Conclusion: The study demonstrates feasibility and benefits of a continuous, presence-based CLMRS pipeline, achieving substantial gains in detection and identity tracking under real-world field conditions, while highlighting training/quantisation challenges and underscoring the need for robust data protection and human-in-the-loop safeguards.

Abstract: An estimated 138 million children remain in child labour worldwide, and the monitoring systems used by affected sectors, built on periodic household visits and interviews, systematically under-detect them. We present a real-time computer-vision pipeline, built and operated solely as a research prototype, that studies the feasibility of giving Child Labour Monitoring and Remediation Systems (CLMRS) a continuous, presence-based evidence channel. The pipeline combines a multi-task person and face detector (YOLO26x backbone in the CerberusDet framework), cascaded age estimation pairing MiVOLO v2 with a child-specialist model for ages 0-12, ByteTrack tracking, ArcFace and DINOv2 re-identification, and track-level fusion producing reviewable per-person records. The detector raises person mAP@0.5 from 0.390 to 0.683 over the previous-generation baseline; the child specialist reaches 1.944 years MAE on children-only validation, where widely used open-source stacks err by 18-23 years. FP8 TensorRT compilation yields a 1.77x speedup at +0.002 years MAE, bringing the pipeline above twice real-time on embedded hardware. On 26.8 hours of proxy video the system finds 634 unique child candidates versus 285 for its predecessor. We further report a seventeen-day unattended field pilot on a farm in Zimbabwe (38.7 million frames, six cameras) evaluated against a daily attendance register: software tuning improved detection yield 36-fold, and identity consolidation under a simultaneity veto cut over-reporting from 9.1x to 1.8-3.9x with zero proven-false merges. We document training and quantisation failures alongside successes, and the data-protection and human-in-the-loop safeguards such a system requires.

</details>


### [26] [AMPLIFAI: A Multiphase CT Dataset for Benchmarking Clinical Reasoning in LI-RADS Assessment of Liver Lesions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14778)
*Pranav Kulkarni,Nikhil Shah,Amritansh Suryavanshi,Jana Delfino,James Tonascia,Jade Wong-You-Cheong,Barton Lane,Joseph Chirico,Jeffrey D. Hirsch,Ang Li,Heng Huang,Florence X. Doo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces AMPLIFAI, the first public multiphase abdominal CT dataset with LI-RADS labels and segmentation for three features (arterial phase hyperenhancement, washout, enhancing capsule) to enable AI research for LI-RADS-based HCC diagnosis; documents dataset via Datasheets for Datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the lack of large, publicly available, high-quality labeled datasets for LI-RADS AI, within the context of HCC where imaging-based LI-RADS is critical.

Method: Assembles multiphase abdominal CT scans annotated with LI-RADS categories and segmented for three key LI-RADS features; follows the Datasheets for Datasets format; details dataset composition, curation, and annotation pipeline.

Result: Publishes AMPLIFAI as the first public LI-RADS-annotated multiphase CT dataset with feature segmentations; provides comprehensive documentation to support transparent, reproducible research.

Conclusion: A resource to accelerate AI development for LI-RADS characterization and HCC diagnosis, enabling reproducible research and benchmarking in the field.

Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with early detection improving survival from <20\% to >70\%. The standardized LI-RADS criteria establish a biopsy-free, fully imaging-based framework that can serve as a foundation for automating HCC diagnosis with artificial intelligence (AI). However, the lack of large, publicly available datasets with high-quality labels has limited the development of AI models for LI-RADS characterization. We introduce the \textbf{AMPLIFAI} dataset, the first public dataset of multiphase abdominal CT scans annotated with LI-RADS categories and segmented for three major LI-RADS features: arterial phase hyperenhancement, washout, and enhancing capsule. Following the \emph{Datasheets for Datasets} format, this paper details the dataset's composition, curation process, and annotation pipeline to facilitate transparent, reproducible research.

</details>


### [27] [MegaParts: Scaling Part-Aware 3D Object Generation to 300 Parts via Token-Efficient Autoregressive Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14783)
*Manwen Liao,Xinyu Lian,Jian Mao,Kaixu Chen,Li Luo,Jinghao Yan,Wanshui Gan,Qiao Yu,Weitian Zhang,Chunhua Shen,Guang Chen,Bo Dai,Xudong Xu,Zhaoyang Lyu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MegaParts introduces a scalable autoregressive framework for part-aware 3D generation using a token-efficient vector-quantized shape tokenizer and an LLM to generate part-level geometry within a structured sequence, enabling up to 300 parts and long sequences (256k tokens) with improved mesh quality over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing part-aware 3D generation methods do not scale well to objects with many parts due to exploding token length and memory requirements; there is a need for scalable, controllable, and fine-grained part-level generation.

Method: Develop a token-efficient vector-quantized tokenizer that learns discrete latent representations for part-level geometry with adaptive token lengths. Train a large language model to generate object bounding boxes, part bounding boxes, and part shape tokens within a unified structured sequence. Utilize efficient long-context training to handle sequence lengths up to 256k tokens, enabling objects with up to 300 parts.

Result: The approach achieves higher mesh quality than baseline autoregressive and diffusion models, demonstrating that compressed discrete part tokens improve both scalability and geometry fidelity. The framework suggests LLM-native token-efficient autoregressive modeling as a strong alternative to diffusion for large-scale part-aware 3D generation.

Conclusion: MegaParts enables scalable, compositional part-level 3D generation with fine-grained control for complex objects, extending the reachable scale to hundreds of parts without sacrificing fidelity; a promising direction for large-scale, controllable 3D content creation.

Abstract: Part-aware 3D object generation is essential for graphics applications such as controllable modeling, editing, and articulation, where objects are represented as coherent assemblies of semantic parts. However, existing part-aware generation methods, do not scale well to highly complex objects. As the number of parts increases, generating detailed geometry becomes prohibitively expensive in token length and memory. We introduce MegaParts, a scalable autoregressive 3D generation framework to address this challenge by combining structured sequence modeling with a token-efficient vector-quantized shape tokenizer. Our tokenizer learns discrete latent representations for part-level geometry by minimizing token usage subject to high-fidelity reconstruction, enabling adaptive-length tokenization based on geometric complexity. On top of this compact representation, we train a large language model to generate object bounding boxes, part bounding boxes, and part shape tokens within a unified structured sequence. Combined with efficient long-context training strategy, our token-efficient formulation scales to objects with up to 300 parts and sequence lengths up to 256k tokens. This substantially extends the scale of part-aware 3D generation while preserving compositional structure and enabling fine-grained part-level control. Our method achieves higher mesh quality than baseline autoregressive and diffusion models, showing that compressed discrete part tokens improve not only scalability but also the achievable fidelity of generated geometry. These results suggest that LLM native token-efficient autoregressive modeling is a compelling alternative to diffusion for large-scale part-aware 3D generation. The project page is available at https://expmaster.github.io/megaparts_webpage.

</details>


### [28] [Qwen-Video-Edit: Instruction-Based Video Editing by Repurposing an Image Editing Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14790)
*Yunpeng Bai,Yossi Gandelsman,Michaël Gharbi,Qixing Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Repurposes an instruction-based image edit model to edit videos by embedding per-frame video VAE latents into a tiled pseudo-image space, with lightweight input/output projections and image-prior transfer, finetuned on a large editing dataset; temporal refinement is optional.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the cost and complexity of instruction-based video editing by leveraging mature image-editing priors and latent-space alignment, and to test whether per-frame video latents lie in a space compatible with image editing.

Method: Tile Wan-2.1 video-VAE latent frames into one large virtual image; reuse the editor's image positional encoding for each tile; introduce lightweight input/output projections warm-started from the editor's patchify/unpatchify to map between video latents and image latents; initialize to embed a static video as an image; fine-tune on Ditto-1M editing triplets; optionally apply a few denoising steps from Wan-2.2 as a temporal enhancer.

Result: Zero-training observations show the stock image editor can edit a video delivered as a contact sheet; it is indifferent to whether tokens come from joint encode or per-frame encodes; it can edit genuine video latents even without fine-tuning to some degree; fine-tuning reduces fidelity gaps, yielding recognizable edits; temporal enhancement provides additional coherence.

Conclusion: Per-frame video latents remain close to the image domain, enabling transfer of mature image-editing priors with minimal adaptation; this offers a cost-effective alternative to video-conditioned backbones, though fidelity and temporal coherence may still benefit from limited fine-tuning or temporal augmentation.

Abstract: Instruction-based video editing is commonly built on video-pretrained generative backbones: a video diffusion transformer is adapted, at considerable cost, to condition on a source video and an editing instruction. In this report we explore a different route and show that a strong instruction-based image editing model can edit videos by operating directly on video-VAE latents. Starting from Qwen-Image-Edit, we arrange the latent frames of a Wan~2.1 video VAE as tiles of one large virtual image, reuse the editor's image positional encoding for every tile, and bridge the two latent spaces with a pair of lightweight input/output projections warm-started from the editor's own patchify and unpatchify layers, so that at initialization a (static) video is embedded exactly as an image the model already understands. The whole system is then fine-tuned on the public Ditto-1M editing triplets, and a few denoising steps of Wan~2.2 serve as an optional temporal enhancer. We motivate the design with a chain of zero-training observations: the stock image editor already edits a video presented as a contact sheet; it is indifferent to whether the sheet's tokens come from one joint encode or from per-frame encodes stitched in latent space; and it even edits genuine video latents zero-shot to a clearly recognizable degree, leaving fine-tuning only a fidelity gap to close. Our results suggest that, despite the large investment in training video latent spaces, per-frame video latents remain close enough to the image domain that mature image editing priors transfer with minimal adaptation. Project Page: https://yunpeng1998.github.io/Qwen-Video-Edit-Page; Code: https://github.com/yunpeng1998/Qwen-Video-Edit; Model: https://huggingface.co/yunpeng1998/Qwen-Video-Edit.

</details>


### [29] [Zero-Shot Adaptation of Medical Vision Foundation Models for High-Frequency Micro-Ultrasound Prostate Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14796)
*Ayusha Abbas,Saram Abbas,Kabita Adhikari*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Zero-shot prostate segmentation in micro-ultrasound using MedSAM plus lightweight post-processing; achieves near-expert accuracy without training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate prostate boundary delineation is essential for PSA density calculations and biopsy decisions. Conventional ultrasound blurs boundaries; micro-ultrasound offers higher resolution but speckle hampers segmentation. Supervised methods require data and generalize poorly across scanners.

Method: Use MedSAM, a foundation model trained on 1.5M medical images, with spatial prompts to localize the prostate. Apply CLAHE to sharpen the outer wall, binary dilation to recover missed pixels, and Fourier smoothing (4 modes, s=1.05) to refine the boundary. Evaluate bounding-box and point-click prompts on 75 patients (2,621 slices) from the Micro-Ultrasound Prostate Segmentation dataset; hold-out test set of 20 patients.

Result: On the held-out set, boundary-distance error decreased by 45%. Dice improved from 0.749±0.043 to 0.865±0.029; HD95 dropped from 217.2±36.9 px to 120.1±26.1 px. Across the cohort, Dice reached 0.859. The method’s mean overlap was not significantly different from three non-expert rater groups (p>0.19) and it produced 38–52% better inter-patient consistency. Point-click prompts performed poorly (best Dice=0.350) due to speckle; a bounding box suffices for deployment without data collection or retraining.

Conclusion: A practical zero-shot segmentation pipeline for micro-ultrasound prostate boundaries is feasible. Bounding-box prompts suffice, enabling easy clinic deployment without data annotation or model fine-tuning, while achieving Dice and boundary accuracy approaching non-expert human performance.

Abstract: Prostate cancer claims a life every 80 seconds. Early detection is needed to prevent disease progression, and both PSA density calculation and biopsy decisions rely on knowing the exact boundary of the gland. Conventional ultrasound at 6-12 MHz blurs this boundary, missing one in three high-risk cancers. Micro-ultrasound (29 MHz) improves resolution threefold but introduces dense acoustic speckle that obscures the outer wall; given the same image, two clinicians draw outlines differing by over 10% in area. Supervised methods are costly and generalise poorly across scanners. Can a foundation model segment the prostate with no training data?
  We present the first zero-shot pipeline for this modality: MedSAM, pre-trained on over 1.5 million medical images, localises the prostate; we then apply CLAHE to sharpen the outer wall, binary dilation to recover missed pixels, and Fourier smoothing (4 modes, s=1.05) to refine the boundary. MedSAM requires a spatial prompt, so we evaluate bounding-box and point-click strategies across 75 patients of the Micro-Ultrasound Prostate Segmentation dataset (2,621 slices).
  On the 20-patient held-out test set, the pipeline reduces mean boundary-distance error by 45% (Dice 0.749+/-0.043 to 0.865+/-0.029; HD95 217.2+/-36.9 to 120.1+/-26.1 px), reaching Dice 0.859 across the cohort. Its mean overlap shows no significant difference from the three non-expert rater groups (p>0.19), while segmenting 38-52% more consistently (lower inter-patient standard deviation). Point-click prompts fail regardless of placement (best Dice=0.350), because speckle gives no stable local contrast. Only an approximate bounding box is required, so any clinic can deploy it without data collection, annotation, or retraining.

</details>


### [30] [Where the Cost Falls: A Deployment-Aware Adoption Order for Stability Enhancements to Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14811)
*Rowan Hussein,Mohamed Ouf*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A systematic analysis of four architectural enhancements to cycle-consistent GANs for unpaired image-to-image translation, revealing how cost distribution across components governs practical adoption under compute or latency constraints, with self-attention being the costliest; proposes an evaluation protocol and reports results on horse-to-zebra translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address persistent failures in cycle-consistent GANs—training instability (oscillation/collapse), texture drift despite cycle consistency, and missed local artifacts by a global discriminator—and to understand how four proposed enhancements interact with training and deployment rather than only final image quality.

Method: Baseline cycle-GAN for unpaired translation is incrementally augmented with four enhancements: 1) Wasserstein objective with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP), 2) VGG19 perceptual loss on the cycle reconstruction, 3) multi-scale discriminators, and 4) self-attention. Each is added one at a time on a fixed control and then combined. The authors document failure modes (collapse, reconstruction artifacts) and visualize sample diagnostics, report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Kernel Inception Distance (KID) for the combined model, and analyze the training cost distribution and deployment implications. They apply the methodology to horse-to-zebra translation and propose a protocol covering variants, perceptual similarity, and downstream segmentation for ranking enhancements by measured evidence.

Result: The enhancements partition sharply by where their cost falls in the architecture, rather than by run-to-run variation. WGAN-GP, perceptual loss on cycle reconstruction, and multi-scale discriminators modify training dynamics without altering the deployed generator, while self-attention increases memory roughly quadratically with feature-map size and is thus the least favorable for resource-constrained teams. The four enhancements can be integrated sequentially and in combination, with targeted mitigation of observed failure modes (collapse and texture-reconstruction artifacts). The authors report FID and KID for the combined model and call for a standardized protocol to fairly compare variants across perceptual similarity and downstream tasks. They emphasize an adoption order under compute/latency budgets and highlight memory bottlenecks as a central consideration for deployment.

Conclusion: Choosing enhancements should consider not only final output quality but where in the architecture the cost resides. In resource-constrained settings, WGAN-GP, perceptual loss, and multi-scale discriminators offer training benefits without changing the shipped model, whereas self-attention, despite potential quality gains, imposes prohibitive memory costs. A standardized evaluation protocol is needed to rank variants across perceptual and downstream metrics and to guide the deployment sequence.

Abstract: Teams that adopt cycle-consistent adversarial networks for unpaired image-to-image translation meet the same obstacles: adversarial training oscillates or collapses, cycle consistency preserves coarse layout while finer texture drifts, and a single discriminator judging global realism misses local artifacts. Four enhancements address these failures, and they are usually compared on output quality alone. We show that they also divide sharply by where their cost falls, and that this division, which follows from the architecture and not from any particular run, yields an adoption order for teams under a compute or latency budget. A Wasserstein objective with gradient penalty, a VGG19 perceptual loss on the cycle reconstruction, and multi-scale discriminators change training only, so a team can adopt or drop them without altering what ships. Self-attention alone persists into the deployed generator, with memory growing as the square of the feature-map size, which makes it the one component a resource-constrained team should defer. We integrate all four onto a lightly tuned baseline for horse-to-zebra translation, introduced one at a time on a fixed control and then combined, and for each we give the failure mode it targets and how it integrates. We document the collapse and reconstruction-artifact modes the baseline produced, report what visual inspection of saved samples showed for each variant, and report Fréchet Inception Distance and Kernel Inception Distance for the combined model. We specify the protocol still needed, covering the individual variants, perceptual similarity, and downstream segmentation, to rank these enhancements on measured evidence.

</details>


### [31] [OvDSGG: End-to-End Open-Vocabulary Dynamic Scene Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14835)
*John Helsby,Yi Yang,Bodo Rosenhahn,Michael Ying Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An end-to-end open-vocabulary dynamic scene graph generator (OvDSGG) that uses an open-vocabulary spatial and temporal backbone, a Triplet Feature Extraction Module, and a Visual-Language Alignment Module to enable open-vocabulary DSGG without heavy distillation; it is evaluated on a new Action Genome–based benchmark with Base/Novel splits and shows strong zero-shot performance while remaining competitive in closed-set settings; code and benchmark are released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current DSGG methods are closed-set and fail to cover long-tail/novel concepts; open-vocabulary models either rely on pretrained LMs with multi-stage training/cost, or lack end-to-end integration. There is a need for a unified, efficient open-vocabulary DSGG framework with good generalization.

Method: Propose OvDSGG architecture: (1) open-vocabulary Spatial Backbone and Temporal Backbone to extract visual features; (2) Triplet Feature Extraction Module to bridge spatial and temporal streams and produce subject–predicate–object representations; (3) Visual-Language Alignment Module that learns an adaptive decision boundary in a joint visual-language space for open-vocabulary recognition, avoiding costly knowledge distillation; (4) a new open-vocabulary DSGG benchmark (Base/Novel splits for objects and predicates) derived from Action Genome; (5) evaluation against open-vocabulary baselines.

Result: OvDSGG significantly outperforms open-vocabulary baselines on the proposed benchmark, with zero-shot Recall@K improvements of 10.0–20.4 percentage points; closed-set DSGG performance remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: An effective end-to-end open-vocabulary DSGG framework that integrates open-vocabulary vision-language alignment and cross-modal reasoning, validated on a rigorous baseline benchmark; code and benchmark are publicly available.

Abstract: Dynamic scene graphs (DSGs) capture spatio-temporal interactions across videos as $\langle$subject, predicate, object$\rangle$ triplets, and underpin downstream tasks such as video captioning, video question answering, and action analysis. However, end-to-end dynamic scene graph generation (DSGG) methods are closed-set: they recognize only objects and predicates from a fixed training vocabulary and struggle with the long-tailed distribution of rare concepts, severely limiting their real-world applicability. Existing open-vocabulary models typically inherit pretrained large language models, resulting in multi-stage training and inference with substantial cost. We introduce OvDSGG, the first end-to-end framework for open-vocabulary DSGG. OvDSGG builds on top of an open-vocabulary Spatial Backbone and a Temporal Backbone; we further propose a Triplet Feature Extraction Module that bridges them, and a Visual-Language Alignment Module that preserves open-vocabulary recognition by learning an adaptive decision boundary in the joint visual-language feature space, without expensive knowledge distillation in existing methods. We further introduce a rigorous open-vocabulary DSGG benchmark adapted from Action Genome, with disjoint Base/Novel splits for both objects and predicates. OvDSGG significantly outperforms open-vocabulary baselines across all metrics, with zero-shot Recall@$K$ scores 10.0--20.4 percentage point higher than the next-best baseline, while on closed-set DSGG remaining competitive with state-of-the-art models. Code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/jhelsby/OvDSGG/.

</details>


### [32] [Zero-MELO: Test-Time Evidence Calibration with Multimodal LLMs for Zero-Shot Micro-Gesture Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14854)
*Chengyan Wang,Hanliang Xie,Yueyi Yang,Haoyu Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A test-time evidence calibration framework (Zero-MELO) for micro-gesture recognition with multimodal LLMs, using a tree search to collect fine-grained visual cues, a calibration module to reduce score biases, and a multi-cue fusion component; yields strong gains over Qwen2.5-VL on iMiGUE and MA-52.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs struggle with fine-grained, motion-centric tasks like micro-gesture recognition due to single-pass inference and bias toward language/motion-agnostic appearances. There is a need for localized evidence and test-time guidance to improve reasoning and reliability.

Method: Introduce a tree search mechanism to progressively acquire localized, fine-grained visual evidence; a test-time calibration module to mitigate score biases; a multi-cue fusion module to integrate evidence from multiple cues; diagnose zero-shot MGR errors in NLL space to identify bottlenecks.

Result: Mean-class accuracies: 26.84% on iMiGUE and 22.10% on MA-52, significantly higher than Qwen2.5-VL baselines of 16.15% and 10.20%. Code will be released at the project page.

Conclusion: The proposed test-time evidence calibration framework enhances both reasoning detail and reliability for MLLMs in motion-centric tasks, achieving substantial performance gains and providing a practical approach for future work in MGR and related domains.

Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general video understanding, their capability in fine-grained and motion-centric tasks remains limited. This limitation is particularly critical in micro-gesture recognition (MGR), where micro-gestures (MGs) - subtle, short-duration, and spatially localized human movements - serve as key discriminative signals for implicit affective analysis, yet are easily neglected following common prompting practices. Although MGR has been intensively studied by many discriminative approaches, the use of MLLMs for MGR is underexplored, with notably poor performance. We hypothesize that the motion-sensitive representation ability of MLLMs is constrained by their inherent single-pass forward inference, which can be substantially enhanced through carefully designed test-time guidance. Motivated by this, building on our prior findings regarding temporal insensitivity in Video LLMs, we diagnose zero-shot MGR errors in the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) space. We observe that MLLMs suffer from two bottlenecks: 1) insufficient localized evidence and 2) severe score biases driven by language and motion-agnostic appearances. Thus, we propose a novel test-time evidence calibration framework that improves both reasoning details and prediction reliability. Specifically, we introduce a tree search mechanism to progressively acquire localized, fine-grained visual evidence, coupled with a test-time calibration module to mitigate score biases. The multi-cue fusion module then integrates evidence from multiple cues without relying on a single cue for final prediction. Our framework achieves mean-class accuracies of 26.84\% on iMiGUE and 22.10\% on MA-52, significantly outperforming the Qwen2.5-VL baseline, which produces 16.15\% and 10.20\%, respectively. The code will be available at https://zero-melo.github.io/Zero-MELO.

</details>


### [33] [Beam-Wise Statistical Background Subtraction for Static Roadside LiDAR: A Cross-Sensor Benchmark Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14868)
*Alexander Baumann,Marcel Vosshans,Thao Dang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Beam-wise statistical background subtraction for statically mounted LiDAR; introduces HighwayScene dataset and extends CoopScenes for reproducible evaluation; shows per-beam temporal models with spatial filtering improve precision without sacrificing recall and real-time capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Systematic cross-sensor evaluation and reproducible studies for static roadside LiDAR background subtraction are missing; need robust, transferable methods for static setups.

Method: Per-beam temporal modeling of background; complementary statistical strategies to capture dominant and multi-modal background structures; spatial filtering in angular and 3D domains; combination with lightweight per-beam models and spatial consistency filtering.

Result: Robust and transferable background subtraction across scenes and heterogeneous sensing technologies; precision improved with spatial filtering, while recall remains high and real-time capability maintained.

Conclusion: Beam-wise statistical modeling is effective for static roadside LiDAR background subtraction; datasets and implementations are publicly released to enable reproducible evaluation.

Abstract: Background subtraction is a key preprocessing step for infrastructure-based LiDAR perception, enabling efficient isolation of dynamic traffic participants without semantic annotations. However, systematic cross-sensor evaluations and reproducible studies for static roadside LiDAR are missing. This paper presents a comparative benchmark of beam-wise statistical background subtraction for statically mounted LiDAR sensors. We formulate background estimation as a per-beam temporal modeling problem and investigate complementary statistical strategies that capture dominant as well as multi-modal background structures, combined with spatial filtering in the angular and 3D domain. To enable reproducible evaluation, we introduce HighwayScene, a new multi-LiDAR dataset recorded in a static roadside setup, and extend the public CoopScenes dataset with static/dynamic point-wise annotations. Across multiple scenes and heterogeneous sensing technologies, we demonstrate that beam-wise statistical modeling provides a robust and transferable solution. Combining lightweight per-beam models with spatial consistency filtering substantially improves precision while maintaining high recall and real-time capability. All datasets, annotations, and implementations are publicly released.

</details>


### [34] [SpIn-ViT: Designing a Sparsity-Induced Vision Transformer That Is Mechanistically Interpretable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14922)
*Philip H. Lee,Parth Padalkar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SpIn-ViT is an end-to-end trainable framework uniting pretrained ViT with a modified sparse autoencoder to align sparse patch-level features with image classification, yielding better accuracy and interpretability than post-hoc SAE methods and enabling compact neurosymbolic rule-sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address misalignment between post-hoc SAEs (trained on frozen ViT representations) and downstream classification objectives, by jointly training the ViT and SAE to obtain semantically coherent, localized, interpretable representations without sacrificing predictive performance.

Method: Joint end-to-end training of a pretrained Vision Transformer and a modified Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) that produces sparse patch-level representations aligned with the image classification objective; evaluates on nine benchmarks using classification accuracy, quantitative interpretability metrics, AI-based and human evaluations; also extracts interpretable rule-sets from SAE neurons to build neurosymbolic models.

Result: SpIn-ViT achieves 8.84% higher average classification accuracy vs state-of-the-art post-hoc SAE; AI-based interpretability score ~4x higher; human-evaluation score >2x higher; neurosymbolic models from SpIn-ViT’s neurons achieve 5.97% higher accuracy and require 58.8% smaller rule-sets than neurosymbolic models from SOTA post-hoc SAE.

Conclusion: End-to-end alignment of ViT and SAE enables semantically meaningful neuron activations that localize image regions, improving both predictive performance and interpretability, and enabling compact, effective neurosymbolic models.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability has recently expanded to Vision Transformers (ViTs), with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) increasingly used as post-hoc tools to decompose internal representations into sparse and more interpretable features. However, because post-hoc SAEs are trained on frozen representations after the ViT has already been optimized, their latent features are not directly aligned with the downstream classification objective. We introduce SpIn-ViT, a framework that jointly trains a pretrained ViT and a modified SAE end-to-end, directly aligning sparse patch-level representations with image classification. SpIn-ViT learns semantically coherent neuron activations that localize meaningful image regions while maintaining competitive predictive performance. We evaluate SpIn-ViT across nine image-classification benchmarks using classification accuracy, quantitative interpretability metrics, AI-based and Human evaluations. Compared with the previous state-of-the-art post-hoc SAE method, SpIn-ViT achieves 8.84% higher average classification accuracy, an AI-based interpretability score nearly four times as high, and a human-evaluation score more than twice as high. We further extract interpretable rule-sets using the SAE neurons to create neurosymbolic models which achieve 5.97% higher average classification accuracy while requiring a 58.8\% smaller rule-set than the neurosymbolic models created from the SOTA post-hoc SAE method.

</details>


### [35] [PaSTel: Anchoring Histology in Spatial Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Hierarchical Bio-Prior Contrastive Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14924)
*Azim Dehghani Amirabad,Junchao Zhu,Pushpak Pati,Walid Abdelmoula,Tommaso Mansi,Rui Liao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PaSTel introduces a hierarchical, biology-informed multimodal pretraining for spatial transcriptomics by (1) TF-IDF gene weighting at spots, (2) KEGG pathway anchors for global semantics, and (3) regional clustering for meso-scale structure, yielding superior representations over standard vision/vision-omics encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ST links tissue morphology to gene expression but current methods rely on ubiquitous housekeeping genes and independent spot-patch alignment, which obscure informative signals and ignore spatial dependencies essential for tissue organization. A multiscale, biology-informed pretraining could produce more discriminative, transferable representations.

Method: Three-level integration: spot-level TF-IDF reweighting identifies spatially informative genes; functional level uses curated KEGG pathways as anchors to encode global biological semantics; regional level aggregates neighboring spots via spatial clustering to model meso-scale tissue structure; joint pretraining aligns histology images with gene expression leveraging these priors.

Result: PaSTel outperforms existing vision and vision-omics encoders across multiple downstream tasks on spatial transcriptomics data, showing that multiscale biological priors yield more informative and transferable representations.

Conclusion: Incorporating multiscale biological priors (spot, functional, regional) yields more discriminative, transferable multimodal representations for spatial transcriptomics than prior vision-only or vision-omics approaches.

Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) links tissue morphology with molecular programs, motivating multimodal pretraining methods that align histology images with gene expression. However, existing approaches suffer from two key limitations: spatially informative gene selection is often dominated by ubiquitous housekeeping genes, leading to weakly discriminative representations, and independent spot-patch alignment fails to capture spatial dependencies that are critical for tissue organization. To address these challenges, we introduce PaSTel, a hierarchical multimodal pretraining framework that integrates biological priors at three levels. At the spot level, TF-IDF reweighting is used to identify spatially informative genes; at the functional level, curated KEGG pathways serve as anchors for encoding global biological semantics; and at the regional level, spatial clustering aggregates neighboring spots to model meso-scale tissue structure. Across multiple downstream tasks, PaSTel consistently outperforms existing vision and vision-omics encoders, demonstrating that incorporating multiscale biological priors yields more informative and transferable representations for spatial transcriptomics.

</details>


### [36] [Looks Can be Deceiving: Annotator and Reviewer Performance Across Imagery Sources in Crowd-Sourced Aerial Damage Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14942)
*Thomas Manzini,Priyankari Perali,Raisa Karnik,Stephen Johnson,Robin R. Murphy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: First empirical study of annotator/reviewer performance across multi-source aerial imagery (drone, crewed aviation, and satellite) in post-disaster building damage labeling; finds higher revision rates for lower-resolution sources and persistent disagreement after single reviews; proposes three recommendations for adaptive, budget-aware quality control in multi-source curation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address lack of established best practices for allocating human labeling effort in large multi-source aerial datasets; evaluate how accuracy and QC propagate across diverse image sources in a real-world post-disaster setting.

Method: Empirical analysis of a post-disaster building-damage dataset across 9 disasters with 20k+ buildings per source; 187 annotators; two QC stages: a single-reviewer pass and a consensus-committee review; measured revision rates by source at each stage.

Result: Two key findings: (1) initial annotations are revised more for lower-resolution sources (25.27% for crewed aviation, 36.95% for satellite); same ordering at all stages. (2) A single reviewer reduces but does not resolve disagreement: post-review revisions by committee still occur (6.85% drone, 14.05% crewed, 20.86% satellite). Implication: uniform review allocation leaves more residual disagreement in low-res imagery.

Conclusion: Proposes three recommendations for multi-source dataset curation, aligning with adaptive task assignment and budget-aware quality control to improve efficiency and accuracy in multi-source labeling workflows.

Abstract: This paper presents the first known empirical investigation of annotator and reviewer performance across multi-source remotely sensed imagery, evaluating human labeling across drone, crewed aviation, and satellite views. Because existing aerial imagery datasets rely predominantly on single-source imagery, there is no currently established state of practice for efficiently allocating human labor to curate large-scale, multi-source aerial datasets. This work addresses this limitation by analyzing annotator and reviewer performance within a post-disaster building damage assessment dataset of 9 disasters, where 20041 buildings in drone, 20695 buildings in crewed aviation, and 33392 buildings in satellite imagery were labeled. These labels, provided by 187 annotators, were then refined through two successive quality-control stages: a single-reviewer pass followed by a consensus-committee review. Our analysis reveals two findings that raise questions for standard crowd-sourcing practices. First, initial annotations were revised by the final committee at rates that rise steeply from higher- to lower-resolution sources (25.27% for crewed aviation and 36.95% for satellite), with the same ordering at every observed workflow stage. Second, a single individual review reduced but did not resolve this disagreement: after review, the committee still revised 6.85% of drone, 14.05% of crewed, and 20.86% of satellite labels. These observations suggest that, in workflows like this one, uniform review allocation leaves the most residual disagreement in lower-resolution imagery. Based on this evidence, and consistent with prior work on adaptive task assignment and budget-aware quality control, this paper offers three recommendations for multi-source dataset curation.

</details>


### [37] [Benchmarking Frontier Text-to-Image Models on Image-Description Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14976)
*Sajjad Abdoli,Ghassan Al-Sumaidaee,Ahmed Rashad*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Under heavy, compositionally demanding prompts, production T2I systems show meaningful gaps; Gemini 3 Pro Image leads narrowly over FLUX.2, with Ideogram and Hunyuan trailing; evaluation reveals object-counting, geometric artifacts, and garbled/omitted text as main failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess robustness of state-of-the-art text-to-image systems beyond average-case prompts by focusing on prompts with precise object counts, multi-object attribute binding, legible embedded text, and explicit spatial constraints, using an independent MECE rubric.

Method: Select 48 hardest prompts from the DataSeeds.AI Sample Dataset via automated complexity scoring; generate images with Hunyuan 3.0, Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro), Black Forest Labs FLUX.2, and Ideogram 3.0; independent evaluation using a MECE rubric authored by GPT-5.4-Pro; Gemini 3 Pro Image 3.1 Pro Preview determines criterion satisfaction; full rubrics, scores, and failure annotations are available on request.

Result: Gemini 3 Pro Image ranks first with 84.8/100, narrowly ahead of FLUX.2 at 82.3/100; Ideogram 3.0 and Hunyuan 3.0 score 65.7/100 and 63.3/100, respectively.

Conclusion: Leading systems primarily lose points due to object miscounting and geometric artifacts, while trailing systems more frequently produce garbled text; Ideogram 3.0 often omits requested elements; full per-sample rubrics and annotations are available from the authors upon request.

Abstract: Text-to-image models are typically reported on average-case prompts, which understates the gap between systems on compositionally demanding requests involving precise object counts, multi-object attribute binding, legible embedded text, and explicit spatial constraints. We evaluate four production text-to-image systems: Hunyuan 3.0, Gemini 3 Pro Image ("Nano Banana Pro"), Black Forest Labs FLUX.2, and Ideogram 3.0. The evaluation uses the 48 hardest prompts drawn from the DataSeeds.AI Sample Dataset (DSD), selected through an automated complexity-scoring pass over the full corpus. Every generated image is graded using an independent-judge rubric. GPT-5.4-Pro authors an atomic, weighted, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) evaluation rubric, while Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview independently determines whether each criterion is satisfied. Gemini 3 Pro Image ranks first with a score of 84.8/100, narrowly ahead of FLUX.2 at 82.3/100. Ideogram 3.0 and Hunyuan 3.0 score 65.7/100 and 63.3/100, respectively. Failure analysis shows that the leading systems primarily lose points through object miscounting and geometric artifacts, whereas the trailing systems more frequently produce garbled text. Ideogram 3.0 also frequently omits requested elements. Full per-sample rubrics, scores, and failure annotations are available from the authors upon request.

</details>


### [38] [Risk-Adaptive Edge--Cloud Visual Reasoning for Communication-Efficient Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14991)
*Meng Ma,Shuyang Li,Naigang Wang,Ruimin Ke*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Adaptive onboard traffic assessment selectively triggers cloud VLM reasoning to cut cloud traffic while preserving task performance and safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce communication latency and bandwidth of cloud-based vision-language models in time-sensitive tactical scenarios by performing conservative local processing and delaying cloud queries until necessary.

Method: An onboard VLM and lightweight detector assess temporal traffic conditions and path-relative hazards to decide when to request cloud reasoning; cloud model provides tactical advice; critical control (validation, vehicle control, AEB) remains on-board; evaluated in CARLA under multiple network profiles and scenarios including delayed-roadwork ablation.

Result: Matched task success rate with periodic cloud access while reducing cloud requests by 54.1%; fewer AEB activations; semantic events trigger pre-audit cloud requests; lane changes slightly longer under selective access but robust cloud traffic reduction across network profiles.

Conclusion: Onboard traffic assessment serves as a practical trigger for selective VLM inference, enabling substantial cloud traffic reductions with minimal impact on performance and safety; the approach is robust to network variations and can be generalized to similar edge-cloud VLM deployment tasks.

Abstract: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) offer greater contextual reasoning capabilities than smaller onboard models, but frequent visual uploads increase communication overhead and add network and inference latency to tactical decisions. We present a risk-adaptive edge-cloud architecture in which onboard traffic assessment determines when cloud reasoning is requested. An onboard VLM and a lightweight detector capture temporal traffic conditions and path-relative hazards for conservative local response and selective cloud access. The cloud model provides tactical advice, while validation, vehicle control, and automatic emergency braking remain local. In CARLA experiments, our method matched the task success rate of periodic cloud access while reducing cloud requests by 54.1% and recording fewer automatic emergency braking (AEB) activations. In a delayed-roadwork ablation, semantic events triggered requests before the next scheduled audit. Across three emulated network profiles, the method continued to reduce cloud traffic, although lane changes took longer than with periodic access. Onboard traffic assessment therefore served as a practical trigger for selective VLM inference in these experiments.

</details>


### [39] [Registration-Free Hyperspectral Reconstruction from RGB via a Permutation-Invariant Gram-Matrix Principle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14994)
*Jiangsan Zhao,Masayuki Hirafuji,Seishi Ninomiya,Jakob Geipel,Wei Guo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Permutation-invariant Gram-matrix supervision enables RGB-to-HSI spectral super-resolution without image registration or known CRF, achieving robust, near-state-of-the-art results across diverse scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To relax two common but brittle assumptions in HR-HSI reconstruction: precise spatial registration between LR-HSI and HR-RGB, and a known camera response function. Removing these constraints improves practical applicability across heterogeneous sensors.

Method: Introduce a permutation-invariant supervision principle: the Gram matrix of unmixed abundance maps is invariant to pixel ordering and can be used to align RGB-to-HSI mappings without spatial correspondence or CRF. Train a residual spectral super-resolution network that maps HR-RGB directly to HR-HSI by matching abundance Gram matrices, with no paired supervision. Evaluate robustness by permuting HR-RGB pixels (inverse reindexing) and across diverse benchmarks.

Result: The method achieves accuracy comparable to methods that rely on registration/CRF and paired supervision, while remaining robust when those assumptions are violated. A full random permutation of HR-RGB does not degrade reconstruction, in contrast to a competing fusion method that collapses. Loss ablations indicate that performance primarily stems from the permutation-invariant principle rather than the specific Gram-matrix discrepancy used.

Conclusion: Permutation-invariant Gram-based supervision provides a practical, sensor-agnostic route to high-resolution hyperspectral fusion, reducing dependency on sensor calibration and alignment while maintaining accuracy across indoor, natural, and remote-sensing data.

Abstract: Reconstructing a spatially and spectrally high-resolution hyperspectral image (HR-HSI) from a low-resolution HSI (LR-HSI) and a high-resolution RGB image (HR-RGB) usually assumes precise registration and a known camera response function (CRF). Both assumptions are difficult to satisfy with different sensors. We remove both through a permutation-invariant supervision principle: the Gram matrix of an unmixed abundance map depends on shared material composition but not on pixel ordering. Matching abundance Gram matrices therefore allows RGB-to-HSI mapping to be learned without spatial correspondence and without a predefined CRF. Under a full random permutation of HR-RGB pixels, a state-of-the-art fusion method collapses, whereas our reconstruction is unchanged after inverse reindexing for evaluation. Building on this principle, a residual spectral super-resolution function maps HR-RGB directly to HR-HSI without registration, known CRF, or paired supervision. Across indoor, natural-scene, and remote-sensing benchmarks, the method achieves accuracy comparable to approaches that require these assumptions while remaining robust when they are violated. Loss ablations further show that reconstruction accuracy is largely insensitive to the specific discrepancy used to match the Gram matrices, indicating that performance arises primarily from the permutation-invariant principle rather than loss tuning.

</details>


### [40] [FZ-VLM: A Two Stage Florence-Zephyr Vision Language Model Framework for Pulmonary Nodule Characterization and Clinical Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15004)
*Pramit Dutta,Jenita Manokaran,Richa Mittal,Ryan Appleby,Eranga Ukwatta*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Two-stage Florence-Zephyr Vision-Language Model (FZ-VLM) for unified structured pulmonary nodule characterization in lung CT, combining attribute extraction from CT slices and description/decision generation, with strong evaluation metrics and safety considerations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses time-consuming post-detection radiology workflow and inter-observer variability by unifying radiological attribute extraction and narrative decision support into a single framework.

Method: Stage 1: Fine-tune Florence-2 to extract radiological attributes (anatomical location, margin characteristics, attenuation type, diameter) from expert-annotated 2D axial CT slices. Stage 2: Use Zephyr-7B to generate nodule descriptions, follow-up recommendations, and longitudinal analyses from Stage 1 attributes.

Result: Stage 1: location accuracy 77.18%, margin 67.96%, attenuation 79.13%; diameter MAE 2.58 mm; outperformed GPT-4 baselines and human baseline. Stage 2: radiologist evaluation – accuracy 93.9%, completeness 98.6%, clinical relevance 76.1%, overall 89.5%. Safety: outputs mostly clinically safe; some follow-up recommendations require expert review.

Conclusion: First two-stage VLM framework for structured nodule characterization and clinical decision-making, showing promise to streamline workflow and reduce variability, with areas for further validation and safety oversight.

Abstract: Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and Computed Tomography (CT) is a primary imaging tool for screening and followup assessment. After pulmonary nodule detection, radiologists manually assess anatomical location, diameter, margin characteristics, and attenuation type to support risk assessment and clinical decision-making. However, this post-detection workflow is time-consuming and can be affected by inter-observer variability. Existing Artificial Intelligence methods often focus on isolated tasks, limiting their use as a unified, clinically grounded interpretation framework. This study presents FZ-VLM, a two-stage Florence-Zephyr Vision Language Model framework for unified structured pulmonary nodule characterization in lung CT. The framework uses a fine-tuned Florence-2 model to extract radiological attributes from expert-annotated 2D axial CT slices, while a Zephyr-7B model uses these attributes to generate nodule descriptions, follow-up recommendations, and longitudinal analyses. Results showed that the Stage 1 model achieved 77.18\% accuracy for anatomical location, 67.96\% accuracy for margin characteristics, and 79.13\% accuracy for attenuation type, with a Mean Absolute Error of 2.58 mm for diameter estimation, outperforming evaluated GPT-4-based baselines as well as the human baseline. Expert radiologist evaluation of Stage 2 showed 93.9\% accuracy, 98.6\% completeness score, 76.1\% clinical relevance, and an overall score of 89.5\%. Safety analysis showed that most outputs were clinically safe, although some follow-up recommendations still required expert review. To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first two-stage Vision-Language Model framework for structured nodule characterization and clinical decision-making.

</details>


### [41] [MetaReason: Precise Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning via Editing Meta Information for Solving Geometry Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15006)
*Penghao Yin,Haomin Wang,Qihong Tang,Xiaoye Qu,Hongjie Zhang,Xiao-Ping Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MetaReason is a multimodal reasoning framework for plane geometry that uses structured meta-information to build high-fidelity visual states, enabling accurate auxiliary-line construction and reasoning. It introduces TutorGeo (17k image-to-meta samples, 60k text traces, 60k multimodal traces) and ExamGeo for evaluation, and achieves strong results via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, outperforming open-source models and rivaling proprietary ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current vision-language models rely heavily on text-only reasoning and struggle with geometry tasks that require precise visual reasoning. Intermediate visual states often suffer from inaccurate geometric representations and low rendering fidelity, resulting in unreliable outputs. A need exists for accurate, controllable visual representations to support robust geometry reasoning.

Method: Parse geometric images into structured meta-information; apply controllable edits with predefined tools to synthesize high-fidelity visual states (auxiliary lines, states); perform reasoning on augmented views; construct TutorGeo with image-to-meta, text traces, and multimodal traces; train with a combination of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to develop robust multimodal reasoning.

Result: MetaReason significantly outperforms existing open-source models and is competitive with proprietary models on the constructed tasks, demonstrating robust multimodal reasoning capabilities.

Conclusion: Structured meta-information and high-fidelity visual synthesis enable reliable multimodal geometry reasoning, with TutorGeo and ExamGeo providing comprehensive data and benchmarks to support training and evaluation.

Abstract: Although visual reasoning is crucial for solving complex geometry tasks, existing vision-language models rely heavily on text-only reasoning. Some recent methods introduce intermediate visual states to facilitate reasoning, but they are often hindered by inaccurate geometric representations and low rendering fidelity, ultimately leading to unreliable outputs. To address these limitations, we propose MetaReason, a framework for multimodal reasoning in plane geometry that leverages structured meta-information to enable accurate auxiliary-line construction. The framework first parses geometric images into meta-information, performs controllable edits with predefined tools to synthesize high-fidelity visual states, and then conducts reasoning based on these augmented views. To support this framework, we construct TutorGeo, a comprehensive dataset containing 17k image-to-meta conversion samples, 60k text-only reasoning traces, and 60k interleaved multimodal reasoning traces. Using this dataset, we combine supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to develop robust multimodal reasoning capabilities. We also introduce ExamGeo, a benchmark derived from real-world examination problems that enables systematic evaluation across varying difficulty levels. Experimental results demonstrate that MetaReason significantly outperforms existing open-source models and achieves competitive performance against proprietary models.

</details>


### [42] [DualMiT-Net: Local-Global Transformer-Convolutional Fusion for Breast Mass Segmentation in Mammographic Regions of Interest](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15019)
*Alibek Kamiluly,Milana Muratova,Yash Patel,Fan Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A dual-branch network (DualMiT-Net) combines local mass-focused features with global breast context for breast mass segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CBIS-DDSM with Dice 0.9375 and IoU 0.8834.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast mass segmentation is challenging due to low contrast, irregular shapes, and boundaries blending with surrounding tissue. A model that integrates fine-grained mass details with broader context can improve segmentation accuracy and consistency.

Method: DualMiT-Net with a local MiT-B5 encoder and a global EfficientNet-B5 encoder. Features are shared at deeper encoder levels and fused progressively in a single decoder. A spatial gate modulates global information during decoding. Four input representations were evaluated, selecting percentile-windowed mammograms with a Gabor texture response. Trained on the CBIS-DDSM mass subset with patient-level split; exponential moving average (EMA) weights were used during training.

Result: Mean Dice coefficient: 0.9375; mean IoU: 0.8834, over three training runs. Outperformed six standard encoder-decoder baselines trained under the same data and settings.

Conclusion: Integrating local mass information with wider breast context via a dual-branch, gated fusion architecture yields accurate and consistent breast mass segmentation, surpassing standard baselines on CBIS-DDSM.

Abstract: Breast mass segmentation is an important step in computer-aided mammography, but it remains difficult because masses can have low contrast, irregular shapes, and boundaries that blend with surrounding breast tissue. To address this problem, we present DualMiT-Net, a dual-branch network that uses both a focused view of the mass and a wider view of the surrounding tissue. The local branch uses a Mix Transformer (MiT-B5) encoder to learn mass shape, texture, and boundary information, while the global branch uses an EfficientNet-B5 encoder to learn surrounding breast context. Features from the two branches are shared at the deeper encoder levels and are then progressively fused in a single decoder. A spatial gate controls how much global information is added during decoding. We also evaluated four input representations and selected a percentile-windowed mammogram combined with a Gabor texture response. The model was trained and evaluated on the mass subset of the Curated Breast Imaging Subset of the Digital Database for Screening Mammography (CBIS-DDSM) using a patient-level split. Across three training runs, DualMiT-Net with exponential moving average weights achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.9375 and a mean Intersection over Union of 0.8834. It also achieved better Dice and IoU scores than six standard encoder-decoder baselines trained using the same data and training settings. These results show that combining local mass information with wider breast context can provide accurate and consistent breast mass segmentation.

</details>


### [43] [Geometry-Calibrated Closed-Form Shrinkage for SAR Despeckling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15028)
*Xuran Hu,Mingzhe Zhu,Djordje Stanković,Yujie Zhu,Zhenpeng Feng,Yifang Ban,Ljubiša Stanković*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A geometry-calibrated, closed-form, training-free SAR despeckling method using log-Yeo–Johnson transform and orthonormal group dictionaries, achieving competitive accuracy with a single analytically determined degree of freedom.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To despeck SAR imagery while preserving scattering structures without relying on tunable parameters or extensive training.

Method: Apply log-Yeo–Johnson transform; form groups of similar patches; encode each group on an orthonormal left singular basis; apply coefficient shrinkage with exact soft-thresholding due to orthonormal dictionary; use a random-matrix argument to convert regularization into a single geometry-calibrated degree of freedom; the dictionary is learned from noisy data, causing speckle absorption proportional to group aspect ratio; singular projection Gaussianizes coefficient noise; resulting estimator is deterministic and training-free.

Result: The method ranks first in 18 of 24 PSNR/SSIM comparisons against 12 published methods on three synthetic benchmarks and shows the lowest mean deviation from the theoretical speckle model across six real-SAR configurations from five sensors; code is provided.

Conclusion: The framework delivers a parameter-free, robust despeckling solution with analytical calibrations, strong cross-dataset performance, and practical applicability without training data.

Abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) despeckling is an inverse-recovery problem in which multiplicative non-Gaussian noise must be suppressed without erasing scattering structures. We revisit a nonlocal sparse estimator that applies a log--Yeo--Johnson transformation, stacks similar patches into groups, codes each group on its own left singular basis, and shrinks the resulting coefficients. Three quantities usually treated as tunable are shown to be fixed by this construction. First, the group dictionary is orthonormal, so the weighted Lasso admits an exact coefficient-wise soft-threshold solution: the iterative inner solver is unnecessary, and the two apparent weighting matrices are the numerator and denominator of a single threshold field rather than independent modules. Second, because the dictionary is estimated from the noisy group itself, its retained subspace absorbs speckle in proportion to the group aspect ratio $γ=p^2/K$; a random-matrix argument converts the corresponding regularization constant into a geometry-calibrated correction and collapses patch size, group size, and shrinkage scale into one analytically determined degree of freedom. Third, singular projection makes the coefficient noise nearly Gaussian at every tested look number, which locates the point at which an exact speckle likelihood ceases to be informative. The resulting estimator is deterministic, training-free, and applies one set of analytically determined settings to every image and sensor. It ranks first in 18 of 24 PSNR/SSIM comparisons against twelve published methods on three synthetic benchmarks, and attains the lowest mean deviation of the ratio image from the theoretical speckle model over six real-SAR configurations from five sensors. Code is available \href{https://github.com/Teriri1999/Geometry-Calibrated-Closed-Form-Shrinkage-for-SAR-Despeckling}{here}.

</details>


### [44] [Generation of Synthetic Fingerphotos with GANs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15029)
*Conor Miller-Lynch,Sandip Purnapatra,Syed Konain Abbas,Lambert Igene,Faraz Hussain,Soumyabrata Dey,Stephanie Schuckers*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Synthetic fingerphotos generated with StyleGAN2-ADA and StyleGAN3 are evaluated for realism, privacy preservation, and diversity, providing a quantitative baseline and open-source code for evaluating synthetic fingerphotos in contactless fingerprinting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome data scarcity and privacy concerns in contactless fingerprinting by using synthetic data to develop, test, and benchmark systems.

Method: Train/apply StyleGAN2-ADA and StyleGAN3 to generate fingerphotos; assess realism and privacy by comparing biometric feature statistics of real vs synthetic data, compute cross-match scores between real and synthetic, and synthetic-synthetic match scores; provide evaluation code.

Result: Quantitative comparisons and a benchmarking point for future work; demonstrates feasibility of synthetic fingerphotos for evaluation and development; code released.

Conclusion: Synthetic fingerphotos can serve as a useful resource for developing and evaluating contactless fingerprinting, enabling privacy-preserving data sharing and standardized benchmarks; further work can enhance realism and privacy.

Abstract: Contactless fingerprinting is an emerging approach to biometric authentication that allows users to scan their fingerprints without touching a scanner. Due to the limited amount of contactless fingerprint data available and the security risks associated with sharing real individuals' fingerprints, it is valuable to explore methods of generating synthetic data that can be used in place of - or in conjunction with - real data to develop and evaluate contactless fingerprinting systems. In this paper, we present and evaluate synthetic fingerphotos generated using StyleGAN2-ADA and StyleGAN3, existing image generation architectures. We evaluate the realism, privacy preservation, and variety of the synthetic fingerphotos by comparing their biometric feature statistics to those of real fingerphotos, computing match scores between real and synthetic fingerphotos, and computing match scores between different synthetic fingerphotos. This paper provides a quantitative comparison point for future evaluations of synthetic fingerphotos. The evaluation code is made available at https://github.com/cmillerlynch/fingerphoto-gan.

</details>


### [45] [MOSS-VL Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15045)
*Pengyu Wang,Chenkun Tan,Shaojun Zhou,Qirui Zhou,Yanxin Chen,Xingyang He,Huazheng Zeng,Jijun Cheng,Chenghao Wang,Xiaomeng Qian,Pengfei Wang,Zhan Huang,Shanqing Gao,Wei Huang,Longjun Cao,Wu Ran,Jie Liu,Changtai Zhu,Hongkai Wang,Yixian Tian,Chenghao Liu,Zhen Ye,Xinghao Wang,Botian Jiang,Guoguo Feng,Zhaoye Fei,Ruixiao Li,Mingshu Chen,Yang Gao,Qinyuan Cheng,Shimin Li,Xipeng Qiu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MOSS-VL is a real-time capable vision-language model family that enables perceiving while generating, achieving strong proactive behavior and faster response, with open-source release and competitive performance on streaming benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable true real-time interaction in vision-language models by integrating perception during generation, improving proactive and streaming capabilities while maintaining off-line competence and open reproducibility.

Method: Co-design across the stack: the language decoder uses gated cross-attention to see vision; a synthesized interaction corpus trains when to speak, stay silent, and revise; a staged curriculum concentrates real-time-specific training in a light final stage on top of a strong offline foundation. Offline baseline is MOSS-VL-Instruct; real-time variant is MOSS-VL-Realtime. 11.3B parameter model with visual tokens outside the decoded sequence, enabling faster time-to-first-token.

Result: On four streaming benchmarks, MOSS-VL-Realtime achieves the best average on three and second on the fourth, surpassing open-source streaming models; shows strong proactive behavior (OmniMMI Proactive Alerting: 66.0 vs 37.5). It widens the time-to-first-token advantage over Qwen3-VL-8B from 2.8x to 5.1x as visual context grows. All five checkpoints, curriculum, and real-time inference code are released.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that real-time perception integrated into vision-language models yields superior proactive and streaming performance, with scalable, open-source resources for reproducibility and further research.

Abstract: We present MOSS-VL, an open vision-language model family that treats real-time interaction -- perceiving while it speaks -- as a first-class capability. It is co-designed across the stack: the language decoder attends to vision only through gated cross-attention, so the model can naturally see incoming frames while generating; a synthesized interaction corpus supervises when to speak, when to stay silent, and when to revise; and a staged curriculum concentrates all real-time-specific training in one light final stage over a strong offline foundation. Offline, MOSS-VL-Instruct is competitive at comparable scale and leads temporal-reasoning video sets. Across four streaming benchmarks, MOSS-VL-Realtime posts the best average on three (second on the fourth) among open-source streaming models, sweeping the three subsets that squarely test proactive behavior -- 66.0 vs. 37.5 for the best baseline on OmniMMI Proactive Alerting. With 11.3B parameters but visual tokens outside the decoded sequence, MOSS-VL widens its time-to-first-token advantage over same-backbone Qwen3-VL-8B from 2.8x to 5.1x as visual context grows. We release all five checkpoints, the training curriculum, and the real-time inference code at https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-VL.

</details>


### [46] [Frequency and Edge-Guided Segment Anything Model for Remote Sensing Image Semantic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15054)
*Feng Gao,Zizhe Pan,Haoting Wang,Ruzhuang Hua,Jingchao Cao,Junyu Dong,Qian Du*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FE-SAM introduces a Frequency-Modulated Adapter and an Edge-guided Refiner to enhance SAM for remote sensing image semantic segmentation, achieving improved performance by adaptive frequency features and multi-scale edge information across three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address two key limitations of SAM in RSISS: (i) insufficient adaptation of SAM features to the diverse land-cover types, and (ii) semantic ambiguity at object boundaries that impedes precise delineation.

Method: Frequency-Modulated Adapter (FMA) adaptively decomposes and modulates frequency-domain features to emphasize informative high- and low-frequency components suitable for different land-cover types. EGRefiner integrates multi-scale edge-enhanced information from the input image to improve boundary delineation in segmentation.

Result: FE-SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three RSISS benchmark datasets, outperforming existing methods. The authors also provide source code at the given repository.

Conclusion: FE-SAM offers a scalable and efficient framework for RSISS by combining adaptive frequency-domain feature modulation with edge-aware refinement, enhancing SAM's segmentation quality for land-cover mapping.

Abstract: Remote sensing image semantic segmentation (RSISS) has attracted significant attention due to the growing demand for fine-grained land cover information. The Segment Anything Model (SAM), proposed as a foundation vision model, offers strong segmentation performance and generalization capabilities for RSISS tasks. However, existing SAM-based approaches face two limitations: (1) Insufficient adaptation of SAM's features to the diverse characteristics of land cover types. (2) Semantic ambiguity at object boundaries, which hinders accurate delineation. To address these limitations, we propose Frequency and Edge-guided SAM (FE-SAM), a scalable and efficient framework for RSISS. Specifically, we introduce a Frequency-Modulated Adapter (FMA) that adaptively decomposes and modulates frequency-domain features based on the input data. It selectively enhances informative high- and low-frequency components corresponding to different land cover types. Furthermore, to improve SAM's ability to capture fine-grained details, we design EGRefiner, which integrates multi-scale edge-enhanced information extracted from the input image. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that FE-SAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source codes are available at: https://github.com/oucailab/FE-SAM.

</details>


### [47] [MEDR: Query-Independent Frame Selection via Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15058)
*Xinlei Pu,Weijie Shi,Wen Yang,Yi Cao,Hao Chen,Yuanjun Liu,Wenwei Ding,Jia Zhu,Jiajie Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MEDR offers a training-free, query-independent frame selection for long videos by Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring, enabling a fixed frame subset reusable across questions with modest accuracy gains on multimodal LLM benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform sampling can miss brief, informative events; query-dependent frame selection hinders reuse across questions; a fixed, query-independent selection could preserve coverage and reduce computation while enabling reuse.

Method: Constructs complementary visual, motion, and text signals into signal-specific temporal events. Uses Dynamic Rescoring to iteratively recompute each candidate frame’s score based on signal strength, new event coverage, and temporal proximity to the selected set, yielding a fixed subset without observing the query.

Result: On Video-MME benchmarks, MEDR yields 0.63%–0.89% accuracy gains. On LongVideoBench’s long-video subset, gains up to 1.23% with Qwen3-VL-8B. Overall accuracy improves by 0.53% while reusing the same frame set across all questions about a video.

Conclusion: A training-free, query-independent frame selection approach can improve multimodal LLM performance with reusable frame sets, offering modest but consistent gains and reduced inference redundancy.

Abstract: Frame selection is a fundamental component of multimodal large language models, enabling long videos to be processed under limited visual-token and computational budgets. Uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but may miss informative content that appears only briefly. To alleviate this limitation, query-dependent methods can retrieve question-relevant frames. However, because the selected frames depend on the current question, the same visual input cannot be directly shared across different questions, and frame selection must be repeated in multi-turn video dialogue. This motivates us to seek a query-independent frame selection method that preserves the reusability of a fixed visual input while improving the coverage of informative events beyond uniform sampling. We propose Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring (MEDR), a training-free and query-independent frame selection method. Multi-Signal Event Modeling organizes complementary visual, motion, and text signals into signal-specific temporal events. Dynamic Rescoring then iteratively reevaluates each candidate relative to the current selected set, updating its score according to frame-level signal strength, additional event coverage, and temporal proximity. The resulting fixed frame set is constructed without observing the query and can be reused across different questions. On the standard benchmark evaluations, MEDR improves model accuracy by 0.63%-0.89% on Video-MME. On the long-video subset of LongVideoBench, it improves accuracy by up to 1.23% with Qwen3-VL-8B. MEDR further improves overall accuracy by 0.53%, while reusing exactly the same frame set for every question about a video.

</details>


### [48] [EgoTac: In-the-wild Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15060)
*Wenkang Zhang,Chengbo Yuan,Zicheng Zhang,Zhengxue Cheng,Yang Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EgoTac is a vision-to-tactile model that infers tactile signals from egocentric human videos using a large image-tactile dataset, enabling zero-shot tactile predictions and improved contact estimation for tactile-aware robotics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile data are hard to collect at scale, while egocentric human video data with rich contact events is plentiful. Inferring tactile priors from vision could enable scalable tactile-aware Robot Learning.

Method: Train a generalizable model on a unified corpus of over 5.7 million image-tactile pairs, predicting both continuous force data and binary contact signals from egocentric video inputs.

Result: In-domain force error < 0.06 N; out-of-domain contact prediction surpasses state-of-the-art; captures real tactile rise/fall patterns; enables zero-shot predictions on unconstrained real videos; data diversity and volume scales improve performance.

Conclusion: EgoTac provides a scalable approach to extract tactile priors from egocentric videos, facilitating broad tactile-aware robot learning.

Abstract: Touch is fundamental to dexterous manipulation, yet most egocentric human data increasingly used for robot learning lacks tactile information. Directly collecting large-scale tactile data is challenging due to sensor limitations, while human video data is abundant, contact-rich, and easily scalable. This motivates a natural question: can tactile signals be inferred purely from vision? To address this, we introduce EgoTac, a generalizable model that predicts rich tactile information directly from egocentric human videos. EgoTac is trained on a unified corpus of over 5.7M image-tactile pairs, covering both continuous force measurements and binary contacts. By learning from this diverse dataset, EgoTac captures nuanced touch dynamics across varied interactions. Experiments demonstrate strong performance: in-domain prediction achieves an average force error below 0.06N. On out-of-domain contact prediction benchmarks, EgoTac consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art contact estimator. It also captures the rise and fall patterns of real tactile data and enables zero-shot predictions on unconstrained real-world videos. Scaling analyses further reveal that both data diversity and volume improve performance steadily. Overall, EgoTac provides a scalable pathway to extract tactile priors from egocentric human videos, enabling broadly applicable tactile-aware robot learning.

</details>


### [49] [Do Visual Grounding Decoders Need Feed-Forward Networks? A Controlled Study over Frozen Vision-Language Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15061)
*Tarun Tomar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Attention-only decoders can largely match or exceed FFN-enhanced decoders when using a frozen vision-language model for visual grounding; FFN adds limited, dataset-dependent gains and incurs more parameters, whereas attention-only decoders with similar capacity can reduce parameter count and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether feed-forward networks in visual grounding decoders provide essential computation beyond what a pretrained vision-language model already encodes, and quantify trade-offs in performance, parameters, and latency.

Method: Compare three decoder configurations using frozen VLM features: A4 (four-block attention-only), S4 (four-block attention-plus-FFN), and A8 (eight-block attention-only parameter control). Evaluations on RefCOCOg, Ref-Adv-s, and FineCops-Ref datasets, with metrics including IoU@0.5, and record trainable-decoder parameters and cached-end latency to assess efficiency.

Result: A4 matches or slightly exceeds S4 on RefCOCOg and Ref-Adv-s.
