Although deep learning has shown considerable potential in computational pathology, comprehensive benchmarks that integrate tissue classification and region segmentation within a unified analytical framework remain limited. This study presents a two-stage deep learning framework for multi-class tissue classification and pixel-level histopathological region segmentation, accompanied by a systematic comparison of state-of-the-art architectures at each stage. For tissue classification, six models, a custom convolutional neural network, VGG16, DenseNet, MobileNetV3, a custom Vision Transformer, and YOLO11, are evaluated on a combined dataset of 39,000 images derived from LC25000 and LungHist700. The models distinguish between adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and normal lung tissue. YOLO11 achieves the best classification performance, with an accuracy of 98.38%, a five-fold cross-validation accuracy of 98.21 +/- 0.35%, and a macro F1-score of 0.98. For region segmentation, U-Net, ResNet-encoder U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and YOLO11-seg are evaluated using the GlaS gland segmentation benchmark. DeepLabV3+ obtains the highest Intersection over Union of 0.80 and a Dice score of 0.89, while YOLO11-seg achieves a comparable Intersection over Union of 0.79 using approximately 14x fewer parameters. The best-performing classification and segmentation models are subsequently integrated into an end-to-end framework, providing an accurate, computationally efficient, and reproducible baseline for automated histopathological image analysis.

</details>


### [124] [BagShift: Measuring How Patch Selection Changes the Evidence Seen by Whole-Slide MIL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15970)
*Ruicheng Yuan,Zhenxuan Zhang,Liwei Hu,Anbang Wang,Haijie Xu,Jiawei Luo,Guang Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BagShift isolates the effect of patch selectors in whole-slide MIL by pairing deployments that keep features and predictor fixed while varying the selector, revealing how deployment constraints alter observed evidence and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how deployment-related changes to the MIL selector affect evidence and predictions, separate from case-mix and feature representation, and to propose a robust evaluation framework.

Method: Introduce BagShift, a paired protocol that fixes features and predictor and varies the patch selector under a fixed budget (128 patches). Compare two views: sampling across tissue vs concentrating around a coordinate, across PANDA, CAMELYON16, and external lung subtyping. Measure performance with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) and observe evidence retention (e.g., tumor retention). Also test unioning repeated localized observations before a single MIL pass.

Result: Across PANDA: two views reduce QWK by 1.57 and 17.96 points on the ×100 scale. On CAMELYON16, localized views retain tumor in only 10.0% of micrometastases; matched exposure does not consistently recover the loss. External lung subtyping shows a much smaller response. Unioning repeated local observations before one nonlinear MIL pass improves PANDA QWK by 7.87 points. Key claim: patch count governs computation, not observed evidence; deployment evaluations should report preserved evidence and aggregation strategy.

Conclusion: Deployment evaluations for MIL should report both the evidence preserved by the selector and how multiple localized observations are aggregated. Localized sampling can dramatically alter observed evidence, and aggregation strategies can mitigate but not fully compensate for selection effects.

Abstract: Whole-slide multiple-instance learning (MIL) observes only the patches admitted by its selector. Deployment can alter this selector through compute limits, tissue masking, or regional workflows, even when the patch count is unchanged. We introduce BagShift, a paired protocol that changes the selector for the same case while holding its features and predictor fixed, thereby isolating selector response from case mix. With equal 128-patch budgets, sampling across the tissue or concentrating around one coordinate exposes markedly different evidence: on PANDA, the two views reduce quadratic weighted kappa by 1.57 and 17.96 points, respectively (QWK reported on the $\times100$ scale). On CAMELYON16, lesion annotations withheld from model development show that localized views retain tumor in only 10.0\% of micrometastatic observations, and matched exposure does not consistently recover the loss. The same fixed-count stressor produces a much smaller response on external lung subtyping, although differences in relative coverage make cross-task severity descriptive. When repeated localized observations are available, unioning their patches before one nonlinear MIL pass improves PANDA QWK by 7.87 points over averaging regional predictions. Patch count specifies computation, not observed evidence; deployment evaluations should report both what a selector preserves and how repeated observations are aggregated.

</details>


### [125] [CM-MAE: A Physics-Guided Cross-Modal Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Vision-Wireless Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15972)
*Yubo Zhang,Yiyao Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CM-MAE: self-supervised vision–wireless pretraining for cross-scenario representation transfer using soft contrastive alignment and masked joint decoding, improving cross-domain fusion representations on DeepSense 6G.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address robustness of joint camera–wireless representations across viewpoint, traffic, illumination, and propagation changes; enable cross-scenario transfer without ray-traced paths or labels.

Method: Self-supervised dual-branch pretraining with a soft contrastive alignment loss that builds a target distribution from similarities between measured beam-power profiles; a masked joint decoder reconstructs hidden visual patches and wireless angular clusters under modality dropout; differential-rate fine-tuning for fast fusion-head adaptation while encoders update slowly.

Result: On a sequence-disjoint DeepSense 6G protocol, soft alignment improves matched linear-probe transfer average from 24.88% to 29.49%; mild fusion fine-tuning yields 77.38% Top-1 on unseen Scenarios 6–8; optional transductive normalization reaches 78.69%. The approach uses only RGB frames and 64-beam power vectors (no ray-traced paths or beam-index labels).

Conclusion: Soft alignment enhances cross-scenario representation transfer in vision–wireless fusion; results warrant interpretation as transfer diagnostics rather than beam-prediction claims, highlighting robustness gains through self-supervised cross-modal pretraining.

Abstract: Synchronized camera and wireless measurements observe the same scene through different physical channels. The central difficulty is that a representation learned in one deployment can fail when viewpoint, traffic, illumination, and propagation geometry change. This paper presents CM-MAE, a self-supervised vision--wireless pretraining framework for cross-scenario representation transfer. The evaluated real-data model uses only RGB frames and the measured 64-beam received-power vector available in DeepSense 6G; it does not use ray-traced paths, calibrated depth, or beam-index labels during pretraining. Its central pretraining term is a \emph{soft contrastive alignment loss}. Instead of making the synchronized image--wireless pair the only positive pair, this loss builds a target distribution from similarities between measured beam-power profiles, so nonidentical samples with similar directional responses are not forced apart as false negatives. A masked joint decoder provides the complementary local objective by reconstructing hidden visual patches and wireless angular clusters under modality dropout. After pretraining, a differential-rate fine-tuning rule lets a new fusion head adapt quickly while the encoders move slowly. Under a sequence-disjoint DeepSense 6G protocol, adding the soft alignment loss improves a matched linear-probe transfer average from 24.88\% to 29.49\%. Mild fusion fine-tuning reaches 77.38\% Top-1 accuracy on unseen Scenarios 6--8, and optional transductive normalization adaptation reaches 78.69\%. Since the fusion setting uses the contemporaneous 64-beam power vector at inference, these results should be read as representation-transfer diagnostics, not as proactive beam-prediction or reduced-sweeping claims.

</details>


### [126] [A Plug-and-Play 2D Motion Interface for Real-World Motion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15984)
*Kaname Yokoyama,Norimichi Ukita*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes a plug-and-play 2D Motion Interface that lets 3D-pretrained Motion Language Models (MoLMs) accept 2D motion inputs without fine-tuning, achieving competitive performance with 3D inputs and outperforming models trained from scratch on 2D data; includes a monocular real-world video motion dataset and a real-video adapter; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoLMs rely on 3D motion representations, but obtaining accurate 3D motion from monocular videos is challenging, hindering real-world deployment of MoLMs.

Method: Introduce a plug-and-play 2D Motion Interface that bridges 2D motion inputs to 3D-pretrained MoLMs without modifying or fine-tuning the original models; construct a monocular real-world video motion evaluation dataset and develop a real-video adapter to validate performance under monocular pose estimation.

Result: Experiments on public datasets show that 2D inputs via the interface perform comparably to 3D inputs across multiple MoLMs and better than training MoLMs from scratch on 2D data; the monocular real-world video dataset and real-video adapter demonstrate the practicality of 2D motions in monocular pose estimation.

Conclusion: 2D motion serves as a practical, plug-and-play interface for deploying MoLMs in real-world motion understanding scenarios, reducing dependence on accurate 3D pose estimation.

Abstract: Motion Language Models (MoLMs) typically understand human motions by tokenizing 3D motion and processing the resulting tokens using a language model. However, obtaining accurate 3D motions from monocular videos is challenging, limiting their real-world applicability. To address this issue, we introduce a plug-and-play 2D Motion Interface that enables 3D-pretrained MoLMs to accept 2D motion inputs without modifying or fine-tuning the original models.
  Experiments on public datasets show that our method achieves performance comparable to 3D motion inputs across multiple MoLMs and outperforms training MoLMs from scratch on 2D motions. We further construct a monocular real-world video motion evaluation dataset and introduce a real-video adapter, demonstrating the usefulness of 2D motions over 3D motions under the evaluated monocular pose-estimation setting. These results suggest that 2D motion provides a practical interface for deploying MoLMs in real-world motion understanding settings. Code is available at https://github.com/irajisamurai/2D-Motion-Interface.

</details>


### [127] [Depth-guided Multi-view Exposure Bracketing for HDR Robot Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16014)
*Jinnyeong Kim,Juhyung Choi,Woohyeok Kim,Sunghyun Cho,Seung-Hwan Baek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DMEB is a single-shot HDR method for multi-view, low-bit-depth cameras that uses depth-guided confidence-aware fusion across views to handle extreme illumination. It is evaluated on a new large-scale dataset (121 real scenes + 20 CARLA sequences) and serves as a strong reference for HDR perception in multi-camera and depth-sensor robotic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is currently no comprehensive benchmark for HDR perception in multi-sensor robotic systems, especially under extreme illumination. A large-scale, real-and-synthetic dataset is needed to evaluate HDR perception across multi-camera setups and sensor fusion pipelines.

Method: Depth-guided Multi-view Exposure Bracketing (DMEB): distribute greatly different exposures across multiple low-bit-depth cameras in a single shot, then fuse using depth-guided confidence-aware fusion to produce an enhanced HDR image.

Result: A large-scale dataset is introduced: 121 real-world scenes with modest to ultra-high dynamic range and 20 synthetic CARLA sequences. DMEB establishes a strong reference on this dataset and demonstrates the viability of this sensor configuration for robust HDR perception across multi-camera and depth-sensor systems.

Conclusion: DMEB provides a strong baseline for single-shot HDR in multi-sensor robotic systems and highlights the potential of multi-view, depth-guided fusion in challenging illumination conditions. The accompanying dataset offers a valuable benchmark for future HDR perception research in real-world and simulated robotic settings.

Abstract: Achieving reliable single-shot high dynamic range (HDR) imaging under extreme illumination conditions remains a long-standing challenge, yet no comprehensive benchmark exist for evaluating HDR perception in multi-sensor robotic systems. To fill this gap, we introduce a large-scale dataset collected via a custom robotic vision platform and an iPhone 13 Pro: 121 real-world scenes spanning modest and ultra-high dynamic range conditions, alongside 20 synthetic video sequences from the CARLA simulator. As a reference pipeline for this dataset, we propose Depth-guided Multi-view Exposure Bracketing (DMEB), a single-shot HDR method that distributes drastically different exposures across multi-view low-bit-depth cameras and fuses them via depth-guided confidence-aware fusion. Evaluations on our dataset show that DMEB establishes a strong reference point and highlight the promise of this sensor configuration for robust HDR perception in diverse multi-camera and depth sensor system.

</details>


### [128] [Multi-scale Decomposed Convolution Refinement Network for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16015)
*Mingsheng Zheng,Zirui Jiang,Bo Liu,Yupeng Chen,Jun Zhang,Kai Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MDCRNet introduces multi-scale decomposed convolution refinement with hierarchical learning and discriminative metric learning for VI-ReID, achieving state-of-the-art results on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB; code is available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle cross-modal discrepancies and limited discriminative power in visible-infrared person re-identification, addressing gaps in semantic mining, cross-modal fusion, and robust feature constraints.

Method: A Hierarchical Learning Module (HLM) consisting of four Hierarchical Decomposed Convolution Attention (HDCA) blocks with lightweight channel attention and multi-scale spatial perception. A Joint Discriminative Metric Loss (JDML) that includes a Granularity Discriminative Loss (GDL) to optimize intra-identity compactness and inter-identity separability across modalities.

Result: Empirical evaluation on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB shows state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks; code for MDCRNet is released.

Conclusion: MDCRNet demonstrates effective integration of hierarchical multi-scale feature learning and cross-modal discriminative metric learning, advancing VI-ReID performance and offering a reusable framework for cross-modal person re-identification.

Abstract: Visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) suffers from cross-modal discrepancies and limited discriminative capabilities, leading to suboptimal recognition performance. Current approaches exhibit limitations in semantic mining, cross-modal fusion and feature constraints. To tackle these challenges, we propose MDCRNet, a Multi-scale Decomposed Convolution Refinement Network that enhances cross-modal feature learning and discriminative metric learning. Specifically, we introduce a Hierarchical Learning Module (HLM) containing four Hierarchical Decomposed Convolution Attention (HDCA) modules, each equipped with lightweight channel attention and multi-scale spatial perception blocks to capture multi-scale spatial dependencies. Moreover, we develop a Joint Discriminative Metric Loss (JDML) incorporating a novel Granularity Discriminative Loss (GDL) that simultaneously optimizes intra-identity compactness and inter-identity separability across modalities. Extensive experiments on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB datasets demonstrate that MDCRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Kevin-zms/MDCRNet.

</details>


### [129] [TR-GS: High-Fidelity Sparse-View CT Volumetric Rendering via t-Distribution Gaussian Splatting and Ray-Confidence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16042)
*Zedong Xiao,Yiren Wang,Zhou Liu,Xiaolin Liu,Zhangji Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TR-GS introduces a robust Gaussian-splatting framework for sparse-view CT using projectable Student's t-distributions and a ray-confidence mechanism with wavelet regularization, improving reconstruction quality over baselines on both synthetic and real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse-view CT reduces projection requirements and radiation exposure but induces structural artifacts and reconstruction uncertainty. A robust volumetric representation is needed for accurate medical visualization and downstream applications.

Method: Replace standard Gaussian primitives with projectable Student's t-distribution primitives. Introduce a ray-confidence model that modulates their degrees of freedom based on local ray observability. Apply confidence-guided 3D wavelet regularization to balance high-frequency detail preservation with noise suppression.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show TR-GS improves over representative baselines in most evaluated settings and remains competitive in the remaining cases.

Conclusion: TR-GS yields high-quality sparse-view CT volumetric representations suitable for downstream medical multimedia applications (e.g., XR visualization and interactive clinical rendering) and is licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Abstract: High-fidelity 3D medical visualization supports applications such as clinical assessment and surgical planning. Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) can reduce projection requirements and associated radiation exposure, but limited observations may introduce structural artifacts and reconstruction uncertainty. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient explicit representation for volumetric rendering, existing CT methods based on standard Gaussian primitives may be sensitive to unreliable observations under sparse-view acquisition. We present TR-GS, a Gaussian-splatting framework for sparse view CT volumetric rendering. TR-GS replaces standard Gaussian primitives with projectable Student's t-distribution primitives and introduces a ray-confidence model that regulates their degrees of freedom according to local ray observability. Confidence-guided 3D wavelet regularization is further used to balance high-frequency detail preservation and noise suppression. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that TR-GS improves over representative baselines in most evaluated settings and remains competitive in the remaining cases. The resulting volumetric representations may support downstream medical multimedia applications, including XR-based visualization and interactive clinical rendering.

</details>


### [130] [TISC: A Text-Driven Image Semantic Communication System for Faithful Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16100)
*Feifan Zhang,Yuyang Du,Xiaoyan Liu,Soung Chang Liew*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes TISC, a text-driven image semantic communication framework using Tree-Structured Attribute Semantic Extraction (TSASE) and Initial Noise Optimization (INO) to improve semantic fidelity in I2T and T2I.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address semantic loss in I2T and semantic faithfulness variability in diffusion-based T2I, which hamper faithful image reconstruction under low-bandwidth semantic communication.

Method: Introduce TSASE to decompose semantic extraction into global scene, background, and object-level attributes (including spatial position, shape/pose, color, material, etc.). Introduce INO to select initial diffusion noise seed at transmitter via a comprehensive similarity score combining visual and semantic consistency.

Result: Experiments across multiple datasets show TSASE improves object-position recovery and semantic description faithfulness; INO parameter study validates the noise-seed configuration.

Conclusion: TISC with TSASE and INO enhances semantic faithfulness in the reconstructed image and demonstrates effective low-bandwidth semantic communication with diffusion-based generative models.

Abstract: Generative image semantic communication converts an image into a text description and then performs text-to-image reconstruction at the receiver via diffusion-based generative models. This paradigm has attracted broad attention due to its extremely low bandwidth cost. However, existing methods still face two critical bottlenecks across image-to-text (I2T) semantic extraction at the transmitter and text-to-image (T2I) semantic reconstruction at the receiver: (i) semantic loss and distortion in I2T, where holistic image descriptions may omit fine-grained object attributes and spatial-position information, causing the generated text to deviate from the original image semantics; and (ii) insufficient semantic faithfulness in T2I, where even with the same semantically faithful text description, different initial noise settings may lead diffusion-based reconstruction to produce images with different levels of semantic consistency with the original image. These issues jointly limit the semantic faithfulness of image reconstruction. To address them, we propose TISC, a text-driven image semantic communication framework tailored for faithful reconstruction. TISC incorporates two key designs: (1) Tree-Structured Attribute Semantic Extraction (TSASE), which decomposes semantic extraction into global scene, background, and object-level attribute descriptions, covering spatial position, shape/pose, color, material, and other physical attributes for each detected object; and (2) an Initial Noise Optimization (INO) mechanism, which selects an initial noise seed at the transmitter according to a comprehensive similarity score that jointly considers visual and semantic consistency. Experiments on multiple datasets show that TSASE improves object-position recovery and semantic description faithfulness, while the INO parameter study supports the adopted configuration for noise selection.

</details>


### [131] [Beyond Similarity Matching: Structured Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Referring Segmentation in 3DGS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16103)
*Yizhao Wang,Xinfa Wang,Jingbo Wang,Jingbo Wang,Guantao Zhang,Yafeng Han,Guohong Gao,Yuhe Xia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: QAGaussian advances open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian Splatting by learning query-conditioned Gaussian slots, a relation-aware slot graph, and an adaptive router, achieving state-of-the-art segmentation without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of global text–region similarity in 3DGS that cause target–reference confusion, granularity mismatch, part–whole leakage, and relation violations; require query-conditioned representations and relational reasoning across multiple granularities.

Method: Learn multi-scale Gaussian slots conditioned on the input query; build a language-conditioned, edge-weighted slot graph capturing target-reference, attributes, part–whole, and contextual relations; apply a granularity-adaptive router to fuse region-, object-, part-, attribute-, and relation-aware masks; perform relation-constrained refinement for spatial, part–whole, attribute, and geometric consistency; pretrain on Mosaic3D-5.6M for Gaussian–text alignment and evaluate on independent benchmarks without target-dataset fine-tuning.

Result: Avg. mIoU 47.2 and Avg. F1 63.2; outperforms strongest 3DGS baseline by 2.7 mIoU and 2.9 F1; Part-mIoU 38.6→43.4; Rel-mIoU 44.4→50.8; reduces target-reference confusion from 10.8 to 7.4; code released at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: Query-conditioned slot learning with relation-aware graph reasoning and adaptive routing effectively improves open-vocabulary referring segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting, demonstrating robust performance across metrics without fine-tuning.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary referring segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) requires a neural model to select Gaussian primitives according to free-form language expressions. Existing 3DGS-based methods usually rely on global text-region similarity, which is weak for queries involving attributes, reference objects, spatial relations, and fine-grained parts. This often causes target-reference confusion, granularity mismatch, part-whole leakage, and relation violations. We propose QAGaussian, a query-adaptive neural reasoning framework for language-guided Gaussian primitive selection. QAGaussian first learns query-conditioned multi-scale Gaussian slots as differentiable candidates whose receptive fields are shaped by the input expression. It then builds a relation-aware slot graph with language-conditioned edge weighting to propagate target-reference, attribute, part-whole, and contextual evidence. A granularity-adaptive router softly combines region-level, object-level, part-level, attribute-aware, and relation-aware mask branches, followed by relation-constrained refinement for spatial, part-whole, attribute, and geometric consistency. QAGaussian is pretrained only on Mosaic3D-5.6M for Gaussian-text alignment and evaluated on independent benchmarks without target-dataset fine-tuning. It achieves 47.2 Avg. mIoU and 63.2 Avg. F1, outperforming the strongest 3DGS referring baseline by 2.7 mIoU points and 2.9 F1 points. It also improves Part-mIoU from 38.6 to 43.4, Rel-mIoU from 44.4 to 50.8, and reduces target-reference confusion from 10.8 to 7.4. These results demonstrate that query-conditioned slot learning, relation-aware graph reasoning, and adaptive routing provide an effective neural modeling strategy for open-vocabulary referring segmentation in 3DGS. The code is available at https://github.com/zqeslwyz/QAGaussian.

</details>


### [132] [Nexus: Structured Synergy for Efficient Text-to-Image Generation using Rectified Flow Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16104)
*Yizhao Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Nexus combines sparse, linear-complexity diffusion with low-bit, per-expert training (MoE FFNs and gated DeltaNet attention) to deliver SDXL/SD3-quality text-to-image generation with much higher inference efficiency, enabling edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for text-to-image face high computational demands, quadratic memory/compute scaling, and memory footprints that hinder high-resolution synthesis and edge deployment.

Method: Integrate sparse architecture, linear-time computation, and low-bit quantization through MoE (mixture-of-experts) feed-forward layers, gated DeltaNet attention, and per-expert low-bit training; jointly optimize these components for efficiency and quality.

Result: Achieves generation quality comparable to mainstream models such as SDXL and SD3 while delivering markedly higher inference efficiency; validated on COCO and LAION datasets.

Conclusion: Nexus offers a scalable, efficient diffusion/flow matching framework that preserves image quality while reducing resource requirements, enabling high-resolution generation and potential edge deployment.

Abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models have made significant progress in text-to-image generation, yet high computation, quadratic complexity, and large memory footprint hinder high-resolution synthesis and edge deployment. We propose Nexus, which integrates sparse architecture, linear complexity, and low-bit quantization. It combines MoE feed-forward layers, gated DeltaNet attention, and per-expert low-bit training to reduce computation and memory. Their joint optimization allows Nexus to achieve generation quality comparable to mainstream models such as SDXL and SD3 while delivering markedly higher inference efficiency. Experiments on COCO and LAION validate its effectiveness.

</details>


### [133] [SUGFW+: An Uncertainty-guided Feature Weighting Framework for Cold Start Active Adaptation of SAM in Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16110)
*Xiaochuan Ma,Ning Zhu,Jia Fu,Lanfeng Zhong,Hanyu Jiang,Bin Song,Kang Li,Guotai Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A SAM-based framework (SUGFW+) for Cold Start Active Learning in medical image segmentation that uses patch-level features and uncertainty from SAM, aggregates them into discriminative image-level representations (PGDR), selects samples via a Greedy Strategy with Clustering and Uncertainty (GSCU), and tightly couples sample selection with training through Uncertainty-Prompted Fine-Tuning (UPFT), achieving state-of-the-art results on four public datasets; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce annotation cost in medical image segmentation by leveraging strong, generalizable embeddings from foundation models (SAM) for effective cold-start sample selection, and to tightly integrate selection with model adaptation.

Method: (1) PFUC: extract patch-level feature embeddings and uncertainty from SAM. (2) PGDR: aggregate patch embeddings into global, discriminative image-level representations with uncertainty awareness. (3) GSCU: greedy sample selection balancing diversity (clusters) and uncertainty. (4) UPFT: fine-tune SAM in a sample-efficient way during training, coupling selection and training. (5) Evaluation on four public datasets demonstrating improved performance; code released.

Result: SUGFW+ achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing CSAL methods on four public datasets for medical image segmentation under low annotation budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed SUGFW+ framework effectively exploits SAM embeddings for cold-start active learning and adaptation, with a tight integration of sample selection and fine-tuning that yields superior performance. The approach is modular (PFUC, PGDR, GSCU, UPFT) and reproducible (code release).

Abstract: Cold Start Active Learning (CSAL) is important in improving the performance of a medical image segmentation model with low annotation budget by querying a small subset for annotation from an unlabeled training set. Existing CSAL methods typically rely on inefficient dataset-specific Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) to map the unlabeled images into a feature space for sample selection. Recently, the advent of foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) offer a promising alternative as the pre-trained model can provide strong generalizable feature embeddings, and allow high performance in downstream tasks after fine-tuning (adaptation). However, how to systematically exploit SAM's inherent embeddings for cold-start sample selection during adaptation with low annotation budget remains underexplored. To address this, we propose an extended SAM-based Uncertainty-guided Feature Weighting (SUGFW+) framework for CSAL and adaptation of SAM. Specifically, it leverages the SAM for Patch-level Feature and Uncertainty Calculation (PFUC), and introduces a Patch-based Global Distinct Representation (PGDR) module that aggregates patch-level embeddings into highly discriminative, uncertainty-aware image-level features. These features are then utilized by a Greedy Selection with Cluster and Uncertainty (GSCU) strategy to combine diversity and uncertainty during sample selection. Unlike prior CSAL methods that decouple sample selection from model training, SUGFW+ tightly integrates these two stages via an Uncertainty-Prompted Fine-Tuning (UPFT) process of SAM in model training. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that SUGFW+ achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing CSAL methods. Code is available at https://github.com/HiLab-git/SUGFW-plus.

</details>


### [134] [TokenSTFormer: A Tokenized Spatial-temporal Attention Model for Holistic Motion Analysis in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16122)
*Dong Chen,Kenneth M. C. Cheung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This work introduces ScoliGait, a dataset of 1,516 gait videos with X-ray records for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) screening, and TokenSTFormer, a spatiotemporal transformer that tokenizes spatial and temporal features to improve representation and convergence, achieving state-of-the-art results (accuracy ~0.79) compared with a vanilla Vision Transformer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AIS screening is limited by subjectivity, required expert interpretation, and low scalability. A gait-based, attention-driven approach aims to enable scalable, cost-effective screening by leveraging holistic motion features.

Method: Construct the ScoliGait dataset (1,516 gait video clips with corresponding X-ray records) and propose TokenSTFormer, a model that tokenizes spatial and temporal semantics to enhance feature representation; compare against a vanilla Vision Transformer encoder.

Result: State-of-the-art performance with improved metrics over ViT, reporting an accuracy of 0.79.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of gait-based AIS screening with attention-based models, highlighting potential for scalable clinical applications and guiding future research in scoliosis detection.

Abstract: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) is a prevalent spinal deformity in adolescents that, if left untreated, can result in severe health outcomes. Traditional screening methods are limited by subjective interpretation, reliance on professional expertise and low scalability. To address these challenges, we present ScoliGait dataset, which comprises 1,516 gait video clips paired with corresponding X-ray records. We also introduce TokenSTFormer, a novel model that tokenizes spatial and temporal semantics to enhance feature representation and convergence. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing vanilla Vision Transformer encoder across key metrics, including accuracy of 0.79. This study highlights the potential of leveraging holistic motion features derived from gait video and attention-based models for scalable, cost-effective AIS screening, paving the way for future clinical applications in scoliosis detection.

</details>


### [135] [Graph Neural Assisted Actor-Critic for Latency-Efficient Edge Vision System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16142)
*Alam Noor,Luis Almeida,Kai Li,Jiyan Wu,Miguel Gutiérrez Gaitán,Eduardo Tovar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GCN-assisted A2C DRL framework to selectively transmit pixel-group areas from UAV video to reduce latency and false detections, leveraging a Graph ConvNet to exploit pixel correlations and a Lagrangian dual optimization to enforce latency constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latency in UAV surveillance degrades operator effectiveness; transmitting full frames yields high latency; existing DRL methods are not optimized for pixel-level transmission efficiency and latency constraints.

Method: Introduce a GCN-assisted A2C DRL model. The GCN learns hidden representations of pixel-group correlations and supervises the A2C policy, which selects a subgroup of pixels to transmit instead of the full frame. A Lagrangian dual form with gradient descent enforces latency constraints and mitigates constraint-violation penalties during optimization.

Result: Experiments show reduced video frame transmission latency and lower false detection rate compared to other DRL and state-of-the-art models.

Conclusion: The proposed GCN-assisted A2C framework effectively reduces UAV video transmission latency while maintaining or improving detection performance, demonstrating the viability of pixel-group selective transmission in latency-constrained UAV vision systems.

Abstract: UAV on-board vision systems are widely used for different activities, including monitoring in no-fly zones. In this case, the vision-equipped UAV streams a video to a ground server where an operator assists its activities. The latency of video transmission has a profound impact on the effectiveness of the operator assistance. However, most techniques available for video transmission still incur significant latency costs. In this paper, we propose a graph convolutional neural network-assisted (GCN-Assisted A2C) deep reinforcement learning (DRL) system model to find the optimal pixel-correlated area of a suspicious object. We combine the Lagrangian dual form with gradient descent to prevent lack of convergence and over- and under-penalization constraint violation during latency optimization. The proposed system model sends a sub-group pixel-correlated area of the frame from the UAV to the server rather than the transmission of the whole video frame. The proposed framework utilizes the GCN model to explore hidden representations of feature-correlated groups of pixels. Moreover, the GCN supervises the A2C model, which selects a subgroup to enhance transmission latency, thus supervising the training of UAV actions in A2C. Experimental results show that GCN-assisted A2C reduces video frame transmission latency together with false detection rate in UAV vision systems over other DRL and state-of-the-art models.

</details>


### [136] [KeyID: Decoupled Drafting and Keyframe Editing for Identity-Preserving Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16154)
*Jianjie Luo,Yiming Zhong,Haoming Shen,Yupeng Xiao,Zhenguo Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: KeyID is a training-free Identity-Preserving Video Generation (IPVG) framework that decouples video dynamics from identity injection using two components: (1) Reference-Aware Video Generation, producing an identity-agnostic video draft aligned to multiple references, and (2) Identity-Preserved Keyframe Editing, injecting the target identity via sparse keyframe correction and motion interpolation. It shifts from dense frame supervision to sparse refinement, enabling multi-subject references and complex sequential actions without training. It outperforms prior work and won runner-up in Track 2 (Sequential Action) of ACM Multimedia 2026 IPVG Grand Challenge; code available at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address high tuning costs and limited input-level enhancements in Identity-preserving video generation, while maintaining rigid identity consistency over long sequences. Need a training-free, modular approach that scales to multi-subject references and sequential actions.

Method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) Reference-Aware Video Generation to produce an identity-agnostic draft aligned with multiple references; (2) Identity-Preserved Keyframe Editing to inject the target identity through sparse keyframe corrections followed by motion interpolation. The approach shifts supervision from dense frame-level to sparse keyframe-level refinement, enabling a capacity trade-off favorable to prompt adherence and identity fidelity. The design is modular and training-free, extensible to multi-subject references and complex action sequences.

Result: The method outperforms prior works on automatic and human evaluations on the official IPVG challenge benchmark, achieving runner-up in Track 2 (Sequential Action). Code is released.

Conclusion: KeyID demonstrates that decoupling video dynamics from identity injection via sparse keyframe refinement can achieve robust identity preservation in long, complex sequences without additional training, and is extensible to multi-subject references and sequential actions.

Abstract: Identity-preserving video generation (IPVG) requires synthesizing videos that are faithful to both reference subjects and text prompts. Existing methods are often hindered by high tuning costs or limited input-level enhancements, struggling to maintain rigid identity consistency during complex, long-sequence actions. To address these limitations, we propose KeyID, a training-free IPVG framework that decouples the synthesis of video dynamics from the injection of identity. Specifically, KeyID comprises two components: (1) Reference-Aware Video Generation, which produces an identity-agnostic video draft aligned with multiple references, and (2) Identity-Preserved Keyframe Editing, which integrates the target identity via sparse keyframe correction and subsequent motion interpolation. By shifting from dense frame-level supervision to sparse keyframe-level refinement, KeyID effectively resolves the capacity conflict between prompt adherence and identity fidelity. Crucially, our modular design allows seamless extension to multi-subject references and complex sequential action generation without additional training. KeyID outperforms prior works and is validated by automatic and human evaluations on the official challenge benchmark, ultimately securing the runner-up position in the Track 2 (Sequential Action) of the ACM Multimedia 2026 IPVG Grand Challenge. Source code is available at https://github.com/WISLab-GDUT/KeyID.

</details>


### [137] [Beyond Clear Skies: Synthetic Seasonal and Weather Variations for Real-World Drone Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16191)
*Tamara R. Lenhard,Andreas Weinmann,Tobias Koch*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SDV-W extends SynDroneVision with adverse-weather and seasonal variation for urban drone detection. 55,187 annotated high-resolution images across three urban environments, three seasons, and weather conditions including rain, snow, and fog at multiple severities; enables matched clean-adverse comparisons and quantifies condition-specific detector degradation. Evaluated with representative YOLO models on real-world data; improves robustness and reduces misses/false alarms; complements general synthetic data; public release upon acceptance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world drone detectors struggle under adverse weather and appearance variation. Real data covering such conditions is scarce, expensive to annotate, and difficult to sample systematically. Synthetic data offers controllable variation, scalable annotations, and reproducible experiments.

Method: Systematic extension of SDV to adverse-weather and seasonal domain shifts. Rendered 55,187 annotated high-resolution images from three urban environments across three seasons and weather types (rain, snow, fog) at multiple severities, preserving SDV's scene and trajectory. Enables matched clean-adverse comparisons and quantification of condition-specific detector degradation. Evaluation conducted across representative YOLO models on real-world datasets.

Result: SDV-W improves detector reliability under adverse appearance shifts, reduces missed detections and false alarms, and is most effective as a complement to general-purpose synthetic drone-detection data.

Conclusion: SDV-W is a valuable, scalable resource for robust drone detection under adverse conditions and will be publicly released upon paper acceptance.

Abstract: Reliable drone detection under real-world deployment conditions requires training data that spans the full operational design domain, including adverse weather and seasonal appearance variation. However, acquiring and annotating such data at scale remains highly resource-intensive, as adverse-weather conditions are inherently difficult to control, reproduce, and sample systematically. Existing datasets therefore typically provide only limited coverage of such conditions. Conversely, synthetic data offers a scalable alternative: environmental variation becomes controllable, while modern game-engine-based pipelines provide realistic rendering and automatic annotations. Leveraging this potential, we introduce SynDroneVision-Weather (SDV-W), an systematic extension of SynDroneVision (SDV) targeting adverse-weather and seasonal domain shifts in urban drone detection. SDV-W comprises 55,187 annotated high-resolution images from three urban environments, rendered across three seasonal configurations and diverse weather conditions, including rain, snow, and fog at multiple severity levels. By preserving SDV's scene and trajectory configuration, SDV-W enables matched clean-adverse comparisons and quantification of condition-specific detector degradation. Across representative YOLO models and real-world datasets, we show that SDV-W improves detector reliability under adverse appearance shifts, reduces missed detections and false alarms, and is most effective as a complement to general-purpose synthetic drone-detection data. SDV-W will be publicly released upon paper acceptance.

</details>


### [138] [Picking the Right Image to Classify: Reliable-Input Selection in Teledermatology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16198)
*Fabian Gröger,Marco Weishaupt,Philippe Gottfrois,Simone Lionetti,Linda Wermelinger,Nipun Ranasekara,Ludovic Amruthalingam,Alexander A. Navarini,Marc Pouly*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An oracle can select a correctly classified image per case and boost weighted F1 by ~20 percentage points, but no training-data-free selectors substantially close this gap; reliable-input selection remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Teledermatology images suffer distribution shifts (lighting, angle, distance, focus, framing) between training and deployment. When multiple images exist per case, selecting the most reliably classifiable image could improve accuracy, motivating a study of reliable input selection.

Method: Benchmark four training-data-free selectors (embedding norm, neighborhood consensus, perturbation stability, model confidence) across six dermatology datasets and nine frozen backbones; compare to an oracle that sees true labels; also test a small labeled reference set and a fusion of confidence with Mahalanobis distance.

Result: The oracle raises weighted F1 by about 20 percentage points on average across datasets and backbones. No training-data-free selector substantially narrows the gap to the oracle. The best data-free approach is the model’s own confidence, but it yields only modest gains. A small labeled reference set does not help; a fusion of confidence and Mahalanobis distance still leaves most of the gap.

Conclusion: This is the first study to introduce and benchmark reliable input selection in dermatology, highlighting a clinically important but unsolved problem and setting a baseline for future research.

Abstract: Dermatology models face distribution shifts in teledermatology settings, where submitted images differ from the training data in lighting, angle, distance, focus, and framing. These test-time images are ordinary clinical photographs, but some fall outside the model's training conditions, leading the model to often misclassify them due to shifts in acquisition between training and deployment. When multiple images of the same case exist (several photos of one patient or lesion), a natural way to improve accuracy is therefore to select the image the model is most likely to classify correctly. We call this task reliable-input selection. An oracle that, for each case, selects a correctly classified image when one exists raises weighted F1 by about 20 percentage points on average across six dermatology datasets and nine frozen backbones. This oracle is an upper bound that sees the labels, whereas a selector must choose blindly. Capturing this gain in practice is hard. A selector that needs no pretraining data applies to any frozen model, including those whose data is not public. It must judge reliability from quantities the model exposes at inference: its embeddings, their norms, and its confidence. We benchmark four such training-data-free selectors: the embedding norm, the neighborhood consensus among a case's images, the stability of the prediction under small perturbations, and the model's own confidence. No training-data-free selector substantially narrows this oracle gap. The best of them is the model's own confidence, but it recovers only a small part of the gap on the clinical datasets. A small labeled reference set does not help either: the best selector overall, a fusion of confidence and Mahalanobis distance, still leaves most of the gap. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce and benchmark reliable input selection, a clinically important, unsolved task.

</details>


### [139] [PCT-Prompt: A Prompt-Guided Transformer Framework for Dense Prediction Tasks in Point Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16225)
*Dejun Zhang,Yanzi Bai,Yiqi Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A two-branch Transformer framework, PCT-Prompt, augments a standard Transformer backbone with a prompt-guided feature branch for dense 3D point-cloud prediction. It introduces a fine-grained multi-scale geometry extraction block (geometry-sensitive abstraction) and a PnP-3D layer, plus a prompt learning block that generates and refines tokens via cross-attention, and a prompt drop mechanism to balance local detail and global consistency. It shows improved performance on ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and DALES, indicating better adaptability to dense prediction tasks in real-world scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense prediction on point clouds requires strong priors about local geometry and global context. Standard Transformers may underperform due to weak priors; a prompt-guided branch can inject structured local information and refine predictions through cross-attention, improving accuracy and robustness.

Method: Two-branch architecture: (1) standard Transformer backbone for global feature extraction from point clouds; (2) prompt-guided feature branch with (a) fine-grained feature extraction block using a geometry-sensitive abstraction layer to capture multi-scale local geometry, and a PnP-3D layer to fuse local context with global regularization; (b) prompt-refined feature learning block that generates prompt tokens and refines them via cross-attention; a prompt drop mechanism progressively removes prompt information across Transformer layers to balance local details with global consistency.

Result: Experiments on ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and DALES show that PCT-Prompt improves the adaptability of standard Transformers to dense prediction tasks, achieving strong performance in real-world scenarios.

Conclusion: PCT-Prompt effectively enhances standard Transformers for dense point-cloud prediction by integrating a prompt-guided local feature branch with global backbone, achieving notable improvements and practical applicability.

Abstract: Standard Transformers have proven effective in point cloud object classification, but their performance in dense prediction tasks within complex scenes is often hindered by weak prior assumptions. To address this challenge, we propose PCT-Prompt, a novel framework that enhances standard Transformers by introducing a prompt-guided feature branch to improve performance in dense prediction tasks. The standard Transformer branch leverages pre-trained models for global feature extraction from point cloud data, serving as the backbone for processing high-level features. Meanwhile, the prompt-guided feature branch consists of two key components: a fine-grained feature extraction block that captures multi-scale geometric features using geometry-sensitive abstraction layer, along with the PnP-3D layer to integrate local context with global regularization. The second component, the prompt-refined feature learning block generates prompt tokens, which are subsequently refined through cross-attention mechanisms. Additionally, we introduce a prompt drop mechanism that progressively removes prompt information across Transformer layers, balancing local details and global consistency. Experimental results on the ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and DALES datasets demonstrate that PCT-Prompt significantly improves the adaptability of standard Transformers to dense prediction tasks, achieving strong performance in real-world scenarios.

</details>


### [140] [GaussianDWM++: Language-Grounded 3D Gaussian Driving World Model for Unified Scene Understanding, Editing, and Multi-Modal Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16234)
*Tianchen Deng,Xuefeng Chen,Shuang Wu,Qu Chen,Jiajun Zhu,Bo Dai,Jianfei Yang,Hesheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified foundation-feature Gaussian driving world model that encodes 3D semantics via Gaussian primitives distilled from vision-language features, enabling language-grounded reasoning, 4D editing, and multi-modal generation with state-of-the-art results on driving benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing driving world models (DWMs) emphasize conditional scene generation and rely on coarse representations (points, occupancy, BEV), which limits explicit 3D understanding and fine-grained alignment between text and 3D structure; a compact, open-vocabulary semantic representation is needed to support language-grounded reasoning and controllable 4D editing.

Method: Introduce a foundation-feature Gaussian tokenizer that distills Qwen/SigLIP visual-language features into 3D Gaussian primitives to form a compact open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic field; design a geometry-aware Gaussian adapter with importance-aware hierarchical selection and text-conditioned Perceiver-style cross-attention to aggregate dense Gaussian primitives into world tokens; apply a KL-based Gaussian–image distribution alignment objective to align Gaussian world tokens with foundation image tokens; leverage this aligned representation to enable instruction-controllable scene editing (e.g., weather changes, dynamic vehicle manipulation) and multi-modal generation.

Result: Extensive experiments on broad driving benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance across scene understanding, visual grounding, planning-oriented reasoning, and controllable 4D generation tasks; code and datasets to be released on GitHub.

Conclusion: A unified framework that integrates 3D semantic representation, language-grounded reasoning, and controllable 4D generation within a Gaussian world model, enabling open-vocabulary in-text alignment and editability of dynamic driving scenes, with strong empirical results and planned open-sourcing.

Abstract: Driving World Models (DWMs) have recently advanced rapidly with generative models, yet most existing methods mainly focus on conditional scene generation and lack explicit 3D scene understanding, language-grounded reasoning, and controllable 4D editing capabilities. Moreover, commonly used point cloud, occupancy, or BEV representations make it difficult to achieve fine-grained alignment between textual information and the underlying 3D scene structure. To address these limitations, we propose a foundation-feature Gaussian driving world model that unifies scene understanding, language-grounded reasoning, controllable 4D editing, and multi-modal generation within a single framework. Specifically, we introduce a foundation-feature Gaussian tokenizer that directly distills Qwen/SigLIP visual-language features into 3D Gaussian primitives, building a compact open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic field. We further design a geometry-aware Gaussian adapter that combines importance-aware hierarchical selection with text-conditioned Perceiver-style cross-attention to aggregate dense Gaussian primitives into compact world tokens. To improve representation compatibility, we introduce a KL-based Gaussian--image distribution alignment objective that aligns Gaussian world tokens with foundation image tokens. Based on the aligned Gaussian representation, our framework further supports instruction-controllable scene editing, including weather-conditioned generation and dynamic vehicle manipulation. Extensive experiments on broader driving benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across scene understanding, visual grounding, planning-oriented reasoning, and controllable 4D generation tasks. We will release the code and datasets publicly on Github.

</details>


### [141] [Convolution-Free Holistic Multivariance Decomposition Layer for Efficient Hyperspectral Image Classification Tensor Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16241)
*Süha Tuna,Ülker Başar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces Holistic Multivariance Decomposition (HMD) as end-to-end differentiable neural network layer family (HMD-0/1/2) for hyperspectral image classification, delivering superior accuracy vs classical tensor decompositions with fewer parameters and comparable stability to CNNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigid tensor decompositions fail to capture complex spatio-spectral dependencies; conventional CNNs are compute-intensive and parameter-heavy for hyperspectral data; need efficient, stable, expressive feature extractors.

Method: Defines HMD as a layer that explicitly separates independent mode variations from cooperative higher-order interactions using learnable matrix-valued supports; presents three approximants HMD-0, HMD-1, HMD-2; integrated with a downstream classifier and trained end-to-end via backprop; evaluated on three benchmark hyperspectral datasets; compared against Tucker, CP, Tensor Train, and CNN baselines.

Result: HMD layers outperform classical tensor decompositions in classification accuracy; HMD-1 and HMD-2 achieve generalization and training stability comparable to 2D/3D-CNNs while reducing feature-extractor parameter count.

Conclusion: HMD offers a robust, parameter-efficient substitute for traditional convolution in multidimensional hyperspectral image classification, maintaining stability during training and enabling end-to-end optimization.

Abstract: Feature extraction for hyperspectral image classification is conventionally addressed using rigid tensor decompositions that fail to capture complex spatio-spectral interdependencies, or heavily parameterized convolutional neural networks that are computationally expensive. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces the Holistic Multivariance Decomposition (HMD) framework as a novel, end-to-end differentiable neural network layer. By explicitly separating independent single mode variations from cooperative higher dimensional interactions via learnable, matrix valued supports, the proposed HMD-0, HMD-1 and HMD-2 approximants are optimized jointly with a downstream classifier via backpropagation. Comprehensive evaluations across three benchmark HS datasets demonstrate that the higher level HMD layers achieve superior classification accuracy compared to classical learnable tensor baselines, including Tucker, Canonical Polyadic, and Tensor Train decompositions. Furthermore, HMD-1 and HMD-2 achieve a generalization capacity and training stability comparable to standard 2D and 3D-CNNs while requiring significantly fewer feature extractor parameters. These results demonstrate that the HMD framework provides a structurally robust substitute for traditional convolution in multidimensional HS image classification, offering high parameter efficiency and stability throughout the optimization process.

</details>


### [142] [SCOUT: Semantic Concept Discovery for Open-Vocabulary Editing of face Recognition Templates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16251)
*Leon Todorov,Peter Rot,Peter Peer,Vitomir Štruc,Klemen Grm*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCOUT introduces an end-to-end framework to discover and edit semantic concepts directly in face recognition templates, enabling open-vocabulary editing with stable, identity-preserving manipulation across CNN/ViT/Swin backbones, without re-encoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap in template-space interpretability and editing for face recognition by enabling scalable, semantic, open-vocabulary edits beyond manual neuron inspection or fixed attribute labels.

Method: SCOUT learns sparse template representations, derives semantic hypotheses for latent features from natural-language descriptions, validates feature stability, and provides controllable semantic directions for direct template editing. The edits are supported by independent inversion models for visualization, enabling end-to-end interpretability without re-encode pipelines across CNN, ViT, and Swin backbones.

Result: SCOUT discovers interpretable concepts beyond standard attribute labels and enables controllable, identity-aware template manipulation with negligible impact on identity matching. Edited templates can be decoded by separate inversion models for visualization and evaluation, demonstrated across CNN, ViT, and Swin architectures.

Conclusion: SCOUT offers a scalable, open-vocabulary approach to semantic editing of face recognition templates directly in template space, with stable, interpretable directions and inversion-based visualization, generalizing across multiple backbone architectures.

Abstract: Face recognition templates are compact identity representations, yet they also encode rich semantic information about facial appearance. Prior work has shown that templates can be inverted to images or indirectly manipulated through image-editing pipelines, but direct semantic editing in template space remains largely unexplored. Existing interpretability methods for face recognition often rely on manual neuron inspection or predefined attribute labels, limiting scalability and semantic flexibility. To address this gap, we propose SCOUT (Semantic Concept Discovery for Open-VocabUlary Editing of Face Recognition Templates), an end-to-end framework for discovering and directly manipulating semantic concepts in face recognition templates using mechanistic interpretability. SCOUT learns sparse template representations, generates semantic hypotheses for latent features from natural-language descriptions, and validates their stability. The resulting features act as controllable semantic directions for direct editing, avoiding costly edit--re-encode pipelines. Experiments with face recognition models using CNN, ViT, and Swin backbones show that SCOUT discovers interpretable concepts beyond standard attribute labels and enables controllable, identity-aware template manipulation with negligible impact on identity matching. We further show that edited templates can subsequently be decoded with independent inversion models for visualization and evaluation.

</details>


### [143] [Defake-o3: From Speculative Rationales to Verifiable Evidence for Explainable AIGI Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16259)
*Bowen Deng,Jiahui Zhan,Yikun Ji,Haozhen Yan,Jianfu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Defake-o3 is an explainable AIGI detector that combines interactive visual search with an Evidence Verifier to provide grounded, verifiable explanations. It introduces GroundFake for grounded detection and FakeFrontier for out-of-distribution evaluation, achieving stronger detection and explanation quality than prior MLLM-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The surge of AI-generated images demands detectors that are not only accurate but also explainable and reliable. Existing MLLM-based detectors often produce speculative, ungrounded rationales and may miss subtle artifacts from new generators. There is a need for verifiable, localized evidence and robust evaluation resources.

Method: Defake-o3 uses iterative visual inspection of suspicious regions, guided by an Evidence Verifier trained on human-grounded annotations. Reinforcement learning rewards favor grounded evidence and penalize baseless claims. GroundFake provides localized bounding-box evidence with visual grounding, artifact-specific annotations, corrected reasoning trajectories, and supervision for valid/invalid evidence. FakeFrontier offers an out-of-distribution benchmark built from real images and outputs of 10 recent generators, plus an MLLM-based protocol to assess evidence quality and persuasiveness.

Result: Defake-o3 improves both detection accuracy and explanation quality, yielding more localized, verifiable, and persuasive evidence. GroundFake and FakeFrontier, along with additional OOD benchmarks, demonstrate robustness to generator variety and the effectiveness of verifier-guided evidence alignment.

Conclusion: Integrating interactive evidence inspection with a trained Evidence Verifier yields grounded, verifiable explanations for AIGI detection. The associated GroundFake dataset and FakeFrontier benchmark provide valuable resources for evaluating and advancing explainable detection in dynamic generative settings.

Abstract: The rapid progress of image generation models calls for AI-generated image (AIGI) detectors that are not only accurate but also explainable and reliable. While MLLM-based detectors can provide natural language explanations, existing methods often generate speculative rationales: they rely on vague or hallucinated artifacts, miss subtle localized flaws from the latest generators, and fail to provide evidence that can be visually verified. We present Defake-o3, an explainable AIGI detector that moves from speculative rationales to verifiable evidence. It combines interactive visual search with verifier-guided evidence alignment: the model iteratively zooms into suspicious regions to inspect fine-grained details, while an Evidence Verifier, trained from human verification annotations, provides reinforcement learning rewards that favor grounded evidence and penalize baseless claims. To support this objective, we construct GroundFake, a dataset designed for grounded explainable detection, with localized bounding-box evidence, human verification based on visual grounding and artifact specificity, corrected reasoning trajectories, and valid/invalid evidence supervision. We further introduce FakeFrontier, an out-of-distribution benchmark built from real images and outputs of 10 recent generators, together with an MLLM-based protocol for evaluating evidence quality and persuasiveness. Experiments on GroundFake, FakeFrontier, and additional out-of-distribution benchmarks show that Defake-o3 improves both detection accuracy and explanation quality, producing more localized, verifiable, and persuasive evidence.

</details>


### [144] [Seeing Before Answering: Training-Free Visual Layer Profiling for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16263)
*Ruchen Liu,Yi Yang,Yiming Xu,Michael Ying Yang,Monika Sester,Bodo Rosenhahn*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Layer usefulness in LLaVA-style VLMs is not fixed; a data-free predictor based on representation geometry (Visual Dataset Entropy) can identify promising layers, reducing the need for exhaustive search; Gromov-Wasserstein distance is informative only as a diagnostic after projection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The common practice of routing visual tokens through a fixed late layer is fragile and task/backbone-dependent; an efficient, data-free method to predict which layer will best align vision and language could save compute and improve performance.

Method: Evaluate two VLMs across seven image/video benchmarks; perform exhaustive layer-wise inference to establish oracle best layers. Introduce Visual Dataset Entropy (VDE) computed on sample-level visual embeddings and Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance as an alignment signal. Profile both pre-projector (frozen vision tower) and post-projector (trained multimodal projector) representations. Use 100 unlabeled task samples to compute VDE and GW.

Result: Exhaustive search is expensive; the default layer is sub-optimal in 13 of 14 model-task pairs. Pre-projector VDE tracks layer-wise accuracy and, for SigLIP-based LLaVA-Video, the top-ranked layers cover the oracle best; for CLIP-based Video-LLaVA, VDE provides region-level guidance. GW does not transfer pre-projector and flattens post-projector, serving better as an alignment diagnostic than a selector. Overall, VDE offers a training-free policy that narrows candidate layers for limited downstream verification while GW is more diagnostic after projection.

Conclusion: Representation-geometry-based signals (VDE) can forecast layer usefulness in LLaVA-style VLMs without labeled data, enabling efficient layer selection and reducing the need for exhaustive search. GW remains useful mainly as an alignment diagnostic post-projection. Practically, use VDE pre-projector to shortlist a handful of candidate layers and verify with minimal downstream checks.

Abstract: LLaVA-style Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pass visual tokens from a fixed late layer of the vision backbone, typically the penultimate one, to the language model. We first show that this hidden convention is fragile: across 2 VLMs and 7 image and video benchmarks, the default layer is sub-optimal in 13 of 14 model-task pairs, and the best layer shifts with both task and visual backbone. Finding that layer by exhaustive layer-wise inference is prohibitively expensive, and no better fixed default exists. We therefore ask whether layer usefulness can instead be predicted from representation geometry. We study matrix-based entropy, introduced for unimodal layer analysis, which we compute over sample-level visual embeddings as Visual Dataset Entropy (VDE); and Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance, introduced for encoder-level VLM model selection, which we repurpose as a layer-wise visual--language alignment signal. Transferring these to LLaVA-based models is not obvious a priori: the vision tower is frozen while the multimodal projector is trained, so we profile both sides of the projector. We find that VDE transfers, and GW does not. Computed from 100 unlabeled task samples without downstream inference, pre-projector VDE tracks layer-wise accuracy and its top-ranked layers cover the oracle best layer on every task for the SigLIP-based LLaVA-Video, while giving region-level guidance for the CLIP-based Video-LLaVA. Post-projector profiles show that the projector reshapes visual geometry but does not erase the performance-relevant trend, leaving $\mathrm{VDE}_{\mathrm{pre}}$ the stronger signal. GW instead flattens after projection and is best read as an alignment diagnostic rather than a selector. VDE thus offers an interpretable, training-free policy that narrows the visual-layer search to a handful of candidates for limited downstream verification.

</details>


### [145] [CoM$^3$eT: A foundation model for medical image analysis through federated, multidimensional context integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16268)
*J. Raphael Schäfer,Kai Geissler,Till Nicke,Chiara Tappermann,Karoline Heber,Eike Petersen,Habib Mergan,Lars Ole Schwen,Nick Weiss,Annika Gerken,Jan Hendrik Moltz,Tom Bisson,Isil Dogan O,Tim-Rasmus Kiehl,Norman Zerbe,Sefer Elezkurtaj,Robin S. Mayer,Nadine Flinner,Peter Wild,Isabel Dahm,Felix Peisen,Heinrich von Busch,Robert Grimm,Sebastian Arndt,Lisa Siegler,Matthias Stefan May,Antje Prasse,Natalia Artysh,Fabian Kiessling,Johannes Lotz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified, attention-based medical foundation model (CoM^3eT) that handles pathology and radiology, sparse/dense outputs, and 2D/3D inputs; achieves strong performance with <2.5% trainable parameters and enables federated, hardware-light deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical foundation models are often confined to a single specialty and a single output type, hindering cross-modality generalization. There is a need for a unified, data-efficient foundation model that spans modalities, task types (sparse/dense), and input dimensionalities, while supporting federated learning across hospitals.

Method: Introduce CoM^3eT, a multidimensional attention-based transformer that learns co-representations across modalities (pathology and radiology), output types (sparse/dense, report generation), and input dimensions (2D and higher-D). It uses multitask training across diverse datasets (five tomographic, four whole-specimen, and three 2D) and enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning (}<2.5% of parameters). Evaluations include open-competition performance and federated-learning scenarios with consumer hardware.

Result: Outperformed other medical foundation models across a broad suite of datasets, including sparse/dense predictions and report generation. Achieved performance comparable to full fine-tuning with less than 2.5% trainable parameters. In federated hospital settings, matched pooled-data training performance over internet connections on consumer-grade hardware.

Conclusion: CoM^3eT provides a unified, scalable, and data-efficient medical foundation model that bridges specialties and output types, enabling broader research access and practical deployment in federated, resource-constrained environments.

Abstract: Medical foundation models improve generalization when training AI models with limited labeled data, but remain confined to a single specialty, such as pathology or radiology, and to either sparse or dense outputs, such as classification or segmentation. Here, we present CoM$^3$eT (Co-representation Multidimensional Multitask Medical Transformer), a medical vision foundation model that unifies pathology and radiology, sparse and dense predictions, and two- and higher-dimensional inputs by modeling multidimensional context with attention. CoM$^3$eT outperformed other medical foundation models in an open competition spanning five tomographic, four whole-specimen, and three two-dimensional datasets, covering sparse and dense prediction tasks as well as report generation. When adapted across diverse clinical applications, training fewer than 2.5% of parameters achieved performance comparable to full fine-tuning, enabling research without access to high-performance GPU clusters. Applied to federated learning across hospitals, this approach achieved performance comparable to pooled-data training over internet connections and with consumer-grade hardware.

</details>


### [146] [TransAnyText: Translating Arbitrary Text in E-commerce Images via Structured Visual Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16284)
*Xiaoan Liu,Lichen Ma,Zipeng Guo,Yu He,Xiaoyan Su,Shaojie Guo,Hao Yang,Jingling Fu,Xiaolong Fu,Zhen Chen,Yu Guo,Fei Wang,Xinyi Liu,Yongjun Zhang,Ke Zhang,Junshi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TransAnyText introduces a structured visual-code framework that translates image text by generating renderable HTML patches, enabling controllable, editable outputs for cross-border e-commerce imagery; it uses a two-stage separation of semantic generation (VLM) and pixel rendering (diffusion), plus a three-stage post-training pipeline and new dataset/benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-border e-commerce requires accurate multilingual translations while preserving product visual identity and enabling easy edits; existing cascaded or end-to-end methods struggle to simultaneously satisfy translation quality, visual fidelity, and editability.

Method: Decouples semantic generation from pixel rendering. A vision-language model handles visual understanding, cross-lingual translation, and structured visual generation; a diffusion model handles background inpainting and pixel-level refinement; deterministic HTML patch rendering synthesizes the final image. A three-stage post-training pipeline—supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for image-to-code mapping, privilege-gap weighted self-distillation (PWSD) for style/layout token learning, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for task-level optimization. Introduces TransAnyDataset and TransAnyBench for multilingual e-commerce image translation datasets and benchmarks.

Result: Extensive experiments show competitive performance against cascaded pipelines, open-source end-to-end models, and closed-source image editing systems; demonstrates effective, controllable, and editable translation of e-commerce images.

Conclusion: The work substantiates a viable, modular approach to cross-border e-commerce image translation that separates semantic reasoning from pixel rendering, enabling controllable outputs and a dedicated multilingual dataset/benchmark for progress in this domain.

Abstract: Cross-border e-commerce image translation is essential for global retail, where product images, banners, and detail pages need to be produced in different languages. Existing methods struggle to achieve accurate translation, faithful visual identity preservation, and easy-to-edit outputs, simultaneously. To address these challenges, we introduce TransAnyText, a structured visual code framework that reformulates image text translation as generating renderable HTML patches from source images and target languages. Our framework decouples semantic generation from pixel rendering: a vision-language model (VLM) handles visual understanding, cross-lingual translation, and structured visual generation, while a diffusion model performs background inpainting and pixel-level refinement, followed by deterministic rendering to synthesize the final image. Based on this formulation, we develop a three-stage post-training framework, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) establishes the image-to-code mapping, privilege-gap weighted self-distillation (PWSD) improves the learning of style and layout tokens, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) further optimizes task-level performance. We further introduce TransAnyDataset and TransAnyBench, a multilingual dataset and benchmark for e-commerce image translation. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against cascaded pipelines, open-source end-to-end models, and closed-source image editing systems, providing an effective, controllable, and editable solution for cross-border e-commerce image translation.

</details>


### [147] [Audio-Visual Segmentation via Depth-Guided Collaborative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16285)
*Zhaojin Fu,Yuyang Hong,Qi Yang,Zili Wang,Kun Ding,Shiming Xiang,Bin Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DGCM-AVS introduces depth-aware tri-modal AVS with a Depth-Aware Dynamic Modulator and Depth-Guided Progressive Fusion to improve cross-modal alignment and object separation, achieving notable gains on AVSS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AVS models largely ignore geometric cues like depth, limiting cross-modal alignment and robustness when localizing sounding objects; integrating depth aligns perceptual spatial structure with audio-visual evidence.

Method: Proposes a tri-modal framework DGCM-AVS with (1) Depth-Aware Dynamic Modulator to separate adjacent objects while maintaining intra-object consistency, and (2) Depth-Guided Progressive Fusion that uses depth as an intermediate bridge to progressively align audio with visual features, enabling joint audio-visual-depth modeling.

Result: Compared to state-of-the-art, achieves relative improvements of 10.2% in M_J and 8.7% in M_F on the AVSS dataset, demonstrating depth as a promising modality for AVS.

Conclusion: Depth provides a valuable spatial structure cue for AVS; the proposed depth-informed tri-modal architecture advances cross-modal localization and invites further exploration of depth in multimodal segmentation.
