Abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) is a fundamental task in multimodal perception that performs pixel-level segmentation of sounding objects in videos by leveraging both visual and audio cues. It has broad applications in video understanding, human-computer interaction, and autonomous driving. However, most existing AVS methods do not explicitly model geometric cues such as relative distance and occlusion, thereby limiting the robustness of cross-modal alignment. In human perception, spatial structure is naturally integrated with audio-visual evidence to accurately localize sounding objects. Motivated by this, we incorporate estimated depth as a spatial structural cue for AVS and propose DGCM-AVS, a tri-modal framework that jointly models audio, visual, and depth information. Specifically, we design a Depth-Aware Dynamic Modulator to improve the separation of adjacent objects while preserving intra-object feature consistency. Furthermore, we propose Depth-Guided Progressive Fusion, which uses depth as an intermediate bridge to progressively align audio cues with visual features. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, DGCM-AVS achieves relative improvements of 10.2 percent in M_J and 8.7 percent in M_F on the AVSS dataset. We believe our study highlights depth as a promising yet underexplored modality for AVS and may encourage further research in this direction.

</details>


### [148] [PosterText: Towards Unified Visual Text Generation and Editing for E-commerce Poster](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16289)
*Xiaoan Liu,Lichen Ma,Zipeng Guo,Yu He,Xiaoyan Su,Shaojie Guo,Jingling Fu,Xiaolong Fu,Hao Yang,Tongxuan Liu,Yu Guo,Fei Wang,Xinyi Liu,Yongjun Zhang,Junshi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified Text Patch Generation and Editing framework (PosterText) for e-commerce posters that treats text patches as atomic units and supports generation, patch addition/deletion/modification, with optional style control, trained via a four-stage curriculum and evaluated on a patch-level dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the gap between end-to-end poster generation and multi-stage editing pipelines, enabling flexible, precise editing of existing posters while preserving global coherence and enabling reference-guided styling.

Method: Formulates a Text Patch Generation and Editing task with four atomic operations on text patches (generate, add, delete, modify). Proposes PosterText, a unified model trained via a four-stage curriculum: (1) text rendering pretraining, (2) instruction-following training, (3) reinforcement learning for preference alignment, (4) spatial guidance self-distillation for execution refinement. Builds a large-scale patch-level dataset and a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation.

Result: Empirical results show PosterText achieves competitive performance relative to existing generation and editing methods, validating the effectiveness of the unified framework.

Conclusion: A unified, patch-based approach to e-commerce poster generation and editing is viable and effective, with a contributing dataset and benchmark to support evaluation and further research.

Abstract: Automated e-commerce poster design requires both high-quality poster generation and flexible editing of existing designs. However, most existing methods either target end-to-end poster generation or follow multi-stage design pipelines, with limited capability for flexible and precise editing of existing posters. To enable unified generation and editing of e-commerce posters, we introduce Text Patch Generation and Editing, a unified task formulation that treats text patches as atomic units and covers four operations: poster generation, patch addition, patch deletion, and patch modification, with optional reference-guided style control. Based on this, we propose PosterText, a unified model trained with a four-stage curriculum, including text rendering pretraining, instruction-following training, reinforcement learning for preference alignment, and spatial guidance self-distillation for execution refinement. We further construct a large-scale dataset with patch-level annotations and a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PosterText achieves competitive performance against existing generation and editing approaches, validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [149] [Cross-View Urban Sensing: Mapping Subjective Streetscape Perception via AlphaEarth Embeddings and Urban Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16310)
*Peilin Li,Pengfei Chen,Jingyu Wang,Zhifeng Yang,Tiansheng Chen,Mengjie Gong,Xiao Cheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CVLNet uses cross-view learning to predict street-level perception from AlphaEarth embeddings and urban context, without SVI at inference. It achieves high accuracy (Adjusted R^2 ~0.76) across four SE Asian cities, enabling citywide perception maps and inequality analysis via WorldPop and Deficit Palma Ratio; demonstrates remote sensing as scalable alternative to SVI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome uneven SVI coverage and updates; enable scalable mapping of perceptual urban qualities; quantify exposure inequality.

Method: Cross-view Learning Network with per-task adaptive gating; uses AlphaEarth embeddings and multi-source urban contextual data; trained with labels from pretrained SVI-Percept; evaluates on four cities; ablation studies; produces citywide maps; integrates with WorldPop; uses Deficit Palma Ratio for inequality.

Result: Median road-segment Adjusted R^2 = 0.76; 5.9–11.3% improvement over baselines across five perceptual dimensions; AlphaEarth + context features are complementary; extended coverage from 13–31% to full road network; citywide maps produced; inequality quantified.

Conclusion: Remote sensing-based approach can substitute SVI at scale for streetscape perception mapping and urban inequality assessment; enables comprehensive, population-aware planning insights.

Abstract: Residents' perception of the urban streetscape is an important factor in public health, active mobility, and social wellbeing. Street view imagery (SVI) has emerged as a widely used data source for assessing these perceptual qualities, yet its uneven coverage and irregular updating limit large-scale measurement. Here, we present CVLNet, a Cross-View Learning Network that predicts street-level perception from AlphaEarth embeddings and multi-source urban contextual data without requiring SVI at inference. CVLNet applies per-task adaptive gating to jointly model five perceptual dimensions, using labels from the pretrained SVI-Percept model as ground truth. The proposed method is evaluated across four Southeast Asian cities: Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, and Manila. CVLNet achieves a median road-segment-level Adjusted $R^{2}$ of 0.76 and consistently outperforms the baseline models, with gains ranging from 5.9--11.3% across the five perceptual dimensions. Ablation experiments show that AlphaEarth features and urban contextual features contribute complementary information. We further produce citywide road-level streetscape perception maps for five subjective perceptual dimensions across all four cities, extending perception estimation from the 13--31% of the road network directly covered by available SVI to the complete road network of each city. Integrating these maps with WorldPop gridded population data, we quantify exposure inequality across population-density, demographic, and land-use groups using the Deficit Palma Ratio. These results demonstrate that remote sensing can serve as a scalable alternative to SVI for citywide streetscape perception mapping, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of urban environmental inequality.

</details>


### [150] [Deep Thought Alignment: Trajectory-Level Latent Distillation for Video Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16316)
*Ao Shen,Yongheng Zhang,Yinghui Li,Manning Wang,Di Yin,Xing Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Latent-OPD augments on-policy distillation with latent trajectory-level supervision and a progressive teacher-lookahead, yielding consistent gains in video reasoning, especially with fewer frames or longer videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce the computational burden of video reasoning in Large Multimodal Models by transferring reasoning capabilities to smaller models, and to tighten supervision beyond output-token predictions by constraining latent representations that accumulate evidence.

Method: Augment On-Policy Distillation (OPD) with trajectory-level latent distillation focused on the end-of-trajectory hidden state, and introduce a progressive teacher-lookahead strategy that aligns middle-to-late student layers with progressively deeper teacher layers.

Result: Latent-OPD consistently outperforms output-only OPD across six video reasoning benchmarks, with more pronounced gains in scenarios with limited frames, long videos, or tasks requiring complex evidence aggregation.

Conclusion: Latent-OPD is an effective framework for frame-efficient video reasoning, improving latent supervision and judicious teacher-student alignment to enhance performance on video reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) for video reasoning have long been hindered by the high computational cost of processing vast amounts of visual information. This dilemma motivates the transfer of the reasoning capabilities of large models to smaller, more efficient ones. On-Policy Distillation (OPD) offers a promising solution by matching output-token distributions along student-generated trajectories. However, video reasoning often depends on evidence accumulated across multiple frames. In this context, output-level supervision only captures information expressed through token predictions and does not directly constrain the latent representations formed during reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-OPD, which augments OPD with trajectory-level latent distillation. Specifically, our method focuses on the position at the end of each trajectory, where hidden states effectively summarize the accumulated visual evidence and reasoning context. Furthermore, we introduce a progressive teacher-lookahead strategy, which aligns middle-to-late student layers with increasingly deeper teacher layers. Experiments on six video reasoning benchmarks show that Latent-OPD consistently outperforms output-only OPD. Notably, the improvements are particularly pronounced in scenarios with limited frames, long videos, or tasks requiring complex evidence aggregation. These results establish Latent-OPD as a highly effective approach to frame-efficient video reasoning.

</details>


### [151] [LaGSplat: Inferring Physics-Governed Interactive Simulation from Monocular Video Using Latent Lagrangian Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16324)
*Louen Pottier*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LaGSplat is a latent-Lagrangian, Gaussian Splatting framework that learns physics-governed dynamics from monocular video and allows interactive forces (unseen during training) to drive the reconstructed object in real time in 2D/3D.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To infer interactive, physically plausible dynamics from limited visual data without measured forces, enabling controllable manipulation of deformable or rigid objects from monocular videos.

Method: Introduce a low-dimensional latent state q that serves as generalized coordinates of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and as the conditioning input to a Gaussian Splatting decoder with moving primitives μ_i(q). External forces f map to latent generalized forces via J(q)^T f, enabling dynamics in the latent space that project to the observed object. Training uses monocular video plus sensor data; inference supports arbitrary forces and real-time rendering; dynamics are governed by a dissipative Euler-Lagrange equation over a few coordinates.

Result: Validated on tasks increasing in difficulty from rigid to deformable, and from autonomous to force-driven real systems; demonstrated interactive use where forces of any magnitude/direction can be applied and the response rendered in real time in 2D/3D; the approach provides bounded, plausible responses to unseen forces, avoiding divergence typical of unconstrained predictors.

Conclusion: A low-dimensional latent Lagrangian with Gaussian Splatting enables physically plausible, interactive manipulation from monocular video, bridging dynamics and neural rendering. This framework trades generality for stability and realism under unseen forces, outperforming purely pixel-space predictors by enabling explicit force-to-dynamics mapping.

Abstract: We present LaGSplat (Latent Lagrangian Gaussian Splatting), a framework that infers interactive, physics-governed dynamics from one or a few monocular videos. At inference it lets a user push on the filmed object, rigid or deformable, with an external force that was never measured, annotated, or seen during training. This is possible because a low-dimensional latent state $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ plays two roles at once: it is the generalised coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder. The inductive bias of this decoder, whose primitives are explicit points $μ_i(\mathbf{q})$ that move with the object, is what lets a force $f$ applied in the image pull back into a latent generalised force $J(\mathbf{q})^\top f$ and enter the equations of motion, which pixel-space (CNN) or neural-field (NeRF) decoders cannot do. We validate LaGSplat on test cases of increasing difficulty, from rigid to deformable and from autonomous to forced real systems, combining monocular video and sensor measurements. We further demonstrate interactive use: forces of arbitrary magnitude and direction can be applied to the reconstructed object at any time, its response rendered in real time, in 2D or 3D. Assuming a dissipative Euler-Lagrange equation over a few generalised coordinates trades generality for a bounded, plausible response to unseen forces, where an unconstrained predictor diverges.

</details>


### [152] [GRNEdit: Efficient General Video Editing from a New Binary-Evidence Perspective in Generative Refinement Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16328)
*Feng Xie,Jiagao Hu,Fuhao Li,Zepeng Wang,Yuxuan Chen,Dahua Gao,Fei Wang,Daiguo Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GRNEdit is a two-stage, lightweight framework for instruction-based video editing that encodes editing intent as local retain-or-flip decisions over binary bits, achieving strong performance with minimal conditioning parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To model editing intent efficiently without heavy conditioning (e.g., large branches or source concatenation) by representing semantics in a compact bitwise latent space and leveraging a two-stage refinement process.

Method: Stage I encodes discrete source codes into continuous evidence signals and uses a null-prompt identity pathway to emphasize content preservation; Stage II compares edited states to source-preserving references to revise unresolved target-bit decisions, all within a GRN backbone trained on ~0.6M pairs with <3% conditioning parameters.

Result: GRNEdit-2B and GRNEdit-8B achieve OpenVE-Bench scores of 4.03 and 4.18, with the 2B model outperforming many 14B open-source editors and the 8B model on par with leading editors, despite compact conditioning.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that editing semantics can be effectively modeled as local bitwise decisions guided by coordinate-wise evidence, yielding strong performance with lightweight conditioning and a small training set; further work could explore generalization and robustness across diverse editing tasks.

Abstract: Instruction-based general video editing seeks to unify diverse editing operations within a single, intuitive interface. Existing approaches often rely on resource-intensive conditioning, using either heavyweight branches or costly source concatenation. Is there any efficient way to model editing intent? Thus, we introduce GRNEdit, a lightweight two-stage framework. GRN inspires our approach by encoding visual semantics through combinations of bits. Through task-specific fine-tuning, we take this representation further and recast editing semantics as local retain-or-flip decisions over individual bits. Source information is consequently modeled as coordinate-wise evidence supporting the observed binary states, while the GRN backbone remains responsible for resolving their global composition into coherent generative semantics. In Stage I, a compact encoder translates discrete source codes into continuous evidence signals, which GRN assimilates throughout binary refinement. Inspired by null-prompt training for classifier-free guidance, we further assign the null condition an editing-specific meaning: an empty instruction denotes no edit and is supervised through source reconstruction. This identity pathway not only implicitly strengthens evidence utilization and content preservation in Stage I, but also produces a source-preserving state in the same representation space as the edited state. Stage II can therefore directly compare each edited state with its source-preserving counterpart and use their discrepancy to revise unresolved target-bit decisions. Trained on only 0.6M pairs with less than 3\% conditioning parameters, GRNEdit-2B and GRNEdit-8B achieve scores of 4.03 and 4.18 on OpenVE-Bench. The 2B model outperforms multiple 14B open-source editors, while the 8B model performs on par with leading open-source editors.

</details>


### [153] [Unlocking Motion in Expressions: Temporal Calibration for Referring Video Object Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16332)
*Yiwen Jiang,Zhengtong Zhu,Ruixin Zhang,Jiaqing Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EMC provides an explicit, expression-driven mechanism to calibrate motion cues in RVOS, via MSP, MIC, and STSC, achieving improved robustness across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of explicit modeling of how motion semantics in language expressions influence the use of motion information for temporal reasoning in RVOS.

Method: Introduce MSP to extract motion-control signals from expressions, STSC to construct temporal stages aligned with the expression, and MIC to calibrate motion influence during temporal decision making within a unified cross-modal framework.

Result: Empirical superiority on six standard RVOS benchmarks (Ref-YouTubeVOS, Ref-DAVIS17, MeViS, A2D-Sentences, JHMDB-Sentences).

Conclusion: Explicitly unlocking motion semantics via EMC improves adaptability to semantic requirements and demonstrates strong performance with a portable code release.

Abstract: Referring Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to segment referred objects at the pixel level in video sequences based on natural language descriptions. Existing methods typically introduce motion information within a unified cross-modal temporal modeling framework, where language cues are used for target localization and segmentation. However, the dependency of expressions on motion semantics is not explicitly modeled, making it difficult to adaptively adjust the use of motion information according to different semantic requirements. To address these issues, we propose an Expression-driven Motion Calibration (EMC) framework for RVOS that explicitly unlocks and leverages the motion semantics within expressions. The proposed method extracts interpretable motion control signals from expressions via a Motion Signal Processing (MSP) module, and employs a Motion Influence Calibration (MIC) module to adjust the contribution of motion cues during temporal decision making. In addition, a Semantic Temporal Stage Construction (STSC) module is introduced to build expression-relevant temporal stages, providing a compact temporal candidate space for motion calibration. Through extensive evaluation on six standard benchmarks, including Ref-YouTubeVOS, Ref-DAVIS17, MeViS (valid/valid$^u$), A2D-Sentences, and JHMDB-Sentences, the superiority of our method is validated. We will release the code on https://github.com/Jeven7/EMC.

</details>


### [154] [SIGMA-Lane: Scale-pyramId Gated MAmba for Temporally Consistent Video Lane Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16338)
*Tiancheng Zhang,Mengmeng Wang,Yan Gao,Xiangjie Kong,Guojiang Shen,Jiaxin Du*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SIGMA-Lane introduces occlusion-aware state contamination handling in SSM-based temporal lane detection via dual gating on the write and fusion paths, plus Structural Spatial Retrieval (SSR), to improve temporal stability under heavy occlusion while maintaining competitive F1 and mIoU on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video lane detection suffers from occlusion where temporal cues become unreliable. Existing occlusion-aware refinements supply obstacle masks but do not directly protect the state-update path, causing persistent errors as occlusions propagate through time.

Method: Model the problem as state-space model (SSM) temporal propagation. Add occlusion-aware gates on the SSM write and residual-fusion paths to regulate entry of current observations into memory and their fusion after propagation. After coordinate-consistent affine alignment, combine two paths: (1) SSM-consistent dual-gating for temporal filtering and (2) Structural Spatial Retrieval (SSR) to recover missing lane structure from aligned historical priors.

Result: Empirical evaluation on VIL-100 and OpenLane-V shows improved temporal stability under heavy occlusion, with competitive F1 and mIoU scores relative to baselines.

Conclusion: Treat occlusion-induced failures as state contamination in SSM-based temporal models. The dual-gating mechanism plus SSR provides robust temporal memory and effective structure recovery, yielding more stable lane predictions under occlusion without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Video lane detection requires predictions that remain stable across frames, yet severe vehicle occlusions can break temporal cues. In streaming recurrent models, corrupted observations may enter the hidden state and produce errors that persist into later frames. Existing occlusion-aware refinements usually provide obstacle masks as auxiliary inputs, so the state-update path is only indirectly protected. We propose SIGMA-Lane, which treats this failure mode as state contamination in State Space Model (SSM)-based temporal modeling. SIGMA-Lane places occlusion-aware gates on the SSM write and residual-fusion paths, controlling how current observations enter temporal memory and are fused back after temporal propagation. After coordinate-consistent affine alignment, the model combines two complementary paths: SSM-consistent dual-gating for temporal filtering and Structural Spatial Retrieval (SSR) for recovering missing lane structure from aligned historical priors. Experiments on VIL-100 and OpenLane-V show improved temporal stability under heavy occlusion, with competitive F1 and mIoU scores.

</details>


### [155] [Depth-Dominant Skeleton Detection for Natural Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16367)
*Chengkun Rao,Yixuan Deng,Min Li,Yangjun Ou,Ye Li,Ziwei Luo,Zhaojing Wang,Junwei Tang,Bangchao Wang,Xiaoyun Yan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DDSkel proposes a depth-dominant skeleton detection paradigm with an asymmetric encoder that fuses RGB into depth features; achieves state-of-the-art performance on SymPASCAL with only 36% of the parameters of the prior best method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RGB-only skeleton detection struggles on complex scenes due to color/texture complexity. Depth images provide clearer contours and inter-region spatial relations, suggesting a depth-dominant modality can alleviate detection difficulty.

Method: DDSkel uses an asymmetric encoder design where the depth branch is the main pathway and the RGB branch is lightweight (about 12% of the depth branch parameters). RGB features are fused into depth features, yielding a simple yet effective architecture.

Result: DDSkel outperforms all state-of-the-art approaches on the challenging SymPASCAL dataset, achieving this with 36% of the trainable parameters of the current best method.

Conclusion: A depth-dominant skeleton detection paradigm is viable; leveraging depth as the primary modality with a compact RGB auxiliary branch can achieve superior performance with substantially fewer parameters.

Abstract: To date, all natural scene skeleton detection follows the paradigm of taking RGB images as the sole input; despite notable progress, methods under this paradigm suffer significant performance degradation on complex-content images. We observe that depth images are inherently insensitive to color and texture, and can provide clear regional contours and inter-region spatial relationships, which naturally alleviates the difficulty of skeleton detection in complex scenarios. Motivated by this observation, this paper proposes for the first time a novel skeleton detection paradigm where depth images serve as the dominant modality and RGB images act as the auxiliary, and accordingly presents a model DDSkel (short for Depth-Dominant Skeleton Detection) under this paradigm. DDSkel employs an asymmetric encoder design to fuse RGB information into depth features, with the RGB modality branch having only 12% the parameters of the depth modality branch. DDSkel has a simple structure without intricate designs. Nevertheless, with only 36% of the trainable parameters of the current best method, DDSkel outperforms all state-of-the-art approaches on SymPASCAL, the most challenging dataset with a large volume of complex images.

</details>


### [156] [Joint Flow Matching Enables Continuous Dose-Conditioned Cell Morphing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16424)
*Lea Bogensperger,Manuela Merlo,Martin Baumgartner,Michael Krauthammer,Bernard Ciraulo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Joint flow matching for dose-conditioned single-cell morphing via dual-timestep modeling of cell latents and drug concentration; enables continuous dose control and concentration estimation; shows generalization to unseen doses with competitive per-concentration metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of discrete-dose or distribution-to-distribution perturbation models by enabling explicit, continuous handling of drug concentration and a reversible mapping that supports dose-conditioned morphing.

Method: Dual-timestep joint flow matching that jointly models cell latent representations and drug concentration in an invertible flow framework; produces a monotonic dose-response geometry in latent space; enables concentration estimation from cell morphology and generalizes to unseen doses.

Result: Competitive or improved per-concentration metrics on two compounds compared to representative baselines; additional capabilities (continuous dose control, concentration estimation, dose generalization) unavailable to discrete-class methods.

Conclusion: Joint flow matching provides continuous dose control and concentration-aware perturbation modeling, with monotonic latent dose-response and generalization to unseen doses, enhancing predictive capabilities beyond discrete-dose approaches.

Abstract: Generative modeling has shown increasing promise for predicting cellular perturbation effects under chemical compound treatments. Existing approaches either model perturbation as a distribution-to-distribution mapping without explicit concentration handling, or treat concentration as a discrete class label, precluding continuous dose control. We introduce a joint flow matching approach that simultaneously models cell latents and drug concentration via a dual-timestep formulation, enabling dose-conditioned single-cell morphing through the invertibility of flow matching. The joint formulation induces a monotonic dose-response geometry in latent space and additionally supports concentration estimation from cell morphology. As proof of concept, we further demonstrate generalization to an unseen dose held out during training. Empirically, our method achieves competitive or improved per-concentration metrics on two compounds compared with representative baselines, while enabling capabilities structurally unavailable to discrete-class methods.

</details>


### [157] [Contrastive Energy Fields for Inference-Time Procedure Planning in Instructional Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16457)
*Mohamed Afham,Christoph Reich,Oliver Hahn,Daniel Cremers,Stefan Roth*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CEFITO leverages an action-conditioned representation space and task-constrained optimization to prune irrelevant actions at inference, achieving state-of-the-art in procedure planning on two benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches (feed-forward or diffusion-based) predict action sequences without enforcing task-specific logical constraints, causing plausible-but-irrelevant actions to appear in plans.

Method: Train a predictor to produce an action-conditioned representation; cast planning as a constraint-aware optimization problem over the action space; during inference, omit actions deemed irrelevant by the constraints, yielding a more focused plan.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on two standard procedure planning benchmarks (no numeric values provided in abstract).

Conclusion: Explicitly reasoning over the action space and pruning irrelevant actions at inference enhances planning effectiveness and efficiency compared with prior methods.

Abstract: Procedure planning seeks to estimate a sequence of actions to transition from an observed initial state to a given goal state. Current procedure planning approaches directly predict action sequences from latent representations using feed-forward neural networks or diffusion-based inference. These paradigms treat every action as plausible, lacking the ability to enforce task-specific logical constraints that render certain actions irrelevant or not plausible. We propose CEFITO, a procedure planning approach that learns a predictor to express an action-conditioned representation space. Based on this representation space, we formulate procedure planning as a task-constrained optimization problem. Unlike prior methods, CEFITO explicitly reasons over the action space by omitting irrelevant actions during inference-time planning. This reformulation enables effective procedure planning and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on two established procedure planning benchmarks.

</details>


### [158] [Shared-Structure 4D Spectral Gaussian Representation for Sparse-View Spectral CT Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16463)
*Jiancheng Fang,Shaoyu Wang,Wenjun Xia,Yang Chen,Qiegen Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 4D-SG with shared Gaussian geometry and GSC-Net improves sparse-view spectral CT reconstruction, outperforming a Gaussian baseline across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address angular undersampling and spectral coupling in sparse-view spectral CT by learning a factorized, continuous 4D representation that separates shared spatial structure from spectral variation.

Method: Propose SharedStructure 4D-Spectral Gaussian Representation (4D-SG) that learns shared Gaussian geometry from full-spectrum structural projections and employs Gaussian-wise Spectral Density Curve Network (GSC-Net) to predict Gaussian raw density transformations. This factorization avoids independent channel geometry optimization and yields a continuous 4D representation from discrete spectral measurements for unobserved channels.

Result: Evaluated on six datasets (synthesized, simulated projection, and real projection) with 50 views, achieving best average performance. Compared with the strongest Gaussian baseline: PSNR 36.61 dB vs 35.56 dB; SSIM 0.914 vs 0.909; LPIPS 0.194 vs 0.208.

Conclusion: The 4D-SG approach effectively handles sparse-view spectral CT, offering improved reconstruction quality over a Gaussian baseline.

Abstract: Sparse-view spectral computed tomography (CT) reconstructs energy-resolved attenuation volumes from limited projection views, requiring simultaneous handling of angular undersampling and spectral coupling. We propose a SharedStructure 4D Spectral Gaussian Representation (4D-SG) that learns shared Gaussian geometry from full spectrum structural projections and uses a Gaussian-wise Spectral Density Curve Network (GSC-Net) to predict Gaussian raw density transformations. This factorization separates shared spatial structure from spectral attenuation variation, avoids independent channel geometry optimization, and establishes a continuous 4D-SG representation from discrete spectral measurements for unobserved spectral channel queries. Experiments on six synthesized, simulated projection, and real projection datasets with 50 views demonstrate the best average performance. Compared with the strongest Gaussian baseline, 4D-SG improves PSNR from 35.56 dB to 36.61 dB, increases SSIM from 0.909 to 0.914, and reduces LPIPS from 0.208 to 0.194, demonstrating its effectiveness for sparse-view spectral CT reconstruction.

</details>


### [159] [Sterilizable Scene Graph Generation for Operating Rooms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16469)
*Nick Lemke,Ssharvien Kumar Sivakumar,Antoine P. Sanner,John Kalkhof,Henry John Krumb,Ghazal Ghazaei,Anirban Mukhopadhyay*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SG-NCA: a lightweight Neural Cellular Automata–based scene graph generation framework for surgical videos; achieves comparable performance to baselines with 55x fewer parameters and runs on fanless edge devices, enabling privacy-preserving, OR-ready intraoperative scene understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a critical need for efficient, privacy-preserving, low-latency scene understanding in the operating room. Classic scene graph generation models are large and hardware-hungry, conflicting with hygiene, latency, and data privacy constraints.

Method: Introduces SG-NCA, the first scene graph generation method built on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA). It uses NCA-based multiclass segmentation for object detection and feature extraction, paired with a lightweight relation predictor to form graphs. The approach emphasizes deployment on fanless devices and dental (surgical) settings.

Result: Empirical evaluation on cataract and cholecystectomy videos shows performance comparable to established baselines while reducing parameters by 55×. Demonstrated deployment on fanless edge devices and a downstream application (surgical video captioning), supporting privacy-preserving, OR-ready understanding of intraoperative scenes.

Conclusion: SG-NCA demonstrates that NCAs can support structured scene representations in surgery, delivering a compact, privacy-preserving SGG framework suitable for OR deployment and downstream tasks like captioning.

Abstract: Scene graph generation from surgical video enables a holistic and structured understanding of surgical scenes by modeling objects and their semantic relationships. Despite recent advances, state-of-the-art approaches rely on large, parameter-heavy deep learning models that are impractical for deployment in the operating room (OR) due to hardware footprint, hygiene constraints, latency, and data privacy concerns. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first scene graph generation method built on NCAs and the first NCA framework capable of learning structured representations. We introduce SG-NCA, a lightweight scene graph generation framework based on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), designed for inference in fanless devices critical for OR hygiene protocols. SG-NCA is the first scene graph generation combining NCA-based multiclass segmentation for efficient object detection and feature extraction with a lightweight relation predictor. We evaluate SG-NCA on videos of cataract surgery and cholecystectomy, demonstrating performance comparable to established baselines while requiring 55x fewer parameters. We showcase deployment on fanless edge devices better suited for the OR and demonstrate downstream applications such as surgical video captioning, highlighting SG-NCA's potential for affordable, privacy-preserving, and OR-ready intraoperative scene understanding.

</details>


### [160] [RISE: Roadside Infrastructure Sequence Understanding across 3D Tracking and Structured Vision-Language Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16480)
*Yanbo Jiang,Haotian Zheng,Jiahao Wang,Hanxiao Ren,Yitao Xu,Yining Xing,Zehong Ke,Hao Cheng,Yiqian Tu,Jinhao Li,Zhiyuan Xuan,Fang Zhang,Jianqiang Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RISE couples calibration-aware, image-only 3D multi-view tracking with a structured vision-language QA pipeline for roadside sequences, achieving non-LiDAR 3D tracks (66.9 MOTA) and a large RISE-VQA dataset (33.9k QA pairs); results show domain-adaptation and temporal context help, but spatial grounding, future localization, and interaction reasoning remain challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve robust 3D tracking in calibrated multi-camera roadside setups without LiDAR and enable grounded vision-language reasoning over driving scenes.

Method: Two components: (1) metric 3D tracking via SAM3 video identities + calibration-guided mask agreement, producing calibration-conditioned 3D tracks without 3D training. (2) structured VLR: a human-reviewed MLLM pipeline to mine clips and an Oracle to produce bbox-grounded QA with full context, preventing future evidence leakage; dataset RISE-VQA; evaluation bench RISE-Bench with intersection-held-out splits and deterministic metrics.

Result: 66.9 MOTA on 20 clips across 6 intersections; RISE-VQA: 33,910 QA pairs, 557 clips, 16 intersections, 61 roadside views; RISE-Bench reveals domain adaptation and temporal context gains, with persistent challenges in spatial grounding, future localization, and interaction reasoning.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of calibration-conditioned multi-view tracking and vision-language reasoning in roadside settings; provides a large, grounded QA dataset; highlights key failure modes and directions for improvement.

Abstract: We present RISE (Roadside Infrastructure Sequence Understanding and Evaluation), a framework spanning metric 3D tracking and structured vision-language reasoning in roadside sequences. For metric tracking, our image-only method combines SAM3 video identities with calibration-guided mask agreement for multi-view identity association, recovering persistent 3D tracks without LiDAR or task-specific 3D training. Its calibration-conditioned geometry allows the procedure to be instantiated at different calibrated multi-camera intersections without layout-specific retraining. On 20 human-reviewed clips from six intersections, the generated tracks achieve 66.9 MOTA within the defined multi-view evaluation scope. For structured vision-language reasoning, a human-reviewed MLLM pipeline mines high-value clips and uses a constrained full-context Oracle to construct bbox-grounded predictive QA without exposing future evidence to evaluated models. The resulting RISE-VQA dataset contains 33,910 QA pairs from 557 clips across 16 intersections and 61 roadside views. Its intersection-held-out RISE-Bench evaluates semantic choices, coordinates, future boxes, and interaction sets with deterministic task-specific metrics. Experiments show consistent benefits from domain adaptation and generally from temporal context, while revealing persistent challenges in spatial grounding, future localization, and interaction reasoning.

</details>


### [161] [Remote-Sensing City Layout Extraction with MLLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16484)
*Zigan Zhou,Kai Li,Yupeng Deng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: End-to-end framework "Code-as-City" converts a single top-down urban scene image into an executable city code and renderable 3D layout via multimodal LLMs, enabling coupled 2D/3D outputs and editable regeneration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of conventional outputs (detection boxes, masks, vectors) that lack object identities, relations, topology, and regeneration rules; provide an executable, editable city layout from images.

Method: An image model generates a five-class semantic layout prior. Three sequential MLLM passes refine roads, land-cover regions/relations, and buildings, guided by the prior. Deterministic normalization converts records into a city graph and a restricted layout program. Executing the program renders a 3D city layout and an orthographic semantic projection; pixel-level comparison with masks validates alignment; named objects/relations/editing operations support synchronized regeneration of both views.

Result: Evaluated on CityLayout-100: 41.1% mean IoU and 48.3% global IoU, indicating the framework can translate visual observations into inspectable, editable city code with coupled planar and 3D outputs.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of turning images into executable, editable city representations with integrated 2D/3D outputs; highlights potential for advanced urban analysis and design workflows, while underscoring typical challenges such as reliance on LLMs, data limitations, and alignment guarantees.

Abstract: Remote-sensing systems usually describe urban content with detection boxes, semantic masks, or vector boundaries. Such outputs locate classes and support image-plane scoring, yet they do not by themselves constitute an executable layout that retains object identities, typed relations, topology, and regeneration rules. Code-as-City instead casts urban-layout extraction from a single top-down image as constrained code generation with a multimodal large language model (MLLM). An image model first produces an aligned five-class semantic layout prior. Three ordered MLLM passes use the image and this prior to recover roads, land-cover regions and relations, and buildings. Deterministic normalization converts the accumulated records into a city graph and a restricted layout program. Executing the program creates a renderable 3D city layout and an orthographic semantic projection over shared geometry. The projection admits pixel-level comparison with remote-sensing masks, while named objects, relations, and editing operations remain available for synchronized regeneration of both views. Evaluated on the 100 scenes of CityLayout-100, the complete framework obtains 41.1% mean intersection-over-union and 48.3% global intersection-over-union. This result provides quantitative evidence that visual observations can be translated into inspectable, editable city code with coupled planar and 3D outputs.

</details>


### [162] [HiFi-BRep: High-Fidelity Latent Representation for Robust B-Rep Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16485)
*Junhao Hou,Chenqi Luo,Pufan Wang,Jiaying Lu,Yusheng Liu,Feiwei Qin,Meie Fang,Kun Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HiFi-BRep introduces a topology-aware encoder and a single-stage decoder to generate high-fidelity, valid B-Reps by mitigating padding/feature contamination and non-differentiable validity enforcement, achieving improved structural validity and geometric fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep generative B-Rep methods suffer from representation brittleness (padding noise and feature contamination in latent space) and generation brittleness (cascaded errors due to sequential generation and non-differentiable validity checks). A robust, differentiable, joint geometry-topology synthesis is needed.

Method: 1) A topology-aware encoder uses learnable queries to remove padding and topology-guided attention to prevent feature contamination, yielding a high-fidelity latent representation. 2) A single-stage decoder jointly predicts geometry and topology in parallel, incorporating core manifold constraints as a differentiable learning objective to enable mutual guidance and avoid cascading errors.

Result: Empirical results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both structural validity and geometric fidelity on B-Rep generation tasks; the approach is validated by extensive experiments and is accompanied by publicly available code and models at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: HiFi-BRep offers a robust, differentiable framework for high-quality B-Rep synthesis by coupling topology-aware encoding with a unified geometry-topology decoder, mitigating representation and generation brittleness and enabling reliable, high-fidelity B-Reps.

Abstract: Boundary representation (B-Rep) generation is a fundamental task in computer-aided design, yet the direct synthesis of high-fidelity and structurally valid B-Reps remains a major challenge. Existing deep generative methods suffer from two forms of brittleness: representation brittleness, caused by padding noise and feature contamination in the latent space, and generation brittleness, stemming from sequential error propagation and a train-inference mismatch due to non-differentiable validity enforcement. We propose HiFi-BRep, a novel framework that addresses these limitations through two synergistic contributions. First, a topology-aware encoder constructs a high-fidelity latent representation by eliminating padding via learnable queries and preventing feature contamination with topology-guided attention. Second, a single-stage decoder jointly predicts geometry and topology in parallel, embedding core manifold constraints as a differentiable learning objective. This design ensures mutual guidance between geometry and topology while avoiding cascaded errors. Extensive experiments show that HiFi-BRep significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both structural validity and geometric fidelity, providing a robust solution for high-quality B-Rep synthesis. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/1nnoh/HiFi-BRep.

</details>


### [163] [MLLM-Guided Semantic Correction for Text-to-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16513)
*Junhao Chen,Zheqi Lv,Keting Yin,Shengyu Zhang,Zhou Zhao,Feiyang Chen,Xinyu Duan,Baoxing Huai,Fei Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Training-free mid-generation semantic correction for text-to-video diffusion using multimodal LLM feedback, via an in-loop latent trajectory intervention without model updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic errors such as missing objects, incorrect attributes, or mismatched actions are common in text-to-video generation. Existing corrections are limited to pre- or post-sampling stages; there is a need for in-loop semantic supervision to improve alignment and fidelity.

Method: Introduce two modules: (1) Semantic Assessment Supervisor that produces intermediate preview frames for semantic evaluation and deviation diagnostics, and (2) Semantic Modification Assistant that intervenes in the latent diffusion trajectory during inference using feedback from multimodal LLMs, enabling continuous self-reflection and correction without modifying model parameters.

Result: Demonstrates improved semantic alignment, visual fidelity, and temporal consistency across multiple benchmarks, achieved in a training-free manner by correcting the generation trajectory during sampling.

Conclusion: In-loop semantic correction driven by MLLM feedback provides effective, parameter-free improvement in video synthesis; the approach can be extended to other generative tasks requiring semantic fidelity.

Abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models and Transformer architectures have led to significant progress in text-to-video generation. However, these models often suffer from semantic errors such as missing objects, incorrect attributes, or mismatched actions. Although some semantic correction methods perform optimization before sampling or refinement after sampling, how to detect and correct semantic deviations during the video generation process remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a training-free, interpretable mid-generation correction framework that integrates multimodal large language model (MLLM) feedback directly into the diffusion sampling loop. Our framework achieves diffusion trajectory correction by injecting semantic evaluation signals during video synthesis, enabling the model to optimize the generated content through continuous self-reflection. We propose two key modules: a Semantic Assessment Supervisor that generates intermediate preview frames for semantic evaluations and deviation diagnostics, and a Semantic Modification Assistant that corrects semantic drift during inference via a controllable latent trajectory intervention. Our method improves semantic alignment, visual fidelity, and temporal consistency without modifying model parameters. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks.

</details>


### [164] [Matched Outcomes, Divergent Gaze: How Foveated MLLMs Search Compared to Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16514)
*Mohamed Amine Kerkouri,Marouane Tliba,Aladine Chetouani,Ulas Bagci,Alessandro Bruno*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Multimodal LLMs can match humans on presence and target acquisition under a human-matched foveated input, but their gaze dynamics diverge, revealing a process-level gap not captured by standard attention metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether MLLMs replicate human visual search dynamics and attention alignment, beyond outcome accuracy, using human-like foveation.

Method: Three general-purpose MLLMs are tested under identical, human-matched foveated views on COCO-Search18. Fixations are driven fixation-by-fixation. Assess decision (target present), efficiency (first-saccade target acquisition), and gaze process (scanpath dynamics); compare to human scanpaths; analyze entropy, amplitude, and self-consistency; determine whether retinal input reproduces human looking patterns in space and time.

Result: Models reach ceiling performance for target presence and frequently acquire targets on the first saccade, outperforming humans in some metrics. However, the gaze process is non-human: all models exhibit low-entropy, large-amplitude, self-consistent scanpaths that align with themselves far more than two humans do. Retinal-input matching reproduces where humans look but not the temporal unfolding of looking. Standard alignment metrics (answer-alignment, saliency) miss the process-level axis, so zero-shot models can excel on outcome/spatial tasks but not on temporal/process-level aspects of human vision.

Conclusion: Process-level dynamics of attention are not captured by common metrics, so zero-shot MLLMs cannot be certified as human-like vision. New process-aware metrics are needed to assess temporal and attentional dynamics, beyond outcome and spatial alignment.

Abstract: Human visual search is serial: the fovea must land on a candidate to confirm it, and those landings form a scanpath. Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs), given the same foveated input, search as humans do bears on their use as models of human vision and on attention-alignment scores. We compare three general-purpose MLLMs with human eye-movement scanpaths on goal-directed search (COCO-Search18), driving each model fixation by fixation through an identical, human-matched foveated view and assessing it along three axes: the decision of target presence, the efficiency of reaching the target, and the gaze process itself. The axes dissociate. On the decision and on target acquisition the models match or exceed humans, detecting present targets near ceiling and reaching them on the first saccade more often than people do. The gaze process is not human. Under the human-matched condition, all three share one signature: low-entropy, large-amplitude, self-consistent scanpaths that agree with themselves far more closely than two humans agree with each other. That is consistent with a single-pass, non-serial architecture rather than a limit of acuity. Matched retinal input reproduces where humans look but not how the looking unfolds in time, and no degradation regime recovers human-like search at human-like success. The gap sits on a process axis that answer-alignment and saliency metrics do not measure. Because they miss it, such metrics cannot certify human-like vision, and zero-shot models suit outcome and spatial questions but not temporal, process-level ones.

</details>


### [165] [Ultra: Unsupervised Cross-Task Optimization for Reliable Restoration Segmentation Collaboration under Adverse Weather](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16589)
*Shiqin Wang,Zhiqian Li,Haoyuan Du,Junming Chen,Jiayuan Li,Tianrun Xu,Haoyang Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Ultra: an unsupervised restoration-segmentation collaborative framework for adverse-weather UDA-ASS that uses direction selection and causal effect estimation to avoid hallucination, achieving state-of-the-art segmentation and better restoration, with generalization to related tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Under severe degradation and lack of target-domain supervision, existing cross-task guidance between restoration and segmentation is unidentifiable and prone to hallucination, harming performance.

Method: CTDN generates candidate optimization directions by exploiting complementary visual structure and semantic cues and supports cooperative direction selection between restoration and segmentation. CMIL shifts cross-task transfer from correlation-based propagation to causal effect assessment, applying intervention-based filtering to suppress hallucination spread.

Result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art segmentation on three UDA-ASS benchmarks; achieves superior unsupervised restoration compared to existing methods; generalizes to unsupervised restoration and object detection collaboration tasks.

Conclusion: The Ultra framework enables reliable cross-task collaboration by explicit direction selection and causal effect estimation, mitigating hallucinations and improving both restoration and segmentation under unsupervised domain shifts; code will be released.

Abstract: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Adverse Weather Semantic Segmentation (UDA-ASS) aims to transfer semantic knowledge from labeled normal-weather images to unlabeled adverse environments. Existing approaches implicitly assume that restoration and segmentation provide mutually beneficial guidance. However, under severe degradation and without target-domain supervision, the validity of cross-task optimization directions becomes fundamentally unidentifiable, leading to hallucination-driven error propagation. In this work, we propose a novel Unsupervised Restoration-Segmentation Collaborative Learning Framework (Ultra), which reframes cross-task interaction as direction selection under uncertainty and causal effect estimation, enabling reliable collaboration through candidate direction generation and intervention-based filtering. In detail, we propose CTDN and CMIL. The former exploits complementary visual structures and semantic information to generate candidate optimization directions and performs cooperative direction selection between restoration and segmentation. The latter reformulates cross-task information transfer from correlation-based propagation into causal effect assessment, suppressing hallucination propagation. Extensive experiments on three widely used UDA-ASS benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art segmentation performance. Beyond segmentation, our framework achieves better unsupervised restoration results than existing UDA-ASS restoration methods and generalizes to unsupervised restoration and object detection collaboration tasks. Code and models will be available at https://github.com/Wang-Shiqin/Ultra.

</details>


### [166] [Towards Zero-Shot Domain Generalization for ID Cards Presentation Attack Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16591)
*Mario Nieto-Hidalgo,Juan M. Espin,Juan E. Tapia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Prototypical Network head with EfficientNet-V2-b0 uses four genuine samples per class and episodic training across card domains to achieve cross-country PAD with ~9% EER, outperforming softmax and CLIP baselines on multi-country and DLC-2021 benchmarks, enabling privacy-preserving, scalable onboarding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Publicly available genuine samples for ID-PAD are scarce; systems need robust generalization across diverse national IDs with minimal data collection to enable scalable, privacy-preserving onboarding.

Method: A prototypical network head built on EfficientNet-V2-b0; creates class prototypes from four genuine samples; episodic training fixes PAD classes while varying the card domain to learn universal attack cues across domains.

Result: On a large multi-country dataset and the DLC-2021 benchmark, the method achieves an average Equal Error Rate of about 9%, outperforming conventional softmax and CLIP zero-shot baselines even when trained with data from a single source country.

Conclusion: The approach enables accurate, privacy-preserving PAD with minimal data collection, facilitating scalable cross-jurisdictional remote onboarding.

Abstract: Presentation-Attack Detection (PAD) for national ID cards is limited by the lack of publicly available genuine samples, making it difficult for systems to generalize across countries. This paper introduces two main innovations: (1) a Prototypical Network head using an EfficientNet-V2-b0 backbone that requires only four genuine samples per class to create reliable prototypes; and (2) an episodic training regime that keeps PAD classes fixed while varying the card domain, allowing the network to learn universal attack cues.
  Evaluated on a large multi-country dataset and the public DLC-2021 benchmark, this method achieves an average Equal Error Rate of around 9\%, outperforming conventional softmax and CLIP zero-shot baselines even with data from a single source country. This approach provides accurate, privacy-preserving PAD while minimizing data collection, facilitating scalable cross-jurisdictional remote onboarding.

</details>


### [167] [Interactive Whole Slide Images for RL-based Tumour Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16607)
*Mohamad Mohamad,Francesco Ponzio,Maxime Gassier,Nicolas Pote,Xavier Descombes*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An end-to-end RL framework segments tumors directly on whole-slide images by viewing the slide as a hierarchical, multi-resolution environment and navigating with movement, zoom, and selection actions; PPO-based actor-critic yields fast inference and competitive coarse segmentation compared to patch-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WSIs are huge and tumors are sparsely distributed, making patch-based, preselected candidates inefficient. An end-to-end RL approach can leverage global context and sequential exploration to perform segmentation directly on full slides.

Method: Model WSIs as a hierarchical multi-resolution environment. An agent chooses actions (move, zoom, select tumor) to navigate the slide, processing local observations and a global thumbnail within an actor-critic framework trained with PPO. The system performs direct sequential segmentation without predefined patch pools.

Result: Demonstrates feasibility of direct sequential segmentation on full slides. Achieves comparable coarse segmentation quality to patch-based approaches at similar magnification, with inference time reduced to a few seconds per slide. Ablation studies show environment design and action-space granularity significantly affect performance.

Conclusion: Treating WSIs as interactive environments is a promising direction for RL-based computational pathology and can enable fast, end-to-end analysis without patch preselection.

Abstract: Whole-slide image (WSI) analysis remains computationally challenging due to the extremely large spatial resolution of slides and the sparse distribution of tumour regions. We propose an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework for sequential tumour segmentation directly on WSIs. Instead of treating the slide as a predefined collection of candidate patches, we formulate the WSI itself as a hierarchical multi-resolution environment through which an agent navigates using movement, zooming, and tumour selection actions. The agent jointly processes local observations and a global thumbnail representation within an actor-critic architecture trained using proximal policy optimization (PPO). Experiments on pulmonary adenocarcinoma WSIs demonstrate the feasibility of direct sequential tumour segmentation on full slides, achieving comparable coarse segmentation quality relative to patch-based approaches operating at similar magnification levels, while reducing inference time to a few seconds per slide. We further analyse the impact of environment design and action-space granularity. Our results suggest that modelling WSIs as interactive environments provides a promising direction for RL-based computational pathology

</details>


### [168] [Beyond Accuracy: Assessing Calibration of Geospatial Foundation Models and Their Sensitivity to Distribution Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16614)
*Nils Lehmann,Jakob Gawlikowski,Burak Ekim,Isaac Corley,Xiao Xiang Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GeoFMs are typically ranked by clean accuracy, but this ignores calibration and robustness under corruption and distribution shift. Across 16 encoders and multiple tasks, EO pretraining does not outperform ImageNet pretraining in clean conditions and under shift leads to more overconfidence. Representational rigidity (CKA) links to this degradation. Uncertainty methods (temperature scaling, deep ensembles) fail to counteract degradation; Gaussian-process probes help under severe cloud but worsen clean data. Selective prediction (abstention) cannot reliably avoid confidently wrong predictions. The paper advocates multi-condition, multi-metric benchmarking to better reflect real-world deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployment of GeoFMs in critical earth observation tasks requires reliable confidence estimates and robustness to distribution shifts and corruptions, not just high clean accuracy. A narrow evaluation protocol risks overestimating real-world performance and stability.

Method: Empirical study over 16 frozen encoders, 4 classification and 5 segmentation datasets, and 2 orthogonal corruption axes. Evaluates calibration, distribution shift, and robustness. Uses centered kernel alignment (CKA) to probe representation dynamics. Tests three uncertainty quantification methods (temperature scaling, deep ensembles, Gaussian-process probe). Conducts selective prediction experiments with abstention.

Result: All encoders degrade under corruption; ranking changes across conditions. EO-pretrained and ImageNet-pretrained encoders perform similarly on clean accuracy and calibration; EO pretraining provides no greater shift stability. Under shift, EO encoders become more overconfident than ImageNet ones. CKA indicates EO embeddings are more rigid, losing task information while remaining overconfident. Temperature scaling and deep ensembles do not mitigate degradation; Gaussian-process probes reduce ECE under severe cloud but inflate it on clean data. Abstention strategies fail to reliably skip confidently wrong predictions.

Conclusion: Benchmark practices should be expanded beyond clean accuracy to include calibration, shift robustness, and uncertainty under multiple conditions. Evaluations across diverse metrics are necessary to align model development with real-world deployment needs.

Abstract: Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) are most commonly ranked and selected by accuracy on standard benchmark conditions via averaged ranks. We show that this protocol is too narrow: the promised deployment in critical EO tasks requires further angles of analysis, mainly calibration, the agreement between a model's confidence and its correctness. Across 16 frozen encoders, four classification and five segmentation datasets, and two orthogonal stress axes, every encoder degrades as corruption intensifies, and the ranking changes as well. Across the four classification benchmarks, EO-pretrained and ImageNet-pretrained encoders are indistinguishable on clean accuracy and clean calibration, and EO pretraining provides no more stability under shift than ImageNet pretraining. Under shift the GeoFMs drift further into overconfidence than the ImageNet-pretrained encoders, at every grade and in every corruption family. A centered kernel alignment (CKA) analysis ties this to representational rigidity: EO-pretrained embeddings move less under corruption while losing just as much task information and remaining overconfident. We apply three commonly explored uncertainty quantification methods and find that temperature scaling and deep ensembles cannot counteract the degradation, while a Gaussian-process probe roughly halves ECE under severe cloud only by tripling it on clean data. In selective prediction experiments, we find that confidence-based abstention cannot defer around confidently wrong predictions, and advocate that benchmark rankings and evaluations should therefore operate across a multitude of conditions and metrics to more holistically evaluate model development progress and close the gap to real world deployment scenarios.

</details>


### [169] [HarmTrace: Anchor-Calibrated Decoupled Optimization for Fine-Grained Target Identification in Harmful Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16622)
*Yujia Li,Yiqun Zhang,Zihan Cheng,Yijie Huang,Tenglong Ye,Zihan Wang,Xiaocui Yang,Shi Feng,Yifei Zhang,Daling Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Extends multimodal harmful meme detection with fine-grained target identification, introducing Meme3W and a strict JRA metric; presents HarmTrace with CTPO and VPA to decouple and calibrate target-identity from harmfulness, achieving large gains in JRA and harmfulness accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Harmful meme detection often predicts harmfulness without correctly identifying the attacked target or evidence; a fine-grained, jointly correct target-identification is needed for robust, trustworthy detection.

Method: Introduce Meme3W to unify datasets with human-verified annotations; propose Joint Record Accuracy (JRA) as a strict metric requiring both harmfulness and all target-identification fields to be correct. Develop HarmTrace with entity-aware supervised fine-tuning and Conditional Target-identification Policy Optimization (CTPO), using a Virtual Positive Anchor (VPA) for target-identification normalization.

Result: HarmTrace improves both JRA and harmfulness accuracy across evaluated backbones; e.g., JRA on Qwen3-VL-8B rises from 17.58% to 52.51%. Code released at the provided URL.

Conclusion: Target-aware, anchor-calibrated optimization effectively aligns harmfulness prediction with fine-grained target identification, demonstrating substantial gains on unified meme benchmarks and highlighting the importance of joint evaluation metrics.

Abstract: Multimodal harmful meme detection is typically formulated as image--text harmfulness classification. A model may correctly predict harmfulness while misidentifying the attacked target or its supporting evidence. We therefore extend harmful meme detection with fine-grained target identification, asking what type of target is attacked, who is targeted, and where the target appears in the meme. The model predicts harmfulness for every meme and, for harmful memes, outputs the target category, target entity, textual mention, and visual region. To support this task, we introduce Meme3W, which unifies multiple public harmful meme datasets and provides human-verified annotations for harmful instances. We further introduce Joint Record Accuracy (JRA), a strict record-level metric requiring the harmfulness label and all target-identification fields to be jointly correct. Experiments with representative multimodal large language models reveal a substantial gap between harmfulness accuracy and JRA. To narrow this gap, we propose HarmTrace, an anchor-calibrated decoupled optimization framework. HarmTrace strengthens target-entity supervision through entity-aware supervised fine-tuning. It then applies Conditional Target-identification Policy Optimization (CTPO) to decouple harmfulness and target-identification advantages, restricting target-identification optimization to label-correct responses for harmful examples. CTPO uses a Virtual Positive Anchor (VPA) as a fully correct reference for target-identification advantage normalization. HarmTrace improves both JRA and harmfulness accuracy across the evaluated backbones, with JRA on the Qwen3-VL-8B backbone increasing from 17.58\% to 52.51\%. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llly1234/HarmTrace-for-Harmful-Memes.

</details>


### [170] [DRAFE: Domain-Robust Asymmetric Fusion of Heterogeneous Detection Transformers for Cross-City Fine-Grained Traffic Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16632)
*Divine Yao Agbobli,Geoffery Eyram Agorku,Israel Afriyie,Kwadwo Amankwah-Nkyi,Marvin Osei-Kuffour,Richmond Owusu Duah,Bright Seglah,Kelvin Asamoah Terkper,Kwabena Amoako Adjei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DRAFE: a domain-robust ensemble method for cross-city fine-grained traffic detection, fusing LW-DETR and RF-DETR via asymmetric fusion. Two-stage training with pseudo-label expansion and human refinement yields a curated corpus; challenge-finetuning on Hafnia Track 6. Inference includes anchor-conditioned matching, reliability-weighted fusion, agreement-aware recalibration, and complementary hypothesis recovery. Achieves 0.4022 mAP (6th/25) on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 6, outperforming a baseline ensemble by 0.0553 mAP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the persistent challenge of fine-grained vehicle recognition with robust cross-city generalization. Cross-city variations (appearance, DAM, sensors) impede single-model detectors; an ensemble leveraging complementary detectors and domain-informed fusion may improve generalization and localization under domain shifts.

Method: Two-stage training: (1) pretrain complementary detectors on diverse public traffic datasets using pseudo-label expansion and human-in-the-loop annotation refinement to create a curated corpus of 6,049 images and 203,619 annotations; (2) challenge-compliant fine-tuning on Project Hafnia Track 6. At inference: (a) anchor-conditioned class-consistent matching; (b) reliability-weighted coordinate fusion; (c) agreement-aware confidence recalibration; (d) complementary hypothesis recovery. Ensemble consists of independently trained LW-DETR and RF-DETR detectors.

Result: On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 6, DRAFE achieved 0.4022 mAP, ranked sixth among 25 teams, and improved by 0.0553 mAP over a preliminary ensemble evaluated under identical benchmark conditions.

Conclusion: DRAFE demonstrates that domain-robust asymmetric fusion and careful inference-time fusion strategies can yield competitive performance for cross-city, fine-grained traffic object detection. The two-stage training with pseudo-labeling and human refinement also highlights the value of curated data. Potential limitations are not stated and could include sensitivity to pseudo-label quality and the need for diverse public data to maintain cross-city generalization.

Abstract: Deep learning-based object detectors are fundamental to intelligent transportation systems, enabling traffic monitoring, vehicle analytics, and infrastructure management. However, achieving both fine-grained vehicle recognition and robust cross-city domain generalization remains challenging. We present the Domain-Robust Asymmetric Fusion Ensemble (DRAFE), which combines independently trained LW-DETR and RF-DETR detectors for cross-city fine-grained traffic object detection. DRAFE employs a two-stage training strategy that first pretrains complementary detectors on diverse public traffic datasets using pseudo-label expansion and human-in-the-loop annotation refinement, producing a curated corpus of 6,049 images and 203,619 annotations, before challenge-compliant fine-tuning on the Project Hafnia Track 6 dataset. At inference, DRAFE applies anchor-conditioned class-consistent matching, reliability-weighted coordinate fusion, agreement-aware confidence recalibration, and complementary hypothesis recovery. On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 6, DRAFE achieves 0.4022 mAP, ranks sixth among 25 participating teams, and improves by 0.0553 mAP over a preliminary ensemble evaluated under identical benchmark conditions.

</details>


### [171] [How Sampling Strategy Affects Imbalance Mitigation in LiDAR Segmentation: A Study of Structured vs. Random Point-Based Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16673)
*Antonis Savva,Christos Kyrkou,Theocharis Theocharides*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Benchmark study on class-imbalance mitigation for 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation across three datasets (DALES, S3DIS, STPLS3D) and two architectures (KPConv, RandLA-Net). Inverse-frequency weighting degrades performance, while uniform weighting often rivals complex losses, with results strongly shaped by sampling strategy (structured vs. random) and data acquisition characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D LiDAR data exhibit severe class imbalance; unlike 2D vision, the transferability of imbalance mitigation techniques to 3D is unclear. A systematic, cross-dataset, cross-architecture benchmark is needed to identify robust strategies that account for sampling regimes and real-world data acquisition effects.

Method: Evaluate six reweighting schemes and five imbalance-aware losses on three LiDAR datasets (DALES, S3DIS, STPLS3D) using two point-based nets (KPConv, RandLA-Net). Compare against uniform weighting. Analyze loss landscapes under structured (nearest-neighbor/structured sampling) and random sampling, examine interaction with imbalance ratio and dataset geometry, and report per-class and aggregate metrics.

Result: Inverse-frequency weighting degrades performance by up to 12% and can cause catastrophic failures for minority classes. Uniform weighting performs within ~2% of complex losses for structured sampling (KPConv) but yields larger gaps with random sampling (RandLA-Net, up to 4.6%). Loss landscapes show that, for structured sampling, imbalance ratio shapes geometry on real data but decouples on synthetic data; for random sampling, landscape sensitivity depends strongly on dataset geometry regardless of imbalance. Overall, for the two architectures tested, the effectiveness of mitigation approaches depends on the interaction of sampling strategy, imbalance severity, and data acquisition characteristics.

Conclusion: Mitigation strategies for 3D LiDAR imbalance cannot be universally chosen from 2D practices. Sampling strategy and real-world data acquisition characteristics crucially determine which approaches work; uniform weighting can be competitive with complex losses in certain regimes, while naive inverse-frequency weighting can be detrimental. Practitioners should consider sampling design and dataset geometry when selecting imbalance mitigation.

Abstract: Class imbalance in LiDAR point clouds poses challenges for semantic segmentation in autonomous navigation and urban mapping. While 2D vision has numerous mitigation techniques, their effectiveness in 3D remains unclear. We benchmark six reweighting schemes and five imbalance-aware losses across three datasets (DALES, S3DIS, STPLS3D) using two architectures (KPConv, RandLA-Net). Inverse-frequency weighting degrades performance by up to 12% compared to uniform weighting, with catastrophic failures in minority classes. Uniform weighting performs within 2% of complex losses for structured sampling (KPConv) but benefits less for random sampling (RandLA-Net, up to 4.6% gap). Loss landscape analysis reveals a complex interplay: for structured sampling, imbalance ratio determines landscape geometry on real LiDAR data but decouples from it on synthetic data; for random sampling, landscapes show high sensitivity to dataset geometry regardless of imbalance ratio. For the two evaluated point-based architectures, these results suggest that the interaction between sampling strategy (structured vs. random), imbalance severity, and data acquisition characteristics shapes which mitigation approaches are effective.

</details>


### [172] [Bridging the Gap between Labeled and Unlabeled Data via Unified Flow with Feature Memory Bank](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16681)
*Shanwen Wang,Xin Sun,Danfeng Hong,Junyu Dong,Patrick Le Callet*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes a remote sensing semi-supervised semantic segmentation method (UFFM) that uses Unified Flow and a Feature Memory Bank to reduce bias in pseudo-labels and align labeled/unlabeled feature representations, achieving state-of-the-art results on RS datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In semi-supervised semantic segmentation, training labeled and unlabeled data separately leads to dominance by labeled data and poor pseudo-label quality, especially under domain shifts between RS data and existing models. There is a need for a unified training objective and dynamic feature alignment to improve pseudo-labels and cross-domain consistency.

Method: Introduce Unified Flow (UF) that blends an external visual foundation model with an RS-domain teacher to produce less biased pseudo-labels and jointly optimize labeled and pseudo-labeled data under a unified objective. Add a Feature Memory Bank (FMB) that dynamically updates class-specific features during training to reduce feature discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled data via class-feature alignment.

Result: Extensive experiments on remote sensing datasets show the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of UF and FMB in reducing bias and bridging the optimization/representation gap.

Conclusion: UFFM is effective for RS semi-supervised segmentation, addressing pseudo-label bias and feature-domain gaps, with code released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Although semi-supervised semantic segmentation ($\text{S}^4$) utilizes abundant unlabeled data to reduce manual labeling burdens, independent training of labeled and unlabeled data causes the former to dominate, which severely degrades pseudo-label quality. To address this challenges, we propose a novel remote sensing (RS) $\text{S}^4$ method via unified flow with feature memory bank (UFFM). Specifically, UFFM comprises two key innovations: unified flow (UF) and feature memory bank (FMB). The UF is a new training flow that generates less biased pseudo-labels by combining an external visual foundation model (VFM) with an RS domain teacher, and jointly optimizes labeled and pseudo-labeled data under a unified training objective. The FMB is a novel memory module for $\text{S}^4$ that dynamically updates class-specific features during training and reduces the feature discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled data through class-feature alignment.
