To verify the effectiveness of our model, we conduct extensive experiments on RS datasets. The experimental results show the superiority of our method over SOTA $\text{S}^4$ methods. Moreover, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our contributions in bridging the optimization and feature representation gap between labeled and unlabeled data. Our code is released at \href{https://github.com/wangshanwen001/RS-UFFM}{https://github.com/wangshanwen001/RS-UFFM}.

</details>


### [173] [PersonaShot: Benchmarking Person-Centric Narrative Continuity in Multi-Shot Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16717)
*Yuji Wang,Yuheng Chen,Teng Hu,Ran Yi,Yijia Hong,Han Feng,Weijian Cao,Chengjie Wang,Lizhuang Ma,Jiangning Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces PersonaShot, the first person-centric benchmark for narrative continuity in multi-shot video generation, with ~1,000 segments and 16 metrics across physical continuity, affective dynamics, and cinematic grammar.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize appearance or single-shot quality and neglect cross-shot coherence and criterion-specific evaluation needed for physical, emotional, and relational continuity across cuts.

Method: Construct PersonaShot dataset (~1,000 multi-shot segments), define 16 metrics over three temporal levels (within-shot states, cross-shot transitions, sequence trajectories), and develop lightweight criterion-specific evaluators grounded in visual, temporal, or relational evidence via a multimodal teacher. Align evaluators with expert human judgments.

Result: Reveals distinct capability profiles among SOTA models and a gap between perceptual quality and cross-shot narrative continuity; visually compelling videos often exhibit physical-state resets, abrupt affective shifts, or broken cinematic relations; human studies show strong agreement between evaluators and expert judgments.

Conclusion: Provides a benchmark and criterion-aligned evaluators for rigorous assessment of multi-shot narrative continuity, enabling targeted improvements and better alignment between perceptual quality and coherent cross-shot storytelling.

Abstract: Video generation is rapidly evolving from single-shot clips to multi-shot narratives, where the human character serves as the core narrative anchor. However, existing benchmarks mainly assess character appearance or individual-shot quality, without measuring whether physical and emotional states remain coherent across cuts. They also rarely provide criterion-specific evaluation methods, although physical continuity, facial dynamics, and cinematic relations require different visual, temporal, and relational evidence. To address these limitations, we introduce PersonaShot, the first person-centric benchmark for narrative continuity in multi-shot video generation. PersonaShot contains approximately 1,000 multi-shot segments and 16 metrics spanning physical continuity, affective dynamics, and cinematic grammar. \textbf{\textit{1)} Narrative Continuity Benchmark:} We evaluate character coherence across three temporal levels: within-shot states, cross-shot transitions, and sequence-level trajectories. \textbf{\textit{2)} Human-Aligned Specialist Evaluators:} We distill reasoning from a large multimodal teacher into lightweight criterion-specific evaluators, each grounded in the visual, temporal, or relational evidence required by its metric, and align them with expert human judgments. \textbf{\textit{3)} Systematic Evaluation and Insights:} Our evaluation reveals distinct capability profiles across state-of-the-art models and a clear gap between perceptual quality and cross-shot narrative continuity. Even visually compelling videos frequently exhibit physical-state resets, abrupt affective shifts, and broken cinematic relations across shots. Human studies further demonstrate strong agreement between our evaluators and expert judgments.

</details>


### [174] [CytoFormer: A Molecularly Supervised Cell Foundation Model for Histopathology Cell Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16718)
*Jialu Yao,Songhao Li,Alina Yu,Zhi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CytoFormer learns a reusable, label-efficient cell-type representation from paired spatial transcriptomics and H&E; achieves strong cross-organ accuracy, good transfer to unseen cell types, and superior active-learning performance for histology.</n


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable scalable, accurate cell-type identification from routine histology without relying on slow, hand-annotated labels by pathologists; leverage molecular identity to supervise morphology.

Method: Assemble 81 Xenium sections across 16 organs; derive per-cell labels via clustering, marker-gene annotation, organ-wise human review, and QC; map to common organ cell types; train CytoFormer with multi-task per-organ classification heads; evaluate on spatially held-out tissue; compare encoder freezing against pathology foundation models; assess active-learning label efficiency.

Result: CytoFormer attains 0.85 accuracy and macro-F1 0.78 across 16 organs; its predictions preserve tissue architecture in held-out sections; linear-head probes on CytoFormer features outperform six pathology foundation models on four benchmarks, including unseen organs/cell types; in active learning, embeddings enable F1 0.82 in detecting normal epithelium amid looks-like tumour with few annotations, beating baselines by 0.13 in F1.

Conclusion: CytoFormer delivers a label-efficient, reusable representation for cell-level analysis of routine histology, with strong cross-organ performance and transferability, including in data regimes with limited annotations.

Abstract: Identifying cell types directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology would enable single-cell analysis at scale, but training such models has relied on manual pathologist annotations, which are slow, expensive and unreliable for many cell types. We instead supervise morphology with molecules. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics profiles individual cells in situ on a section that can afterwards be stained with H&E, so that molecular identity and morphology are observed for the same physical cell. We assembled 81 such paired Xenium sections spanning 16 organs, derived per-cell labels by clustering, marker-gene annotation, organ-wise human review and quality control, and mapped them onto the cell types commonly reported in each organ. This yielded 15.4 million cells, each with a paired H&E image patch and one of 23 cell types, on which we trained CytoFormer, a cell foundation model with a multi-task, per-organ classification head. On spatially held-out tissue CytoFormer reached an accuracy of 0.85 and a macro-F1 of 0.78 across all 16 organs, and its predictions reproduced the tissue architecture of an entire held-out section. The representation also transfers: with the encoder frozen, a linear head on CytoFormer features performed better than six pathology foundation models on four expert-annotated benchmarks, including on organs and cell types that were not part of pretraining. Finally, in an interactive active-learning setting, CytoFormer's embeddings are markedly more label-efficient than existing pathology foundation models, detecting normal epithelium amid look-alike tumour with an F1 of 0.82 from only a few annotations and leading the strongest baseline by 0.13 in F1. CytoFormer turns paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics into a reusable, label-efficient representation for cell-level analysis of routine histology.

</details>


### [175] [Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Image Dataset Quality Assurance in Multi-Center Breast MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16725)
*Chiara Tappermann,Steffen Renisch,Lars Ole Schwen,Hans Meine,Horst K. Hahn,Eike Petersen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Unsupervised QA for multi-center breast MRI using anomaly and OOD detection; introduces a 17-type anomaly benchmark from six public datasets and compares four methods (projection with domain features and positional encoding; 3D reconstruction with augmented objective; two hybrid OOD detectors). Finds medium-far/far-OOD robustly detected; near-OOD and unseen external data show method-specific gaps; 3D reconstruction and projection with adaptation perform best; hybrids fail without domain-specific tuning; implants/mastectomies remain challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: -Regulatory emphasis on data quality for high-risk medical AI; need scalable automated QA to detect corrupted/inconsistent data across centers as datasets grow.

Method: 1) Build a controlled AD benchmark of 17 QA-relevant anomaly types (protocol violations, processing errors, incorrect anatomical regions) from six public datasets, plus a radiological anomaly taxonomy grounded in human visual perception. 2) Include near-, medium-far-, far-OOD samples, in-distribution, and external normal data. 3) Evaluate four methods: (a) projection-based with domain-specific feature extractor and novel positional encoding; (b) 3D reconstruction-based with full-volume extension and augmented training objective; (c) two unmodified hybrid OOD detectors.

Result: - Medium-far and far-OOD samples detected reliably across methods. - Near-OOD and external normal data from unseen institutions expose method-specific weaknesses. - 3D reconstruction-based method: AUROC 0.936 with strong generalization. - Projection-based method with positional encoding: AUROC 0.954 overall, highest performance. - Hybrid methods exhibit critical failure modes and do not generalize across modalities/anatomies without domain adaptation. - Implants and mastectomies remain challenging for all methods.

Conclusion: The work establishes a practical, scalable framework for unsupervised dataset QA in medical AI pipelines, providing a benchmark, taxonomy, and guidance on method selection and generalization. It highlights the necessity of domain-specific adaptation and acknowledges persistent gaps (implants/mastectomies) and the risk of relying on a single method.

Abstract: Corrupted, inconsistent, or anomalous data silently threatens the safety and reliability of medical AI. Despite growing regulatory recognition of dataset quality assurance (QA) for high-risk medical AI, scalable automated detection remains underdeveloped. We employ unsupervised anomaly detection (AD) and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection as an automated dataset QA mechanism for multi-center dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI.
  We build a controlled AD benchmark of 17 realistic QA-relevant anomaly types from six public datasets (protocol violations, processing errors, incorrect anatomical regions) and propose a taxonomy of radiological image anomalies based on human visual perception, enabling fine-grained analysis of AD failure modes. The benchmark includes near-, medium-far-, far-OOD samples, as well as in-distribution and external normal data. Four methods are evaluated: a projection-based method extended with a domain-specific feature extractor and a novel positional encoding, a reconstruction-based approach extended to full 3D volumes with an augmented training objective, and two unmodified hybrid OOD detection methods.
  Medium-far- and far-OOD samples are detected reliably, whereas near-OOD samples and external normal data from unseen institutions expose method-specific differences. The 3D reconstruction-based approach best balances detection performance (AUROC: 0.936) and generalization to unseen institutions. The projection-based method with positional encoding achieves the highest overall detection performance (AUROC: 0.954). Both hybrid methods exhibit critical failure modes, confirming that methods validated for one modality or anatomy may not generalize without domain-specific adaptation. Implants and mastectomies remain an open challenge for all methods. Our results establish a foundation and practical guidance on scalable unsupervised QA in medical AI pipelines.

</details>


### [176] [TRACE-Bench: Decomposing and Diagnosing Multi-Reference Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16765)
*Haoran Wang,Chaofan Ma,Ran Yi,Lizhuang Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TRACE-Bench unifies multi-reference image generation tasks via four atomic operators (Anchor, Disentangle, Apply, Compose) and a compositional formula framework. It builds ~1.6k evaluation cases across 1–8 operator slots, enabling operator-aligned scoring and diagnostic trees. Empirical results show bottlenecks in disentanglement and attribute binding, not scene composition, with best models reaching 0.74 attribute fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address fragmentation in existing benchmarks for multimodal generation and enable diagnostic, capability-focused evaluation across combinatorial reference prompts.

Method: Define four atomic operators, represent prompts as compositional formulas over f, g, ⊕, and C; construct TRACE-Bench from 631 templates and ~4,000 reference images; develop operator-aligned evaluation and diagnostic tree; evaluate 9 state-of-the-art models.

Result: Evaluation reveals that primary bottlenecks lie in disentanglement (g) and attribute binding (⊕) rather than composition (C); maximum reported attribute fidelity score is 0.74; ~1.6k test cases across 1–8 slots provide diagnostic granularity.

Conclusion: A capability-oriented, operator-based benchmark enables fine-grained diagnostics for multi-reference generation and identifies where current models underperform; emphasis should be placed on improving disentanglement and binding capabilities to raise attribute fidelity.

Abstract: Despite recent advances in unified multimodal models for multi-reference image generation, existing benchmarks remain organized around predefined task types (e.g., "subject composition"), which are ill-suited to this combinatorial setting and lead to fragmented coverage, uncontrolled complexity, and little diagnostic value. Recognizing that diverse multi-reference tasks share a common set of atomic operations, we adopt a capability-oriented perspective and formalize four operators: Anchor ($f$), Disentangle ($g$), Apply ($\oplus$), and Compose ($C$). Any multi-reference prompt can then be represented as a compositional formula over these operators, whose structural complexity is quantified by the number of operator slots. Building on this formulation, we construct TRACE-Bench, comprising approximately 1,600 evaluation cases across slot counts 1--8, built from 631 formula templates and around 4,000 reference images spanning diverse artistic styles and real-world subjects. The formula structure directly drives an operator-aligned evaluation protocol for per-capability scoring and a diagnostic tree analysis for recursive failure localization. Evaluating 9 leading models reveals insights invisible to holistic scoring: the primary bottleneck lies in disentanglement ($g$) and attribute binding ($\oplus$) rather than scene-level composition ($C$), with even the best model scoring only 0.74 on attribute fidelity. Project page: https://amuseum-whr.github.io/TraceBench

</details>


### [177] [Calibration-Free Vehicle Speed Estimation: A Monocular Keypoint-Template Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16785)
*Gaofeng Su,Keya Li,Raja Sengupta,Kara M. Kockelman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Calibration-free monocular speed estimation using a 36-keypoint vehicle template and per-frame homography updates; compares keypoint-only tracking vs warped optical flow; achieves MAEs ~9–15% and high within-20% accuracy on VS13 and BrnoCompSpeed, improved with edge trimming; enables low-cost, citizen-based speed enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable accurate vehicle speed estimation from monocular video without camera calibration or roadway references, supporting low-cost speed enforcement via portable devices.

Method: A 36-keypoint vehicle template is tracked with a YOLO-based keypoint detector. A homography matrix is updated each frame. Two estimation strategies are evaluated: (1) keypoint-only tracking and (2) warped optical flow with dense spatial aggregation. Speeds are projected into metric space via homography; tested on 400+ roadside/overhead clips (30–100 mph).

Result: On VS13 and BrnoCompSpeed datasets: warped optical flow achieved MAEs of 15.0% and 9.7% and 77.9% and 93.1% within ±20%. After trimming 10% edge outliers: MAEs improved to 11.7% and 7.6% and within-±20% accuracy to 85.3% and 95.4%. Speeds span 30–100 mph.

Conclusion: The approach addresses limitations of existing vision-based methods, enabling low-cost, efficient speed enforcement using portable devices (dashcams/smartphones) and supporting citizen-based traffic safety programs.

Abstract: This paper proposes a calibration-free framework for reliably and effectively estimating vehicle speeds from monocular videos, without relying on roadway features, camera calibration, or roadway-feature-based reference objects. The proposed framework estimates vehicle speeds using a 36-keypoint vehicle template and a homography matrix updated at each frame. A YOLO-based keypoint detection module is trained on diverse datasets, and two estimation strategies are compared: keypoint-only tracking and warped optical flow with dense spatial aggregation. Speed is estimated by projecting displacements into metric space using the homography, with validation conducted on over 400 video clips from roadside and overhead datasets, covering speeds from 30 to 100 mph. The method achieves reliable speed estimation on the VS13 and BrnoCompSpeed datasets, with the warped optical flow method delivering MAEs of 15.0% and 9.7%, respectively, and 77.9% and 93.1% of estimates falling within +/-20% error. After applying a 10% trim to remove edge-of-frame outliers, performance improves to MAEs of 11.7% and 7.6%, with within-+/-20% accuracy increasing to 85.3% and 95.4%. This work addresses key limitations of existing vision-based approaches and enables low-cost and efficient speed enforcement using portable devices such as dashcams and smartphones, thereby supporting citizen-based enforcement programs for traffic safety.

</details>


### [178] [HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16859)
*Weiliang Chen,Haowen Sun,Jun Gao,Jiawei Chi,Hanyang Wang,Qiyu Dai,Yihao Li,Hao Li,Jingnan Gao,Yi-Hsin Hung,Xingzhuo Guo,Shangchen Miao,Zhiyuan Shi,Xiang Li,Fengrui Tian,Weihua Du,Ziqi Huang,Shenyuan Gao,Siqiao Huang,Mingyu Liu,Yifei Li,Shizun Wang,Xi Wang,Tianqi Zhang,Xue Luo,Xiyin Ren,Jinshan Ren,Xiaoyang Shen,Xiaobo Hu,Zhiyang Dou,Mingyu Ding,Yichao Yan,Xinchao Wang,Yizhou Wang,Shilong Liu,Wenzhao Zheng,Yueqi Duan,Yuan Gong,Ziwei Liu,Ming-Yu Liu,Jialong Wu,Jiangran Lyu,Fangfu Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An interpretable, hierarchical evaluation framework for world models (HarnessEval-W) that produces a verifiable evidence tree by decomposing evaluation cases into subproblems solved by sub-agents; demonstrates on 18 models and 330 cases; results align with human preferences; open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks yield scalar scores without interpretable reasoning; world models require verification of physics, causality, and state evolution; need transparent justification of performance.

Method: Agentified evaluation pipeline; interpret context; decompose into subproblems; spawn specialized sub-agents with context/tools; parent agent aggregates evidence into final verdict; produces evidence tree; open-sourced.

Result: Applied to 18 world models across 330 evaluation cases; judgments align with human preferences; provides fine-grained, verifiable diagnoses per rollout.

Conclusion: Enables transparent, inspectable evaluation; invites community contributions; can evolve with more cases and skills.

Abstract: A benchmark should deliver more than a scalar score: what makes an evaluation trustworthy is the reasoning that justifies the score. This is especially critical for world models, where judging a rollout requires understanding whether physics, causality, and world state evolve correctly. Humans spot such violations naturally, yet no existing benchmark automates this capability: metrics are computed brute-force, leaving no reasoning chain that can be examined or verified. We introduce HarnessEval-W, an agentified evaluation pipeline that brings the harness paradigm from the LLM ecosystem to world model benchmarking. Rather than applying a fixed rubric, HarnessEval-W interprets the context of each evaluation case, decomposes the evaluation question into measurable subproblems, and spawns specialized sub-agents, each equipped with tailored context and diagnostic tools to reason over its own subproblem. The parent agent then validates the gathered evidence and summarizes it into the final verdict. This hierarchical workflow turns every evaluation into a transparent evidence tree whose complete reasoning chain justifies the result. We apply HarnessEval-W to 18 representative world models over 330 evaluation cases. Its judgments closely align with human preferences while providing verifiable, fine-grained diagnoses of every generated rollout. We open-source the full pipeline as a live benchmark and invite the broad community to contribute to grow new skills and evaluation cases as world models evolve.

</details>


### [179] [SplatGuide: Geometric Priors from 3D Gaussians for Pose-Free Novel View Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16863)
*Yejun Zhang,Zihan Wang,Xu Ji,Yihao Wang,Yuxin Hou,Junyuan Fang,Juho-Matti Kilpeläinen,Arno Solin,Hamed Rezazadegan Tavakoli,Esa Rahtu,Juho Kannala*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SplatGuide unifies geometry, occlusion, and features from a single 3DGS forward pass to enable pose-free, photorealistic novel-view synthesis via three complementary signals, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3DGS-plus-diffusion pipelines extract only a single signal (rendered pixels or learned features) and ignore per-Gaussian visibility cues, causing an information disconnect among renderable geometry, visibility cues, and learned features.

Method: From one 3DGS forward pass, generate three signals: (1) rendered images as pixel-aligned geometric conditioning; (2) per-Gaussian source-view indices rendered into a target-view voting map for occlusion-aware reference selection; (3) reconstruction tokens providing feature-level guidance via cross-attention. All signals are reused for rendering, reference voting, and feature guidance in a diffusion framework.

Result: Empirical evaluation across RealEstate10K, DL3DV, Tanks-and-Temples, and Mip-NeRF 360 shows state-of-the-art pose-free novel-view synthesis; on RealEstate10K with a moderate number of inputs, it surpasses the ground-truth-pose baseline.

Conclusion: By reusing a single 3DGS reconstruction to supply pixel conditioning, per-Gaussian occlusion-aware voting, and reconstruction-token guidance, SplatGuide closes the information disconnect and yields coherent, photorealistic novel views; the approach demonstrates the benefit of unified multi-signal utilization from one forward pass and suggests avenues for richer per-sample visibility cues and integration with diffusion.

Abstract: Generating photorealistic novel views from unposed images requires both 3D geometric understanding and the ability to synthesize unseen content. A natural strategy combines feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction with multi-view diffusion. Yet prior pipelines extract at most one signal from the reconstruction, either pixel rendering or learned features, while none exploits per-Gaussian visibility for occlusion-aware reference selection. This *information disconnect* leaves renderable geometry, visibility cues, and learned features unused. SplatGuide closes this disconnect by reusing a single 3DGS scene across three complementary roles. Rendered images provide pixel-aligned geometric conditioning. Per-Gaussian source-view indices are rendered into a target-view voting map for occlusion-aware reference selection. Reconstruction tokens supply feature-level guidance via cross-attention. All three signals derive from the same reconstruction forward pass. Across RealEstate10K, DL3DV, Tanks-and-Temples, and Mip-NeRF 360, SplatGuide achieves state-of-the-art pose-free novel view synthesis. On RealEstate10K, with a moderate number of input views, it surpasses the ground-truth-pose baseline.

</details>


### [180] [An Empirical Study of Training Pixel-Space Text-to-Image Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16887)
*Dengyang Jiang,Ruoyi Du,Zhennan Chen,Dongyang Liu,Zanyi Wang,Mingzhe Zheng,Xiangpeng Yang,Huanqia Cai,Aiming Hao,Yuming Jiang,Peng Gao,Harry Yang,Steven Hoi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Pixel-space diffusion models lag in training efficiency; a latent-to-pixel pipeline with careful transition can match or surpass latent-space models and offers large inference-speedups (~3.2–4.8x).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the practical gap: many pixel-space diffusion studies focus on small-scale or class-conditional settings, yet training at scale is slow and its competitiveness with latent-space models is uncertain.

Method: Conduct a large-scale empirical study of pixel-space diffusion. Propose a latent-to-pixel strategy that first learns generative priors in latent space and then transitions to pixel space during post-training. Systematically evaluate design choices for the transition (weight initialization, data composition, prediction target, decoder architecture, noise schedule) to derive a practical recipe.

Result: Direct large-scale pixel-space pre-training converges more slowly than latent-space training. The latent-to-pixel approach yields pixel-space models that match or exceed latent-space counterparts and delivers 3.18–4.75× end-to-end inference speedups.

Conclusion: The study provides empirical insights and practical guidelines for pixel-space generation and demonstrates that a latent-to-pixel strategy is a viable path to high-performance, fast pixel-space diffusion models.

Abstract: This paper investigates an increasingly important topic in generative modeling: pixel-space diffusion models. Although numerous studies have explored this topic, most focus on small-scale or class-conditional settings. Consequently, a practical recipe for training pixel-space models that rival or exceed well-established latent-space counterparts remains elusive. Through a comprehensive empirical study, we first observe that direct large-scale pre-training in pixel space converges substantially more slowly than in latent space. This observation motivates a latent-to-pixel strategy that acquires generative priors efficiently in latent space and transitions to pixel space during post-training. We then systematically investigate the key design choices governing this transition, including weight initialization, data composition, prediction target, decoder architecture, and noise schedule, and identify a practical recipe that makes the resulting pixel-space models match or outperform their latent-space counterparts while delivering 3.18 to 4.75 times end-to-end inference speedups. We hope that our findings provide useful empirical insights and practical guidelines for future research on pixel-space generation.

</details>

# cs.CG [[Back]](#toc)

### [181] [On graphically local versions of metric embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15779)
*Vishesh Jain,Duan Tu*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Graphically local metric embedding can be as hard as preserving all pairwise distances. A construction with a max-degree-3 graph shows any embedding into l2 that preserves only the graph edges within a (1+ε) factor requires m = Ω(ε^{-2} log n), matching the Johnson–Lindenstrauss bound for all-pairs embedding. The degree-3 bound is tight: for max degree 2 (or treewidth 2), G-isometric embeddings into 2D normed spaces are always possible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the complexity of embedding a finite metric space while approximately preserving only a subset of pairwise distances defined by a sparse graph, and to identify the thresholds where such local embeddings are as hard as global embeddings or become tractable.

Method: Provide a general reduction from graphically local embedding to global embedding, and give a concrete construction: a Euclidean space X on n points with a maximum-degree-3 graph G=(X,E), such that any embedding into ℓ2^m preserving E-distances up to (1+ε) requires m = Ω(ε^{-2} log n). Also prove tightness of degree bounds by showing degree-2 cases admit G-isometric embeddings into 2D normed spaces.

Result: Demonstrates a lower bound m = Ω(ε^{-2} log n) for preserving a sparse set of distances, matching the JL upper bound for all-pairs embedding, thus showing local embedding can be as hard as global embedding. Establishes that the max-degree-3 condition is tight; for graphs with max degree ≤2 (or treewidth ≤2), any metric space can be embedded G-isometrically into 2D normed spaces.

Conclusion: The difficulty of graphically local metric embedding aligns with the global embedding problem at the critical threshold of degree 3; this sharpens our understanding of when local distance preservation suffices or remains as hard as preserving all pairwise distances, extending prior results on noncontracting embeddings.

Abstract: We consider the problem of graphically local metric embedding, i.e. embedding points from an arbitrary finite metric space into a target metric space while preserving, up to a small distortion, only a subset of the pairwise distances specified by a bounded degree graph $G$.
  We provide a general reduction showing that, in many cases, this is no easier than embedding the points while approximately preserving all pairwise distances. As an illustration of our general reduction, we show that there exists a Euclidean metric space $X$ on $n$ points along with a graph $G = (X,E)$ of maximum degree $3$ such that any embedding of $X$ into $\ell_2^m$ which only preserves distances specified by $E$ up to a relative error of $(1+\varepsilon)$ must satisfy $m = Ω(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$.
  Our lower bound matches the upper bound on the dimension coming from the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma for approximately preserving all pairwise distances; previously, such a lower bound was known only for the class of noncontracting embeddings [Schechtman-Shraibman, Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2009]. Moreover, the condition that the maximum degree of the graph is $3$ is best possible: for graphs $G$ of maximum degree $2$ (or more generally, treewidth at most $2$), any metric space embeds $G$-isometrically into any two-dimensional normed space.

</details>


### [182] [Geometric Burning Under $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ Metrics, and Beyond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15954)
*Shahin Kamali,Saba Yazdani*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: NP-hardness persists for geometric burning under L1/L∞; gives improved approximations: 2+ε (baseline) for anywhere and point burning, then 7/4+ε for anywhere burning, and 3151/1620+ε (~1.9451)+ε for point burning; extends L∞ result to fixed dimension d≥3 with (2−1/2^{d+1}+ε); transfers to all Lp via norm comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend geometric burning analysis beyond Euclidean metric to L1 and L∞ to exploit their geometry, obtain tighter approximations, handle higher dimensions, and unify across p-norms.

Method: Utilize the axis-aligned geometry of L1/L∞ balls (diamonds/cubes) to design coverings with radii in {0,...,k−1}, derive approximation algorithms via geometric partitioning and ε-approximation techniques; establish NP-hardness; extend wherever-burning strategies to higher dimensions; apply norm-comparability to transfer results across p-norms.

Result: Established NP-hardness for L1/L∞ geometric burning; achieved (2+ε)-approx for both anywhere and point burning; improved to 7/4+ε for anywhere burning; 3151/1620+ε for point burning; in L∞ for fixed d≥3, (2−1/2^{d+1}+ε); mapped results to all 1≤p≤∞ via standard norm comparisons.

Conclusion: L1/L∞ geometry enables sharper approximation guarantees for geometric burning and allows dimension- and norm-wide generalizations, while maintaining NP-hardness; provides a cohesive framework to extend Euclidean results to other norms.

Abstract: Burning is a discrete-time model for propagation in which a new fire starts in each round, while each existing fire expands by one unit of distance along the underlying metric. In geometric burning, the input is a finite point set, and the goal is to burn all points in as few rounds as possible. Equivalently, burning a point set in $k$ rounds corresponds to covering it with metric balls of distinct radii in $\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}$; the objective is to minimize $k$. Previous work has studied the problem mainly under the Euclidean metric. In this paper, we study geometric burning under the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ metrics. The problem remains NP-hard in both settings.
  The $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ metrics provide additional geometric structure, which allows us to obtain improved approximation guarantees, especially for anywhere burning. We first present a simple $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for both anywhere burning and point burning. We then improve the anywhere burning approximation to $7/4+\varepsilon=1.75+\varepsilon$, and give a $(3151/1620+\varepsilon)$-approximation for point burning, where $3151/1620<1.9451$. We also extend the anywhere burning result under $L_\infty$ to every fixed dimension $d\ge 3$ to achieve a $\left(2-\frac{1}{2^{d+1}}+\varepsilon\right)$-approximation. Finally, using standard comparisons between planar $L_p$ distances, we transfer our $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ algorithms, together with known Euclidean burning algorithms, to obtain approximation guarantees for every fixed $1\le p\le\infty$.

</details>


<div id='cs.RO'></div>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [183] [SpotlessGS: Relightable 3D Gaussian Splatting under Dynamic Illumination for Robotic Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14713)
*Liang Hong,Jiaxin Wei,Simon Schaefer,Stefan Leutenegger,Jaehyung Jung*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Joint lighting optimization within Dark Gaussian Splatting to create relightable 3D reconstructions using spherical harmonics for spatial variation and an MLP BRDF, improving rendering quality and downstream robotic perception.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots in dark/poorly lit environments rely on onboard lights that cause uneven illumination, degrading perception. 2D image enhancement lacks reliable supervision and breaks multi-view geometry; a 3D relightable model with unified lighting estimation can preserve geometric consistency and improve downstream tasks.

Method: Extend DarkGS by integrating learning-based lighting optimization without explicit light calibration, introduce a low-frequency illumination model using spherical harmonics to capture spatially varying residual and ambient lighting, and employ an MLP-based BRDF to model non-Lambertian reflectance. Evaluate on synthetic and real datasets and validate benefits for a robotic perception downstream task.

Result: The method mitigates illumination artifacts, improves rendering quality, and yields better quantitative performance than prior approaches. Downstream robotic perception tasks show improved performance using the relightable 3D model.

Conclusion: A calibration-free, relightable 3D reconstruction framework that combines joint lighting optimization, SH-based illumination, and learned BRDF to enhance perception in challenging lighting conditions, with potential applicability to broader illumination-robust 3D vision tasks.

Abstract: Robots operating in dark or poorly lit environments rely on onboard lights, which often produce uneven illumination that degrades downstream perception tasks. Prior approaches based on 2D image enhancement lack reliable supervision and fail to preserve multi-view geometric consistency. To address these limitations, we extend Dark Gaussian Splatting (DarkGS) toward a more accurate and flexible relightable 3D reconstruction framework. First, we eliminate the need for explicit light parameter calibration by jointly optimizing lighting parameters within the Gaussian Splatting framework. Second, we introduce a low-frequency illumination model based on spherical harmonics (SH) to capture spatially varying residual and ambient lighting effects. Third, we incorporate an MLP-based Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) to model non-Lambertian reflectance. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates illumination artifacts while improving rendering quality and quantitative performance over prior approaches. We further validate its benefits for robotic perception through a downstream task.

</details>


### [184] [MISTac: A Vision-Based Tactile Sensor for Minimally Invasive Surgery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14772)
*Robin Koch,Annabella Mascot,Rayan Younis,Martin Wagner,Stefanie Speidel,Mark Cutkosky,Ingo Sieber,Roberto Calandra*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MISTac is a high-resolution vision-based tactile sensor for palpation in MIS, featuring an 8 mm replaceable tip and modular hardware, demonstrating tissue classification with ~84% LOOCV accuracy in vivo; open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of tactile feedback in minimally invasive surgery and enable palpation-based tissue classification and intra-operative localization.

Method: Developed MISTac with a replaceable 8 mm tip; modular 3D-printed case supporting bulky illumination and imaging hardware; achieved optical resolution of 176.68 μm, tactile resolution of 250 μm, and force sensitivity of 24.3 mN; collected tactile data in vivo and trained a machine learning model for tissue classification using leave-one-out cross-validation.

Result: In vivo usability demonstrated; tissue classification task achieved ~84% aggregate accuracy in LOOCV; device open-sourced at GitHub.

Conclusion: MISTac demonstrates the feasibility of vision-based tactile sensing to augment MIS with tissue classification capability; a small but meaningful step toward integrating tactile feedback in MIS, with an open-source release for community development.

Abstract: Minimally invasive and robot-assisted surgery offer many advantages over traditional open surgery, but deprive surgeons of tactile feedback and the ability to palpate tissue with their fingers. To address this lack of tactile feedback, we introduce the MISTac, a high resolution vision-based tactile sensor specifically designed for palpation in MIS. The sensor has a replaceable sensor tip with a diameter of 8 mm which allows it to fit through the trocars used in minimally invasive surgery. Its modular 3D-printed case design allows the use of bulky off-the-shelf illumination and imaging hardware that can easily be exchanged and upgraded. The sensor has an optical resolution of 176.68 $μm$, a tactile resolution of 250 $μm$, and can resolve forces as little as 24.3 mN. An in vivo study with the sensor shows its usability in minimally invasive surgery. We trained a machine learning model with the tactile data collected in the trial on a tissue classification task achieving an aggregate accuracy of ~84% in a leave-one-out cross validation. Tactile sensors have the potential to one day aid surgeons during minimally invasive surgery with tasks such as tissue classification or intra-operative tumor localization; MISTac is a small step towards this vision. We open-source MISTac at https://github.com/lasr-lab/mistac

</details>


### [185] [Imagining Recovery: Inference-Time Counterfactual Realignment for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14822)
*Yanyan Zhang,Disheng Liu,Kai Ye,Chaoda Song,Xinpeng Li,Mohsen Hariri,Vikash Singh,Yu Yin,Vipin Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoRe is a training-free recovery framework for vision-language-action (VLA) robotic manipulation that uses counterfactual reasoning at inference to realign policy after deviations, without failure data or retraining; it imagines a continuation from a recent viable state to the current goal using synthesized observations and minimally adjusts the robot and scene to rejoin the imagined path, avoiding physical trial-and-error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current recovery methods for VLA systems rely on failure data, policy retraining, or external corrective agents, which increases data requirements and risks. VLA models are fragile to online disruptions (goal changes, scene/robot perturbations) and need robust, policy-agnostic recovery that preserves task progress.

Method: CoRe detects deviations, then privately imagines how the policy would proceed toward the current goal from a recent viable state. It uses synthesized observations (instead of real execution) to simulate continuation, and applies minimal realignment of the robot and scene to rejoin the imagined path, after which control is returned to the policy. The approach is training-free and does not require failure data or task-specific recovery training.

Result: Across multiple simulators, VLA backbones, and real-world settings, CoRe improves success rates by up to 85.0 percentage points toward near-nominal levels and reduces physical restorations by 42.2%, without policy fine-tuning or failure-specific recovery training.

Conclusion: CoRe offers a general, training-free solution for robust VLA recovery, enabling real-time counterfactual realignment that preserves progress and handles mid-episode goal changes and perturbations with lower risk and data requirements.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have improved the flexibility and generality of robotic manipulation, yet they remain fragile to online disruptions, such as changes in task goal, scene configuration, or robot state. Existing recovery methods often require failure data, policy retraining, or external corrective agents, introducing additional data requirements and execution risks. We propose Counterfactual Realignment (CoRe), a training-free framework that recovers a frozen VLA at inference time without failure data. Upon detecting a deviation, CoRe imagines how the policy would continue toward the current goal from a recent viable state, using synthesized observations in place of physical execution, and then minimally realigns the robot and scene to rejoin this imagined continuation before returning control to the policy. Recovery is therefore planned without physical trial-and-error, preserves completed task progress, and handles both mid-episode instruction changes and physical perturbations in a unified manner. Extensive experiments across multiple simulators, VLA backbones, and real-world settings show that CoRe improves success rates by up to 85.0 percentage points to near-nominal levels while reducing physical restorations by 42.2%, without policy fine-tuning or failure-specific recovery training.

</details>


### [186] [Modeling and Control of an Eel-Inspired Soft Robot for Design Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14860)
*Zhangjingyi Jiang,Mark Campbell*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FEM-based elastic-rod + hydrodynamics model for eel-inspired soft robot enables design optimization and control; slight asymmetry improves maneuverability with similar speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a physics-grounded platform to explore design choices, control policies, and material degradation effects in anguilliform soft swimmers to guide model-based estimation and control.

Method: Elastic rod Finite Element Method to represent soft robot; coupled with a hydrodynamic force model; simulate control strategies; analyze design variations and material degradation.

Result: Slightly asymmetric designs achieve greater maneuverability while maintaining comparable swimming velocity; the approach demonstrates the effectiveness of proposed control methods and identifies robust configurations and degradation implications.

Conclusion: The coupled FEM-hydrodynamics framework is a valuable design tool for optimizing task-specific performance and assessing resilience to material property changes in eel-inspired soft robots.

Abstract: Anguilliform locomotion is a highly efficient swimming mode; the advent of new materials for soft robots enables the development of an eel-inspired soft robot. This paper presents a simulation model of an eel-inspired soft robot designed for anguilliform swimming. This model can aid in design optimization and the development of model-based estimation, reasoning, and control systems. A Finite Element Method (FEM) model of an elastic rod is used to capture the soft materials of the robotic fish, which makes it particularly amenable to variation over time as the material properties change. The material model is coupled with a hydrodynamic force model to simulate the behavior of a soft, elongated robot in water. The model is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control approaches in achieving desired swimming behaviors. It also provides insights into design decisions, including the robustness of different system configurations and the impact of material degradation and failure. The results show that slightly asymmetric designs are advantageous, offering comparable swimming velocities but greater maneuverability. This model can be used to guide future robotic design decisions aimed at optimizing performance for specific tasks.

</details>


### [187] [Real-time Estimator of Actuator Control and Health (REACH) on an Eel-Inspired Soft Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14865)
*Zhangjingyi Jiang,Myungsun Park,Michael T. Tolley,Mark Campbell*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: REACH: a real-time actuator health estimator for soft swimming robots using a sigma-point filter and hypothesis testing to detect actuator degradation amid nonlinearities and time-varying changes; evaluates sensor types (GPS, IMU, Bend Sensor) and sensor placement; demonstrates robust health prediction across multiple gaits and with noisy/manufacturing-variability data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater soft robots suffer actuator degradation in harsh environments. Real-time health estimation enables mission continuation or safe return by detecting actuator failure and degradation.

Method: Model-based estimator (soft robot model) combined with a sigma-point filter and formal statistical hypothesis testing. Evaluates three sensor types (GPS, IMU, Bend Sensor) with one sensor per actuator. Also studies sensor quantity/placement (IMU vs Bend Sensor). Compares three swimming gaits (linear, wide turn, tight turn). Validates fault estimation via a filter-consistency test. Experimental validation uses bend-sensor data from a fish robot under noisy conditions and manufacturing variation.

Result: REACH with bend sensor and IMU both adequate; IMU requires two sensors, bend sensor requires three for full actuator health insight. All three gaits allow accurate health prediction with minor performance differences. The estimator is statistically consistent in fault detection. Experimental data show robustness to noise and manufacturing variation.

Conclusion: REACH is effective for real-time actuator health estimation in soft swimming robots, handling nonlinear dynamics and degradation, with validated robustness to sensor noise and manufacturing variability.

Abstract: An actuator health estimation algorithm for a soft swimming robot that can perform anguilliform swimming is developed. Due to harsh operational environments of underwater robots, and the common degradation of soft robot materials and actuators, accurate estimation of actuator functionality is necessary for robots to perform their missions as well as return to base in the event of actuator degradation and failure. Termed REACH (Real-time Estimator of Actuator Control and Health), the architecture employs a soft robot model, sigma point filter, and a formal statistical hypothesis test to adequately capture the nonlinearities and changes over time. The performance of REACH using three sensor types (GPS, IMU, and Bend Sensor) with one sensor on each actuator is compared, demonstrating that both bend sensor and IMU are adequate choices. Sensor quantity and placement are evaluated for IMU and bend sensor, showing two sensors are sufficient for IMU, whereas three sensors are needed for bend sensor. Three swimming gaits (linear swimming, wide turning, tight turning) are compared, demonstrating that REACH can successfully predict actuator health for all three gaits, with minimal differences in performance. A filter validation method shows the fault estimation algorithm is statistically consistent in finding the correct degradation. The approach is experimentally evaluated using bend sensor data collected from a fish robot, demonstrating that REACH can successfully estimate actuator health with noisy data and variations in manufacturing.

</details>


### [188] [Geometry-Aware Online Mapping for 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14902)
*Thai Luu,Quan Tran,Hieu Phan,Tuan Dang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Geometry-aware, mapping-thread densification methods improve online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS-SLAM) by preserving transmittance, initializing camera scale from depth/intrinsics, and guiding expansion to high-residual regions, yielding consistent rendering gains with negligible overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline 3DGS reconstructions rely on heavy per-frame optimization and density heuristics that don’t transfer well to online SLAM with strict per-keyframe budgets and growing maps. A decoupled, geometry-aware approach is needed for robust, real-time mapping.

Method: Introduce three geometry-aware methods that run in the mapping thread: (1) transmittance-preserving densification to maintain consistent visibility-based density; (2) camera-aware scale initialization using depth measurements and camera intrinsics; (3) error-guided densification that concentrates new primitives in regions with high residuals. These methods are decoupled from pose optimization budgets.

Result: Rendering quality improves consistently with negligible overhead in online SLAM; demonstrates a coupling between photometric residuals and pose uncertainty; plans to open-source the code to promote reproducibility.

Conclusion: Geometry-aware, decoupled mapping strategies enhance 3DGS-SLAM performance and robustness, reducing brittleness of offline heuristics and enabling efficient online mapping; open-source release will aid reproducibility and community validation.

Abstract: Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has enabled efficient photorealistic view synthesis and is rapidly being adopted in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) systems for online mapping. In these systems, a Gaussian map must be expanded and refined incrementally while tracking runs in real time, so initialization and density control directly determine where limited computation and iterations are spent. This contrasts with offline 3DGS reconstruction, where such heuristics can be amortized over long optimization schedules. However, most 3DGS-SLAM pipelines inherit initialization and density-control heuristics from offline reconstruction, which can become brittle under the strict per-keyframe optimization budgets and incremental map growth of online SLAM. In this work, we revisit these heuristics in a decoupled 3DGS-SLAM setting and propose three geometry-aware methods that operate in the mapping thread: transmittance-preserving densification, camera-aware scale initialization from depth and intrinsics, and error-guided densification that focuses new primitives on high-residual regions. Our results show consistent improvements in rendering quality with negligible overhead, highlighting the coupling between photometric residuals and pose uncertainty in online SLAM. We will open-source our code to the community to foster growth and validate reproducibility.

</details>


### [189] [From Continuous Design to Delay-Aware Discrete Synthesis: Guaranteed High-Bandwidth Joint Control for PMSM Drives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14937)
*Edmundo Pozo Fortunić,Mehmet C. Yildirim,Sami Haddadin*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Delay-aware, discrete-time PMSM current-control framework for robotic joints that directly designs a discrete PI controller with bandwidth and delay guarantees; analytically derives minimum sampling rate, controller gains, and DC-link voltage; validated by simulations and hardware experiments showing reduced hardware requirements vs traditional continuous-time design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern robotic joints require high-bandwidth current control over wide speed/torque ranges, where discretization, communication and computation delays cannot be neglected. Traditional designs discretize after continuous-time design, making delay effects and sampling frequency choices heuristic and potentially suboptimal.

Method: Develop a task-aware, delay-extended discrete-time joint model that explicitly includes physical communication and computation delays. Use this model to synthesize a discrete PI current controller with guaranteed bandwidth and delays. Derive analytical expressions for the minimum sampling frequency, controller gains, and DC-link voltage needed to meet specified performance across the operating envelope. Validate via simulations across dynamic requirements and hardware experiments on a custom robotic joint.

Result: Simulation and hardware results indicate substantially lower sampling frequency and DC-link voltage requirements compared with conventional continuous-time design, while meeting the specified performance across the operating envelope.

Conclusion: The proposed delay-extended, task-aware discrete-time framework provides explicit guarantees on bandwidth and delay, reduces hardware requirements, and is validated both in simulation and real embedded implementation, offering a practical path for robust PMSM current control in dynamic robotic joints.

Abstract: The increasing dynamic demands of modern robotic joints require current controllers to achieve high bandwidth over wide operating ranges of speed, acceleration, and torque, where communication, computation, and discrete-time effects can no longer be neglected. Conventional PMSM current controllers are typically designed in continuous time and subsequently discretized, leaving the sampling frequency and the impact of implementation delays largely to heuristic selection and iterative validation. This paper introduces a task-aware, delay-extended discrete-time joint model that explicitly accounts for physical communication and computation delays and enables direct synthesis of a discrete PI current controller with prescribed bandwidth and delay guarantees throughout the operating envelope. The framework analytically determines the minimum required sampling frequency, controller gains, and DC-link voltage needed to satisfy the specified motor and joint performance. Simulations across a range of dynamic requirements validate the methodology and demonstrate substantially reduced sampling-frequency and DC-link-voltage requirements compared with conventional continuous-time-based design. Experiments on a newly developed custom robotic joint further validate the proposed framework under real embedded implementation conditions.

</details>


### [190] [SkillComposer: Learning Reusable Skills for Natural-Language Robot Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14944)
*John Woods,Hasti Seifi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SkillComposer uses an LLM-based generate-test loop to create robot programs in simulation, with an online library-learning system that compresses recurring function sequences into reusable macro skills, improving success rates and usability for manipulation and caregiving tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lower the barrier to programming robots for complex, multi-step tasks and address LLM weaknesses in decomposition and reuse of prior solutions.

Method: An interactive generate-test loop where an LLM iteratively generates and revises robot programs before execution; successful programs are stored in an online library-learning system that abstracts recurring function sequences into macro skills for future tasks.

Result: Ablation experiments and a user study with 12 participants show evaluator-guided generation and learned abstractions improve success and usability and reduce user effort.

Conclusion: Learning reusable macro skills via an online library-learning system enhances NL robot programming performance and user experience in simulation.

Abstract: Natural-language interfaces can lower the barrier to programming robots, but existing systems struggle when users request complex tasks. While large language models (LLMs) perform well with simple commands, they often struggle to generate code for multi-step tasks, decompose high-level instructions, or reuse prior solutions. We present SkillComposer, an interactive natural-language robot programming system for simulation environments that continually learns reusable program abstractions. SkillComposer uses a generate-test architecture in which an LLM iteratively generates and revises robot programs before execution. Successful programs are stored and processed by an online library-learning algorithm that compresses recurring function sequences into reusable macro skills for future tasks. We evaluate SkillComposer through ablation experiments and a user study with 12 participants to determine its effectiveness on manipulation and robot caregiving tasks. The results show that evaluator-guided generation and learned abstractions improve success rates and usability while reducing user effort in natural-language robot programming.

</details>


### [191] [Evidence of Absence: Cross-Modal Abductive Risk Perception to Sustain World Models When Vision Fails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14952)
*Cong Xu,Ravi Sankar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An abductive, modality-agnostic framework uses acoustic cues to sustain a world-model under degraded vision, achieving earlier hazard alerts and fewer false alarms via a structured multi-modal approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To preserve prediction-critical world-state content when the primary visual modality is occluded or degraded by leveraging complementary auditory evidence and modeling the absence of co-evidence as evidence of hidden causes.

Method: Instantiate an abductive framework acoustically: a microphone-array front-end estimates bearing of engine/tire sources and extracts approach-rate evidence (Doppler if a stable tone exists; broadband looming otherwise). The event “signature present, visual co-evidence absent” triggers abductive inference of a hidden road user, emitting a calibrated risk advisory (not a control command). Recoverability of the hidden state is analyzed via identifiability (shared vs modality-unique information), with cueing cast as Neyman-Pearson detection under a fixed false-alarm budget. Evaluated on real occluded-approach recordings at blind junctions, comparing hazard warning latency, false alarms, localization, calibration, and robustness under degraded vision.

Result: Hazard warnings occur on average 1.7 s before LOS entry; matches the sustained-window variant of a published acoustic baseline in detection rate with 42% fewer false alarms; localization median 3.4° once in view; expected calibration error 0.034; hazard-awareness score >0.87 under vision degradation that collapses a vision-only channel to 0.03; calibration transfers to unseen junctions with minimal loss; the signature classifier does not transfer; moving-ego noise limits deployment.

Conclusion: The abductive, cross-modal approach can sustain hazard awareness under occlusion with improved false-alarm performance and localized outputs, though generalization of the signature classifier and robustness to ego-motion noise are limiting factors.

Abstract: A structured world-state (entities, relations, context, and predictive cues) is designed to preserve prediction-critical content when perception degrades, but it presumes observations to populate it; when the primary visual modality is occluded or degraded, those observations may be missing. We address how to sustain the world model from a complementary modality by treating the absence of expected co-evidence as evidence of a hidden cause. The abductive framework is modality-agnostic; this article instantiates it acoustically. A microphone-array front-end estimates the bearing of engine and tire sources and extracts approach-rate evidence (Doppler when a stable tone exists, a broadband looming readout otherwise); the event "signature present, visual co-evidence absent" then triggers abductive inference of a hidden road user, emitting a calibrated risk advisory rather than a control command. Recoverability of the hidden state is analyzed as an identifiability question separating shared from modality-unique information, and cueing is cast as Neyman-Pearson detection under an explicit false-alarm budget. On real occluded-approach recordings at blind junctions, the method warns a mean 1.7 seconds before line-of-sight entry, matches the sustained-window variant of the published acoustic baseline's detection rate with 42% fewer false alarms, localizes to 3.4 degrees median once in view, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.034), and keeps hazard awareness above 0.87 under staged vision degradation that collapses a vision-only channel to 0.03. We also measure the method's limits: calibration transfers to an unseen junction almost losslessly, the signature classifier does not, and moving-ego noise is the binding deployment constraint.

</details>


### [192] [GaussMemory: Task-Driven 3D Gaussian Scene Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14986)
*Zhiqiang Hu,Shouren Huang,Masatoshi Ishikawa*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Active, end-to-end learned 3D memory (GaussMemory) using Gaussian splatting improves long-horizon manipulation and outperforms strong baselines on LIBERO and VLABench benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon robotic manipulation needs persistent, task-relevant spatial memory. Existing 3D memory systems are passive, treating all elements equally. A memory that learns what to remember and how to update it can better support complex tasks.

Method: Introduce GaussMemory with 3D Gaussian Splatting as a persistent geometric substrate. Jointly learn memory update and readout in an end-to-end framework, enabling bidirectional guidance between task needs and memory strategy. Evaluate on LIBERO (Goal, Long-10) and VLABench (Track 1, Track 6) against MemoryVLA and π0-FAST.

Result: GaussMemory outperforms MemoryVLA on LIBERO Goal and Long-10; on VLABench it surpasses π0-FAST by +5.2% (Track 1) and +6.0% (Track 6).

Conclusion: The paper advocates a shift from passive storage to active, learned memory that jointly optimizes what to remember and how to update it, achieving measurable gains on established benchmarks through the GaussMemory architecture.

Abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally relies on persistent spatial memory. However, existing 3D memory systems function merely as passive recorders: they store observations using fixed, hand-crafted rules, treating every scene element--whether a critical grasp target or an irrelevant background wall--with equal importance. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift from passive storage to active, task-driven spatial memory. We argue that a robot's memory should not simply record what it sees, but actively learn how to remember--discovering which objects to track precisely, how aggressively to update them, and what to discard, all learned end-to-end without hand-designed rules. Crucially, this active paradigm is realized by unifying memory update and readout as two sides of the same cognitive process, enabling bidirectional flow where task needs shape update strategies and vice versa. To instantiate this vision, we introduce GaussMemory, which leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting as a persistent geometric substrate. On LIBERO, GaussMemory outperforms MemoryVLA on Goal and Long-10; on VLABench, it surpasses $π_0$-FAST by +5.2% (Track 1) and +6.0% (Track 6).

</details>


### [193] [HP2-SLAM: Adaptive Hybrid ICP for Robust and Efficient LiDAR SLAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14996)
*Nam Tran,Thu Tran,Hieu Phan,Thai Luu,Toan Nguyen,William J. Beksi,Tuan Dang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HP2-SLAM introduces a planarity-aware adaptive threshold in a neighborhood-size adaptive hybrid ICP, balancing point-to-point and point-to-plane residuals for robust, real-time LiDAR SLAM. It achieves strong generalization without learning or dataset-specific tuning and outperforms geometry-based baselines on public datasets within a full SLAM pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the brittleness of learning-based LiDAR SLAM (training data requirements, compute, generalization gaps) and the weaknesses of traditional ICP in planar or repetitive scenes by devising a geometry-based method that is robust, simple, and efficient.

Method: A neighborhood-size adaptive hybrid ICP with a planarity-aware adaptive threshold that classifies correspondences by local geometry and density, guiding a principled mix of point-to-plane and point-to-point residuals. Integrated into a complete SLAM pipeline with submap management, loop closure detection, and pose graph optimization; no feature engineering, learning, or dataset-specific tuning.

Result: The method consistently outperforms strong geometry-based baselines on publicly available datasets and runs in real time on commodity hardware.

Conclusion: Strategic geometric adaptation—specifically planarity-aware, density-informed thresholding in a hybrid ICP framework—can achieve robustness and generalization without sacrificing simplicity or efficiency.

Abstract: Achieving robustness, accuracy, and efficiency simultaneously remains a central challenge in light detection and ranging (LiDAR) simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). While learning-based approaches deliver strong benchmark performance, they often require extensive training, substantial computational resources, and struggle to generalize to unseen or degenerate environments. Geometry-based methods are efficient and interpretable, yet their performance degrades in planar or repetitive scenes due to limitations of standard iterative closest point (ICP) formulations. We present HP2-SLAM, a minimalist yet robust LiDAR SLAM framework built around a neighborhood-size adaptive hybrid ICP. Our key insight is a planarity-aware adaptive threshold that dynamically classifies correspondences based on local geometric structure and density, thereby enabling a principled balance between point-to-plane and point-to-point residuals. This formulation stabilizes alignment in both structured and degenerate environments without feature engineering, learning modules, or dataset-specific tuning. Integrated into a complete SLAM pipeline with submap management, loop closure detection, and pose graph optimization, HP2-SLAM consistently outperforms strong geometry-based baselines across publicly available datasets while maintaining real-time performance on commodity hardware. Our results demonstrate that carefully designed geometric adaptation can achieve strong generalization and robustness without sacrificing simplicity or efficiency.

</details>


### [194] [NPU Offloading of a Frozen Visual Encoder for Robot Policy Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15002)
*Hyojun Yun,Seungjae Won,Hyungpil Moon*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Offloading a frozen visual encoder to an NPU reduces training energy per sample but increases training time and slightly lowers policy success rate compared with a GPU-only baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether moving the forward pass of a frozen encoder to a low-power accelerator can lower overall energy consumption during policy training, and quantify the trade-offs with training time and policy performance.

Method: An asynchronous CPU/GPU/NPU pipeline was built for an AR-Actor policy: the frozen ResNet18 visual encoder and first encoder layers were offloaded progressively to an Aries2 NPU (INT8) while the FP32 action predictor trained on a GPU (RTX 5060 Ti). Four levels of offloading (L1–L4) were tested against a GPU-only baseline. Each condition trained for 30k steps with three seeds; GPU power vs combined GPU/NPU power tracked energy; training time per sample and peak GPU memory were recorded. Final policies evaluated over 300 seeds and 4,500 rollouts.

Result: Energy per sample decreased 17.1% at L1 (ResNet18 + first encoder layer) and 27.9% at L4 (ResNet18 + all four encoder layers). Training time per sample rose 15.2% (L1) to 37.7% (L4). Peak GPU memory dropped ~19.8–20.7%. Overall success rate: GPU-only 93.33%; NPU conditions 91.44–92.89% (0.44–1.89 percentage points lower).

Conclusion: Offloading a frozen visual encoder to an NPU can reduce training energy but increases training time and slightly reduces policy performance; the choice of offloading level should balance energy constraints with acceptable performance loss.

Abstract: When a robot policy is trained for a new task or dataset, its visual encoder can be frozen and only its action generation module trained, reducing training cost. Freezing removes the encoder's backward pass, but its forward pass must still run at every training step because the input images change, so it keeps consuming GPU compute. We therefore ask whether moving this computation to a low power AI accelerator such as an NPU can reduce total energy despite the added data transfer and longer training time, and how it affects policy performance. We built an asynchronous training pipeline that uses both a GPU and an NPU for the AR-Actor specialist. The frozen visual encoder runs in A8W8 INT8 on a Mobilint Aries2 NPU, while the FP32 action expert is trained on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti GPU. We compared a GPU-only baseline with four conditions, L1 to L4, which gradually extend NPU offloading from one to four Transformer encoder layers. Each condition was trained for 30,000 steps with three random seeds. We measured GPU board power for the GPU-only condition and combined GPU and NPU board power for the NPU conditions. Energy per sample decreased by 17.1% in L1, which offloaded ResNet18 and the first encoder layer, and by 27.9% in L4, which offloaded ResNet18 and all four encoder layers. In contrast, training time per sample increased by 15.2% in L1 and 37.7% in L4, and peak allocated GPU memory decreased by 19.8 to 20.7%. The 15 resulting policies were each evaluated with the same 300 environment seeds, for a total of 4,500 simulator rollouts. The combined success rate was 93.33% for GPU-only and 91.44 to 92.89% for the NPU conditions. These results show that NPU offloading of a frozen visual encoder can reduce training energy, but it increases training time and lowers policy success rate by 0.44 to 1.89 percentage points compared with GPU-only training.

</details>


### [195] [ForceU-VLA: A Force-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model for Embodied Ultrasound Scanning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15009)
*Xingzheng Wu,Cheng Zhang,Guihao Yan,Xifeng Hu,Zhi Liu,Qing Cai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ForceU-VLA combines force-feedback and ultrasound imagery through FUSFM and SAMM to enable stable, high-quality autonomous ultrasound scanning; introduces a large force-aware dataset (ForceU-VLA-Data) with 450 expert trajectories and ~100k multimodal frames across two organs and five views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the weak coupling between force and ultrasound modalities and the lack of scanning-stage awareness, which limit modelling of dynamic probe–tissue interactions during robotic/embodied ultrasound scanning.

Method: Proposes Force-Ultrasound Synergistic Fusion Module (FUSFM) to fuse visual ultrasound and force feedback for stable probe guidance; Stage-Adaptive Modulation Mechanism (SAMM) to adapt multimodal features across scanning stages; introduces ForceU-VLA-Data, a real-world dataset with force, image, and action signals from two organs, five scanning views, 450 expert trajectories and ~100,000 synchronized frames; source code at GitHub.

Result: Experimental results show significant improvements in contact stability and probe pressure regulation, leading to higher-quality ultrasound acquisition, better task execution, and enhanced system reliability.

Conclusion: Demonstrates effectiveness of a force-aware, stage-adaptive embodied ultrasound framework and provides a public dataset and code to facilitate further research and deployment.

Abstract: Embodied intelligent ultrasound scanning enables the automation and standardization of the ultrasound examination process by integrating perception, decision-making, and execution capabilities. However, existing methods suffer from loosely coupled modeling between force and ultrasound modalities and lack awareness of scanning stages, which limits their ability to capture dynamic probe-tissue interactions. To address these issues, we propose ForceU-VLA, a force-aware Vision-Language-Action model for autonomous embodied ultrasound scanning, which leverages force signals and ultrasound image feedback throughout the scanning process to enable accurate and high-quality ultrasound acquisition. Firstly, we propose a Force-Ultrasound Synergistic Fusion Module (FUSFM) that synergistically fuses ultrasound visual and force-feedback information to provide stable, reliable guidance for probe motion. Secondly, a Stage-Adaptive Modulation Mechanism (SAMM) is proposed to accommodate the task requirements across different scanning stages by adaptively modulating multimodal features to enhance their representation quality. Additionally, we introduce ForceU-VLA-Data, a real-world, force-aware embodied ultrasound dataset that integrates visual, force, and action signals, including data from two organs across five representative clinical scanning views, and comprising 450 expert-collected trajectories with approximately 100,000 synchronized multimodal frames. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that ForceU-VLA significantly improves contact stability and probe pressure regulation in embodied ultrasound scanning, thereby effectively enhancing task execution quality and overall system reliability. The source code is available at https://github.com/VMVLab/ForceU-VLA.

</details>


### [196] [MotionGS-SLAM: Event-Modulated Gaussian Splatting for Motion-Blur Robust SLAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15024)
*Zhiqiang Hu,Shouren Huang,Masatoshi Ishikawa*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces MotionGS-SLAM: a blur-forward model for vision-based SLAM that uses event-modulated Gaussian kernels to capture blur formation, enabling joint optimization of intra-exposure camera trajectories and 3D geometry; shows strong gains under severe motion blur.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based SLAM degrades catastrophically with motion blur, and deblurring is ill-posed. A physics-based forward-model leveraging high-temporal-resolution event data can render blur a tractable, information-rich cue.

Method: Model blur formation within the rendering pipeline using an event-modulated Gaussian kernel with spatial modulation (anisotropic, motion-aligned brush strokes) and temporal modulation (exposure sampling density based on velocity). Perform joint optimization of intra-exposure camera trajectories and 3D scene geometry using blur-aware photometric and event-based constraints.

Result: Extensive experiments report significant improvements in trajectory accuracy and map quality under severe high-motion conditions, compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: A physics-based blur model integrated with event data yields robust SLAM under heavy blur, enabling accurate pose and map recovery when traditional vision systems fail.

Abstract: Current Vision-based SLAM systems fail catastrophically when motion blur corrupts the visual input, as they attempt the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering sharp content from degraded observations. We present MotionGS-SLAM, which fundamentally reimagines motion blur handling through a paradigm shift: rather than removing blur artifacts, we reformulate the challenge as a well-constrained forward problem that generatively models blur formation within the rendering pipeline. By leveraging event cameras' microsecond temporal resolution and immunity to motion blur, we introduce a novel event-modulated Gaussian kernel that dynamically adapts each Gaussian's rasterization based on precise motion cues. Our dual-modulation mechanism transforms 2D Gaussian projections from isotropic dots into anisotropic, motion-aligned elliptical brush strokes (spatial modulation) while adaptively varying exposure integral sampling density based on local velocity (temporal modulation). This physics-based approach enables joint optimization of intra-exposure camera trajectories and 3D scene geometry through blur-aware photometric and event-based constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in trajectory accuracy and map quality under severe high-motion conditions.

</details>


### [197] [PACE: Phase-Progress-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Embodied Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15026)
*Chengye Song,Jiawei Zhang,Rui Song,Shengqi Wang,Xiangrong Zhang,Ziyi Wang,Huanbin Zhou,Hongzhou Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PACE introduces a phase-progress-aware credit-assignment approach for long-horizon manipulation, featuring a Global-Local Cooperative Value-Correction Critic (GLC-Critic) and Progressive Policy Distillation (PPD). It enables step-level credit signals and credit-conditioned policy updates, yielding significant gains over baselines in both simulation and real-world robotic arms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon manipulation tasks span hundreds of control steps with success or failure only revealed at episode end. Without step-level credit, policy improvement struggles to differentiate progress from stagnation. Existing post-training methods relying on demonstrations or interactions are insufficient for fine-grained credit signals.

Method: (1) GLC-Critic aggregates visual and motion-difference features within local temporal windows to infer phase and intra-phase progress, applying residual correction to a discretized remaining-cost distribution to enable step-level credit assignment. (2) Progressive Policy Distillation converts credits into positive/negative conditions via task-wise thresholds and trains a credit-conditioned action-generation policy: protect pretrained policy with high-credit positives, then incorporate all credits to learn the quality boundary; inference uses the difference between conditional outputs to amplify high-credit behaviors.
