Result: Extensive simulations and diverse real-world robotic-arm experiments show that PACE consistently achieves significant improvements over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: PACE provides effective credit assignment and policy refinement for long-horizon manipulation, enabling step-level credit signals and credit-conditioned policy updates with robust gains across simulation and real-world tasks.

Abstract: Post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) models typically relies on expert demonstrations and policy interaction trajectories. However, in long-horizon manipulation, a single episode often spans hundreds of control steps and multiple phases, while success or failure is only revealed at episode termination. Policy improvement therefore requires step-level credit signals to distinguish behaviors that advance the task from those that stall or regress. We present PACE, a credit-assignment framework for post-training on long-horizon manipulation, centered on a phase-progress-aware critic. PACE consists of two key modules: (1) the Global-Local Cooperative Value-Correction Critic (GLC-Critic) aggregates visual and motion-difference features within local temporal windows to infer the phase and intra-phase progress of each step, and applies residual correction to a discretized remaining-cost distribution accordingly, enabling step-level credit assignment; (2) Progressive Policy Distillation (PPD) converts credit into positive and negative conditions via task-wise thresholds and trains a credit-conditioned action generation policy: it first protects the pretrained policy with high-credit positive samples, then incorporates all positive and negative credits to learn the quality boundary, and at inference amplifies high-credit behaviors through the difference between conditional outputs. Extensive simulation experiments and diverse real-world robotic-arm experiments demonstrate that PACE consistently achieves significant improvements over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [198] [Max-Q Selective Imitation for Human-in-the-Loop Online Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15088)
*Zihang Wang,Yishan Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-component HIL online RL method combining MC Q-chunk critic with Monte Carlo returns for chunk-level action-value regression and max-Q selective imitation for actor updates, enabling rapid learning from human interventions. Empirically, it achieves near-100% success in minutes on real robots and >96% in ~30 minutes in simulation, outperforming HIL-SERL, EXPO, and E2HiL on success-time frontier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable real-robot, human-in-the-loop RL that quickly leverages interventions while continuing to improve beyond the human prior; tackle credit assignment for interventions and distribution shift due to partial autonomy.

Method: (1) MC Q-chunk critic regresses chunk-level action values onto Monte Carlo returns from the replay buffer, performing sample-average (behavior) policy evaluation so interventions get direct credit. (2) Max-Q selective imitation updates the actor by imitating, at each state, the higher-Q action between the current policy action and a buffer sample under a hard winner-take-all rule, automatically switching learning focus between interventions and on-policy self-improvement. Overall, a standard critic ensemble mean scores candidates; no softening of targets or score-gap thresholds.

Result: Real USB pick-and-insert with 20 demonstrations: 99% success within 30 minutes; HIL-SERL ~5 hours. In simulation on Peg Insertion and Square: ACT/Flow Q-chunk variants ≥96% within ~30 minutes; outperforms HIL-SERL, EXPO, and E2HiL on the success–time frontier.

Conclusion: The proposed ACT QChunk-MCBC approach yields substantially faster convergence and competitive robustness in HIL online RL for robotic tasks, with strong empirical gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

Abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HIL) online reinforcement learning for real robots must absorb human interventions quickly while continuing to improve beyond the human prior. We present a training method for this setting based on two components. First, an \emph{MC Q-chunk} critic regresses chunk-level action values onto Monte Carlo returns from the replay buffer, performing sample-average (behavior) policy evaluation so that intervention trajectories are credited directly rather than diluted by current-policy TD backups. Second, \emph{max-Q selective imitation} updates the actor by imitating, at each state, the higher-$Q$ action between the current policy action and a buffer sample under a hard winner-take-all rule. This rule automatically switches between learning from interventions and on-policy self-improvement: when the autonomous policy is stronger, targets align with the policy distribution, reducing the policy--target-sample gap that otherwise induces execution-time distribution shift. In practice we score candidates with a standard critic ensemble mean to reduce comparison noise, without softening targets or introducing score-gap thresholds. On a real USB pick-and-insertion task with 20 demonstrations, ACT QChunk-MCBC attains 99\% success within 30 minutes of HIL training, whereas HIL-SERL requires about 5 hours to converge. In simulation on Peg Insertion and Square, ACT/Flow Q-chunk variants similarly reach $\ge$96\% success within roughly half an hour of effective training, outperforming HIL-SERL, EXPO, and E2HiL on the success--time frontier.

</details>


### [199] [StructRL: Structured Action-Space Exploration for Flow-Based VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15139)
*Jiarui Yang,Bin Zhu,Jingjing Chen,Na Zou,Yanwei Fu,Jianggang Zhu,Yu-Gang Jiang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Structured Noise Dilution affects in-chain noise; StructRL relocates stochasticity to action space via a deterministic ODE decoder, action-space noise, and last-step replay, yielding better exploration and OOD performance in flow-based VLA with RL across multiple models and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for temporally smooth, action-group-scaled exploration in flow-based VLA for robotics; in-chain noise is ineffective due to dilution and lacks structured correlation.

Method: Three couplings: (i) deterministic ODE-based decoder for the latent flow-to-action mapping; (ii) structured noise injected directly in the action space; (iii) last-step replay to avoid assigning likelihoods to intermediate denoising states during policy-gradient updates.

Result: In three flow-based VLA models and across simulated benchmarks and two real-world tasks, StructRL improves exploration efficiency and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance compared to prior in-chain baselines.

Conclusion: Relocating stochasticity to the action space with structured noise leads to more effective exploration and robust RL adaptation for flow-based VLA; supports broader application and better OOD generalization.

Abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are now widely used for continuous robotic manipulation, and online reinforcement learning (RL) is emerging as a key technique for adapting them to new tasks. Existing RL methods typically inject stochasticity inside the denoising chain, often through isotropic or temporally independent noise. However, effective robot exploration calls for structured noise: temporally smooth and scaled differently across action groups. We show that simply switching the in-chain noise to a structured form does not suffice: noise added at an intermediate flow time can be weakened by the remaining denoising steps before execution, a phenomenon we call \emph{Structured Noise Dilution}. We propose \textbf{StructRL}, which avoids dilution by relocating policy stochasticity to the action space via three coupled choices: (i) a deterministic ODE decoder, (ii) structured noise injected directly in the action space, and (iii) last-step replay, where policy-gradient updates avoid assigning likelihoods to intermediate denoising states. This keeps structured exploration tied to the executed action while providing a tractable training signal for the flow decoder. Across three flow-based VLA models on multiple simulated manipulation benchmarks and two real-world tasks, StructRL improves exploration efficiency and OOD performance over prior in-chain baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured action-space exploration for adapting flow-based VLA with RL. \textbf{Project page:} https://flyfaerss.github.io/structrl/

</details>


### [200] [Low-Rank Dynamics-Effective Latent Carriers for Counterfactual Rollout in Learned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15156)
*Yang Liu,Yuming Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A rank-4 low-rank patch can steer a 192-d hidden-state world model's autonomous rollout along a counterfactual velocity-edit trajectory in a 2D collision task, demonstrating a compact, dynamics-effective intervention interface rather than a fixed intrinsic state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether small, directly addressable hidden-state edits can enforce counterfactual trajectories in learned world models and how such edits propagate during autonomous rollout.

Method: Train a recurrent world model (192-d hidden state) in a two-object, two-dimensional collision environment. Define a local velocity-edit family and verify native representation/rollout of edited futures. Build rank-k carriers from factual-to-counterfactual hidden changes and learn a map from the factual state and requested edit to carrier coefficients. Find the smallest rank (rank-4) that satisfies replication criteria. Apply a single rank-4 patch at an anchor to redirect a 12-step autonomous rollout without future observations or teacher forcing. Test across independent checkpoints and nearby times. Include controls (equal-norm random, wrong-object, wrong-time) and a stress test contrasting intended position edits.

Result: A rank-4 patch suffices to redirect the future for 12 steps during autonomous rollout; the intervention is robust across independently trained models and nearby intervention times; simple randomized/out-of-distribution controls do not explain the effect, though a stress test reveals that not all intended edits guarantee success; interventions are characterized as dynamics-effective rather than mapping to a fixed intrinsic state.

Conclusion: The study identifies a compact, rank-4 intervention interface for velocity edits that can steer the future dynamics of a learned world model during autonomous rollout, challenging the notion of a single latent state dimension governing predictions and highlighting a practical approach to targeted future computation editing.

Abstract: World models may predict the future without making clear which parts of their hidden state actually drive those predictions. We ask whether a small, directly addressable hidden-state change can place a learned world model on the intended counterfactual trajectory and then let the model continue that future on its own. We study a recurrent world model with a 192-dimensional hidden state in a controlled two-object, two-dimensional collision environment. For a bounded family of local velocity edits, we first verify that the model can natively represent and roll out the edited future. We then construct candidate low-rank carriers from training-only factual-to-counterfactual hidden differences and learn a map from the factual state and requested edit to carrier coefficients. On the registered rank grid, rank 4 is the smallest tested rank that satisfies the full development-panel criteria. A single rank-4 patch at the anchor is sufficient to redirect a 12-step autonomous rollout, with no future observations, teacher forcing, or repeated correction. The frozen procedure satisfies the preregistered replication rule across independently trained checkpoints and remains usable across nearby intervention times. Random equal-norm, wrong-object, and wrong-time controls do not explain the effect. A position-edit stress test provides a negative contrast: the intended position patch can pass the raw rollout criteria, but no-patch and random controls can pass the same criteria, and wrong-object specificity is not established. Thus, successful editing alone is not enough. We use dynamics-effective to describe an intervention that changes the model's future computation in a sustained and target-specific way under autonomous rollout. The rank-4 result identifies a compact intervention interface for the tested velocity-edit family, not a closed four-dimensional state or an intrinsic state dimension.

</details>


### [201] [LAPF: LLM-Agent-Based Path Finder Using the UAVScenes Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15175)
*Yousef Emami,Mohammadhossein Homaei,Hao Zhou,Miguel Gutiérrez Gaitán,Atefeh Hajijamali Arani,Rui Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LLM-Agent-Based Path Finder (LAPF) for UAV navigation in town-scale outdoor environments; integrates perception, memory, planning, and action with chain-of-thought reasoning; shows bounded hazard-driven corrections and near-optimal paths with minimal clamp events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of traditional optimization/ML/RL methods in uncertain, outdoor, dynamic environments by enhancing LLM-assisted navigation with agentic capabilities (memory, planning, tool interaction) to improve generalization and adaptability.

Method: Develop LAPF architecture that closes the perception–memory–planning–action loop; leverage prior navigation experiences; enable chain-of-thought reasoning; map detected hazards to bounded corrective actions; dynamically refine waypoint decisions based on environmental feedback; evaluate with three independent trials per method in town-scale outdoor open-field and obstacle-injected scenarios.

Result: Mean path lengths: 512.83 m (open-field) and 506.37 m (obstacle-injected) versus straight-line optimum 497.33 m; path-length reductions of 17.2% and 15.6% relative to CoT prompting; absolute path efficiencies of 97.1% and 98.1%; LAPF uniquely couples every detected hazard to a bounded, metric-neutral corrective action with zero clamp events in both scenarios, while CoT prompting shows 9.7–14.0 events.

Conclusion: LAPF demonstrates enhanced agentic navigation with robust hazard handling and near-goal stability, offering improved generalization and safety over prior LLM-assisted approaches; effective integration of perception, memory, planning, and action in a closed-loop cognitive architecture for UAV navigation.

Abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous navigation in complex outdoor environments, where dynamic conditions and mission requirements require intelligent adaptive decision-making. Existing optimization-based, Machine Learning (ML), and Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches often rely on predefined models or task-specific training, limiting their generalization and adaptability in uncertain scenarios. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted approaches offer promising reasoning capabilities but remain constrained by limited agentic functionality, including insufficient memory, planning, and tool interaction mechanisms.This paper proposes an LLM-Agent-Based Path Finder (LAPF) framework for autonomous UAV navigation in town-scale outdoor environments. LAPF extends LLM-assisted navigation by integrating perception, memory, planning, and action modules into a closed-loop cognitive architecture. The proposed agent leverages prior navigation experiences, performs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, couples each detected hazard to a bounded corrective action, and dynamically refines waypoint decisions based on environmental feedback.The three independent trials per method demonstrate that LAPF achieves mean path lengths of 512.83 m and 506.37 m, compared to the straight-line optimum of 497.33 m, corresponding to path length reductions of 17.2% and 15.6% relative to CoT prompting and absolute path efficiencies of 97.1% and 98.1% in open-field and obstacle-injected scenarios, respectively. Furthermore, LAPF is the only evaluated approach that couples every detected hazard to a bounded, metric-neutral corrective action while maintaining near-goal stability, with zero clamp events in both scenarios, whereas CoT prompting increases from 9.7 to 14.0 events.

</details>


### [202] [Remember Smarter: Visual History Compressor and Hyperbolic Experience Space for Robotic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15269)
*Dai Zhou,Jiexi Yan,Tong Li,Yuxuan Wang,Cheng Deng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RS is a plug-and-play memory module for long-horizon robot policies that combines a visual-history branch with bidirectional spatial Mamba and causal temporal Mamba and an asynchronous hyperbolic experience-memory branch using a Poincare VAE to improve memory retention and experience reuse, boosting LIBERO-Plus performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon robot policies need compact access to recent observations and reusable experience without expanding the Vision-Language-Action context.

Method: Visual-history branch compresses multi-view patch histories via bidirectional spatial Mamba and causal temporal Mamba, exposing memory to action-facing hidden states through residual cross-attention without altering the VLM token stream. Experience branch stores final-layer VLM states in a Poincare VAE space, organizes them hierarchically, and asynchronously converts retrieved experience into geodesic prompt tokens to support action inference.

Result: Adaptation to pi0 yields LIBERO-Plus total success rising from 53.6% to 70.6%, with substantial gains observed in real-robot experiments evaluating memory retention and experience utilization.

Conclusion: RS provides a modular memory-augmentation that integrates compact visual-history and hyperbolic experience memory, enabling improved long-horizon policy performance while preserving the VLA pipeline; demonstrated clear performance gains on standard benchmarks and real-robot tests.

Abstract: Long-horizon robot policies require compact access to recent observations and
  reusable experience without expanding the vision-language-action (VLA)
  context. We introduce Remember Smarter (RS), a plug-and-play module with
  complementary visual-history and hyperbolic experience-memory branches. Its
  visual branch compresses multi-view patch histories using bidirectional
  spatial Mamba and causal temporal Mamba, then exposes the resulting memory to
  action-facing hidden states through residual cross-attention while leaving the
  VLM visual-token stream unchanged. Its experience branch stores successful
  final-layer VLM states in a Poincare VAE space, organizes them hierarchically,
  and asynchronously converts retrieved experience into geodesic prompt tokens
  without blocking action inference. When adapted to pi0, RS increases total
  success on LIBERO-Plus from 53.6% to 70.6% and
  achieves substantial
  performance gains in real-robot experiments designed to evaluate memory
  retention and experience utilization.

</details>


### [203] [VTInstructor: Visual Trajectory Prompting for Navigation Instruction Generation in Continuous Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15284)
*Haolin Yang,Yuxing Long,Zihan Yang,Hao Dong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VTInstructor is a novel VLN instruction-generation framework for continuous environments that converts implicit trajectory geometry from dense ego-centric RGB streams into explicit visual trajectory prompts, enabling state-of-the-art natural language generation and improved downstream navigation without relying on navigation graphs, maps, or scene reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In continuous environments, agent observations are dense RGB streams without explicit trajectory cues or discrete viewpoint graphs, hindering instruction generation and dataset construction. There is a need to bridge perception and language generation without reliance on pre-built maps or scene reconstructions.

Method: EDTC condenses long RGB trajectories into navigation-critical keyframes; VTP overlays path, turn, and goal cues onto anchors; VTMod injects the trajectory signals into the visual encoder; VT-GRPO calibrates spatial injection during training. The framework does not require a navigation graph, pre-built map, or scene reconstruction.

Result: On R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val Unseen benchmarks, VTInstructor achieves state-of-the-art natural-language-generation metrics, surpassing strong baselines by +0.357 CIDEr (R2R-CE) and +0.109 CIDEr (RxR-CE Val Unseen). It raises a frozen follower’s success rate to 63.3% (+14.7 percentage points) and provides consistent data-augmentation gains of +3 SR on downstream navigation tasks.

Conclusion: VTInstructor effectively converts implicit trajectory geometry into explicit visual prompts, enabling high-quality instruction generation in continuous environments without navigation graphs or maps and delivering tangible gains in both NL generation and downstream navigation performance.

Abstract: Navigation instruction generation from ego-centric RGB video in continuous environments is an important yet challenging task for human-robot interaction and scalable dataset construction. Prior instruction generators assume discrete viewpoint graphs with panoramic observations, where trajectory structure is explicit; in continuous environments, however, the agent receives only a dense RGB stream, making trajectory cues difficult to recover. We propose VTInstructor, the first VLN instruction generation framework for continuous environments. Our key idea is to convert implicit trajectory geometry into explicit visual trajectory prompts: EDTC condenses long RGB trajectories into navigation-critical keyframes, VTP overlays path, turn, and goal cues onto these anchors, VTMod injects the resulting trajectory signals into the visual encoder, and VT-GRPO further calibrates this spatial injection during training, all without requiring a navigation graph, pre-built map, or scene reconstruction. On the challenging R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val Unseen benchmarks, VTInstructor sets a new state of the art across all standard NLG metrics, surpassing the strongest baseline by +0.357 CIDEr and +0.109 CIDEr, respectively. Beyond automatic metrics, VTInstructor-generated instructions raise a frozen follower's success rate to 63.3%, a +14.7 percentage-point gain over the best competing instruction source, and provide consistent data augmentation gains of +3 SR points on downstream navigation tasks.

</details>


### [204] [PhaseLoRA: Control-Regime-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation for Continuous-Action Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15285)
*Yufei Guo,Yinan Wu,Haoran Duan,Guiguang Ding,Jungong Han*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PhaseLoRA introduces a phase-aware, lightweight LoRA-based PEFT for continuous-action VLA policies that modulates the adaptation direction over action chunks using two weakly supervised descriptors. It yields large gains on LIBERO and outperforms higher-rank baselines, with ablations confirming the necessity of temporal conditioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitation of temporally static PEFT adapters in continuous-action manipulation where control regimes change over a rollout (approach, contact, grasp, transport, placement), requiring phase-dependent adaptation.

Method: PhaseLoRA adds a time-conditioned modulation of the LoRA left factor at each action-chunk prediction by using two weakly supervised descriptors (fine-control tendency and event/boundary intensity). The backbone remains frozen while the effective low-rank update direction varies over time, enabling phase-aware adaptation without large parameter overhead.

Result: On LIBERO, PhaseLoRA improves average success rate by 12.2 points over a matched-parameter high-rank LoRA baseline and surpasses stronger LoRA variants. Ablations show random temporal modulation and scalar gating fail to reproduce full performance; update-direction analyses reveal structured temporal variation aligned with the predicted descriptors.

Conclusion: Within-trajectory (phase) conditioning is an effective, lightweight PEFT axis for continuous-action VLA policies, enabling better performance with small parameter overhead through temporally-varying adaptation.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is a natural way to adapt pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but most adapter designs apply temporally static updates throughout a control rollout, overlooking the phase-dependent nature of continuous-action manipulation. Such policies traverse distinct regimes, including approach, contact transition, grasping, transport, and placement, each requiring different adaptation behaviors. We propose \textbf{PhaseLoRA}, a lightweight LoRA parameterization that conditions adaptation at each action-chunk prediction step using two weakly supervised descriptors: fine-control tendency and event/boundary intensity. PhaseLoRA modulates the LoRA left factor in the action expert, allowing the effective low-rank update direction to vary over time while keeping the backbone largely frozen. On LIBERO, PhaseLoRA improves average success rate by 12.2 points over a matched-parameter high-rank LoRA baseline and outperforms stronger LoRA variants. Ablations show that random temporal modulation and scalar gating do not reproduce the performance of the full model, while update-direction analyses reveal structured temporal variation associated with the predicted control descriptors. These results establish within-trajectory conditioning as an effective lightweight PEFT axis for continuous-action VLA policies.

</details>


### [205] [SCORE: Shape-Conforming Regions for Flight in Enclosed, Degraded Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15289)
*Eric Minwoo Kim,Jong-Kook Kim*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Non-convex, shape-conforming keep-out regions for UAVs in confined spaces using a nonconformity score on a signed distance field, enabling distribution-free coverage guarantees and better preservation of usable free space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enclosed environments degrade perception, making conservative convex keep-out regions inflate and occlude narrow passages. A distribution-free guarantee is desirable to bound perception error and safety under uncertainty.

Method: Define a nonconformity score on the signed distance field (SDF) to produce a non-convex keep-out that follows obstacle geometry. Enhance usability with: (1) voxelwise union of complementary sensor observations to certify voxels missed by any single sensor; (2) adaptive margin around obstacles that accounts for measured visibility without requiring weather labels or online ground-truth feedback.

Result: On real subterranean data, the proposed approach retains more usable free space than convex baselines at the same certified coverage and yields safer closed-loop flight.

Conclusion: Distribution-free, shape-conforming keep-out enables safer UAV navigation in cluttered, perceptually challenging environments by avoiding unnecessary bulging and better preserving free space under uncertainty.

Abstract: Autonomous UAVs enter enclosed environments such as caves and collapsed structures that confine the vehicle and degrade perception. Conformal prediction provides a distribution-free guarantee by calibrating how far an obstacle keep-out must expand to absorb perception error at a target coverage level. However, existing keep-out regions use convex primitives whose bulges consume narrow passages and grow as perception degrades. Our main contribution defines the nonconformity score on a signed distance field (SDF). This produces a non-convex keep-out that tightly follows obstacle geometry and avoids the unnecessary bulging of equal-margin convex regions. Two supporting components keep this geometry usable as perception degrades. First, a voxelwise union of complementary sensor observations certifies voxels that any single sensor misses. Second, the margin around the obstacle adapts to measured visibility without weather labels or the online ground-truth feedback that single-pass flight cannot provide. Results on real subterranean data show that the resulting distribution-free, shape-conforming keep-out retains more usable free space than convex baselines at the same certified coverage, and produces safer closed-loop flight.

</details>


### [206] [MM-BEV: Enhancing Timeliness by Computing Where and When it Matters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15437)
*Liangkai Liu,Kang G. Shin*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MM-BEV is a real-time multimodal BEV system that prioritizes safety-critical perception to reduce compute. It introduces four mechanisms (temporal ROI selector, ROI-aware feature extraction with sparse voxelization, latency-aware coordination, asynchronous scheduling) to compute where and when it matters. It achieves ~2x–3x latency reductions on nuScenes and a real robot setup, with negligible loss in geometry-critical recall and minimal drop in safety-critical recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high computational cost of multimodal BEV perception and real-time deployment challenges by exploiting three overlooked opportunities: structured sparsity in inputs, timing misalignment between modalities, and the fact that many detections do not influence immediate planner actions.

Method: 1) Criticality-ranked temporal ROI selector using motion-extrapolated detections from prior frames; 2) Sparse, ROI-aware feature extraction with shared-shape camera crops at context-adaptive resolution and ROI-aware LiDAR voxelization; 3) Latency-aware coordinator that adapts LiDAR sweeps, image resolution, and keyframes to scene dynamics and TTC; 4) Asynchronous scheduler that decouples sensing from inference and skips stale frames.

Result: On nuScenes, MM-BEV reduces inference latency by 1.96x and end-to-end latency by 2.93x, with no loss in geometry-critical recall and only a 0.2 percentage-point drop in safety-critical recall. On a Clearpath Husky A300 with Ouster-128 LiDAR, BEV cameras, and Jetson AGX Orin, mean latency reduced by 2.11x, demonstrating real-world viability.

Conclusion: MM-BEV demonstrates that safety-critical, real-time multimodal BEV is feasible by prioritizing mandatory work and leveraging structured sparsity, temporal ROI, and latency-aware coordination. The approach achieves substantial latency reductions with minimal impact on critical recall, indicating practical potential for real autonomous systems.

Abstract: Multimodal bird's-eye-view (BEV) perception combines LiDAR depth accuracy with dense camera semantics, but its high computational cost and imperfect sensing conditions make real-time deployment challenging. Existing methods largely compress individual detectors and overlook three opportunities: structured sparsity within camera and LiDAR inputs, timing misalignment between modalities, and the fact that many detected objects do not affect the planner's immediate action. We present MM-BEV, a real-time multimodal BEV system guided by a simple principle: compute where and when it matters. MM-BEV divides perception into mandatory work for safety-critical objects within braking distance of the ego vehicle and with short time-to-collision (TTC), and optional work for less urgent regions. It prioritizes mandatory work and reduces or sheds optional work under tight compute budgets. MM-BEV integrates four mechanisms: (1) a criticality-ranked temporal ROI selector based on motion-extrapolated detections from prior frames; (2) sparse, ROI-aware feature extraction using shared-shape camera crops at context-adaptive resolution and ROI-aware LiDAR voxelization; (3) a latency-aware coordinator that adapts LiDAR sweeps, image resolution, and keyframes according to scene dynamics and TTC; and (4) an asynchronous scheduler that decouples sensing from inference and skips stale frames. On nuScenes, MM-BEV reduces inference latency by 1.96x and end-to-end latency by 2.93x, with no loss in geometry-critical recall and only a 0.2 percentage-point drop in safety-critical recall. On a Clearpath Husky A300 equipped with an Ouster-128 LiDAR, BEV cameras, and a Jetson AGX Orin, MM-BEV further reduces mean latency by 2.11x, demonstrating its potential for real-world autonomous systems.

</details>


### [207] [Accelerating Mixed Discrete-Continuous Motion Planning via Neural Graphs of Convex Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15440)
*Ananya Trivedi,Sarvesh Prajapati,Mohamed Khalid M Jaffar,Zhexin Xu,David Rosen,Taskin Padir*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Learning-accelerated Graph of Convex Sets for motion planning via Graph Attention Networks to predict candidate paths and a ranking network to select near-optimal plans, enabling large speedups in online replanning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GCS yields discrete-graph-based optimization that couples discrete decisions with continuous trajectories but is computationally heavy for online replanning.

Method: Replace costly convex relaxation in GCS with a Graph Attention Network producing candidate paths; a lightweight ranking network orders by estimated cost; evaluate in that order and stop early.

Result: Achieves up to 100x speedups over nominal GCS with 100% success across convex/non-convex settings; near-optimal suboptimality; validated on 3D quadrotor, 7-DoF manipulator, planar pushing.

Conclusion: Learning-based pruning provides real-time capable GCS planning while maintaining high success; code at provided URL.

Abstract: Motion planning problems such as collision-free navigation and contact-rich manipulation can be naturally formulated as optimization problems that couple discrete decisions with continuous trajectories. The Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) framework offers a practical solution to these problems. It represents discrete decisions as nodes of a graph and encodes continuous trajectories in the edges connecting them. However, the resulting optimization subproblems can become computationally prohibitive for online replanning.
  In this work, we propose a learning-based strategy to mitigate this limitation. Specifically, we replace the costly convex relaxation step required by nominal GCS with a single forward pass through a Graph Attention Network that predicts a set of highly probable candidate paths through the graph. A lightweight ranking network then orders these candidates by their estimated trajectory cost. Evaluating them in this order, we terminate our search early while still recovering a near-optimal motion plan. We validate the resulting pipeline across diverse robotic tasks, including collision-free motion planning for a 3D quadrotor and a 7-DoF manipulator, and planning through contact for planar pushing. Across both convex and non-convex cost and constraint settings, our approach yields up to two orders of magnitude speedup over nominal GCS while maintaining a 100% success rate, at the cost of some suboptimality in the recovered solutions. Code implementations and video demonstrations can be found at https://neural-gcs.github.io/.

</details>


### [208] [GUIDER: Evaluating Goal-Free Human Intent Inference for Teleoperated Manipulation on Real-Robot Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15446)
*Nicholas Kenny,Cesar Alan Contreras,Basile Ouedraogo,Rustam Stolkin,Manolis Chiou,Maria Kyrarini*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GUIDER, a goal-free probabilistic framework, is evaluated for human intent inference in robotic manipulation. On robotic-arm data, online updates and constraints are used. Across 20 steps in 3 scenarios (tea, medicine), it always included the correct grasp-candidate set, with a time-to-confident-prediction of 3.7 s, time before first grasp 49.6 s, prediction stability 96.4%, and perceptual-phase runtimes ~4.5 s (mean 4.857 s, median 4.474 s).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess accuracy and efficiency of intent inference during assistive manipulation; enable reliable human-robot collaboration by predicting grasp-relevant intents.

Method: Deploy GUIDER on robotic-arm data; incorporate online probability updates, workspace limits, support-plane filtering, and a grasping mode prioritizing feasible grasp regions; preserve original temporal conditions; evaluate in three manipulation scenarios across 20 steps.

Result: In all cases, the intended grasp was within the correct candidate set; showed rapid and stable predictions; quantified timings and runtime.

Conclusion: GUIDER demonstrates effective, timely intent inference in manipulation tasks with robust performance metrics; supports efficient assistive robotics, though generalizability beyond the tested scenarios remains to be demonstrated.

Abstract: This paper presents an evaluation of a goal-free probabilistic framework for human intent inference during robotic manipulation. We deploy the Global User Intent Dual-phase Estimation for Robots (GUIDER) on data collected from a robotic arm to test the manipulation phase across various assistance scenarios, including making tea and fetching medicine. To support operation, we add online probability updates, workspace limits, support-plane filtering, and a grasping mode that prioritizes feasible grasp regions, all of which are tested on the recorded data while preserving its original temporal conditions. Across 20 manipulation steps in three scenarios, GUIDER estimated human intent within the correct grasp-candidate set in all cases and achieved a time to confident prediction of 3.7 s, a remaining time before first grasp of 49.6 s, a prediction stability of 96.4%, and a runtime of 4.857/4.474 s (mean/median) per perceptual phase of intent.

</details>


### [209] [Detachable Wire Drive : Reconfigurable Robot Architecture with Shared Actuators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15461)
*Takahiro Hattori,Kento Kawaharazuka,Kei Okada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes Detachable Wire Drive for sharing heavy actuators across multiple morphologies; uses a Wire Detach Unit to split/reconnect drive paths; validated with a 2-DOF rigid arm, a continuum arm, and two grippers, showing reliable detachment and seamless switching between configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional modular robots require dedicated actuators for each module, increasing weight, volume, and cost. Sharing heavy/expensive actuators across morphologies aims to improve efficiency and versatility.

Method: Introduce a Wire Detach Unit that physically splits and reconnects wire drive paths so motors can be consolidated into a common base. Develop and demonstrate three interchangeable modules (2-DOF rigid arm, continuum arm, two grippers) attached to a single shared actuator set, along with a control framework to manage configuration transitions.

Result: Experimental validation shows mechanical reliability of the detachment/reconnection process and that the control framework can seamlessly manage transitions between configurations, confirming the viability of a shared-actuator reconfigurable system.

Conclusion: Detachable Wire Drive enables more efficient, multi-functional robotic systems by centralizing actuators while preserving modularity; supports scalability to additional morphologies and tasks.

Abstract: Reconfigurable robots offer significant potential for adapting to diverse tasks; however, conventional centralized architectures often require dedicated actuators for each module, leading to substantial increases in overall system weight, volume, and cost. To address these challenges, this paper presents the "Detachable Wire Drive," a reconfigurable robotic system that enables the sharing of heavy and expensive actuators across various morphologies. The core of this system is the "Wire Detach Unit," a mechanism designed to physically split and reconnect wire drive paths, allowing motors to be consolidated into a common base unit. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by developing a 2-DOF rigid arm, a continuum arm, and two distinct grippers, all of which are interchangeably attached to, and driven by, a single shared actuator set. Experimental results validate the mechanical reliability of the detachment process and the control framework's ability to seamlessly manage transitions between configurations, highlighting a path toward more efficient and multi-functional robotic systems.

</details>


### [210] [Vision-Based Tactile Intelligence for Robotics: Sensing, Learning, and Embodied Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15490)
*Peng Zhou,Jun Hu,Sihan Chen,Zeqing Zhang,Haofei Ma,Zhenyu Lu,Sichao Liu,Xueqian Wang,Pai Zheng,Xiang Li,Shan Luo,Jia Pan,David Navarro-Alarcon,Chenguang Yang,Michael Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey of vision-based tactile sensors (VBTSs) that treats sensing hardware, learning methods, simulation, and datasets as an integrated system, providing a hardware taxonomy, a hierarchical view of learning from low-level signals to policies, and discussion of simulation/datasets with sim-to-real transfer and cross-sensor adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome sparse, low-dimensional tactile data from conventional sensors by leveraging high-resolution image-based tactile observations, enabling richer perception and control in contact-rich robotic tasks.

Method: The paper organizes VBTS literature into a hardware taxonomy (elastomer design, sensor geometry, and optical configuration), presents a hierarchical learning framework from signal understanding to task policies and foundation models, and surveys simulation platforms and tactile datasets, including cross-sensor adaptation and sim-to-real transfer, to propose an integrated sensing-and-learning system.

Result: A structured, holistic framework that guides sensor design, AI methods, simulation, and data collection; identifies how hardware choices influence learning capabilities and transferability, and collates open challenges in coherent, scalable tactile intelligence for robotics.

Conclusion: The review advances tactile intelligence by connecting hardware, AI architectures, simulation, and datasets, outlining open challenges and directions to accelerate development of VBTS-driven perception and manipulation in contact-rich tasks.

Abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for robots in contact-rich tasks, yet many tactile sensors still provide sparse, low-dimensional signals that do not capture sufficient information for complex robotic perception and interaction. Vision-based tactile sensors (VBTSs) offer a powerful alternative by con-verting contact-induced deformation of a soft interface into im-ages. The image-based formulation gives VBTSs high-resolution, information-rich tactile observations that enable complex robotic tasks. This review surveys the full VBTS pipeline and treats sensing hardware, learning methods, simulation, and datasets as an integrated sensing-and-learning system. We 1) organize representative VBTSs into a hardware taxonomy structured by deformable elastomer design, sensor size and shape, and optical system design to guide future sensor development; 2) present a hierarchical view of learning-based tactile intelligence from low-level signal understanding to task-level policies and foundation models; and 3) examine simulation platforms and tactile datasets as a scaling layer, together with sim-to-real transfer and cross-sensor adaptation for training, benchmarking, and deployment. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions for VBTSs in robotics. By providing a holistic view of how hardware, AI architectures, simulation, and datasets interact, this review aims to advance tactile intelligence for contact-rich robotic tasks.

</details>


### [211] [Temporal Logic Guided Universal Task Representations for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15509)
*Hao Zhang,Zhangli Zhou,Zhen Kan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR:  LOTUS is a temporal logic–inspired universal task representation framework for RL. It uses LTL formulas to model task relationships, treats the LTL encoder as a policy for updates, and employs the bisimulation metric for theoretical guarantees and robustness. Empirically, it improves learning efficiency, generalization, and representation quality across diverse tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve generalizable task representations that work across diverse environments and task structures while avoiding degradation from gradient signals in RL controllers.

Method: Develop a task representation architecture that extracts semantics from Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas, integrates an update mechanism that views the LTL encoder as a policy, and uses the bisimulation metric to guarantee behavioral equivalence, optimality fidelity, and trajectory robustness.

Result: LOTUS accelerates convergence by over 20% in single-task scenarios, yields 15–45% higher success rates on unseen manipulation tasks, and improves generalization by over 25% in complex multi-task environments with deeper sub-goals and conjunctions.

Conclusion: LOTUS provides a universal, robust task representation framework compatible with any RL algorithm, offering theoretical guarantees via bisimulation and demonstrated empirical gains in efficiency and generalization; code and resources are publicly available.

Abstract: Task guided agents demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of complex tasks. However, most existing task representation algorithms are tailored to specific contexts and struggle to generalize across diverse scenarios. Moreover, they typically depend on gradient signals from reinforcement learning controllers to update their weights, which can degrade both representation quality and learning efficiency. To overcome these limitations, we propose LOTUS, a temporal logic inspired universal task representation framework that can be seamlessly integrated into any RL algorithm to enhance agent performance across diverse task settings. Specifically, we design a novel task representation architecture capable of modeling relationships and extracting task semantics from LTL formulas. We further introduce a more effective update mechanism that treats the LTL encoder as a policy, thereby improving representation capacity. To enhance stability and robustness, LOTUS leverages the bisimulation metric, which provides theoretical guarantees for LTL representation, including behavioral equivalence, optimality fidelity, and trajectory robustness. Experimental results show that LOTUS outperforms most existing methods in learning efficiency, generalization capability, and representation quality. Specifically, LOTUS accelerates convergence over 20% in single-task scenarios, achieves a 15%-45% higher success rate in unseen manipulation tasks, and improves generalization performance over 25% in complex multi-task environments with increased sub-goal depth or conjunctions. The corresponding code, videos, and appendix are available at: https://lotus-website.github.io/.

</details>


### [212] [Degenerate in Whose Frame? An Equivariance Condition for Degeneracy Detection in LiDAR Registration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15532)
*Yujie Zhang,Chunlei Zhao,Yuzong Lin,Yuxuan Guo,Xiaohui Jia,Jinyue Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Per-axis degeneracy labels for LiDAR registration are not robust scene properties; only an equivariant, body-frame-independent metric (M = sum J_i^T J_i) yields stable, scale-invariant degeneracy information; empirical labels change with frame choice, and remapping corrections differ.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether per-axis degeneracy labels are intrinsic to the scene and derive an invariant degeneracy criterion.

Method: Theoretically analyze how the information matrix H transforms under body-frame changes (congruence vs similarity), use adjoint reparameterization, and formulate Hv = lambda Mv. Identify when the metric is equivariant and define M = sum_i J_i^T J_i. Empirically test across 365 frame pairs from four public sequences, examining label stability and remapping corrections.

Result: Congruence preserves nullity but does not preserve per-axis labels; degeneracy thresholds are not frame-invariant. A rigid-body tuned metric exists only at zero screw pitch. The equivariant metric M yields dimensionless, scale-invariant, frame-independent generalized eigenvalues; threshold transfers empirically across sequences. However, across data, per-axis footprints still vary; remapping corrections differ by body-frame choice in 44.5–69.5% of pairs (median 0.7–4.0 mm, max 0.87 m).

Conclusion: The reported per-axis degeneracy labels are not inherently frame-independent; only an equivariant, rig-adapted metric provides a robust degeneracy criterion. The root issue lies in the reporting quantity (per-axis labels) rather than the threshold magnitude; adopting an equivariant metric and reporting its eigenstructure is recommended for robust LiDAR registration degeneracy analysis.

Abstract: Degeneracy detectors for LiDAR registration commonly return six per-axis binary labels. We ask whether these labels are properties of the scene. Under a body-frame change, the point-to-plane information matrix transforms by congruence, H' = Ad(T)^T H Ad(T), not similarity. Congruence preserves nullity and, through the adjoint reparameterization, identifies the same physical twist subspace; the per-axis footprint and a thresholded spectrum need not be invariant. In a noise-free circular tunnel, shifting the origin by one metre changes which degrees of freedom are flagged. A generalized criterion Hv = lambda Mv is universally frame-independent over positive-semidefinite information forms if and only if its metric rule is equivariant. No fixed metric qualifies, while a rig-adapted one exists only at zero screw pitch, met in one of nineteen surveyed calibrations. The equivariant point-displacement metric M = sum_i J_i^T J_i yields dimensionless, scene-scale-invariant generalized eigenvalues. They are invariant to body frame, consistent changes of length unit and scene scales; the threshold also transfers empirically across sequences. Across 365 frame pairs from four public sequences, labels rarely change at practical extrinsic magnitudes, yet a remapping estimator's correction differs between body-frame choices on 44.5-69.5% of pairs, with a median of 0.7-4.0 mm and a maximum of 0.87 m. The per-axis footprint changes even under the equivariant metric, placing the fundamental issue in the reported quantity.

</details>


### [213] [Contact Modes Are Strata: What Geometric Structure Buys in Discrete-Continuous Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15541)
*Phone Thiha Kyaw,Jonathan Kelly*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Treat contact modes as actual strata in configuration space and plan as a walk over strata with within-stratum geodesics; enables fast integrated discrete-continuous planning for contact-rich manipulation without pre-specified contact sequences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the discrete-continuous coupling in contact-rich manipulation by making contact mode changes explicit as-dimensional structure in the planning problem.

Method: Model the configuration space as a stratified space where each contact mode is a stratum; plan paths that traverse strata, with segments within a stratum being geodesics; no mode/contact sequence is fixed in advance.

Result: In two simulated tasks, the planner returns solutions within seconds without requiring any a priori mode, contact sequence, or stratum specification.

Conclusion: Viewing contact mode changes as actual strata and planning as a walk over strata with geodesic segments provides an effective, mode-agnostic framework for fast planning in contact-rich manipulation.

Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a discrete question and a continuous one at once, namely which contacts are active and how to move while they hold. The two are coupled by a change of dimension, since each contact that a robot maintains confines its motion to a lower-dimensional manifold. We make that coupling the explicit object of planning by observing that a contact mode is not merely analogous to a stratum of the configuration space; it is one. A plan is then a walk over strata whose within-stratum segments are geodesics. On two contact-rich manipulation tasks in simulation, pushing a T-shaped block around obstacles and reorienting a cube in a dexterous hand, our planner returns solutions within seconds with no mode, contact sequence, or stratum given in advance.

</details>


### [214] [MistyPilot: Enabling Social-Robot Control through Multi-Agent LLM Skill Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15549)
*Xiao Wang,Lu Dong,Ifeoma Nwogu,Srirangaraj Setlur,Venu Govindaraju*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A hierarchical multi-agent LLM system, MistyPilot, routes natural-language instructions to two specialized agents (Physically Interactive Agent and Social Interaction Agent) via a Task Router to orchestrate Misty robot skills; shows high accuracy and user-perceived usability; code to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the integration gap between natural-language instructions and diverse, real-time robotic behaviors. Interactive tasks require blending reactive physical control with stateful social dialogue; existing interfaces demand manual API composition and runtime state management.

Method: Proposes a two-agent architecture guided by a Task Router: Physically Interactive Agent handles sensor-triggered control and direct skill invocation; Social Interaction Agent manages dialogue-oriented task-state management and multimodal response generation. Social Agent reuses previous results when possible and performs full generation otherwise. Evaluated on five component-level suites with real hardware, plus a preliminary 12-participant user study; scalability up to ~100 skills.

Result: Mist yPilot achieves high accuracy on routing, sensor-skill binding, task-state parsing, and result reuse; lower variance than a single-agent baseline; participants report positive usability and interaction quality; code will be publicly available.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility and benefits of multi-agent LLM orchestration for social robots, enabling scalable skill composition and efficient interaction management. Provides groundwork for broader deployment, though further large-scale validation and generalization to other robots are warranted.

Abstract: Programming small social robots from natural-language instructions requires more than invoking isolated APIs. Interactive tasks combine reactive physical behaviors with stateful social behaviors, while existing interfaces often require developers to manually compose APIs into skills, configure their parameters, bind sensor events to skills, and manage task states at runtime. We present MistyPilot, a multi-agent LLM framework that interprets high-level natural-language instructions and orchestrates the corresponding skills on the Misty social robot. A Task Router dispatches each instruction to one of two specialized agents: a Physically Interactive Agent for sensor-triggered robot control and direct skill invocation, and a Social Interaction Agent for dialogue-oriented task-state management and context-dependent multimodal response generation. To improve efficiency, the Social Interaction Agent reuses previously generated results when applicable and invokes full generation otherwise. We evaluate MistyPilot on five component-level suites, with sensor bindings and skill invocations executed on the physical Misty robot, and a preliminary user study with 12 participants. MistyPilot attains high accuracy on routing, sensor-skill binding, task-state parsing, result reuse, and skill extension up to 100 skills, and lower variance than an otherwise identical single-agent baseline, while participants report positive perceptions of usability and interaction quality. The code will be made publicly available via the project page.

</details>


### [215] [ReForce: Learning Force-aware Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15560)
*Yuhang Wu,Lingqi Zeng,Changwei Jing,Jianglong Ye,Xiaolong Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ReForce introduces a force-aware retargeting framework that adds a residual force predictor to kinematic retargeting, improving contact accuracy and manipulation on force-driven tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The embodiment gap between human demonstrations and robot actuation is prominent because manipulation is governed by contact forces, not just kinematics. Existing retargeting is mostly kinematic and may miss necessary force interactions for dexterous manipulation.

Method: A general force tracker trained on large-scale simulation interactions predicts a residual on the kinematically retargeted action to achieve the desired contact force. This enables online force-aware teleoperation and offline data translation, and the predictor aligns robot hand forces with intended contacts.

Result: In both simulation and real hardware, ReForce yields lower force-tracking error and stronger multi-finger contact engagement on contact-rich tasks such as paper-cup grasping and tongs manipulation.

Conclusion: Incorporating force-aware residuals into retargeting bridges the embodiment gap, enabling more faithful reproduction of human intent in contact-rich manipulation and supporting both real-time teleoperation and offline data translation.

Abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable data source for dexterous manipulation, but transferring them to robot actions remains challenging due to the embodiment gap. Today's retargeting is mostly kinematic, yet manipulation is decided by force, which governs how the hand interacts with the object and how the object moves. In this paper, we present ReForce, a Force-aware Retargeting method that turns human motion and forces into robot actions that reproduce the intended contact. ReForce predicts a residual on the kinematically retargeted action to reach the desired force, using a general force tracker trained on large-scale simulation interactions. It supports both online force-aware teleoperation and offline data translation. In simulation and on real hardware, ReForce achieves lower force-tracking error and stronger multi-finger contact engagement on contact-rich tasks such as paper-cup grasping and tongs manipulation.

</details>


### [216] [Not All History Helps: Velocity-Aware Selective Memory for Long-Horizon End-to-End Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15573)
*Yuchen Liu,Ziying Song,Shengkai Zhang,Jiannan Chen,Peiliang Wu,Lei Yang,Bin Sun,Yan Gong,Li Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: StableDrive introduces Selective Momentum Memory (SMM) and Motion-Stage Training Scaffold (MSTS) to stabilize long-horizon planning for autonomous driving, achieving state-of-the-art results on nuScenes MomAD, LT-nuScenes, and NAVSIM without extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper targets unreliable priors from self-generated history and within-horizon motion-stage evolution. Existing methods rely on historical planning states as temporal context, which can become stale or conflict with the current motion stage, hindering long-horizon planning.

Method: Propose Selective Momentum Memory (SMM) implemented via a Mamba selective state-space operator to regulate the influence of the previous self-predicted planning state; introduce Motion-Stage Training Scaffold (MSTS) that uses motion-stage, long-horizon trajectory, and longitudinal-motion supervision to guide stage-aware motion learning; MSTS is removed at inference; a fixed parameter midpoint between two architecture-aligned endpoints yields a deployable single SMM planner without ensembling or extra inference cost.

Result: On nuScenes under the MomAD protocol, StableDrive achieves state-of-the-art performance across planning metrics from 1 to 6 s, reducing average collision rate by 23.3%, TPC by 30.9%, and L2 by 11.8% over the previous best for each metric. On LT-nuScenes, it reduces 6-s collision rate by 23.81%, TPC by 10.90%, and L2 by 6.37%. On NAVSIM v1 and v2, it attains the highest PDMS/EPDMS in all three reported settings, including a 5.7-point EPDMS gain on v2 navhard over the prior best.

Conclusion: StableDrive delivers robust, deployable long-horizon planning by stabilizing cross-cycle history and leveraging stage-aware learning, achieving consistent SOTA performance across diverse autonomous-driving benchmarks without additional inference-time computation.

Abstract: Reliable long-horizon planning remains a key challenge in end-to-end autonomous driving. By accounting for future motion evolution and potential consequences, it provides forward-looking guidance for safe and consistent driving in evolving traffic environments. Existing methods use historical planning states as temporal context. Self-generated history may become stale or conflict with the current motion stage, introducing unreliable priors. We propose StableDrive to address cross-cycle historical reliability and within-horizon motion-stage evolution. Selective Momentum Memory (SMM), implemented with a Mamba selective state-space operator, controls the influence of the preceding self-predicted planning state on the current cycle. Motion-Stage Training Scaffold (MSTS) uses motion-stage, long-horizon trajectory, and longitudinal-motion supervision to guide stage-aware future motion learning and is removed before inference. A fixed parameter midpoint between two architecture-aligned endpoints yields a single deployable SMM planner without model ensembling or extra inference-time computation. On nuScenes under the MomAD evaluation protocol, StableDrive achieves SOTA performance across all reported planning metrics from 1 to 6 s, reducing average collision rate by 23.3%, TPC by 30.9%, and L2 by 11.8% over the best previously reported value for each metric. On the curated Longitudinal-Transition nuScenes (LT-nuScenes), StableDrive reduces 6-s collision rate by 23.81%, TPC by 10.90%, and L2 by 6.37%. On NAVSIM v1 and v2, StableDrive achieves the highest PDMS/EPDMS in all three reported settings, including a 5.7-point EPDMS gain on v2 navhard over the previous best.

</details>


### [217] [Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Efficient VLA Inference via Speculative Inference and Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15636)
*Chunyu Qi,Zhuoran Song,Jian Weng,Haozhe Jiang,Xueyuan Liu,Naifeng Jing,Guanghui He,Xiaoyao Liang,Haibing Guan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SpecVLA introduces a state-aware, algorithm-system co-design to extend action length and reduce latency in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) for robotics by speculative long-horizon predictions in inactive states with a lightweight verifier (sVLA), aided by a heterogeneous GPU+robotic accelerator and speculative dataflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models are computationally heavy and have short predictive action lengths, hindering real-time robotic deployment. Exploiting the natural active/inactive interaction patterns of robotic environments can improve efficiency without sacrificing reliability.

Method: 1) State-aware VLA inference paradigm; 2) Construct a smaller verifier model (sVLA) using differential residuals and block-wise mixed-precision quantization; 3) Hardware architecture with GPU + robot-specific accelerator; 4) Speculative dataflow decoupling VLA and sVLA for parallel execution.

Result: On OpenVLA and RDT with LIBERO and ManiSkill benchmarks, SpecVLA substantially reduces end-to-end latency while preserving task success rates, enabling real-time manipulation with high efficiency and reliability.

Conclusion: SpecVLA demonstrates that long-action-length speculative prediction, when paired with timely verification and state-aware scheduling, can deliver real-time, reliable embodied AI performance through algorithm-system co-design.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in the field of embodied AI, but their high computational cost and limited predicted action length hinder real-time deployment. Although Dadu-Corki, a dedicated accelerator for efficient embodied AI, has been introduced, it does not exploit the inherent interaction patterns between the robot and its environment, which results in a relatively short predicted action length. We observe that robotic environments naturally alternate between active states-where precise actions are crucial-and inactive states-where actions have limited impact on task success. This insight enables a new scheduling opportunity: long-action-length speculative prediction in inactive states, paired with selective verification in active states.
  We propose SpecVLA, an algorithm-system co-design framework that adaptively balances action length, inference latency, and task reliability. On the algorithm side, SpecVLA introduces a state-aware VLA inference execution paradigm and a hardware-friendly construction of a smaller verification model (sVLA) using differential residuals and block-wise mixed-precision quantization. On the system side, we develop a heterogeneous architecture consisting of a GPU and a robotic-specific hardware module, along with a speculative dataflow that decouples VLA and sVLA through parallel execution. Comprehensive evaluations on OpenVLA and RDT across LIBERO and ManiSkill benchmarks show that SpecVLA reduces end-to-end latency significantly while preserving task success rate. By enabling long-action-length speculative prediction with timely verification, SpecVLA achieves real-time robotic manipulation with both high efficiency and reliability.

</details>


### [218] [Robo-Dopamine 2.0: History-Conditioned and OOD-Aware Process Reward Modeling for Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15680)
*Yijie Xu,Haopeng Jin,Run Zhou,Shengbang Liu,Sixiang Chen,Hongyang Cheng,Sicheng Hu,Peterson Co,Jinwen Luo,Huajie Tan,Shanghang Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Robo-Dopamine 2.0 introduces a history- and OOD-aware process reward for refining VLA policies; uses pairwise rewards with reference panels and observed rollout history, plus an OOD-aware signed progress space and a Signed-Hop Curriculum. It improves visual order consistency and real-world manipulation success, with new datasets and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address compounding errors, scene changes, and off-trajectory states in VLA policies; overcome sparse rewards and temporal ambiguity from static before-after rewards; improve OOD robustness.

Method: Two-stage reward model: (1) history-conditioned pairwise rewards using source-aligned reference panels for synthetic OOD queries and observed rollout history for online queries while preserving endpoints; (2) OOD-aware signed progress space representing valid progress, robustness, failure, recovery. Training via Signed-Hop Curriculum with transition-aware replay to order coarse execution before fine-grained progress calibration. Also introduces OOD trajectory dataset and a five-family benchmark.

Result: Improved VOC mean from 0.967 to 0.986 and OOD-robust VOC from 0.906 to 0.958. With 400k pairwise rewards and 25% replay, Signed-Hop achieves 0.9872 mean VOC vs 0.9858 baseline. In RL, full model achieves 86.8% mean RoboTwin success and 71/80 successful real-world insertions.

Conclusion: The proposed history- and OOD-aware reward modeling plus curriculum learning yields improved robustness to OOD and real-world performance for VLA-based robotic manipulation; the approach effectively discriminates robustness-preserving variations from failures and enhances exploration.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models improve robotic manipulation but remain vulnerable to compounding errors, scene changes, and off-trajectory states. Reinforcement learning can refine pretrained VLA policies, yet sparse success signals hinder exploration, while engineered dense rewards are costly and task-specific. Existing learned visual reward models often rely on static before-after observations, causing temporal ambiguity and weak discrimination between robustness-preserving variations and task-invalid failures under out-of-distribution (OOD) execution. We introduce Robo-Dopamine 2.0, a history- and OOD-aware process reward model with a pairwise prediction interface. It combines (1) history-conditioned pairwise rewards that use source-aligned reference panels for synthetic OOD queries and observed rollout history for online queries, while preserving the queried endpoints, and (2) an OOD-aware signed progress space that represents valid progress, robustness, failure, and recovery. A Signed-Hop Curriculum with transition-aware replay learns coarse execution ordering before fine-grained progress calibration. We also construct an OOD trajectory dataset and a five-family benchmark. Reference panels improve mean visual order consistency (VOC) from 0.967 to 0.986 and OOD-robust VOC from 0.906 to 0.958. With the same 400K pairwise-reward budget, Signed-Hop training with 25% replay reaches 0.9872 mean VOC, compared with 0.9858 for a matched-pool shuffled control. In downstream reinforcement learning, the full model achieves 86.8% mean RoboTwin success and 71/80 successful real-world insertions.

</details>


### [219] [GAINS: Leveraging Inconsistent Human Intervention Signals in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15707)
*Xinyi Zhang,Yinuo Zhao,Pei Ren,Lechun Jiang,Huiqian Jin,Lei Sun,Dapeng Wu,Zhengping Che,Chi Harold Liu,Jian Tang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GAINS uses distributional RL with quantile Q-networks to model return variability caused by sparse rewards and imperfect human interventions, and introduces a pessimistic exploration strategy to enable safe, sample-efficient learning under human corrections. It outperforms state-of-the-art intervention-based methods, achieving higher task success and better recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human-in-the-loop RL for real-world manipulation is hindered by imperfect human actions and, more critically, delayed/inconsistent intervention signals. Existing work addresses action quality but not timing; GAINS targets this gap to enable robust learning under practical human supervision.

Method: Apply distributional reinforcement learning via quantile Q-networks to capture the distribution of returns under inconsistent human interventions. Build a pessimistic exploration strategy on top of this distributional representation to promote safety and sample efficiency when leveraging human corrections. Evaluate on four simulated manipulation tasks and two real-world scenarios, comparing to state-of-the-art intervention-based methods (e.g., RLIF).

Result: GAINS achieves a 22% higher task success rate than RLIF and increases recovery success by up to 43% in failure scenarios across tested tasks.

Conclusion: Modeling the variability of returns due to human imperfection is crucial for deploying intervention-based RL in real-world manipulation. The distributional and pessimistic approaches in GAINS yield safer, more data-efficient learning and improved performance when human guidance is noisy or delayed.

Abstract: Correcting robot manipulation policies through human intervention holds great promise for real-world deployment, yet human operators are inherently imperfect in both the actions they provide and the timing of their intervention signals. While the former has been extensively discussed in reinforcement learning (RL), the latter remains underexplored. At high control frequencies, human intervention signals are often delayed and inconsistent across time and state space. In this work, we present GAINS, a framework for leveraging inconsistent human intervention signals in RL. At the core of GAINS, we employ distributional RL with quantile Q-networks to model the return variability induced by sparse task rewards and inconsistent human interventions. Building on this distributional representation, we introduce a pessimistic exploration strategy that promotes safe and sample-efficient learning under human corrections. We evaluate GAINS on four diverse simulated manipulation tasks and two challenging real-world scenarios against state-of-the-art intervention-based methods. GAINS achieves a 22% higher task success rate than RLIF and improves recovery success by up to 43% in failure scenarios. These results highlight the importance of modeling return variability induced by human imperfection for real-world deployment of intervention-based learning.

</details>


### [220] [Some Modifications to Our End-to-End UAV Planner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15741)
*Junjie Lu,Bailing Tian*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Enhances YOPO by introducing a two-piece MINCO parameterization, multi-homotopy prediction via motion primitives, adaptive-speed feasibility with barrier penalties, and a ranking loss to improve trajectory safety, expressiveness, and path directness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome soft-constrained optimization pathologies in YOPO (conflicting costs, non-convexity across homotopy classes, limited spatial expressiveness) and to enable safer, more informative, and efficient planning.

Method: - Adopt a two-piece MINCO parameterization to trade time for smoothness without changing spatial profile.
- Lift YOPO's multi-modal prediction to span distinct homotopy classes; use each motion primitive as a homotopy anchor that confines the trajectory to a feasible basin without explicit safe-flight corridors or front-end search.
- Impose barrier penalties on velocity and acceleration, plus a curvature-dependent speed limit whose gradient acts only on velocity, yielding adaptive speed and deceleration in clutter or sharp turns.
- Replace score regression with a ranking loss to prevent small score errors from reordering the candidate set.

Result: Yields richer trajectory representations, safer obstacle avoidance, and more direct flight paths.

Conclusion: The modifications address YOPO's limitations by enabling multi-modal, adaptive-speed, and more expressive trajectory planning, improving safety and directness of paths.

Abstract: The one-stage planner YOPO maps a single depth image and the robot state directly to a set of candidate trajectories, trained by backpropagating through differentiable trajectory costs. This yields dense, geometrically informative supervision, but inherits the pathologies of soft-constrained optimization: the safety cost competes with the smoothness and goal-reaching terms, is non-convex across homotopy classes, and the single-piece polynomial is limited in expressiveness. In this report, we summarize several effective modifications. We adopt a two-piece MINCO parameterization, trading time for smoothness without altering the trajectory's spatial profile. We further lift YOPO's multi-modal prediction to span distinct homotopy classes, treating each motion primitive as a homotopy anchor that confines the trajectory to a feasible basin - without explicit safe-flight-corridor construction or front-end search. For dynamic feasibility, we impose barrier penalties on velocity and acceleration together with a curvature-dependent speed limit whose gradient acts only on the velocity, producing an adaptive-speed behavior that decelerates in cluttered regions or sharp turns. We replace score regression with a ranking loss, preventing small score errors from reordering the candidate set. These yield richer trajectory representations, safer obstacle avoidance, and more direct flight paths.

</details>


### [221] [Making two action heads agree: coordination mechanisms and a runtime collapse certificate for flow-matching policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15748)
*Jinhui Sun,Wei Zhou,Bowen Yang,Xinliang Xiao,Li Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Coordinating dual-head flow-matching policies in multimodal prediction; training-supported discrete partitions yield robust coordination; a chance-corrected bound based on diversity clarifies feasibility; LIBERO-Plus shows residual false alarms; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address false alarms and coordination challenges when two kinematically equivalent prediction branches operate on different modalities; understand what mechanisms coordinate them and at what cost.

Method: Empirical study across two robot environments and a non-robotic testbed, classifying coordination mechanisms into four categories. The paper derives a chance-corrected coordination bound using Gini-Simpson diversity, and evaluates on LIBERO-Plus with a preregistered intervention. It includes ablations on latent sharing, consistency regularization, and discrete partitions, plus providing code and configurations.

Result: Findings include: (1) an auxiliary latent shared by both branches but absent from the flow-matching construction is erased at population optimum (dead end); (2) sharing source noise can coordinate or anti-coordinate depending on the representation map; (3) consistency regularization yields intermediate coordination but reduces valid-pair rate; (4) training-supported discrete partitions achieve near-ceiling coordination robustly; (5) a coordination bound based on branch diversity is derived; (6) LIBERO-Plus shows benign multimodality adds 1.57 percentage points of false alarms to the residual, which remains the strongest evaluated failure signal; preregistered token intervention does not meet its false-alarm criterion; all code and configurations are released.

Conclusion: Effective coordination in dual-head flow-matching requires mechanisms like training-supported discrete partitions; a theoretical diversification-based bound provides a label-free diagnostic for coordination vs. collapse; in practice, residual false alarms persist and can be quantified with the proposed metrics, with code available for replication.

Abstract: A dual-representation flow-matching policy decodes each predicted motion into joint and end-effector spaces, and the residual between the two kinematically equivalent decodings provides a physically interpretable runtime signal. On multimodal tasks, however, independently sampled branches may choose different valid modes, causing false alarms. We study how to coordinate the two branches and at what cost. Across two robot environments and a non-robotic testbed, the tested mechanisms fall into four classes. An auxiliary latent shared by both branches but absent from the flow-matching construction is erased at the population optimum, a provable dead end confirmed within a prespecified 2% equivalence band. Sharing source noise can coordinate or anti-coordinate: its effect changes sign with the representation map and tracks the alignment of decoder mode basins. Consistency regularization gives intermediate coordination but reduces the valid-pair rate, while training-supported discrete partitions achieve near-ceiling coordination robustly.
