We further derive a chance-corrected coordination bound based only on each branch's Gini-Simpson diversity, yielding an attainable region and a label-free certificate that separates coordination from collapse when zero mismatch is ambiguous. On LIBERO-Plus, benign multimodality adds 1.57 percentage points of false alarms to the residual, which remains the strongest evaluated failure signal; the preregistered token intervention does not meet its false-alarm criterion or produce a seed-robust detection change. Code, models, and per-run configurations are available at https://github.com/kimo423/dual-head-coordination.

</details>


### [222] [Tac4Loco: Learning Spatiotemporal Plantar Pressure Representations for Humanoid Locomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15766)
*Ziyun Liu,Sikai Guo,Zheng Li,Jiahang Cao,Haichao Liu,Pei Qu,Yinghong Zhang,Jinni Zhou,Jun Ma*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Tac4Loco uses tactile plantar pressure data with a topology-preserving representation and a dual-branch spatiotemporal encoder to train with an asymmetric actor-critic, enabling robust humanoid locomotion on uneven terrains and zero-shot generalization to unseen terrains; code will be released open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humanoid robots operating on complex terrains experience highly variable plantar support due to foot placement errors, ground properties, and transient dynamics. Robust locomotion requires adaptation to uneven terrain and uncertain foot–ground interactions.

Method: Introduce Tac4Loco, a tactile-perceptive framework that uses multi-array plantar pressure as direct feedback. It uses a topology-preserving ordinal representation to map simulated and physical sensor signals into a shared observation space, with a dual-branch encoder to extract spatial and temporal representations. The learned spatiotemporal features are combined with augmented proprioception (including terrain estimation cues) and fed into an asymmetric actor-critic policy learner.

Result: In both simulation and real-world experiments, Tac4Loco improves tracking performance and support adaptation on inclined, partial, asymmetric, and changing-support terrains. It achieves zero-shot deployment on unseen compliant and unstructured terrains (e.g., foam platform, gravel road). Open-source code and experimental configurations will be released.

Conclusion: The proposed tactile-perceptive framework leverages the topology of plantar pressure to enhance perception and control, yielding robust, transferable locomotion policies for humanoid robots across diverse terrains with strong generalization to unseen environments.

Abstract: Humanoid robots are expected to traverse complex terrains, where the plantar support may vary dramatically due to foot placement errors, ground properties, and transient dynamics.
  To achieve robust locomotion, the robots are required to adapt to uneven terrain and uncertain foot--ground interactions.
  Existing locomotion policies rely primarily on proprioception or exteroceptive terrain perception, where the former provides only indirect evidence of plantar support, while the latter predicts contact conditions before touchdown but cannot observe the actual support in real-time.
  Although some studies incorporate plantar contacts as an auxiliary perception, they rely mainly on summary statistics, overlooking the spatial topology of plantar pressure, which provides a more direct characterization of the realized contact state.
  To bridge this gap, we present Tac4Loco, a tactile-perceptive framework that incorporates multi-array plantar pressure as direct feedback for humanoid locomotion.
  We formulate a topology-preserving ordinal representation to map simulated and physical sensor signals into a shared observation space,
  with a dual-branch encoder for extracting their spatial and temporal representations. Subsequently, the learned spatiotemporal features are integrated with augmented proprioception including terrain estimation cues, and provided to an asymmetric actor-critic architecture for policy learning.
  Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate improved tracking performance and support adaptation on terrains with inclined, partial, asymmetric, and changing support. We further demonstrate its zero-shot deployment on unseen compliant and unstructured terrains, including a foam platform and a gravel road. All code and experimental configurations will be released as open-source to facilitate reproducibility.

</details>


### [223] [Reliable Piezoresistive Strain Sensing Through Physical Limits and Uncertainty Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15784)
*Carmen Ballester,Víctor Muñoz,Dorin Copaci,Dolores Blanco*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Physics-informed probabilistic inverse modeling plus a three-state reliability monitor improves trust in soft piezoresistive sensors by detecting in-range/out-of-range/abnormal readings; validated with Gaussian Processes showing high accuracy and coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Soft piezoresistive sensors exhibit nonlinear, hysteretic behavior with limited calibrated range. Probabilistic regressors provide uncertainty but do not account for sensor limits; there is a need to detect when readings come from outside admissible ranges or when the sensor is failing to prevent unsafe decisions.

Method: Develop a physics-guided input feature set and a physics-informed probabilistic inverse model (Gaussian Process) combined with a risk factor that fuses prediction uncertainty with strain and strain-rate limits into a three-state monitor (nominal, out-of-range, abnormal). Evaluated on a Nitinol wire and a silver-coated polyamide thread.

Result: Gaussian Process regression achieved fit scores of 0.90–0.95 with RMSE 0.26%–0.15%. Empirical coverage of 96% against the 95% target. The monitor detected 95% of out-of-range cases and 100% of abnormal conditions while remaining reliable under nominal operation.

Conclusion: Reporting confidence alongside estimates enables systems to withhold action when readings are unreliable or out of bounds, eliminating the need for extensive failure-label data for soft materials and enhancing safety in wearable and soft robotic applications.

Abstract: Soft piezoresistive strain sensors are one of the most common sensing solutions for wearable and soft robotic applications due to their flexibility and compliance. However, their resistance response is nonlinear and hysteretic, and a sensor can be pushed past its calibrated workspace or misbehave inside it, carrying that error into a decision or control loop. Probabilistic regressors track confidence but ignore those limits. A predictive mean can look unremarkable even when the reading comes from a sensor outside its admissible range or already failing internally, so a confident-looking estimate is not the same as a trustworthy one. This paper proposes a reliability framework pairing a physics-informed probabilistic inverse model, built on physics-guided input features, with a risk factor fusing uncertainty with strain and strain-rate limits into a three-state monitor. Tests on a Nitinol wire and a silver-coated polyamide thread with a Gaussian Process raised fit scores to 0.90-0.95 (RMSE 0.26%-0.15%) and a 96% empirical coverage against the 95% target. The monitor caught 95% of out-of-range and 100% of abnormal conditions while staying reliable under nominal operation. A sensor that reports confidence alongside its estimate lets a system withhold action instead, since it needs no labeled failure examples, which are hard to collect for soft materials.

</details>


### [224] [ViTaR: Visuo-Tactile Residual Adaptation for Foundation VLA Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15816)
*Yi Wang,Renjun Wu,Jinyan Liu,Xuesong Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ViTaR adds bounded tactile modulation to a frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, via a two-stage adaptation (Effect-Guided Modeling and Residual Action Modulation) that uses real-time visuotactile data to generate small, scaled residual corrections. It yields strong gains on UniVTAC (61.3% avg success, +30.6pp over the frozen VLA) and transfers to real robots, outperforming tactile baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLAs encode broad visual-semantic priors but lack awareness of local contact events; modifying VLAs risks forgetting and online reinforcement is brittle under near-failure contact. The goal is to preserve pretrained capabilities while integrating tactile feedback through bounded corrections.

Method: A two-stage adaptation: (1) Effect-Guided Modeling selects and justifies local corrections based on outcome-grounded evidence; (2) Residual Action Modulation translates this evidence into a bounded, continuously-scaled residual that modulates the frozen VLA’s outputs using real-time visuotactile observations.

Result: On UniVTAC (7 contact-rich tasks), ViTaR achieves 61.3% average success, a 30.6pp improvement over the frozen VLA base, and surpasses purpose-built tactile baselines. Physical-robot experiments demonstrate transfer to real sensor noise and dynamics.

Conclusion: Bounded tactile modulation enables effective integration of tactile feedback without retraining or unbounded influence on pretrained priors, preserving generalization while improving performance in contact-rich manipulation; ViTaR shows strong cross-domain evidence from simulations to real robots.

Abstract: As Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models scale toward real-world deployment, contact-rich manipulation exposes a critical blind spot: these policies encode broad visual-semantic priors yet remain unaware of local contact events, producing identical actions whether contact is established, lost, or destabilized. Existing remedies either modify VLA internals, risking catastrophic forgetting, or demand online reinforcement under near-failure contact conditions. Both grant tactile unbounded influence over action generation, conflicting with the priors that make VLAs generalizable. We introduce ViTaR, which reframes tactile feedback from an action-generating perceptual input to an execution modulator that selects and scales bounded residual corrections atop a frozen VLA, preserving pretrained capabilities by construction. ViTaR decomposes adaptation into two stages: Effect-Guided Modeling determines whether and which correction is locally justified via outcome-grounded preference evidence, and Residual Action Modulation converts this evidence into a residual choice with continuously scaled gain from real-time visuotactile observations. On the UniVTAC benchmark spanning seven contact-rich tasks, ViTaR achieves 61.3% average success, a 30.6 percentage-point improvement over its frozen VLA base that also surpasses purpose-built tactile baselines. Physical-robot experiments confirm that bounded tactile modulation transfers to real sensor noise and dynamics.

</details>


### [225] [Scaling Manual-Grounded Appliance Manipulation with Data Synthesis and Unified Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15863)
*Yuxing Long,Lei Kang,Ziyan Yu,Yuzheng Gao,Bin Cheng,Jiyao Zhang,Xiaoqi Li,Haolin Yang,Dongjiang Li,Hui Shen,Hao Dong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MAGE is a scalable data-synthesis pipeline that creates large, manually grounded datasets (UseAppliance) via a Hierarchical Appliance Graph (HAG) to enable long-horizon, robust appliance manipulation planning. An end-to-end model (AppliancePlan, 7B params) trained on this data achieves major gains on open-loop planning and real-robot sim-to-real transfer, demonstrating progress toward general-purpose household robotics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Household robotics require long-horizon, state-dependent planning under disturbances. There is a lack of diverse, task-oriented datasets aligned with manual instruction for planning. The work aims to bridge this gap by automatically generating grounding and planning data from appliance manuals.

Method: Introduce Hierarchical Appliance Graph (HAG) to extract part grounding, planning, and recovery data from manuals; synthesize UseAppliance dataset with 89K+ part annotations, 53K+ manipulation tasks, 33K+ closed-loop steps across 22 appliance categories; develop AppliancePlan (7B params) for manual-grounded manipulation planning; validate on RealAppliance-Bench and real robots (six appliances).

Result: On RealAppliance-Bench, AppliancePlan (7B) achieves >10x improvement over best baseline in open-loop planning and outperforms state-of-the-art models across tasks; real-robot experiments show effective sim-to-real transfer across six appliances.

Conclusion: MAGE enables scalable generation of task-focused grounding data and a capable planning model, advancing open-ended, manual-grounded appliance manipulation and supporting progress toward general-purpose household robotics.

Abstract: Operating household appliances requires long-horizon planning that is state-dependent and robust to disturbances, yet existing large models fall short, as no sufficiently diverse, task-oriented dataset exists to support such planning. To bridge this gap, we propose MAGE, a scalable data synthesis pipeline that introduces a novel Hierarchical Appliance Graph (HAG) to automatically generate part grounding, long-horizon planning, and closed-loop recovery data from appliance manuals. With MAGE, we build UseAppliance, the first large-scale dataset for manual-grounded appliance manipulation planning, spanning 22 appliance categories with 89K+ part annotations, 53K+ manipulation tasks, and 33K+ closed-loop adjustment steps. Built on UseAppliance, we develop AppliancePlan, an end-to-end model for manual-grounded appliance manipulation planning. On RealAppliance-Bench, AppliancePlan with only 7B parameters achieves over 10x the best baseline on open-loop planning and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models across all tasks. Real-robot experiments on six household appliances further confirm effective sim-to-real transfer, marking an important step toward general-purpose household robotics.

</details>


### [226] [GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15875)
*GigaBrain Team,Angen Ye,Axiang Sun,Can Jin,Chenxi Cheng,Chong Shi,Dengke Shang,Dingqian Zhang,Guan Huang,Guangqiang Wang,Guangqing Ding,Guo Li,Hangcong Li,Hengyu Zhong,Hongtao Lu,Jianbo Qin,Jiming Mao,Jing Zhu,Jindi Lv,Jingzhi Cui,Junjie Xie,Junyi Bao,Kai Liu,Lei Yuan,Limin Long,Lv Feng,Mingming Yu,Peng Li,Pengfei Yi,Qi Li,Qianli Zhang,Qingfang Li,Qitang Hu,Rui Zhang,Shaoyan Sun,Shibo Sun,Shiying Duan,Tenghui Chen,Tianze Liu,Weijie Ke,Wenyao Xue,Xiaofeng Wang,Xiaoyu Tian,Xinyu Liu,Xinze Chen,Yang Wang,Yankai Wang,Yejun Zeng,Yifan Li,Yifei Nie,Yilong Li,Yilong Liu,Yongchao Feng,Yumeng Wang,Yun Ye,Zhichao Liu,Ziheng He,Zonghai Yang,Zheng Zhu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GigaBrain-0.7 is an embodied foundation model with a 3-system architecture, trained on ~37k hours of heterogeneous embodied data, using one-stage alignment to unify understanding and action, yielding improved zero-shot, instruction following, and task success across diverse embodiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the generalization gap in vision-language-action (VLA) systems by scaling data, refining architecture, and enabling cross-embodiment generalization through unified, large-scale pretraining and alignment.

Method: Three-system architecture (understanding, prediction, action) with one-stage alignment training. Pretraining on over 37,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data across multiple embodiments and tasks.

Result: Outperforms prior models (GigaBrain-0 series, π0.5) in zero-shot capabilities, language-conditioned instruction following, and post-training task success rates; demonstrates robust adaptability on Maker H01 and common robot embodiments in home and industrial settings.

Conclusion: Shows the effectiveness of a unified embodied foundation model with extensive pretraining and one-stage alignment for cross-embodiment generalization; code and weights to be released.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a dominant paradigm for generalist embodied agents, demonstrating strong complex and long-horizon task completion in structured settings. Yet it remains an open question whether current VLA systems can benefit from more effective architectural design, scale to substantially larger and more heterogeneous data regimes, and achieve broader generalization across tasks and embodiments. To this end, we present GigaBrain-0.7, an embodied foundation model with substantially improved generalization across diverse robot embodiments. Specifically, GigaBrain-0.7 unifies understanding, prediction, and action through a three-system architecture, scales pretraining to over 37,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, and introduces one-stage alignment training that jointly optimizes vision-language understanding and multi-embodiment action generation. Compared with the preceding GigaBrain-0 series and prior state-of-the-art models including $π_{0.5}$, GigaBrain-0.7 achieves substantial improvements in foundation zero-shot capabilities, language-conditioned instruction following, and post-training task success rates. In particular, on our in-house Maker H01 platform and mainstream robot embodiments, GigaBrain-0.7 demonstrates strong task adaptability and completion ability across both home and industrial scenarios. All training code and pretrained model weights will be released.

</details>


### [227] [Grouping Auction-Consensus Algorithm for Decentralized Task Allocation in Multi-Robot Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15884)
*Jose Rodriguez,Sven Koenig,Wenjie Dong,Qi Lu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Grouping Auction-Consensus (GACA) improves decentralized MRTA by grouping spatially proximate tasks, yielding near-optimal performance with faster convergence compared to CBBA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CBBA’s task-level bidding is poorly aligned with the min-sum objective of minimizing total team travel distance, leading to suboptimal, especially in spatially distributed environments; a scalable approach is needed for decentralized MRTA.

Method: Extend CBBA with a two-phase auction-consensus framework. Introduce nearest-neighbor preprocessing to partition tasks into spatially coherent groups. Agents perform group-level bidding—claiming whole groups, acquiring partial groups, or contesting groups—with a consensus phase to resolve conflicts.

Result: On MT-SR-IA, evaluated against MILP ground-truth. Across 4 swarm sizes and 4,000 test worlds, GACA achieves median percent optimality of ~97% vs CBBA’s 81–84%; converges in equal or fewer iterations. Scalability tests over 3,280 additional instances (swarm sizes 5–20, tasks 10–50) show gains generalize across configurations.

Conclusion: Grouping-based bidding effectively aligns with the min-sum objective, delivering near-optimal allocations and robust scalability in decentralized MRTA across diverse problem settings.

Abstract: Decentralized multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) is essential for scalable and resilient autonomous systems. The Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm (CBBA) is a widely adopted decentralized baseline. However, its individual task-level bidding is poorly aligned with the min-sum objective of minimizing total team travel distance, leading to suboptimal allocations in spatially distributed environments. This paper introduces the Grouping Auction-Consensus Algorithm (GACA). This decentralized MRTA framework adopts the two-phase auction-consensus architecture of CBBA while fundamentally redesigning its bidding mechanism to reason over groups of spatially proximate tasks. A nearest-neighbor preprocessing step partitions tasks into spatially coherent groups before allocation. Agents then iteratively propose structured group-level actions: claiming unassigned groups, acquiring partial groups, or contesting groups held by other agents. Competing actions are resolved through a consensus phase. Operating in the MT-SR-IA problem class, GACA is evaluated against CBBA using a Mixed-Integer Linear Program as the ground-truth optimality reference. Across four swarm sizes and 4,000 test worlds, GACA achieves a median percent optimality of approximately 97% compared to 81--84% for CBBA, while converging in equal or fewer iterations. A scalability evaluation over 3,280 additional problem instances spanning swarm sizes of 5 to 20 agents and task counts of 10 to 50 confirms that these gains generalize robustly across a wide range of problem configurations.

</details>


### [228] [Tactile Sim2Real without Tactile Simulation via Bottlenecked Latent Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15897)
*Fan Yang,Youngsun Wi,Jinhao Yu,Nima Fazeli,Dmitry Berenson*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A sensor-agnostic Sim2Real framework (SBLR) uses an oracle tactile sensor for policy learning and latent reconstruction to map real sensors to the oracle domain, achieving strong zero-shot transfer across tactile sensors and outperforming physics-based baselines in Peg Insertion/Gear Meshing tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile-sensing sim-to-real is hindered by diverse, sensor-specific models and high fidelity requirements; current domain-knowledge-heavy simulations are error-prone and costly. The work aims to avoid sensor-specific modeling while retaining fidelity.

Method: Two-stage policy training: (1) train policies in the oracle sensor latent space (point-cloud + finger-tip forces) as a simulator-native signal; (2) train a bottlenecked latent reconstructor to map real sensor information to the oracle latent, capturing information loss. Alignment between oracle and real sensors is learned from unpaired random-play data via rectified-flow-based transformation networks trained on nearest-neighbor pseudo-pairs. Evaluation uses three simulation tasks and hardware experiments on Peg Insertion and Gear Meshing with GelSight Mini and DIGIT sensors.

Result: SBLR achieves 85-97.5% zero-shot success without sensor-specific modeling, matching or approaching an oracle with direct tactile simulation; outperforms a physics-based tactile-simulation baseline by 7.5-15%.

Conclusion: A sensor-agnostic sim-to-real framework enables high-transfer performance across diverse tactile sensors without calibration or sensor-specific modeling, demonstrating robust zero-shot transfer in contact-rich tasks.

Abstract: Robot sensor designs, particularly tactile sensors, are highly diverse and evolve rapidly. Modeling each sensor in simulation demands substantial domain expertise and computational approximations can degrade the fidelity of the simulated signals. We propose Sim2Real via Bottlenecked Latent Reconstruction (SBLR), a framework that avoids sensor-specific simulation entirely by (1) training policies on a simulator-native oracle sensor that is easy to construct without modeling any particular sensor (e.g. we use a point-cloud and finger-tip forces as a tactile oracle), and (2) aligning real sensor latent embeddings to those of the oracle sensor at inference time. Policy training proceeds in two-stage: the policy first learns from the oracle sensor latents, then a bottlenecked latent reconstruction adapts it to the information loss expected when using the real sensor instead of the oracle. The alignment between oracle and real sensor is learned from unpaired random-play data collected in both simulation and the real world, using rectified-flow-based transformation networks trained on nearest-neighbor pseudo-pairs. Simulation experiments on three contact-rich tasks show that SBLR matches or approaches the performance of an oracle with direct access to tactile simulation. Hardware experiments on Peg Insertion and Gear Meshing with GelSight Mini and DIGIT sensors demonstrate 85-97.5% zero-shot success without requiring any sensor-specific modeling or calibration, outperforming a physics-based tactile simulation baseline by 7.5-15%.

</details>


### [229] [Pre-training Visual Dexterity in Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15917)
*Sarthak Kamat,Adam Rashid,Satvik Sharma,Aseem Doriwala,Chelsea Finn,Phillip Isola,C. Karen Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SPD demonstrates simulation-only teleoperation pre-training for dexterous manipulation, enabling on-embodiment trajectories and improving real-world fine-tuning with a 56-DoF bimanual system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dexterous hands offer rich manipulation capabilities but suffer from data scarcity; real teleoperation is costly to scale, and human hand videos are off-embodiment with lossy pose estimation. Simulation-based, on-embodiment data from VR can provide scalable pre-training sources.

Method: Collect 75 hours of multi-task dexterous manipulation via VR teleoperation from five operators (on-embodiment). Pre-train a causal transformer on a sequence modeling objective in simulation. Fine-tune on 1–2 hours of real demonstrations on a 56-DoF bimanual dexterous setup. Conduct ablations on history conditioning and short action chunks.

Result: Simulation pre-training yields better performance than training from scratch when fine-tuning with limited real data. Ablations show the benefits of history conditioning and short action chunks for reactive control.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training in dexterity is viable and data-efficient. VR-based on-embodiment teleoperation can serve as a scalable pre-training source for real-world dexterous manipulation, reducing data requirements for real-world fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large-scale pre-training has made robot policy fine-tuning increasingly data-efficient, but this progress has largely been driven by datasets and embodiments built around simple parallel-jaw grippers. Dexterous, multi-fingered hands remain comparatively data-starved because real teleoperation is costly to scale, while human hand video is off-embodiment and requires lossy pose estimation and retargeting. We introduce Simulation Pre-training for Dexterity (SPD), a pre-training framework for dexterous manipulation that uses data entirely collected in simulation. In SPD, humans manipulate virtual objects inside a VR headset, enabling on-embodiment trajectories and robot-free collection. With the help of five operators, we collect 75 hours of multi-task dexterous manipulation over one week, and use it to pre-train a causal transformer on a sequence modeling objective. We study the benefits of simulation pre-training on real-world tasks by fine-tuning on 1-2 hours of physical demonstrations on a 56-DoF bimanual dexterous setup. We find that our approach outperforms training behavior cloning policies from scratch, showing that simulation teleoperation is a viable pre-training source for real-world dexterous manipulation. We perform ablation studies, measuring the benefits of history conditioning and short action chunks for reactive control.

</details>


### [230] [RAPAC-DP: Response-Aligned Pending-Action Compensation for Diffusion Policies under Delayed Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15924)
*Tao Wang,Wei Wang,Jianhui Wang,Qi Wang,Weidi Huang,Bing Xu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RAPAC-DP mitigates cloud-side latency in imitation-learning by using a pending-action sequence as conditioning to a compensation pathway; achieves substantial latency robustness without requiring delayed data; shows strong results on Kinetix and RoboMimic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address performance degradation caused by communication and computation delays in cloud-based imitation-learning policies, without needing explicit system dynamics or delayed demonstrations.

Method: Introduce RAPAC-DP: encode already-scheduled actions into a pending-action sequence that conditions a parameter-efficient compensation pathway. When delays are negligible, bypasses to recover the base policy. Train using delay-conditioned samples derived from delay-free demonstrations. Applicable to diffusion- and flow-based action generators.

Result: On Kinetix, at the largest fixed delay, retains 81.4% of delay-free performance. On RoboMimic tasks, mean success rate 0.633 across three tasks.

Conclusion: Pending-action compensation is an effective strategy for mitigating cloud-induced delays in imitation-learning, with a general approach that does not require explicit dynamics or extra delayed demonstrations.

Abstract: Cloud-side inference gives imitation-learning policies access to greater computational resources, but communication and computation delays can degrade control performance. To compensate for these delays, we propose RAPAC-DP, a response-aligned pending-action compensation framework designed for both diffusion- and flow-based action generators. RAPAC-DP encodes the actions already scheduled for execution before the cloud response arrives into a pending-action sequence that serves as the conditioning input to a parameter-efficient compensation pathway. When delay effects are negligible, bypassing this pathway exactly recovers the frozen base policy. For training, RAPAC-DP constructs delay-conditioned samples from delay-free demonstrations, requiring neither explicit system dynamics nor additional delayed demonstrations. At the largest fixed delay tested on Kinetix, RAPAC-DP retained 81.4% of its overall delay-free performance. At the largest fixed delay tested on each RoboMimic task, it achieved a mean success rate of 0.633 across the three tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pending-action compensation for cloud-deployed imitation-learning policies.

</details>


### [231] [Revisiting Open-Loop Execution in Robotics: Toward Reactive, Higher-Performing Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15938)
*Michael Zeng,Abhinav Agarwal,Ajay Bati,Brian Lee,Siddharth Ancha,Russ Tedrake*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Long open-loop prefixes help imitate non-Markovian demonstrations, but hurt reactivity; with sufficiently long context, reactive, closed-loop policies outperform open-loop strategies, suggesting long-context reactive policies are a principled, more effective alternative.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation learning for robotic manipulation typically uses long open-loop execution to mitigate errors and latency, yet the exact mechanisms remain unclear. The study seeks to disentangle the roles of non-Markovian demonstrations, compounding errors, and context length in shaping performance.

Method: Empirical evaluation across four simulation tasks and two real-world tasks. Systematically vary open-loop horizon and policy context length, compare closed-loop (reactive) versus open-loop policies, quantify the effect of non-Markovianity, and assess the contribution of compounding errors to performance differences.

Result: Expert non-Markovianity dominates the relationship between task success and open-loop horizon. Compounding errors matter but have a weaker impact in this setting. When context is sufficiently long, open-loop execution ceases to be beneficial, and reactive, closed-loop policies achieve the best performance.

Conclusion: Long-context, reactive policies are a principled and superior alternative to long open-loop execution for imitation learning in manipulation tasks; improving context richness and reactivity should be the focus rather than extending open-loop prefixes.

Abstract: Action chunking --- the practice of predicting a sequence of actions and executing a prefix open-loop --- has emerged as a key enabler of recent progress in imitation learning for robotic manipulation. However, executing long open-loop prefixes reduces reactivity, limiting policies' ability to correct for errors. Further, the mechanisms underlying these performance benefits remain poorly understood: prior works cite mitigating compounding errors, absorbing inference latency, or smoothing motions, but provide limited controlled evidence or guidance for preserving reactivity. In this work, we argue that long open-loop execution primarily helps short-context policies imitate "non-Markovian demonstrations". Across four simulation and two real-world tasks, we show that expert non-Markovianity strongly shapes the relationship between task success and open-loop execution horizon. Further, we investigate the impact of compounding errors --- the prevailing explanation for long open-loop execution in prior work --- and find that while they matter, expert non-Markovianity has a much stronger impact in our experimental setting. Finally, we show that when policies are provided with a sufficiently long context, open-loop execution is no longer beneficial and the most reactive, closed-loop policies perform best. While imitation learning has seen great success using long open-loop execution, our findings motivate long-context, reactive policies as a more principled and performant paradigm.

</details>


### [232] [Rotate Disks to Reach Farther: Design and Modeling of a Novel Reconfigurable Tendon Driven Manipulator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15946)
*Sabyasachi Dash,Yangkun Liu,Will Hunter,John Golden,Girish Krishnan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces reconfigurable tendon-driven continuum manipulators with independent disk rotation to reroute tendons (MDL and CDR). Presents a PCS-based static model within a potential energy framework, validated experimentally with low tip errors, and with computation times an order of magnitude faster than Cosserat rod solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expand the deformation capabilities of tendon-driven continuum manipulators by enabling local, programmable tendon rerouting through rotating spacer disks, yielding richer 3D backbone shapes while maintaining computational efficiency for potential real-time control.

Method: Two designs: Manual Disk Locked (MDL) and Continuous Disk Rotor (CDR) enabling disk rotations before and during operation. A predictive static model based on piecewise constant strain (PCS) under a potential energy minimization framework is developed, incorporating (a) disk rotations, (b) discrete tendon paths between disk segments, (c) rigid disk thickness, and (d) tendon elasticity.

Result: Experimental validation shows an average tip error of 1.2% of total length for parallel tendon routing and ~3% when multiple disks are rotated. The approach achieves an order of magnitude faster computation than the state-of-the-art Cosserat rod solver.

Conclusion: Reconfigurable disk-based tendon routing expands the deformation repertoire of TDCMs and, with a PCS-based energy model, yields accurate predictions at significantly reduced computation times, enabling faster or real-time control and design exploration.

Abstract: Rerouting the tendon path in tendon driven continuum manipulators (TDCMs) enables a broad range of deformation modes. This work presents a Reconfigurable TDCM design which allows independent rotation of intermediate spacer disks, thereby locally rerouting the tendon and achieving non-trivial backbone spatial deformations. Two such designs, (a) Manual Disk Locked (MDL) and (b) Continuous Disk Rotor (CDR) manipulators are presented to achieve disk rotations before and during operation, respectively. A predictive static model based on the piecewise constant strain (PCS) assumption is developed within a potential energy minimization framework, incorporating (a) disk rotations, (b) discrete tendon paths between disk segments, (c) rigid thickness of spacer disks, and (d) elasticity of the tendons. The model is validated against experimental results, demonstrating an average tip error of $1.2\%$ of the manipulator's total length for parallel tendon routing and around $3\%$ for the case when multiple disks are rotated. The computation time is an order of magnitude lower than the state of the art Cosserat rod solver.

</details>


### [233] [Tabletop Pen Manipulation With a Vision-Guided 4-DoF Arm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15968)
*Anirudh Rangarajan,Bibit Bianchini*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Low-cost 4-DoF robotic arms can perform perception-guided sorting tasks by compensating for missing wrist rotation with corrective sweeps; a fixed overhead camera plus YOLO-OBB and pose estimation enables direct and reoriented grasps, achieving 196 direct grasps and 130 reorientation sweeps across 326 motions, suggesting task-informed engineering can overcome actuation underactuation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Make accessible 4-DoF arms capable of handling arbitrarily oriented objects by using perception and planning to compensate for underactuation; demonstrate a low-cost solution for sorting tasks.

Method: A fixed overhead camera observes a ~$200 Waveshare RoArm-M2-S arm. An YOLO-OBB detector localizes utensils; camera intrinsics + ArUco-based pose estimate map pixel coords to robot coordinates. A color classifier labels utensil color. The orientation angle guides strategy: near-aligned objects are grasped directly; steeper orientations are corrected via sweeps before grasping and sorting into color bins. Evaluation uses 326 motions across 7 utensil types.

Result: Out of 326 motions, 196 were direct grasps and 130 required corrective sweeps to reorient objects up to 90 degrees. The approach achieved successful color sorting despite the missing wrist rotation, indicating perception-driven planning can compensate for underactuation in this task.

Conclusion: Perception-informed planning can mitigate missing degrees of freedom in simple pick-and-place tasks for low-cost robots. The method shows promise for broader adoption but may be constrained by object variety, lighting, and fixed-camera setup; further work could explore robustness and generalization across more objects and tasks.

Abstract: Low-cost four-degree-of-freedom (DoF) arms are among the most accessible robotic platforms. But they are, in theory, underactuated for picking up in situations where objects are at arbitrary orientations, a task that appears to require five degrees of freedom: the planar position (x and y), the height (z), a wrist rotation to align the gripper with the object, and gripper actuation, of which a four-DoF arm lacks the wrist rotation. This work shows that perception and motion planning can enable such an arm, a roughly $200 Waveshare RoArm-M2-S, under a fixed overhead camera to detect and color-sort writing utensils without that joint. A YOLO11n-OBB (You Only Look Once, oriented bounding box) detector locates each writing utensil; camera intrinsics and an ArUco reference pose convert its pixel coordinates to robot coordinates; and a color classifier labels it. The detected orientation angle determines the motion strategy: utensils close to the arm's fixed approach direction are picked up directly, and those at steeper angles are reoriented via corrective sweeps until they are graspable, after which they are picked up and sorted into the assigned color bin. Across 326 logged motions on seven writing utensils, the arm made 196 direct grasps and 130 corrective sweep passes, correcting misalignments up to 90 degrees, suggesting that clever task-informed engineering can compensate for a missing degree of freedom on tasks like this one.

</details>


### [234] [Learning Varying Physical Therapist-Patient Interactions for Robot-mediated Upper Limb Task-Specific Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15995)
*Jia Quan Loh,Vincent Crocher,Marlena Klaic,Denny Oetomo,Ying Tan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TP-GMM learning-from-demonstration to capture personalised therapist-patient interaction in task-specific exercises; aligns patient kinematics with therapist torques; evaluated against LUT across 14 mock pairs and 3 tasks; TP-GMM slightly better and generalizes to unseen task variations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rehabilitation robotics have not delivered significant benefits, possibly due to poor modeling of personalized PT-patient interaction and limited practice variability. Preserve personalized interaction across varying practice conditions while increasing TST dosage.

Method: Learn from demonstrations using Task-Parameterised Gaussian Mixture Models (TPGMM) to map patient joint kinematics to therapist-applied torques; generalize to novel task variations; benchmark against a Look-Up Table; study conducted with 14 mock therapist-patient pairs over 3 tasks with six variations each.

Result: Both TP-GMM and LUT reproduce interactions in unseen variations; TP-GMM shows a slight performance advantage over LUT; reconstruction accuracy improves with task complexity, drawing closer to the actual interaction as complexity increases.

Conclusion: TP-GMM-based Learning-from-Demonstration can preserve personalized therapist-patient interactions and generalize to new task variations, potentially improving the effectiveness of Task-Specific Training in rehabilitation robotics.

Abstract: Upper extremity motor function recovery is positively linked to Task-Specific Training (TST) and sufficient therapy dosage. Rehabilitation robots can increase TST dosage via controlled, repetitive treatment and free therapists to simultaneously manage other patients, but it has yet to demonstrate significant benefits over conventional treatment. This is potentially linked to inaccurate robotic representation of personalised physical therapist-patient interaction and lack of practice variability during TST. Hence, we advocate for robotic interventions that preserve the personalised physical therapist-patient interactions when delivering TST for patients across varying practise conditions. We propose a Learning-from-Demonstration framework using Task-Parameterised Gaussian Mixture Models (TPGMM) to learn personalised physical therapist-patient interaction in Task-Specific exercises, mapping patient joint kinematics to therapist-applied torques using few demonstrations. The model is generalised to reconstruct therapist torques in new task variations. The framework was evaluated on physical interactions from 14 mock "therapist-patient" pairs over three tasks of increasing complexity, each with six variations. A benchmark comparison against a Look-Up Table was conducted. The results show both methods reproducing interactions in unseen task variations that deviate slightly from the actual interaction, with TPGMM slightly outperforming LUT. Both methods reproduced interactions that gets increasingly closer to the actual interaction as task complexity increases.

</details>


### [235] [Benchmarking Identity-Sensitive LLM Outputs for Surveillance and Security Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16030)
*Nneka Hyman,Jasmine Khan,Raj Korpan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Identity-conditioned prompts lead to readable differences in LLM-generated surveillance/ security robot designs; readability varies with prompt conditions and demographic identities across 236 labels, establishing readability as an initial benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether demographic identity cues in prompts systematically influence LLM-generated robot design descriptions and to understand potential fairness and accessibility implications in early-stage robotics documentation.

Method: Experiment with 236 demographic identity labels applied across single-label and model-augmented prompt conditions; assess readability as a baseline metric for identity-conditioned variation in generated designs; situate findings within a broader suite of lexical, semantic, sentiment, syntactic, and fairness analyses.

Result: Significant differences in readability observed across prompt conditions, design dimensions, and demographic identities.

Conclusion: Readability alone cannot determine fairness or social appropriateness but provides an interpretable baseline within a broader benchmarking framework that includes lexical, semantic, sentiment, syntactic, and fairness-focused analyses.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate textual robot design specifications, interaction policies, and risk assessments during early-stage robot development. Such outputs may influence how surveillance and security robots are conceptualized, documented, and ultimately implemented. This paper evaluates whether identity-conditioned prompts produce systematic differences in LLM-generated surveillance and security robot design descriptions. Using 236 demographic identity labels across single-label and model-augmented prompt conditions, we analyze readability as an initial benchmark for evaluating accessibility and identity-conditioned variation in generated robot design descriptions. The results show significant differences in readability across prompt conditions, design dimensions, and demographic identities. Although readability cannot determine whether an output is fair or socially appropriate, it provides an interpretable baseline within a broader benchmarking framework that also includes lexical, semantic, sentiment, syntactic, and fairness-focused analyses.

</details>


### [236] [ScenarioCharacterization: A Modular Toolkit for Characterizing Safety across Trajectory Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16041)
*Ingrid Navarro,Yutong Duan,Jonathan Francis,Jean Oh*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An open-source, modular, config-driven framework (ScenarioCharacterization) for automated, dataset-agnostic profiling of driving scenarios in trajectory datasets, via a three-layer pipeline (dataset adapter, characterizer, analysis) with schema-based communication; demonstrated on Waymo Open Motion, Argoverse2, nuPlan; available on GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable consistent, reusable scenario profiling across heterogeneous driving datasets, reducing integration effort and enabling downstream analyses.

Method: Three-layer pipeline: dataset adapter maps datasets onto a common Scenario representation; characterizer performs feature extraction, behavior probing, and criticality scoring at scenario and agent levels; analysis layer provides visualization and analyses. All layers communicate via Pydantic-validated schemas, configuration-driven to allow plugging new datasets without rewriting code.

Result: Shown example outputs on three datasets; open-source; design and APIs described; outlines downstream uses; GitHub repo provided.

Conclusion: The framework enables easy dataset plug-in and provides a scalable, modular approach for driving-scenario characterization; facilitates cross-dataset analyses and reuse.

Abstract: We introduce ScenarioCharacterization, an open-source framework for automated, dataset-agnostic profiling of driving scenarios in trajectory datasets. Our framework is packaged as a modular, configuration-driven pipeline of three layers: a dataset adapter that maps custom datasets onto an open Scenario representation, a characterizer that performs feature extraction, behavior probing, and criticality scoring at scenario and agent levels, and an analysis layer for scenario visualization and feature, score, and probe analyses. Because the layers communicate only through Pydantic-validated schemas composed via configurations, a new dataset can easily plug in without rewriting the characterization and analysis stack.
  This technical report describes the design and APIs, shows example outputs on Waymo Open Motion, Argoverse2, and nuPlan, and discusses downstream uses of the approach. The framework is available at https://github.com/navarrs/ScenarioCharacterization.

</details>


### [237] [SurgVIL: Scaling Surgical Robot Imitation Learning with Open-source Surgical Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16058)
*Xinhao Chen,JuoTung Chen,Nigel Nelson,Antony Goldenberg,Jesse Haworth,Sean D. Huver,Axel Krieger*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SurgVIL scales surgical robot imitation learning by leveraging open-source surgical videos with weakly supervised kinematics, improving generalization from phantom demonstrations to real-tissue tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data scarcity of synchronized video-action demonstrations in real clinical tissue; phantom data are fully labeled but lack visual diversity; a scalable, multi-source approach is needed to bridge domain gaps.

Method: Fuse kinematically labeled phantom demonstrations with open-source surgical videos. Since the videos lack robot motion labels, estimate approximate kinematics as weak supervision. Train policies across multiple backbones (ACT, π0, GR00T-H) on needle pick-up and cholecystectomy cutting tasks.

Result: Incorporating surgical videos substantially improves generalization to real-tissue and out-of-distribution scenarios across the tested backbones, indicating a scalable path from phantom training to generalizable surgical policies.

Conclusion: SurgVIL demonstrates a viable, scalable approach to scaling surgical robot imitation learning by combining labeled phantom data with open-source videos, enabling better generalization and broader data coverage for real-world policies.

Abstract: Learning-based surgical robot autonomy requires large-scale demonstrations with synchronized videos and robot actions, but such data are exceedingly rare in clinical or realistic tissue settings because robot kinematics are typically inaccessible outside controlled research systems. In contrast, phantom data collected on research platforms provide accurate action labels but lack the visual diversity of real tissue. We propose SurgVIL, a framework for scaling surgical robot imitation learning using open-source surgical videos. SurgVIL combines kinematically labeled phantom robot demonstrations with surgical videos from open-source datasets and online sources for policy learning. Since these videos lack robot motion labels, we estimate approximate kinematics as weak supervision. We evaluate SurgVIL on two da Vinci robot tasks: needle pick-up and cholecystectomy cutting. Across ACT, $π_0$, and GR00T-H backbones, adding surgical videos substantially improves generalization to real-tissue and out-of-distribution settings, suggesting a scalable path from phantom training toward generalizable surgical robot policies.

</details>


### [238] [US-VLA: An Ultrasound Vision-Language-Action Model for Embodied Abdomina](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16074)
*Cheng Zhang,Xingzheng Wu,Guihao Yan,Xifeng Hu,Zhi Liu,Mei Wu,Qing Cai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: US-VLA is a vision-language-action model for automated ultrasound scanning that uses a ultrasound-aware expert fusion module and a real-world US-VLA-Data dataset to guide sequential probe manipulation; claims competitive performance and potential generalization in abdominal ultrasound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome generalization and stability issues in reinforcement learning and learning-assisted ultrasound scanning caused by hand-crafted rewards and data scarcity, by encoding semantic clinical goals and providing real-time guidance across devices and populations.

Method: Introduce an ultrasound-aware expert fusion module that integrates ultrasound observations with contextual information to produce semantic feedback; develop US-VLA-Data with five standard planes for liver and kidney, comprising 320 expert scanning trajectories and ~80,000 synchronized timesteps; implement US-VLA to generate sequential probe manipulation actions under real-time ultrasound feedback; release source code.

Result: Extensive experiments show US-VLA achieves competitive performance on ultrasound probe manipulation tasks, indicating effectiveness and promising generalization within the evaluated abdominal setting.

Conclusion: US-VLA demonstrates the feasibility of semantically guided, real-time ultrasound scanning with potential generalization beyond the evaluated abdominal scenarios; dataset and code release facilitate reproducibility and further research.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence-assisted ultrasound scanning enhances diagnostic reliability and efficiency by providing real-time guidance for standardized image acquisition and reducing operator dependence. However, existing reinforcement learning and learning-assisted ultrasound scanning methods typically rely on carefully designed reward functions or extensive interaction data, which limits their generalization ability and stability across different devices, patient populations, and complex clinical scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose an ultrasound vision-language-action model (US-VLA) for automated ultrasound scanning that explicitly encodes clinical semantic goals and generates sequential probe manipulation actions under real-time ultrasound feedback. In particular, we first design an ultrasound-aware expert fusion module to jointly integrate ultrasound observations with auxiliary contextual information, enabling semantic ultrasound feedback to effectively guide the scanning process. Then, we construct US-VLA-Data, a real-world dataset covering liver and kidney examinations, which includes five clinically defined standard planes and comprises 320 expert scanning trajectories with approximately 80,000 synchronized timesteps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that US-VLA achieves competitive performance in ultrasound probe manipulation tasks, indicating its effectiveness and promising generalization within the evaluated abdominal ultrasound setting. The source code is available at https://github.com/VMVLab/US-VLA.

</details>


### [239] [Unified Condition-Action Modeling for Accurate One-Step Action Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16153)
*Xinyu Zhou,Zikun Cai,Kuangji Zuo,Gen Li,Boyu Ma,Yanshuo Lu,Yutong Song,Mingqi Yuan,Jiayu Chen,Jianfei Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Unified Condition-Action modeling (UCA-Flow) integrates conditions and actions into a single token sequence, enabling joint learning, faster inference, and higher success in robot manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion/flow policies often treat conditions as auxiliary signals rather than jointly evolving with action trajectories, which can limit performance under tight latency constraints.

Method: Represent observation, timestep, interval conditions and actions as tokens and process them with a Unified Condition-Action Transformer; employ dynamic condition representation reconstruction during generation; introduce an improved dual-pass supervision over u and v for optimization.

Result: Achieves a 9.3 percentage point increase in average success rate over the strongest baseline; offers 45.6x and 33.4x speedups over DP3 and Simple DP3; remains 4.3x and 2.3x faster than one-step FlowPolicy and MP1, respectively.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling conditions and actions in a unified token space enables accurate, fast one-step action generation for robot manipulation, with substantial efficiency gains and improved performance.

Abstract: Robot manipulation requires policies that are both accurate and efficient, as robot control must respond to changing observations under tight latency constraints. Recent diffusion and flow policies are promising, but they often treat conditions as auxiliary signals rather than jointly evolving them with action trajectories. We find that this limitation can be effectively mitigated by a \textbf{simple yet effective unified condition-action modeling design} that represents conditions and actions in a shared token space, allowing a compact model to achieve high performance while improving both inference speed and accuracy. Therefore, we propose UCA-Flow, a unified condition-action modeling framework for accurate one-step action generation. Our method unifies observation conditions, timestep conditions, interval conditions, and action tokens into a single sequence, and processes them with a Unified Condition-Action Transformer for joint condition-action representation learning. As a result, condition representations are dynamically reconstructed according to the current generation stage, highlighting information most relevant for action refinement. Furthermore, we introduce an improved dual-pass supervision scheme over $u$ and $v$ for stronger optimization of unified condition-action modeling. UCA-Flow improves the average success rate by 9.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline, while achieving $45.6\times$ and $33.4\times$ speedups over DP3 and Simple DP3, and remaining $4.3\times$ and $2.3\times$ faster than one-step FlowPolicy and MP1, respectively.

</details>


### [240] [SparkVLA: Stop-Aware Hierarchical VLA with Adaptive Action Chunking for Long-Horizon Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16172)
*Xunyao Lei,Renjun Wu,Tianlin Huo,Xuesong Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SparkVLA unifies stop and execution-length decisions in a single ranking over candidates, improving hierarchical Vision-Language-Action performance; introduces Anchor-Conditioned Context Encoding and Stop-Aware Action-Prefix Selection; demonstrates strong gains on RoboCerebra and real-robot experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In hierarchical VLA, the decision of when to terminate a subtask and how far to execute an action are mutually dependent. Existing architectures optimize these decisions separately, leading to suboptimal performance due to asymmetric information.

Method: Formulate stopping and action-prefix length as a single ranking among a unified candidate set that includes Stop and every action-prefix. Use an Anchor-Conditioned Context Encoding module to cache a history-aware subtask anchor encoding (onset-state memory and goal semantics). Apply a Stop-Aware Action-Prefix Selection head that scores all candidates via full self-attention at chunk boundaries (bn attention) for efficiency; relies on offline ordinal preferences instead of threshold tuning.

Result: On RoboCerebra, SparkVLA achieves 47.12% success rate, surpassing the official hierarchical baseline by 30.57% and the strongest reproducible method by 26.83%. Real-robot experiments on multi-step tasks validate gains on physical hardware.

Conclusion: The unified ranking approach eliminates the need for threshold tuning and leverages history-aware anchors and stop-aware scoring to improve hierarchical VLA performance, with strong results in both simulated benchmarks and real hardware.

Abstract: At every re-observation point in a hierarchical Vision-Language-Action (VLA) system, two interface decisions must be made: when to terminate the current subtask and how far to execute the proposed action chunk. These decisions are mutually dependent---the optimal stopping point depends on what the executor plans to do, while the optimal execution length depends on where the subtask boundary lies---yet existing architectures evaluate them in isolation, an asymmetry neither module can overcome alone. We present SparkVLA, a stop-aware hierarchical VLA that resolves this mutual dependency by formulating both decisions as a single ranking: Stop competes against every action-prefix length in a unified candidate set, and the system selects the highest-scoring option, eliminating threshold tuning and requiring only offline ordinal preferences. An Anchor-Conditioned Context Encoding module caches a history-aware subtask anchor encoding onset-state memory and goal semantics, guiding visual-token pruning toward task-relevant regions; a Stop-Aware Action-Prefix Selection head scores all candidates via full self bnattention at chunk boundaries for efficiency. On RoboCerebra, SparkVLA achieves 47.12% success rate, surpassing the official hierarchical baseline by 30.57% and the strongest reproducible method by 26.83% Real-robot experiments on multi-step tasks further validate these gains on physical hardware.

</details>


### [241] [RoboStriker: Latent-Space Strategic Games for Autonomous Humanoid Boxing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16195)
*Kangning Yin,Kaige Liu,Zhe Cao,Wentao Dong,Weishuai Zeng,Tianyi Zhang,Qiang Zhang,Jingbo Wang,Jiangmiao Pang,Yang Li,Ming Zhou,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A latent-space, two-player zero-sum game (RoboStriker) for humanoid combat that constrains exploration to a decoder-reachable latent manifold learned from predefined boxing motions, enabling stable self-play and successful real-robot deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between strategic multi-agent reinforcement learning and physically feasible action in contact-rich humanoid tasks; prevent catastrophic balance failures from exploring raw motor spaces by constraining exploration to a learned latent space.

Method: Formulate a two-player latent-space zero-sum Markov game. Propose RoboStriker: a hierarchical framework that distills boxing motion expertise into a bounded latent manifold and uses Latent-Space Neural Fictitious Self-Play for co-evolution. Train in a structured latent space and execute via a motion decoder. Validate with extensive simulations and real-robot experiments; code and supplementary materials released.

Result: Latent-space reasoning substantially outperforms direct exploration in raw action space, reducing balance failures and improving tactical performance (win rates, striking efficiency). Real-world humanoid deployment successfully validated.

Conclusion: Constrained latent-space strategic exploration enables robust, competitive humanoid combat policies and can generalize beyond raw motor spaces, with demonstrated transfer to real robots.

Abstract: Achieving human-level competitive intelligence and physical agility in humanoid robots remains a profound challenge, particularly in contact-rich and highly dynamic tasks such as boxing. While Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning offers a principled framework for strategic interaction, its direct application to unstructured raw motor spaces inevitably leads to joint-level physical collapse, preventing the emergence of any viable combat tactics. To resolve this fundamental conflict between strategic exploration and physical feasibility, we formulate the humanoid combat task as a novel two-player latent-space zero-sum Markov game. Under standard regularity and approximate best-response assumptions, we show that the latent formulation induces an equivalent game over the decoder-reachable action manifold, providing an approximate-Nash interpretation of the resulting self-play dynamics. To instantiate this theoretical formulation, we propose RoboStriker, a hierarchical framework that decouples high-level reasoning from low-level execution. It first distills the tracking expertise of predefined boxing motions into a topologically bounded latent manifold. This structured latent foundation subsequently drives multi-agent co-evolution via Latent-Space Neural Fictitious Self-Play. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that gaming within this structured latent space substantially outperforms direct exploration. By constraining strategic exploration through a pretrained motion decoder, RoboStriker substantially reduces the catastrophic balance failures observed in raw action-space methods and achieves superior tactical performance in both competitive win rates and striking efficiency. Finally, we successfully deploy and validate our learned combat policies on real-world humanoid robots. Our code and video and supplementary materials are available at RoboStriker.

</details>


### [242] [Deep Probabilistic Indoor Gas Source Localization via Physical Dependency-Guided Sequential Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16221)
*Seunghwan Kim,Hyungjin Kim,Junhee Lee,Hyondong Oh*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A deep probabilistic, physics-informed framework for indoor gas source localization that sequentially infers wind and concentration fields to estimate the source, improving performance under sparse/noisy data and enabling real-time operation on embedded GPUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate indoor gas source localization is hindered by complex dispersion due to walls/obstacles and by the computational cost of high-fidelity models; a real-time, robust solution is needed for safety.

Method: A deep probabilistic model that embeds indoor gas transport physics through sequential conditional inference: first infer wind and concentration fields, then update the source posterior using these fields, allowing physics-guided inference to improve robustness with sparse observations.

Result: The approach outperforms representative GSL baselines in simulations and enables accurate, efficient active GSL; real-robot experiments demonstrate feasibility of online operation on embedded GPUs.

Conclusion: Integrating physics-informed gas transport with sequential probabilistic inference yields robust, real-time GSL under sparsity/noise and supports scalable deployment on resource-constrained platforms.

Abstract: Reliable gas source localization (GSL) is critical to safety in industrial and urban environments, yet remains challenging indoors because walls and obstacles interact with airflow to create complex gas dispersion. High-fidelity models such as computational fluid dynamics and filament models can capture these effects, but their computational cost limits online use. We propose a deep probabilistic framework that infers the source posterior from sparse and noisy measurements collected by a mobile robot. Unlike end-to-end models that directly infer source estimates from measurements, the proposed method incorporates physical dependencies of indoor gas transport, where wind and source location govern the concentration field. These dependencies are embedded through sequential conditional inference, in which inferred wind and concentration fields guide source posterior estimation. This structure improves localization under sparse and noisy observations. Evaluations show that the proposed method outperforms representative GSL baselines and enables accurate and efficient active GSL in simulations. Real-robot experiments demonstrate the feasibility of online operation on an embedded GPU.

</details>


### [243] [HiPHI: A Large-Scale Benchmark for High-Precision Human Motion and Object-Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16222)
*Jiahao Ji,Ji Ma,Runhan Zhang,Runyi Yu,Wenjia Wang,Weiheng Chi,Qianqian Peng,Weichao Yan,Yongfei Gu,Ye Tian,Ting Wu,Longwei Li,Chun Yuan,Ruoli Dai,Lei Han*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HiPHI: a 600+ hour high-fidelity whole-body human motion dataset with physics-grounded interactions, guided by FrameNet, including sub-millimeter mocap and object trajectories, plus benchmarks for diversity, grounding, and physical AI; aims to advance humanoid policy learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing datasets either lack precise physical states (web videos) or have limited behavioral coverage (lab motion capture). There is a need for scalable, high-fidelity, diverse motion data with interaction grounding to train and evaluate humanoid policies.

Method: Optical motion capture pipeline; over 600 hours of data; sub-millimeter marker tracking; mesh-level object trajectories; theoretical framework grounding with FrameNet; creation of benchmarks for motion-space diversity, interaction grounding, object consistency, and physical AI tasks.

Result: HiPHI expands motion coverage compared to existing motion datasets while maintaining high-fidelity interaction quality; provides scalable data foundation for training, evaluating, and generalizing humanoid policies in real-world embodied tasks; potential extension to motion priors in computer graphics.

Conclusion: HiPHI enables scalable humanoid policy learning with comprehensive motion and interaction data; frames a path for broader use and extensions to motion priors.

Abstract: Humanoid intelligence requires learning over an extremely diverse space of whole-body motions and physically grounded interactions. However, existing embodied datasets remain fundamentally limited: internet-scale video data lack precise physical states and interaction grounding, while laboratory motion datasets provide high fidelity but only narrow behavioral coverage. This mismatch creates a critical bottleneck for scalable humanoid policy learning. We present HiPHI, a 600+ hour scale high-fidelity whole-body human motion dataset designed to systematically maximize coverage of the human motion and interaction manifold. HiPHI is theoretically guided by FrameNet, a linguistic framework organizing human primitives. Created using an optical motion capture pipeline, HiPHI provides sub-millimeter spatial marker tracking accuracy for full-body human motion and mesh-level object trajectories. We further introduce a benchmark suite evaluating motion-space diversity, interaction grounding, object consistency, and physical AI applications. Our analyses demonstrate that HiPHI significantly expands motion coverage compared to existing motion datasets while maintaining high-fidelity interaction quality, and establishes a scalable data foundation for training, evaluating, and generalizing humanoid policies in real-world embodied tasks, where similar extensions are also applicable to motion prior models in computer graphics.

</details>


### [244] [Planner-Conditioned Diffusion for Coordinated Multi-Agent Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16229)
*Marcus Yu Siong Teo,Jeric Lew,Tanishq Duhan,Guillaume Sartoretti*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PCDP introduces a planner-conditioned diffusion policy for multi-agent exploration, enabling diverse long-horizon trajectories and coordination via local reranking; achieves strong performance on simulation and real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve scalable, non-redundant, long-horizon multi-agent exploration without heavy handcrafted coordination; diffusion planners offer long-horizon trajectories but suffer from limited behavioral diversity and controllability, motivating a multimodal, planner-aware policy that can be reused across agents.

Method: Train a single diffusion policy conditioned on an explicit planner identity, trained on demonstrations from multiple planner styles to learn a multimodal trajectory distribution. Reuse this single-agent policy across all agents and implement coordination through local reranking to select joint trajectories with minimal overlap among nearby agents.

Result: PCDP matches the perfect success rate of diffusion baselines while improving mean max-agent travel, total team travel, and agent imbalance. Reranking on a single-planner baseline yields only marginal gains, indicating planner-conditioned multimodality drives the gains. Qualitative results and real-robot experiments show emergent spatial separation without explicit repulsion.

Conclusion: Planner-conditioned diffusion with local reranking yields scalable, diverse, and controllable multi-agent exploration, achieving strong simulation and real-world performance and highlighting multimodality as the key for coordination.

Abstract: Coordinated multi-agent exploration requires not only efficient individual coverage but also non-redundant coverage across agents over extended planning horizons. Conventional approaches rely on hand-crafted coordination rules, while end-to-end multi-agent learning methods are difficult to scale and train. Diffusion-based planners such as DARE offer a promising alternative by generating long-horizon trajectories instead of single-step actions, but existing methods are trained on a narrow planner distribution, limiting behavioral diversity and inference-time controllability. We propose a Planner-Conditioned Diffusion Policy (PCDP) for graph-based multi-agent exploration. PCDP is trained on demonstrations from multiple planner styles with planner identity as an explicit conditioning input, enabling a single shared model to learn a multimodal trajectory distribution and generate diverse, controllable trajectory candidates from the same observation. Rather than learning coordination end-to-end, we reuse this multimodal single-agent policy across all agents and introduce coordination through local reranking, in which nearby agents jointly select the trajectory combination with minimal predicted overlap. We evaluate PCDP against classical and diffusion-based baselines on 100 held-out maps in a four-agent simulation setting. PCDP matches the perfect success rate of the diffusion-based baselines while improving mean max-agent travel, total team travel, and agent imbalance. Crucially, reranking alone over a single-planner baseline yields only marginal gains, indicating that planner-conditioned multimodality is the main contributor to improved coordination. Qualitative simulation results and real-robot experiments with two agents further validate that diverse long-horizon trajectory generation produces emergent spatial separation between agents without any explicit repulsion mechanism.

</details>


### [245] [Cyclops: LiDAR as a Camera That Dreams in Color](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16264)
*Wei Gao,Jian Shu,Mingle Zhao,Maani Ghaffari,David Kong,Chengzhong Xu,Hui Kong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Cyclops translates sparse NRS-LiDAR intensity into RGB video to enable camera-free, all-day perception. It densifies LiDAR intensities with a frozen module, then transports latent features to the RGB distribution via Latent Bridge Matching using a learned velocity field in few ODE steps. Temporal attention mitigates flicker, and a differentiable terminal reward optimizes the velocity field along the trajectory. Experiments show RGB-synthesized video boosts RGB-model performance (segmentation, lane detection, colorization) under diverse lighting, outperforming LiDAR baselines and conventional cameras in near-dark conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the modality gap between sparse LiDAR intensity and dense RGB data to enable robust, camera-free perception across lighting conditions. Leverage pre-trained RGB models by translating LiDAR signals into RGB-like representations and reduce inter-frame flicker.

Method: 1) Freeze a pre-trained densification module to convert sparse LiDAR intensity projections into dense latent representations that capture geometric richness. 2) Use Latent Bridge Matching (LBM) to map the latent to the target RGB distribution via a learned velocity field solved with few-step ODE integration. 3) Incorporate temporal attention to inject prior-frame context and stabilize visuals across frames. 4) Model the velocity field as a policy optimized with a differentiable terminal reward to maximize terminal fidelity along the ODE path. 5) Apply the synthesized RGB to standard RGB models for perception tasks (segmentation, lane detection, colorization).

Result: Synthesized RGB frames under various lighting, including near-dark, enable RGB-trained perception models to significantly outperform both LiDAR baselines and traditional cameras on semantic segmentation, lane detection, and colorization. The method reduces modality gap and improves all-day perception performance.

Conclusion: Cyclops demonstrates feasibility of converting sparse LiDAR intensity into RGB video to support camera-free perception. The approach integrates a frozen densification module, Latent Bridge Matching with a velocity field optimized via a differentiable terminal reward, and temporal attention to mitigate flicker. This yields improved task performance across lighting conditions and tasks, validating the modality-bridging pipeline.

Abstract: Conventionally, robotic perception relies heavily on cameras due to the rich semantic texture they provide. However, their performance degrades significantly in low-light or high-dynamic-range environments. Conversely, while Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) captures illumination-invariant geometric and intensity properties, the resulting data are typically single-channel and sparse, creating a significant modality gap when applying vision models pre-trained on RGB datasets. In this paper, we propose Cyclops, a framework that translates sparse Non-Repetitive Scanning LiDAR (NRS-LiDAR) intensity into RGB video, enabling camera-free inference for all-day perception tasks. Our approach first converts sparse LiDAR intensity projections into dense representations via a frozen pre-trained densification module, serving as a geometrically rich source condition. The dense intensity latent is then transported toward the target RGB distribution through Latent Bridge Matching (LBM) with a learned velocity field in a few ODE integration steps. To mitigate inter-frame flickering, we inject prior-frame context via temporal attention layers and further formulate the velocity field as a policy optimized by a differentiable terminal reward that encourages terminal fidelity through backpropagation along the ODE trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized RGB, including those generated under near-dark conditions, enable standard RGB-based perception models to substantially outperform both LiDAR baselines and conventional cameras on semantic segmentation, lane detection, and point cloud colorization across diverse lighting conditions.

</details>


### [246] [Marker-Constrained Pose-Graph Correction for Cross-Platform Georeferencing in GNSS-Denied Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16281)
*Marco Giberna,Jose Luis Sanchez Lopez,Holger Voos*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Georeference lightweight odometry and dense reconstructions in GNSS-denied environments using pre-surveyed Cholesteric Spherical Reflector (CSR) markers to anchor outputs to a common LUREF frame via marker-constrained pose-graph optimization; real-time marker processing with sub-second trajectory correction; significant drift reduction observed in UAV/UGV emulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNSS-denied operations require reliable, common spatial references across heterogeneous sensors (odometry and dense mapping). Pre-surveyed visual anchors enable alignment to a geodetic frame without GNSS.

Method: Deploy camouflage-matched CSR markers (iMarkers) as pre-surveyed anchors. Perform coarse similarity alignment between LiDAR-odometry and RTAB-Map reconstruction and enforce marker-constrained pose-graph optimization to express all outputs in LUREF. Evaluate with two handheld sessions (UAV/UAV-emulating and UGV-emulating), relocate one marker among six surveyed positions, and quantify drift correction; real-time marker processing and sub-0.25 s trajectory correction per session.

Result: Marker-anchor correction reduced revisit inconsistency by 97.9% (UAV) and 99.1% (UGV); improved held-out anchor prediction vs one-time alignment; cross-session dense reconstructions achieved median 58 cm NN distance without cross-session registration; marker processing real-time; trajectory correction <0.25 s per session.

Conclusion: Pre-surveyed CSR-based anchors enable georeferencing of lightweight odometry and dense reconstructions in GNSS-denied operation with real-time marker processing and substantial drift reduction, demonstrating proof-of-concept feasibility.

Abstract: Autonomous operation in GNSS-denied environments requires heterogeneous mapping pipelines to maintain a consistent spatial reference. This paper presents a framework using camouflage-matched fiducial markers fabricated from Cholesteric Spherical Reflectors (CSRs) as pre-surveyed visual anchors.
