No gradient or parameter updates are performed.

Result: On RoboMemArena, BATON improves task success by 11.6% and cumulative success by 14.9% over the SOTA baseline.

Conclusion: Subtask-centric exploration with transition-aware memory reduces exploration cost from multiplicative to additive, provides clear attribution of failures to stages, and eliminates the need for parameter updates, yielding improved long-horizon performance.

Abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation chains many contact-rich skills into one multi-stage task. Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly master the individual skills, yet the chain still fails: errors compound beyond the policy's ability to correct, and one subtask silently constrains the next. A promising recipe freezes the VLA and puts an LLM agent in charge: it plans in language, moves in free space with analytic primitives, invokes the VLA only for contact-rich segments, and writes adaptation into language memory. Applied to long horizons, it breaks twice. (1) Competence comes from whole-task exploration at test time, whose cost is multiplicative in stages: if one stage needs T episodes, a K-stage task needs about T^K, and a failure does not reveal which stage caused it. (2) It has no representation of transitions: the VLA primitive carries an exit but no entry condition, so a subtask can succeed in a form its successor cannot use. We present BATON. Against (1), BATON makes the subtask the unit of exploration: each is explored in the cheap short-horizon regime and its solution stored in memory; a long-horizon trajectory is then composed from these solutions rather than discovered whole. Cost becomes additive (T*K) and every failure is attributed to a single stage. Against (2), BATON equips exploration with a transition-aware memory. Within a subtask, a verifier agent governs the invocation transition: the VLA is called only after the wrist view confirms the scene is ready. Across subtasks, a handoff transition restores an entry state disturbed by the predecessor's residue, and a lookahead transition selects the strategy whose outcome the successor can inherit. No parameters are updated. On the long-horizon benchmark RoboMemArena, BATON improves task success by 11.6% and cumulative success by 14.9% over the SoTA.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [272] [Learning Discrete Riemannian Metrics for Physical Fields with Cochain-Frame Equivarianc](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14556)
*Dongzhe Zheng,Christine Allen-Blanchette*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RHMP reframes mesh-based physics learning by fixing coboundaries and learning SPD cochain metrics, enabling cochain-frame equivariance, exact topological identities, and improved generalization across physics benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conservation laws are topological and should be preserved exactly; existing neural surrogates conflate topology and geometry, learning unconstrained propagation. A principled architecture is needed to separate and respect topology while learning geometry.

Method: Fix the cellular coboundaries d_k from oriented incidence; learn symmetric positive-definite cochain metrics H_k for geometry-dependent propagation. Use metric-weighted Hodge blocks d_k^T H_{k+1} d_k to enforce cochain-frame equivariance and preserve cochain identities (d_{k+1}d_k=0) and positive semi-definite operators; ensure exact Abelian curvature invariance.

Result: Evaluated on seven physical benchmarks spanning fluids, electromagnetism, gauge fields, and variable-mesh CFD. RHMP achieved the best overall performance, with the largest gains where topology, learned geometry, and field structure interact.

Conclusion: RHMP demonstrates that separating topology (preserved exactly by fixed d_k) from learnable geometry (H_k) yields exact topological identities, stable energetics, and superior performance across diverse physics tasks; it supports an architectural principle for physics-informed graph neural networks.

Abstract: Physical fields on meshes require a separation between topology and geometry: conservation laws are topological and should be exact, while geometry, material response, and anisotropic coupling must be learned from data. Existing neural surrogates often mix these roles inside unconstrained message passing. We introduce Riemannian Hodge Message Passing (RHMP), which turns this separation into an architectural principle. RHMP fixes the cellular coboundaries ($d_k$) determined by oriented incidence and learns symmetric positive-definite cochain metrics ($H_k$) for geometry-dependent propagation. Treating $H_k$ as the learned metric motivates cochain-frame equivariance: physical propagation should be invariant to orthogonal changes of the hidden cochain feature basis. RHMP implements this principle with metric-weighted Hodge blocks ($d_k^\top H_{k+1}d_k$), yielding exact cochain-complex identities ($d_{k+1}d_k=0$), nonnegative Hodge energies, positive-semidefinite operators, and exact Abelian curvature invariance. Across seven physical benchmarks spanning fluids, electromagnetism, gauge fields, and variable-mesh CFD, RHMP achieves the best overall performance, with the largest gains when topology, learned geometry, and field structure interact.

</details>


### [273] [Forward Pass Domain Adaptation (Without Cross-Layer Backpropagation)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14563)
*Rivaan Patil,Simon Dennis,Hao Guo,Kevin Shabahang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FPO bypasses backward passes, enabling efficient fine-tuning of LLMs with 2.7–3.2× throughput and ~40% lower peak memory, while keeping off-domain benchmarks within seed-noise of baseline. It relies on a late-layer gradient approximation and a per-layer diagnostic to identify viable adaptation; uses a single output error signal applied to target layers with no inter-layer signals or autograd graph. Evaluated on multiple model families; SFT localization to FPO's target layers is possible but costlier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increase fine-tuning efficiency by eliminating backward propagation through the model body, achieving higher throughput and lower memory without sacrificing performance.

Method: Empirical observation that late transformer layers' output-layer error approximates the true gradient (cosine similarity ~0.47–0.59); introduce a two-minute per-layer diagnostic to quantify this approximation; compute a single output error signal and apply it to each target layer; no inter-layer signal propagation; no autograd graph; evaluate on three model families; optionally localize SFT to FPO's layers.

Result: Throughput gains of 2.7–3.2× with ~40% less peak memory; in-domain perplexity improved; off-domain benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Winogrande) remain within seed-noise of baseline; localizing SFT to FPO layers is feasible but at 2.2× wall-clock cost.

Conclusion: FPO shows that targeted late-layer adaptation with a single output-derived error signal can enable efficient fine-tuning, preserving performance on many benchmarks; full-network fine-tuning does not reliably reproduce these benefits.

Abstract: Forward-Pass-Only MLP training (FPO) adapts large language models without a backward pass through the model body, achieving 2.7--3.2x the throughput of standard fine-tuning at ~40% less peak training memory, while leaving off-domain benchmarks within seed-noise of baseline, a property that full-network fine-tuning does not reliably reproduce. FPO rests on a single empirical observation: at late layers of a transformer, the output-layer prediction error approximates the true gradient with cosine similarity 0.47--0.59 across six public models we survey. We introduce a two-minute diagnostic that quantifies this approximation per layer for any model, identifying where late-layer adaptation is viable. Informed by the diagnostic, FPO computes a single error signal at the output and applies it to each target layer. No signal is propagated between layers, and no autograd graph is constructed at any point. We evaluate FPO on three model families (OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-8B, Falcon3-7B). Across all three, FPO produces in-domain perplexity improvement and leaves MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, and Winogrande within seed-noise of baseline. Localizing SFT to FPO's target layers to enter this regime is also feasible, but at 2.2x the wall-clock cost of FPO.

</details>


### [274] [Coarse-to-Fine Multi-Resolution Diffusion Models for Trajectory Generation in Urban Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14570)
*Wen Ye,Muyan Weng,Chuizheng Meng,Hao Niu,Yizhou Zhang,Yan Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MR-Traj is a multi-resolution diffusion model for synthetic trajectory generation that decomposes trajectories into coarse milestones and fine segments. It captures spatial-temporal dependencies across scales, achieving comparable global-distribution fidelity to SOTA while improving fine-grained pattern modeling and downstream task performance, and increases output diversity to reduce linkage risk in seed-guided releases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public trajectory data are constrained by privacy concerns, limiting utility for urban analytics. Existing methods focus on global distribution alignment but ignore multi-resolution mobility patterns critical for practical tasks. A hierarchical, multi-resolution approach aims to preserve utility across scales.

Method: MR-Traj treats trajectories as compositions of coarse milestones and fine-grained segments and learns a diffusion process at multiple resolutions. It injects stochasticity at each resolution level to generate diverse trajectories, enabling better capture of hierarchical spatial-temporal dependencies and reducing trajectory linkage risk.

Result: Experiments show MR-Traj matches state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in global distribution similarity, but outperforms SOTA in modeling fine-resolution mobility patterns and supporting downstream urban mobility tasks. The multi-resolution stochasticity yields more diverse trajectories and lowers linkage risk in seed-guided data release. Code is publicly available.

Conclusion: A principled multi-resolution diffusion framework can effectively generate large-scale, diverse synthetic trajectories that preserve global statistics while enhancing fine-grained mobility realism and utility for downstream tasks, with practical privacy benefits.

Abstract: Understanding human mobility is critical for a wide range of urban applications, including traffic management, epidemic control, and urban planning. However, due to privacy concerns, the availability of large-scale public trajectory data remains limited, posing challenges for downstream mobility analysis. Existing methods for synthetic trajectory generation primarily focus on matching global distribution similarity, while often overlooking mobility patterns across different spatial and temporal resolutions that are essential for practical utility.
  To address these challenges, we propose a novel multi-resolution diffusion framework, MR-Traj, for large-scale trajectory generation. MR-Traj explicitly models trajectories as compositions of coarse-grained milestones and fine-grained segments, enabling the capture of complex spatial-temporal dependencies at multiple resolutions. Experimental results demonstrate that MR-Traj achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in terms of global distribution similarity, while consistently outperforming them in modeling fine-resolution mobility patterns and supporting downstream urban mobility tasks. In addition, by introducing stochasticity at multiple resolution levels, MR-Traj generates more diverse trajectories, which empirically reduces trajectory linkage risk under a seed-guided data release setting. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ray0202/MR-Traj.

</details>


### [275] [Geometry Is Not Robustness: A Trajectory-Level Study of PGD Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14594)
*Dhairysheel Durgule*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Trajectory-level PGD diagnostics (loss evolution, gradient alignment, steps-to-failure) map optimization dynamics but do not reliably indicate robustness across regimes; steps-to-failure best separates robustness levels, whereas mean loss and gradient alignment tend to be similar across models with different robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether trajectory-based metrics genuinely reflect adversarial robustness or merely the geometry of optimization during PGD attacks.

Method: 20-step PGD with random initializations and multiple restarts for robustness evaluation; full PGD trajectories recorded for 3000 clean-correct samples per model; compare clean-trained vs adversarially-trained CNNs on Fashion-MNIST across robustness regimes; diagnose with loss evolution, gradient alignment, and failure timing.

Result: A clear model robustness hierarchy emerges, yet trajectory metrics contribute unevenly. Steps-to-failure distributions clearly separate robustness regimes and reflect functional resistance; mean loss trajectories and gradient alignment show little differentiation across models with varying robustness. Trajectory diagnostics describe optimization geometry but do not independently measure robustness.

Conclusion: Trajectory-level diagnostics should complement standard robustness measurements, with interpretability contingent on robustness regime and attack strength; not a replacement for final robustness metrics.

Abstract: Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) is widely used to evaluate adversarial robustness, typically via final adversarial accuracy, which does not capture model behaviour throughout the attack. Recent work proposes trajectory-level diagnostics, such as loss evolution, gradient alignment, and steps-to-failure, for deeper insight into adversarial optimisation dynamics. However, whether these diagnostics reliably indicate robustness strength remains unclear. We conduct a trajectory-level investigation of PGD attacks on convolutional neural networks trained on Fashion-MNIST. We compare clean-trained and adversarially-trained models across multiple robustness regimes, using rigorous 20-step PGD evaluations with random initialisation and multiple restarts for robustness measurement, and single-initialisation trajectory recording for diagnostics. We record full PGD trajectories across 3000 clean-correct samples per model and analyse loss evolution, gradient alignment, and failure timing across attack iterations. Our results reveal a clear robustness hierarchy across models; however, trajectory metrics do not contribute equally to its identification. Mean loss trajectories and gradient alignment patterns appear quantitatively similar across adversarially-trained models with substantially different robust accuracies. In contrast, steps-to-failure distributions provide a clearer separation of robustness regimes, directly reflecting functional resistance to adversarial perturbation. These findings indicate that trajectory-level diagnostics describe optimisation geometry but do not independently measure adversarial robustness. Their interpretability depends on robustness regime, attack strength, and multi-metric evaluation. Trajectory-level analysis should be a complementary diagnostic tool, interpreted in context, rather than a replacement for standard robustness measurements.

</details>


### [276] [DumpsterCluster: From Dumpster Diving to Serving LLaMA-70B on $60 GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14614)
*Zeyu Cao,Xuan Guo,Cheng Zhang,Cheuk Hang Lau,Ilia Shumailov,Yiren Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A 128-GPU DumpsterCluster built from second-hand GPUs is economically viable for LLM inference, but its environmental sustainability hinges on energy sources; emissions can far exceed current-gen hardware if electricity is not clean.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether repurposing retired AI GPUs into a DumpsterCluster for modern LLM inference is economically viable and environmentally sustainable, and to identify conditions under which this path makes sense.

Method: Assembled a 128-GPU DumpsterCluster from second-hand components and operated it for one year; applied pipeline-parallel optimizations; benchmarked on LLaMA-70B throughput using V100 GPUs; compared total cost of ownership and energy/carbon metrics against a modern 8-GPU system.

Result: Economically, the DumpsterCluster (~$22k) yields substantial cost advantages over a ~$600k 8-GPU system. It achieves competitive LLaMA-70B throughput after pipeline-parallel optimizations. Environmentally, energy per token is higher; under grid-average carbon intensity, second-hand systems emit ~4x more per token for 8B and >40x for 70B vs current-gen hardware. Viability is region-dependent, favoring low electricity costs and clean energy.

Conclusion: Repurposing retired GPUs can be a viable pathway to expand AI capacity and reduce upfront costs, but only when paired with low-carbon electricity and regions with favorable energy economics; otherwise, environmental impact can negate economic benefits.

Abstract: As AI datacenters retire functional GPUs, vast quantities of still capable accelerators enter secondary markets. This paper investigates whether these retired GPUs can find a productive afterlife to form a DumpsterCluster that can serve modern LLM inference, and under what conditions such repurposing is economically viable and environmentally sustainable. We physically built a 128-GPU DumpsterCluster from scratch using only second-hand components and ran it for one year. At current market prices (\$22K for the DumpsterCluster vs. \$600K for an 8-GPU B200 system), the economic advantages are substantial. Through pipeline-parallel optimizations, our V100 based DumpsterCluster achieves competitive LLaMA-70B throughput, validating production viability. However, our deployment reveals critical context dependencies. Older GPUs consume significantly more energy per token, making total cost of ownership favorable only in regions with inexpensive electricity. Under grid-average carbon intensity, second-hand systems can produce approximately 4x higher total carbon emissions per token for 8B models, and over 40x for 70B models, compared to current-generation hardware. These findings show that GPU afterlife is not universally sustainable - hardware repurposing must be strategically coupled with low carbon energy sources. When deployed in regions with favourable energy economics and clean electricity, second-hand GPUs offer a viable pathway for expanding AI capacity while advancing affordability, energy security, and environmental responsibility.

</details>


### [277] [Calibrated Trust, Not Sharper Prediction: An Empirical Test of Uncertainty Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14617)
*Surya Saka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uncertainty-fusion pipelines in legal AI show limited predictive gains and notable calibration risks; removing Dempster‑Shafer and using conformal selective prediction yields high automation with calibrated trust (~97% automation, ~0.5% error escape).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether integrating uncertainty estimation tools improves real-world case-outcome prediction in law, and assess calibration, safety, and deployment implications of such pipelines.

Method: Test on 1,000 ECtHR cases (LexGLUE/FairLex), ~4,750 per-fact tests, comparing three evidence estimator families (A: raw LLM, B: LLM via fusion pipeline, C: term-frequency baseline) across two frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5); components include Bayesian odds, Dempster-Shafer fusion, conformal prediction; evaluate AUROC, calibration (ECE), and label safety; remove Dempster-Shafer, recalibrate, apply class-conditional risk control with conformal selectivity on full 1,000-case set.

Result: Findings: (1) On discrimination (AUROC ≈ 0.83) the fusion pipeline offers no gain over raw LLM or baseline; frontier LLM alone is strongest. (2) Naive LLM + Bayesian odds + Dempster-Shafer doubles calibration error (ECE 0.16 → 0.46) due to prior mismatch, reproducible across models. (3) Dempster-Shafer fusion is unsafe on long chains, often producing confident but wrong labels; recommended removal. (4) With Dempster-Shafer removed, recalibrated, and deployed with conformal selective-prediction and class-conditional risk control, full 1,000-case set achieves 96.8% accuracy with 0.5% errors escaping and 96.3% caught for review, vs 85.9/3.8/72.1 for untuned baseline. Overall contribution: calibrated trust and operational reliability rather than sharper predictive accuracy; automation is achieved through selective prediction rather than unconditional accuracy gains.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-fusion pipelines in legal AI primarily enhance calibrated trust and operational deployment via selective automation; remove unsafe components (Dempster–Shafer), ensure recalibration, and rely on conformal prediction for prudent escalation rather than pursuing higher discriminative metrics.

Abstract: A recurring proposal in legal AI is to improve case-outcome prediction by fusing uncertainty tools (evidence graphs with belief propagation, sequential Bayesian odds updating, Dempster-Shafer combination, and conformal prediction) into one pipeline. We test this on 1,000 real European Court of Human Rights cases from LexGLUE and FairLex, predicting whether the Court found a Convention violation from the case's fact paragraphs. We compare three families across two frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5) as per-fact evidence estimators: (A) the raw LLM, (B) the LLM routed through the fusion pipeline, and (C) a term-frequency baseline through the same pipeline. Across roughly 4,750 tests we find: (1) on discrimination (AUROC around 0.83) the pipeline yields no improvement over either the raw LLM or the baseline; a frontier LLM used directly is the strongest single discriminator. (2) Naively composing an LLM with Bayesian-odds and Dempster-Shafer fusion more than doubles calibration error (ECE from about 0.16 to 0.46) via a prior-mismatch mechanism that replicates across both models. (3) Dempster-Shafer fusion is actively unsafe on long chains, committing confidently to wrong labels at below-chance accuracy; we recommend removing it. (4) The pipeline's genuine value is operational: routed through a conformal selective-prediction layer, the system decides which cases to automate and which to escalate. After removing Dempster-Shafer, recalibrating, and applying class-conditional risk control on the full 1,000-case set, the tuned engine auto-clears at 96.8 percent accuracy with 0.5 percent errors escaping and 96.3 percent caught for review, versus 85.9 / 3.8 / 72.1 for an untuned baseline. The contribution of such pipelines in law is calibrated trust, not sharper prediction.

</details>


### [278] [PIKFNO: An Interpretable Neural Operator Based on Physics Informed Kernel Function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14619)
*Yuan Guo,Hanshu Chen,Zhuojia Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-informed kernel–based neural operator (PIKFNO) constrains the trunk with physics-informed kernel functions derived from governing equations, uniting kernel-methods with neural operators; two construction strategies; shows high accuracy, interpretability, and data-efficient generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address interpretability and data efficiency limitations of existing neural operators (e.g., DeepONet) by embedding kernel-based physics into the operator design and aligning with meshless collocation kernel expansions.

Method: PIKFNO imposes physics-informed kernel functions on the trunk network. Two construction strategies: (1) data-driven kernel learning, yielding kernels that act as nonsingular fundamental solutions; (2) transformations of analytical fundamental solutions to build kernels. Aligns with kernel expansions used in meshless collocation.

Result: Numerical experiments demonstrate high predictive accuracy, improved interpretability, and superior generalization under limited training data.

Conclusion: PIKFNO provides a new, efficient, physically consistent, and interpretable neural operator framework, bridging kernel methods and neural operators for physics-informed learning.

Abstract: This work proposes a new interpretable neural operator framework, termed the Physics Informed Kernel Function Neural Operator (PIKFNO), which explicitly incorporates physics informed kernel functions derived from governing equations into the neural operator architecture. Unlike traditional neural operators such as DeepONet, which rely on deep networks to implicitly learn basis functions, PIKFNO constrains the trunk network through physics informed kernel functions, thereby aligning its operator structure with the kernel expansions used in meshless collocation methods. Two construction strategies are introduced: one learns kernel functions directly from data, where the learned kernel can be regarded as a nonsingular fundamental solution, while the other builds them through transformations of analytical fundamental solutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that PIKFNO achieves high predictive accuracy with substantially improved interpretability and superior generalization under limited training data. The proposed framework offers a new pathway for developing efficient, physically consistent, and interpretable neural operators.

</details>


### [279] [Explaining Reinforcement Learning Decisions in Self-adaptive Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14620)
*Jasmina Gajcin,Juan C. Rosero,Ivana Dusparic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EARL is a Python library that provides counterfactual explanations for reinforcement learning by exploring What-if scenarios, enabling user-friendly explanations of agent behavior in realistic self-adaptive systems such as CitiBike simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning policies, particularly deep RL, often lack transparency, harming user trust and complicating verification. Counterfactual explanations are intuitive and can improve understanding and trust in RL policies within real-world, self-adaptive systems.

Method: Proposes Explanations using Alternative Realities for Reinforcement Learning (EARL), a Python library that generates counterfactual explanations in RL by constructing What-if scenarios to clarify agent behavior. Demonstrates applicability with a CitiBikes simulation and provides evaluations of performance in real applications.

Result: EARL demonstrates feasibility of generating counterfactual explanations in realistic RL-based systems and shows applicability to self-adaptive settings like CitiBike simulations, with evaluations indicating practical utility and potential improvements in explainability and trust.

Conclusion: EARL advances RL explainability by enabling counterfactual explanations in realistic RL contexts, supporting better understanding and trust in autonomous systems; future work may address scalability, user studies, and integration with verification workflows.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been extensively used in autonomous and self-* systems, but RL policies, especially deep RL ones relying on neural networks, lack transparency and are difficult to understand. This can lead to diminished user trust, and makes for a more challenging verification of systems. To address this challenge, this paper introduces Explanations using Alternative Realities for Reinforcement Learning (EARL), a Python library to produce counterfactual explanations in RL settings. This library allows the user to produce explanations by exploring What-if scenarios to clarify agent behavior by comparing possible outcomes. Counterfactual explanations have been shown to be intuitive and user-friendly in psychology research, but have only recently been explored in RL, with existing implementations usually limited to toy examples and benchmarks. EARL supports counterfactual explanation generation in realistic RL-based self-adaptive systems. To demonstrate its applicability, we demonstrate its use in a simulation of CitiBikes, a self-adaptive bike-sharing system, and we provide evaluations showing how it performs in real applications.

</details>


### [280] [Metaplasticity as adaptive gradient preconditioning for incremental learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14634)
*Isabelle Aguilar,Zayn Andre Zainal,Omid Kavehei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SynGAP is a task-free continual learning method that uses an online, gradient-based metaplasticity mechanism: a bounded multiplicative mask derived from an EMA of the Fisher Information Matrix to precondition gradients and mitigate forgetting without episodic memory or task labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To solve catastrophic forgetting in non-stationary environments without explicit task delineation, by translating continuous biological metaplasticity into a stable optimization-based regularization.

Method: Compute an exponential moving average of the Fisher Information over a data stream; convert this into a bounded multiplicative mask that preconditions gradients during optimization, attenuating updates to historically important parameters.

Result: Empirically outperforms baselines: on Split CIFAR-100, ~4x accuracy gain over EWC++ and ~10% over ER, with reduced forgetting; on CORe50, ~68% accuracy, about 10% above optimizer baselines; claims memory efficiency and edge applicability.

Conclusion: Continuous biological metaplasticity can be formalized as stable gradient-based regularization, yielding a robust, memory-efficient framework for task-free continual learning.

Abstract: Biological intelligence naturally prevents catastrophic forgetting through Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory, a macroscopic consolidation process driven at the local level by synaptic metaplasticity: the continuous, history-dependent neuromodulation of individual synapses. While artificial neural networks struggle with the stability-plasticity dilemma in non-stationary environments, existing solutions often require task labels or incur massive memory overhead, diverging from biological reality. Re-framing this localized neuromodulation as an optimization-driven process, we introduce $\textbf{SynGAP}$: $\textbf{Syn}$aptic $\textbf{G}$eometric $\textbf{A}$daptive $\textbf{P}$reconditioning. SynGAP is a task-free continual learning framework based on adaptive gradient preconditioning. Rather than relying on explicit episodic triggers, SynGAP simulates real-time metaplasticity by maintaining an exponential moving average of the Fisher Information Matrix over a continuous data stream. During the optimization step, these dynamic metaplastic states are translated into a bounded multiplicative mask that preconditions raw gradients, selectively attenuating updates to critical historical parameters. Empirical evaluations demonstrate SynGAP's superior ability to mitigate catastrophic forgetting compared to established baselines. On the Split CIFAR-100 benchmark, SynGAP delivers a $4\times$ increase in accuracy compared to EWC++ and outperforms Experience Replay (ER) by almost $10\%$, while reducing the forgetting measure by over $10\%$ against both methods. Furthermore, on the CORe50 benchmark, SynGAP achieves about $68\%$, a $10\%$ improvement over optimizer baselines. By mathematically formalizing continuous biological metaplasticity as stable gradient-based regularization, SynGAP offers a highly robust and memory-efficient solution for adaptive intelligence at the edge.

</details>


### [281] [Fractional Optimizers Meet Fractal Activation Functions: An Empirical Study of Multi-Scale Optimization in Neural Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14636)
*Sebastian Raubitzek,Georg Goldenits,Sebastian Schrittwieser,Philip König,Kevin Mallinger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fractional optimization and fractal activations interact in a performance-dependent way: some fractional methods pair well with certain fractal activations, especially regularization-style fractional scaling; Grünwald–Letnikov memory aids perturbed surfaces; adaptive memory improves plain memory substitutions, but there is no universal improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how fractional optimization techniques (memory-based fractional derivatives) interact with fractal activation functions (multi-scale, self-similar nonlinearities) in neural network training, and whether their combination yields systematic gains across benchmarks.

Method: Experimentally evaluate various fractional optimizer families on standard benchmark surfaces (Ackley and Himmelblau) in vanilla and Weierstrass-perturbed forms, then train feed-forward networks on ten classification datasets using conventional and fractal activations. Comparisons include standard optimizers, regularization-style fractional scaling, explicit/adaptive memory-based fractional optimizers, and other representative methods.

Result: Findings show selective, not universal, benefits from combining the two directions. Regularization-style fractional scaling performs well with certain fractal activations; Grünwald–Letnikov memory is most beneficial on perturbed surfaces; adaptive memory improves plain memory substitutions in several cases, supporting cautious use of fractional memory as a controllable, direction-specific tool.

Conclusion: The study suggests adaptive memory-based fractional optimization is a promising direction as a controlled alternative to universal replacement, with benefits dependent on activation style and surface perturbation; overall, the interaction is useful but selective.

Abstract: Fractional optimization methods and fractal activation functions are two independent directions for improving neural network training. Fractional optimizers extend first-order optimization through fractional derivatives and memory effects, whereas fractal activations introduce multi-scale nonlinear representations based on self-similar Weierstrass- and Blancmange-type functions. Here, we investigate their interaction within a unified experimental framework. We evaluate fractional optimizer families on Ackley and Himmelblau benchmark surfaces, in standard form and with additive Weierstrass-type perturbations, and then in feed-forward neural networks with conventional and fractal activations on ten classification datasets. The comparison includes standard methods, regularization-style optimizers, explicit and adaptive memory-based fractional optimizers, and other representative literature methods. Overall, fractional optimization and fractal activations show useful but selective pairings. Regularization-style fractional scaling performs well with selected fractal activations in network training, while Grünwald--Letnikov memory is most relevant on perturbed surfaces. Adaptive memory improves plain memory substitution in several cases, supporting controlled fractional memory as a promising direction rather than a universal replacement.

</details>


### [282] [Early Cycle Charge Trajectory Generative Prediction and Full Life Cycle Health Management of Iron-Chromium Flow Batteries Based on FlowBD-E1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14637)
*Suyang Zhuang,Zekun Jiang,Tianhang Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An early-cycle, generative forecasting framework (FlowBD-E1) for Fe-Cr redox flow batteries predicts full future V/I trajectories and health (SOH) from the first few cycles, enabling long-horizon prognostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-duration stationary storage requires proactive degradation detection. Fe-Cr redox flow batteries use abundant materials but suffer from slow chromium kinetics, hydrogen evolution, membrane crossover, and electrolyte imbalance, which slowly reshape charge trajectories. Existing prognostics focus on Li-ion or scalar health metrics; this work aims to forecast complete V/I trajectories to diagnose ageing early.

Method: FlowBD-E1 combines a multi-scale convolutional encoder, a lifecycle Transformer, and an age-aware FiLM decoder to generate future charge voltage/current profiles. It compares deployment strategies: single-step latent extrapolation (SLE), recursive latent forecasting (RLF), and teacher-forced updating (TFU). Trained on the first 9 of 289 cycles of an industrial 33 kW Fe-Cr RFB to forecast remaining cycles and SOH. Evaluation uses joint V/I MAPE and SOH MAPE, with ablations against LSTM/TCN baselines.

Result: RLF achieved a joint V/I MAPE of 0.731% over the remaining lifecycle and SOH MAPE below 1%. Ablation tests show the age-aware generative architecture outperforms LSTM and TCN baselines and maintains sub-percent errors under industrial validation.

Conclusion: Early-cycle trajectory generation can convert a short commissioning record into a long-horizon diagnostic signal for flow-battery management, enabling prognostics and health assessment from limited initial data.

Abstract: Long-duration stationary energy storage requires batteries whose degradation can be detected before substantial capacity loss has accumulated. Iron-chromium redox flow batteries are attractive for this role because they use abundant and low-cost active species, yet their operation is shaped by slow chromium kinetics, hydrogen evolution, membrane crossover and electrolyte imbalance. These coupled processes gradually reshape the full charge voltage/current (V/I) trajectory, but most battery prognostic studies either focus on lithium-ion cells or compress ageing into scalar capacity and state-of-health (SOH) labels. Here we study an industrial 33 kW Fe-Cr redox flow battery and introduce FlowBD-E1, an early-cycle generative forecasting framework that predicts complete future charge V/I trajectories from only the first few cycles. The model combines a multi-scale convolutional encoder, a lifecycle Transformer and an age-aware FiLM decoder, and we compare three deployment strategies: single-step latent extrapolation (SLE), recursive latent forecasting (RLF) and teacher-forced updating (TFU). Using the first 9 of 289 cycles, RLF achieved a joint V/I mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.731% over the remaining lifecycle and produced SOH estimates below 1% MAPE. Ablation and independent-sequence tests showed that the age-aware generative architecture outperformed LSTM and TCN baselines and retained sub-percent errors under industrial validation. These results suggest that early-cycle trajectory generation can turn a short commissioning record into a long-horizon diagnostic signal for flow-battery management.

</details>


### [283] [Randomly initialized autoencoders: fixed points and edge-of-chaos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14638)
*Leonid Berlyand,Roman Sarapin,Yitzchak Shmalo,Victor Slavin,Sasha Sodin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces local and global edge-of-chaos concepts for autoencoders and analyzes their fixed-point stability using random matrix theory (spectral methods for local EoC; Sudakov-Fernique for global EoC).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand existence, stability, and basins of attraction of autoencoder fixed points by leveraging edge-of-chaos ideas and contractive properties; adapt EoC to autoencoders to address perturbations.

Method: Define local and global EoC for autoencoders; analyze local EoC via spectral techniques from random matrix theory; analyze global EoC using the Sudakov-Fernique inequality for Gaussian processes.

Result: Provides a theoretical framework linking autoencoder contraction properties to EoC notions and establishes analytic conditions/bounds for stability and perturbation robustness across scales.

Conclusion: The edge-of-chaos framework for autoencoders offers a principled lens to study stability and robustness of fixed-point dynamics, integrating contraction concepts with RMT tools.

Abstract: In this paper we study autoencoders, a special class of deep neural nets (DNNs) whose performance can be characterized via their fixed points. This perspective naturally raises questions of existence, stability, and basins of attraction of these fixed points. These questions are addressed via the contractive properties of autoencoders, and are closely related to the notion of edge-of-chaos.
  Edge-of-chaos (EoC) is an important notion in the theory of DNNs. It describes the critical regime separating ordered and chaotic signal propagation through a randomly initialized network. Initialization at or near this critical regime offers several theoretical and practical advantages, including stability of the network w.r.t. perturbations of the input. EoC was previously introduced for broad classes of neural networks using mean-field averaging methods. In this paper we modify the notion of EoC for the study of autoencoders. Specifically, we introduce local and global EoC for autoencoders that control local (small) and global (arbitrary) perturbations of the input respectively.
  The study of stability of autoencoders falls within the scope of nonlinear problems in Random Matrix Theory (RMT). Our analysis of local EoC is based on spectral techniques of RMT, whereas global EoC is studied by employing Sudakov-Fernique inequality for Gaussian processes.

</details>


### [284] [Valid Per-Field Selective Risk Control for Document Extraction: Three Failure Modes, a Validity Ladder, and When Conditioning Pays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14639)
*Bhaskar Gurram*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Per-field accept/review with selective risk is evaluated and hardened against three failure modes in real document-extraction; introduces a validity ladder of fixes and multiple certify-able methods (Mondrian Learn-then-Test, Support-bin) with mixed success across settings; releases reg-gated Apache-2.0 tooling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trust contracts for document-extraction require controlling error rates among accepted fields; real pipelines silently violate these guarantees, motivating a rigorous, tiered validity framework and certified results.

Method: Empirical study on 13,859 genuine claude-sonnet-5 fields from 800 CORD receipts; diagnose three failure modes (document clustering, score-refit leakage, tie-mass pathology); implement a validity ladder with tiered guarantees; evaluate via fit/val splits, Mondrian Learn-then-Test with exact binomial tails, Support-bin taxonomy; cross-validate on claude-haiku-4/5 and haiku/qwen; conduct human-gold audit with Fleiss' kappa; release under Apache-2.0.

Result: Found three failure modes; validity ladder improves control with metrics: learned fusion: coverage 0.318, risk 0.096 (alpha 0.10); production variant 0.326; per-group PAC certificates: field-iid 0.171/0.068, cluster-corrected 0.140, doc-iid 0.060; Support-bin wins across tiers (p<1e-4 with Bonferroni); pooled thresholds perform on higher-accuracy corpora; frozen configuration verified on claude-haiku-4/5; blind human audit shows accepted-set risk 1.3% vs 10% budget (Fleiss' kappa 0.83).

Conclusion: Open-source with seed-pinned, regression-gated procedures; multiple tiers provide guarded, though sometimes conservative, risk control; results favor the Support-bin approach for certifiable control on the studied data.

Abstract: Per-field accept/review with selective risk at most alpha -- accept a field only if the error rate among accepted fields is controlled -- is the trust contract document-extraction systems need, and the natural procedure silently violates it on real documents. On 13,859 genuine claude-sonnet-5 fields from 800 CORD receipts (49.0% correct) we diagnose three failure modes: document clustering (design effect 1.84-2.45), score-refit leakage (coverage 0.416 at risk 0.127, violating alpha=0.10 in 95% of splits), and a tie-mass pathology (a degenerate score collapses the threshold grid, 0.030 to 0.001). We organize the fixes as a validity ladder, guarantee form stated per tier. A fit/val split protocol restores expected-selective-risk control for a learned fusion: coverage 0.318 at risk 0.096 at nominal alpha=0.10, no tolerance band (production variant 0.326) -- an on-average point whose realized risk exceeds alpha in 47.5% of resplits, not a certificate. Mondrian Learn-then-Test with exact binomial tails yields per-group PAC certificates: field-iid 0.171 at risk 0.068, cluster-corrected 0.140, doc-iid 0.060 -- the only tier matching documents, honestly near-vacuous today. Support-bin, the pre-specified provenance taxonomy, wins every rigor tier on the sonnet CORD capture (p<1e-4, Bonferroni-corrected) -- a win that does not replicate on the same documents under haiku or qwen -- while on higher-accuracy corpora pooled thresholds win: conditioning helps exactly where pooled cannot certify, subsumed by a learned score elsewhere. A frozen-configuration confirmation on selection-untouched claude-haiku-4-5 held at both risk levels, and a blind three-annotator human-gold audit verifies the practical tier's accepted-set risk at 1.3% against its 10% budget (Fleiss' kappa=0.83; labels err one-sidedly pessimistic). Released Apache-2.0 with seed-pinned, regression-gated procedures.

</details>


### [285] [BDIP-Net: Dual-Interaction Graph Learning for Property Prediction of Bilayer Materials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14640)
*An Vuong,Chen Zhao,Jin Hu,Shui-Qing Yu,Xintao Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for efficient construction and prediction of stacked bilayer materials using a DFT-quality workflow and an interaction-aware graph neural network.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the high computational cost of DFT-based optimization and the lack of explicit interaction-type modeling in existing ML models for bilayer materials.

Method: 1) MatterSim-D3-based structural optimization to generate DFT-quality bilayer structures from monolayers and stacking configurations. 2) BDIP-Net, a graph neural network with explicit intra-layer and inter-layer interaction representations and adaptive message fusion for property prediction. 3) Evaluation on BiDB, HetDB, and SAMBA (homobilayers, heterobilayers, twisted bilayers).

Result: The MatterSim-D3 workflow closely reproduces DFT-PBE-D3 optimized structures; BDIP-Net consistently outperforms existing GNN and potential-based approaches for bilayer property prediction.

Conclusion: The integrated framework enables efficient, accurate bilayer structure generation and property prediction, supporting scalable discovery across diverse bilayer systems.

Abstract: Stacked bilayer materials exhibit rich stacking-dependent properties driven by the interplay between strong intra-layer bonding and weak inter-layer van der Waals interactions. The computational discovery of such materials is challenging because accurate structure generation typically relies on expensive DFT-based optimization, while existing machine-learning models often fail to explicitly distinguish different interaction types during property prediction. To address these challenges, we propose a machine-learning framework for efficient construction and property prediction of stacked bilayer materials. The framework employs a MatterSim-D3-based structural optimization workflow to generate DFT-quality bilayer structures from monolayer building blocks and stacking configurations at substantially reduced computational cost. For property prediction, we introduce BDIP-Net (Bilayer Dual-Interaction Potential Network), a graph neural network that explicitly models intra-layer and inter-layer interactions through interaction-specific potential representations and adaptive message fusion. We evaluate the proposed framework on BiDB, HetDB, and SAMBA, encompassing homobilayers, heterobilayers, and twisted bilayer systems. Results show that the MatterSim-D3-based workflow closely reproduces DFT-PBE-D3 optimized structures, while BDIP-Net consistently outperforms existing graph neural network and potential-based approaches for bilayer property prediction.

</details>


### [286] [Training and Evaluating Ethical Reinforcement Learning Agents on Per-Episode Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14642)
*Prabhjyot Singh,Majid Ghasemi,Mark Crowley*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Four ethical-RL training methods evaluated on Craftax show similar mean reward but differing per-episode ethics; ESR yields near-constant per-episode violations, while Lagrangian and weight-sweep methods exhibit higher per-episode violations; evaluation should target per-episode distribution, not just mean metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reward misspecification allows unethical behavior in RL; a single deterministic governance objective may fail to constrain episodic violations. The study investigates whether different training objectives control per-episode ethics and how evaluations should be structured to reveal episodic risks.

Method: Compare four approaches: scalar penalties with termination; linear multi-objective weight sweep; adaptive Lagrangian constraint; non-compensatory utility optimized per episode under the Expected Scalarized Returns (ESR) criterion. Use a detector-based protocol counting every violation across all episodes in Craftax. Assess performance on mean return vs mean violation rate; also examine per-episode distributions and include an observation-augmentation control.

Result: On the mean return–mean violation frontier, methods are indistinguishable. Per-episode, ESR maintains ~one violation per episode (worst-decile 1.04 ± 0.07), Lagrangian ~1.14 ± 0.03, weight-sweep ~2.20 ± 0.20. An observation-augmentation control attributes separation to the training objective rather than observations; per-episode guarantees incur no extra cost on the frontier.

Conclusion: If ethical violations do not average out across episodes, evaluation and training should target the per-episode distribution rather than the mean to reliably assess and enforce ethical behavior.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents trained on a single reward signal exploit the gap between the designed reward and the intended behavior. This is particularly a problem when we are trying to imbue ethical behavior into RL agents. An agent can look ethical on average while concentrating its violations in a few bad episodes, and a creature in the environment harmed in one episode is not restored by good conduct in another. We compare four ways of training ethical behavior in Craftax, an open-ended survival benchmark. The four are: scalar penalties with termination, a linear multi-objective weight sweep, an adaptive Lagrangian constraint, and a non-compensatory utility optimized per episode under the Expected Scalarized Returns (ESR) criterion. All are evaluated under a single detector-based protocol that counts every violation in every episode without censoring. On the frontier of mean return against mean violation rate, the four methods are indistinguishable; per episode they separate sharply. At matched mean return, the ESR agent holds its stated budget of one violation in effectively every episode (worst-decile 1.04 +/- 0.07 violations), the Lagrangian leaks past the same budget (1.14 +/- 0.03), and the weight sweep's worst episodes double it (2.20 +/- 0.20). An observation-augmentation control attributes the separation to the training objective rather than to what the agent observes, and the per-episode guarantee costs nothing on the mean frontier. When ethical violations do not average away across episodes, we argue both training and evaluation must target the per-episode distribution rather than the mean.

</details>


### [287] [DUET: Dual-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Same-Weight Disagreement for Prohibition Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14644)
*Zihan Li,Feifei Li,Wenhui Que*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DUET: a token-selective on-policy distillation method to enforce prohibition compliance in LLMs by contrasting two teachers with and without prohibition visibility; achieves strong violation suppression while preserving normal utility across large LLM variants and external safety benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LLM deployments use runtime prohibitions (policies, PII redlines, tool boundaries) that differ per request/tenant. Traditional post-training approaches (SFT, DPO) struggle: SFT hides violations in compliant labels; DPO’s sequence-level signals miss token-localized violations. There is a need for token-level supervision that isolates the prohibition signal without confounding model capacity or mismatch.

Method: DUET trains two identical-weight teachers: a positive teacher that sees the prohibition and a negative teacher that does not. Per-token disagreement between the two teachers isolates the prohibition’s causal effect, providing a clean supervision signal. Two mechanisms are used: (1) signal cleaning: discard tokens where both teachers agree, removing redundant/prefix-corrupted signals; (2) preference-directed learning: push the student toward the positive teacher and away from the negative at the token level, embedding DPO-style optimization directly into on-policy distillation (OPD) without offline preference data. Evaluation uses an industrial Prohibition-Compliance benchmark spanning five task families (explicit refusal, paraphrase robustness, over-refusal); experiments on 1.5B–8B Qwen variants; comparisons against teacher models and distillation baselines.

Result: DUET achieves 72.3–85.2% violation compliance while preserving 88–93% normal utility across 1.5B–8B Qwen models. Outperforms teacher baselines and other distillation methods. External SysBench evaluation shows improved safety alignment with minimal degradation on GSM8K and MATH-500.

Conclusion: Token-localized, on-policy distillation with a prohibition-visibility versus prohibition-absent teacher pair provides clean supervision for prohibition compliance, delivering strong safety performance with minimal utility loss. Demonstrates practical efficacy for industrial deployments and cross-task robustness; potential limitations include computational cost of dual teachers and reliance on accurate prohibition signals.

Abstract: Real-world LLM deployments increasingly rely on runtime-injected prohibitions--enterprise policies, PII redlines, tool boundaries--that vary per request and per tenant. Conventional post-training is structurally ill-suited: SFT hides the violation signal in compliant labels, and DPO's sequence-level preferences mismatch token-localized violations. We propose DUET, a token-selective on-policy distillation method for prohibition compliance. DUET pairs a teacher that sees the prohibition (positive) with an identical-weight teacher that does not (negative). Because the two teachers differ only in prohibition visibility, their per-token disagreement isolates the prohibition's causal effect--yielding a clean supervision signal uncontaminated by model capacity or mismatch. This disagreement drives two complementary mechanisms: signal cleaning, which discards agreement tokens as redundant or prefix-corrupted, and preference-directed learning, which pushes the student away from the negative teacher and toward the positive one at token granularity, embedding DPO-style optimization directly into OPD without offline preference data. We construct an industrial Prohibition-Compliance benchmark spanning five task families covering explicit-refusal, paraphrase robustness, and over-refusal. Across 1.5B-8B Qwen variants, DUET achieves 72.3-85.2% violation compliance while preserving 88-93% normal utility, dramatically outperforming teacher model and other distillation baselines. External evaluation on SysBench confirms improved safety alignment with minimal degradation on GSM8K and MATH-500.

</details>


### [288] [Efficient Neural-Network-Based High-Resolution Radiative Transfer for CO___ Retrieval, and Application to Interferometric Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14645)
*Jordan Lontsi Tedongmo,Yann Ferrec,Laurence Croizé,Pablo Musé,Gabriele Facciolo,Andrés Almansa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MLP surrogate replaces expensive full-physics radiative transfer for CO2/CH4 retrieval, enabling efficient forward modeling for NanoCarb while preserving spectral accuracy and Jacobian sensitivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce uncertainties in CO2/CH4 emission estimates and enable high revisit/spatial coverage with spaceborne measurements; full-physics RT is computationally expensive, motivating surrogate modeling.

Method: Train a feedforward multilayer perceptron to predict top-of-atmosphere radiances in the CO2 weak band. Use a combined MAE loss on radiances and RT Jacobians to preserve spectral accuracy and sensitivity to geophysical parameters, and couple the MLP surrogate with the NanoCarb instrumental response to create an efficient forward model.

Result: The MLP-based RT surrogate yields an efficient and precise forward model for NanoCarb measurements, showing promising results for CO2 concentration retrieval.

Conclusion: A physics-informed ML surrogate can significantly accelerate forward modeling for spaceborne CO2/CH4 retrievals, enabling higher revisit and spatial coverage while maintaining accuracy, with immediate applicability to the SCARBOn NanoCarb project.

Abstract: Studying climate change requires reducing uncertainties in CO2 and CH4 emission estimates to better distinguish anthropogenic from natural sources, which motivates spaceborne measurements with improved revisit frequency and spatial coverage. In this context, the Horizon Europe SCARBOn project assesses a low-cost satellite constellation featuring the NanoCarb imaging interferometer as its core sensor for monitoring CO2 and CH4 emissions in the atmosphere. However, estimating CO2 and CH4 concentrations with high revisit and spatial coverage poses significant challenges: full-physics retrieval algorithms commonly used rely on repeated high-resolution radiative transfer (RT) simulations, which are computationally expensive when using line-by-line RT models. As an alternative, we propose in this study a feedforward multilayer perceptron (MLP) surrogate designed to accurately and efficiently predict top-of-atmosphere radiances in the CO2 weak band, using a combined mean absolute error (MAE) loss on radiances and RT Jacobians to preserve both spectral accuracy and sensitivity to geophysical parameters. Coupling the MLP-based RT surrogate with the NanoCarb instrumental response yields an efficient and precise forward model for NanoCarb measurements, which shows promising results for CO2 concentration retrieval.

</details>


### [289] [iFuzz-Meta: An Interpretable Fuzzy Learning Framework Bridging Top-Down and Bottom-Up Knowledge Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14646)
*Xiaowei Jiang,Daniel Leong,Beining Cao,Nan Zhou,Yingtao Ren,Yu-Cheng Chang,Thomas Do,Chin-Teng Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Interpretable fuzzy-rule meta-learning (iFuzz-Meta) links semantically meaningful prototypes to neural models, enabling interpretable inference and cross-domain generalization via knowledge-guided regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the trade-off between performance and interpretability in neural networks; preserve human-understandable rules and prototypes; study how these rules adapt across tasks; leverage priors to guide learning.

Method: Proposes iFuzz-Meta: interpretable fuzzy rule-based learning; fuzzy rules tied to semantic/spatial prototypes in feature space; meta-learning analyzes rule reorganization across tasks; knowledge-guided regularization with top-down-bottom-up integration using theoretical priors as soft inductive biases.

Result: Empirical results show interpretable reasoning and stable cross-domain generalization across tasks/domains.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates a viable path toward explainable, knowledge-aware fuzzy systems, combining interpretable rules, meta-learning, and priors to guide semantically meaningful adaptation.

Abstract: Interpretable representation learning remains a key challenge in modern neural computation, particularly when models are expected not only to perform but also to explain their reasoning. This paper introduces iFuzz-Meta, an interpretable fuzzy rule-based learning framework that preserves human-understandable reasoning structures within modern neural architectures. Each fuzzy rule corresponds to a semantic and spatial prototype defined in the original feature space, enabling transparent inference and direct interpretability. Meta-learning is employed as an analytical paradigm to examine how these interpretable rules reorganize across tasks and domains, providing a principled means to link algorithmic adaptation with cognitive representation. A knowledge-guided regularization mechanism further enables a top-down-bottom-up integration, in which theoretical priors act as soft inductive biases while data-driven learning refines and extends them. This dual process ensures that adaptation proceeds along semantically and physiologically meaningful trajectories, rather than arbitrary parameter shifts. Evaluations demonstrate that iFuzz-Meta achieves interpretable reasoning and stable cross-domain generalization, establishing a potential general pathway toward explainable and knowledge-aware fuzzy systems.

</details>


### [290] [SMOPD: Selective Token-Entropy Masking for Dirty-History Multi-Turn On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14647)
*Chenyang Jiang,Changhan Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Selective masking of low-entropy tokens during multi-turn on-policy distillation (SMOPD) stabilizes OPSD, yielding +1.0–2.5 pp SHARDED accuracy on LiC with Qwen3 across 1.7B/4B/8B models; token-level uncertainty is a stronger stabilization signal than final-answer correctness; the approach is parameter-free with zero inference-time overhead; outcome-scalar augmentation can be detrimental.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dirty-history rollouts in multi-turn OPSD cause brittleness as later turns entrench earlier errors; uniform distillation dilutes signal by allocating loss to tokens with little corrective value. A lightweight, parameter-free method focusing on token-level uncertainty could stabilize learning without increasing inference cost.

Method: For each middle-turn, compute per-token student entropy; mask the lowest-entropy 20% of tokens from the clipped generalized Jensen-Shannon distillation loss; final-answer and FULL-preservation losses remain unchanged. Compare this to a correctness-scaling variant that multiplies a detached reliability proxy by final-answer correctness.

Result: On LiC with Qwen3 models, SMOPD improves SHARDED-view accuracy by 1.0–2.5 percentage points in single-seed 1.7B, 4B, and 8B comparisons; a small 4B multi-seed check shows a +1.7pp mean SHARDED gain (p = 0.022). Adding the outcome scalar is harmful at 1.7B (-4.0pp) and remains scale-dependent when combined with masking (+1.3pp at 4B, neutral at 1.7B, -0.5pp at 8B). These results suggest token-level uncertainty is a more reliable stabilization signal than final-answer correctness in dirty-history OPSD, while causal mechanism tests and broader benchmarks remain for future work.

Conclusion: A zero-parameter, zero-inference-overhead stabilization via selective masking of low-entropy middle-turn tokens; token-level uncertainty dominates as a stabilization signal in the evaluated dirty-history OPSD setting. Further causal validation and broader benchmarking are needed.

Abstract: Dirty-history rollouts make multi-turn on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) brittle: once a student emits an erroneous intermediate reply, later turns are conditioned on that reply, and uniform distillation can spend loss on tokens that carry little corrective signal. We introduce SMOPD (Selective Masking for On-Policy Distillation), a loss-only stabilization method for multi-turn OPSD. For each generated middle-turn reply, SMOPD ranks token positions by student entropy and removes the lowest-entropy 20% from the clipped generalized Jensen-Shannon distillation loss; final-answer and FULL-preservation losses are unchanged. This design targets token-level uncertainty rather than coarse trajectory outcomes, adds no parameters, and has zero inference-time overhead. We compare SMOPD with a correctness-scaling variant that multiplies a common detached reliability proxy using final-answer correctness. On LiC with Qwen3 models, SMOPD improves SHARDED-view accuracy by 1.0-2.5 percentage points in single-seed 1.7B, 4B, and 8B comparisons, and a small 4B multi-seed check shows a +1.7pp mean SHARDED gain over baseline (two-tailed p = 0.022). Adding the outcome scalar is harmful without masking at 1.7B (-4.0pp) and remains scale-dependent when combined with masking (+1.3pp at 4B, neutral at 1.7B, and -0.5pp at 8B). These archived aggregate results suggest that token-level uncertainty is a more reliable stabilization signal than scalar final-answer correctness in this evaluated dirty-history OPSD setting, while leaving causal mechanism tests and broader benchmark validation to future work.

</details>


### [291] [Discrete Diffusion Language Models Are Training-Free Multi-Label Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14649)
*Pawan Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training-free multi-label classification using discrete masked-diffusion LMs (dLLM-SetScore) with per-label yes/no prompts; fixes slot-position bias by per-label, single-slot scoring; evaluates LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across six datasets; shows competitive gains and provides theoretical/performance analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome need for task-specific fine-tuning and training data in multi-label NLP tasks, while avoiding label-order artifacts and exploiting discrete diffusion LMs for robust, training-free inference.

Method: For each candidate label, pose a short yes/no question at a masked position and compare probabilities of the two answer tokens. Avoid task-specific fine-tuning or NLI training data. Use a 200-example labelled validation slice to select thresholds, temperature, and prompt wording. To avoid slot-position bias, place all labels in separate, identical answer slots with the same syntactic position. Evaluate LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on six datasets against multiple baselines (NLI models, autoregressive LLMs, SetFit, supervised classifiers). Prove permutation invariance, analyze decision thresholds under weighted Hamming loss, and derive shortlist ceilings for recall and F1. Explore a local Joint Set Refinement step, found negative as it reduces F1.

Result: The method yields training-free improvements in macro-F1 and micro-F1 on several datasets where Instruct checkpoints provide the best results among training-free methods; LLaDA-Instruct attains leading scores on Reuters and ECtHR within the protocol; permutation-invariance is established; thresholds and shortlists are theoretically characterized; the Joint Set Refinement step lowers F1 (negative result).

Conclusion: dLLM-SetScore demonstrates that training-free multi-label classification with discrete diffusion LMs is viable, highlights the importance of per-label slot design to remove order artifacts, and provides theoretical insights on thresholding and recall/F1 budgets; identifies limitations (e.g., potential F1 degradation with refinement, artifacts from initializations) and points to future work on more robust refinement strategies and broader dataset coverage.

Abstract: We present dLLM-SetScore, a training-free method that uses discrete masked-diffusion language models for multi-label text classification. For each candidate label, it asks a short yes/no question and compares the probabilities of the two answer tokens at one masked position. The method uses no task-specific fine-tuning or training on textual-entailment datasets; a 200-example labelled validation slice selects thresholds, temperature, and prompt wording.
  We first show that placing all labels in one prompt creates a strong slot-position asymmetry: the first answer slot is predicted positive on $99.4\%$ of GoEmotions examples and $100\%$ of Reuters examples. Per-label scoring places every label in the same syntactic position, making predictions invariant to label order and avoiding this artifact. We evaluate LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on six datasets against NLI models, an autoregressive LLM, SetFit, and supervised classifiers. On the five datasets shared by both diffusion families, Instruct checkpoints improve macro-F1 in 9 of 10 comparisons and micro-F1 in 8 of 10, although these comparisons do not identify the cause. Within our protocol, LLaDA-Instruct records the highest training-free values for both Reuters and ECtHR metrics. We prove permutation invariance, characterize thresholded decisions under weighted Hamming loss, and derive shortlist ceilings for recall and F1. An exploratory local Joint Set Refinement step lowers F1 from biased and unbiased initializations and is retained as a negative result.

</details>


### [292] [Paired Exact-Reset Evaluation of a Prediction-Derived Medium-to-Full World-Model Cascade](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14650)
*Malo de Pastor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Paired-exact-reset evaluation shows a Medium-derived predictive interface provides a small, reliable routing signal to switch to a Full predictor, reducing decision cost by ~0.00255, but there is no evidence of causal sufficiency, compute savings, closed-loop value, or broad cross-family generality; sequential routing does not outperform fixed policies except at very low compute prices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether a fast, intermediate predictor (Medium) can reliably indicate when to switch to a more expensive, more accurate Full predictor to reduce task-specific decision loss, under controlled exact-reset physical outcomes.

Method: Use a paired evaluation and audit protocol: ensure all candidate actions are executed from the same reset state; Medium and Full operate on the same candidate set and task; use the paired physical-loss difference as the routing target. Evaluate on a fresh PushT bank (V106, 1,600 states, 39 tasks, 3 checkpoint pairs) comparing a frozen prediction-interface router against Medium, Full, and a latency-advantaged task-only router. Prospectively seal a second PushT (V107) with stronger current-state control using DINO features and all five actions, with no DINO latency charged. Independent PyBullet audit supports a composite task-prediction-regime router. Measure coded cost reductions (overhead-inclusive decision cost) and latency, and report state-clustered 95% intervals.

Result: The prediction interface lowers priced physical decision cost by 0.002549 (state-clustered 95% CI [-0.002867, -0.002238]); one-sided 95% upper bound -0.002286), with negative effects across all three checkpoint pairs. A controlled-PyBullet audit supports a composite task-prediction-regime router. The sequential router remains slower than fixed policies, with advantages only at low compute prices.

Conclusion: Evidence supports incremental routing information from the tested prediction interface beyond a deliberately favored current-DINO control, but it does not establish causal sufficiency, compute savings, closed-loop value, or cross-family generality.

Abstract: Existing adaptive-inference and world-action-model systems use cheap-stage outputs or predicted futures to allocate additional computation. We study a narrower question: under paired exact-reset physical outcomes, can a Medium-derived interface predict when switching to a separately frozen Full predictor improves task-specific decision loss enough to justify sequential overhead? Our contribution is a paired evaluation and audit protocol, not a new generic routing rule: all candidate actions are executed from the same reset state, Medium and Full act on the same candidate set and task, and their paired physical-loss difference defines the routing target. On a fresh PushT bank (V106; 1,600 states, 39 tasks, three checkpoint pairs), a frozen prediction-interface router lowers overhead-inclusive decision cost relative to standalone Medium, standalone Full, and a latency-advantaged task-only router. We then prospectively seal a second 1,600-state PushT confirmation (V107) against a stronger current-state control using the task, a dimension-matched projection of current DINO features, and all five candidate actions, with no DINO encoder latency charged. The prediction interface lowers priced physical decision cost by 0.002549 (state-clustered 95% interval [-0.002867, -0.002238]; one-sided 95% upper bound -0.002286), with negative effects for all three checkpoint pairs. A controlled-PyBullet audit independently supports a composite task-prediction-regime router. The sequential router remains slower than fixed policies, and its advantage is restricted to low compute prices. The evidence supports incremental routing information in the tested prediction interface beyond one deliberately favoured current-DINO control, but not causal sufficiency, compute saving, closed-loop value, or cross-family generality.

</details>


### [293] [Pushing the Limits of High-Resolution Weather Forecasting through Data Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14652)
*Yang Zhao,Peisong Niu,Tian Zhou,Ziqing Ma,Guanlong Ma,Rong Jin,Huiling Yuan,Liang Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-centric approach (BaguanHR) uses variable-wise super-resolution to synthesize extensive 0.1° data from ERA5, enabling high-resolution ML forecasting by mitigating coarse-to-fine information loss; achieves superior performance to ML baselines and IFS-HRES on most 72-h lead times, and reveals a power-law scaling where doubling data reduces RMSE by ~4.6-4.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limited availability of high-resolution data (~0.1°) for long-lead forecast training; decades of reanalysis are only at 0.25°, and direct transfer from 0.25° to 0.1° is hampered by irreversible information loss.

Method: Proposes BaguanHR, shifting from model transfer to data transfer. Demonstrates SR has lower conditional entropy and input amplification than forecasting; performs variable-wise SR to synthesize 0.1° data from ERA5; builds synthetic-plus-real dataset; compares to ML-based methods and IFS-HRES across 72 and 120-hour lead times; investigates scaling with data.

Result: Outperforms ML-based methods and IFS-HRES on >85% of lead times within 72 hours; clear data bottleneck; observes power-law scaling: twofold data reduces RMSE by 4.6% (72h) and 4.9% (120h).

Conclusion: Data-centric approach via variable-wise SR is effective and simple; enables long coarse-resolution reanalyses to train high-res models; SR provides robust resolution transfer due to lower conditional entropy.

Abstract: The development of 0.1$^{\circ}$ global weather forecasting models based on machine learning (ML) is constrained by the limited availability of high-resolution data, as decades of reanalysis are only available at 0.25$^{\circ}$ resolution. While existing approaches fine-tune 0.25$^{\circ}$ forecast models on limited 0.1$^{\circ}$ samples, we show that this transfer is hindered by the irreversible information loss inherent in coarse-resolution forecasting. Therefore, we propose BaguanHR, a framework that shifts the focus from transferring models to transferring data. We first show that super-resolution (SR) has lower conditional entropy and input amplification than forecasting, making it a more robust vehicle for resolution transfer. By leveraging this advantage through variable-wise SR, we synthesize extensive 0.1$^{\circ}$ data from ERA5. BaguanHR's performance on the synthetic-plus-real dataset exceeds both ML-based methods and IFS-HRES, achieving superior performance across over 85% of the lead times within 72 hours. Furthermore, our findings highlight a power-law scaling effect, as a twofold increase in data reduces RMSE by 4.6% for 72-hour forecasting and 4.9% for 120-hour forecasting. Our results demonstrate that scaling high resolution ML-based forecasting is primarily a data bottleneck, and that variable-wise super-resolution provides a simple yet general solution to unlock long coarse-resolution reanalyses for high-resolution training.

</details>


### [294] [Do Uncertainty Signals Help? A Systematic Study of Uncertainty-Aware Decoding with Rollback Mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14653)
*Xianzong Wu,Xiaohong Li,Yuejun Guo,Xinyang Liu,Tianlin Li,Junjie Wang,Qiang Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uncertainty-aware rollback decoding improves code generation in LLMs by using uncertainty signals to detect unreliable regions and revert to earlier valid prefixes at inference time, without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertainty quantification is widely used to measure model confidence, but its potential to enhance LLM-based code generation remains underexplored. This work investigates whether uncertainty signals can guide at-inference-time rollbacks to improve code generation quality, aiming to enhance reliability without retraining.

Method: Introduce uncertainty-aware rollback decoding. At inference, compute token-level uncertainty signals, identify unreliable generation regions, and roll back to previously valid prefixes. Evaluate across seven code LLMs, five code generation benchmarks, and eight uncertainty signals under a unified decoding setup. Include a component-controlled ablation to separate feedback-guided rollback from localization effects.

Result: Rollback decoding improves over equal-budget restart on standard benchmarks, with gains up to 0.26 pass@1 and 0.35 AvgTestPassRate on functional code benchmarks, and up to 6.4 percentage points in Patch-Aligned Safe Rate on Dsec-Python. Information-theoretic signals (token entropy, negative log-likelihood) perform best overall. Feedback-guided rollback provides main improvement; uncertainty localization offers additional gains under fixed check/budget/rollback/branch decay.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware rollback decoding is an effective, training-free strategy to improve LLM-based code generation. Appropriate uncertainty signals—especially entropy and NLL—enable reliable rollback, with feedback-guided mechanisms driving most of the gains, though localization adds value in certain configurations.

Abstract: Prediction uncertainty is a widely adopted metric for quantifying model confidence, with downstream applications spanning model explanation, data selection, and prediction rollback. Despite its demonstrated utility, the potential of uncertainty quantification to enhance code generation in large language models (LLMs) remains largely underexplored, raising a critical question: to what extent can uncertainty serve as an effective signal for improving LLM-based code generation?
  To answer this question, we study uncertainty-aware rollback decoding, an inference-time strategy that uses uncertainty signals to identify unreliable generation regions and roll back to earlier valid prefixes without retraining the model. We evaluate this framework on seven code LLMs, five code generation benchmarks, and eight token-level uncertainty signals under a unified decoding setup.
