We evaluate six production research systems and find that the benchmark is far from saturated: at high effort, the strongest system reaches only 0.363 soft F1 and 0.133 hard F1. Performance degrades as target volume and hierarchy depth increase, with incomplete discovery, missing enrichment, and incomplete evidence construction remaining major bottlenecks. The benchmark and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/perplexityai/wandr.

</details>


### [319] [Real-Time State-of-Health Estimation and Online Degradation Prognosis from Partial Battery Discharge Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14764)
*Begoña Ispizua,Serio Gil-López,Leire Arrizabalaga,Ibai Laña*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-informed deep learning for lithium-ion battery SOH using partial discharge data from arbitrary voltage ranges, enabling accurate SOH estimation (MAPE < 4%) and real-time degradation trend forecasting without fixed protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need robust SOH estimation under heterogeneous, real-world operation with incomplete discharge data; real-time aging detection without historical data.

Method: Integrates physics-informed degradation dynamics with data-driven learning to estimate SOH from incomplete discharge curves across arbitrary voltage ranges; introduces a real-time degradation trend estimator that detects aging transitions without prior data.

Result: MAPE < 4% in SOH estimation from partial data; real-time degradation forecasting that continuously integrates usage; effective across arbitrary discharge segments; outperforms fixed-protocol methods.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that SOH estimation from partial data and real-time degradation forecasts are feasible and broadly applicable, reducing dependence on fixed discharge protocols and enabling adaptive battery health monitoring.

Abstract: With the increasing integration of renewable energy sources, energy storage systems have become essential, making the accurate estimation of their State of Health (SOH) and degradation behavior critical. In this work, we propose a physics-informed deep learning approach for lithium-ion battery SOH prediction using incomplete discharge curves extracted from arbitrary voltage ranges, thereby reflecting realistic and heterogeneous operating conditions. The proposed method combines data-driven learning with physically motivated degradation dynamics to ensure consistent and reliable SOH estimation from partial discharge information, achieving a MAPE below 4$\%$. In addition, a real-time degradation trend estimation strategy is introduced to detect key aging transitions without requiring prior knowledge or historical data, making it applicable to a wide range of batteries. Overall, our approach enables SOH estimation from arbitrary discharge segments and a real-time degradation forecast that continuously integrates all usage, overcoming previous methods that rely on fixed protocols or early, non-adaptive predictions.

</details>


### [320] [ER-KANs: Efficient and Robust Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Data-Scarce Scientific Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14773)
*Harshil Lodhiya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ER-KAN is a robust, compact variant of efficient-KAN that uses shared Gaussian RBF bases, curriculum noise injection, and entropy-weighted adaptive regularization to perform well in noisy, data-scarce settings; it matches MLP accuracy at moderate noise and degrades gracefully with noise, introduces a noise degradation ratio metric, and is validated across eight analytic functions and two PINNs, though Burgers' equation PINN convergence is a limitation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark papers in efficient-KAN have relied on clean data, which can obscure architecture differences and overestimate robustness. The study targets noisy, data-scarce regimes and seeks to improve robustness and provide a standard reporting metric.

Method: Introduce ER-KAN with: (1) shared Gaussian RBF bases across all edges in a layer for locality and parameter efficiency; (2) curriculum noise injection during training to teach noise robustness; (3) entropy-weighted adaptive regularization to mitigate overfitting at small sample sizes. The network has 595 parameters. Evaluations include eight analytic functions (N in {50, 200, 500}, sigma in {0, 0.03, 0.1}), a damped harmonic oscillator physics-informed neural network (PINN) where ER-KAN achieves 4.2x lower solution MSE than MLP, and a Burgers' equation PINN where all models fail to converge.

Result: Compared to Chebyshev KAN, vanilla KAN, and standard MLP, ER-KAN shows significantly more graceful degradation under input noise: test MSE increases by 10.6x for ChebyKAN, 7.9x for KAN, 1.7x for MLP, and only 1.4x for ER-KAN when sigma=0.1. In eight analytic problems, ER-KAN with 595 parameters matches MLP accuracy at moderate noise and degrades more gracefully as noise grows. On the damped oscillator PINN, ER-KAN reduces solution MSE by 4.2x relative to MLP. On Burgers' PINN, no model converges, highlighting genuine limitations. A new noise degradation ratio is proposed as a complementary metric and recommended as a standard reporting metric for efficient-KAN work.

Conclusion: ER-KAN offers a robust, parameter-efficient approach for noisy, data-scarce settings and identifies error amplification under noise with a simple, interpretable metric. The authors advocate adopting the noise degradation ratio as a standard reporting practice and acknowledge limitations in some PINN cases (e.g., Burgers' equation).

Abstract: The efficient-KAN literature---covering Chebyshev, wavelet, and radial-basis-function variants of the original Kolmogorov-Arnold Network---has been benchmarked almost entirely on clean data. We show that this choice conceals a large capability difference between architectures: ChebyKAN's test MSE (evaluated against clean ground truth) increases by a factor of 10.6x when training data is corrupted with sigma=0.1 noise, versus 7.9x for vanilla KAN, 1.7x for a standard MLP, and just 1.4x for our proposed ER-KAN.
  ER-KAN combines three design choices targeting the noisy, data-scarce setting: shared Gaussian RBF bases across all edges in a layer (providing locality and efficient parameterisation), curriculum noise injection during training (explicitly teaching noise robustness), and entropy-weighted adaptive regularisation (preventing overfitting at small N). The result is a 595-parameter network that matches MLP accuracy at moderate noise while degrading far more gracefully as noise grows.
  We evaluate on eight analytic functions (N in {50, 200, 500}, sigma in {0, 0.03, 0.1}), on a damped harmonic oscillator physics-informed neural network where ER-KAN achieves 4.2x lower solution MSE than MLP, and on a Burgers' equation PINN where all models fail to converge---a genuine limitation we report rather than suppress. We introduce the noise degradation ratio as a simple complementary metric and recommend it become a standard reporting requirement for efficient-KAN papers.

</details>


### [321] [p-Spin Glass Network Efficient Single-Batch Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14774)
*Vladimer Khasia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces p-Spin Glass Network that achieves memory efficiency (8x parameter compression; activation memory bounded to O(B·T·D)), sample efficiency (matches Transformer asymptotics with 8x fewer sequences), single-batch stability (stable with micro-batch size 1), and modality-agnostic temporal credit assignment (works on subword and raw byte streams); aims to remove large-batch requirement for stable deep learning and enable continual learning and edge AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern sequence models require massive memory footprints and large-batch optimization, which limit sample efficiency and continual learning. A network architecture that reduces memory, stabilizes optimization, and supports cross-modal temporal credit assignment could unlock data-efficient and edge-friendly learning.

Method: Proposes p-Spin Glass Network with native ternary quantization to compress internal parameters by 8×. Utilizes exact implicit gradients to strictly bound activation memory to O(B·T·D). Demonstrates stability and convergence at extremely small micro-batch sizes. Architecture appears modality-agnostic, supporting discrete subword and raw byte streams.

Result: 1) Memory efficiency: 8× parameter compression; activation memory bound to O(B·T·D). 2) Sample efficiency: matches Transformer baseline asymptotically with 8× fewer training sequences. 3) Single-batch stability: smooth, monotonic convergence at micro-batch size 1. 4) Modality-agnostic stability: robust temporal credit assignment across discrete subword and long-horizon raw byte streams.

Conclusion: Removes the large-batch requirement for stable deep learning, laying groundwork for continual learning and edge AI.

Abstract: Modern sequence models heavily rely on massive memory footprints and large-batch stochastic optimization, barriers that restrict sample efficiency and continual learning. We introduce the $p$-Spin Glass Network, a novel architecture that overcomes these limitations, structurally manages optimization variance and yields four noticeable capabilities: 1. It enforces memory efficiency: native ternary quantization compresses internal parameters by $8\times$, while exact implicit gradients strictly bound activation memory to $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot T \cdot D)$. 2. it demonstrates sample efficiency, matching the asymptotic performance of a Transformer baseline while utilizing $8\times$ fewer training sequences. 3. Method enables single-batch stability and smooth, monotonic convergence at a stochastic micro-batch size of $1$. 4. Finally, this stability proves modality-agnostic, maintaining robust temporal credit assignment across both discrete subword and long horizon uncompressed raw byte streams. Ultimately, this work removes large batch requirement for stable deep learning, establishing a foundation for continuous learning and edge AI.

</details>


### [322] [NRCD: An Open Database of Collegiate Running with Unified Performance Standardization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14776)
*Jonathan A. Karr,Ryan M. Fryer,Ben Darden,Nicholas Pell,Kayla Ambrose,Evan Hall,Ramzi K. Bualuan,Nitesh V. Chawla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces the National Running Club Database (NRCD), the first large-scale, openly available collegiate running dataset, plus a standardization pipeline and governance, enabling robust longitudinal and environmental analyses including gender-stratified modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lack of publicly accessible, bulk-downloadable collegiate running data; existing sites limit analyses to small samples and skew by gender; need to study environmental factors and gender equity.

Method: Aggregate 128,963 performances from 28,913 athletes across 1,336 meets in XC, indoor/outdoor track, and road, spanning 2004–2026; Aug 2023+ includes course distance, elevation, weather, venue metadata; community governance; open submission and expert approval; release of 'nrcd' Python package; unified performance standardization pipeline; recommendations for gender-stratified modeling.

Result: Dataset composition: 36.3% women; 97.7% of XC rows with weather fields; comprehensive metadata in later seasons; standardization lowers median within-athlete cross-meet variability by 51.0% for women and 34.4% for men; live database with growing meet volume.

Conclusion: Dataset and pipeline enable longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental-confounder studies, and gender-equity research in collegiate sport; released under FAIR principles; supports research in those areas.

Abstract: Collegiate running in the United States generates thousands of race results annually in cross country and track and field, yet no large-scale dataset has been publicly available for research. Existing websites such as Athletic.net, MileSplit, and TFRRS host results but do not support bulk download, restricting prior analyses to ~500 performances, often skewing studies toward male athletes. We introduce the National Running Club Database (NRCD), the first openly available collegiate running dataset at scale: 128,963 approved performances from 28,913 athletes across 1,336 meets in four sports (cross country (XC), indoor and outdoor track, and road races), 36.3% women, spanning 2004 through 2026. Within that single export, meets from August 2023 onward carry comprehensive course distance, elevation gain and loss, weather at race time, and track venue metadata (97.7% of XC rows with weather fields); earlier seasons back to 2004 are included with sparser metadata. NRCD is community-governed through open submission and expert approval and is maintained as a live database whose meet volume has grown yearly. We release a unified performance standardization framework that operationalizes established distance, elevation, and heat adjustments in one pipeline. Furthermore, we recommend gender-stratified modeling. On XC, full standardization lowers median within-athlete cross-meet variability by 51.0% (women) and 34.4% (men) versus raw times. We release the dataset and pipeline with a python package `nrcd' under FAIR principles, supporting longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental-confounder studies, and gender-equity research in collegiate sport.

</details>


### [323] [Is Grokking a Loss of Normal Hyperbolicity of the Interpolation Manifold?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14803)
*Suvinava Basak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The sharp grokking transition likely arises from smooth contraction along a stable zero-loss manifold, not a loss of normal hyperbolicity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether the grokking generalization transition is a bifurcation (loss of normal hyperbolicity) or a gradual drift along the zero-loss manifold.

Method: Define the residual Jacobian J and analyze the smallest nonzero singular value σ_min^+ (for squared loss, the slowest normal-restoring rate). Evaluate σ_min^+ and the six smallest singular values across five seeds for a two-layer ReLU network trained to grok modular addition under squared loss.

Result: σ_min^+ does not collapse at the transition; it is near zero before memorization and attains its largest values during the transition. The six smallest singular values behave identically; no subspace-local collapse is observed. Results are reproduced across seeds.

Conclusion: Preliminary evidence favors the smooth-contraction picture over the bifurcation hypothesis. A single Adam-run does not prove absence of a bifurcation but constrains where it could hide.

Abstract: A recent line of work recasts the post-memorization phase of grokking as constrained optimization: once a network interpolates the training set, weight decay drives a slow drift along the zero-loss manifold toward lower norm. In the language of dynamical systems, this is a fast-slow system in which the interpolation manifold plays the role of a slow manifold. We ask a question that this framing makes natural but the existing literature does not address: is the sharp generalization transition a loss of normal hyperbolicity of that manifold: a fold- or bifurcation-like event in which a normal restoring direction goes flat? Or does the manifold stay uniformly attracting while generalization happens by smooth drift? We propose a simple, optimizer-agnostic diagnostic: the smallest nonzero singular value $σ_{\min}^{+}(\mathbf J)$ of the residual Jacobian, which, for the squared loss, equals the slowest normal restoring rate of the manifold. On a two-layer ReLU network trained to grok modular addition under squared loss, $σ_{\min}^{+}(\mathbf J)$ does not collapse at the transition; it is near zero only before memorization and attains its largest values during the transition. The result holds across five seeds, and the six smallest singular values behave identically; there is no subspace-local collapse either. This is preliminary evidence against the bifurcation hypothesis and in favor of the smooth-contraction picture. We are explicit that a single-setting, gradual-transition experiment under Adam optimizer does not prove the absence of a bifurcation; it constrains where one could hide.

</details>


### [324] [Disentangling Homophily and Rarity: Explaining Failure in Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14823)
*Preben M. Ness,Fariz Ikhwantri,Dusica Marijan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Homophily—not rarity—primarily governs node classification difficulty; heterophilic nodes are not inherently harder to classify, and their information can often be recovered by retraining the final classification layer, challenging subgroup-generalisation claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle whether the difficulty of classifying heterophilic nodes arises from their heterophily or from their rarity, by comparing subgroup generalisation versus neighbourhood aggregation explanations using GNNs across multiple datasets.

Method: Empirical evaluation of six GNNs on five datasets with varying levels of homophily, focusing on node-wise classification performance for heterophilic vs. homophilic nodes and investigating the effects of retraining the classification head/ final linear layer.

Result: Homophilic nodes are easier to classify even when rare, challenging the subgroup framing. The information needed to classify heterophilic nodes can be recovered by retraining the classification head, or just the final linear layer, indicating that misrepresentation of heterophilic nodes by GNNs can be mitigated without changing the base feature extractor.

Conclusion: The study supports that homophily predicts classification ease, undermines the notion that heterophily alone makes heterophilic nodes harder to classify, and shows that the needed discriminative information often resides in the final classification layer rather than in the graph aggregation itself.

Abstract: Are heterophilic nodes in a graph harder to classify because they are heterophilic or because they are rare? Some existing work frames classification of such nodes as a subgroup generalisation problem, where a model performs well on the majority group at the expense of the rare group. Others explain this as a problem of neighbourhood aggregation in graph neural networks (GNNs). We assess these two viewpoints through a detailed evaluation of six GNNs on five datasets of varying homophily, and find that homophilic nodes tend to be easier to classify, even when they are rare---challenging the subgroup framing. However, our findings also nuance existing beliefs about how GNNs misrepresent heterophilic nodes. We demonstrate that the information needed to classify heterophilic nodes correctly is often recoverable by retraining the classification head of a model, or even just the final linear classification layer.

</details>


### [325] [M-LINKX: Multiview Graph Learning for Brain Cognitive Disease Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14847)
*An Phan,Yufei Jin,Xingquan Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M-LINKX is a multi-view graph-learning framework that uses segment-based EEG inputs to construct multiple functional connectivity graphs (defined by connectivity metric, frequency band, and topology filter) for dementia classification, fusing views with trainable weights and averaging segment-level predictions to produce subject-level accuracy, achieving top results on two datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG signals for dementia diagnosis are noisy, non-stationary, and vary across individuals; segment-based processing and multi-view representations may better capture discriminative information and inter-channel interactions.

Method: Split EEG into fixed-length segments; for each segment, compute channel-level features and construct several FC graphs based on different metrics, frequency bands, and topology filters. Avoid message passing; instead, learn representations from node features and adjacency matrices, fuse graph-view representations with trainable view weights, and obtain subject-level predictions by averaging segment-level probabilities.

Result: On CAUEEG (HC/MCI/Dementia) and AHEAP (HC/AD/FTD) datasets, M-LINKX achieves best subject-level performance under the reported experimental settings.

Conclusion: Multi-view functional connectivity integrated with a graph-learning fusion framework can enhance EEG-based dementia classification; code and data are publicly available for replication.

Abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) is a non-invasive and relatively low-cost procedure that measures brain electricity for the detection of cognitive diseases. EEG-based classification of dementia-related conditions, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), remains challenging because EEG signals are noisy, non-stationary, and vary across subjects. Segment-based learning provides a practical way to model long EEG recordings by converting them into fixed-length inputs. For each segment, discriminative information may be explored by using signals within each channel (i.e. electrode), as well as interactions between EEG channels. In this paper, we propose M-LINKX, a multi-view graph learning framework for EEG-based dementia classification. For each segment, we extract channel-level node features and construct multiple functional-connectivity (FC) graph views, where each view is defined by a specific combination of connectivity metric, frequency band, and topology filter, respectively. Instead of relying on message passing over the constructed graphs, M-LINKX follows a simple design in modeling node features and adjacency-based connectivity representations. The graph-view representations are fused using global trainable view weights, and subject-level prediction is obtained by averaging segment-level probabilities. Experiments on two three-class EEG datasets with different diagnostic groups, CAUEEG (HC/MCI/Dementia) and AHEAP (HC/AD/FTD), show that M-LINKX achieves the best subject-level performance under the main experimental settings. Our study suggests that multi-view functional connectivity can improve EEG-based dementia classification when integrated with an appropriate graph-learning architecture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/anphantt/MLINKX.

</details>


### [326] [Can Neural Networks Learn by Experimenting on Themselves? Self-Interventional Learning from Functional Consequences to Predictive Self-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14894)
*Michał Tomaszewski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SIL perturbs its own structure, learns a predictive self-model, and uses predictions to guide future structure changes; in a synthetic setup it recovers key structure but not all synergy; with more interventions error drops (0.0335 -> 0.0148) and rank correlation improves (0.629 -> 0.883); ablations show mapping accuracy is crucial; however, model-guided action doesn't beat a direct empirical-memory policy and CIFAR-10/ResNet validation shows no robustness benefit; overall SIL is promising but incomplete and not universally better than direct strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable a system to learn about its own internal functional organization by self-generated interventions, constructing a predictive self-model that can generalize to unexecuted interventions and guide subsequent structural actions.

Method: Introduce Self-Interventional Learning (SIL): perturb the system's own functional structure, observe consequences, train a predictive self-model, generalize to unexecuted interventions, and use predictions to guide later structural actions. Evaluated in a construction-known synthetic system with varied intervention budgets and confirmatory seeds, plus ablation experiments on mapping accuracy and a comparison to a direct empirical-memory policy; CIFAR-10/ResNet validation assesses robustness relative to direct repair search.

Result: SIL recovered critical structure, redundancy, and replaceability; synergy was not reliably recovered. Increasing intervention budget from 4 to 56 reduced held-out prediction error from 0.0335 to 0.0148 and increased Spearman correlation from 0.629 to 0.883. In a matched ablation, preserving the correct intervention–consequence mapping reduced prospective prediction error by 81.3%, while using the same learned self-model for action reduced normalized regret by 31.7% relative to ignoring it. Model-guided action did not significantly outperform a direct empirical-memory policy, and CIFAR-10/ResNet validation showed no robustness advantage over equal-budget direct repair search.

Conclusion: SIL constitutes a viable intervention-driven framework for learning predictive knowledge about a network’s own functional organization, but the self-model remains incomplete and is not universally superior to simpler direct strategies.

Abstract: Machine-learning systems usually model external data, while their internal functional organization is analyzed by external observers. This work introduces Self-Interventional Learning (SIL), in which a neural system perturbs its own functional structure, observes consequences, learns a predictive self-model, generalizes to unexecuted interventions, and uses predictions to guide later structural action. In a construction-known synthetic system, SIL recovered critical structure, redundancy, and replaceability, while synergy was not reliably recovered. Across 30 fresh confirmatory seeds, increasing the pairwise intervention budget from 4 to 56 reduced held-out prediction error from 0.0335 to 0.0148 and increased Spearman correlation from 0.629 to 0.883. In a matched ablation, preserving the correct intervention--consequence mapping reduced prospective prediction error by 81.3%, while using the same learned self-model for action reduced normalized regret by 31.7% relative to ignoring it. However, model-guided action did not significantly outperform a direct empirical-memory policy, and powered CIFAR-10/ResNet validation showed no robustness advantage over equal-budget direct repair search. These results support SIL as an intervention-driven framework for learning predictive knowledge about a network's own functional organization, while showing that the self-model remains incomplete and is not universally superior to simpler direct strategies.

</details>


### [327] [Degeneracy Counting Quantum Algorithm using Decoherence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14941)
*Malay Marut Das,Mark A. Novotny,Yaroslav Koshka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CTPQsd# counts global optima by measuring a small four-qubit probe within a canonical thermal pure quantum (CTPQ) state, avoiding full minimization or tomography. Numerical experiments up to 20 qubits show exact and near-degenerate counting via temperature thresholds, reducing tomography to a four-qubit probe.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counting global optima is #P-hard; existing approaches rely on full optimization or large-scale tomography. The work proposes a scalable degeneracy-counting scheme by linking probe decoherence to problem degeneracy within a CTPQ framework.

Method: Prepare a joint CTPQ state of a small probe S and the problem P. Use a perturbative relation between the decoherence measure of S and the degeneracy of P when S and P are in this state. Measure only S (four qubits) to infer degeneracy, tested on diagonal random-energy Hamiltonians (maximally unstructured QP testbed). Classical simulations for up to 20 qubits examine the sensitivity to temperature, energy range, size, and degeneracy; identify a temperature threshold for exact degeneracy and a lower threshold for counting near-degenerate minima within a chosen energy tolerance.

Result: First numerical demonstration that degeneracy can be counted via the probe's decoherence without enumerating minima. Exact counting is possible above a temperature threshold; a second, lower threshold yields a window to count near-degenerate minima within a user-defined tolerance. Measurement confined to S reduces tomography from the full problem Hilbert space to a four-qubit probe.

Conclusion: CTPQsd# offers a scalable, probe-based route to degeneracy counting, circumventing full Hilbert-space tomography. Its practical viability hinges on accurate temperature control and the behavior of non-diagonal problem Hamiltonians; further work needed to extend beyond diagonal random-energy problems and toward experimental realization.

Abstract: Counting the global optima of a classical optimization problem is a #P-hard task. We develop the canonical thermal pure quantum (CTPQ) state-based degeneracy counting (CTPQsd#) algorithm that determines the number of global optima of a classical optimization problem P by measuring only a small probe S, without finding individual minima. The method exploits a perturbative relation between the decoherence measure of S and the degeneracy of P when S and P are together in a CTPQ state. We provide the first numerical demonstration that this relation can be used to count the global minima, applying it to problems encoded by diagonal random-energy Hamiltonians as a maximally unstructured testbed for classical binary optimization problems. Classical simulations of up to 20 problem qubits quantify the algorithm's sensitivity to variations in the temperature of the CTPQ state, the Hamiltonian energy range, the problem size, and degeneracy. We establish the temperature threshold for determining the exact degeneracy and identify a second, lower threshold that provides a temperature window to count near-degenerate minima within a user-defined energy tolerance. By confining measurement to S, the protocol replaces tomography over the exponentially large problem Hilbert space with tomography over a small probe represented by only four qubits.

</details>


### [328] [PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14951)
*Ying-Qiu Zheng,Alex Fung,Stephen M Smith,Rogier B Mars,Saad Jbabdi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PathFinder introduces a path-based joint low-rank decomposition to connect datasets without a shared dimension, unifying existing joint methods and enabling cross-modal pattern discovery and missing-data prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To analyze and integrate multimodal datasets that do not share a common axis, by exploiting partial overlaps and connectivity to reveal shared structure.

Method: PathFinder leverages chains of pairwise shared dimensions to construct a global joint decomposition. Many conventional joint matrix decomposition methods emerge as special cases within this framework, and the approach enables joint estimation of common patterns across modalities via linking paths between data matrices.

Result: Provides a unifying framework that can discover cross-dataset patterns and predict missing data or modalities, with applicability across modalities, species, and scales.

Conclusion: PathFinder serves as a general umbrella for joint decomposition methods, expanding the scope of cross-dataset analysis beyond one-to-one dimensional mappings.

Abstract: Low-rank matrix decompositions can uncover patterns and structure in data and have a number of different applications across many disciplines. Extensions to "joint" low-rank decompositions have been proposed to link datasets from different modalities. While these methods enable the discovery of common patterns across modalities, they require that all the multimodal data share one or more dimensions. We propose a new analysis method, PathFinder, that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily all share a dimension. The key insight is that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices do share some dimension, and that there are one or more paths that link across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This enables the joint estimation of common patterns across different modalities, species, or scales, where a one-to-one mapping across all data along some dimension is not necessarily available. We show that PathFinder is a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases. It can be used to discover common patterns across disparate datasets and to make predictions for missing data or modalities.

</details>


### [329] [LLM-based Framework for Generating and Verifying Parallel DEVS Statecharts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14956)
*Vamsi Krishna Vasa,Hessam S. Sarjoughian,Edward J. Yellig*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An agentic PDEVS-LLM framework is proposed to assist human modelers in generating and verifying PDEVS statecharts by generating plausible facts, correcting inconsistencies via propositional logic entailment, and verifying logical correctness through manually created Timed Automata, with an iterative human-in-the-loop and a basic completeness/accuracy metric, showing improved logical consistency across example systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the accuracy and verifiability of PDEVS statecharts by integrating LLM-generated plausible facts with formal verification, addressing inconsistencies in fact generation and behavioral structure.

Method: 1) Use an agentic LLM to generate plausible facts from a system description prompt. 2) Apply a controlled-correction mechanism using propositional logic entailment to verify plausibility of facts. 3) Extract key behavioral conditions from the description and have the LLM produce facts accordingly. 4) Verify plausible facts against behavioral conditions (finite iterations). 5) Generate modification prompts to reduce errors in facts. 6) Verify the statechart's logical correctness by manually creating and verifying a Timed Automata representation for deadlock and reachability. 7) Allow iterative, incremental regeneration by a human modeler. 8) Introduce a basic correctness metric for completeness/accuracy of behavioral traits. 9) Demonstrate with a collection of example systems of varying complexity to assess capabilities and limitations of LLMs.

Result: The evaluation reports substantial improvement in the logical consistency of generated PDEVS statecharts when using the proposed verification mechanism, with more coherent and accurate behavioral traits and state-transition structures.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates a viable human-in-the-loop approach to producing more accurate PDEVS statecharts by coupling LLM-assisted fact generation with formal propositional-logic and Timed Automata verification; it highlights improved consistency but relies on manual Timed Automata steps and leaves room for automation and broader benchmarking.

Abstract: The development of models demands sound modeling and simulation knowledge as well as domain knowledge. Every model should accurately represent a system's dynamics and be verifiable. Toward this objective, this research introduces an agentic PDEVS-LLM framework to assist human modelers in generating and verifying PDEVS statecharts for behavior modeling of atomic Parallel Discrete Event System Specification (PDEVS) models. The framework supports (re)generating plausible facts from a system description prompt using the agentic LLM used for generating plausible facts. Inconsistencies in plausible facts lead to incorrect PDEVS statecharts having logical structure and behavioral inaccuracies. A controlled-correction mechanism is developed to verify the logical consistency of the plausible facts. The agentic LLM is used to generate key behavioral conditions from the system description prompt. The plausible facts are then verified against the behavioral conditions using propositional logic entailment for a finite number of times. The verification results enable the generation of modification prompts that can reduce errors in generated plausible facts, resulting in more accurate PDEVS statecharts. To verify a statechart's logical correctness, its Timed Automata counterpart is manually created and verified for deadlock and reachability properties. The human modeler may regenerate plausible facts and PDEVS statecharts iteratively and incrementally. A basic correctness metric is introduced to quantify the completeness and accuracy of the expected behavioral traits of the PDEVS statechart models. A collection of example systems with varying levels of complexity is developed to demonstrate the capabilities and limitations of LLMs. The evaluation of the proposed verification mechanism shows a substantial improvement in the logical consistency of generated statecharts.

</details>


### [330] [Command-Space Counterfactual Explanations for Pareto-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14963)
*Joanikij Chulev,Hendrik Baier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CF-ZOO provides command-space counterfactual explanations for Pareto Conditioned Networks (PCNs) by minimally perturbing the desired-return command to flip the agent's action, using a boundary-seeded search in a black-box setting, yielding actionable, user-aligned explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Make the (state, command)→action mapping in PCNs transparent and actionable, addressing opacity and horizon-conditioning ambiguities; enable explanations that reflect user trade-offs.

Method: Define return-command interventions with a return-only PCN variant; adapt adversarial machine learning techniques to RL explanations; introduce boundary-seeded directional search (CF-ZOO) to navigate the command-action landscape in a black-box setting.

Result: Produces actionable, intuitive explanations such as 'If your trade-off shifted toward X, the agent would choose Y.' The boundary-seeded search improves over purely local optimization by avoiding poor local minima in the command-action landscape.

Conclusion: CF-ZOO offers a practical framework for explaining PCNs via counterfactuals in command space, aligning explanations with user preferences and enhancing interpretability of multi-objective RL policies.

Abstract: Pareto Conditioned Networks learn multiple multi-objective reinforcement learning behaviours by conditioning a single policy on a desired return command. However, the local mapping from command and state to action remains opaque. We propose command-space counterfactual explanations for PCNs: given a fixed state, original command, and foil action, we search, in a black-box setting, for a minimally changed desired-return command under which the same trained policy would choose the foil. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate PCN explanations as return-command interventions, using a return-only PCN variant that avoids the added ambiguity of horizon-conditioning. Second, we adapt adversarial machine learning methods to reinforcement-learning explanations. Third, we introduce a boundary-seeded directional search that improves over purely local optimization in the command-action landscape, resulting in our proposed approach CF-ZOO. The resulting explanations are actionable and intuitively expressed in the user's own preferences: "If your trade-off had shifted slightly towards X, the agent would have chosen Y."

</details>


### [331] [A Physiology-Informed Digital Twin Framework for Simulating Liver Health Progression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14969)
*Sumaiya Afroz Mila,Sandip Ray*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A physiology-informed digital twin (HEPATWIN) models longitudinal liver function and disease progression (NAFLD to cirrhosis) using mechanistic hepatic metabolism, personalized inputs, and stage-transition calibration, validated on NIDDK NAFLD data to forecast multi-year biomarker trajectories and support NASH detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a mechanistic, personalized, non-invasive tool for predicting liver health trajectories and disease progression, addressing limitations of purely data-driven models and ensuring clinically interpretable biomarker dynamics.

Method: A unified systems-level liver model incorporating carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, and detoxification, with patient-specific inputs (diet, activity, baseline biomarkers); stage-transition calibration to align outputs with population biomarker distributions across NAFLD, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; longitudinal simulation and multi-year forecasting; validation on the NIDDK NAFLD dataset; assessment of NASH detection capability.

Result: Longitudinal biomarker estimates fall within clinically acceptable ranges; multi-year trajectory forecasts are feasible; simulated biomarkers retain clinical signal sufficient for competitive NASH detection compared with models using ground-truth lab data.

Conclusion: Physiology-informed digital twins hold promise for personalized, non-invasive liver health monitoring, enabling long-horizon prognosis and disease staging, with potential applicability to other organ systems.

Abstract: We present a physiology-informed digital twin of the human liver designed for longitudinal simulation of liver function and early-stage disease progression. The model, referred to as HEPATWIN, integrates key hepatic processes, including carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, and detoxification, within a unified systems-level framework to generate clinically observable biomarker trajectories. Unlike purely data-driven approaches, HEPATWIN incorporates mechanistic representations of liver physiology and patient-specific inputs such as diet, activity, and baseline biomarkers to simulate disease evolution over time. To ensure consistency with clinical progression patterns, we introduce a stage-transition-driven calibration mechanism that aligns simulated outputs with population-level biomarker distributions across disease stages, including NAFLD, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Validation using the NIDDK NAFLD dataset demonstrates that HEPATWIN produces longitudinal biomarker estimates within clinically acceptable ranges and can forecast trajectories over multi-year horizons. Furthermore, simulated biomarkers retain sufficient clinical signal to support downstream NASH detection with competitive performance relative to models using ground-truth laboratory data. These results highlight the potential of physiology-informed digital twins for personalized, non-invasive diagnosis and prediction of organ health in general and liver health monitoring in particular.

</details>


### [332] [Do Geometry-Aware Positional Encodings Help Transformers in Spatial Imperfect-Information Games?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14982)
*Wenji Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Geometry-aware HexRoPE improves belief tracking and imitation data efficiency but not overall win rate in a hexagonal imperfect-information game.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether geometry-aware positional encodings enhance a Transformer’s ability to represent map geometry and track hidden entities over time in spatial imperfect-information games, without proposing a new encoding.

Method: Four-level benchmark on a hexagonal naval pursuit game: geometry/topology probes, exact-Bayes hidden-target tracking, offline policy imitation at 1k and 10k games, and 7,200 fixed-seed games versus three legacy opponents. Comparisons across matched Transformer backbones include HexRoPE, no encoding, rectangular relative bias, and graph bias. Metrics: exact-belief posterior cross-entropy, policy action accuracy, and win rate, with statistics on D6-transformed test orbits and a larger map; Holm-adjusted p-values and confidence intervals reported.

Result: HexRoPE reduces exact-belief posterior cross-entropy by 0.278 on D6-transformed test orbits and by 0.329 on a larger map. At 1k games, policy action accuracy improves by 4.63 percentage points over no encoding and 2.05 points over rectangular relative bias; gains shrink to 1.55 and 0.41 points at 10k games. However, win rate declines by 1.56 percentage points relative to no encoding (95% CI [-4.50, 1.17]), i.e., not statistically significant. Rectangular bias shows strong D6 belief-conistency but fails to extrapolate from radius 3 to 4; graph bias yields only a small blocked-edge gain. Overall, geometry inductive bias enhances belief estimation and data-efficient imitation, but does not automatically translate to stronger closed-loop play.

Conclusion: Geometric inductive bias helps belief estimation and data-efficient imitation in spatial imperfect-information settings, but does not necessarily improve closed-loop performance such as win rate.

Abstract: Transformers applied to spatial imperfect-information games must represent map geometry while tracking hidden entities through time. We ask whether geometry-aware positional encodings improve these capabilities, without claiming a new positional encoding. We construct a four-level benchmark on a hexagonal naval pursuit game: controlled geometry and topology probes, an exact-Bayes hidden-target tracking task, offline policy imitation at 1k and 10k games, and 7,200 fixed-seed games against three legacy opponents. Across matched Transformer backbones, HexRoPE reduces exact-belief posterior cross-entropy relative to no positional encoding by 0.278 on D6-transformed test orbits and 0.329 on a larger map; both hierarchical-bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero, and both Holm-adjusted p-values are below 0.001. At 1k games, HexRoPE improves policy action accuracy by 4.63 percentage points over no encoding and 2.05 points over rectangular relative bias; the gains shrink to 1.55 and 0.41 points at 10k games. However, HexRoPE does not improve aggregate gameplay win rate: its paired effect over no encoding is -1.56 percentage points (95% CI [-4.50, 1.17]). Rectangular relative bias is strongest on D6 belief consistency but fails sharply when extrapolating from radius 3 to radius 4, while graph bias provides only a small blocked-edge gain. The results show that geometric inductive bias improves belief estimation and data-efficient imitation, but those representation gains do not automatically produce stronger closed-loop play.

</details>


### [333] [Lipschitz Bandits with Arbitrary Feedback Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15036)
*Yuhao Liu,Yu Chen,Longbo Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Lipschitz bandits with arbitrary feedback delays: stochastic setting using an elimination-based algorithm and adversarial setting using EXP3; both achieve regret tilde{O}(T^{(dz+1)/(dz+2)} + sqrt{D}) over horizon T with total delay D; dz differs by setting; delays add a sqrt{D} term while delay-free regret is preserved otherwise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address learning with delayed feedback in Lipschitz bandit problems over continuous action spaces, where rewards are revealed after arbitrary delays, in both stochastic and adversarial regimes; understand how delays affect regret and how to design algorithms that adapt to delayed feedback while exploiting Lipschitz structure.

Method: Develop an elimination-based algorithm for the stochastic Lipschitz bandit with delays and an EXP3-based algorithm for the adversarial variant. Define and use the zooming dimension dz appropriate to each setting. Analyze regret under total delay D and show a unified bound tilde{O}(T^{(dz+1)/(dz+2)} + sqrt{D}).

Result: Proposed algorithms achieve regret bounds that match delay-free Lipschitz bandit results up to an additive sqrt{D} term due to delays. The bound highlights the impact of the delay budget on learning performance and extends known results to arbitrary feedback delays.

Conclusion: Delays contribute an additional sqrt{D} overhead while preserving the main learning rate dictated by the Lipschitz geometry via the zooming dimension. The results unify stochastic and adversarial analyses under a common framework and suggest that near-optimal performance is achievable even with substantial feedback delays.

Abstract: The Lipschitz bandit problem extends the traditional multi-armed bandit framework to continuous action spaces by assuming that the reward functions satisfy a Lipschitz condition. This work investigates Lipschitz bandits under arbitrary feedback delays, where reward signals are not received immediately upon taking an action but after an arbitrarily chosen delay. We consider both stochastic and adversarial reward settings, proposing an elimination-based algorithm and an EXP3-based algorithm, respectively. For both settings, our algorithms achieve a regret bound of $\tilde{O}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}+\sqrt{D}\right)$ over a time horizon $T$ with total delay $D$, where the main difference between settings lies in the definition of the zooming dimension $d_z$. Our bounds match existing delay-free regret guarantees for Lipschitz bandits and characterize the additional $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{D})$ impact introduced by feedback delays.

</details>


### [334] [Certifying Compressed Language Models: An Audit and a Statistical Toolkit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15046)
*Amogh Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Equivalence claims for compressed models are fragile: churn often dwarfs net accuracy deltas, and many claims lack margins or per-item outputs. The authors propose a paired equivalence-testing framework with a declared margin, certified per-item evidence, and full data release; they validate it with a controlled GPTQ vs AWQ experiment and prescribe a five-line reporting standard applicable to any comparison of similar models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the insufficiency of current equivalence claims in model compression by requiring verifiable, item-level evidence and explicit margins, enabling reproducible, quantitative assessments.

Method: Audit of 1,707 model–task cells drawn from public per-item evaluation dumps (1.3B–405B items). Assess churn relative to net delta; preregister an audit of 17 equivalence claims; develop and apply a paired equivalence test at a declared margin with certification tables derived from observed disagreement under compression. Conduct a controlled experiment pairing GPTQ and AWQ on byte-identical calibration samples across five seeds. Release all per-item outputs, protocols, and code.

Result: Churn is ~5× the net accuracy delta; 16 of 17 claims eligible but none specify a prospective margin or release per-item outputs; many claims provide insufficient data to assess numerically; in a pilot, changing the calibration draw reversed method ordering in 5 of 8 confirmatory cells (H3). The authors propose a five-line reporting standard and emphasize full transparency (outputs, protocols, code).

Conclusion: Equivalence claims should be supported by explicit margins and item-level evidence via paired testing; the approach is generalizable to comparisons between similarly powerful models and demands full data transparency.

Abstract: A fraction of a point of benchmark accuracy is the usual evidence that a compressed model is equivalent to its original. That quantity is least informative when two models are most alike: a net delta is what survives cancellation between opposing per-item changes, and cancellation is most complete in the regime equivalence claims occupy. Across an atlas of 1,707 paired model-by-task cells mined from public per-item evaluation dumps (1.3B-405B), churn runs roughly five times the net accuracy delta, and cells scoring identically to their baseline still disagree on individual items. In a preregistered audit of 17 equivalence claims from three registered frames (method papers, model cards, vendor documentation), 16 are eligible. None states a prospective numerical equivalence margin, and none releases task-matched per-item outputs, though 3 release outputs for other tasks only; 5 report too little to assess numerically, so a reader cannot check them at any sample size. We audit evidential sufficiency, not truth: no claim is called false. We supply the missing instrument: paired equivalence testing at a declared margin, with certification tables giving the items an evaluation needs, computed from disagreement observed under compression, not from independent-binomial variance. A controlled experiment pairs GPTQ and AWQ on byte-identical calibration samples across five seeds. Under the frozen eight-cell decision rule H3 is supported: changing the calibration draw was sufficient to reverse the observed method ordering in 5 of 8 confirmatory cells. The reporting standard we propose is five lines: declare a margin, run the paired test, report churn beside net delta, cite the sample size you met, release per-item outputs. It applies to any comparison between two models alike enough to be worth comparing. All per-item outputs, protocols and code are released.

</details>


### [335] [Online Convex Optimization with Dueling Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15050)
*Yiyang Lu,Hareshkumar Jadav,Mohammad Pedramfar,Ranveer Singh,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a reduction that turns binary dueling feedback into approximate gradients, enabling standard first-order online convex optimization (OCO) methods in adversarial settings; achieves first nontrivial regret bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dueling (pairwise comparison) feedback is natural but underexplored in adversarial OCO. The goal is to enable learning from binary preferences and establish regret guarantees.

Method: A simple reduction converts dueling feedback into approximate gradients, allowing the use of standard first-order optimization methods.

Result: The reduction yields regret transfer and first results in this setting: overall regret O(T^{3/4}) for static, adaptive, and dynamic scenarios; under extra structure, improved rates: O(T^{2/3}) for smooth objectives and O(sqrt(T log T)) for strongly convex functions.

Conclusion: The proposal provides a practical, gradient-based framework for adversarial OCO with dueling feedback, with nontrivial regret bounds and potential for further improvements under structural assumptions.

Abstract: We study online convex optimization with dueling (pairwise comparison) feedback, where the learner observes only a binary preference between two queried points. While dueling feedback is well understood in discrete or stochastic settings, the adversarial convex setting has remained unexplored. We propose a simple reduction that converts dueling feedback into approximate gradients, enabling the use of standard first-order methods. We show that regret guarantees transfer under this reduction, yielding the first results for this setting, including $\mathcal{O}(T^{3/4})$ static, adaptive, and dynamic regret. Under additional structure, we obtain improved rates of $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ for smooth objectives and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \log T})$ for strongly convex functions.

</details>


### [336] [A Unified Mamba--MoE Surrogate for Closed-Loop Simulation and Measurement-Window Forecasting of Inverter Transients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15051)
*Haoguang Wang,Huy Hoang Le,Akhila Kandivalasa,Christian Moya,Marcos Netto,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unified Mamba surrogate with mixture-of-experts routing handles both closed-loop simulation and measurement-window forecasting of inverter transients, achieving similar accuracy with 13% fewer parameters and 94–96% empirical coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To efficiently model transient dynamics of inverter-based resources and enable joint tasks (simulation and forecasting) with reliable uncertainty quantification.

Method: A Mamba backbone augmented with a router network to assign data-dependent weights to specialized experts (MoE). Task conditioning and adaptive conformal prediction provide task-specific outputs and prediction intervals. A single backbone replaces two separate specialists; evaluated on a grid-following inverter with controller hardware-in-the-loop validation.

Result: The unified Mamba–MoE surrogate matches the low-error performance of dedicated Mamba specialists while reducing parameters by 13%. Prediction intervals achieve 94–96% coverage. For transient dynamics, MoE routing yields lower errors across all outputs compared to a shared backbone without routing. HIL validation shows efficient adaptation by updating only the shared output head with limited data.

Conclusion: MoE routing within the Mamba framework enables a compact, multi-task surrogate that preserves accuracy and provides reliable uncertainty estimates for both closed-loop simulation and short-horizon forecasting of inverter transients, with practical hardware-in-the-loop applicability.

Abstract: This paper proposes a Mamba surrogate model with mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing to represent the transient dynamics of inverter-based resources. A Mamba surrogate model is a predictive machine learning model built on the Mamba architecture. MoE routing uses a router network to assign data-dependent weights to specialized subnetworks (experts). The resulting Mamba--MoE surrogate can perform two tasks: (i) closed-loop simulation and (ii) measurement-window forecasting of inverter transients. A single Mamba backbone with task conditioning and expert routing serves both tasks, replacing two separate specialists. Task-matched objectives fit each prediction form, and an adaptive conformal layer provides prediction intervals for both tasks. For the considered grid-following inverter, the unified surrogate model remains in the same low-error regime as a Mamba specialist pair while using 13% fewer parameters. The prediction intervals achieve 94--96% empirical mean marginal coverage across the two tasks. For transient dynamics---that is, beyond the vicinity of an equilibrium point---our surrogate model with MoE routing yields lower errors across all outputs in both tasks compared to a shared Mamba backbone without expert routing. A controller hardware-in-the-loop simulation validates our results and shows that adapting only the shared output head with limited measured data reduces held-out forecasting error.

</details>


### [337] [GATTA: Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15084)
*Zsombor Bánfi,András Gézsi,András Formanek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GATTA uses test-time augmentation for graph active learning, aggregating predictions from multiple augmented views with a consistency-based filter, to improve uncertainty estimates. This boosts simple acquisition strategies (e.g., Entropy, Least Confidence), matches or surpasses complex methods, and scales well across architectures and graph sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Active learning on graph-structured data suffers from unreliable uncertainty estimates and high computational cost when using complex acquisition strategies. TTA offers potential robustness by combining multiple augmented views, but label-preserving graph augmentations and view consistency must be managed. The work proposes to leverage TTA for more reliable active learning with efficient compute.

Method: Introduce GATTA: generate multiple augmented views of a graph, obtain predictions from each, aggregate uncertainties across views, and apply a consistency-based filtering to drop views with unreliable predictions. Evaluate across multiple datasets, GNN architectures, and acquisition strategies; compare against MC Dropout and other methods; analyze augmentation types and filtering strategies; provide guidelines for deployment.

Result: Uncertainty-based methods (Entropy, Least Confidence) benefit most from TTA, achieving competitive performance with less computational overhead than sophisticated acquisition functions. GATTA generalizes across architectures, outperforms MC Dropout, and scales with ensemble size and graph size. Empirical analysis offers practical guidelines on augmentation types and filtering for effective deployment.

Conclusion: Augmenting simple active-learning baselines with test-time augmentation yields strong, efficient performance for graph data. TTA reduces implementation complexity and computational cost while delivering robust uncertainty estimates, making TTA a practical path to strong graph active learning.

Abstract: Test-time augmentation (TTA) has proven effective for improving model robustness and uncertainty estimation in computer vision, yet its application to graph-structured data remains largely unexplored. We introduce GATTA (Graph Active Learning with Test-Time Augmentation), a framework for enhancing active learning by aggregating predictions across multiple augmented views to produce more reliable uncertainty estimates. To address the challenge of label-preserving graph augmentations, GATTA incorporates a consistency-based filtering mechanism that discards augmented views yielding unreliable predictions. We systematically evaluate GATTA across multiple graph datasets, GNN architectures, and acquisition strategies. Our results show that simple uncertainty-based methods, such as Entropy and Least Confidence, benefit most from TTA, achieving performance competitive with more sophisticated and computationally expensive approaches. GATTA generalizes across architectures, outperforms model-side ensemble methods such as MC Dropout. We further show that GATTA scales efficiently with both ensemble size and graph size. Extensive analysis of augmentation types, strengths, and filtering strategies provides practical guidelines for effective deployment. Our findings demonstrate that augmenting simple methods with TTA offers a more efficient path to strong active learning performance than engineering complex acquisition functions, enabling practitioners to achieve competitive results with lower computational overhead and reduced implementation complexity.

</details>


### [338] [EMASAM: a Computationally Efficient Sharpness-Aware Minimization via EMA-Guided Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15105)
*Tanapat Ratchatorn,Masayuki Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EMASAM is a computationally efficient variant of SAM that uses an EMA shadow model to define perturbations, eliminating the extra gradient step while preserving generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sharpness of the loss landscape is linked to generalization; SAM improves generalization but requires an extra gradient computation for perturbations, increasing cost.

Method: Define perturbation direction via the discrepancy between the current model and an EMA shadow model; perturb away from the EMA center toward less stable regions without using loss gradients in the perturbation step; avoids an additional backpropagation and reduces gradient-induced instability from noisy mini-batch gradients.

Result: The approach yields similar generalization benefits to SAM with lower computational cost and improved training stability, as evidenced by experiments showing efficiency and robustness.

Conclusion: EMASAM provides a cheaper, stable alternative to SAM that retains its generalization advantages by leveraging EMA-based perturbations and avoiding extra gradient computations.

Abstract: Recent progress in optimization research has highlighted the sharpness of the loss landscape as a key factor in narrowing the generalization gap. Motivated by this insight, Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) was proposed as a training strategy that enhances generalization. Despite the promising performance, SAM suffers from its twice computational cost due to its core algorithm requiring an extra gradient computation during the perturbation step. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Exponential Moving Average Sharpness-Aware Minimization (EMASAM), a computationally efficient variant of SAM. EMASAM does not require the loss gradient in the perturbation step. Instead, EMASAM defines the perturbation direction based on the discrepancy between the main model and the EMA shadow model. This perturbation travels away from the stable average position toward the less stable area, acting as a softer yet cheaper alternative to SAM's worst-case scenario perturbation. Moreover, since EMASAM's perturbation does not rely on noisy mini-batch gradients, it mitigates the gradient-induced instability inherent in SAM. Hence, EMASAM eliminates the need for an extra backpropagation while also preserving the generalization ability of the SAM-style training. Several experiments have been performed and confirm the efficiency and robustness of our method.

</details>


### [339] [Global Federated Learning Strategies for Building Efficient Personalized Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15107)
*Seongyoon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The dissertation studies heterogeneity in Federated Learning (FL) and aims to achieve simultaneous global knowledge preservation and local personalization. It identifies feature-vector collapse as a primary bottleneck, proposes representation-magnitude alignment to mitigate local-global discrepancy, and uses global-feature distillation to prevent forgetting during local alignment. It also reevaluates global initialization in personalized reward modeling, showing that with sufficient local fine-tuning a single global initialization can outperform multiple global models for personalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In FL with non-iid data, both global model performance and user-specific personalization degrade. The work seeks strategies that (i) address representation-level misalignment between local and global models, (ii) avoid forgetting global knowledge during local alignment, and (iii) optimize the use of global initializations under preference heterogeneity to enhance personalization.

Method: (1) Diagnose feature-vector collapse as a fundamental bottleneck and propose a method to equalize representation magnitudes between local and global models. (2) Analyze local alignment-induced forgetting and introduce a distillation-based approach using the global model's feature vectors to preserve global knowledge while achieving local alignment. (3) Empirically study federated personalized reward modeling with heterogeneous preferences, comparing multiple global initiations versus a single global initialization under varying degrees of local fine-tuning.

Result: 1) Addressing representation magnitude disparity mitigates feature-vector collapse and improves cross-client generalization. 2) Feature distillation from the global model enables local alignment without sacrificing global knowledge, reducing forgetting. 3) In personalized reward modeling with heterogenous preferences, a single global initialization can surpass multiple global initializations when ample local fine-tuning is allowed, reframing the role of global initializations in FL.

Conclusion: The work redefines how global knowledge and personalization interact in FL under heterogeneity, offering practical strategies that jointly preserve global representations and enable robust personalization. It highlights the potential to simplify initialization strategies (favoring a single global init) and to rely on targeted distillation and magnitude-alignment techniques to combat representation and forgetting challenges.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a practical framework that can train models on distributed user data while guaranteeing data privacy; however, due to heterogeneity in which each user has a different data distribution, problems frequently arise where both global and personalization performance deteriorate simultaneously. This dissertation presents methodologies for building efficient personalized models by identifying which strategies are effective in the global training stage and by showing how to preserve global knowledge while securing user-specific performance during local adaptation. First, we show that as data heterogeneity increases, the collapse of feature vectors is a more fundamental bottleneck than classifier weights, and propose a method that directly mitigates the discrepancy in representation magnitude between local and global models. Second, we analyze that a training approach that strengthens local alignment can induce forgetting of global knowledge (e.g., categories not observed locally), and propose a method that achieves both local alignment and global knowledge preservation by combining feature distillation based on the global model's feature vectors. Third, in federated personalized reward model learning with preference heterogeneity, we empirically verify the conventional belief that "increasing the number of global models yields better initialization," and we show that when sufficient local fine-tuning is allowed, a single global initialization can instead provide stronger personalization performance. This study redefines the role of global initialization under data and preference heterogeneity and provides practical training strategies that simultaneously satisfy global knowledge preservation and personalization.

</details>


### [340] [Probability-Preserving Transformer for the Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15112)
*Mushtaq Ali,Muzamil Tariq,Niaz Ali Khan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Transformer model for TDSE solving with hard unitarity constraint ensuring probability conservation; claims exact unitarity and faster computation than soft-constraint approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TDSE solving is computationally intensive; soft-constraint transformers cannot guarantee probability conservation; a physically exact, efficient surrogate is desirable.

Method: A transformer architecture that enforces TDSE probability conservation as a hard constraint, intrinsically guaranteeing unitarity across temporal evolution without retraining.

Result: Empirical results indicate the hard-constraint model is physically exact and computationally superior to soft-constraint methods.

Conclusion: Hard-constrained unitarity yields accurate, efficient TDSE solutions and eliminates the need for retraining; promising for reliable quantum dynamics surrogates.

Abstract: Solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) via traditional numerical methods is computationally intensive. Transformer models offer a compelling alternative, but standard implementations rely on soft constraints that cannot rigorously guarantee probability conservation. Here, we introduce a Transformer architecture that enforces TDSE probability conservation as a hard constraint. The design intrinsically ensures unitarity across temporal evolution without requiring repeated retraining. Our empirical findings show that this hard-constraint approach is not only physically exact but also computationally superior to conventional soft-constraint methods.

</details>


### [341] [Decision-Driven Regularization: A Blended Model for Learning and Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15124)
*Gar Goei Loke,Qinshen Tang,Yangge Xiao,Xun Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bi-objective decision-driven regularization for contextual optimization that balances prediction accuracy and decision cost, connecting to robust optimization and SPO+, with empirical gains over standard baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To avoid overfitting and suboptimal decisions in integrated learning-optimization, the paper argues for explicit control of prediction accuracy within the optimization objective and addresses uncertainty/ambiguity in the cost function via a surrogate and a hyperparameter.

Method: Introduce a bi-objective framework that jointly learns outcomes from features and minimizes decision cost, via decision-driven regularization. Provide a surrogate for the cost function that depends on a new hyperparameter. Show connections to robust optimization and regret minimization, leading to models closely related to, and generalizing, SPO+..

Result: Numerical experiments on synthetic data show that the proposed model is superior to benchmarks (OLS, Random Forest, XGBoost, SPO+, Perturbation Gradient, Learning-to-Rank) in terms of decision quality and predictive performance.

Conclusion: The framework generalizes SPO+ and links to robust and regret-based formulations, offering improved decision performance and robustness in integrated learning-optimization; demonstrated effectiveness on synthetic studies, with potential for broader applicability.

Abstract: In contextual optimization, the decision-maker seeks optimal decisions to minimize a cost function, that varies based on observed features. This context is common in many business applications ranging from on-demand delivery and retail operations to portfolio optimization and inventory management. In this paper, we study the learning and optimization approach, which first learns how outcomes result from the features, and then selects optimal decisions based on these outcomes. We focus on the integrated learning and optimization literature, and identify that a lack of control for prediction accuracy can lead to overfitting and a loss of decision effectiveness against simple separate learning and optimization models. Instead, we propose a bi-objective formulation that balances prediction accuracy and cost minimization, termed decision-driven regularization. It also addresses ambiguity in the definition of the cost function via a surrogate that depends on a new hyperparameter. We additionally show that alternative perspectives for formulating the problem, namely robust optimization and regret minimization, lead to models that are closely related to our proposed model. As a consequence, our framework generalizes models such as SPO+. Our model is shown to be numerically superior to other benchmarks, such as OLS, Random Forest, XGBoost, SPO+, Perturbation Gradient, and Learning and Rank, in our synthetic studies.

</details>


### [342] [PureTD: Reinforcement Learning for Backgammon Money Games with No Evaluation-time Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15146)
*Alexander L. Strehl*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-play reinforcement learning without evaluation-time search can reach near state-of-the-art backgammon play, learning both checker play and cube actions; cubeful money games outperform 1-ply search engines like GNU Backgammon/Open Sage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether removing evaluation-time search and relying on self-play can achieve high strength in backgammon, extending the legacy of Tesauro's TD-Gammon.

Method: Train from scratch using self-play RL with minimal hand-coded logic and no expert features; simultaneously learn checker play and doubling cube decisions; no evaluation-time search is used.

Result: The approach attains near-state-of-the-art playing strength; in cubeful money games, the search-free model evaluates faster and outperforms GNU Backgammon and Open Sage under a one-move (1-ply) look-ahead.

Conclusion: Pure self-play reinforcement learning can reach high levels of backgammon performance without evaluation-time search, implying broader potential for RL-based agents in complex games and suggesting efficiency benefits over traditional search-based engines.

Abstract: We revisit Tesauro's TD-Gammon for backgammon money games in the setting of no evaluation-time search. Both checker play and cube action (use of the doubling cube) are learned from scratch via self-play reinforcement learning (RL), with minimal hand-coded logic and no expert features. In this setting, we demonstrate that pure self-play RL suffices to train models that reach near-state-of-the-art playing strength. Specifically, for cubeful money games, our search-free model evaluates faster and is substantially stronger than the open-source engines GNU Backgammon and Open Sage running a one-move (1-ply) look-ahead search.

</details>


### [343] [FinFraudBench: A Heterogeneous Graph Benchmark for Financial Fraud Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15177)
*Yixuan Chen,Hongyu Zhan,Jie Sheng,Weiyu Han,Shuai Chen,Tianyi Zhang,Xiao Tan,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A large-scale heterogeneous graph benchmark for financial fraud detection (FinFraudBench) with two datasets, preserving six entity types and fourteen edge types, addressing realism and class imbalance, plus standardized evaluation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To align graph-based fraud detection benchmarks with real-world financial ecosystems by preserving multi-entity, multi-relational structure and realistic operating conditions (scale, imbalance, limited labels).

Method: Two heterogeneous graph datasets (CreditCard-Fraud, BankTrans-Fraud) with up to 8.99M nodes and 89.23M directed typed edges, six entity types, fourteen edge types, natural fraud rates. A standardized evaluation protocol for ranking and imbalance-sensitive classification, plus baseline evaluations.

Result: Empirical evaluation reveals current graph-method limitations in realistic settings and offers insights and directions for future research.

Conclusion: FinFraudBench provides a realistic, large-scale benchmark and evaluation protocol to advance research in heterogeneous graph-based financial fraud detection.

Abstract: The increasing complexity of digital financial systems has reshaped financial fraud detection from isolated transaction classification into relational risk reasoning over interconnected financial entities. This shift has motivated graph-based fraud detection, where models identify fraudulent nodes by exploiting dependencies among customers, cards, merchants, categories, and locations. However, despite rapid progress in graph-based methods, existing public benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world financial systems in two important aspects. First, they often simplify financial ecosystems into homogeneous or single-node-type multi-relational graphs, failing to preserve the multi-entity and multi-relational nature of financial data. Second, they rarely provide large-scale heterogeneous financial graph datasets with realistic operating conditions such as extreme class imbalance and limited label availability, making it difficult to assess the practical effectiveness of current methods. To address these gaps, we present FinFraudBench, a heterogeneous graph benchmark for financial fraud detection. FinFraudBench contains two heterogeneous graph datasets (CreditCard-Fraud and BankTrans-Fraud) with up to 8.99M nodes and 89.23M directed typed edges. Each dataset preserves six financial entity types, fourteen directed edge types, and natural fraud rates that mirror deployment constraints. With these datasets, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol covering both ranking and imbalance-sensitive classification metrics, and evaluate representative baselines. Extensive experiments yield empirical insights into current methods' limitations and suggest promising avenues for future research. FinFraudBench is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FinFraudBench-B002.

</details>


### [344] [MiNO: Cotangent-bundle propagator learning for PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15187)
*Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan,Bum Jun Kim*

Main category: cs.LG
