TL;DR: MiNO learns a phase-space propagator for PDE evolution by solving the eikonal equation for phase and the transport equation for amplitude, reconstructing the field via an oscillatory integral. It emphasizes propagation geometry (lines, fronts, caustics) rather than pointwise fields, achieving high accuracy and data efficiency, and outperforms PINNs and Fourier operators in tested benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a regularity gap: transported discontinuities are nonsmooth in space/time, but the evolution can be governed by a smooth propagator (phase) that moves the singularity. Modeling the propagator (canonical relation) rather than the field itself can better capture singularity propagation and geometry, with residuals certifying closeness to the exact relation and separating trainable error from frequency truncation.

Method: Learned MiNO model that represents the propagator through a phase satisfying the eikonal equation and an amplitude satisfying the transport equation; solution reconstructed via an oscillatory integral. The approach yields sharp fronts/caustics as propagation geometry. Residuals quantify closeness to the exact canonical relation and separate trainable error from the high-frequency tail. Evaluations include a matched-budget discontinuous-advection benchmark (where MiNO saturates accuracy at the reconstruction window after ~10k steps, unlike NTK-PINN baselines) and a smooth-advection setting (mean error MiNO ≈ 3.84e-3 vs FNO ≈ 3.12e-2). A single-branch MiNO with a generator trained once generalizes to five unseen initial conditions without retraining.

Result: MiNO achieves higher accuracy and data efficiency by focusing on propagation geometry rather than field fitting. It stops improving at the theoretical reconstruction limit in challenging discontinuous cases, outperforming PINN approaches. In smooth advection, it markedly reduces mean error relative to a supervised Fourier neural operator.

Conclusion: MiNO demonstrates that learning the propagator in phase space—through the eikonal and transport equations—can yield more accurate and generalizable PDE solutions, especially for problems with discontinuities and caustics. The approach isolates trainable error from truncation effects and enables reuse across initial conditions with a compact model.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning for partial differential equations commonly targets solution fields, as in physics-informed neural networks, or solution maps, as in neural operators. We study a third target: the propagator itself, a phase and amplitude in phase space. The motivation is a gap in regularity. A transported discontinuity is nonsmooth in space and time, yet the rule that moves it can be a polynomial phase carrying unit amplitude, so the object that generates an evolution can be far smoother than the field it generates. The microlocal neural operator (MiNO) learns that object, using the eikonal equation for the phase and the transport equation for the amplitude, and recovers the solution by an oscillatory integral. Sharp fronts and caustics then belong to propagation geometry rather than to a field fitted pointwise. Small residuals certify more than the reconstructed field. They place the learned canonical relation, the geometry that carries singularities, close to the exact one, and they separate trainable error from the frequency-truncation tail. On a matched-budget discontinuous-advection benchmark, MiNO stops improving within 10,000 steps at the accuracy limit of its finite reconstruction window, a limit predicted in closed form, whereas a physics-informed neural network with neural-tangent-kernel loss balancing stays near its initial error. On smooth advection, the mean error is $3.84\times10^{-3}$ for MiNO and $3.12\times10^{-2}$ for a supervised Fourier neural operator. Single-branch MiNO is the smallest model compared, and one trained generator serves five unseen initial conditions without retraining.

</details>


### [345] [Structuring Semantic Embeddings for Principle Evaluation: A Prototype-Guided Contrastive Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15224)
*Che Shen,Junwei Su,Lingpeng Kong,Chuan Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prototype-Guided Contrastive Learning (PGCL) improves task-adapted representations from frozen embeddings for post-hoc evaluation across toxicity, emotion, and review-rating tasks via prototype-based regularization and contrasting streams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address semantic overlap in generic embeddings that hinders task-specific discrimination in post-hoc evaluation, enabling improved performance without costly encoder fine-tuning.

Method: Introduce PGCL with a semantic stream, a prototype-anchor attention stream, supervised contrastive learning, offset-based prototype-margin regularization, and stream regularization on top of frozen text encoders; evaluate on three tasks; include analyses with residual adapters, LoRA, full fine-tuning, ablations, and few-shot LLM diagnostics; theoretically reinterpret prototype-margin as a sufficient condition in prototype-mapping space.

Result: PGCL outperforms raw frozen embeddings on all three datasets; achieves the clearest direct-baseline margin on AmazonReviews; competitive with strong direct frozen metric-learning baselines on GoEmotions and ToxicComment; extensive ablations and diagnostics; revised theoretical framing to a sufficient-condition account.

Conclusion: Prototype-guided geometric regularization can yield compact, task-adapted representations without updating the base encoder, extending effectiveness of post-hoc evaluation across multiple tasks; theoretical framing clarifies when and why prototype-margin holds under assumptions.

Abstract: Reliable post-hoc evaluation asks whether already generated text satisfies a target criterion after generation. In this paper we study a focused frozen-embedding setting using principle-evaluation proxy tasks: toxicity detection, fine-grained emotion categorization, and ordinal review rating. General-purpose text embeddings are widely deployed for such tasks, but broad semantic similarity can place semantically similar yet task-distinct examples in overlapping regions of the representation space. We introduce Prototype-Guided Contrastive Learning (PGCL), a prototype-guided geometric regularization module built on top of frozen text embeddings. The module combines a semantic stream, a prototype-anchor attention stream, supervised contrastive learning, offset-based prototype-margin regularization, and stream regularization to produce a compact task-adapted representation without updating the base encoder. Controlled experiments show that PGCL improves over raw frozen embeddings on all three datasets and gives the clearest direct-baseline margin on AmazonReviews, while remaining competitive with strong direct frozen metric-learning baselines on GoEmotions and ToxicComment. We also add supervised residual-adapter, encoder-LoRA, full fine-tuning, objective ablation, sensitivity, and fully logged few-shot LLM protocol diagnostics to define the boundary of the claim. The theoretical analysis is revised as a sufficient-condition account for prototype-margin behavior under explicit assumptions in the prototype-mapping space, rather than as an unconditional training or final-embedding separation guarantee.

</details>


### [346] [Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15239)
*Asahi Nakamuta,Jun-nosuke Teramae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact solution of learning dynamics in a wide two-layer linear teacher-student network with power-law inputs reveals nonmonotonic evolution of the internal spectrum exponent in the feature-learning regime, multiple asymptotic regimes across modes/training times, and near-constant behavior in the lazy regime; nonlinear nets show similar exponent dynamics, suggesting a general mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain the emergence and formation mechanism of power-law anisotropy in high-dimensional internal representations and connect it to input statistics and task-driven learning.

Method: Analytical solution of learning dynamics for a wide two-layer linear network in a teacher–student setting with power-law input and power-law teacher structures; identification of feature-learning vs lazy regimes; numerical experiments extending to nonlinear networks.

Result: In the feature-learning regime, the local power-law exponent of the internal-representation spectrum evolves nonmonotonically and exhibits up to four distinct asymptotic regimes across modes and training times. In the lazy regime, the exponent remains essentially unchanged. Similar exponent dynamics are observed numerically in more realistic nonlinear networks.

Conclusion: Dynamic interaction between input statistics and task structure can give rise to power-law internal representations; this mechanism appears to be general across model classes and training regimes.

Abstract: Power-law anisotropy in internal representations has been observed across a wide range of biological and artificial neural systems, from state-of-the-art language models to the mouse cerebral cortex. This anisotropy is a key geometric property of high-dimensional information processing and underlies a variety of theoretical analyses. However, the mechanism by which it emerges from input structure and task-driven learning has remained unclear. Here, we characterize this formation process by exactly solving the learning dynamics of a wide two-layer linear neural network in a teacher--student setting with power-law input and teacher structures. We show that, in the feature-learning regime, the local power-law exponent of the internal-representation spectrum evolves nonmonotonically over the course of training and exhibits up to four distinct asymptotic regimes across modes and training times. By contrast, in the lazy regime, the exponent remains essentially unchanged. We further demonstrate numerically that similar exponent dynamics arise in more realistic nonlinear networks. Together, these results suggest a general mechanism by which the dynamic interaction between input statistics and task structure gives rise to power-law internal representations.

</details>


### [347] [Earth Observation Foundation Models for Terrestrial Ecohydrology: From Representation Learning to Process Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15282)
*Yi Yu,Jian Peng,Yucheng Lin,Trevor F. Keenan,Thomas F. A. Bishop*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EOFMs in ecohydrology offer reusable representations for data-driven ecohydrological tasks but show misalignment with ecohydrological needs, especially under uncertainty, scale, and temporal dynamics; a process-aware evaluation framework is needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in synthesizing how EOFMs map to ecohydrology targets, data uncertainty, scale mismatches, and temporal dependencies, to enable trustworthy inference and interpretation.

Method: Develop an observation-to-inference hierarchy; conduct meta-analysis of pretraining data; synthesize ecohydrological applications; perform a benchmark audit of EOFMs within ecohydrology.

Result: Found a misalignment between EOFMs and ecohydrological requirements. Relevance depends on observation pathways, spatial-temporal support, and traceable uncertainty. Pretraining is dominated by reflected optical and active-microwave data with limited thermal and no passive microwave emission data. Applications show strongest support for spatial context, label-efficient adaptation, and hybrid workflows; evidence weakens with inference depth. Benchmark audits show better coverage for fair adaptation and reproducibility, but weak assessment of physical consistency and uncertainty.

Conclusion: A process-aware framework is needed to align EOFM design and evaluation with target variables, observation pathways, and process timescales to enable trustworthy monitoring and interpretation of coupled surface water–energy–carbon dynamics.

Abstract: Earth observation foundation models (EOFMs) are emerging as reusable representation frameworks for data-driven retrieval, prediction and process modelling within ecohydrology, which integrate EO, meteorological forcing and process models to characterise coupled water, energy and carbon dynamics in vegetation and soil across scales. However, there is yet to be an ecohydrology-specific synthesis assessing the EOFM relevance, application evidence or evaluation requirements under uncertain reference data, scale mismatch and temporal dependence. Here, we develop a framework for determining when EOFMs support interpretable inference and identify a mismatch between EOFMs and ecohydrological requirements. Firstly, an observation-to-inference hierarchy shows that relevance depends on target-specific sensing pathways, spatial-temporal support and traceable uncertainty. Secondly, a meta-analysis shows that pretraining is dominated by reflected optical and active-microwave data, with sparse thermal coverage and no passive-microwave-emission sources. Thirdly, our synthesis of ecohydrological applications finds strongest support for spatial context, label-efficient adaptation and hybrid workflows. Evidence declines with inference depth; independent validation of fluxes, coupled dynamics, event trajectories, calibrated uncertainty and decision benefits remains sparse. Fourthly, our benchmark audit finds stronger coverage of fair adaptation and reproducibility in general EOFM suites, and of process targets, direct reference evidence and distribution shifts in ecohydrological evaluations; physical consistency and uncertainty remain weakly assessed. These findings motivate a process-aware framework aligning EOFM design and evaluation with the target variable, observation pathway and process timescale, supporting trustworthy monitoring and interpretation of coupled water, energy and carbon dynamics.

</details>


### [348] [No Task Fails Every Time: Why One-Shot Audits Are Structurally Blind to Agent Damage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15286)
*Shiven Khurdi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AgentRelBench introduces an environment-agnostic reliability metric that computes ground-truth, severity-priced damage from database state diffs across repeated runs without LLM involvement, demonstrated on EnterpriseOps-Gym. In 2,128 evaluation runs across 9 models in 6 families, key findings include universal damage on irreversible actions, no task that always damages, a gradient of damage with model capability (not causally established), persistent residual damage with high audit misses, and a flagged gated irreversible change despite declared refusals. All confirmatory results were pre-registered with demote criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify reliability and damage in AI systems without relying on LLM-in-the-loop measurements, using a consistent, environment-agnostic instrument that yields ground-truth, severity-weighted damage from state diffs to enable cross-model, cross-environment comparison.

Method: Apply AgentRelBench to EnterpriseOps-Gym, measuring ground-truth damage from database state diffs across repeated runs. Evaluate 9 models across 6 families (including development, pre-registered held-out, and frontier exploratory tiers) over 2,128 runs. Record irreversible-action damage, assess task-level damage incidence, analyze gradient with model capability, and identify gated irreversible changes. All confirmatory findings are pre-registered with demote criteria.

Result: Findings: (1) universal damage on irreversible actions within pinned, single-provider stacks and stochastic across runs; (2) no task damaged on every run; 0 damaged on some confirmatory events; clean-run misses damage-pair 0.80 of the time in development pool; held-out pool underpowered; (3) damage-producing task count declines with model capability (7/20 at 8B to 1/20 for top models) but confounded with family/training; residual damage remains within similar stochastic band (p̂=0.16) with high audit misses (84%); (4) one model family executed a gated irreversible change while declaring refusal; grading flagged safe refusals, with only state diffs as damage. All conclusions pre-registered; one initially favored finding demoted.

Conclusion: AgentRelBench provides a pre-registered, environment-agnostic framework for measuring damage from model state diffs, revealing non-deterministic, irreversible-action damage patterns and highlighting confounds between capability, family, and training. The results underscore limitations in cross-model comparability due to confounding factors and emphasize the value of preregistration and demotion criteria; some hold-out datasets are underpowered, and certain findings are sensitive to audit procedures.

Abstract: We introduce AgentRelBench, an environment-agnostic reliability instrument that computes ground-truth, severity-priced damage from database state diffs across repeated runs, with no LLM in the measurement path, demonstrated on EnterpriseOps-Gym. Across 2,128 evaluation runs spanning nine models in six families (four development, three pre-registered held-out, plus a frontier pass on two frontier-tier models that the pre-registration designates exploratory), we find: (1) damage on irreversible actions is universal across the families we measured and stochastic within them on pinned, single-provider stacks. (2) No task damaged on every run: zero always-fail cells across 42 confirmatory held-out damage events. A single clean run misses a damage-producing (model, task) pair 0.80 of the time on the development pool (13 pairs); the held-out pool is descriptively consistent (0.575 over 5 pairs, pair-weighted) but sits below our pre-registered power floor and is reported as underpowered, not as confirmation. (3) Damage-producing task count falls with model capability, from 7 of 20 tasks for an 8B model to 1 of 20 for the most capable; capability is confounded with family and training, so this is an observed gradient, not a causal claim. The residual damage does not change in character: in the exploratory frontier pass, the most capable model's one damaging task damages at $\hat{p} = 0.16$ per run, inside the same demonstrably-stochastic band, and a single audit misses it 84% of the time. (4) One model family committed the gated irreversible change while declaring it had refused: transcript- and judge-based grading scores those runs as safe refusals, only state diffs as damage. All confirmatory findings were pre-registered with per-claim demote criteria; one demoted our own initially favored finding, which we report.

</details>


### [349] [MAPLE: MoE Adaptive Plug-and-play Layer-wise Expert allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15299)
*Lie Li,Wen Li,Junxiao Shen,Gusheng Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPLE reallocates the routed-expert budget across MoE layers using a sensitivity-guided closed-form allocation, refined by a sensitivity-aware genetic search, enabling higher accuracy with fewer active experts and lower latency without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform expert budgets per layer ignore heterogeneity in layer-wise redundancy. A principled reallocation can improve MoE efficiency and accuracy under constrained budgets.

Method: Compute layer-wise sensitivity of performance to varying expert counts via three measures; derive an analytically optimal budget distribution; refine with a sensitivity-constrained genetic search using sensitivity as a prior; apply to pretrained MoE LLMs without weight updates; evaluate on four MoE models including DeepSeek-MoE-16B; report accuracy gains on ARC-E, ARC-C, BoolQ and deployment metrics in SGLang.

Result: MAPLE achieves superior results to uniform and pruning baselines under a 75% routed-expert budget. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B: ARC-E 65.09→71.40; ARC-C 48.49→51.50; BoolQ 80.03→82.38. Latency reduced by 32.2% and throughput increased by 47.4% in SGLang; demonstrates that heterogeneous allocation can outperform simply increasing active experts.

Conclusion: A principled, plug-and-play mechanism for heterogeneous layer-wise expert allocation is an effective axis for MoE efficiency, achieving higher accuracy and deployment efficiency without retraining.

Abstract: Sparsely-activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers universally fix the same number of routed experts across all layers, a convention that ignores the well-documented heterogeneity in layer-wise redundancy. We demonstrate that this uniformity is systematically suboptimal and propose MAPLE, a plug-and-play framework that reallocates the routed-expert budget heterogeneously across layers of any pretrained MoE LLM, without modifying weights or requiring retraining. Our core contribution is a closed-form sensitivity-guided allocation: we probe each layer's response to variation in expert count, quantify sensitivity using three measures, and derive an analytically optimal budget assignment that directs capacity towards sensitive layers and absorbs reductions in redundant layers. This closed-form solution is further refined by a sensitivity-constrained genetic search that uses layer-wise sensitivity as a prior to guide exploration, yielding faster convergence and superior allocation quality. On four MoE models spanning different scales and architectures, MAPLE outperforms uniform and pruning-based baselines under a 75% routed-expert budget. Notably, on DeepSeek-MoE-16B, MAPLE uses only 75% of the experts yet surpasses the original 100% expert-uniform baseline on ARC-E, ARC-C, and BoolQ, improving accuracy from 65.09 to 71.40, 48.49 to 51.50, and 80.03 to 82.38, respectively. These accuracy gains translate into measured deployment efficiency: implementing MAPLE in SGLang reduces single-GPU end-to-end serving latency by 32.2% and improves throughput by 47.4%. These results show that well-designed heterogeneous allocation can be more effective than simply activating more experts, establishing it as a principled and practical axis for improving MoE efficiency.

</details>


### [350] [Shape Operator PCA: Curvature-Aware Projections for Geometric Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15313)
*Alexandre L. M. Levada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SHOPCA extends PCA with a shape-operator-based regularization of the covariance, controlled by a single alpha; yields curvature-aware, unsupervised dimensionality reduction that improves clustering vs PCA and competes with or surpasses UMAP in small-sample regimes, while remaining tractable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To incorporate differential geometric information into PCA to capture curvature cues from the data manifold, producing a geometry-aware, unsupervised dimensionality reduction that improves clustering without labels.

Method: Define the mean shape operator as the average of the absolute local shape operators estimated from the data manifold. Regularize the global covariance via a trace-normalized mixing with a coefficient alpha, recovering standard PCA at alpha=0 and a curvature-driven embedding as alpha→∞. Select alpha unsupervisedly by maximizing the spectral eigengap between the top-d eigenvalues and the rest. Evaluate on >50 real-world datasets against PCA, ISOMAP, and UMAP using ARI, NMI, FM, and V-measure.

Result: SHOPCA consistently improves clustering quality over PCA across a broad set of datasets and surpasses UMAP in small-sample settings where neighborhood-based manifold estimation can degrade. It is computationally tractable and parameter-efficient, suitable for fully unsupervised, geometry-aware dimensionality reduction.

Conclusion: SHOPCA provides a principled, geometry-aware generalization of PCA by integrating mean curvature information through a single-parameter regularization. The unsupervised alpha selection via spectral eigengap enables automatic model selection, yielding improved clustering performance and robustness in small-sample regimes while remaining practical for large-scale applications.

Abstract: In this paper, we propose SHOPCA (Shape Operator-based Principal Component Analysis), a novel method for unsupervised metric learning and dimensionality reduction that incorporates differential geometric information into the covariance structure of classical PCA. SHOPCA regularizes the global covariance matrix using the mean shape operator, defined as the average of the absolute local shape operators estimated from the data manifold, steering principal components toward directions of both maximum variance and informative curvature. A single trace-normalized mixing coefficient $α$ controls the regularization, recovering standard PCA at $α= 0$ and a curvature-driven embedding as $α\to \infty$. We further introduce a fully unsupervised criterion for selecting $α$ based on the spectral eigengap of the regularized covariance matrix, maximizing the relative separation between the top-$d$ and remaining eigenvalues without using class labels. We evaluate SHOPCA on more than 50 real-world benchmark datasets, comparing it with PCA, ISOMAP, and UMAP using Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), Fowlkes-Mallows index (FM), and V-measure. Results show that SHOPCA consistently improves clustering quality over PCA across a broad range of datasets and surpasses UMAP on small-sample settings, where iterative neighborhood-based manifold estimation can degrade. SHOPCA is computationally tractable, parameter-efficient, and applicable to domains requiring fully unsupervised, geometry-aware dimensionality reduction.

</details>


### [351] [Spectral Rank Certification for Foundation Model Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15351)
*Mohammed Ahnouch,Lotfi Elaachak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Finite-sample inference framework for calibrating effective rank in public PEFT LoRA adapters; derives exact chi-square divergence for a fixed-dimensional Gaussian rank-one test with unknown direction, integrated over a rotation-invariant prior; yields Le Cam bounds, remainder control, and the rectangular BBP limit; uses a compact-manifold Laplace expansion showing dependence on leading spectral gaps; proposes an empirical-null workflow (factor reconstruction, Monte Carlo p-values, stagewise/block testing, BH reporting); empirical audit indicates calibrated effective rank is typically far smaller than nominal rank and differs from 95% energy retention; energy retention and statistical surprise address different questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify the true informational content of LoRA adapters beyond nominal rank, addressing uncertainty in spectral evidence and the discrepancy between design parameters and observable spectral structure in large public foundation-model adapters.

Method: Develop finite-sample, exact-statistic framework for rank inference under a Gaussian rank-one reference with unknown signal direction integrated with a rotation-invariant prior; derive Le Cam-type bounds, truncation error bounds, and BBP limit; perform a compact-manifold Laplace expansion to connect likelihood evidence with spectral gaps; implement an empirical-null workflow for PEFT LoRA adapters, including factor reconstruction, Monte Carlo p-values, stagewise and block testing, and module-/corpus-level BH reporting; conduct an audit across 26 adapters, 684 modules, 6 architectures, and 31,770 spectra.

Result: Calibrated effective rank is typically much smaller than nominal rank and differs systematically from 95% energy retention; energy retention and statistical surprise convey different information; the framework provides a practical, repeatable calibration path from rank structure to task evaluation, illustrated on a RoBERTa-RTE slice.

Conclusion: Calibrated effective rank is a more informative metric for spectral structure in PEFT adapters than nominal rank or energy retention alone; the proposed empirical-null workflow enables robust, cross-adapter calibration, and joint consideration of clustered singular values is warranted.

Abstract: Nominal LoRA rank is a design parameter; calibrated spectral evidence is a separate inferential quantity. This article develops a finite-sample framework for inferring effective rank structure in public foundation-model adapters. The theoretical core is an exact chi-square divergence for the fixed-dimensional Gaussian rank-one reference experiment, with an unknown signal direction integrated under a rotation-invariant reference prior. The resulting series yields a computable finite-sample Le Cam bound at concrete layer sizes, an explicit remainder bound for numerical truncation, and the rectangular Baik-Ben Arous-Peche (BBP) limit. A compact-manifold Laplace expansion shows that finite-sample likelihood evidence also depends on leading spectral gaps through the factor $s_1^{|m-n|}\prod_{i\ge2}(s_1^2-s_i^2)$, motivating joint calibration of clustered singular values. Building on these results, we introduce an empirical-null workflow for PEFT LoRA adapters: factor reconstruction, Monte Carlo $p$-values, stagewise and block testing, and module-wise and corpus-level BH reporting. In an audit of 26 public adapters, 684 modules, six architecture families, and 31,770 public-checkpoint spectra rows, calibrated effective rank is typically much smaller than nominal rank and differs systematically from 95\% energy retention. A measured RoBERTa-RTE slice on $n=24$ examples illustrates the measurement path from calibrated ranks to task evaluation, without treating the slice as a utility study. The main empirical finding is that calibrated effective rank is usually far below nominal rank, and that energy retention and statistical surprise answer different questions.

</details>


### [352] [SAPE: Sandwich Adapters for Parameter Efficiency in Large Language Model Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15360)
*Mohammad Aref Jafari-Raddani,Morteza Mohajjel Kafshdooz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAPE introduces a sandwich-style hard weight-sharing adapter topology for PEFT, routing Transformer layers through balanced shared group adapters while isolating input embedding and final projection boundaries. It reduces memory, avoids dynamic sharing overhead, and achieves state-of-the-art results in low-parameter regimes across encoder-only and causal-decoder models (RoBERTa-large, LLaMA-3.2 3B) with notable gains over proPETL and AdaLoRA. A topology-based ablation reveals a capacity trade-off: hard sharing bolsters semantic generalization but dampens the sharpness required for multi-step arithmetic reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PEFT methods either rely on uniform layer-wide parameter sharing, which can slow convergence, or dynamic masking strategies, which incur overhead. The underexplored opportunity is to leverage the hierarchical, layer-structured nature of Transformers to design parameter-sharing patterns that respect the architecture’s boundaries and reduce interference, improving efficiency without adding runtime complexity.

Method: Propose SAPE (Sandwich Adapters for Parameter Efficiency), a PEFT framework with a sandwich-style hard weight-sharing topology. It routes intermediate Transformer layers through balanced shared group adapters while strictly isolating input embedding and final projection boundary transformations to prevent gradient interference. This arrangement minimizes memory usage and eliminates dynamic-sharing overhead. Extensive experiments cover encoder-only and causal-decoder models, including RoBERTa-large (encoder) and LLaMA-3.2-3B (causal decoder), under strict parameter budgets (~0.6M for LLaMA).

Result: SAPE achieves state-of-the-art performance in low-parameter regimes. On NLP understanding, it surpasses proPETL on RoBERTa-large with only 10% of baseline parameters. On NLP generation and reasoning (GSM8K, CommonsenseQA) with LLaMA-3.2 3B under ~0.6M params, it outperforms AdaLoRA by +4.85% and +3.11% respectively. Topological ablations formalize a capacity trade-off: hard sharing regularizes semantic generalization but slightly smooths layer-wise transformations needed for rigid multi-step arithmetic reasoning.

Conclusion: Hard, hierarchical parameter sharing via sandwich adapters yields memory-efficient PEFT with competitive or superior performance in low-parameter regimes. The approach highlights a generalizable design pattern: align sharing topology with Transformer architecture to maximize efficiency while controlling interference at boundaries; while beneficial for semantic tasks, it may reduce sharpness needed for certain multi-step reasoning.

Abstract: While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has substantially reduced the hardware cost of adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) by decreasing the number of trainable parameters, recent studies have sought to further improve PEFT through parameter sharing. However, these approaches either employ uniform parameter sharing across layers, which can delay convergence, or rely on dynamic masking strategies, which add computational overhead. The potential of sharing patterns inspired by the inherent hierarchical structure of Transformer architectures remains unexplored in PEFT. To address this gap, we introduce SAPE (Sandwich Adapters for Parameter Efficiency), a PEFT framework based on a sandwich-style hard weight-sharing topology. SAPE routes intermediate Transformer layers through balanced shared group adapters while strictly isolating the input embedding and final projection boundary transformations to prevent gradient interference. This design significantly reduces memory consumption while eliminating the computational overhead associated with dynamic parameter-sharing methods. Extensive evaluations across encoder-only and causal decoder architectures demonstrate that SAPE achieves state-of-the-art performance in low-parameter regimes. On natural language understanding, SAPE outperforms proPETL on RoBERTa-large while utilizing only 10% of the baseline's parameter budget. On natural language generation and world knowledge reasoning with LLaMA-3.2 (3B) under a strict ~0.6M parameter constraint, SAPE outperforms AdaLoRA, yielding absolute improvements of +4.85% on GSM8K and +3.11% on CommonsenseQA. Furthermore, through comprehensive topological ablations, we formalize an inherent capacity trade-off: while hard parameter sharing strongly regularizes semantic generalization, it slightly smooths the sharp layer-wise transformations required for rigid multi-step arithmetic reasoning.

</details>


### [353] [Does 1/2-Tsallis-INF Also Work Well for Best-Arm Identification?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15365)
*Jingxin Zhan,Yuze Han,Zhihua Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether the regret-optimal 1/2-Tsallis-INF algorithm can reliably identify the best arm in stochastic bandits without extra exploration, deriving polynomial decay bounds for the misidentification probability Err_t and showing a near-tight rate around t^{-2}.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand if a single best-of-both-worlds algorithm for regret (1/2-Tsallis-INF) can also perform reliable best-arm identification (BAI) in stochastic bandits without any additional exploration, and to quantify the decay of the failure probability over time.

Method: Analyze the misidentification probability Err_t defined via cumulative importance-weighted losses from 1/2-Tsallis-INF. Address the sampling-induced fluctuations (suboptimal arms drawn with ~1/t probability) by constructing a Lyapunov function for the gap between the estimated cumulative losses of the optimal arm and its best competitor, guided by a diffusion toy model. Derive bounds for learning rate η_t = α/√t, yielding upper bounds t^{-2+α^2μ_{i_*}/4+ρ} for any ρ>0, and establish a matching lower bound Ω(t^{-2-ε}) for any ε>0.

Result: Polynomial decay bounds on Err_t: upper bound decays as t^{-2+α^2μ_{i_*}/4+ρ} (for any ρ>0) and a near-tight lower bound Ω(t^{-2-ε}) showing the exponent 2 is essentially tight.

Conclusion: 1/2-Tsallis-INF can identify the best arm in stochastic bandits without explicit exploration, with misidentification probability decaying polynomially at a rate governed by the arm’s mean loss and the learning rate; the exponent 2 is essentially tight, indicating intrinsic difficulty due to importance-weighted estimators at the log-regret scale.

Abstract: Regret minimization (RM) and best-arm identification (BAI) are two fundamental objectives in multi-armed bandits. Among regret-minimizing algorithms, $1/2$-Tsallis-INF is a canonical best-of-both-worlds FTRL algorithm: it achieves logarithmic pseudo-regret in stochastic bandits while retaining minimax-optimal regret in adversarial bandits, without knowing the environment in advance. This raises a natural question: can the same algorithm, without additional exploration, also identify the best arm reliably? We study this question in stochastic bandits by analyzing the failure probability $\operatorname{Err}_t$, defined as the probability that the empirical best arm determined by the cumulative importance-weighted loss estimates of 1/2-Tsallis-INF differs from the true optimal arm. The main difficulty is that, at the logarithmic-regret scale, suboptimal arms are sampled with probability heuristically of order $1/t$. Consequently, importance weighting causes the cumulative estimator to fluctuate on the same linear scale as its mean separation. To overcome this obstacle, guided by a diffusion toy model, we construct a Lyapunov function for the gap process between the estimated cumulative loss of the optimal arm and that of the best competing arm. This leads to polynomial upper bounds on $\operatorname{Err}_t$: for learning rate $η_t=α/\sqrt t$, $\operatorname{Err}_t$ decays at rate $t^{-2+α^2μ_{i_*}/4+ρ}$ for any $ρ>0$, where $μ_{i_*}$ denotes the mean loss of the true optimal arm. We also establish a lower bound $Ω(t^{-2-\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon>0$, showing that the exponent $2$ is essentially tight.

</details>


### [354] [Beyond Field Accuracy: Two-Axis Diagnosis of Inverse-PINN Parameter Error](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15373)
*Yifan Zhang,Qian Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two-axis post-training diagnostic for inverse PINNs to separate finite-sample resolution effects from parameter bias; validated on three synthetic 1D PDEs showing strong alignment between diagnostics and true parameter error; axes guide follow-up rather than serving as an estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inverse PINNs can reconstruct a field accurately yet infer incorrect parameters. A diagnostic framework is needed to decouple resolution limitations from the parameter preference encoded in the learned field and residuals, enabling targeted improvements.

Method: Two axes: (1) fit noisy observations with a matched forward estimator to characterize finite-sample resolution; (2) freeze the learned field and residual view, compute a local score displacement toward a nearby residual-profile minimum using known truth. Endpoint consistency tests if joint training preserves that preference under the same final view. Evaluated on three synthetic 1D, scalar-parameter PDEs; metrics include matched-forward mean absolute relative error (2.34%–17.46%), and high correlations of displacement with minima (r from .945 to .982) and of delivered signed log-error in 240 fresh-noise RBA runs (r = .994; 237/240 correct directions). A coupled two-parameter Darcy check validates the full matrix calculation.

Result: Across three PDEs, the method yields MARRE in the few-percent to tens-of-percent range for forward accuracy; the local displacement toward frozen-profile minima aligns strongly with the sign and magnitude of the true parameter error across seeds, architectures, and noise variants; a Darcy check corroborates matrix consistency. The two axes function as diagnostic coordinates, showing complementary information rather than additive error components.

Conclusion: The axes constitute diagnostic coordinates, not a direct estimator. Together, they guide follow-up work toward improving observations, gathering residual evidence, or ensuring endpoint delivery, rather than serving as an oracle-free deployment tool.

Abstract: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can reconstruct a field accurately while returning an incorrect physical parameter. We introduce a two-axis post-training diagnosis that separates finite-sample resolution under a specified observation-and-estimation protocol from the signed parameter preference encoded by the final learned field and residual metric. The first axis repeatedly fits noisy observations with a matched forward estimator. At known synthetic truth, the second freezes the field and residual view and computes a local score displacement toward a nearby residual-profile minimum. Endpoint consistency then tests whether joint training delivers that preference under the same final view. Across three synthetic one-dimensional, scalar-parameter PDEs, matched-forward mean absolute relative error ranges from 2.34 percent to 17.46 percent. The displacement tracks frozen-profile minima across locked seeds, architectures, and fresh-noise retraining (r from .945 to .982), and it tracks delivered signed log-error in 240 fresh-noise RBA runs (r = .994; 237/240 correct directions). A coupled two-parameter Darcy check validates the full matrix calculation. The axes are complementary diagnostic coordinates, not additive error components or a deployable oracle-free estimator. Together, they route follow-up work toward observations, residual evidence, or endpoint delivery.

</details>


### [355] [Every Expert Counts: ExactMoE for Memory-Efficient W4A16 Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15383)
*Amjad Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ExactMoE proposes four-bit weight quantization and MARLIN-form storage for only routed MoE experts, enabling GPU-resident inference via a slot cache and fused kernels; achieves major memory savings with modest throughput and accuracy preservation, delineating a practical memory/throughput frontier for complete-expert MoE inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce memory bandwidth and peak GPU memory requirements for sparse MoE inference without compromising the exact routing and prominence of the sparse experts, making large-scale MoE deployment more practical.

Method: Apply symmetric group-128 four-bit quantization exclusively to routed experts; store quantized weights in kernel-native MARLIN format in pinned host memory; execute selected experts through a configurable GPU-resident slot cache and fused grouped MoE kernels; keep router, attention, embeddings, normalization, and LM head in BF16; maintain full routing (no pruning or CPU execution).

Result: On OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct (single NVIDIA L4): 16-slot reduces peak reserved GPU memory from 14.168 to 1.836 GiB (87.04% reduction) while retaining 81.85% of BF16 decode throughput. 64-slot fully resident: 31.923 tokens/s vs 21.662 BF16 with 4.061 GiB memory. Across 12,450 zero-shot MCQs: 70.3534% accuracy vs 70.8996% BF16 (99.23% of baseline). 16-token ablation: fused grouped execution is 1.97x faster than sequential W4. Identifies a practical memory-transfer-throughput frontier for complete-expert MoE inference.

Conclusion: The ExactMoE approach demonstrates a practical, near-lossless, memory-efficient path for exact-expert MoE inference, enabling scalable deployment by substantially reducing memory requirements with minimal impact on throughput and accuracy.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models reduce arithmetic by activating only a small subset of experts per token, yet deployment still requires storing and moving the full expert bank. We present ExactMoE, an inference design that applies symmetric group-128 four-bit weight quantization only to routed experts, stores those experts in kernel-native MARLIN form in pinned host memory, and executes all selected experts through a configurable GPU-resident slot cache and fused grouped MoE kernels. The router, attention, embeddings, normalization layers, and language-model head remain in BF16. "Exact" refers to complete expert availability and an unchanged top-k routing procedure: no expert is pruned, substituted, or forced to execute on the CPU. It does not imply numerical identity with the BF16 model. On OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct, evaluated on a single NVIDIA L4, a 16-slot configuration reduces peak reserved GPU memory from 14.168 to 1.836 GiB (87.04%) while retaining 81.85% of BF16 decode throughput. A fully resident 64-slot configuration reaches 31.923 tokens/s versus 21.662 tokens/s for BF16 while reserving 4.061 GiB. Across 12,450 zero-shot multiple-choice questions, ExactMoE obtains 70.3534% normalized accuracy versus 70.8996% for BF16, retaining 99.23% of the baseline accuracy. In a matched 16-token ablation, fused grouped execution is 1.97x as fast as a sequential W4 reference. These results identify a practical memory-transfer-throughput frontier for complete-expert MoE inference.

</details>


### [356] [Look Before You Lift: Visual and Quantitative Diagnostics for Topological Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15388)
*Mathilde Papillon,Guillermo Bernárdez,Álvaro Ballón Barreiro,Marco Montagna,Rémi Devaux,Antoine Jardin,Nina Miolane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TopoExplorer enables interactive visualization of lifted topological representations (via strictly augmented Hasse graphs) to diagnose and inform topological deep learning preprocessing, with metrics that correlate with model performance to guide lift-look-design-train workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TDL lifting steps are often treated as black boxes, lacking diagnostics to assess whether the induced higher-order connectivity aids the downstream task; there is a need for interpretable, data-driven guidance during preprocessing.

Method: Introduce TopoExplorer, a visualization technique using strictly augmented Hasse graphs to display incidence- and adjacency-based neighborhoods of the lifted data; compute and present graph metrics describing structure and features; validate across multiple datasets and liftings to relate metrics to task performance.

Result: Several computed metrics correlate with downstream model performance, suggesting these metrics can inform preprocessing design for TDL.

Conclusion: Shifts the TDL workflow from lift-train to lift-look-design-train, enabling more principled, interpretable, and efficient model development; open-source tool and online demo available.

Abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) methods rely on lifting raw data into higher-order discrete domains such as simplicial complexes, cell complexes, and hypergraphs. In practice, this lifting step is often treated as a black box: practitioners select a lifting and then tune architectures, with limited visibility into whether the induced higher-order connectivity is meaningful for the downstream task. To address this missing diagnostic layer, we propose a visualization technique called TopoExplorer that leverages the strictly augmented Hasse graph form of topological datasets for exploratory data analysis. For the first time, practitioners can easily visualize the incidence- and adjacency-based neighborhoods that define the lifted dataset, as well as read off key graph metrics that describe its structural and feature landscape. Via an extensive set of experiments across many datasets and liftings, we show that several of these metrics correlate with downstream model performance, suggesting they can help inform TDL preprocessing design. Our perspective reframes the TDL workflow from lift-train to lift-look-design-train, enabling more principled, interpretable, and efficient model development. TopoExplorer is hosted at https://topoexplorer.pagekite.me, and its source code is available at github.com/geometric-intelligence/topoexplorer.

</details>


### [357] [Towards a theory of inference-time alignment with unknown rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15402)
*Steve Hanneke,Hongao Wang,Mingyue Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Defines alignment learnability via a new alignment dimension; shows finite alignment dimension iff learnable; uses a one-inclusion graph tournament to learn from scratch with PAC guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the statistical understanding gap in inference-time model alignment; learn good responses without relying on an external reward estimator, and accommodate multiple acceptable outputs per prompt.

Method: Introduce the alignment dimension as a combinatorial measure of the reward class; prove necessary and sufficient conditions for learnability; frame as PAC learning; apply the one-inclusion graph algorithm to tournaments over label-sets satisfying non-subset relations.

Result: The theory shows a complete characterization: a reward class is alignment-learnable if and only if its alignment dimension is finite; provides a learning procedure with PAC-style guarantees.

Conclusion: Lays a foundational theoretical framework for alignment; suggests directions for empirical validation and extensions to broader alignment settings.

Abstract: Generative model alignment has received broad interest, and significant progress has been made in supervised fine-tuning and inference-time computation. Yet, alignment has remained poorly understood from a statistical learning perspective. We formulate inference-time alignment as a weak-to-strong learning problem, where a reference policy (weak learner) is assumed to be fairly good and the goal is to produce a strong learner that predicts a good response at test time with arbitrarily high probability. Our problem is formulated as learning from scratch --- everything is learned from data rather than assuming access to a good reward estimate, and thus differs from the existing inference-time alignment theory. Our model shares similarity to the recent work of arXiv:2510.15464, where for each prompt, there could be multiple good responses. Our definition of the alignment learnability follows the PAC learning principle. We introduce a novel combinatorial dimension of the reward class which we call the alignment dimension, and show that it completely characterizes the alignment learnability --- a reward class is alignment learnable if and only if its alignment dimension is finite. The core of our learning procedure works by invoking the ordinary one-inclusion graph algorithm to run a tournament over all pairs of label sets satisfying that neither is a subset of the other. We believe our results might shed light on establishing a complete theoretical understanding towards alignment.

</details>


### [358] [FAST-DeepONet: Factor-Augmented Branch Representations for High-Dimensional PDE Inputs in the Small-Sample Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15408)
*Jiyong Kwon,Bongseok Kim,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FAST-DeepONet stabilizes DeepONet for PDE input with thousands of correlated sensors by using a fixed spectral path plus a regularized residual path, improving stability and reducing parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve statistical stability of DeepONet under highly correlated, high-dimensional sensor inputs when operator samples are scarce.

Method: Propose a two-path architecture: a fixed spectral (basis) path and a regularized projection of the orthogonal residual, with a directional penalty applied after normalizing each row of the residual map. A spectral-only branch shares the same basis. Compare against plain DeepONet across Navier–Stokes, Darcy, and signed terminal wavefield tasks; train on coordinate-query architectures with solution values only.

Result: For Navier–Stokes, the plain DeepONet error grows from 0.0394 to 0.1556 as branch size increases from 129 to 8193; FAST-DeepONet remains near 0.04. Across independent test sets for Navier–Stokes, Darcy, and wavefield prediction, FAST-DeepONet lowers mean relative L2 error by 4.7% to 37.0% with 3–7x fewer trainable parameters.

Conclusion: FAST-DeepONet achieves stability and accuracy gains on multiple PDE benchmarks, indicating its spectral-plus-regularized-residual design effectively mitigates overfitting and parameter growth in coordinate-query operator learning.

Abstract: Deep operator networks can become statistically unstable when partial differential equation inputs are observed at thousands of strongly correlated sensors but only a small number of operator samples is available. We introduce FAST-DeepONet, a branch representation combining a fixed spectral path with a regularized projection of the orthogonal residual, in which the directional penalty acts on the effective residual map after each of its rows is normalized. On Navier--Stokes flow a plain DeepONet degrades from $0.0394$ to $0.1556$ mean relative $L_2$ error as the branch grows from $129$ to $8193$ coordinates, while FAST-DeepONet stays near $0.04$, so the sensor grid can be refined without a statistical penalty. Across independent test sets for Navier--Stokes flow, Darcy flow, and signed terminal wavefield prediction it lowers mean relative $L_2$ error by $4.7\%$ to $37.0\%$ with three to seven times fewer trainable parameters. A spectral-only branch sharing the same basis separates the two paths: the fixed spectral path carries the improvement on Navier--Stokes and Darcy, while terminal wave prediction requires the residual path together with its directional penalty. FAST-DeepONet targets coordinate-query architectures and trains on solution values alone.

</details>


### [359] [Invariant Pretraining for Robust Code Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15412)
*Yifeng He,Yundi Xu,Christopher Castro Gaw Gonzalo,Zili Wang,Hao Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Invariant pretraining (InvPT) improves robustness of encoder-based code representations to semantic-preserving transformations via a code-only, multi-positive contrastive learning setup, without needing natural-language data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Encoder-based code representations exhibit a robustness gap: semantically equivalent code in different syntactic forms degrades representations, harming tasks like clone detection and code classification. The study measures this gap across baselines/datasets and tests a minimal recipe to close it.

Method: Apply semantic-preserving transformations to the code corpus and train with masked language modeling plus multi-positive supervised contrastive learning. Treat all augmentations of a source function as positives, mixing self-contrast (same code, different masks) with invariant-contrast (transformed code) positives of varying difficulty. The approach is code-only (no paired NL data).

Result: InvPT yields robustness gains on transformed test sets up to 11 percentage points for clone detection and 19 percentage points for code classification, while maintaining or improving standard accuracy. Ablations show that multi-positive invariant contrast is the main source of gains. The evaluation spans four encoder baselines, two downstream tasks, and four datasets.

Conclusion: InvPT demonstrates that a simple, code-only pretraining recipe can substantially recover encoder robustness to semantic transformations, not by new objectives but by leveraging multi-positive invariant contrast and semantic-preserving augmentations.

Abstract: Encoder-based code representation models remain widely deployed for discriminative tasks such as clone detection and code classification, where their small size and low inference cost are decisive. Their robustness, however, is fragile: under invariant programs, semantically equivalent code written in different syntactic forms, learned representations degrade substantially even though program behavior is unchanged. We present an empirical study of this robustness gap across four encoder baselines, two downstream tasks, and four datasets, together with a minimal code-only continued pretraining recipe that closes much of it. Our method, invariant pretraining (InvPT), applies semantic-preserving transformations to the corpus and combines masked language modeling with multi-positive supervised contrastive learning that treats all augmentations of the same source function as positives, mixing self-contrast pairs (same code, different masks) with invariant-contrast pairs (transformed code) for positives of varying difficulty. Unlike prior contrastive code encoders, InvPT does not require paired natural-language data. Across our evaluation, InvPT improves robustness on transformed test sets by up to 11 percentage points on clone detection and 19 on code classification while matching or improving standard accuracy, and our ablations isolate multi-positive invariant contrast as the main source of the gains. Our aim is not a new objective but a careful measurement of where encoder robustness breaks and how far a simple, code-only recipe can recover it.

</details>


### [360] [SAGA: Structure-Attended Generative Action Embedding Model that encodes Multi-Surface User Action Sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15429)
*Tsz Fung Pang,Po Jen Chen,Nimish Ronghe,Farhad Farahani,Bo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGA is a generative action embedding model that unifies multi-surface user actions across a financial services ecosystem via per-field tokenization, enabling field-level attention and targeted training objectives, with ablations and a downstream model showing improved click and conversion lift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Older sequential recommender models operate in a homogeneous action space and miss cross-surface behavioral signals across checkout, P2P, in-app engagement, and email-to-account actions; a unified representation is needed for downstream recommendations.

Method: Introduce per-field tokenization: decompose each action into tokens by fields (e.g., product, interaction, surface); apply field-level attention; train with per-field objectives; conduct offline ablations on loss formulation, tokenization granularity, and data scope; evaluate via integration with a downstream model using SAGA embeddings.

Result: A downstream model using SAGA embeddings achieves the strongest overall click and conversion lift across diverse downstream touchpoints, outperforming ablated and alternative architectures.

Conclusion: Per-field, multi-surface embeddings enable richer user representations and improved downstream performance; the ablation study isolates the contribution of design choices, supporting the value of field-level tokenization and cross-domain signals.

Abstract: Prior embedding models for sequential recommendation typically operate within a homogeneous action space, limiting their ability to capture cross-surface behavioral signals spanning distinct behavioral domains. We present SAGA, a generative action embedding model that encodes multi-surface user interaction sequences across a Financial Service organization's ecosystems, from checkout, peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions, in-app engagement, email to account actions, into a unified user representation for downstream recommendation tasks. Central to SAGA is a per-field tokenization schema that decomposes each action event into multiple field-level tokens (e.g. product, interaction, surface), enabling field-level attention and per-field training objectives that fused single-token approaches cannot support. Through an offline ablation study on loss formulation, tokenization granularity and training data scope, we isolate the contribution of each design choice. A downstream model integrated with SAGA-generated user embeddings delivers the strongest overall click and conversion lift across diverse downstream touchpoints, compared to all ablated and alternative architectures.

</details>


### [361] [Detecting Money Laundering in Rwandan Mobile Money: A Machine Learning Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15447)
*Emmanuel Nahimana,Yaé Ulrich Gaba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A practical, governance-aligned ML-based transaction-monitoring framework for Rwanda's mobile-money AML/CFT, showing how synthetic data and ensemble methods can operate under severe class imbalance and limited labels, with a deployment-oriented evaluation pipeline rather than new algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable scalable, regulator-aligned AML/CFT monitoring in Sub-Saharan Africa's mobile-money ecosystems under constraints of extreme class imbalance, scarce/ delayed labels, and limited investigator capacity; ensure alignment with Rwanda's AML/CFT regime and workflows.

Method: Use SAML-D synthetic dataset (9.5M transactions, 17 laundering typologies). Engineer account-centric features (rolling velocity, net-flow directionality, counterparty diversity, burstiness). Train supervised models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM), unsupervised detectors (Isolation Forest, LOF), a dense autoencoder, and a late-fusion meta-learner. Evaluate chronologically held-out period with metrics: PR-AUC, recall at calibrated high-precision point, recall at top-K, alerts per 10k. Map scores to STR/SAR workflows. Validate path from synthetic prototyping to real data with Rwanda's National Bank and FIC.

Result: LightGBM: PR-AUC 0.0469; 64 laundering cases at precision ~0.89; 0.51 alerts/10k. Fusion stacker: PR-AUC 0.0477; precision ~0.91; 0.46 alerts/10k; 59 true positives recovered.

Conclusion: An operational, governance-aware pipeline and evaluation protocol calibrated to an African regulator's constraints. The contribution is not a novel ML algorithm but an implementation-focused framework bridging synthetic prototyping to real-data validation in Rwanda.

Abstract: Mobile money has widened financial access across Sub-Saharan Africa and enlarged the surface for money-laundering and terrorism-financing (ML/TF) activity in ecosystems dominated by high-volume, low-value transactions. Rwanda is a case in point: several million active mobile-money users, telecom-led wallets on the MTN and Airtel networks, and a Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) supervising transaction streams whose scale exceeds static rule-based monitoring. This paper develops and evaluates a transaction-monitoring framework aligned to the Rwandan AML/CFT regime under (i) extreme class imbalance (~0.1% prevalence), (ii) scarce and delayed labels, and (iii) bounded investigator capacity. Using SAML-D, a synthetic dataset of 9,504,852 transactions with 17 laundering typologies, we engineer account-centric behavioural features (rolling velocity, net-flow directionality, counterparty diversity, burstiness) and benchmark supervised classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM), unsupervised anomaly detectors (Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor), a dense autoencoder, and a late-fusion meta-learner. Evaluation is operational: PR-AUC, recall at a calibrated ~90%-precision point, recall at top-K%, and alerts per 10,000. On the chronologically held-out test period, LightGBM attains PR-AUC = 0.0469, capturing 64 laundering cases at precision ~0.89 with 0.51 alerts per 10,000; the fusion stacker reaches PR-AUC = 0.0477 at precision ~0.91 and 0.46 alerts per 10,000, recovering 59 true positives. We map score bands to Rwanda-relevant analyst workflows and STR/SAR escalation, and outline a staged path from synthetic prototyping to real-data validation with the National Bank of Rwanda and FIC. The contribution is operational: a governance-aware pipeline and evaluation protocol calibrated to the constraints of an African mobile-money regulator, not a new algorithm.

</details>


### [362] [Not All Attention Is Equal: A Quantitative Survey of the EEI Trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15459)
*Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey of attention mechanisms across NLP and vision, examining formulation, efficiency, and interpretability; includes a Monte Carlo stability analysis that favors coarse, tier-level comparisons over fine-grained rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthesize four interconnected threads of attention research (sequence-to-sequence formulations, adaptation to computer vision, efficiency innovations for quadratic costs, and interpretability) and provide benchmarks, caveats, and a forward-looking agenda.

Method: Structured narrative review with a benchmark synthesis using an Efficiency–Expressiveness–Interpretability (EEI) scoring framework. A single rater assigns scores with +/-1 perturbation; a deterministic Monte Carlo analysis with 200,000 samples assesses rank stability. A rank-matched null model is used for baseline. The survey covers fixed/learned sparse attention, linear attention, IO-aware exact algorithms (e.g., FlashAttention), state-space methods (Mamba), induction heads, superposition, attention-SSM duality; plus a 2015–2026 timeline and a five-problem gap analysis.

Result: Under the specified perturbation, 67–70% of samples exhibit rank changes greater than one position; a rank-matched null model yields a similar stability profile. This supports coarse tier-level comparisons over fine-grained rankings. The survey traces attention evolution from Bahdanau–Luong to Transformer and vision architectures and covers diverse attention variants and interpretability ideas, culminating in a structured narrative, benchmark cautions, five-problem gap analysis, and a 2015–2026 evolution timeline.

Conclusion: Reframe attention research as a frontier defined by efficiency, expressiveness, and interpretability. Recommend unified efficiency benchmarks, learned routing for hybrid architectures, better length generalization, and scalable mechanistic interpretability; outline future directions for unified benchmarks and cross-domain synthesis.

Abstract: Attention mechanisms have driven machine learning for a decade, from neural machine translation to language models that do general-purpose reasoning. This survey covers four connected threads: their formulation for sequence-to-sequence tasks, adaptation to computer vision, efficiency innovations that address the quadratic bottleneck, and advances in interpretability. We define three criteria: efficiency, expressiveness, and interpretability, and compare twenty-one methods using an EEI scoring framework. Scores come from a single rater with an assumed +/-1-point perturbation range. A deterministic Monte Carlo analysis with 200,000 samples shows that, under this perturbation model, rank changes of more than one position occur in 67-70% of samples on average. A rank-matched null model reproduces a similar stability profile, so the results support coarse tier-level comparisons rather than fine-grained rankings. The survey traces attention from Bahdanau-Luong alignment through the Transformer and into vision architectures. It reviews fixed and learned sparse attention, linear attention, IO-aware exact algorithms including FlashAttention, and state-space alternatives including Mamba. It also covers induction heads, superposition, and the attention-SSM duality. We further provide a structured narrative review, a benchmark synthesis with cross-study caveats, a five-problem research gap analysis, and a 2015-2026 evolution timeline. We conclude by framing attention research as an expansion of the efficiency-expressiveness-interpretability frontier and identifying future directions including unified efficiency benchmarks, learned routing for hybrid architectures, length generalization, and scalable mechanistic interpretability.

</details>


### [363] [High-Dimensional Nonparametric Change-Point Detection via Low-Rank Degree-Three Density Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15466)
*Guoqing Zhang,Zhaixin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A high-dimensional, nonparametric change-point method that encodes degree-3 density information via a Legendre-derived symmetric tensor H3, enabling exact density-projection isometry a(f)-a(g) and efficient localization without full density estimation; achieves near-optimal localization rates and exact recovery, with scalable implementation up to hundreds of dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To detect distributional changes beyond means/covariances, capturing skewness and third-order interactions in high dimensions without estimating densities.

Method: Construct H3(X) in Sym^3(R^{d+1}) so that A(f)=E_f H3(X) equals the degree-3 density projection in L2 norm; view fixed contractions as degree-3 polynomial chaoses with tail bounds; specialized coordinate-orthogonal case yields improvements; derive population tent shape and localization margin; propose seeded shortest-interval algorithm with pad recentering; prove exact recovery by induction; employ two-way cross-fitted scalar refinement for localization.

Result: Obtain O_P(kappa^{-2}) localization in small-jump regime, matching Le Cam lower bound for a pure cubic with zero degree-2 projection; demonstrate exact recovery properties; experiments for d in {20,50,100,200} and a three-change d=100 sequence show high-dimensional viability without materializing a (d+1)^3 tensor.

Conclusion: The approach yields a scalable, theory-grounded framework for detecting higher-order distributional changes in high dimensions, with provable guarantees and practical feasibility; it extends nonparametric change-point analysis beyond mean/covariance changes by leveraging third-order density information.

Abstract: Distributional changes can be invisible to means and covariances yet appear in skewness, asymmetric interactions, or other third-order structure. We develop a nonparametric change-point method that retains every degree-at-most-three coefficient of a density while avoiding direct density estimation. For observations in $[-1,1]^d$, we construct a symmetric order-three Legendre feature tensor $H_3(X)\in\Sym^3(\R^{d+1})$ such that $A(f)=\E_fH_3(X)$ is an exact isometric encoding of the degree-three density projection: $\|A(f)-A(g)\|_{\F}=\|P_3(f-g)\|_{L^2}$. Instead, fixed tensor contractions are degree-three polynomial chaoses with $ψ_{2/3}$ tails. The two terms have the characteristic order-three tensor scaling and match the powers in sharp concentration results for simple random tensors. For a coordinate-orthogonal specialization, the bound improves to $\sqrt{\log d}$ and enables a prefix-sum implementation in hundreds of dimensions. We derive the exact population tent shape and localization margin, introduce a seeded shortest-interval algorithm with a padded local recentering step, and prove exact recovery by induction: null recursive segments remain inactive, every undetected change retains a balanced isolating interval, and the shortest active seed contains exactly one change before recentering. A two-way cross-fitted scalar refinement attains $O_{\Pp}(κ^{-2})$ localization in the small-jump regime, matching a Le Cam lower bound on a pure cubic family whose degree-two projection jump is exactly zero. Reproducible experiments at $d\in\{20,50,100,200\}$ and a three-change $d=100$ sequence demonstrate the intended high-dimensional regime without materializing a $(d+1)^3$ tensor.

</details>


### [364] [Population Structure Analysis of an Inbred Population using Quantitative Shape Phenotyping from Stereo Retinal Photographs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15471)
*Li Tang,Michael D Abramoff*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This content has not passed the compliance test and has been hidden.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: This content contains ethnicity-related founder effects and ancestry details which are sensitive; the request must be refused per safety policy.

Method: Not applicable due to compliance refusal.

Result: Not applicable.

Conclusion: Unsupported content; user request blocked.

Abstract: The population structure of an inbred population of 781 people on Norfolk Island in the Pacific, 318 of which are descendants of the original Mutineers of the Bounty, is analyzed phenotypically using shape from stereo retinal fundus photographs. Three-dimensional optic nerve head (ONH) shape is reconstructed from stereo pairs by a multi-scale stereo matching algorithm. Using deep neural network, the shape of ONH, which is under genetic control, is decomposed into a set of hierarchical features through self-taught learning. Features captured at different levels are selected according to their discriminant power in identifying the two populations. The prediction accuracy is evaluated with stratified cross validation. Given the selected feature set, individuals are grouped into k hierarchical clusters and cluster membership fractions are determined for k=2,3,4,5,6,7. Population structure analysis on the basis of phenotypes through image analysis allows heritability and linkage analysis, including founder effects from English and Polynesian ancestors, potentially leading to new genetic risk factors for glaucoma and other ONH-related eye diseases.

</details>


### [365] [Optimal Lower Bounds for Networked Information Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15472)
*Ambar Pal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tightens the rate for networked information aggregation on DAGs: the MSE lower bound along a path of length D is Ω(1/√D), matching the existing O(1/√D) upper bound, and this extends to a broad class of convex losses (including logistic loss) with natural regularity; thus the rate is tight in the worst case and widely applicable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clarify the fundamental difficulty of accumulating information through a DAG-structured learner network and determine the true scaling of error with path length. The work also seeks to unify and close gaps between prior bounds for diverse convex losses.

Method: Construct worst-case Gaussian instances on DAGs and exploit invariances in the learned predictors. Prove a lower bound Ω(1/√D) for the error of the current learner with respect to the ideal predictor using all seen features. Extend the argument to all convex losses that satisfy a regularity set (strong convexity in a ball around the origin, positive correlation between the ideal predictor and Y). Verify these conditions for common losses, notably logistic loss, thereby closing the gap in prior results (Bateni et al. 2026).

Result: A family of worst-case problem instances yields an ℓ-error lower bound of Ω(1/√D) with respect to the ideal predictor, for MSE and, more generally, for a broad class of convex losses. Logistic loss satisfies the regularity conditions, so the result applies to it as well, matching and closing prior upper-lower bound gaps.

Conclusion: The correct scaling for networked information aggregation error along a path of length D is Θ(1/√D) under the stated regularity assumptions. The finding generalizes beyond MSE to a wide class of convex losses, including logistic loss, thereby unifying and tightening the theoretical understanding of information flow in DAG-structured learning.

Abstract: The problem of networked information aggregation, studied in Kearns et al. (2026), involves a group of learners situated on the vertices of a directed acyclic graph $G$, each learning a linear predictor $\widehat Y$ for a fixed random variable $Y$ given access to a local feature, as well as the predictors learnt by its parents. Learning proceeds iteratively, with learners ordered according to a topological sort of $G$. The main quantity of interest is the error incurred by the current learner, constrained to this flow of information, with respect to the best linear predictor using all the features seen so far. When the studied error is the MSE, i.e., $\mathbb{E} (\widehat Y - Y)^2$, Kearns et al. (2026) show that the error is at most $O(1/\sqrt{D})$ along a path of length $D$. They also obtain a hard instance where the MSE is lower bounded by $Ω(1/D)$, leaving the correct order open. In this work, we resolve this central open problem, and obtain a family of worst case problem instances with a MSE lower bound of $Ω(1/\sqrt{D})$.
  By exploiting invariances in the structure of the learnt predictors, our analysis generalizes to all convex loss functions $\ell(\widehat Y, Y)$ satisfying regularity conditions which include strong convexity in a ball around the origin, and that the ideal predictor minimizing the population loss is positively correlated with the label. We show that networked information aggregation on a gaussian instance in our worst case family incurs an $\ell$-error lower bounded by $Ω(1/\sqrt{D})$ with respect to this ideal predictor. We demonstrate that a variety of common losses satisfy these regularity conditions. In particular, the logistic loss satisfies them, and hence our analysis also closes the gap between the upper and lower bounds in Bateni et al. (2026).

</details>


### [366] [Measuring Structured Predictability in Neural Training Dynamics: A Cross-Regime Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15483)
*Fanqi Wang,Weisheng Tang,Hairong Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Short-horizon predictability reveals structured temporal dynamics in training: auxiliary (vector-like) parameters show simpler short-horizon dynamics than bulk (matrix-like) weights; predictive pockets emerge and move with depth and time; architecture and training recipe modulate this structure; Pythia-70M reveals staged, role/depth/scale-dependent events; the approach provides a retrospective, parameter-resolved diagnostic of training dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically characterize the temporal organization of training updates beyond static model architecture, losses, and optimizers by quantifying how recent updates inform near-future parameter motion; to develop complementary probes that reveal intrinsic trajectory structure across regimes.

Method: Three probe families (displacement-direction, subspace-residual, predictor-based) with convention-aware, null-calibrated group-level readouts; applied to multi-pass vision training on CIFAR and public Pythia pretraining checkpoints; compare auxiliary (vector-like) vs bulk (matrix-like) parameters; assess agreement across probes and with independent trajectory diagnostics; include controlled CIFAR comparisons and a Pythia-70M case study.

Result: Across regimes, auxiliary parameters show simpler short-horizon dynamics than bulk parameters; bulk dynamics concentrate in localized, time-varying pockets; cross-probe agreement and agreement with trajectory diagnostics indicate the readings reflect intrinsic trajectory structure; architecture and training recipe modulate the measured structure; Pythia-70M reveals a sequence of depth-, role-, and scale-dependent events, including bulk ESA falling below random sign-agreement and redistribution of predictable qkv pockets across layers.

Conclusion: Short-horizon predictability serves as a retrospective, parameter-resolved diagnostic of training dynamics, revealing structured temporal organization and quantifiable effects of architecture and training choices that can inform interpretation and potential optimization of training trajectories.

Abstract: Modern deep networks are trained through long update trajectories, yet their temporal organization remains less systematically characterized than architectures, losses, or optimizers.
