We study short-horizon predictability as a measure of temporal redundancy: where, when, and under which training conditions recent updates contain information about near-future parameter motion. We combine three complementary probe families, displacement-direction, subspace-residual, and predictor-based probes, with convention-aware, null-calibrated group-level readouts, and apply them to multi-pass vision training on CIFAR and public Pythia pretraining checkpoints. Across both regimes, vector-like tensors such as normalization parameters and biases (auxiliary parameters) exhibit simpler short-horizon dynamics than matrix-like feature-transforming weights (bulk parameters), whose predictable behavior concentrates in localized, time-varying pockets. Agreement within and across probe families, and with independent trajectory diagnostics, indicates that these measurements capture intrinsic trajectory structure, while probe differences distinguish complementary forms of temporal organization. Controlled CIFAR comparisons further show that architecture and training recipe systematically modulate the measured structure. A Pythia-70M case study further exposes a sequence of role-, depth-, and scale-dependent events, including bulk ESA falling below the random sign-agreement level and the emergence and redistribution of predictable qkv pockets across layers. These results position short-horizon predictability as a retrospective, parameter-resolved diagnostic of training dynamics.

</details>


### [367] [QSMP: finding representative time series subsequences through Quick Shift+Matrix Profile](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15492)
*Carlos H. Mendoza-Cardenas,Rogers F. Silva,Austin J. Brockmeier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QSMP identifies representative waveforms in long time series by density-guided clustering of subsequences, linking Quick Shift with Matrix Profile to enable a space-efficient clustering approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long time series require concise, interpretable summaries for visualization and downstream tasks (classification/forecasting). Existing methods can be space-intensive; QSMP aims to provide a scalable, representative set of waveforms.

Method: Adapt Quick Shift (a mode-seeking clustering algorithm) to cluster time-series subsequences using a density estimate guided by the Matrix Profile similarity search structure. This yields a space-efficient clustering of subsequences in a long time series.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real datasets shows QSMP effectively summarizes and visualizes long time series by extracting representative waveforms and does so with superior space complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: QSMP provides a practical, scalable tool for summarizing long time series through representative waveforms, enabling improved visualization and potential benefits for downstream tasks.

Abstract: Finding representative waveforms in long time series has scientific and practical value in many domains, as it enables summarization and visualization of large time series datasets, and downstream tasks like classification and forecasting. We present here QSMP, a method to find representative waveforms in long time series through a density-guided clustering of time series subsequences. Our method makes a novel connection between Quick Shift, a mode-seeking algorithm, and the Matrix Profile, a time series similarity-search data structure, to adapt Quick Shift to the clustering of subsequences in long time series, with a space complexity that is superior to the state-of-the-art method. Our experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that QSMP can be a valuable tool to summarize and visualize long time series by finding representative waveforms.

</details>


### [368] [PERO: Efficient Robust Post-Training Foundation Models for Encrypted Traffic Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15504)
*Wumei Du,Jiarong Wen,Kaiyu Zhang,Zi Yang,Yiqin Lv,Longfei Zhang,Dong Liang,Zheng Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PERO is an efficient robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models that uses a lightweight risk proxy to identify high-risk samples for targeted fine-tuning, achieving robustness with lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) overlooks tail-risk; robust objectives (e.g., CVaR) are computationally prohibitive for large models; there is a need for scalable, risk-aware post-training in encrypted traffic classification.

Method: PERO introduces a lightweight proxy to estimate per-sample risk, selects a subset of high-risk samples, and updates the foundation model using only this subset, decoupling risk estimation from expensive large-model optimization.

Result: Empirical experiments on encrypted traffic datasets show that PERO achieves competitive or superior robustness and average performance compared with strong robust post-training methods, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs.

Conclusion: PERO offers a practical, scalable robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models, balancing tail-risk handling with efficiency.

Abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is vital for network security, yet real-world deployments are inherently sensitive to rare but high-loss errors such as misclassification of malicious traffic. The encrypted traffic foundation model, as a promising general-purpose technique, can achieve impressive overall performance. However, employing standard objectives such as empirical risk minimization often overlooks high-risk tail events, and commonly used performance metrics hardly reflect robustness limitations in risk-sensitive scenarios. Directly applying robust optimization objectives, such as conditional value-at-risk, to post-training is computationally prohibitive for large models, as identifying high-loss samples exhausts substantial computation. To this end, we propose Pre-Evaluation Robust Optimization (PERO), an efficient robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models. PERO employs a lightweight proxy to estimate sample-wise risk and selects a subset of high-risk samples to update the foundation model, decoupling risk estimation from expensive large-model optimization. Extensive experiments on typical encrypted traffic datasets show that PERO achieves competitive or superior robustness and average performance compared to outstanding robust post-training methods, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs.

</details>


### [369] [UniFed-VLM: Federated Instruction Tuning for Vision-Language Models with Multiple Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15516)
*Pengyu Wang,Baochen Xiong,Xiaoshan Yang,Yifan Xu,Zhang Qimeng,Haifeng Chen,Changsheng Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes UniFed-VLM, a federated instruction-tuning framework for vision-language models under joint heterogeneity in tasks, modalities, and model architectures; introduces FedCSA (subspace-aligned aggregation of adapters with dynamic weighting and compensation) and TCoD (two-stage collaboration with Mutual Distillation Adapter and mixture-of-experts distillation); shows improved average performance across benchmarks compared with existing FL methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable privacy-preserving fine-tuning of large vision-language models when data is distributed and heterogeneous across clients (tasks, modalities, architectures); address challenges of parameter scale and heterogeneity in realistic FL settings.

Method: Two-stage framework: FedCSA performs subspace-aligned aggregation of parameter-efficient adapters with dynamic weighting and compensation to mitigate heterogeneity conflicts; TCoD enables knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models via a Mutual Distillation Adapter and a mixture-of-experts-based distillation strategy.

Result: Empirical evaluation on multiple benchmarks shows UniFed-VLM achieves stronger average performance across diverse tasks compared with existing federated learning methods for VLMs.

Conclusion: UniFed-VLM effectively handles multi-dimensional heterogeneity (tasks, modalities, architectures) in federated instruction tuning for VLMs and demonstrates practical improvements; code available at the referenced repository.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in multimodal understanding and generation. However, fine-tuning of VLMs typically relies on centralized data, which raises privacy concerns in certain domains (e.g. healthcare). Federated Learning (FL) provides a natural solution by enabling model training without sharing raw data. However, applying FL to VLM instruction tuning is highly challenging. VLMs have substantial parameter scales, and in real-world scenarios, clients exhibit significant heterogeneity in tasks, modalities, and model architectures.
  Existing methods mainly focus on simplified settings and are unable to handle such multi-dimensional heterogeneous scenarios. In this work, we study federated instruction tuning under joint heterogeneity in tasks, modalities, and model architectures.
  We propose UniFed-VLM, a unified federated instruction tuning framework for VLMs that addresses multiple types of heterogeneity. It consists of two key components: 1) Federated Compensated Subspace Aggregation (FedCSA), which performs subspace-aligned aggregation of parameter-efficient adapters with dynamic weighting and compensation to mitigate heterogeneity-induced conflicts; 2) Two-stage Collaborative Distillation (TCoD), which enables effective knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models via a Mutual Distillation Adapter (MDA) and a mixture-of-experts-based distillation strategy. We conduct experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, and the results show that UniFed-VLM achieves stronger average performance across diverse tasks compared with existing FL methods. The source code is available at: https://github.com/wangpengyu2004/UniFed-VLM.

</details>


### [370] [Guaranteed Adaptive Modality Acquisition: When the Policy Chooses Its Own Calibration Group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15520)
*Melika Baghi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RouteCert enables calibration guarantees under adaptive input acquisition by conditioning on terminal input patterns; provides two finite-sample constructions and a counterexample for policy-dependent groupings; validated on ECG and masked multimodal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multimodal systems where inputs can be acquired at a cost and the final observed pattern depends on the policy, calibration guarantees must adapt to the terminal pattern; standard pattern-conditional guarantees assume a fixed grouping independent of calibration data, which is violated by adaptive policies.

Method: Characterize when pattern-conditional guarantees hold; propose two finite-sample constructions: (1) threshold-free routing with calibration applied at the terminal pattern; (2) simultaneous certification of complete policy-pattern pairs, enabling calibration data to select the deployed policy; provide a counterexample showing the failure of guarantees under policy-dependent grouping; formalize RouteCert.

Result: ECG task: certified policy achieves 71.2% coverage with 7.4% observed disagreement vs cardiologist at 48.8% of the prespecified cost, and every acquisition stage is certified. On masked benchmarks: pointwise certification at terminal patterns yields worst-pattern selective risk 0.034 vs pooled design 0.145 (cap 0.10) with comparable answered fraction 0.350 vs 0.342; budget-matched simultaneous comparison reduces answered fraction to 0.305.

Conclusion: Policy-conditional calibration guarantees are nontrivial under adaptive acquisition; RouteCert provides practical finite-sample certifiable methods and demonstrates robustness across tasks, with per-pattern and per-stage certificates and maintained performance under budget constraints.

Abstract: A multimodal system may begin inference holding only some of its inputs and may acquire the rest at a cost. With adaptive acquisition, the policy determines which inputs are ultimately observed, so we state the guarantee conditional on that terminal input pattern. Conditional calibration normally assumes the grouping map is fixed independently of the calibration sample, which policy-induced grouping does not satisfy. We characterize when pattern-conditional guarantees remain valid and give two finite-sample constructions: threshold-free routing with calibration applied at the terminal pattern, and simultaneous certification of complete policy-pattern pairs, which lets calibration data select the deployed policy. A counterexample shows that a guarantee proved for a calibration-independent grouping map need not transfer once the policy makes the terminal group calibration-dependent. We call the resulting method RouteCert. On a clinical electrocardiogram task with a staged, cost-ordered lead protocol, the certified policy answers 71.2% of held-out patients at an observed 7.4% disagreement with the cardiologist's diagnosis at 48.8% of the prespecified ordinal cost of acquiring every stage, and all three acquisition stages carry their own certificate. On masked multimodal benchmarks, certifying pointwise at each terminal pattern holds observed worst-pattern selective risk, measured against the full-information reference decision rather than the true label, at 0.034 where a pooled design reaches 0.145 against a 0.10 cap, at a comparable answered fraction (0.350 vs 0.342); under the budget-matched simultaneous comparison the answered fraction falls to 0.305.

</details>


### [371] [Spectral Saliency for Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15548)
*Cedar Site Bai,Amber Yijia Zheng,Raymond A. Yeh,Brian Bullins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spectral Saliency Unlearning (SSU) uses thresholded updates along weak singular directions guided by a confident unlearning signal, extending Muon's spectral approach with theoretical justification of forgetting/retention and broad empirical validation across vision, diffusion, and language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve gradient-based machine unlearning by focusing updates on meaningful spectral directions, reducing over-unlearning and preserving utility.

Method: Decompose gradient updates via singular value decomposition, threshold weak singular components, and apply updates only in directions supported by a confident unlearning signal, alongside spectral magnitude normalization inspired by Muon.

Result: SSU demonstrates improved forgetting efficacy while maintaining model utility across image classifiers, diffusion models, and large language models, with a theoretical account from the forgetting-retention trade-off.

Conclusion: SSU offers a principled, scalable spectral approach to machine unlearning with broad applicability and theoretical grounding, potentially outperforming prior spectral/unlearning methods.

Abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) aims to remove the influence of specific training data while preserving model utility. As the name suggests, MU can be viewed as the inverse of learning, using gradient-based updates to reduce the influence of a forget-set by counteracting the previously learned behavior. Recently, Muon, a gradient descent variant, has been introduced. Muon applies spectral magnitude normalization to encourage exploration of rare directions and demonstrates promising performance. Inspired by Muon, we adopt the spectral view for unlearning and propose Spectral Saliency Unlearning (SSU). SSU thresholds weak singular components and updates only those directions supported by a confident unlearning signal. We further provide theoretical justification for this thresholding approach from the perspective of the forgetting-retention trade-off. Experiments across image classifiers, diffusion models, and LLMs demonstrate SSU's effectiveness.

</details>


### [372] [Amortised Post-Hoc Explanation with Exact Preservation for Dynamic Graph Anomaly Detectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15559)
*Iyad Assaad Nekka,Hamida Seba,Walid Khaled Hidouci,Karima Amrouche*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: X-StrGNN provides a post-hoc explanation layer for StrGNN, delivering structural and temporal attributions per edge while preserving detection; shows stability and cost improvements in a controlled study; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explainability gap for StrGNN in dynamic graph anomaly detection to support human analysts and trustworthy decisions.

Method: Wraps a frozen StrGNN with a post-hoc explanation layer producing multiplicative structural and temporal masks per flagged edge. Maintains exact detection pass-through. Conducts a controlled design study comparing gradient attribution, per-instance mask optimization, and amortised parameterisation, under a single protocol, one budget, and three seeds; evaluates Delta AUC, Delta AP, Delta P@100, stability, and cost.

Result: Detection preserved exactly (Delta AUC/AP/P@100 = 0). Attribution cost 0.66 ms per edge. X-StrGNN achieves highest stability (0.913) at 268x lower cost than per-instance optimization; temporal attribution outperforms ablated control; per-instance optimization underperforms the random baseline; code and protocol released.

Conclusion: Post-hoc attribution layer effectively explains StrGNN decisions with minimal overhead, enabling scalable, interpretable anomaly detection in dynamic graphs; provides guidance on attribution strategies and empirical methodology.

Abstract: Anomaly detection in dynamic graphs underpins financial fraud analysis, intrusion detection, and platform integrity, where automated decisions require human-interpretable justifications. StrGNN, the strongest performer in recent benchmarks, produces no explanation: when an edge is flagged, the analyst receives only a score. Explanation metrics are undefined for StrGNN because no attribution vector exists. This paper closes that gap. We present X-StrGNN, a post-hoc explanation layer that wraps a trained, frozen StrGNN and emits, for every flagged edge, dual attributions: a structural attribution identifying which contextual interactions in the enclosing subgraph drove the decision, and a temporal attribution identifying which historical snapshot carried the signal. Both attributions are multiplicative masks identically one in the unexplained pass, so the layer is an exact pass-through: detection is preserved to machine precision, verified rather than asserted (Delta AUC = 0.0000, Delta AP = 0.0000, Delta P@100 = 0.0000). Attribution costs 0.66 ms per edge, making explanation of an entire alarm list feasible. We conduct the first controlled design study of attribution strategies for this architecture, comparing gradient attribution, per-instance mask optimisation, and amortised parameterisation under one protocol, one budget, and three seeds. X-StrGNN attains the highest stability (0.913) at 268x lower cost than per-instance optimisation, and its temporal attribution (1.601 against a measured random floor of 0.973) is separably better than its ablated control, while per-instance optimisation - the most expensive strategy - falls below that floor. Code, protocol, and per-seed measurements are released.

</details>


### [373] [SchurQuant: Groupwise Discrete Optimization for Layer-Wise LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15567)
*Gunjun Lee,Sehwan Son,Younjoo Lee,Byungjun Kim,Jung Ho Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCHURQUANT proposes a backpropagation-free weight-only PTQ method that combines SCHUROPT (analytic suffix elimination and Schur-complement curvature) with discrete refinement, achieving state-of-the-art mean zero-shot accuracy at 2-bit quantization across Llama and Qwen models; 11.88pp gain on 2-bit Qwen3-4B and 9.65pp over baselines, with a broader strategy including teacher reconstruction and regularization for robust performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable accurate weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models under tight memory budgets, addressing two main limitations of existing backpropagation-free PTQ: (i) group decisions ignore the optimal continuous suffix, and (ii) discrete refinements keep a fixed affine quantization grid.

Method: Analytically eliminate the suffix's optimal continuous response to obtain an exact groupwise quadratic with Schur-complement curvature (SCHUROPT). Then alternate closed-form row-wise scale/zero-point refitting with coordinate descent over integer codes. With the GPTQ objective fixed, SCHUROPT optimizes efficiently without backpropagation.

Result: At 2-bit quantization on Qwen3-4B, SCHUROPT yields a mean accuracy improvement of 11.88 percentage points. At higher precision, tighter reconstruction does not consistently improve end-model metrics. SCHURQUANT integrates SCHUROPT with enhancements such as quantized-prefix teacher reconstruction, reference-weight regularization, residual-add targets, and teacher-decision token weighting. Across eight Llama and Qwen models, it achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among evaluated backpropagation-free PTQ baselines, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.65 percentage points at 2 bits.

Conclusion: SCHURQUANT combines the efficient SCHUROPT optimization with teacher-based reconstruction and regularization techniques to deliver state-of-the-art mean zero-shot accuracy for 2-bit weight-only PTQ across diverse LLMs, while providing competitive performance at higher bit-widths.

Abstract: Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) enables the deployment of large language models under tight memory budgets, but accuracy often collapses at 2-3 bits. Existing backpropagation-free PTQ optimizers have two limitations: group decisions ignore the correction that the remaining continuous suffix can absorb, and discrete refinements typically keep the affine quantization grid fixed. We introduce SCHUROPT, which analytically eliminates the suffix's optimal continuous response, yielding an exact groupwise quadratic with Schur-complement curvature. It then alternates closed-form row-wise scale/zero-point refitting with coordinate descent over integer codes. With the GPTQ objective fixed, SCHUROPT improves mean zero-shot accuracy on 2-bit Qwen3-4B by 11.88 percentage points (pp). At higher precision, however, tighter reconstruction does not consistently improve end-model metrics. SCHURQUANT therefore combines SCHUROPT with quantized-prefix teacher reconstruction, reference-weight regularization, residual-add targets, and teacher-decision token weighting. Across eight Llama and Qwen models, SCHURQUANT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the evaluated backpropagation free PTQ baselines, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.65 pp at 2 bits.

</details>


### [374] [Quantum Models with Multi-Stage Training for Compositional Concept Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15601)
*Mina Abbaszadeh,Matilda Karabina Moore,Mehrnoosh Sadrzadeh,Martha Lewis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoCoGen proposes a compositional multimodal model that separates nouns and relations using tensors and variational quantum circuits, trained in two stages (object representations first, then relations). It encodes images with CLIP-derived quantum embeddings and shows improved out-of-distribution relational generalization with far fewer trainable parameters than classical baselines, aided by nonlinear quantum encodings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address compositional generalization in multimodal learning by factorizing meaning into stable primitives (nouns) and relational transformations, enabling robust transfer from object-level to relation-level reasoning.

Method: Two-stage training: (1) learn object representations from single-object image-caption pairs; (2) freeze object parameters and optimize only relational components. Nouns are represented as vectors; relations as higher-order tensors; relations learned as transformations over stable primitives using variational quantum circuits. Images use CLIP-based embeddings encoded with amplitude and angle encodings to explore linear and nonlinear feature mappings. Tests conducted on CLEVR tailored for CoCoGen; multiple tensor/ansatz configurations explored.

Result: Multi-stage training with structured encodings improves out-of-distribution relational generalization and achieves this with orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than classical baselines. Gains stem from the interaction between representation and encoding; nonlinear quantum encodings enhance separability of compositional structure.

Conclusion: Structured quantum representations combined with staged learning offer an effective framework for compositional generalization in multimodal quantum ML; results support potential of quantum-inspired representations to improve relational generalization with efficient parameter use.

Abstract: Compositional Concept Generalization (CoCoGen), the ability to systematically recombine learned primitives in novel contexts, is a key challenge for multimodal learning. In this work, we provide a solution using a compositional model of meaning that separates nouns from relations and uses tensors and variational quantum circuits to train them on data. This model enables us to employ a multi stage training paradigm, one that first learns object representations from single-object image-caption pairs, then subsequently transfers these to the relational stage where object parameters are frozen and optimisation is only applied to relational components. This design explicitly enforces compositional factorisation at the circuit, ensuring that relations are learned as transformations over stable primitives. The training paradigm is tested on the CLEVR dataset developed specificially for CoCoGen. For text, we work with vector representations of nouns and higher order tensor representations of relations using a set of different ansatz. For images, we work with quantum encodings of image embeddings dervied from Open AI's Vision Language tool CLIP and contrast amplitude encoding, which preserves the original embedding geometry, with angle encoding, which introduces nonlinear feature transformations. Our results show that multi-staged training combined with structured encodings significantly improves out of distribution relational generalisation, while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than classical baselines. We find that performance gains arise from the interaction between representation and encoding, with nonlinear quantum encodings enhancing the separability of compositional structure. These findings demonstrate that structured quantum representations and staged learning provide an effective framework for compositional generalisation in multimodal quantum machine learning.

</details>


### [375] [FluxBin: Flexible LUT-based Ultra-low-bit LLM Inference by Algorithm-Kernel Synergy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15602)
*Qingyao Yang,Runming Yang,He Xiao,Wendong Xu,Junyu Chen,Haobo Liu,Chenchen Ding,Ruihan Hu,Yik-Chung Wu,Ngai Wong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FluxBin presents a hardware-aware, algorithm-kernel co-design for ultra-low-bit LLM quantization, achieving up to ~5.9x speedup and ~10x energy savings with 70B-scale models on a single A100, with 4x memory reduction and minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Binary quantization promises extreme compression and acceleration but current work lacks specialized hardware kernels, relying on floating-point arithmetic or dequantization overheads; a hardware-aware co-design is needed to unlock practical speedups for LLMs.

Method: Algorithmic innovations: Decoupled Row-Column Binary Decomposition to boost representational capacity while staying hardware-friendly; Hessian-guided saliency-aware hybrid bases to preserve critical information. Kernel innovations: Lookup Table Building Approach with Scale Fusion to minimize FP ops; Virtual Columnar Mapping to transform irregular/sparse/salient matrices into dense execution on CUDA kernels.

Result: Extensive evaluation shows FluxBin achieves up to 5.92× speedup and 10.19× energy savings across architectures, enabling deployment of 70B-scale models on a single A100 with ~4× memory reduction; accuracy is comparable to heavily finetuned methods.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of a holistic algorithm-kernel co-design (FluxBin) for ultra-low-bit LLM execution, delivering practical acceleration and energy savings without sacrificing accuracy, and enabling large-scale models on commodity hardware.

Abstract: While binary quantization theoretically promises extreme compression and acceleration for Large Language Models (LLMs), existing research often overlooks the necessity of specialized hardware kernels, thus failing to unleash the full acceleration potential due to persistent reliance on expensive floating-point arithmetic or runtime dequantization overheads. To bridge this gap, we propose FluxBin (\textbf{F}lexible \textbf{L}UT-based \textbf{U}ltra-low-bit e\textbf{X}ecution with \textbf{Bin}ary bases), an algorithm-kernel co-design that synergizes post-training quantization with a highly optimized CUDA kernel. Algorithmically, we introduce Decoupled Row-Column Binary Decomposition to enhance representational capacity while maintaining hardware efficiency, complemented by a Hessian-guided saliency-aware hybrid bases that preserve critical information. At the kernel level, we implement a Lookup Table Building Approach with Scale Fusion to reduce floating-point arithmetic, featuring a Virtual Columnar Mapping that transforms irregular, sparse, and salient matrices into dense execution. Extensive evaluations demonstrate FluxBin achieves up to $5.92\times$ speedup and $10.19\times$ energy savings across diverse model architectures, delivering comparable accuracy to heavily fine-tuned methods. This effectively enables the deployment of 70B-scale models on one single A100 GPU with a $4\times$ memory reduction. Code is available at https://github.com/nicyyyy/FluxBin.

</details>


### [376] [Benchmarking Quantum Machine Learning for Power-System Attack Detection: Evaluation Choices Decide the Outcome Before the Models Do](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15617)
*Md Rezwanul Islam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Benchmark claims for quantum ML detectors in power-system security are highly sensitive to evaluation design; eight design choices shift conclusions, calling into question robustness claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess the robustness and comparability of quantum and classical ML detectors for power-system cyberattacks, using public datasets and realistic attack scenarios.

Method: Benchmark fidelity-kernel SVMs and variational classifiers against six tuned classical models on Mississippi State/ORNL data, evaluating under white-box, transfer, decision-based black-box, and poisoning attacks; explore two benchmark tuning choices, with eight total design choices in evaluation and tuning.

Result: Conclusions depend on evaluator choices; large performance splits occur with different protocols (e.g., 0.905 vs 0.594 macro-F1); quantum arm often non-competitive relative to classical; fidelity kernel robust under some attacks but fragile under others; mis-specification and unseeded randomness can produce large artifacts; a positive control reveals accuracy is driven by labels; seeded benchmark released with controls for each choice.

Conclusion: The paper emphasizes that reported performance is contingent on evaluation design; to ensure credible claims, standardized, seeded, and transparent benchmarking is essential, including controls for data-label integrity and attack scenarios.

Abstract: Machine-learning detectors for power-system cyberattacks are themselves attack surfaces, and quantum machine learning has been proposed for them. We benchmark fidelity-kernel SVMs and variational classifiers against six tuned classical models on public power-system attack data (Mississippi State/ORNL), across white-box, transfer, decision-based black-box, and poisoning attacks. Our headline finding is methodological: the benchmark's answers are set by the evaluator's choices before the models. Eight choices -- six in the evaluation protocol, two in the tuning the benchmark itself runs -- each reversed or moved a conclusion at fixed models. The largest is the split: the row-level protocol scores 0.905 macro-F1 where holding whole source files out leaves 0.594, and in the capped matched-dimensionality regime the quantum arm sits within noise of chance with the classical arm 0.024 above it. A fidelity kernel looks most robust until attacked directly (retention 0.886 to 0.064); a mis-fitted surrogate manufactures a 10x asymmetry; an unseeded black-box attack moves 75% between restarts. A positive control explains the accuracy null: the labels, not the pipeline. We give the control that catches each choice and release the seeded benchmark.

</details>


### [377] [In Defense of OCTA: The Reconstruction-Utility Gap in OCT-to-OCTA Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15626)
*Michael Chertok,Alon Tiosano,Orly Gal-Or,Lior Kramarski,Einav Baharav Shlezinger,Irit Bahar,Lior Wolf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: High image-level fidelity in OCTA synthesis does not guarantee clinical utility; downstream-task fidelity (segmentation of retinal vessels) reveals clinically relevant degradation in capillaries and failure to reproduce pathology, raising concerns about relying on perceptual metrics alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate OCT-to-OCTA synthesis not by visual similarity but by its ability to support OCTA-derived biomarkers for diabetic-retinopathy ischemia, addressing the gap between reconstruction quality and clinical usefulness.

Method: A frozen real-OCTA segmenter used as a probe on two synthesis methods (XOCT, TransPro). Downstream Dice evaluated for large vessels vs capillaries; included a matched-blur control to test fabrication versus blur. Retrained on a private Spectralis dataset to test generalization. Qualitative assessment of a neovascular lesion (n=3). Statistics: paired Wilcoxon p<1e-3.

Result: Large-vessel Dice: 0.862 → 0.831 (drop); capillary Dice: 0.798 → 0.635 (fivefold larger loss). TransPro worse overall. Matched-blur control indicates fabricated detail, not blur. Re-training on Spectralis data fails to reproduce the neovascular lesion (qualitative, n=3).

Conclusion: Reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient for clinical utility; downstream-task fidelity is necessary for OCT-to-OCTA synthesis evaluation. This work advocates validating synthetic OCTA via task-relevant metrics (e.g., segmentation-based biomarkers) rather than image similarity metrics.

Abstract: Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) images retinal blood flow, giving capillary-perfusion and foveal-avascular-zone biomarkers that grade diabetic-retinopathy ischemia. Because OCTA hardware is less common than structural OCT, recent work synthesizes it from OCT, reporting strong reconstruction (3D PSNR > 31 dB, SSIM > 0.9). We ask not whether the synthetic image looks similar, but whether it supports the measurements OCTA is acquired for. A frozen real-OCTA segmenter, applied as a probe to two synthesizers (XOCT, TransPro), shows downstream Dice falling with structural fineness: large vessels survive (0.862 -> 0.831) while the fine capillary network collapses (0.798 -> 0.635, five times the large-vessel loss; paired Wilcoxon p < 1e-3), TransPro worse throughout. A matched-blur control shows this detail is fabricated, not blurred. Retrained on a private Spectralis dataset, neither synthesizer reproduces the neovascular lesion (qualitative, n=3). Reconstruction fidelity is not clinical utility; we establish downstream-task fidelity as the evaluation OCT-to-OCTA synthesis needs.

</details>


### [378] [Generalised Transportability via Causal Abstractions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15645)
*Yorgos Felekis,Paris Giampouras,Fabio Massimo Zennaro,Theodoros Damoulas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a model-level, distributionally robust framework for transportability that moves beyond query-by-query criteria by using Causal Abstraction to determine when a single map aligns source/target, and provides certified interventional query intervals in both exact and approximate regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transporting causal conclusions across populations is limited by existing transportability criteria that are query-specific and fail when target data are absent; a unifying, robust framework is needed to decide existence of transport maps and provide quantitative guarantees.

Method: Model-level transport based on shared variables/graph/interventions with differing mechanisms; derive conditions for exact/approximate transportability in Markovian and semi-Markovian settings; formulate distributionally robust optimization over mechanism/env perturbations to obtain certified bounds; interpret approximation error as a quantitative notion of approximate transportability; evaluate on synthetic benchmarks and a real ecological dataset.

Result: Characterizes when a single map exists that makes source and target interventional behavior align; if such a map exists, all target queries transport; in the approximate setting, the best map yields certified intervals for queries; provides bounds for non-transportable cases and guarantees under target-agnostic scenarios; empirical results show the certified intervals bracket the true interventional queries.

Conclusion: Frames model-level transport as a distributionally robust abstraction problem, yielding practical certificates and intervals; demonstrates applicability to Markovian/semi-Markovian settings and real data, bridging transportability and abstraction theory.

Abstract: Transporting a causal conclusion from a source study population to a target one is a fundamental problem in causal inference. The theory of transportability provides a criterion for when this is possible: given experimental data from the source and observational data from the target, it determines whether a target query is identifiable and does so completely; i.e. if the query can be transported, the criterion finds the exact formula. However, it works one query at a time and returns an expression rather than the value itself. It is also silent in two practically important regimes: when the query is not transportable and when no target data exist at all. To tackle both, we take a model-level perspective grounded in Causal Abstraction theory. Source and target share variables, graph, and interventions, differing only at a known set of mechanisms, which makes transportability a special case of same-level abstraction. Thus, instead of asking whether one query transports, we ask whether a single map aligns the source and target across their interventional behaviour. We characterise when such a map exists in both the Markovian and semi-Markovian settings; when it does, every target query transports at once. Our main contribution lies in the approximate case. When no exact map exists, the best approximate one still yields certified query intervals, recasting abstraction error as a quantitative notion of approximate transportability. We formulate model-level transport as distributionally robust optimisation over mechanism and environment perturbations of the unseen target and derive certificates for both challenging regimes: bounds for non-transportable queries, and guarantees under target-agnostic settings. We evaluate our framework on synthetic Markovian and semi-Markovian benchmarks and a real ecological dataset, and we show that the certified intervals bracket the true interventional query.

</details>


### [379] [Learning Auditable Classifier Models: Source-Disjoint Tree Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15725)
*Srikumar Krishnamoorthy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RPTE is a three-stage, fully auditable tree ensemble that decomposes predictions into non-overlapping rule contributions, achieving competitive accuracy with dramatically reduced inspection units.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In clinical and regulated settings, models must be accurate and auditable. Tree ensembles excel in accuracy but are hard to audit; interpretable alternatives trade expressiveness. RPTE aims to combine accuracy with principled, inspectable interpretability.

Method: Stage 1: build supervised symbolic feature vocabulary. Stage 2: grow shallow trees under a source-disjointness constraint (each raw variable assigned to at most one tree) and retain the discovered structures. Stage 3: fit an L1-regularized logistic regression over leaf-region indicators to obtain sparse, jointly optimal coefficients.

Result: On 12 clinical-domain binary benchmarks with repeated stratified 5-fold CV, RPTE is competitive with tuned opaque ensembles and interpretable baselines. It reduces model inspection units 9× to 87× relative to XGBoost and has lower audit complexity than EBM on all datasets; RuleFit is comparable on a subset where rule counts are small but lacks source-disjointness guarantees. Code available.

Conclusion: RPTE provides full auditability by design via additive, non-overlapping rule contributions without severely sacrificing predictive performance; the source-disjointness constraint enhances interpretability and auditability in regulated contexts.

Abstract: Predictive models in clinical and regulated settings must be accurate and fully auditable. Tree ensembles deliver strong accuracy on tabular data, but their sequential boosting couples structure discovery with coefficient estimation, making compact per-prediction auditing difficult. Interpretable alternatives impose structural constraints that limit expressiveness: generalized additive models typically restrict interactions to pairwise terms and post-hoc rule extractors produce overlapping rules that hinder compact interpretation. We introduce Residual Pattern Tree Ensemble (RPTE), a three-stage learning approach, that is built on three key principles: bounded feature budget, source disjointness, and separate coefficient estimation. Stage~1 builds a supervised symbolic feature vocabulary. Stage~2 grows shallow trees under a source-disjointness constraint, where each raw variable is allocated to at most one tree, and retains only the discovered tree structures. Stage~3 solves a single $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression over leaf-region indicators, yielding jointly optimal sparse coefficients. This learning approach ensures that every prediction decomposes into an algebraic sum of named, non-overlapping rule contributions, enabling full auditability by design. Empirical evaluation on twelve clinical-domain binary classification benchmarks using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation shows that RPTE performs competitively against tuned opaque ensembles and interpretable baselines. RPTE reduces model inspection units by 9$\times$ to 87$\times$ relative to XGBoost and maintains lower audit complexity than EBM on all 12 datasets. RuleFit requires comparable or fewer inspection units on three datasets where its rule count is small, but without source-disjointness guarantees. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/srikumar2050/hugiml-core}{this https URL}.

</details>


### [380] [FirstDiff: One-Step Diffusion-Based Anomaly Detection for Multivariate Time Series via Initial Noise Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15727)
*Ali Boudaghi,Alireza Nemati,Hadi Zare*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FirstDiff enables anomaly detection in multivariate time-series by using the predicted diffusion noise from the first reverse-diffusion step, modeling its normal distribution with validation data, and performing inference from a single denoising evaluation instead of a full reverse trajectory; it uses a Diffusion Transformer and achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks with lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based anomaly detection typically relies on the full reverse diffusion to reconstruct data, which is computationally expensive and may ignore informative intermediate denoising representations. There is a need to leverage early denoising information and better model temporal and cross-sensor dependencies.

Method: Model the distribution of predicted diffusion noise under normal behavior using validation data. Perform anomaly detection from the initial reverse-diffusion evaluation using a Diffusion Transformer as the denoising backbone to capture temporal and inter-sensor dependencies, avoiding the full reverse-diffusion trajectory.

Result: Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance while reducing inference cost by using a single denoising-network evaluation instead of the full reverse diffusion process.

Conclusion: Early denoising information is informative for anomaly detection in diffusion-based methods, enabling significant computational savings without sacrificing accuracy; incorporating a Diffusion Transformer strengthens modeling of complex temporal and inter-sensor relationships.

Abstract: Diffusion models have recently shown strong potential for multivariate time-series anomaly detection by learning the distribution of normal data through iterative denoising. Existing diffusion-based approaches, however, typically perform anomaly detection after completing the reverse diffusion process, relying primarily on the final reconstructed signal and overlooking informative representations produced during denoising. This design incurs substantial computational cost and limits the use of intermediate diffusion information for anomaly detection.
  In this paper, we propose FirstDiff, a diffusion-based anomaly detection framework based on the observation that the predicted diffusion noise at the initial reverse-diffusion evaluation already contains sufficient information for accurate anomaly detection. FirstDiff models the statistical distribution of predicted diffusion noise under normal behavior using validation data, enabling anomaly inference from a single denoising-network evaluation rather than completing the reverse diffusion trajectory.
  To model complex temporal and inter-sensor dependencies, FirstDiff employs a Diffusion Transformer as the denoising backbone. Extensive experiments on five public benchmark datasets demonstrate that FirstDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing diffusion inference from the full reverse trajectory to a single denoising-network evaluation.

</details>


### [381] [TinyCast: Probabilistic Zero-Shot Forecasting with Computed Periodicity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15767)
*Armin Steinhauser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TinyCast is an attention-free zero-shot forecaster with 146k parameters that uses a zero-parameter spectral detector to identify dominant periods, folds the context on their phase, and employs a dilated convolutional encoder with a block-autoregressive quantile decoder to emit a predictive distribution. It achieves strong parameter efficiency, claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance at small sizes, and is end-to-end INT8-exportable for embedded deployment without per-signal fitting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve probabilistic forecasting with minimal parameter budgets by exploiting the periodic structure of time-series rather than relying on heavy learning, enabling on-device deployment and end-to-end INT8 inference without per-signal fitting.

Method: Zero-shot approach: use a zero-parameter spectral detector to identify dominant periods, fold the input context by their phase, encode with a dilated convolutional encoder, and generate a predictive distribution via a block-autoregressive quantile decoder. The model has 146,505 parameters and exports in static INT8, enabling end-to-end embedded forecasting without per-signal fitting.

Result: Outperforms or matches all known zero-shot entries on the GIFT-Eval board with established parameter counts, defines a size-accuracy frontier for probabilistic accuracy, and is the only zero-shot entry under 1.4M parameters that emits a predictive distribution without test-data leakage; other entries achieving higher scores require at least ~28x more parameters. On Chronos-ZS and fev-bench, larger models with at least 28x more parameters perform better.

Conclusion: TinyCast demonstrates that a compact, architecture-aligned design targeting periodic structure can deliver probabilistic forecasts at very small scales, with strong so-called zero-shot performance and straightforward embedded deployment potential. Its reliance on periodicity is a strength for certain time-series contexts but may limit applicability where periodic structure is weak or absent.

Abstract: We introduce TinyCast, an attention-free zero-shot forecaster that emits a predictive distribution from 146,505 parameters, on the premise that at this size the periodic structure of a context is worth computing rather than learning. A zero-parameter spectral detector supplies the dominant periods, the context is folded on their phase, and a dilated convolutional encoder and a block-autoregressive quantile decoder model the rest. It is smaller than every zero-shot entry on the GIFT-Eval board whose parameter count can be established. On probabilistic accuracy it defines the size-accuracy frontier. Among zero-shot entries declaring no test-data leakage it is the only one below 1.4M parameters that emits a predictive distribution, and every entry scoring better carries at least that budget. On Chronos-ZS and fev-bench every neural model ahead of it carries at least 28 times its parameters. Because the mixing path is convolutions and matrix multiplications only, it exports to static INT8 and forecasts end to end on an embedded device without per-signal fitting.

</details>


### [382] [Temporal Graph Prototype-conditioned Conformal Prediction for Fraud Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15768)
*Xudong Chen,Shengbo Gong,Lu Cheng,Wei Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProtoCP is a conformal prediction framework for edge-level fraud detection on temporal graphs that improves calibration efficiency and stability under class imbalance and temporal drift by using prototypes and a neighborhood-relative, diffusion-based scoring mechanism; it achieves target coverage with smaller prediction sets on four fraud benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fraud detection on temporal graphs suffers from benign-dominated calibration signals and extreme class imbalance, which lead to inefficient conformal prediction sets with poor calibration. There is a need for distribution-free, risk-aware uncertainty quantification with efficient, targeted calibration.

Method: ProtoCP focuses calibration on fraud-relevant subgraph context using learned prototypes to suppress benign-noise. It introduces a neighborhood-relative nonconformity score with temporal score diffusion to achieve stable class-conditional calibration under drift and imbalance.

Result: Empirical evaluation on YelpChi, S-FFSD, FTFD, and BankSim shows that ProtoCP attains the target coverage with consistently smaller prediction sets than state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks.

Conclusion: ProtoCP provides an effective, distribution-free conformal prediction framework for edge-level fraud detection on temporal graphs, improving calibration efficiency and robustness to class imbalance and temporal drift; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees and has emerged as a principled tool for uncertainty quantification. In edge-level fraud detection on temporal interaction graphs, where false positives and false negatives both carry substantial cost, such coverage guarantees are particularly appealing for risk-aware decision making. However, directly applying existing graph conformal predictors yields inefficient prediction sets due to two recurring properties of fraud data. Fraudulent interactions are often embedded in benign-dominated neighborhoods that dilute calibration signals, while extreme class imbalance leaves scarce labeled-fraud support in the calibration split and leads to overly conservative class-conditional thresholds. To address these issues, we propose ProtoCP, a conformal prediction framework for edge-level fraud detection on temporal graphs. ProtoCP improves calibration efficiency by focusing calibration on fraud-relevant subgraph context and producing more stable nonconformity scores under class imbalance and temporal drift. Specifically, it leverages learned prototypes to suppress benign-dominated noise in the calibration context and introduces a neighborhood-relative scoring mechanism with temporal score diffusion for stable class-conditional calibration. Experiments on four fraud benchmarks (YelpChi, S-FFSD, FTFD, and BankSim) show that ProtoCP achieves the target coverage with consistently smaller prediction sets than state-of-the-art baselines. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Picard1701ent/ProtoCP.git

</details>


### [383] [Learning Stock Trading Policies via Barycenter-Based Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15770)
*Arishi Orra,Himanshu Choudhary,Manoj Thakur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BRaG uses a barycenter-based adversarial IRL to learn stock trading from multiple expert strategies, pretrain via imitation learning, then fine-tune with RL, with control barrier functions to enforce drawdown-based risk constraints; evaluated across four major markets showing improved performance and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning in trading suffers from delayed/noisy rewards, exploration challenges, and difficulty enforcing risk constraints. Leveraging multiple expert strategies via a barycentric aggregation can yield a robust pseudo-expert representation and improve learning stability.

Method: Aggregate heterogeneous expert demonstrations using a performance-weighted Wasserstein barycenter to create a stable pseudo-expert. Pretrain a trading policy with adversarial imitation learning. Fine-tune the policy with reinforcement learning using true market rewards. Incorporate control barrier functions to constrain actions and regularize learning to satisfy drawdown limits.

Result: The approach achieves stronger performance than classical trading rules and recent DRL methods across US, UK, Indian, and Taiwanese markets, with more stable risk characteristics.

Conclusion: BRaG offers a stable, risk-aware framework for stock trading that combines multi-expert imitation via a Wasserstein barycenter with adversarial IL and risk-constraining control barrier methods, yielding robust performance across diverse markets.

Abstract: Designing effective trading strategies using reinforcement learning remains challenging due to delayed and noisy rewards, poor exploration, and the difficulty of enforcing explicit risk constraints. In this work, we propose BRaG, a barycenter-based adversarial inverse reinforcement learning framework for stock trading that learns trading behavior from multiple heterogeneous expert strategies. BRaG aggregates expert demonstrations using a performance-weighted Wasserstein barycenter, yielding a stable pseudo-expert representation that captures shared structure across diverse trading styles. This representation is used to pretrain a trading policy via adversarial imitation learning, which alleviates unstable exploration during reinforcement learning. The pretrained policy is subsequently refined using reinforcement learning with true market rewards. To ensure risk-aware decision-making, BRaG incorporates control barrier functions that constrain action execution and regularize policy learning to satisfy drawdown limits. We evaluate the proposed approach on four major global equity markets, including the US, UK, Indian, and Taiwanese indices. Across all the markets, the proposed approach achieves stronger performance than both classical trading rules and recent deep reinforcement learning methods, while exhibiting more stable risk characteristics.

</details>


### [384] [Routing Divergence Is Not Evidence of Behavioral Influence in Same-Weight MoE Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15787)
*Cedric Caruzzo,Donggeun Yoo,Tae Soo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decompose MoE routing into routing and content terms; routing has limited direct influence; exposure-based analysis suggests measuring exposure before interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address potential blind spots in same-weight self-distillation and MoE routing where identical weights can route tokens differently, questioning whether routing decisions affect behavior.

Method: Exact blockwise decomposition separating a routing term (gate changes at fixed content) from a dense-like content term; quantify routing vs content across seven open-weight checkpoints and two domains; analyze residual-stream exposure; scaling backbones in two models; confirmatory experiments with matched-norm noise, pre-registered PubMedQA patches, and merged-expert probes.

Result: Routing term accounts for ~1.6x of the block-output; exposure of the residual-stream ~3.2x; exposure correlates with routed block’s residual share; backbone scale increases exposure monotonically; common-mode controls support a mass-and-coherence mechanism rather than simple denominator dilution; pre-registered patches show routing term moves outputs by < half the natural context effect and is largely replicated by matched-norm noise, while the content term is strongly direction-specific; exposure remains small at tested boundaries; router movement alone is not evidence of behavioral influence.

Conclusion: Router movement alone does not indicate behavioral influence; first measure exposure, then apply behavioral interventions when decision matter; the content term likely drives directional effects; exposure-based analysis provides robust guidance for MoE alignment and interpretation.

Abstract: Two Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) forward passes can share every weight yet route the same token through different experts. This creates a possible blind spot in same-weight self-distillation, where a demonstration-conditioned teacher supervises a query-only student. We study this mismatch in its single-step form, with frozen weights rather than as a proxy for a full training trajectory. An exact blockwise decomposition separates a routing term, which changes gates at fixed content, from a dense-like content term. Across seven open-weight checkpoints and two domains, the routing term spans only $1.6\times$ as a fraction of block output, while its residual-stream exposure spans $3.2\times$. Exposure is ordered by the routed block's share of the residual. Scaling the always-on backbone in two confirmatory models moves exposure monotonically; common-mode controls support a mass-and-coherence mechanism rather than denominator dilution alone. Preregistered PubMedQA patches on three models show that the full routing term moves outputs by less than half the natural context effect and is largely reproduced by matched-norm noise, whereas the content term is strongly direction-specific. Scale and merged-expert probes show that the narrow block-level range is not universal, although exposure remains small at the tested boundaries. Router movement alone is therefore not evidence of behavioral influence: measure exposure first, and use a behavioral intervention when the decision matters.

</details>


### [385] [A Pre-Specified Construction-Confirmation Test of Operation-Level Causal Transfer Across Finite Isomorphic Symbolic Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15809)
*Xinyi Shan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: One route showing evidence for operation-level cross-domain mapping in a single model and prompt, but evidence is narrow and not generalizable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether hidden-state differences between operations can be added to mapped recipient inputs to move toward corresponding recipient answers, thereby demonstrating operation-level structure across symbolic domains.

Method: Input-specific intervention design in finite isomorphic state spaces with multiple controls (wrong-operation, norm-matched random, no-op) and a two-stage design separating candidate construction from confirmation. Tested on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (layers 20–21) with a pre-specified, frozen candidate route; replication using an NN-based confirmation pipeline.

Result: A single pre-specified prompt route (| integer_mod16--letters16 | successor->predecessor) passed both PyVene splits; confirmation intersection–union p-value = 0.000198; Holm-adjusted p-value = 0.006943. An independent NN interception test reproduced all 12 confirmation estimates and had Holm-adjusted p-value = 0.007141. The result is limited to one route, one candidate, and one model revision/layer window, with replication across two interventions.

Conclusion: Evidence suggests a detectable effect consistent with operation-level structure for a specific route and candidate, but cannot support cross-model generalization, back-end independence, domain-general transfer, or algebraic invariance.

Abstract: Behavioral accuracy, linear decodability, and successful activation interventions do not by themselves show that a model carries an operation-level structure from one symbolic domain to another. We ask a narrower question in finite isomorphic state spaces: if the hidden-state difference between two operations is estimated separately for each source input, does adding that difference to a mapped recipient input move the model toward the corresponding recipient answer? The design compares this input-specific intervention with wrong-operation, norm-matched random, and no-op controls, and separates candidate construction from an independently isolated confirmation split. On a frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model at layers 20--21, one route--domain--operation candidate from a family pre-specified and frozen before confirmation access, transparent | integer_mod16--letters16 | successor->predecessor, passed both PyVene splits; its confirmation intersection--union p-value was 0.000198 and its 36-family Holm-adjusted p-value was 0.006943. A subsequent NNsight 0.7.0 experiment, pre-specified and frozen before its confirmation access, tested only this selected prompt route, without candidate or layer reselection. It reproduced all 12 confirmation effect estimates, confidence intervals, and exact sign-flip p-values numerically; its 36-family Holm-adjusted p-value was 0.007141. The result is therefore limited to one prompt route and one candidate, replicated across two intervention implementations on one model revision and one layer interval. It does not establish cross-model generalization, full-family backend independence, domain-general transfer, or algebraic invariance.

</details>


### [386] [KOALA: Koopman Operator Learning for WiFi-Based Anticipatory Hum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15815)
*Quang-Anh N. D.,Duc Pham Minh,Thao Phuong Pham,Minh Anh Nguyen,Huan X. Nguyen,Tuan Dang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KOALA uses Koopman latent dynamics to predict human motion from WiFi CSI without autoregressive rollouts, achieving robust multi-horizon predictions via a lifted linear dynamics space, residual operator, anchor-delta head, and a temporal-encoder regularizer, outperforming baselines on MM-Fi and WiPose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CSI-based pose estimation treats prediction as instantaneous regression and either ignores temporal dynamics or relies on autoregressive strategies that accumulate error. There is a need for non-autoregressive, long-horizon prediction directly from CSI with stable dynamics.

Method: Lift CSI-derived pose sequences into a learned Koopman latent space where nonlinear dynamics become linear; perform multi-horizon prediction with simple matrix-vector products, avoiding autoregression. Use a residual CSI-conditioned operator to address attractor issues, and an anchor-delta head to prevent trivial copying. Regularize lifting and operator jointly via a Koopman Anchored Latent (KAL) loss operating in the temporal-encoder feature space.

Result: KOALA achieves robust and consistent short- and long-horizon predictions, outperforming all baselines by a substantial margin on MM-Fi and WiPose datasets.

Conclusion: Koopman-based latent dynamics, with targeted regularization and output heads, enables accurate non-autoregressive multi-horizon motion prediction directly from CSI, addressing noise amplification and identity-attractor problems.

Abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) has emerged as a privacy-preserving alternative to cameras for human pose estimation. However, existing approaches treat pose inference as an instantaneous regression problem and do not model temporal dynamics, making future motion prediction infeasible. Naively applying vision-based prediction methods compounds the estimation noise already present in CSI-derived poses, as autoregressive rollouts amplify errors at every step. We propose KOALA, the framework for human motion prediction directly from WiFi CSI, by lifting noisy CSI-derived pose sequences into a learned Koopman latent space where nonlinear dynamics become linear, enabling multi-horizon prediction via simple matrix-vector products without autoregressive iteration or error accumulation. A residual CSI-conditioned operator resolves the identity attractor problem inherent from Koopman formulations, and an anchor-delta prediction head eliminates the degenerate shortcut of copying the current pose across all horizons. To regularise the lifting and operator jointly, we introduce a Koopman Anchored Latent (KAL) loss that operates in the temporal-encoder feature space, enforcing dynamical consistency across prediction horizons without requiring contrastive, spectral, or auxiliary losses. Experiments on MM-Fi and WiPose show that KOALA achieves robust, consistent performance across both short- and long-term prediction horizons, outperforming all baselines by a substantial margin.

</details>


### [387] [Second-Moment Memory in Coordinatewise Adam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15824)
*Jeonseong Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Second-moment memory in Adam can slow convergence under finite-variance stochastic gradients; the expected positive update scales as M2^{-1/2}, implying a lower bound on average progress; long memory degrades optimization even with finite gradient noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify the optimization cost of maintaining moving averages of past squared gradients and whether it hinders progress.

Method: Theoretical analysis using a simple two-point oracle; derive directional bound on the expected positive normalized update; relate to M2 = (1-β2)^{-1}; translate into average-stationarity bound for a smooth convex problem with normalized gap, smoothness, and variance; examine the effect of memory length and stepsize scaling.

Result: After initialization transient, expected positive normalized update is O(M2^{-1/2}); this bound carries into a lower bound on average progress; long second-moment memory slows optimization even when gradient noise has finite variance.

Conclusion: Second-moment memory can suppress optimization progress; memory length (via β2) crucial for convergence; results inform hyperparameter tuning and theoretical understanding of Adam's behavior under stochastic gradients.

Abstract: Adam retains a moving average of past squared gradients in its denominator, but the optimization cost of this memory is not well understood. We show that second-moment memory can itself suppress progress toward the optimum even under finite-variance stochastic gradients. For a simple two-point oracle, the expected positive normalized update is $O(M_2^{-1/2})$ after an initialization transient, where $M_2=(1-β_2)^{-1}$ is the second-moment memory length. We convert this directional bound, under the stated memory and stepsize scaling, into an average-stationarity lower bound of the same order on a smooth convex problem with normalized gap, smoothness, and variance. Long second-moment memory can slow optimization even when the gradient noise has finite variance.

</details>


### [388] [Self-Supervised Auxiliary Task Discovery for Stable Reinforcement Learning in Stock Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15841)
*Arishi Orra,Himanshu Choudhary,Manoj Thakur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A self-supervised RL framework for stock trading that automatically discovers auxiliary tasks using General Value Functions via a meta-gradient mechanism, improving stability and profitability across major indices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-stationary market behavior and noisy rewards make profitable, stable RL trading hard; fixed, manually designed auxiliary tasks may not generalize across regime shifts. Automatic discovery aims to provide adaptive auxiliary supervision.

Method: Two-network setup: a main network learns the trading policy and auxiliary GVF predictions; a secondary network defines auxiliary tasks by learning cumulants and discount factors. Tasks are updated via meta-gradients that optimize long-term trading performance, enabling autonomously discovered auxiliary supervision.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four major equity indices (DJI, FTSE, Sensex, TAIEX) shows that automatically discovered auxiliary tasks yield more robust learning and better trading performance than baselines.

Conclusion: Automatic discovery of GVF-based auxiliary tasks enhances representation learning and policy optimization in RL-based stock trading, offering improved stability and performance across changing market regimes.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained increasing attention as a data-driven approach for stock trading. However, learning a policy that is both profitable and stable remains challenging due to non-stationary market behaviour and noisy reward signals. Auxiliary tasks are often used to improve representation learning and stabilize training, yet they are usually designed manually and depend heavily on prior assumptions about targets and prediction horizons. Such fixed designs may not remain suitable across changing market regimes. In this work, we propose a self-supervised framework that automatically discovers auxiliary tasks to support reinforcement learning for stock trading. The auxiliary tasks are formulated as General Value Functions so that their predictions enrich the learned state representation and assist policy optimization. The framework consists of two networks. The main network learns the trading policy along with the auxiliary predictions, while the secondary network generates the definitions of auxiliary tasks through learned cumulants and discount factors. These tasks are updated using a meta gradient mechanism that accounts for their long-term impact on trading performance and improves training stability. We evaluate the proposed approach across four major equity indices: DJI, FTSE, Sensex, and TAIEX. The empirical results demonstrate that automatically discovered auxiliary tasks lead to more robust learning and improved trading performance compared to existing baselines.

</details>


### [389] [Geometry of Forgetting: Representation Flux in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15854)
*Maksim A. Kazanskii*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RepFlux defines a latent-representation displacement measure during sequential learning and uses FlowLess-R, a representation-space regularizer, to stabilize replay-based continual learning and reduce forgetting across standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Catastrophic forgetting remains a core challenge in continual learning. The dynamics of latent representations during task succession are poorly understood, yet they may predict forgetting and inform mitigation strategies.

Method: Introduce representation flux, a geometric, sample-level measure of representation displacement across training. Demonstrate its correlation with forgetting and its potential as a predictive marker. Propose FlowLess-R, a representation-space regularizer that aligns replay representations with stored references, enabling continued learning. Integrate FlowLess-R into replay-based methods (ER, DER++, ER-ACE) and evaluate on SplitMNIST, SplitFashionMNIST, SplitCIFAR10, and SplitTinyImageNet.

Result: Representation flux strongly associates with catastrophic forgetting; elevated flux can precede performance degradation and links to confidence degradation. FlowLess-R improves final average accuracy and reduces forgetting when added to ER-based methods across multiple benchmarks.

Conclusion: Representation flux is a useful geometric marker of forgetting; stabilizing latent representations via FlowLess-R offers a simple, architecture-agnostic approach to mitigate forgetting in replay-based continual learning.

Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a fundamental obstacle to continual learning, where neural networks lose previously acquired knowledge while learning new tasks. Existing methods primarily mitigate forgetting through parameter regularization or experience replay, while the representation-space dynamics associated with forgetting remain less understood. We investigate latent representation evolution during sequential learning and introduce representation flux, a geometric measure of sample-level representation displacement across training. We show that representation flux is strongly associated with catastrophic forgetting across multiple benchmarks, with temporal analyses indicating that elevated flux can precede subsequent performance degradation. Representation displacement is also associated with confidence degradation, while complementary geometric properties provide additional information about sample-level forgetting. Motivated by these observations, we propose FlowLess-R, a representation-space regularization method that constrains replay representations relative to stored references while allowing continued learning. FlowLess-R is architecture-agnostic and integrates into replay-based methods through a representation-matching term. Experiments on SplitMNIST, SplitFashionMNIST, SplitCIFAR10, and SplitTinyImageNet show improved final average accuracy and reduced forgetting with ER, DER++, and ER-ACE. Our results identify representation flux as an informative geometric marker of forgetting and show that stabilizing latent representations provides a simple strategy for mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

</details>


### [390] [TransfHAR: Self-Supervised Wrist Representations for On-Demand Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15861)
*Aidan Bradshaw,Riku Arakawa,Xin Liu,Karan Ahuja*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TransfHAR uses self-supervised pretraining on coarse wrist IMU activities to learn transferable motion priors for fine-grained, on-demand activity recognition, achieving strong cross-dataset and in-lab performance with a real-time smartwatch app.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Label scarcity and high customization needs for fine-grained wrist activities; unlabeled data from coarse activities can be leveraged to learn general motion structure that transfers to novel, personalized tasks.

Method: Self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled coarse wrist IMU activities to learn transferable motion priors; fine-grained task transfer to manipulative and procedural activities; real-time smartwatch app enabling user-defined activity sets with few demonstrations; evaluation across three offline cross-dataset benchmarks; personalization via minimal demonstrations.

Result: Outperforms or matches fully supervised baselines using complete label sets in three offline cross-dataset evaluations (average +6.2 BA points). In-lab study (n=10) on seven novel wrist activities yields 86.7% BA with five examples/class and 90.4% BA with one-minute-per-class updates.

Conclusion: Broad self-supervised wrist pretraining yields a robust foundation for on-demand, fine-grained recognition, enabling personalized recognition with minimal labeled data and demonstrations.

Abstract: Fine-grained wrist activity recognition can support applications such as procedural step guidance and context-aware assistance, yet acquiring labeled data for every new task, user, and activity granularity remains a bottleneck. We present TransfHAR, a self-supervised wrist IMU framework for on-demand, fine-grained activity recognition by learning transferable motion priors from global, unlabeled activities. We show that self-supervised pretraining on coarse wrist IMU activities (e.g., sitting, walking, exercise) learns motion structure rich enough to transfer to fine-grained manipulative, gestural, and procedural activities (e.g., snapping, stirring, waving) that are absent from pretraining. We implement TransfHAR as a real-time smartwatch application that lets users define and expand their own activity set for personalized recognition from only a few demonstrations. Across three offline cross-dataset evaluations, TransfHAR matches or exceeds fully supervised baselines that use complete label sets with equal or additional sensor channels, by 6.2 balanced-accuracy points on average. In an in-lab study with 10 participants each performing seven novel wrist activities, TransfHAR reaches 86.7% balanced accuracy across participants with five examples per class and 90.4% when updated from a single one-minute recording per class. These results indicate that broad self-supervised wrist pretraining provides an effective foundation for on-demand fine-grained activity recognition.

</details>


### [391] [Feasible and Novel Synthetic Population Generation with Tabular and Sequential Travel Attributes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15867)
*Farbod Abbasi,Zachary Patterson,Bilal Farooq*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A regularized two-stage generative framework for synthetic populations: Stage 1 uses a WGAN-GP with three regularizers (IGP, LDR, CLAP) to improve feasibility, diversity, and novelty in tabular synthesis; Stage 2 uses Transformer and LSTM-Attention to generate sequential travel attributes conditioned on the synthesized profiles; novelty and count-aware metrics assess recovery of valid unseen combinations; results show improvements over vanilla WGAN-GP and strong cross-stage consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address sampling zeros and infeasible zeros in small survey samples while capturing static socio-demographic attributes and sequential travel behaviour (trip chains) for realistic population synthesis.

Method: Stage 1: WGAN-GP for tabular data with three regularizers (IGP, LDR, CLAP) to encourage broader valid coverage and reduce infeasible samples. Stage 2: Transformer and LSTM-Attention models generate sequential attributes (departure time, trip purpose, travel mode) conditioned on the tabular profiles.
