Novelty and count-aware metrics evaluate recovery of valid unseen combinations. Cross-stage validation checks coherence between mobility status and trip chains.

Result: Regularized models improve feasibility by 2.1–3.7 percentage points, novelty by 6.6–10.0 points, F1 by 6.3–8.6 points relative to vanilla WGAN-GP. LSTM-Attention best for matching trip-length distribution; Transformer yields higher sequential F1 (90.6% vs 89.1%). Cross-stage validation confirms consistency between generated mobility status and trip chains.

Conclusion: The proposed regularized two-stage framework effectively mitigates sampling and structural zeros, enhances coverage and novelty in synthetic populations, and produces coherent sequential travel attributes, offering a robust approach for population synthesis from limited data.

Abstract: Synthetic populations are critical inputs for activity-based travel demand models, yet generating realistic populations from limited survey data remains challenging. Small samples miss valid attribute combinations, known as sampling zeros, and generative models may also produce infeasible structural zeros. Moreover, realistic synthetic populations must capture both static socio-demographic attributes and sequential travel behaviour, such as trip chains. This paper proposes a regularized two-stage generative framework to address these challenges, where regularization refers to additional loss terms that guide the generator toward broader valid coverage and fewer infeasible samples. In Stage 1, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty is augmented with three regularization terms, IGP, LDR, and CLAP, to improve feasibility, diversity, and novelty in tabular population synthesis. In Stage 2, Transformer and LSTM-Attention models generate sequential travel attributes, including departure time, trip purpose, and travel mode, conditioned on the synthesized tabular profiles. We also introduce novelty and count-aware metrics to evaluate whether valid unseen combinations are recovered and generated in realistic proportions. Results show that regularized models outperform the vanilla WGAN-GP across feasibility, diversity, and novelty. Regularization increases feasibility by 2.1 to 3.7 percentage points and novelty by 6.6 to 10.0 percentage points, improving sampling-zero recovery without sacrificing feasibility. The F1 score improves by 6.3 to 8.6 percentage points. For sequential attributes, LSTM-Attention best matches the trip-length distribution, while Transformer achieves higher overall sequential F1, 90.6\% versus 89.1\%. Cross-stage validation confirms strong consistency between generated mobility status and generated trip chains.

</details>


### [392] [Deploying Frontier Agentic Technology in MOOSEnger, a Multiphysics-Capable AI Assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15881)
*Zaid Abulawi,Mengnan Li,Guillaume Giudicelli,Yang Liu,Cody Permann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extend MOOSEnger with a locally-hosted model harness for the MOOSE framework; evaluate agentic performance across multiple physics categories, showing GPT-5.2-based agent outperforms Gemma4-based agent and near-baseline models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lower the barrier to using a complex multiphysics framework by providing an agentic, knowledge-driven assistant that can retrieve context, validate inputs, diagnose issues, and learn from runs for persistent memory.

Method: Develop a harness in MOOSEnger targeting locally-hosted models. The harness retrieves contextual knowledge from the MOOSE repository, validates and diagnoses the resulting input via interaction with the simulation executable environment, and stores lessons in persistent memory. Evaluate on a real engineering problem from VT B, and across eight categories (diffusion, Navier–Stokes, phase field, plasticity, porous media flow, solid mechanics, transient heat transfer, reactor mesh generation) with 25 prompts per category. Compare MOOSEnger-Gemma4 against MOOSEnger-GPT-5.2 and baselines (Gemma4, GPT-5.2 without agentic capabilities).

Result: MOOSEnger-GPT-5.2 achieved ~90% success; MOOSEnger-Gemma4 achieved ~76.5% success. Baselines perform poorly (~5% for GPT-5.2 and 0% for Gemma4). This demonstrates the agentic harness substantially improves performance on complex multiphysics tasks.

Conclusion: An agentic harness tailored to a domain framework (MOOSE) markedly enhances automated workflow performance, validating the value of componentized, knowledge-driven agents in scientific computing; future work could explore scalability, generalization to other frameworks, and deeper memory/explanation capabilities.

Abstract: The Multiphysics Object-Oriented Simulation Environment (MOOSE) is an open-source finite-element framework for building multiphysics simulation applications. Using a multiphysics environment effectively demands specialized expertise, creating a barrier for many domain scientists and engineers. MOOSEnger, developed at Idaho National Laboratory (INL), is a domain-specific, tool-enabled AI agent built for the MOOSE Framework. This work extends MOOSEnger with a harness focused on locally-hosted models. The harness gives the agent a full pipeline: it retrieves contextual knowledge from the MOOSE repository, validates and diagnoses the resulting input through interaction with the simulation executable environment, and extracts and stores lessons in a persistent memory.
  The resulting framework is demonstrated on an engineering problem from the National Reactor Innovation Center Virtual Test Bed (VTB), illustrating its potential to support realistic multiphysics simulation workflows. Additionally, the agent performance is evaluated on different categories including diffusion, Navier--Stokes, phase field, plasticity, porous media flow, solid mechanics, transient heat transfer, and reactor mesh generation. Each category consists of 25 prompts/cases. We compare MOOSEnger-Gemma4 against MOOSEnger-GPT-5.2, alongside baseline Gemma4 and GPT-5.2 without agentic capabilities. MOOSEnger-GPT-5.2 shows a slight edge, achieving a 90\% success rate versus 76.5\% for MOOSEnger-Gemma4. The baseline models perform far worse, at just 5\% (GPT-5.2) and 0\% (Gemma4), underscoring the impact of the agentic harness.

</details>


### [393] [Layers Matter: Why Continual Learning Regularization Should Be Layer-Adaptive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15901)
*Brian B. Moser,Ahmed Anwar,Tobias Christian Nauen,Shishir Muralidhara,Federico Raue,René Schuster,Stanislav Frolov,Andreas Dengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Top Hessian eigenvalues per layer, not per-layer Fisher averages, govern forgetting; diagonal Fisher fails to capture this, causing uneven forgetting across layers. A simple eigenvalue-aware regularization, emphasizing early layers, improves both forgetting and new-task performance when applied to EWC and SLCA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual learning methods like EWC rely on per-parameter or per-layer stability signals (Fisher) to prevent forgetting. However, a diagonal Fisher summary per layer omits top eigenvalue information that dominates sensitivity and forgetting, leading to suboptimal regularization and varying forgetting across layers.

Method: Under a block-diagonal Hessian assumption, the authors derive that forgetting decomposes into a sum over layers, weighted by each layer's top Hessian eigenvalue. They show diagonal-Fisher weights cannot recover these top eigenvalues, especially when layers have identical Fisher averages but different top eigenvalues. They quantify the impact of uniform regularization via layer condition numbers and propose a simple recipe: strengthen early-layer protection while allowing deeper layers to adapt. They validate by applying this eigenvalue-aware weighting to EWC and SLCA and reporting improvements.

Result: Theoretical decomposition of forgetting by layer and top Hessian eigenvalues; demonstration that diagonal Fisher cannot capture critical eigenvalue information; identification of a condition-number–dependent cost for uniform regularization; a practical eigenvalue-aware recipe (protect early layers) that yields improved average performance and forgetting metrics when applied to EWC and SLCA.

Conclusion: Layer-wise forgetting is governed by top Hessian eigenvalues; effective continual learning requires eigenvalue-aware regularization that emphasizes early layers. The proposed recipe enhances existing methods (EWC, SLCA) by better balancing stability and plasticity across the network.

Abstract: Continual learning regularizers like EWC fight forgetting by penalizing changes from previous-task parameters with per-parameter importance, typically diagonal Fisher values. Per-parameter looks more flexible than per-layer, but each layer's diagonal Fisher is a weak summary of its actual curvature, missing the top-eigenvalue information that controls forgetting. Adversarial bit-flip attacks and Hessian-spectrum studies show that this missing per-layer sensitivity spans orders of magnitude in neural networks. Under a block-diagonal Hessian assumption, the layer-level analogue of EWC's existing diagonal assumption, we prove three things. Forgetting decomposes as a sum of per-layer terms weighted by each layer's top Hessian eigenvalue. Diagonal-Fisher weights cannot recover this eigenvalue. For instance, two layers with identical Fisher averages can have top eigenvalues differing by a factor as large as the layer width. For the same level of forgetting, uniform regularization loses new-task performance by an amount scaling with the layer condition number. Our theoretical analysis leads to a simple recipe: protect early layers strongly, let deeper layers move. We apply this recipe to EWC and SLCA and show clear improvements in average performance and forgetting metrics.

</details>


### [394] [Information Geometry of Message Passing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15922)
*Mykola Lukashchuk,Kyrylo Yemets,Alex Ledbetter,İsmail Şenöz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NGMP is an edge-local natural-gradient message passing scheme for variational inference on Forney-style factor graphs. It constrains edge marginals to exponential families derived from the Bethe free energy, yielding a stationary condition where the edge natural parameter is the sum of projected messages. It preserves the exact-message portion representable by the receiving family, improving uncertainty calibration over variational message passing, especially in non-conjugate or sequential/batch settings. Demonstrated on Poisson smoothing, heteroskedastic regression, and hourly ETTh forecasting; gains mainly in uncertainty calibration and converge to VMP in conjugate cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve variational inference by leveraging natural-gradient projections to preserve richer representations across edges, particularly for non-conjugate factors and sequential data, thereby improving uncertainty calibration.

Method: Derive from Bethe free energy with an edge marginal constrained to an exponential family. At stationarity, the edge natural parameter equals the sum of two projected messages, each being the natural-gradient projection of the exact BP log-message at the current marginal, equivalently the gradient of its expectation in mean coordinates. This yields a local, edge-specific NGMP rule where each factor's message depends on the receiving marginal. NGMP retains the part of the exact message that the receiving family can represent, unlike VMP which averages the factor under neighboring beliefs. In conjugate cases NGMP coincides with VMP; in non-conjugate or persistent-uncertainty settings NGMP is more accurate.

Result: NGMP provides a local computation framework that improves uncertainty calibration over standard variational message passing. It remains exact in the conjugate limit and outperforms VMP when edge uncertainty persists (e.g., partially observed chains or streaming batches). Empirical validation on Poisson smoothing, heteroskedastic regression, and hourly ETTh forecasting confirms improved uncertainty calibration with NGMP.

Conclusion: NGMP is a flexible, local, edge-aware alternative to VMP for variational inference on factor graphs, especially advantageous in non-conjugate or sequential data regimes. It preserves the representational capacity of the receiving exponential family and yields better uncertainty calibration, with compatibility to standard VMP in conjugate settings.

Abstract: We show that the natural-gradient stationary condition of variational inference has an edge-local form on a Forney-style factor graph. We start from the Bethe free energy and constrain a selected edge marginal to an exponential family. At a stationary point, the natural parameter of that edge equals the sum of two projected messages, one from each incident factor. Each projected message is the natural-gradient projection of the exact belief-propagation log-message at the current receiving marginal, or equivalently, the gradient of its expectation in the so-called mean coordinates. We call the resulting scheme natural-gradient message passing (NGMP). The rule is local; each edge may carry its own exponential family, and the message a factor sends depends on the marginal that receives it. Compared with variational message passing, NGMP keeps the part of the exact message that the receiving family can represent instead of averaging the factor under the neighboring beliefs. The two coincide when the uncertainty on the edges entering a non-conjugate factor vanishes, and NGMP is more accurate when that uncertainty persists, for example, along a partially observed latent chain or when parameters are filtered through successive data batches. Experiments on Poisson smoothing, heteroskedastic regression, and hourly ETTh forecasting confirm this and show that the gain appears mainly in uncertainty calibration.

</details>


### [395] [ReliaGate: Reliability Routing for Low-Stakes Wearable Stress Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15951)
*Jaden Moon,Yu Wu,Arvind Pillai,Andrew Campbell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliaGate is a post-hoc gating mechanism that decides whether to surface or withhold a fixed-label stress prediction, by aggregating cues into a post-hoc correctness score; evaluated on wearable datasets, it shows improved surfaced-label behavior in some benchmarks, but no labeling changes or formal risk guarantees are provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address when to surface a prediction versus withhold it in low-stakes wearable stress monitoring, since simply maximizing aggregate accuracy can hide information gaps and reduce error when withholding may harm users.

Method: After a locked classifier outputs a stress/non-stress label, a post-hoc gate (ReliaGate) uses cues—confidence, signal quality/trust, agreement, train-standardized atypicality, and train-fitted geometry—to compute a correctness score and decide to surface or withhold the label. Evaluation uses four wearable datasets with subject-disjoint folds, validation-selected routing, held-out intervals, and both pooled and per-subject analyses.

Result: ReliaGate tended to outperform baselines on WESAD and UBFC-Phys primary coverage/risk intervals; results on E4 were mixed. The framework enables study of surfaced-label error, availability, and output distribution across subjects, without label revision or explicit clinical/finite-sample risk guarantees.

Conclusion: ReliaGate offers an operational framework to probe surfaced-label error and availability dynamics across individuals in wearable stress monitoring without changing labels or asserting risk guarantees.

Abstract: We study when a wearable stress system should surface a prediction rather than change it. In low-stakes reflection and summary settings, aggregate accuracy is insufficient because withholding can reduce error while leaving some people with little or no information. We formulate fixed-label reliability routing: after a locked classifier emits a protocol-defined stress/non-stress label, a post-hoc gate surfaces that unchanged label or withholds it as unavailable. ReliaGate assembles established confidence, signal-quality/trust, agreement, train-standardized atypicality, and train-fitted geometry cues into a post-hoc correctness score. We evaluate four wearable datasets using subject-disjoint folds, validation-selected routing, paired held-out-subject intervals, and pooled and per-subject analyses. WESAD point estimates favored ReliaGate, UBFC-Phys primary coverage/risk intervals favored ReliaGate, and E4 checks were mixed. ReliaGate provides an operational framework for studying surfaced-label error, output availability, and accepted-output distribution across subjects, without revising labels or providing clinical or finite-sample risk guarantees.

</details>


### [396] [Beat the Counter First: A Baseline for Temporal-Graph Anomaly Detectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15965)
*Omair Shafi Ahmed,Zohair Shafi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A simple, parameter-free baseline (SimpleCount) using a single informative feature per dataset can outperform complex streaming GAD detectors, challenging the value of added modeling complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically evaluate whether the performance gains from complex architectures in streaming GAD justify increased computation; to establish a strong, simple baseline for comparison.

Method: Introduce SimpleCount selecting one scalar feature per dataset from a fixed pool; compare against two temporal-graph detectors and an IsoForest across six datasets (five public, one synthetic); perform paired tests, five-seed SLADE runs; report wall-clock time.

Result: SimpleCount matches/exceeds SLADE on 3/6 datasets and exceeds IsoForest on all 6; SLADE is 23–133x slower; on synthetic datasets pre-event structural scores recover signal up to AUC 0.955; other detectors near random; effect is dataset-dependent.

Conclusion: Added complexity yields mixed benefits; advocate reporting gains relative to a strong one-feature baseline with its compute cost.

Abstract: Progress in streaming, edge-level graph anomaly detection (GAD) has been marked by increasingly elaborate architectures, from count-min-sketch chi square tests to memory-augmented attention networks. Yet the empirical gains attributable to this added complexity have not been systematically evaluated. We propose SimpleCount, a reference with no parameter fitting that selects one scalar feature per dataset from a fixed pool of counts, recencies, first-occurrence indicators, and count-derived transforms. We compare SimpleCount with two temporal-graph detector models and an IsoForest control fitted to the complete feature vector across five public datasets and one synthetic dataset. SimpleCount matches or exceeds SLADE on three of six datasets and exceeds IsoForest on all six. We report paired statistical tests and five-seed SLADE evaluations. SLADE requires 23 to 133x more wall-clock time than SimpleCount. On Synth-Triangle and an additional Synth-Quad probe, pre-event structural scores recover the planted signal at AUC up to 0.955, while all evaluated detector models remain near random. The benefit of complexity is dataset-dependent, and every claimed gain should be reported against a strong one-feature reference together with its compute cost.

</details>


### [397] [A Banach-Space Theory of Markovian Halpern Iteration for Non-Expansive Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15966)
*Ege C. Kaya,Arda Fazla,M. Berk Sahin,Abolfazl Hashemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Variance-reduced Markovian Halpern-type method achieves O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity for fixed-point problems of non-expansive operators, extending from Hilbert to Banach spaces, with high-probability guarantees via norm smoothing and Poisson-equation analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently computing fixed points when oracle samples come from dependent (Markovian) trajectories; vanilla Halpern with Markovian noise has high sample complexity. Need better variance reduction and generalization to Banach spaces.

Method: Introduce variance-reduced Markovian PAGE-Halpern algorithm with refresh and same-state difference blocks; analyze via Poisson equation; displacement-level Halpern bound; extend to finite-dimensional Banach spaces; measure estimator in auxiliary smooth norm to obtain high-probability guarantees; cover non-smooth geometries via norm smoothing.

Result: In Hilbert spaces, O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity; general finite-dimensional Banach spaces with displacement-level bound in the original non-expansiveness norm; high-probability guarantee with the same dependence; non-smooth geometries handled via smoothing.

Conclusion: Provides a substantial improvement over direct block-minibatch Halpern under Markovian sampling; offers a general, variance-reduced, norm-adaptive framework for fixed-point iterations of non-expansive operators, with broad applicability in stochastic optimization and learning.

Abstract: We study stochastic approximation of fixed points of a non-expansive operator when the oracle samples originate from a continuing Markovian trajectory. A direct block-minibatch implementation of Halpern iteration attains an expected last-iterate residual of order $O(\log N/N)$, but accrues a substantive complexity of $\tilde O(ε^{-5})$ Markovian samples. We therefore introduce a variance-reduced Markovian PAGE-Halpern method whose refresh and same-state difference blocks are analyzed through the Poisson equation. In Hilbert spaces, the cocoercivity of $I-T$ results in an $O(ε^{-3})$ sample complexity. Our main result extends this construction to a general finite-dimensional Banach space. A displacement-level Halpern bound replaces the Hilbert-space potential and yields $\tilde O(ε^{-3})$ sample complexity in the original non-expansiveness norm. We also establish a high-probability guarantee with the same leading accuracy dependence by measuring the estimator in an auxiliary smooth norm. Non-smooth sup and block-sup geometries are covered through norm smoothing.

</details>


### [398] [The Limits of Binding in Dual Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15971)
*Kin Ian Lo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dual-encoder binding failures in CLIP-like systems can be explained by depth/geometry constraints under an ideal-encoder model. Three obstructions yield exact laws (e.g., swap margin m(D)=2 b^{-D}) and a depth that grows logarithmically with dimension; the training objective bounds binding rewards by the rate of contrasting a caption with its swap, which vanishes at web scale. Empirically, text-only diagnostics show models operate at 25–35% of their theoretical ceiling, indicating failures are incentive/code-structure limits, not fundamental dimensional limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when dual-encoder binding failures are necessary versus contingent, and to provide a mathematical framework that isolates the structural/topical causes of binding errors in CLIP-like models, with predictions that can be tested across encoders and scales.

Method: Within Kang et al.'s ideal-encoder framework, first show the axioms are satisfiable. Then derive three obstructions to binding: (1) a depth-dependent swap margin law m(D)=2 b^{-D} for recursive role-binding codes; (2) resolvable depth grows only logarithmically with dimension with a single explicit concentration bound; (3) objective throttle theorems bounding the binding-relevant reward by the rate of contrasting a caption with its own swap, which vanishes at web scale; simulations verify the theorems. Also establish a tight smoothness-binding frontier and a constant relating embedding proximity to a paraphrase anchor to the binding margin.

Result: Three formal obstructions yielding exact laws: depth-bound swap margins m(D)=2 b^{-D} for nesting depth D and logarithmic growth of resolvable depth with dimension; the contrastive objective’s binding reward is bounded by the self-swap contrasting rate (vanishing at scale), with the cost of reversed binding proportional to that rate times the mean binding margin. Empirically, a text-only diagnostic across 18 encoders shows ~25–35% of the ceiling, and the per-item ceiling tracks a task difficulty proxy at high correlation. Binding failure in deployed dual encoders is thus framed as an incentive/code-structure limit, with a fixed depth ceiling.

Conclusion: Binding failure is not a fundamental dimension or smoothness limit, but a structural/incentive limit set by architecture and training dynamics. The results imply that to mitigate binding failures one must modify code structure or enable explicit binding mechanisms, as the depth ceiling persists once those factors are fixed.

Abstract: Dual-encoder models such as CLIP score an image-caption pair by a single inner product of two independently computed unit vectors, and fail at binding, often scoring near chance when asked to distinguish "a red car and a blue dog" from "a blue car and a red dog". We give a mathematical account of when this failure is necessary and when it is contingent. Working within the ideal-encoder framework proposed by Kang et al., we first show the relevant axioms are satisfiable, so every impossibility must enter through an added, checkable hypothesis. We then prove three such obstructions. Depth: for recursive role-binding codes the swap margin obeys an exact law $m(D) = 2b^{-D}$ in the nesting depth D, with a finite-dimension version holding up to one explicitly flagged concentration estimate; the resolvable depth grows only logarithmically in the dimension and is single-digit at CLIP scale, the nesting depth of ordinary language. Objective: architecture-free throttle theorems showing that the contrastive objective's entire reward for binding is bounded by the rate at which training contrasts a caption against its own swap, a rate that vanishes at web scale, and that exactly reversed binding costs only that rate times the mean binding margin; both are verified in simulation. Geometry: a tight smoothness-binding frontier: the closer the two swap-related captions must embed to a shared paraphrase anchor, the smaller the binding margin can be, with an exact constant. Measuring its text-only diagnostic across 18 deployed text encoders, every model sits at roughly 25-35% of its ceiling, and the induced per-item ceiling tracks SugarCrepe's subset difficulty at r = 0.99. Binding failure in deployed dual encoders is thus not a dimension or smoothness limit today, but an incentive and code-structure limit, with a proved depth ceiling that remains once those are fixed.

</details>


### [399] [Fiber Fingerprints of Hidden Learning-State Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15976)
*Qinyou Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Present behavior is not a sufficient statistic for described future learning; fiber fingerprints and predictive quotient formalize how future-learning responses can diverge within present-behavior equivalence classes, yielding a minimal predictive representation and canonical predictive fiber.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify and bound what information about history is needed to predict future learning in learning systems, by formalizing equivalence classes of present behavior and their restricted future-learning laws.

Method: Introduce fiber fingerprints and prefix-compatible finite probes; construct a predictive quotient functor; obtain a Nerode-type minimal recursively sufficient representation; define a canonical set-level predictive fiber without assuming smoothness, reversibility, finite rank, or manifold; under a finite-dimensional Hilbert realization decompose response into visible, visible-mode-reuse, and irreducible-new sectors; build a history-reachability bridge; derive graph-Hodge chronology decomposition, a regular switching class with RMS scale sqrt(p) η^{3/2} and finite-scale corrections, and an exact Adam moment section; support claims with Frozen Transformer–LoRA–AdamW studies on Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3.

Result: Reveal a decomposition of response into distinct sectors and a precise bound structure; establish a history-reachability bridge; identify a graph-Hodge chronology decomposition and an Adam moment section; provide boundary conditions where stronger claims fail (e.g., transport, Hodge conjunction, Qwen accessibility, Mistral revelation); demonstrate that under explicit constraints, present behavior is not a sufficient statistic for future learning.

Conclusion: Within the outlined support-, scale-, metric-, and context-resolved boundaries, present behavior does not uniquely determine declared future learning; the framework yields a principled, minimal, and decomposed view of learning dynamics along with explicit limitations.

Abstract: A learning system can occupy execution states that are indistinguishable under every declared present-behavior readout yet respond differently to future training. We formalize this through fiber fingerprints: controlled future-learning response laws restricted to present-behavior equivalence classes. Prefix-compatible finite probes induce a predictive quotient functor, a Nerode-type minimal recursively sufficient representation, and a canonical set-level predictive fiber without assuming smoothness, reversibility, finite rank, or a manifold. Under an explicit finite-dimensional Hilbert realization, response decomposes into visible, visible-mode-reuse, and irreducible-new sectors; a history-reachability bridge retains only distinctions generated by natural training histories. Conditional mechanism results then identify a graph-Hodge chronology decomposition, a regular switching class with root-mean-square scale $\sqrt{p}η^{3/2}$ and finite-scale corrections, and an exact Adam moment section whose immediate adaptive field is constant while common future gradients can reveal hidden moment differences. Frozen Transformer--LoRA--AdamW studies with Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 support a local action backbone, longer-horizon first-return non-closure, and fresh visible-relative completion with output-range reuse and a low-rank irreducible sector. Stronger claims remain bounded by preregistered negative or mixed results: re-anchored transport is unresolved above its measurement floor; the strict finite-grid Hodge--$3/2$ conjunction is unmet despite prospective contraction; Qwen accessibility is not established in the frozen raw moment chart; and Mistral revelation is future-context dependent rather than bank invariant. Within these support-, scale-, metric-, and context-resolved boundaries, present behavior is not a sufficient statistic for declared future learning.

</details>


### [400] [Operator-Theoretic Generalization Bounds for Multitask Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15982)
*Mahdi Mohammadigohari,Thomas Borsani,Giuseppe Di Fatta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Operator-theoretic generalization bounds for deep multi-output nets via Koopman operators on vector-valued RKHSs; analyzes Sobolev and Brownian regimes; provides finite-rank representer and target-transfer results; empirical proxies tested on synthetic and MNIST.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Develop a unified, operator-based framework to bound generalization in deep multi-output architectures by representing layers as Koopman composition operators on vector-valued RKHSs, and to compare Sobolev-RKHS and Brownian/Cameron–Martin regimes.

Method: Represent network layers as Koopman composition operators in vector-valued Sobolev RKHSs; derive Rademacher complexity bounds separating output-coupling (task matrix trace) from layerwise operator norms, Sobolev symbol ratios, determinant factors, and restriction constants; analyze a Brownian regime via anchored derivative-norm in vector-valued Brownian RKHS; obtain layerwise bounds with scaling |W_l|^{1/2} and ||σ_l'||_∞^{1/2}; prove finite-rank representer theorem for shared operator learning; derive exact finite-dimensional squared-loss problem; establish a target-transfer bound when the learned operator is independent of the target sample; propose empirical Sobolev-inspired and Brownian-inspired proxies.

Result: Bounds that separate output coupling from operator-norm/symbol/determinant factors; Brownian regime yields layerwise bounds with sqrt-scaling in layer widths and activation derivatives; neither Sobolev nor Brownian bounds dominate across hypothesis spaces; finite-rank representer theorem; reduction to a finite-dimensional squared-loss problem; target-transfer bound; empirical studies show stabilized proxies and MNIST tests, but do not directly evaluate the proven bounds for rank-deficient architectures.

Conclusion: The work offers complementary, regime-dependent generalization guarantees for multi-output networks via operator-theoretic methods, enabling shared operator learning and finite-dimensional training formulations; empirical proxies provide practical intuition but do not supersede the formal bounds for certain architectures.

Abstract: We develop operator-theoretic generalization bounds for deep multi-output function classes by representing network layers as Koopman composition operators on vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In vector-valued Sobolev RKHSs, we derive Rademacher complexity bounds for invertible and width-expanding injective architectures. The estimates separate the output-coupling contribution, represented by the trace of the task matrix, from the layerwise operator norms, Sobolev symbol ratios, determinant factors, and restriction constants generated by the linear maps. We then analyze a distinct one-dimensional Brownian/Cameron--Martin regime. Using the exact anchored derivative-norm characterization of the vector-valued Brownian RKHS, we obtain layerwise bounds for domain-preserving scalar linear maps and anchored diffeomorphic activations; the corresponding factors scale as $|W_l|^{1/2}$ and $\|σ_l'\|_\infty^{1/2}$, respectively, and do not involve Sobolev smoothness exponents. Because the Sobolev and Brownian results concern different hypothesis spaces, neither is asserted to dominate the other uniformly. We additionally formulate shared operator learning across tasks, prove a finite-rank representer theorem, derive the exact finite-dimensional problem for squared loss, and establish a target-transfer bound when the learned operator is obtained independently of the target sample. Synthetic and MNIST studies examine stabilized Sobolev-inspired and Brownian-inspired complexity proxies; these empirical proxies are not evaluations of the proved bounds for rank-deficient architectures.

</details>


### [401] [Toward Optimal Second-Order Path-Length Guarantee for Adversarial Multi-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15996)
*Mengxiao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper closes the gap on second-order path-length regret for adversarial K-armed bandits by showing the Bubeck et al. (2019) algorithm attains near-optimal regret with known and unknown second-order path length Q_{∞,2}.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address whether a poly(K) sqrt(1+Q_{∞,2}) regret bound is achievable under bandit feedback for second-order path length, improving upon the O(K + sqrt{K Q_{∞,1}}) baseline and matching a square-root lower bound up to logs and constants.

Method: A refined analysis of the Bubeck et al. (2019) algorithm to bound the regret in terms of K, T, and (1+Q_{∞,2}); for the unknown-Q_{∞,2} case, an adaptive restart scheme with a path-length estimator with uniformly bounded increments.

Result: For known Q_{∞,2}, the algorithm achieves O(K log(KT) + sqrt{K log(KT) (1+Q_{∞,2})}) expected regret, matching the Ω(√(K Q_{∞,2})) lower bound up to logs and additive terms. The unknown Q_{∞,2} case is handled by adaptive restart ensuring the same form up to constants.

Conclusion: The open question is resolved: second-order path-length regret in adversarial bandits is achievable with near-optimal dependence on K, T, and Q_{∞,2}, and the adaptive restart scheme removes the need for prior knowledge of Q_{∞,2}.

Abstract: We study second-order path-length regret in adversarial $K$-armed bandits against oblivious loss sequences. Bubeck et al. [2019] designed an algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K+\sqrt{KQ_{\infty,1}})$ regret, where $Q_{\infty,1}$ is the first-order path length, and left open whether $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\text{poly}(K)\sqrt{1+Q_{\infty,2}})$ regret is achievable under bandit feedback, where $Q_{\infty,2}$ is the second-order path length. Somewhat surprisingly, we resolve this question positively by showing that with a more involved analysis, the exact same algorithm of Bubeck et al. [2019] achieves $\mathcal{O}\left(K\log(KT)+\sqrt{K\log(KT)\bigl(1+Q_{\infty,2}\bigr)}\right)$ expected regret when $Q_{\infty,2}$ is known, where $T$ is the horizon. This matches the $Ω(\sqrt{KQ_{\infty,2}})$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors and additive terms. We further remove the knowledge of $Q_{\infty,2}$ using an adaptive restart scheme whose path-length estimator has uniformly bounded increments.

</details>


### [402] [Retrieval-guided Twin Fusion with Similarity-aware Contrast for Molecule-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16005)
*Shunshun Gu,Shengqi Qiu,Hang Zhou,Xiao Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RISEN introduces retrieval-guided twin fusion with similarity-aware contrast for molecule–text alignment, forming twin latent representations per substructure by cross-modal retrieval and attention pooling, and using soft-thresholded contrastive learning to leverage fine-grained substructure–text semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior methods combining graph mining with contrastive learning neglect fine-grained semantic relations between substructures and texts, limiting downstream performance in molecule search and property prediction.

Method: For each substructure query, retrieve relevant textual descriptions and sample molecules sharing similar substructure descriptions; aggregate these via attention pooling to create a twin latent representation that is fused with the original substructure; compute cross-substructure/text similarity to guide cross-modal contrastive learning with soft thresholding.

Result: Empirical results on benchmark datasets show RISEN outperforms existing baselines in molecule-text alignment tasks.

Conclusion: RISEN effectively captures fine-grained substructure–text semantics through retrieval-guided twin fusion and similarity-aware contrast, boosting performance on downstream molecule-text tasks.

Abstract: This paper studies the problem of molecule-text alignment, which aims to project molecules and their textual descriptions into a joint latent space for downstream tasks including molecule search and molecular property prediction. Previous approaches typically combine graph structure mining with contrastive learning to enhance joint representation learning. However, they typically neglect fine-grained semantic relationships between substructures and texts, leading to suboptimal performance on downstream tasks. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Retrieval-guided Twin Fusion with Similarity-aware Contrast (RISEN) for molecule-text alignment. The core idea of RISEN is to construct a latent twin molecule for each substructure with cross-modal retrieval for semantic enhancement. In particular, for each substructure query, we retrieve relevant textual descriptions and sample several molecules that share similar descriptions of substructures. Then, we aggregate their representations via attention pooling for a twin latent representation, which would be further fused with the original substructure for representation enrichment. In addition, we measure the similarity across substructures and texts, which would further guide cross-modal contrastive learning with soft thresholding. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the superiority of the proposed RISEN in comparison with existing baselines.

</details>


### [403] [Breaking the Compression Barrier: Cross-Architecture Compression Boundary Learning via Reverse Regrowth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16010)
*Zhaocen Liu,Satvik Praveen,Yi Sheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BRIDGE reframes model pruning as a boundary-search problem via reverse regrowth, pushing models to extreme sparsity to reveal collapse regions and then selectively regenerating critical parameters to extend the feasible compression limit across CNNs and Transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pruning often yields abrupt performance degradation beyond a sparsity threshold, making it hard to identify how far a model can be compressed without loss. Forward pruning tends to miss the collapse boundary and risks unstable performance; a method that reveals and crosses this boundary is needed.

Method: BRIDGE first drives the model to an extremely sparse state to expose the collapse region, then performs hierarchical regeneration to recover performance. Regeneration proceeds at two levels: coarse-grained layer selection to identify which parts to regrow, and fine-grained parameter selection to recover the critical parameters. The approach is architecture-agnostic and aims to locate the minimal regenerations required to restore accuracy.

Result: Empirical evaluation on CNNs and Transformer architectures shows BRIDGE can recover models from near-collapse, demonstrating architecture-independence. It yields up to 1.49% improvement for unstructured pruning and up to 4.77% for structured pruning compared with baselines. The authors provide the source code at the given repository.

Conclusion: Reverse regeneration can effectively extend the compression limit while maintaining stable performance, offering a general, architecture-agnostic framework for pushing prune-induced sparsity further without catastrophic performance drops.

Abstract: Model compression is critical for deploying networks on resource-constrained edge devices. While pruning-based methods can significantly reduce model size, they often suffer from abrupt performance collapse beyond a sparsity thresh-old, making it difficult to identify the feasible compression limit of the model. To address this challenge, we propose a boundary-Learning reverse regrowth framework, BRIDGE, that reformulates compression as a constructive boundary-search problem. Unlike forward pruning, our method first drives the model to an extremely sparse state to expose the collapse region, and then selectively regenerates the critical structure to restore performance. The proposed framework employs a hierarchical regeneration strategy, including coarse-grained layer selection and fine-grained regeneration parameter selection, to accurately identify which parameters require recovery. Experiments show that our method can recover models from the brink of collapse on both CNNs and Transformer architectures, demonstrating its architecture in-dependence. BRIDGE achieves a performance improvement of up to 1.49% in unstructured pruning and up to 4.77% in structured pruning. These results demonstrate that reverse regeneration can effectively extend the compression limit while maintaining stable performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/EnumaCaliber/BRIDGE.

</details>


### [404] [RagGAD: Rationale-Aware Conditional Gaussian Mixture Normalizing Flow for Unsupervised Graph Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16018)
*Junxin Lu,Jing Zhao,Shiliang Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unsupervised graph anomaly detection RagGAD uses rationale-aware conditional Gaussian mixture normalizing flow to separate stable, robust rationales from spurious correlations, enabling robust detection of anomalies as low-density regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address reliance on homophily and difficulties distinguishing spurious affinities while capturing diverse normal behaviors; improve robustness in complex real-world graphs.

Method: Adaptive rationale disentangler that separates stable rationales from spurious correlations and decomposes rationales into robust and fragile components. Models rationale-non-rationale distributions with Gaussian mixture modeling and employs a robust-fragile rationale mixture learning strategy within a structure-aware distribution space.

Result: Empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets shows RagGAD achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing methods in unsupervised graph anomaly detection.

Conclusion: Mitigates spurious homophily and embraces heterogeneity of normal patterns; anomalies are identified as low-density regions in a structure-aware distribution built from robust and fragile rationales.

Abstract: Graph anomaly detection aims to identify nodes that deviate from normal behavioral patterns within graphs. However, existing methods largely rely on the homophily assumption, which makes it difficult to distinguish spurious affinities and to capture the diverse behaviors of normal nodes,limiting their robustness in complex real-world scenarios. To address this problem, we propose RagGAD, an unsupervised graph anomaly detection framework based on rationale-aware conditional Gaussian mixture normalizing flow. RagGAD introduces an adaptive rationale disentangler to disentangle stable rationales from spurious correlations within node interrelationships, and further decomposes stable rationales into robust and fragile components. The learned rationales capture underlying interaction patterns that characterize normal behaviors under varying conditions, while anomalies emerge as deviations associated with unstable or spurious correlations. To model the intricate distributions of normal and abnormal nodes, RagGAD integrates rationale-non-rationale Gaussian mixture modeling with a robust-fragile rationale mixture learning strategy. By mitigating spurious homophilic correlations and embracing the heterogeneity of normal patterns, RagGAD identifies anomalies as low-density regions within a structure-aware distribution space. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RagGAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [405] [Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16072)
*Yixuan Wang,Yifei Chen,Haichao Zhang,Haozheng Luo,Xander Wu,Jie Ni,Yun Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos,Yijiang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization (SA-MRPO) for RL-based LM reasoning; adapts per-objective saturation to reweight gradients, improving harder objectives while preserving easier ones across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scalarizing multi-objective rewards with a fixed weighted sum (and standardization) yields ineffective gradient distribution: distinct reward profiles can share the same advantage, and weights stay fixed despite objective saturation, wasting updates on already-satisfied objectives.

Method: Introduce SA-MRPO: independently standardize each reward objective and apply batch-level saturation-based discounting to its contribution; can even flip update sign; evaluated on two- and three-objective setups across mathematical reasoning, adaptive reasoning, and coding tasks.

Result: SA-MRPO yields consistent improvements: 12/15 benchmarks for 2-3 objective math reasoning vs GDPO; up to +5% on AIME24; adaptive reasoning: avg +3.8%, up to +9.2% on AMC23; coding: up to +2.3% pass rate; maintains performance on easier objectives.

Conclusion: Saturation-aware reweighting reallocates optimization effort toward under-optimized objectives, improves hard objectives while keeping easy ones satisfied; the method may reverse the update direction, and shows broad gains across domains.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with group-relative advantages has become the de facto standard for post-training language model reasoners. However, when optimizing multiple reward objectives, existing methods typically scalarize the reward vector with a fixed weighted sum before group-wise standardization. We show that this design leads to two fundamental problems: rollouts with distinct reward profiles can receive identical advantages, and all objectives are optimized with fixed relative weights regardless of their current level of saturation. As a result, training continues to allocate gradient budget to already-solved objectives instead of focusing on those with greater remaining headroom. We introduce \textbf{Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization} (SA-MRPO), which standardizes each reward objective independently and adaptively discounts its contribution according to a batch-level estimate of objective saturation. This dynamically reallocates optimization effort toward under-optimized objectives while empirically maintaining performance on those that are already well satisfied. We further show that saturation-aware reweighting can reverse the sign of an update, rather than merely rescale its magnitude. Across mathematical reasoning with two- and three-objective reward combinations, SA-MRPO improves the harder correctness objective over GDPO in 12 of 15 benchmark comparisons, with gains of up to $5\%$ on AIME24. On adaptive reasoning it improves accuracy on all five benchmarks, by $3.8\%$ on average and up to $9.2 \%$ on AMC23, and on coding benchmarks it improves pass rate by up to $2.3\%$, while in all settings maintaining the easier objectives near their already satisfied levels.

</details>


### [406] [DeepOHeat-v2: Self-Improving Operator Learning for Fast and Trustworthy Thermal Optimization in 3D-IC Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16080)
*Xinling Yu,Yixing Li,Ziyue Liu,Xin Ai,Zhiyu Zeng,Hai Li,Zheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeepOHeat-v2 delivers a fast, accurate surrogate for thermal optimization in high-contrast multi-die 3D ICs by combining a discretized physics loss that handles material interfaces with improved conditioning, a matrix-preconditioned optimizer, and a self-improving retraining loop guided by a hotspot trust gate; achieves near-solve accuracy (0.11 K peak-gap) with ~56× speedup over solving at every step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing physics-surrogate approaches struggle with high-contrast geometries due to discontinuous conductivities and severe ill-conditioning, causing inaccurate surrogates and optimization failure. There is a need for robust, fast surrogates that preserve physics across interfaces and adapt to design-distribution shifts.

Method: 1) Train on a discretized physics loss that naturally handles conductivity discontinuities via an energy form. 2) Use this form to reduce the prediction-space loss-Hessian conditioning from κ^2 to κ. 3) Employ a matrix-preconditioned optimizer to improve convergence and accuracy (mean peak temp error reduced from >30 K to 0.55 K). 4) Implement a self-improving framework: a hotspot trust gate flags placements and queries a reference solver; the surrogate retrains on refined solutions, updating only if validation error improves. 5) Evaluate on a multi-die benchmark comparing surrogate results to full solves.

Result: On a multi-die benchmark, the surrogate-true peak gap drops from 1.12 K to 0.11 K, matching a solve-at-every-step optimizer, with a 56× speedup over full solves.

Conclusion: DeepOHeat-v2 effectively addresses the challenges of high-contrast multi-die 3D IC thermal optimization by integrating a discontinuity-aware physics loss, conditioning-aware optimization, and a self-improving retraining loop, yielding high-accuracy results with substantial run-time savings.

Abstract: Thermal-aware optimization of multi-die 3D integrated circuits evaluates many designs, each a costly heat-equation solve. Operator-learning surrogates replace this solve with a fast forward pass, ideally trained from physics alone, without labeled data. DeepOHeat-v1 made such surrogates fast and trustworthy, but only on low-contrast geometries. High-contrast multi-die stacks break it in two ways: discontinuous conductivities make the continuous physics loss ill-defined at material interfaces, and ill-conditioning ($κ_2(A_h) \approx 6 \times 10^4$) puts the discretized strong-form loss beyond first-order optimization. We propose DeepOHeat-v2 to overcome both. First, we train on a discretized physics loss that handles the discontinuities natively; its energy form reduces the prediction-space loss-Hessian conditioning from $κ^2$ to $κ$, and a matrix-preconditioned optimizer cuts the mean peak temperature error from over 30 K to 0.55 K. Second, because optimization leaves the training distribution, we propose a self-improving framework: a hotspot trust gate sends flagged placements to a reference solver, and the surrogate incrementally retrains on the refined solutions, keeping an update only when it improves held-out validation error. On a multi-die benchmark, the surrogate-true peak gap on the returned design falls from 1.12 K to 0.11 K, matching a solve-at-every-step optimizer while running $56\times$ faster.

</details>


### [407] [Towards Reasonable Molecular Structure Elucidation from Infrared Spectroscopy with Chemical Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16082)
*Yusen Tan,Hongyu Zhan,Hai-tao Yu,Changxi Chi,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A model-agnostic, feedback-driven optimization framework (FIRMPO) that enforces exact formula matching and IR spectral consistency to improve molecular structure elucidation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address failures where ML-predicted candidate structures violate chemical constraints (formula or IR), leading to unreliable top predictions.

Method: Formula- and IR-Matched Preference Optimization (FIRMPO) provides chemical feedback as preference signals based on exact molecular formula matching and IR spectral consistency, and is plug-and-play with different structure prediction models.

Result: Extensive experiments on three IR datasets show substantial improvements in top-ranked structure elucidation accuracy over baselines.

Conclusion: FIRMPO offers a general, model-agnostic approach to enforce chemical constraints in structure elucidation, improving reliability and accuracy.

Abstract: Infrared (IR) spectra provide characteristic signals of molecular structure, which are often interpreted by experts via functional-group identification or library matching, making the process time-consuming and ambiguous. Recent machine learning methods have made progress in molecular structure elucidation using molecular formulas and IR spectra. However, these models often infer unreasonable candidate molecular structures, including top-ranked predictions. More specifically, the molecular formula implied by a candidate structure often fails to match the input molecular formula, and the candidate's theoretical IR spectrum is often inconsistent with the observed IR spectrum. To address these issues, we propose Formula- and IR-Matched Preference Optimization (FIRMPO), a general and plug-and-play chemical feedback-driven preference optimization framework for molecular structure elucidation. FIRMPO incorporates chemical feedback as preference signals based on exact molecular formula matching and IR spectral consistency to guide reasonable structure predictions. Unlike generic preference optimization methods, FIRMPO is tailored to molecular structure elucidation while remaining model-agnostic, enabling it to be readily integrated with different structure prediction models in this class. This encourages models to prioritize structures that satisfy the chemical feedback, leading to a substantial improvement in the accuracy of top-ranked predictions. Extensive experiments on three widely used IR datasets show that FIRMPO significantly improves molecular structure elucidation accuracy over existing baselines.

</details>


### [408] [Behaviour Is an Incomplete Measure of Reasoning Development: Cross-surface pre-arrival accessibility and the limits of developmental inference in a recurrent-depth reasoner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16085)
*Simon Lam-Muir*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Behavioural thresholds and decoder readouts do not coherently identify the same cognitive event; in a 30M-parameter model, behaviour, internal probes, and training-time signals diverge, with early internal signals not reliably predicting trained computation; causal interventions are needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Disentangle how observable proxies (behavior, internal probes, training-time signals) relate to underlying computation in a controlled model, evaluating whether common proxies reflect actual acquired capability.

Method: Evaluate a 30M-parameter recurrent-depth relational reasoner in a closed (oracle-defined) world using dense behavioral trajectories, two training surfaces, preregistered pre-arrival hidden-state probes, and explicit untrained/negative controls; separate training-time and inference-time axes; compare symbolic vs verbal surfaces; assess pre-arrival accessibility and its relation to behavior; apply statistical tests against baselines; examine the relation between observed proxies and the trained computation.

Result: Behaviorally, the model shows large differences across surfaces: three-hop competence requires 70 symbolic epochs but 13,055 epochs on the verbal surface, a 186.5x discrepancy; four-hop verbal competence emerges early (8 logical epochs), yet four-hop held-out behavior remains extremely low (0–3/40). Internal probes reveal pre-arrival identity signals (approx. 0.056 vs chance 0.025; p=0.013) and untrained-control baselines similar; pre-arrival accessibility is present upstream (0.102 vs 0.046 zero-step; p=0.001) and at readout (0.062; p=0.004) for a subset of 21/40 classes. However, tracking accessibility across training is not cleanly evaluable because probe eligibility depends on behavioral arrival and measurand; population-level changes are confounded. Overall, behavioural competence, internal accessibility, and training-time development are distinct observables; neither behavior nor decoder accessibility fully identifies the trained computation; causal intervention is the necessary next step.”

Conclusion: The study shows a dissociation between observable proxies and the underlying trained computation, highlighting the need for causal interventions to establish the relationship between training, internal signals, and behavior.

Abstract: Capability development is routinely inferred from behavioural thresholds, from final checkpoints, or from what a decoder can read out of a hidden state. These quantities need not identify the same event. We study a 30M-parameter recurrent-depth relational reasoner in a closed, oracle-defined world, using dense behavioural trajectories, two training surfaces, preregistered pre-arrival hidden-state probes, prospectively checked evaluability, and explicit untrained and negative controls, holding the training-time and inference-time axes separate throughout. Behaviour first: under one frozen acquisition criterion, three-hop competence cost 70 logical epochs on the symbolic surface and 13,055 on the verbal surface, a 186.5-fold contrast, after which verbal four-hop competence cleared in 8 logical epochs. Across the 13,055-epoch grind, four-hop held-out behaviour never exceeded 3/40 and ended at 0/40. Internal measurement next: on the verbal surface a linear probe recovered future-answer identity before behavioural arrival at 0.056159 against uniform chance 0.025, an untrained control of 0.024758 and a population frequency baseline of 0.048309 (p = 0.012987; 16/40 answer classes contributing). Analogous pre-arrival accessibility survived the surface change, reaching 0.1020 against a zero-step control of 0.0460 (p = 0.000999) at the upstream structural position and 0.0618 at the readout comparator (p = 0.004), with 21/40 classes contributing. Finally, the natural attempt to track that accessibility across training was not cleanly evaluable: probe eligibility is defined by behavioural arrival, so the measured population changes with the measurand. Behavioural competence, internal accessibility, and training-time development are distinct observables, and neither behaviour nor decoder accessibility identifies the computation training acquired; causal intervention is the necessary next step.

</details>


### [409] [Unifying Graph Neural Networks Through a Common Layer Equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16097)
*Sai Karthik Navuluru,Siddhartha Shankar Das,Bo Ni,Hongjie Chen,Yu Wang,Baris Coskunuzer,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Franck Dernoncourt,Mahantesh Halappanavar,Tyler Derr,Ryan A. Rossi,Lakshman Tamil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unifying seven-component layer equation for GNNs separates where information moves from what moves, unifying 200+ architectures via function-valued fillings and a fixed-slot discipline, and linking propagation choices to oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and expressivity; it enables component-wise design, comparison, and an empirical inverse problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph neural networks use diverse, bespoke formalisms; a common, checkable design space reveals shared computations, clarifies architectural differences, and supports principled architecture design and analysis.

Method: Introduce a common layer equation with seven components: update domain, channel set, propagation bank, per-channel message maps, channel-fusion operator, ego/residual map, and update map. Distinguish information movement (propagation bank) from content movement (message maps). Use function-valued fillings to cover local message passing, attention, spectral filtering, global communication, relation-specific channels, higher-order domains, and geometric messages. Demonstrate reductions of canonical layers and component assignments across seven nonexclusive architectural families; enforce a fixed-slot discipline to assign operations.

Result: The framework organizes more than 200 architectures in a common space, enables component-wise comparison and generation of structurally consistent architectures, and connects propagation choices to phenomena such as oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and expressivity. It also yields theoretical insights (e.g., operator bounds for one-layer dependencies and global mixing under certain hypotheses) and highlights an empirical inverse problem linking graph/task properties to component choices.

Conclusion: A unified, checkable design space for GNNs that clarifies shared computations, guides architecture design, and provides both theoretical and empirical guidance for selecting components based on task properties.

Abstract: Graph neural networks are commonly described through family-specific equations whose notation obscures shared computations and structural differences. We introduce a common layer equation that represents covered architectures through seven components: an update domain, channel set, propagation bank, per-channel message maps, channel-fusion operator, ego/residual map, and update map. The central factorization separates where information moves, encoded by the propagation bank, from what moves, encoded by the message maps. Function-valued fillings extend the same equation across local message passing, attention, spectral filtering, global communication, relation-specific channels, higher-order domains, and geometric messages.
  We make this unification explicit and checkable through worked reductions of canonical layers and component assignments spanning seven nonexclusive architectural families. A fixed slot discipline assigns operations by computational role and defines the framework's coverage boundary. The decomposition also yields component-level theoretical insights: under endpoint-local messages and node-local updates, operator support bounds one-layer dependencies, and one-layer global mixing requires a full effective operator row under the stated hypotheses.
  The resulting framework organizes more than 200 architectures in a common design space, enables component-wise comparison and generation of structurally consistent architectures, and connects propagation choices to oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophily, and expressivity. It further exposes the empirical inverse problem of mapping measurable graph and task properties to validated component choices.

</details>


### [410] [AsyTO: Asymmetric Temporal Operator for Parameter-Efficient Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16098)
*Xiachong Lin,Du Yin,Hao Xue,Wen Hu,Imran Razzak,Arian Prabowo,Matthew Amos,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AsyTO offers a lightweight, per-variable operator-based framework for multivariate forecasting that factorizes per-variable operators into shared temporal modes with per-variable gains, achieving strong accuracy with linear parameter growth and favorable Pareto trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Typical dilemma in multivariate forecasting: sharing one temporal predictor across variables reduces parameters but constrains history-to-future mappings; learning independent predictors scales badly with variables. The paper reframes the problem by compressing the forecasting operator, not the data, and shows residual, phase-locked seasonal structure is effective.

Method: Introduce AsyTO: factorize the per-variable operator tensor into shared history-reading and future-writing temporal modes with per-variable mode gains; incorporate a low-rank periodic prototype and cycle-separable factorization; end-to-end forecasts use only each variable's history; parameter count grows linearly with number of variables.

Result: Empirical evaluation on eleven benchmarks across multiple horizons shows AsyTO achieves best lightweight error in 30 of 44 dataset-horizon settings, locating on the accuracy-compute Pareto frontier.

Conclusion: AsyTO provides a parameter-efficient, accurate multivariate forecasting approach by exploiting an asymmetric temporal operator structure and phase-locked seasonality; it outperforms dense, phase-blind baselines on standard benchmarks while keeping complexity linear in variables.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series forecasting faces a structural dilemma: sharing one temporal predictor across variables is parameter-efficient but forces heterogeneous variables through an identical history-to-future map, whereas learning an independent predictor per variable restores flexibility at a cost that grows with the product of variable count, context length, and horizon. We argue that this dilemma dissolves once the object being compressed is the forecasting operator rather than the observed series. Auditing per-variable linear history-to-future maps across standard benchmarks, we find that a phase-locked seasonal component paired with a compact residual operator outperforms a dense phase-blind reference in most audited settings. The residual transport is also directional: lag-invariant alternatives consistently underperform asymmetric history-to-future maps. Guided by this structure, we propose AsyTO, an Asymmetric Temporal Operator that factorizes the tensor of per-variable operators into shared but distinct history-reading and future-writing temporal modes with per-variable mode-wise gains, complemented by a low-rank periodic prototype and a cycle-separable factorization of the temporal modes. Each forecast reads only its own variable's history, so parameters and compute grow linearly in the number of variables. Across eleven benchmarks and multiple forecast horizons, AsyTO attains the best lightweight error in 30 of 44 dataset-horizon settings, locating at the accuracy-compute Pareto frontier.

</details>


### [411] [RetroMPA: A Molecular Property-Aware Auxiliary Framework for Enhancing Retrosynthesis Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16111)
*Mianzhi Liu,Fan Xiao,Zhiliang Yu,Huayang Huang,Yuke Li,Yi Yang,Wenbo Liu,Yu Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RetroMPA is a model-agnostic post-hoc chemical knowledge filter that reweights retrosynthesis predictions using a property-aware embedding, yielding consistent top-1 gains across models and datasets with preliminary wet-lab support and open-source code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limited integration of established chemical knowledge priors in data-driven retrosynthesis by introducing a post-hoc, plug-and-play chemical prior without retraining.

Method: A post-hoc, model-agnostic module that uses a property-aware latent embedding space to recalibrate predictive pathways. It plugs into existing data-driven retrosynthesis methods without changing architectures or requiring retraining, and is evaluated on template-based and template-free systems across USPTO-50K and USPTO-Full; wet-lab validation conducted.

Result: Across eight retrosynthesis models, top-1 accuracy increases by an average of 5.50% on USPTO-50K; on USPTO-Full, average improvement is ~2.03%. Wet-lab experiments confirm viable, previously unreported substrate combinations for Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, Bucherer reaction, and Friedel-Crafts acylation. Code is open-sourced at GitHub.

Conclusion: RetroMPA demonstrates that incorporating chemical priors via a post-hoc filter can reliably boost retrosynthesis performance across model families and data scales without retraining, with added wet-lab validation and accessible code.

Abstract: Retrosynthesis is a cornerstone of drug discovery and organic synthesis. While data-driven deep learning models have shown remarkable progress, they autonomously learn reaction patterns from extensive datasets with limited integration of established chemical knowledge as priors.
  To address this limitation, we introduce RetroMPA, a molecular property-aware, post-hoc enhancement module that injects chemical knowledge into the retrosynthesis pipeline. Rather than functioning as an independent SMILES sequence generator, RetroMPA is a broadly applicable, model-agnostic chemical filter designed to recalibrate and optimize the predictive pathways of existing algorithms.
  This plug-and-play framework integrates seamlessly with a range of data-driven retrosynthesis methods, enhancing outputs without modifying model architecture or requiring resource-intensive retraining. By leveraging a property-aware latent embedding space, RetroMPA consistently improves top-1 accuracy across eight representative retrosynthesis models by an average of 5.50% on USPTO-50K.
  Furthermore, we validate its scalability on the large-scale USPTO-Full dataset, achieving an average improvement of about 2.03% across both template-based and template-free architectures.
  Wet-lab experiments provide preliminary support for the practical utility of the framework. These syntheses confirmed viable, previously unreported substrate combinations for classic reaction paradigms---specifically, Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, Bucherer reaction, and Friedel-Crafts acylation---suggesting that RetroMPA can operate beyond mere data fitting. The code is open-sourced at https://github.com/MengzhouLu/RetroMPA.

</details>


### [412] [Multi-Feature Riemannian Hypergraph for Online Test-Time Adaptation of Motor Imagery Brain-Computer Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16134)
*Siqi Li,Zhi Li,Tong Liu,Shuai Zhang,Yanfei Jia,Zhiqiang Yi,Jue Xie,Ni Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces MRieHy, a multi-feature Riemannian hypergraph framework for online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding that improves cross-day transferability by integrating Riemannian-aligned covariance graphs with a second deep-feature hypergraph, fused with adaptive weights and optimized alongside label projections; uses a FIFO online buffer for Riemannian alignment during testing and demonstrates gains on private ECoG and public EEG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-day transferability and real-time operation are key challenges in MI-BCI. Existing hypergraph methods overlook cross-day benefits from Riemannian geometry, limiting transferability. A framework that exploits Riemannian geometry for cross-day alignment within a hypergraph-based online decoder addresses this gap.

Method: Compute Riemannian means of covariance matrices from multi-day training data for distribution alignment; build a hypergraph over these covariance matrices using Riemannian distance; build a second hypergraph over deep features using cosine similarity; fuse the two hypergraphs with adaptively learned weights; jointly optimize with label projection matrices; during online testing, maintain a FIFO buffer, perform Riemannian alignment on buffered data, and decode using the fused hypergraph.

Result: MRieHy achieves notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets.

Conclusion: MRieHy effectively strengthens cross-day transferability and supports online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding by fusing multi-feature Riemannian and deep-feature hypergraphs with adaptive weighting; validated across ECoG and EEG data with improved accuracy relative to baselines.

Abstract: In clinical motor imagery brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) decoding, cross-day transferability and online operation remain two critical challenges. Hypergraphs can improve transferability by capturing higher-order sample relationships, yet existing hypergraph-based methods for online emotion recognition neglect the cross-day benefits of Riemannian geometry widely adopted in EEG transfer learning. To bridge this gap, we propose the Multi-feature Riemannian Hypergraph (MRieHy), a framework tailored for online test-time adaptation in MI-BCI decoding that leverages Riemannian geometry to strengthen cross-day transferability. MRieHy first computes Riemannian means of covariance matrices from cross-day training data to align multi-day distributions. It then constructs a hypergraph over covariance matrices using Riemannian distance, complemented by a second hypergraph over deep features built with cosine similarity. The two hypergraphs are fused via adaptively learned combination weights, jointly optimized with the label projection matrices. During online testing, MRieHy maintains a first-in-first-out buffer of recent samples, performs Riemannian alignment on the buffered data, and decodes with the learned hypergraph. Extensive experiments on a private four-class ECoG dataset and two public four-class EEG datasets validate that MRieHy achieves notable performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [413] [REFLEX: Reflexive Equilibrium Fixed-point Learning for Endogenous eXchanges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16155)
*Vignesh Nagarajan,Shriraghav Ashok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REFLEX is a practical pre-deployment stability margin for ML-driven quote models in OTC corporate bond markets. It uses three measurable dealer-behavior features to predict stability of repeated retraining, validating via simulations and long-run data, and converting an abstract convergence theorem into a market-level safety margin.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address performative prediction risk in adaptive market-making: existing theory uses unobservable objective properties; there is a need for observable, desk-level metrics to pre-empt instability when models learn from the trades they attract.

Method: Define three measurable features: (i) sensitivity of trading volume to tighter quotes, (ii) curvature of the dealer objective around its optimum, and (iii) rate at which informed flow increases as spreads narrow. Combine them into a retraining modulus to yield a pre-deployment stability margin estimated from quote/execution history. Validate via simulations with two and three competing dealers; compare with ordinary retraining and apply a structurally anchored correction. Calibrate using 36 years of public market data across regimes (calm to crisis).

Result: Predicted vs. measured stability align within 8% in simulation; instability for two competitors increases by 1.74x and by 3.16x for three competitors, as predicted. Ordinary retraining becomes unstable at modulus 1.21; the anchored correction converges while blind retraining collapses. Stability headroom decreases about 4.4x for investment grade and 4.3x for high yield when moving from calm to crisis regimes.

Conclusion: REFLEX operationalizes a theoretical convergence result into a market-level safety margin, turning abstract stability conditions into a practical, measurable risk metric for ML-driven quoting in fixed-income markets.

Abstract: In over-the-counter corporate bond markets, dealers compete for client trades by quoting bid and ask prices. Tighter quotes attract more business, but also informed customers more likely to trade ahead of adverse price moves, leaving the dealer holding the risk. As dealers increasingly use machine learning to set quotes, they retrain these models on the trades their own quotes attract, creating a feedback loop in which each model reshapes the market that generates its next training data. The question is therefore not only whether a quoting model performs well, but whether the market it creates stays stable as the model learns from it. Existing performative prediction theory gives a sharp stability condition, yet expresses it through abstract properties of the learning objective a trading desk cannot measure before deployment. We introduce REFLEX, a framework that replaces those unobservable quantities with three measurable features of dealer behavior: how strongly trading volume responds to tighter quotes, how sharply the dealer's objective bends around its optimum, and how quickly informed flow increases as spreads narrow. REFLEX combines these into a single retraining modulus, a pre-deployment stability margin estimated from a desk's own quote and execution history that predicts whether repeated retraining will converge or amplify itself. In simulation, predicted and measured stability agree within 8%, and competing dealers increase instability by 1.74x with two and 3.16x with three, as predicted. Where ordinary retraining becomes unstable at modulus 1.21, a structurally anchored correction converges as blind retraining collapses. Calibrated over 36 years of public market data, stability headroom falls roughly 4.4x for investment grade and 4.3x for high yield from calm to crisis regimes. Ultimately, REFLEX turns an abstract convergence theorem into a market-level safety margin.

</details>


### [414] [A Tree-Structured Approach for Phishing Template and Attacker Attribution Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16158)
*Unai Agirre,Imanol Jerico,Felipe Castaño,Andrea Venturi,Francesco Zola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unsupervised clustering of DOM-based structural features reveals phishing template reuse; introduces level-wise Jaccard Distance for cluster evaluation; demonstrates that HTML structure can detect emerging/zero-day phishing templates and coordinated campaigns beyond reactive defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
