Motivation: Phishing volumes rise due to kits/templates enabling mass, rapid deployment. Existing defenses rely on reactive blocklists or instance-level classifiers and miss structural reuse across sites. Structural fingerprints of HTML DOM could reveal template reuse and coordinated campaigns.

Method: Represent web pages as DOM trees and extract structural features, optionally augmented with HTML tag-based content. Apply unsupervised clustering using three algorithms; study effect of DOM depth on clustering. Assess cluster quality quantitatively (including a novel level-wise Jaccard Distance Score) and qualitatively via visualization with manual inspection.

Result: Structural representations capture hidden similarities across phishing sites, enabling detection of emerging and zero-day templates and supporting analysis of coordinated phishing threats. Comparative clustering results and depth analyses identify robust structural fingerprints for phishing templates.

Conclusion: HTML DOM structure can serve as a robust fingerprint for phishing template reuse, enabling proactive detection of coordinated campaigns and zero-day templates, and complementing traditional reactive defenses.

Abstract: Phishing remains a persistent and evolving cybersecurity threat, with attack volumes reaching record levels. This growth is driven by the industrialization of phishing through widely available phishing kits and reusable templates, which enable cybercriminals to rapidly generate and deploy large numbers of fraudulent webpages. Although surface-level attributes may differ across these websites, their underlying structures often exhibit significant similarities. However, most existing defenses rely on reactive blocklists or supervised classification models that focus on individual phishing instances, limiting their ability to identify structural reuse and detect coordinated phishing campaigns. To address this limitation, this study investigates whether HTML structure can serve as a robust fingerprint for identifying phishing template reuse. We model webpages as Document Object Model (DOM) trees and extract structural features, optionally enriched with HTML tag-based content information. These representations are then clustered using unsupervised learning methods to group structurally similar webpages. Three clustering algorithms are evaluated and compared, while also analyzing how the depth of the extracted DOM-tree affects cluster formation and overall clustering performance. Finally, cluster quality is also evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively, including a novel level-wise Jaccard Distance Score and manual inspection supported by visualization tools. Results demonstrate that structural representations of webpages can effectively reveal hidden similarities across phishing sites, enabling the detection of emerging and zero-day templates and supporting the analysis of coordinated phishing threats

</details>


### [415] [Demystifying Oversmoothing in Sheaf Neural Networks: An Index-Theoretic Criterion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16180)
*Junwen Dong,Yuhan Peng,Hao Li,Huitao Feng,Kelin Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A relative, geometric index-theoretic criterion quantifies anti-oversmoothing in Sheaf Neural Networks, addressing limitations of using dim ker L; introduces GyroSheaf with curved stalks and extends to nonlinear settings; empirical validation across ten models supports the criterion's predictive power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oversmoothing in graph neural nets remains unresolved when using absolute harmonic-space dimension; current analyses fail when dim ker L inflates without increasing discriminative capacity. A relative, geometric measure can compare anti-oversmoothing across different sheaf configurations.

Method: Develop an index-theoretic comparison criterion under natural conditions on stalk transport and global sheaf structure; prove that one sheaf's harmonic space properly contains another's; instantiate with GyroSheaf and use local tangent-space linearization to handle nonlinear stalks; provide a concrete example; perform experiments across ten models to test the criterion.

Result: The criterion correctly predicts anti-oversmoothing behavior: models violating the criterion collapse despite index jumps, while compliant models maintain depth-stable representations; harmonic spaces show containment beyond trivial inflation; GyroSheaf extends the framework to curved stalks successfully via local linearization.

Conclusion: This work provides the first relative, geometric framework to assess anti-oversmoothing capacity in SNNs, offering a robust design/analysis tool and extending applicability to nonlinear stalks; empirical results validate the theoretical criterion.

Abstract: To combat oversmoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks, Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) were proposed as a generalization by equipping the graph with a sheaf structure and replacing the graph Laplacian with a sheaf Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$. Existing analyses connect sheaf diffusion to oversmoothing via the harmonic space ($\ker\mathcal{L}$), taking its absolute dimension as an indicator of anti-oversmoothing capacity. However, absolute dimension alone is not a reliable measure: certain sheaf configurations inflate $\dim \ker \mathcal{L}$ while their harmonic sections remain entirely constant, without enriching discriminative capacity. We instead introduce the first relative, geometric approach, yielding a precise characterisation of anti-oversmoothing capacity. Under natural conditions on stalk transportation and global sheaf structure, we establish an index-theoretic comparison criterion showing that one sheaf's harmonic space genuinely contains another's beyond trivial inflation. We illustrate this with a concrete instance and further introduce \textit{GyroSheaf}, a sheaf with curved gyrovector-space stalks, extending the criterion to the non-linear setting via local tangent-space linearization. Experiments across ten models confirm the theoretical criterion: sheaf models violating the criterion collapse despite possessing index jumps, while compliant models maintain depth-stable representations.

</details>


### [416] [Understanding and Stabilizing Deep Q-Learning via Controlled Bootstrapping and Regulated Value Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16182)
*Bozhou Chen,Yongyi Wang,Hanyu Liu,Xionghui Yang,Wenxin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unified analysis of instability in deep Q-learning across operator bias, estimator sensitivity, and parameter dynamics; introduces stabilization principles and demonstrates improved stability and competitive performance on Atari-100K and Procgen.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work attributes instability to isolated factors; lacks a unified understanding of interactions among sources of instability during recursive value estimation.

Method: Decompose instability into three complementary perspectives: operator-level bias in Bellman bootstrapping, estimator-level sensitivity of greedy action selection to regression noise, and parameter-dynamics imbalance under aggressive data reuse; derive stabilization principles (controlled bootstrapping, ensemble quantile estimation, spike-based parameter regulation); conduct experiments on Atari-100K and Procgen.

Result: Identify a reward-triggered self-reinforcing trap and characteristic parameter spike dynamics; propose stabilization principles; empirical results show improved training stability and competitive performance.

Conclusion: Provides a unified, multi-perspective framework for understanding and stabilizing deep Q-learning, with practical guidelines that enhance stability without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Deep Q-learning (DQL) has achieved remarkable empirical success in reinforcement learning, yet its training process remains notoriously unstable. Existing studies often attribute instability to isolated factors such as overestimation bias or representation learning issues, lacking a unified understanding of how different sources of instability interact during recursive value estimation. In this work, we provide a systematic analysis of instability in deep Q-learning from three complementary perspectives: operator-level bias in Bellman bootstrapping, estimator-level sensitivity of greedy action selection to regression noise, and parameter-dynamics imbalance under aggressive data reuse. We identify a reward-triggered self-reinforcing trap and characteristic parameter spike dynamics, then derive stabilization principles for controlled bootstrapping, ensemble quantile estimation, and spike-based parameter regulation. Experiments on Atari-100K and Procgen demonstrate competitive performance and improved training stability.

</details>


### [417] [Multi-Granularity Sentiment Integration for LLM-Based Multimodal Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16201)
*Shanshan Lin,Yuesheng Wu,Chao Chen,Yizhe Yang,Zhihao Chen,Zexian Yang,Xiangwen Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MGSI introduces multi-granularity temporal modeling for audio/visual signals in LLM-based multimodal sentiment analysis, preserving local and global cues, refining with text guidance, and adapting polarity/intensity before summarizing into pseudo-tokens for a frozen LLM. It outperforms frozen-LLM baselines and rivals strong multimodal methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs provide strong semantic priors for MSA, but audio/visual cues evolve over different temporal scales and are often compressed early, weakening cross-modal alignment and losing fine-grained affective information. A method is needed to preserve multi-scale temporal dynamics and align them effectively with text.

Method: Encode audio/visual streams at short-, medium-, and long-range temporal scales to preserve local variations and global trends. Refine non-text features via text-guided alignment. Apply polarity- and intensity-aware enhancement to handle ambiguous/near-neutral samples. Compress the multimodal representation into a small set of pseudo-tokens to condition a frozen LLM.

Result: On four public benchmarks, MGSI substantially surpasses frozen-LLM baselines and is competitive with strong multimodal methods. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the benefits of multi-granularity temporal modeling, text-guided refinement, and adaptive sentiment calibration.

Conclusion: Multi-granularity temporal modeling combined with text-guided alignment and adaptive sentiment calibration enables effective LLM-conditioned multimodal sentiment analysis with compact pseudo-tokens, delivering strong performance and robustness across datasets.

Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict sentiment polarity and intensity from heterogeneous inputs such as text, audio, and vision. While large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic priors for MSA, effectively incorporating audio and visual signals effectively remains challenging. A key challenge is that audio and visual sentiment cues evolve over different temporal scales, yet many LLM-based methods compress these signals through shallow projection or coarse pooling before fusing them with text, which can weaken cross-modal alignment and erase fine-grained affective information. We propose MGSI, a multi-granularity sentiment integration framework for LLM-based MSA. MGSI first encodes audio and visual streams at short-, medium-, and long-range temporal scales, preserving both local variations and global affective trends. It then refines non-text features through text-guided alignment, and applies polarity- and intensity-aware enhancement to better handle ambiguous and near-neutral samples. The resulting multimodal representation is finally compressed into a small set of pseudo-tokens for efficient conditioning of a frozen LLM. Experiments on four public benchmarks show that MGSI substantially outperforms frozen-LLM baselines and remains competitive with strong multimodal methods. Further ablation and sensitivity analyses support the effectiveness of multi-granularity temporal modeling, text-guided refinement, and adaptive sentiment calibration.

</details>


### [418] [Conditional Evaluation of Language Models with Cheap Auxiliary Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16210)
*Zhi Zhang,Lingfeng Lyu,Yue Kang,Doudou Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LACE is a semi-supervised estimator for conditional LLM evaluation that uses local centering and a ridge control variate to efficiently incorporate cheap signals (judge scores, confidence, etc.) to estimate conditional performance profiles with zero conditional bias and adaptivity, with performance governed by a local R^2; validated across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating conditional performance from gold labels is expensive; cheap auxiliary signals exist but are biased or miscalibrated. A calibration-free, efficient method is needed to leverage these signals for profiling performance.

Method: Local centering: subtract the conditional mean of a cheap signal within the target profile region; linear augmentation has zero conditional mean under this centering. Use a local ridge control variate combining gold-label residual mean from labeled subset with cheap-signal mean from the full item pool. Derive estimators for direct paired model gaps and deployment-weighted scores. Provide first-order adaptivity to the estimated coefficient. Gains are governed by a population local R^2.

Result: Proves calibration-free identification, unbiasedness for grouped profiles, local oracle optimality within centered linear augmentations, and first-order adaptivity. Applies estimators for direct paired model gaps and deployment-weighted scores. Empirically evaluated on MATH-500, ScienceQA, MMLU, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, and ARC.

Conclusion: LACE offers a principled, efficient framework for estimating conditional LLM performance using cheap signals, with strong theoretical guarantees and broad empirical validation across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: Aggregate accuracy hides where models succeed and fail. Estimating conditional performance profiles from gold labels alone is expensive, while cheap auxiliary signals such as LLM-judge scores, pairwise comparisons, confidence scores, and judge-disagreement features can be collected for every benchmark item but are often biased or miscalibrated. We propose LACE (Local Augmented Control-Variate Evaluation), a semi-supervised estimator for conditional LLM evaluation. The key step is local centering: after subtracting the conditional mean of a cheap signal within the target profile region, any linear augmentation has zero conditional mean and therefore cannot change the estimand. The augmentation coefficient is used only for efficiency, and a local ridge control variate combines a gold-label residual mean from the labeled subset with a cheap-signal mean from the full item pool. We prove calibration-free identification, unbiasedness for grouped profiles, local oracle optimality within centered linear augmentations, and first-order adaptivity to the estimated coefficient. The resulting gain formula is governed by a population local $R^2$, which characterizes how the efficiency attainable from the cheap signals varies across profile values. We also derive corresponding estimators for direct paired model gaps and deployment-weighted scores. We empirically evaluate the primary performance-profile estimator on MATH-500, ScienceQA, MMLU, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, and ARC.

</details>


### [419] [Quantifying the Gap Between Laboratory Battery Test Patterns and Field Duty Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16212)
*Chunyang Zhao,Chresten Træholt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study demonstrates a substantial gap between lab battery tests and real-world duty profiles by quantifying six evidence sources with a duty-structure index (DSI) and C-rate metrics; results show that ageing and SOH depend strongly on duty pattern, suggesting explicit reporting of duty profiles is essential for meaningful battery performance metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Laboratory tests do not mirror real-world usage; quantifying this gap enables better interpretation of laboratory ageing results and improves the relevance of performance metrics for fielded batteries.

Method: Compare six evidence sources (controlled cycling, drive-cycle testing, dynamic cycling, NMC811 lab ageing, real EV charging trace, fleet SOH data). Compute usage frequency, usage intensity, C-rate, and DSI based on normalized current dispersion and ramping. Analyze DSI ranges, C-rate ranges, 80% retention ageing points, chemistry-aligned ageing trends, and field-use statistics (daily distance, SOC distribution at charge endings).

Result: DSI and C-rate vary across sources; some field data align differently with lab ageing. In NMC/NCM chemistry, Imperial shows 0.813 retention under standard cycling and 0.865 under drive-cycle ageing, field source median SOH 0.889 with dispersion; field use shows median 137.2 km/day and 56.9% charges ending ≥95% SOC. These results indicate that ageing and performance metrics are conditioned by the duty pattern.

Conclusion: Battery performance metrics are duty-pattern dependent; studies should report explicit duty-profile descriptors along with chemistry, capacity, and ageing metrics to enable meaningful cross-study comparison.

Abstract: Laboratory battery tests provide the main empirical basis for battery performance and degradation studies, but their operating patterns do not directly represent field duty profiles. This paper quantifies the gap by comparing six accessible evidence sources covering controlled cycling, drive-cycle testing, dynamic cycling, NMC811 laboratory ageing, a real electric-vehicle charging trace, and fleet-scale electric-vehicle state-of-health (SOH) data. The analysis combines usage frequency, usage intensity, usage C-rate, and a duty-structure index (DSI) based on normalized current dispersion and ramping. The representative single-segment DSI ranges from 0.630 for the field source trace and 0.699 for NASA to 2.936 for Oxford and 2.855 for Imperial, while usage C-rate ranges from 0.14-0.40 for Imperial, NASA, Stanford, and Hyundai to 2.00 for Oxford. Long-term ageing also differs: the 80 percent retention region occurs near 351 NASA cycles, 6292 Oxford checkpoints, and 1019 Stanford cycles. In chemistry-aligned NMC/NCM evidence, Imperial retains 0.813 under standard cycling and 0.865 under drive-cycle ageing, while the field source has median SOH 0.889 with visible dispersion. Field operation further shows a median use intensity of 137.2 km/day and 56.9 percent of charges ending at or above 95 percent SOC. These results show that battery performance metrics are conditional on the duty pattern that generated them; application-oriented studies should report explicit duty-profile descriptors together with chemistry, capacity, and ageing metrics.

</details>


### [420] [Beyond Peak Backlog: Conditional Energy and Temporal Geometry in Capacity-Constrained Delayed Bandit Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16216)
*Anling Xiang,Yuwen Yang,Yang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies delay-aware online learning with limited backlog tracking in one-point bandit convex optimization. It derives delay-aware regret bounds under a scheduler-side interface, showing delayed terms scale as O(sqrt(E_C d_tot)) (untuned) and O(sqrt(d_tot)) with a public peak bound; strong convexity yields a temporal cost H_A(d); timing matters beyond aggregate delay; a continuous hard family links tracking capacity to zeroth-order budgets; upper bounds require C >= ln T + 1 and a full capacity minimax characterization remains open.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To close the gap between existing O(√(T σ_max)) regret with scarce tracking and the sharper √(d_tot) bound for unlimited delay tracking, by introducing a scheduling interface that decouples rate adaptation from perturbation filtration and analyzes how delayed feedback and capacity constraints influence minimax regret under convex and strongly convex losses.

Method: Introduce a scheduler-side conditional-energy interface that handles dependent importance weights from randomized admission and separates rate adaptation from one-point perturbation filtration. Derive regret bounds under a semi-clairvoyant oracle and a pathwise hard-capacity contract. Extend results to strong convexity to obtain a temporal cost expression. Construct a continuous hard family to relate tracking capacity to zeroth-order query budgets. Establish that upper bounds require C ≥ ln T + 1 and that the full capacity-minimax characterization is incomplete.

Result: Untuned learner achieves delay term O(√(E_C d_tot)); a public constant-factor peak bound removes this E_C factor; with strong convexity the temporal cost is H_A(d)=∑_t σ_t/(A+t). Timing differences can yield polynomially different minimax regrets despite identical delay multisets and capacities. A continuous hard family translates tracking capacity into zeroth-order budgets and reveals capacity-starvation endpoints. Upper bounds necessitate C ≥ ln T + 1; overall, a complete capacity minimax characterization remains open.

Conclusion: Timing and capacity interact nontrivially under curvature; scheduling and perturbation filtration choices affect achievable regret. The proposed framework advances understanding but does not fully resolve the capacity minimax landscape, indicating further work is needed to close gaps and extend to broader settings.

Abstract: What is the right delay complexity when a learner can track only $C$ pending feedback items and discarded feedback is permanently lost? Existing one-point bandit convex optimization guarantees in this model pay $\sqrt{Tσ_{\max}}$, where $σ_{\max}$ is the peak backlog, although unlimited tracking admits the sharper $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}$ dependence on total delay. We introduce a scheduler-side conditional-energy interface that separates rate adaptation from the one-point perturbation filtration and handles the dependent importance weights created by randomized admission. Under the same semi-clairvoyant oracle and pathwise hard-capacity contract, this yields an untuned learner whose delay term scales as $O(\sqrt{E_C d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$, with only an explicit restart factor $E_C$; a public constant-factor peak bound removes this factor while $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ remains unknown. Under strong convexity, the same interface yields the temporal cost $H_A(d)=\sum_t σ_t/(A+t)$. Two delay vectors with identical delay multisets, $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$, $σ_{\max}$, and capacity can nevertheless have polynomially different minimax regret, showing that timing matters under curvature even when aggregate delay summaries agree. Finally, a continuous hard family converts tracking capacity into a zeroth-order query budget and gives a complementary capacity-starvation lower endpoint. The upper bounds require $C\ge \ln T+1$ and do not constitute a complete capacity minimax characterization.

</details>


### [421] [Optimizing Multi-Market Participation of Battery and Electrolyser Systems Based on Field Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16238)
*Chunyang Zhao,Stoyan Trenchev,Shi You,Chresten Træholt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Experimental hardware-informed optimization shows multi-market profitability for a 55 kW BESS and a small PTX electrolyser using Danish market data; highlights importance of realistic device behavior in revenue stacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As renewable penetration grows, fast-response and flexible resources are needed for stability. Markets and ancillary services enable revenue stacking, but many studies neglect real hardware constraints. The work aims to quantify financial viability by incorporating measured hardware limitations into market participation models.

Method: Experimentally characterize a 55 kW/79 kWh BESS and a three-unit 2.4 kW electrolyser, identify ramp, efficiency, and setpoint-tracking characteristics and embed these into a price-driven optimization framework. Evaluate using Danish market data (2022–2025) to compute optimized daily profits for multi-market participation.

Result: Daily profits: 1,749.27 DKK for the BESS and 289.46 DKK for the electrolyser under multi-market participation. Demonstrates business cases for BESS and PTX systems and the value of incorporating experimental performance in multi-market participation across years.

Conclusion: Incorporating experimental hardware behavior is essential for accurate assessment of participation across multiple markets. The work supports the business case for BESS and PTX and suggests future work should expand market coverage and include longer time horizons and additional hardware constraints.

Abstract: The increasing share of renewable energy in power systems creates a need for fast-response and flexible resources to maintain system stability. With the expansion of electricity markets and ancillary service products, opportunities arise to stack revenues across multiple services. Long-term Power-to-X (PTX) electrolysers and short-term battery energy storage systems (BESS) are prevalent flexible resources, yet most studies neglect real hardware behavior, such as ramp limits, efficiency, and setpoint-tracking accuracy. This work presents experimental and modeling results for a 55 kW/79 kWh BESS and an electrolyser comprising three 2.4 kW units. Key characteristics are identified through measurements and embedded into a price-driven optimization framework for participation in the Danish electricity and ancillary service markets, utilizing real market data from 2022 to 2025. The optimized daily profits for multi-market participation are 1,749.27 DKK and 289.46 DKK for the BESS and electrolyser, respectively. With the demonstrated business cases for BESS and PTX systems, this work highlights the importance of incorporating experimental performance when evaluating participation across multiple markets and years.

</details>


### [422] [SAUL: Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16249)
*Jaewan Choi,Junyoung Yang,Sangdon Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAUL reframes LLM unlearning as a constrained optimization with an explicit forgetting constraint, using an augmented-Lagrangian controller and sharpness-aware updates to balance forgetting with utility, achieving favorable trade-offs on TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE, and offering drop-in improvements for other baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlearning in LLMs faces a fundamental trade-off: erasing targeted knowledge without degrading general utility. Prior methods implicitly encode forgetting via objectives, offering limited explicit control. An explicit constraint-based approach promises finer control, stability, and adaptability.

Method: Formulates forgetting as an explicit constraint within a constrained minimization problem. Uses an augmented Lagrangian controller to adaptively apply pressure on forgetting until the constraint is satisfied. Employs sharpness-aware updates on both retain and forget objectives and a dual-optimizer design with role-separated states to stabilize dynamics. Evaluates SAUL on TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE benchmarks, comparing against sharpness- and perturbation-based baselines under benchmark-specific forgetting criteria. Demonstrates that the augmented-Lagrangian controller can also be used as a drop-in modifier to improve post-forgetting utility for representative baselines.

Result: SAUL achieves favorable forgetting-utility trade-offs across TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE compared with baselines. The explicit constraint and adaptive AL pressure lead to robust forgetting while preserving utility. Additionally, the AL controller improves other baselines’ post-forgetting utility when used as a drop-in modifier, highlighting practical value for existing unlearning methods.

Conclusion: Introducing explicit forgetting control via an augmented-Lagrangian framework yields a stable, effective unlearning paradigm for LLMs. SAUL’s combination of explicit contracting, adaptive pressure, sharpness-aware updates, and dual-optimizer separation provides improved forgetting-utility trade-offs and practical applicability as a modifier to existing methods.

Abstract: Machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs) faces a critical trade-off between erasing target knowledge and preserving general utility. We propose SAUL (Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning), which formulates unlearning as a constrained minimization problem following the principle of "forget enough, but no more than necessary." At its core, SAUL formulates forgetting as an explicit constraint with a prescribed satisfaction criterion, whereas prior unlearning methods typically specify the desired level of forgetting implicitly through optimization objectives. An augmented Lagrangian controller adaptively adjusts forget-side pressure according to constraint violation and can eventually deactivate the forget-side update as the prescribed criterion remains satisfied. Sharpness-aware updates on both retain and forget objectives, together with a dual-optimizer design that maintains role-separated states, further stabilize the resulting unlearning dynamics. We evaluate SAUL on the TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE benchmarks, demonstrating favorable forgetting-utility trade-offs over representative sharpness- and perturbation-based baselines under benchmark-specific forgetting criteria. Beyond the complete SAUL framework, we further show on TOFU that applying the augmented-Lagrangian controller as a drop-in modifier to representative baselines improves their post-forgetting utility, demonstrating the practical value of explicit forgetting control.

</details>


### [423] [Efficient Coreset Selection via K-Nearest Neighbor Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16270)
*Yingfan Liu,Leiyu Zhang,Jiadong Xie,Mingzhe Wang,Jeffrey Xu Yu,Jiangtao Cui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A lightweight coreset selection method (KNNG-CS) using a K-nearest neighbor graph to estimate data point importance, avoiding dense distance matrices. It greedily selects representative nodes with linear storage, achieving competitive accuracy with substantial improvements in time and memory over baseline gradient-approximation coreset methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coreset selection aims to replace a large training set with a small, representative subset to reduce training cost. Existing gradient-approximation coreset methods (e.g., CRAIG, cluster-based variants) rely on dense pairwise distances or large bound matrices, incurring high time and memory costs on large datasets, limiting scalability.

Method: Construct a K-nearest neighbor graph to capture local neighborhood structure. Estimate the importance of each data item from its local neighborhood without maintaining a quadratic distance matrix. Greedily select representative nodes based on this importance, using only linear storage in the number of edges.

Result: On four real-world datasets, KNNG-CS achieves accuracy comparable to representative gradient-approximation coreset methods. It reduces selection time by a factor of 2.3x to 41.2x and reduces peak memory usage to 0.3%–7.5% of baseline methods.

Conclusion: KNNG-CS provides a scalable, efficient coreset selection approach that leverages local graph structure to approximate data point importance, delivering competitive model accuracy with substantial gains in time and memory efficiency compared with existing gradient-approximation coreset methods.

Abstract: Coreset selection reduces the cost of model training by replacing a large training set with a small representative subset. Existing gradient-approximation coreset methods such as CRAIG and cluster-based variants can preserve model accuracy. Still, their selection stages often rely on dense pairwise distances or large item-cluster bound matrices, leading to high time and memory costs on large datasets. This paper proposes KNNG-CS, a lightweight coreset selection method based on a $K$-nearest neighbor graph. KNNG-CS exploits local neighborhood structures to estimate the importance of each data item and greedily selects representative nodes without maintaining a quadratic distance matrix. The method requires only linear storage in the number of edges. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that KNNG-CS achieves accuracy comparable to representative gradient-approximation coreset methods, while reducing selection time by $2.3\times$-$41.2\times$ and peak memory to $0.3\%$-$7.5\%$ of the baselines.

</details>


### [424] [Foresight-England: Development of a National-Scale Generative AI Model of Electronic Health Records for Medical Event Prediction across the COVID-19 Pandemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16273)
*Simon Ellershaw,Christopher Tomlinson,Zeljko Kraljevic,Spiros Denaxas,Harry Hemingway,Cathie Sudlow,Angela M. Wood,Anoop D. Shah,Richard Dobson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A national-scale EHR foundation model (Foresight-E) trained on 61M individuals’ data in the NHS to model direct and indirect COVID-19 effects; zero-shot inference across ~40k codes; evaluation framework for 30-day outcomes; 2023 generalization tests; no quantitative results released due to data access pause; serves as methodological template for population-scale EHR models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Advance population-scale EHR modeling to understand pandemic dynamics, direct health impacts, and indirect effects. Demonstrate the feasibility of a national-scale, zero-shot EHR foundation model trained entirely in a secure NHS environment.

Method: Train from scratch a 243M-parameter transformer decoder on de-identified longitudinal EHRs (≈61M individuals) in the NHS England Secure Data Environment. Tokenize and jointly represent ICD-10, OPCS-4, and SNOMED CT codes across absolute and relative timing to form a 40k-code vocabulary. Autoregressively model patient timelines and perform zero-shot inference at inference time. Evaluate on 30-day COVID-19 hospitalization and mortality with demographic and vaccination subgroups. Reserve 10% of data for evaluation (2023 data used for unseen future generalization). Compare against logistic regression and XGBoost. In this abstract, quantitative results are withheld because data access is paused.

Result: Quantitative results are not disclosed due to the NHS data-access pause; the paper provides the tokenisation, architecture, training, inference, and evaluation strategy as a methodological template and case study for building population-scale EHR foundation models.

Conclusion: The work presents a novel, large-scale EHR foundation-model approach, including a robust evaluation framework for COVID-19 outcomes and future generalization, while highlighting practical challenges (data access) that prevent reporting results; it serves as a blueprint for methodology and reproducibility in population-scale biomedical foundation models.

Abstract: Foresight-England (Foresight-E) is the first national-scale generative foundation model of electronic health records (EHRs), developed as a research pilot strictly for COVID-19 research. We evaluated its ability to model the direct and indirect effects of the pandemic. Trained from scratch entirely within the NHS England Secure Data Environment, Foresight-E is a 243-million-parameter transformer decoder. It was trained and evaluated on de-identified, longitudinal EHRs of approximately 61 million individuals, integrating primary/secondary care, death registrations, and COVID-19 data. Training and validation used a 90% subset (54.9 million) spanning November 2018 to December 2022; the remaining 10% (6.1 million) was held out for evaluation. Foresight-E models patient timelines autoregressively, predicting the next medical event given their prior history. At inference, it operates zero-shot, predicting any concept in its ~40,000-code vocabulary without task-specific training. Our tokenisation scheme retains the clinical granularity of ICD-10, OPCS-4, and SNOMED CT codes, jointly representing absolute and relative timing. We designed an evaluation framework for 30-day COVID-19 hospitalisation and mortality, including subgroup analyses by demographic factors and vaccination status. To assess generalisation to unseen future data and the pandemic's indirect effects, we tested the model on medical events from 2023 (beyond its training period), benchmarking against logistic regression and XGBoost. As detailed in the Project Status section, NHS England has paused access to data for the Foresight-E project, meaning quantitative results are currently unavailable. Instead, we share our strategy for tokenisation, architecture, training, inference, and evaluation as a methodological template and case study in the challenges of building population-scale EHR foundation models.

</details>


### [425] [Transfer Learning of Keystroke Dynamics for Cross-Device User Authentication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16334)
*Nuwan Kaluarachchi,Sevvandi Kandanaarachchi,Kristen Moore,Arathi Arakala,Conrad Sanderson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-device keystroke-based authentication using inductive transfer learning to adapt source-device dynamics to a target device, combining adapted data with limited target data to train a robust classifier; achieves 14.2% EER on BBMAS, outperforming prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-device authentication suffers from distribution drift of keystroke patterns across devices with different form factors; single-device models do not generalize well to other devices.

Method: Use inductive transfer learning to adapt keystroke dynamics learned on a source device to a secondary device. Integrate the adapted data with limited training data from the secondary device to robustly train a binary classifier. Extend the feature set to capture richer discriminative dynamics.

Result: On the BBMAS dataset, the proposed system achieves an equal error rate (EER) of 14.2% for cross-device authentication, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: Inductive transfer learning with an expanded feature set effectively mitigates cross-device distribution drift in keystroke dynamics, enabling improved cross-device user authentication; practical deployment would benefit from evaluating on more devices and contexts.

Abstract: Keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) can be used as a behavioural biometric modality for user authentication, with applications such as fraud prevention. While the modality has been shown to work well for single device authentication, its application to cross-device scenarios is more challenging. Dynamics learned on one device (eg., phone) may not be directly applicable to authentication on a secondary device with a different form factor (eg., tablet) due to changes in typing patterns that can lead to distribution drifts. To address this, we propose a cross-device user authentication system based on inductive transfer learning, where keystroke dynamics learned on one device are adapted to a secondary device. The adapted data is then combined with necessarily limited training data for the secondary device, which is used to robustly train a binary classifier. Furthermore, an extended set of keystroke features is used to better capture discriminative dynamics. Experiments on the BBMAS dataset show that proposed system achieves an equal error rate of 14.2% for the cross-device scenario, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [426] [Task-Anchored Representation Shaping for Pre-Trained Model-Based Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16345)
*Zhiming Xu,Huiyu Yi,Zhen-Hao Xie,Baile Xu,Furao Shen,Jian Zhao,Suorong Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAILS is a lightweight post-PTM module for continual learning that uses fixed task anchors to compute latent recall and correct feature representations, addressing cross-task ambiguity without altering the PTM or classifier; achieves improvements with modest overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-task ambiguity arises when task boundaries are artificial and predictions must generalize across tasks; PTMs provide stable representations but do not guarantee reliable cross-task inference.

Method: Attach TAILS to diverse continual learners; maintain fixed task anchors as persistent references to accumulated knowledge; encode each sample's feature relative to anchors, fuse evidence across tasks into latent recall, and apply the latent recall to adjust the feature before the classifier. Decoupled optimization; negligible inference cost; no changes to PTM, base method modules, or classifier.

Result: Reported improvements in classification and task inference across multiple PTM-based continual learning setups with modest parameter overhead and negligible latency.

Conclusion: TAILS offers a representation-level remedy to cross-task ambiguity that is lightweight, broadly compatible, and effective across PTM-based CL paradigms.

Abstract: Pre-trained models (PTMs) provide a strong foundation for continual learning by offering stable representations that facilitate lightweight adaptation to new tasks. However, adapting well to each task does not ensure reliable inference over all learned tasks. Since task boundaries are often artificial and semantically entangled, an input from an unknown task can remain ambiguous even with strong PTM features, making cross-task prediction a key bottleneck. We propose Task-Anchored Inference Latent Shaping (TAILS), a lightweight post-PTM module that can be integrated into diverse continual learners and optimized through a decoupled step. TAILS uses fixed task anchors as persistent references to accumulated knowledge. It interprets each sample's feature representation relative to these references, then composes relevant evidence across tasks into latent recall. Rather than selecting a task-specific path or adjusting classifier outputs, TAILS uses latent recall to directly correct the feature representation before prediction. It therefore resolves cross-task ambiguity at the representation level, while leaving the original PTM, method-specific modules, and classifier unchanged. Extensive experiments across multiple PTM-based continual learning paradigms show that TAILS can improve classification and task-inference performance with modest parameter overhead and negligible inference cost.

</details>


### [427] [OceanDepths: A Global Dataset of Paired Subsurface and Surface Ocean Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16373)
*Simon Donike,Ruben Cartuyvels,Antonino Ian Ferola,Elisa Carli,Diego Fernandez Prieto,Marie-Helene Rio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OceanDepths is the first open, global, AI-ready dataset linking satellite surface fields to co-located subsurface observations, enabling joint surface–subsurface analysis and AI-method development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The oceans are under-observed relative to land/atmosphere. A standardized, high-resolution dataset that pairs surface satellite fields with in situ depth profiles is needed to study mesoscale dynamics and develop AI-based observations/forecasts.

Method: Regridding and aligning satellite L4 surface products (SST, SSS, SSH) with EN4 in situ subsurface temperature and salinity, supplemented by GLORYS12 reanalysis. The dataset spans 2000–2024 at 0.1° resolution and weekly cadence, containing ~9.5 million paired profiles interpolated to 50 depth levels, with a configurable patch-based spatial division.

Result: Demonstrates a subsurface state reconstruction task using simple baselines, illustrating feasibility and the potential for AI tasks like observation-based forecasting; dataset is open and AI-ready, suitable for multi-stage learning.

Conclusion: OceanDepths provides a challenging, high-resolution, long-term testbed for AI methods in oceanography and supports broader efforts in observable-based forecasting and joint surface–subsurface analysis; available at HuggingFace.

Abstract: Despite comprising over 70\% of its surface, the world's oceans are critically underobserved compared to the land surface or the atmosphere.Understanding the global ocean requires jointly observing its surface and subsurface structure, yet no standardized, high-resolution dataset couples satellite surface fields to co-located \emph{in situ} depth profiles in an AI-ready format.Existing resources either consist of model-reconstructed gridded products rather than observations, cover only a single variable or basin, or operate at resolutions too coarse for mesoscale dynamics.We introduce \textsc{OceanDepths}, the first open, global, regridded AI-ready dataset that pairs satellite-derived sea surface temperature (SST), sea surface salinity (SSS), and sea surface height (SSH) L4 products with co-located EN4 subsurface temperature and salinity profiles, complemented by matched GLORYS12 ocean reanalysis data to support comparisons or multi-stage learning.The dataset spans 2000--2024 at \SI{0.1}{\degree}$\times$\SI{0.1}{\degree} spatial resolution and at weekly temporal resolution, covering the entire globe's sea surface and with over 9.5 million paired profiles interpolated to 50 standardized depth levels.We provide a configurable system to split the globe in equally sized spatial patches.The 4D multivariate structure, high resolution, long temporal extent, and extreme sparsity of subsurface observations (${\sim}$0.01\% per depth level) make \textsc{OceanDepths}a challenging testbed for novel AI methods.We demonstrate subsurface state reconstruction as an example task with simple baseline models, but also envision \textsc{OceanDepths}to support the development of observation-based forecast methods and other related tasks.\added{Available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ESA-philab/OceanDepths.}

</details>


### [428] [Coverage-Maximizing Multinomial Subset Routing under Operational Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16375)
*Quan Zhou,Yiyan Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multinomial Subset Routing (MSR) is an online routing framework over K experts using a multinomial policy to sample M experts per round; the routed subset is the distinct sampled experts. Rewards depend on the best expert(s) in the routed subset, which is a non-additive, winner-based reward structure not captured by typical combinatorial bandits. The paper integrates online mirror descent with Blackwell's Approachability (OMD-Approachability) to enforce long-term two-sided constraints under bandit feedback, achieving O(1/√T) regret in reward and constraint violation. Empirical validation on real crowdsourcing data supports the framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by routing scenarios across specialized models where rewards come from the best-performing option among a sampled subset, and where only the winner's reward is observed. Existing combinatorial bandit and subset-selection methods assume additive rewards and deterministic subsets, which misalign with this setting and with long-term operational constraints.

Method: Introduce a multinomial routing policy over K experts and sample M experts each round to form a routed subset. Weights are updated via online mirror descent, while Blackwell's Approachability handles long-term two-sided constraints under bandit feedback (only winner's reward observed). The algorithm is termed OMD-Approachability.

Result: The authors prove an O(1/√T) regret bound for both the reward and the constraint violation, under bandit feedback. They demonstrate practical applicability and validate the method empirically on a real-world crowdsourcing dataset.

Conclusion: MSR provides a novel non-additive reward framework for online routing with stochastic subnet selection, and OMD-Approachability yields tight regret and constraint guarantees. The approach is grounded in practical domains and validated empirically.

Abstract: We introduce Multinomial Subset Routing (MSR), a new online routing framework over $K$ experts in which the learner keeps a multinomial routing policy instead of a deterministic subset of experts. At each round, the learner samples $M$ experts i.i.d. from the multinomial policy, and the resulting set of distinct sampled experts forms the routed subset.
  The reward depends only on the best-performing expert(s) in the routed subset. This reward structure arises naturally in routing across specialized models but is not captured by standard combinatorial bandits or subset-selection methods, which optimize deterministic subsets and typically assume additive rewards. We require the selection to satisfy several long-term, two-sided operational constraints under bandit feedback, observing only the winner's reward each round. We propose OMD-Approachability, combining online mirror descent with Blackwell's Approachability, and prove it achieves $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ regret in both reward and constraint violation. We ground the framework in practical application domains and validate it empirically on a real-world crowdsourcing dataset.

</details>


### [429] [FETERS: Few-Shot Early Time-Series Classification via Effective Ratio Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16385)
*Chen-An Tai,Yujia Wu,Vincent S. Tseng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Few-shot ETSC framework FETERS uses dataset-level stopping ratio chosen by class-wise leave-one-out on the support set, with a penalty-based reward balancing accuracy and earliness; fuses Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations for classification, achieving SOTA in 5-shot across 69 datasets and competitive results in full-shot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ETSC under limited supervision is challenging due to insufficient labeled data for stopping decisions and feature learning. A method that avoids training an extra stopping module and works well with few labeled examples is desirable.

Method: FETERS selects a dataset-level stopping ratio using class-wise leave-one-out evaluation on the support set. It uses a penalty-based reward to manage the accuracy-earliness trade-off and combines Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations for classification, eliminating the need to train an additional stopping module.

Result: In 5-shot experiments over 69 public datasets across 14 domains, FETERS achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the highest average harmonic mean (HM) and best HM on 38 datasets, and outperforms the current SOTA on 44 datasets. It remains competitive in full-shot settings.

Conclusion: FETERS effectively addresses few-shot ETSC by avoiding extra stopping module training and leveraging strong feature representations, yielding strong cross-domain performance and robust accuracy-earliness trade-off in both few-shot and full-shot regimes.

Abstract: Early time-series classification (ETSC) aims to make accurate predictions from partially observed time series as early as possible. Although various stopping mechanisms and feature learning strategies have been developed for ETSC, most existing methods assume access to sufficient labeled training data, which may be unrealistic in applications with limited annotation. Under limited supervision, learning an additional sample-level stopping module and extracting effective classification features can both become challenging. In this paper, we propose FETERS, a few-shot ETSC framework that selects a dataset-level stopping ratio through class-wise leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation on the support set and uses a penalty-based reward function to manage the accuracy-earliness trade-off, thereby avoiding the need to train an additional stopping module. FETERS further combines Rocket-based features with frozen Chronos representations for classification. Extensive experiments on 69 public datasets spanning 14 domains show that FETERS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in the 5-shot setting, with the highest average harmonic mean (HM) and the best HM on 38 datasets, while outperforming the current SOTA method on 44 datasets. FETERS also remains competitive in the full-shot setting, demonstrating its effectiveness in managing the accuracy-earliness trade-off.

</details>


### [430] [SoftModel: A Neural Model That Grows Its Own Topology -- Governed Structural Growth for Continual In-Service Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16409)
*Zhoumin Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a lifelong-learning, growable neural system with total plasticity, governed by a reality gate, enabling structure to grow on demand and be audited; evaluated on continual-learning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the limitations of frozen architectures and fixed topologies in non-stationary, lifelong tasks. Aims to maintain stability through governance rather than immobility and to let capacity grow with demand.

Method: Introduces an algebra of structural operators (width, hierarchy, composition, input interface, grown cycles, attention heads) and a governance mechanism (reality gate) that treats parametric and structural changes uniformly; builds a complete end-to-end system operated by a production LLM; conducts a pre-registered experimental program with a thorough successes/failures map.

Result: Claims stability under lifelong change becomes an audit property of the lifecycle; capacity growth follows demand; ex-ante marginal value of new capacity is unobservable, hence ex-post governance; first-principles evaluation on standard continual-learning benchmarks with governance preserving long-sequence learning; reports both positive and negative outcomes.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that growth-governed, fully plastic models can sustain continual learning without a fixed topology; introduces auditable lifecycle governance and a framework for expanding capacity on demand; emphasizes a comprehensive experiment plan that maps both successes and failures.

Abstract: Today, a neural system is almost always used in two phases -- trained, then deployed -- and in that regime it freezes twice: training ends, and the topology itself was never a degree of freedom. We take the opposite premise as an axiom -- total plasticity: no part of a model, including its structure, is ever frozen -- and derive the governance a lifelong learner then requires. The design's target regime is continual, in-service learning: a long-lived model on a non-stationary stream, whose stability comes from governance rather than immobility and whose capacity follows demand. The result is a growable soft model: an algebra of structural operators (width, hierarchy, composition, input interface, grown cycles, attention heads), each exact at application, budgeted, and audited, with adoption decided solely by a held-out reality gate that treats parametric and structural change uniformly. A complete from-scratch system realizes the whole account; its factory surface is operated end-to-end by a production LLM. Two conclusions follow from the axiom by construction: stability under lifelong change becomes an audit property of the lifecycle, and structure that follows demand removes the silent cap a fixed topology places on later capability where the capacity floor binds. A third is measured: in the worlds where this was measured, the marginal value of new capacity was unobservable before adoption, so workable growth governance took its ex-post form. The same governance extends to evaluative signals, and the core method is evaluated on standard continual-learning benchmarks, where governed growth preserves the ability to keep learning along long task sequences. A pre-registered experimental program adjudicates the mechanism and value claims on the tested problems and reports its failures at full prominence; the map -- positive and negative -- is the contribution.

</details>


### [431] [TRACE-CASH: Trial-History-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Configuration Exploration in Time-Series CASH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16410)
*Yu-Han Huang,Yujia Wu,Vincent S. Tseng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACECASH is a task-local, hybrid sequential optimizer for TS-CASH that uses grouped actor-critic candidate generation with fixed coverage and exploitation rules; it achieves the best rankings (lowest mean rank) on MASE and WQL across 41 dataset-frequency variants, outperforming six baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable controlled, fair comparisons of heterogeneous search methods under a shared TS-CASH protocol and to address the challenges of conditional search spaces, temporal validation, and costly evaluations in time-series forecasting.

Method: Proposes TRACECASH: a task-local hybrid sequential optimizer with a model actor that proposes an initial model; three model-conditioned actors generate temporal, architectural, and training actions; a modelspecific decoder constructs the final configuration; fixed rules govern model coverage, validation-guided exploitation, and exploration after stalled progress; evaluated against six baselines (random, Bayesian, evolutionary, multi-objective, language-model-assisted) across 41 dataset-frequency task variants.

Result: TRACE-CASH exhibits the lowest mean rank on MASE and WQL among all methods; it also records the lowest window-averaged test-MASE rank in the full and late windows, indicating consistent performance advantages.

Conclusion: The complete TRACECASH procedure is competitive among the evaluated methods for TS-CASH, illustrating the benefit of a task-local, structured actor-critic search with a conditional action space and a decoder-driven configuration synthesis.

Abstract: Combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimization (CASH) searches a conditional space in which the selected model determines which hyperparameters are active. In time-series forecasting, temporal choices, chronological validation, and costly evaluations further complicate this search. Controlled comparisons of heterogeneous search methods under a shared time-series CASH (TS-CASH) evaluation protocol remain limited. Within this setting, we study TRACECASH, a task-local hybrid sequential optimizer combining grouped actor-critic candidate generation with fixed rules for model coverage, validation-guided exploitation, and exploration after stalled progress. A model actor proposes an initial forecasting model; three model-conditioned actors generate temporal, architectural, and training actions; and a modelspecific decoder constructs the configuration ultimately evaluated. We compare TRACE-CASH with six alternatives spanning random, Bayesian, evolutionary, multi-objective, and language-model-assisted search across 41 dataset-frequency task variants. TRACE-CASH has the lowest mean rank on both MASE and WQL. Descriptively, it also has the lowest window-averaged test-MASE rank in the predefined full and late windows. These results support the complete TRACECASH procedure as competitive among the evaluated methods.

</details>


### [432] [PertMind: Eliciting Emergent Biological Reasoning in LLM via Reinforcement Learning on Cellular Perturbation Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16419)
*Zhenchao Tang,Xiaogang Xu,Tianxu Lv,Jiahui Guan,Jiale Zhou,Haohuai He,Zhi Song,Hanbo Huang,Jiehui Huang,Jiafei Wu,Zhe Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PertMind uses perturbation atlases as reinforcement-learning environments to train LLMs for biological reasoning, combining supervised initialization with gene, pathway, and format-level RL signals, enabling scalable, transferable reasoning across multiple biological tasks without extensive post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the need for costly manual curation of biological reasoning traces by converting large perturbation–response datasets into computable RL rewards that guide general-purpose biological reasoning in pretrained models.

Method: Initialize with trusted-trajectory supervised signals and integrate multi-level RL signals (gene, pathway, format). Train solely on forward perturbation–response prediction, leveraging measured gene responses as rewards; evaluate transfer to diverse tasks without task-specific post-training.

Result: Improved inference in unseen cellular contexts while preserving general language abilities; zero-shot transfer to reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation; generated biologically meaningful profiles that align gene, cell, and donor representations across multiscale downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Reinforcement learning anchored to experimental endpoints is a scalable approach for transforming expanding biological atlases into training environments that enable general-purpose biological reasoning in pretrained models.

Abstract: Large language models can describe mechanisms, yet scalable post-training still depends on costly, manually curated biological reasoning traces. Here we show that cellular perturbation atlases can instead become reinforcement-learning environments, where measured gene responses provide computable rewards for biological reasoning. We introduce PertMind, which combines trusted-trajectory supervised initialization with gene-, pathway-, and format-level reinforcement signals. Trained only on forward perturbation-response prediction, PertMind improved response inference in unseen cellular contexts while retaining general language capabilities. It also transferred without task-specific post-training to reverse perturbation identification, double-perturbation reasoning, phenotypic-screen prioritization, and biological-process interpretation. PertMind further generated biological profiles that supported competitive gene, cell, and donor representations across multiscale downstream tasks. These results support the hypothesis that reinforcement on experimental endpoints can concentrate reusable biological strategies already accessible to pretrained models. More broadly, perturbation-derived reinforcement learning offers a scalable route for transforming expanding experimental atlases into training environments for general-purpose biological reasoning.

</details>


### [433] [Localized TabICLv2: Scaling Tabular In-Context Learning through k-NN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16429)
*Beimnet Bekele Guta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Localized TabICLv2 uses k-nearest-neighbors retrieval in the Stage 2 representation to reduce inference cost of TabICLv2 without changing architecture, achieving near-full accuracy with substantial speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-context tabular ICL with TabICLv2 incurs attention cost that grows with training-context size, hindering efficiency on large datasets; a scalable alternative is needed for faster inference while preserving performance.

Method: For each test point, retrieve the k nearest training examples based on similarity in the model's Stage 2 row-representation space; perform inference using the localized context; no architectural changes are required; further gains are possible via additional Stage 2 and Stage 3 fine-tuning.

Result: On TabArena classification tasks, the fine-tuned localized model retains 98.64% of Full TabICLv2 accuracy and yields a median 2.18× speedup in batch inference and ~249× speedup in single-query serving.

Conclusion: Localized retrieval-based conditioning effectively reduces inference cost with minimal accuracy loss; fine-tuning can further improve accuracy retention, making it a practical approach for scalable tabular ICL.

Abstract: Foundational models for tabular data have made significant progress in recent years, with TabICLv2 reporting state-of-the-art performance on several tabular classification tasks. However, full-context tabular ICL still suffers from attention cost that grows with the training-context size, which limits its ability to handle large datasets efficiently. Localized TabICLv2 introduces a method that reduces the inference cost of TabICLv2 by retrieving only the k nearest training neighbours for each test point, measured by similarity in the model's Stage 2 row-representation space, rather than using the full training context. This requires no architectural changes, and we show that accuracy retention can be improved through additional Stage 2 and Stage 3 fine-tuning. On TabArena classification tasks, the fine-tuned localized model retains 98.64% of Full TabICLv2 accuracy and it achieves a median 2.18$\times$ speedup in batch inference, and reaches approximately 249$\times$ median speedup in the single-query serving setting.

</details>


### [434] [Reference-free logged energy-oracle recovery for neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems: conforming Riesz reconstruction and archive-level selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16473)
*Karim Bounja,Lahcen Laayouni,Boujemaa Achchab,Abdeljalil Sakat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reference-free, computable energy-based monitor for selecting neural PDE solutions without exact solutions, enabling monotone and bracketed convergence to the logged energy error under refinement and saturation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To recover or bound the energy error of neural PDE approximations when the exact solution energy is unavailable, improving archive selection beyond loss-based criteria.

Method: Introduce a reference-free conforming Riesz monitor derived from the exact residual-energy identity and conforming projection for symmetric coercive variational problems. Use nested conforming refinement to obtain a lower bound that converges to the logged energy error; under saturation, hierarchical enrichment yields a computable upper bound. Analyze order-sensitivity of archive ranking; prove uniform recovery for finite archives; show selection at fine auxiliary resolution and bracket guarantees, plus logging-resolution loss bounds.

Result: The monitor provides an unconditional lower bound that monotonically approaches the logged energy error; under saturation it yields a computable near-oracle bracket and certifies unique logged-oracle selection; finite-archive recovery guarantees convergence to logged-oracle error and enables oracle-like selection with sufficient resolution; energy-scale calibration demonstrated experimentally in diffusion and elasticity problems.

Conclusion: The proposed energy-error monitor replaces inaccessible exact-error minimization with a computable, training-free selection criterion based on the energy-error scale, enabling oracle-level selection with modest post-processing cost.

Abstract: Neural PDE training yields a finite checkpoint archive, yet its logged energy errors are inaccessible without the exact solution, while loss-based selection does not necessarily recover the logged energy oracle. For admissible neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems, we introduce a reference-free selection rule based on minimizing a computable conforming Riesz monitor. The exact residual-energy identity and conforming projection make the monitor an unconditional lower bound converging monotonically to each logged energy error under nested conforming refinement; under saturation, hierarchical enrichment yields a computable upper estimate and hence a lower-upper bracket. A key finding is that archive selection is order-sensitive: unresolved checkpoint-dependent components can reverse the oracle-non-oracle ranking at finite resolution, so checkpointwise recovery alone is insufficient. For finite archives, we prove uniform recovery, yielding convergence to the logged-oracle error and, without saturation, logged-oracle selection at sufficiently fine auxiliary resolution. Under saturation, the bracket gives a computable near-oracle bound and certifies unique logged-oracle selection upon interval separation. We also bound logging-resolution loss and certify oracle inclusion over prescribed comparison trajectories. The resulting criterion replaces inaccessible exact-error minimization by computable, training-independent post-training selection on the intrinsic energy-error scale, requiring only the computed candidates and the variational problem. Experiments on diffusion and elasticity, including a non-manufactured perforated plate, demonstrate energy-scale calibration, oracle-level selection, and modest post-processing cost.

</details>


### [435] [Pallas: A Proactive KV Cache Migration Framework for LLM Inference in AI-RAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16477)
*Tianhang Ding,Jianchun Liu,Hongli Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proactive KV-cache migration (Pallas) minimizes service interruption and inter-token latency during AI-RAN handovers by predicting the target gNB and prefetching the necessary inference state in parallel with ongoing source-side inference, using a prefix-suffix partitioning of tokens and online prefetching window scheduling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In AI-RAN, handovers can detach an active LLM inference from its KV-cache, causing a trade-off: keeping inference at the source saves state but increases ITL, while moving state to the target reduces SIT but requires cache transfer or recomputation, delaying service. A solution is needed to keep locality while minimizing interruptions.

Method: Pallas partitions the token stream into a stable historical prefix and evolving suffix. The target reconstructs the prefix via local prefill while the source streams KV blocks for the suffix. Upon handover, the target assembles both parts into an up-to-date KV cache and resumes decoding locally. An online scheduler selects the prefetching window (when preparation begins) using mobility predictions and runtime telemetry. The approach is prototyped using vLLM and evaluated across three LLMs and 100–500 Mbps inter-gNB links.

Result: Average SIT is reduced by factors of 2.28–89.68× compared with target-side recovery. Average ITL is reduced by 16.0%–50.0% compared with source-side forwarding.

Conclusion: Proactive KV-cache migration via Pallas can substantially improve continuity and responsiveness of AI-powered RAN services during handovers, demonstrating significant reductions in SIT and ITL in realistic networking conditions with a practical vLLM prototype.

Abstract: AI-RAN brings large language model (LLM) serving close to mobile users, but cellular handover can separate an active request from its inference state: the user attaches to a target base station (gNB) while the large and growing key-value (KV) cache remains at the source. Retaining inference at the source preserves service continuity but persistently increases inter-token latency (ITL), whereas recovering the state at the target restores serving locality but requires KV-cache transfer, recomputation, or a combination of both only after handover, directly prolonging service interruption time (SIT).
  This work presents Pallas, a \textit{proactive} KV-cache migration framework that prepares the inference state at the predicted target before handover, in parallel with ongoing source-side inference and token delivery. At the preparation trigger, Pallas partitions the token sequence into a stable historical prefix and an evolving suffix. The target reconstructs the prefix through local prefill, while the source streams the KV blocks generated for the suffix. At handover, the target assembles both portions into an up-to-date KV cache and resumes decoding locally, leaving only unfinished preparation to contribute to SIT. An online scheduler selects the \textit{prefetching window}, which determines how early preparation begins before handover, based on mobility predictions and runtime telemetry. Across three LLMs and $100$--$500~\mathrm{Mbps}$ inter-gNB links, our vLLM-based prototype reduces average SIT by factors of $2.28$--$89.68$ over target-side recovery approaches and lowers average ITL by $16.0\%$--$50.0\%$ compared with source-side forwarding.

</details>


### [436] [Learning Generalizable Reconstruction of High-Dimensional Neural Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16569)
*Anima Kujur,Zahra Monfared*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A windowed PCA-DMD approach reconstructs high-dimensional LFP dynamics via a latent linear Koopman model, achieving strong cross-subject zero-shot generalization and scalable performance, outperforming several DMD variants and validating on external datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstructing long-duration, high-resolution neural recordings (LFPs) across subjects is challenging due to high dimensionality, nonstationarity, and inter-subject variability; existing DMD variants struggle with scalability and cross-subject generalization.

Method: Segment recordings into overlapping windows, project into a compact PCA latent space, learn linear Koopman evolution in that latent space, and reconstruct signals via inverse projection and overlap-add. Compare against Classical DMD, SpDMD, MrDMD, HODMD; assess zero-shot cross-subject generalization, out-of-sample temporal prediction, scalability from 400k–900k samples, and external validation on a 93-channel Allen Neuropixels recording; analyze Koopman spectrum and modes.

Result: On 200,000-sample hippocampal recordings, PCA-DMD outperformed Classical DMD, SpDMD, MrDMD, and HODMD (KLD=0.0761, HD=0.0847). All-pairs cross-subject zero-shot correlations: 0.9504–0.9800; HD=0.0010–0.0072; KLD=0.0005–0.0022. Out-of-sample temporal prediction showed close one-step agreement across unseen intervals and multiple channels. Scalability from 400k to 900k samples: mean correlation ~0.965–0.968 with predictable compute cost. External validation on 93-channel Allen Neuropixels: mean and median channel-wise correlations of 0.7427 and 0.7990, respectively. Koopman spectral analysis revealed eigenvalues concentrated near the unit circle.

Conclusion: PCA-DMD provides an interpretable, generalizable, and computationally scalable framework for reconstructing high-dimensional neural dynamics.

Abstract: Accurate reconstruction of long-duration neural recordings is challenging because local field potentials (LFPs) are high-resolution, multichannel, transient, and variable across subjects. We present PCA-DMD, a scalable operator-theoretic framework that segments LFP recordings into overlapping windows, projects them into a compact PCA space, learns linear Koopman evolution in the latent space, and reconstructs continuous signals through inverse projection and overlap-add aggregation. On 200,000-sample hippocampal recordings, PCA-DMD outperformed Classical DMD, SpDMD, MrDMD, and HODMD, achieving KLD=0.0761 and HD=0.0847. In all-pair cross-subject zero-shot generalization at 300,000 samples, correlations were 0.9504-0.9800, with HD=0.0010-0.0072 and KLD=0.0005-0.0022, without target-subject fine-tuning. Out-of-sample temporal prediction showed close one-step agreement on temporally held-out LFP segments across the unseen interval and multiple channels. Scalability analysis from 400,000 to 900,000 samples showed stable zero-shot reconstruction, with mean correlation remaining about 0.965-0.968 while computational cost increased predictably. External validation on an independent 93-channel Allen Neuropixels recording yielded mean and median channel-wise correlations of 0.7427 and 0.7990, respectively. Koopman spectral and mode analyses revealed dominant eigenvalues concentrated near the unit circle. PCA-DMD therefore provides an interpretable, generalizable, and computationally scalable framework for reconstructing high-dimensional neural dynamics.

</details>


### [437] [Variational Outlier-Robust Gaussian Process Regression with Generative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16606)
*Arslan Majal,Aamir Hussain Chughtai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A robust generative Gaussian process regression (GPR) model that handles observation-specific contamination via latent indicators, learned with a variational generalized EM approach, achieving competitive-to-superior predictive accuracy under outliers while preserving cubic scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPR with Gaussian likelihood is highly sensitive to outliers, which can distort learning and predictions in real data. There is a need for robust modeling that can explicitly account for contaminated observations without sacrificing tractability.

Method: Introduce a generative GPR with contamination-specific latent variables that indicate observation-level contamination. Use a variational generalized EM procedure to infer the latent variables and GPR hyperparameters jointly, enabling adaptive mitigation of outliers. Maintain cubic computational scaling typical of GPR methods.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real datasets with varying contamination scenarios shows the proposed method remains competitive with, and in several cases outperforms, robust GPR baselines in predictive accuracy, while preserving cubic computational complexity.

Conclusion: The approach offers a robust GPR framework that explicitly models contamination and remains computationally scalable. It provides competitive performance under outliers and suggests potential for broader robustness applications, though details on contamination modeling and scalability in very large datasets would be valuable.

Abstract: Outliers can substantially distort Gaussian process regression (GPR) due to its conventional Gaussian observation likelihood, leading to inaccurate model learning and prediction. To address this limitation, this article introduces a generative GPR model that captures observation-specific contamination and adaptively mitigates the influence of outliers. Subsequently, a variational generalized expectation-maximization procedure is used to learn the latent variables and GPR model parameters. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets under different contamination settings demonstrate that the proposed method remains competitive with-and in several cases outperforms-robust GPR baselines in prediction accuracy. Moreover, the proposed method shares the cubic computational scaling of the compared GPR methods.

</details>


### [438] [Hoeffding adaptive splitting trees for data stream classification with concept drift and ensemble learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16659)
*Daniel Nowak Assis,Jean Paul Barddal,Fabrício Enembreck*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two new decision-tree ensemble models, Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees, blend Hoeffding Tree’s periodic splits with adaptive-splitting via change detectors to boost diversity and adaptability in data-stream ensembles, achieving state-of-the-art results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hoeffding Trees provide a solid, periodic-splitting base for data-stream ensembles, but adaptive-splitting approaches can improve performance under concept drift; however, adaptive splits may reduce ensemble diversity when used as base learners. There is a need to balance adaptability with ensemble diversity.

Method: Introduce two novel models called Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees that combine the periodic splitting strategy of Hoeffding Trees with adaptive splitting triggered by change-detection mechanisms to identify performance decay and decide split points.
