Integrate these into ensembles and evaluate on benchmarks with cost analysis and drift adaptation.

Result: Ensemble performance is enhanced and achieves state-of-the-art results across a comprehensive evaluation, including benchmarks, computational cost analysis, and concept drift adaptation.

Conclusion: The proposed Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees successfully merge periodic and adaptive split strategies to improve diversity and adaptability, yielding superior ensemble performance and encouraging broader adoption and further study.

Abstract: Ensembles of decision trees are well-established methods for data stream classification. In ensemble learning, Hoeffding Trees are widely adopted as base learners, performing periodic split attempts according to the Hoeffding bound. Recent studies, however, indicate that this standard splitting mechanism lacks adaptability, while adaptive trees that trigger splits in response to performance degradation have achieved superior results. In this paper, we identify limitations in the use of adaptive-splitting decision trees as ensemble base learners, showing that change detectors often fail to promote sufficient diversity within ensembles. To address this issue, we propose two novel decision tree models, termed Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees. These models combine the periodic splitting strategy of Hoeffding Trees, which fosters ensemble diversity, with adaptive splitting mechanisms that employ change detection algorithms to identify performance decay and determine split points. Experimental results demonstrate that Hoeffding Adaptive Splitting Trees enhance ensemble performance and achieve state-of-the-art results across a comprehensive evaluation, including benchmark comparisons, computational cost analysis, and concept drift adaptation.

</details>


### [439] [UniTAC: Universal Task-Aware Compression via Weighted Distortion Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16696)
*Homa Esfahanizadeh,Matin Mortaheb,Jinfeng Du,Harish Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniTAC introduces a single learned image codec that spans universal (task-agnostic) to task-specialized operation, retrievable at runtime without retraining by transmitting a per-component importance vector as side information to condition encoder/decoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical AI systems face strict bandwidth, latency, and energy constraints while tasks evolve; per-task codecs are brittle and retraining is often infeasible.

Method: A ViT-based codec with token-level conditioning; a per-component importance vector (e.g., gradient attribution) is transmitted as lightweight side information to condition both encoder and decoder. The model is trained once over a broad, randomized family of such vectors under a weighted rate-distortion objective, with a fixed backbone and a single reconstructive output. Runtime re-targeting is achieved by swapping the injected vector to steer fidelity.

Result: On a localized task at 0.034 bpp, UniTAC achieves 91.4% accuracy, 1.9 percentage points shy of a task-based codec (93.3%), and surpasses universal codecs (76.9%). The work also analyzes a diagonal weighted distortion, deriving when it is task-consistent and how weights map to task sensitivity.

Conclusion: A unified codec that bridges universal and task-specific performance, enabling runtime adaptation without retraining. The approach connects weighted rate-distortion theory to practical ViT-based codecs and demonstrates near-task performance under low bitrate.

Abstract: Physical AI systems such as autonomous vehicles and robots rely on timely exchange of high-dimensional sensory signals under tight bandwidth, latency, and energy budgets. Because the task driving downstream decisions evolves over time, a task-specific codec is brittle and retraining one per task is infeasible in the field. We propose UniTAC, a single learned image codec spanning universal (task-agnostic) to task-specialized operation, re-targeted at runtime without retraining. The task is abstracted as a per-component importance vector, derived, e.g., from gradient attribution of any downstream model, and transmitted as low-overhead side information that conditions both encoder and decoder. Trained once over a broad, randomized family of such vectors against weighted-reconstruction distortion, UniTAC keeps a fixed backbone and a single human-viewable reconstruction whose fidelity is steered to the active task by swapping the injected vector. We analyze the underlying weighted rate-distortion problem, characterizing when a diagonal weighted distortion is task-consistent and how weights relate to task sensitivity. Guided by this, we design a Vision Transformer (ViT) codec whose token-level conditioning natively realizes this weight-driven code. On a localized task at 0.034 bpp, a single UniTAC model reaches 91.4% accuracy, only 1.9% below a task-based codec (93.3%) and above universal codecs (76.9%).

</details>


### [440] [The Ethical Decision Head: Operationalizing Normative Ethics in Autonomous Vehicles via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16710)
*Thomas Mbrice,Ammar Ali,Sami Mian,Khai Hern Low,Eric Chen,Arshia Aghajani,Wolf Schäfer,Amin Shirangi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An RL-based Ethical Decision Head (EDH) trains an autonomous-vehicle policy to learn morally-aligned driving via differentiable rewards derived from two ethical theories, revealing a gap between philosophical ethics and human-guided learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address ethical decision-making in high-stakes autonomous driving by embedding normative ethics into learning, and to assess how human preferences shape learned ethics through RLHF.

Method: Develop EDH using deep RL (PPO) in a CARLA-like state space; instantiate two normative frameworks (Utilitarian and Kantian); train with a Bradley–Terry reward model learned from pairwise human preferences over 200 collision-imminent scenarios; use Kantian condition as a stability/control test.

Result: Kantian framing produced stable learning (acts as a constant predictor via the codebook); the Utilitarian agent exhibited a troubling pattern—human raters rewarded self-sacrifice over minimizing casualties, and the agent learned this preference; overall, an asymmetry in learnability between the normative frameworks under human supervision (RLHF).

Conclusion: RLHF may reflect how humans live ethics rather than how philosophers define them; caution is warranted when embedding normative theories in RL for AVs, as learned behavior may diverge from prescriptive ethics and raise safety and governance concerns.

Abstract: As autonomous vehicles (AVs) approach Level 4 and Level 5 operational capability [SAE International, 2018], their on- board decision systems must handle not only safety-critical locomotion but also their subsequent moral weight. This paper details the Ethical Decision Head (EDH), a deep re- inforcement learning (RL) framework that encodes ethical reasoning as a differentiable reward signal, enabling a pol- icy gradient agent to learn morally-aligned driving behavior in scenarios whose state representation is aligned with the CARLA simulation environment [Dosovitskiy et al., 2017]. Two normative frameworks are instantiated and evaluated: a Utilitarian framework minimizing total casualties and a Kan- tian framework enforcing course maintenance as a categori- cal imperative. The EDH is trained via Proximal Policy Op- timization (PPO) [Schulman et al., 2017] against a Bradley- Terry reward model [Bradley and Terry, 1952] learned from pairwise human preference annotations over 200 collision- imminent scenarios. Results reveal an asymmetry in the learnability of normative ethical frameworks under human su- pervision. The Kantian condition, which reduces to a con- stant prediction task under the codebook, serves as a pipeline control: it confirms training stability and rules out infrastruc- ture failure as an explanation for the utilitarian result. The Utilitarian agent learned something more unsettling: human raters rewarded self-sacrifice over casualty minimization, and the model learned that preference faithfully. This divergence between what humans prescribe in theory and what they re- ward in practice suggests that RLHF does not learn ethics as philosophers define it, but as humans live it.

</details>


### [441] [Le Critique: Privileged Value Functions for LLM Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16739)
*Siddarth Venkatraman,Matthieu Dinot,Laurence Aitchison*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two strategies to enhance value-function reinforcement learning for LLMs: Privileged Value Functions (PVF) and TETHER; they provide token-level credit signals and adaptive baselining, outperforming standard value-function baselines and rivaling group-relative methods like GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Group-relative variance-reduction methods (e.g., GRPO) reduce gradient variance but offer only sequence-level credit and face throughput bottlenecks due to straggler rollouts; learned value functions can provide token-level advantages but entail infrastructure and deployment challenges. This work aims to make value-function RL more practical and effective for LLMs by injecting token-level signals and adaptively combining baselines.

Method: 1) Privileged Value Functions (PVF): inject task-relevant token-level signal without biasing the policy objective. 2) TETHER: an adaptive baseline that interpolates between group-relative and value baselines depending on value-function accuracy. Evaluation across several reasoning tasks; comparison with GRPO and standard baselines.

Result: PVF and TETHER consistently improve over the standard value-function baseline across multiple reasoning tasks, and are competitive with or outperform GRPO's mean-baseline.

Conclusion: PVF and TETHER offer practical, effective enhancements for value-function RL in LLMs by addressing token-level credit assignment and adaptive baselining, yielding strong empirical results across reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms for Large Language Models (LLMs) are largely distinguished by their variance reduction strategy. Group-relative methods like GRPO reduce gradient variance by sampling multiple rollouts per prompt, but provide only sequence-level credit. Training is also blocked by straggler rollouts, reducing throughput and increasing off-policyness. Learned value functions theoretically address both problems, providing token-level advantages without requiring large groups. However, additional infrastructure engineering challenges combined with the practical success of critic-free methods have made it difficult to justify their inclusion in RL pipelines. We propose two complementary strategies to improve the performance of value function RL: 1) Privileged Value Functions (PVF) which provide an elegant mechanism to inject additional task-relevant token-level signal without biasing the policy objective; 2) TETHER, a baseline that adaptively interpolates between group-relative and value baselines depending on the value function accuracy. Across several reasoning tasks, both strategies consistently improve over the standard value function baseline, and are competitive with or outperform mean-baseline GRPO.

</details>


### [442] [Would this change your answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16747)
*Adam Karvonen,Euan Ong,Subhash Kantamneni,Samuel Marks*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CHIVE introduces a counterfactual explanation pipeline for LLMs that discovers explanations via prompt edits, finds that common interpretability techniques do not improve the ability to predict counterfactual behaviors, and shows CHIVE-generated data can train models to generalize to out-of-distribution settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To define what makes explanations 'good' by testing their counterfactual simulatability, and to address the lack of evidence that existing interpretability methods improve predictive power for model behavior on counterfactual inputs.

Method: Introduce CHIVE (Counterfactual Hypothesis Investigation Via Edits), an agentic pipeline that spots unexpected model behaviors and probes them with counterfactual prompt edits; apply two experiments: (i) assess whether standard LLM interpretability techniques improve an agent's ability to predict counterfactual behaviors, (ii) generate CHIVE-based training data by recording outcomes of counterfactual experiments and training predictors on them.

Result: Interpretability techniques studied did not yield improvements in predicting counterfactual behaviors; CHIVE produced thousands of high-quality explanations with supporting counterfactual evidence; models trained on CHIVE-generated counterfactual outcomes generalize to various out-of-distribution settings.

Conclusion: CHIVE automates discovery of explanations for naturally occurring LLM behaviors and provides a framework to evaluate and potentially improve methods for explaining LLM behaviors, including generating valuable training data that generalizes across settings.

Abstract: Many areas of AI research, such as language model interpretability and chain of thought faithfulness, seek to explain model behaviors. But what constitutes a "good" explanation? In this work, we evaluate explanations through the lens of counterfactual simulatability-whether the explanation is useful for predicting model behaviors on related counterfactual inputs. To this end, we introduce CHIVE (Counterfactual Hypothesis Investigation Via Edits), a novel agentic pipeline that identifies unexpected model behaviors in the wild and investigates them with counterfactual prompt edits. This yields thousands of high-quality explanations for naturally-occurring model behaviors along with supporting counterfactual evidence. We apply CHIVE in two ways. First, we evaluate whether common LLM interpretability techniques improve an agent's ability to predict counterfactual model behaviors. Surprisingly, we find no uplift from any of the interpretability techniques studied. Second, we use CHIVE to generate training data. We find that training models to predict outcomes of CHIVE-generated counterfactual experiments generalizes to various out-of-distribution settings. Overall, CHIVE automatically discovers explanations of naturally-occurring LLM behaviors, enabling us to evaluate and improve methods for explaining LLM behaviors.

</details>


### [443] [CaliBench: Are the Stochastic Dynamics of Video World Models Physically Calibrated?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16829)
*Jonathan Sadeghi,Jenny Seidenschwarz,Jesse Allardice,Sirish Srinivasan,Benjamin Graham,Jeffrey Hawke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CaliBench introduces a discrete, physically interpretable calibration benchmark for video world models, revealing widespread miscalibration and a tendency to collapse probability mass, and provides a mean normalised total variation (mnTV) metric and protocol for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks score individual generations or coarse distribution similarity, failing to test fine-grained aleatoric uncertainty for specific phenomena. A calibrated, interpretable test requires known reference distributions in a discrete space.

Method: Define outcome spaces with closed-form reference distributions (e.g., binomial, Bernoulli, uniform dice/cards/lottery, skewed roulette color). Evaluate models by scoring the generated outcomes in these discrete bins, decompose performance into scorability (fraction of scoreable generations) and calibration (total variation distance from reference). Use a chi-squared test for calibration significance (calibration is the null). Test nine scenes across six image-to-video models, with 32 generations per condition, report mnTV and per-model calibration.

Result: Across models/scenes, probability mass concentrates on a small number of outcomes; many model-scenario pairs show significant miscalibration, with extreme cases collapsing to single outcomes. Roulette often yields low scorability due to ambiguous ball placement. No model dominates across all nine scenes; calibration issues persist.

Conclusion: The authors release the evaluation protocol and mnTV metric for fair comparisons of new models, highlighting the need for calibration-focused evaluation in video world models and providing a concrete framework to diagnose and compare uncertainty handling.

Abstract: Video world models approximate the stochastic distribution of physical outcomes through generative sampling, but existing benchmarks score individual generations or compare distributions coarsely over a whole dataset, leaving the fine-grained aleatoric uncertainty of specific phenomena untested. We introduce CaliBench, which scores outcomes in a physically interpretable discrete space - a bin index, a die face, a suit, a colour - rather than a learned feature space such as in FID, so the distance from a known reference distribution is measured directly. We curate outcome spaces whose reference is known in closed form (binomial Galton boards, Bernoulli forks, uniform dice/cards/lottery, a skewed European-roulette colour), enabling an exact calibration test. We decompose performance into two orthogonal axes that a single accuracy metric conflates: scorability, the fraction of generations yielding a scoreable outcome, and calibration, the total variation distance from the reference on that sample. A chi-squared test assesses significance; as calibration is its null hypothesis it can evidence only miscalibration, and at N=32 per cell detects only large deviations. We apply it to nine scenes and six image-to-video models (WAN-2.7, SeeDance-2.0, HappyHorse-1.0, Veo 3.1, Runway Gen-4.5, Cosmos3-Super), 32 generations each. Models consistently concentrate probability mass on a few outcomes rather than reproducing the reference. Most scene-model combinations are significantly miscalibrated, in the extreme collapsing to one outcome, as Veo 3.1 does on dice. On roulette, generations often leave the ball ambiguously placed, giving several models low scorability. Performance varies by scene: no model dominates all nine. We release the protocol and a metric (mean normalised total variation, mnTV) for comparing new models against our results.

</details>


### [444] [Proteus: Incremental Memory Activation for Long-Context Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16844)
*Reza Bayat,Ali Behrouz,Vahab Mirrokni,Aaron Courville*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proteus introduces incremental memory activation to memory-augmented sequence models, progressively expanding memory capacity to alleviate early-token pollution; yields consistent, context-length–dependent gains across language modeling, reasoning, and long-context retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static memory in long-context models allows early tokens to use excessive degrees of freedom, causing interference and limiting capacity for later context. An adaptive memory capacity schedule could mitigate pollution and improve retention.

Method: A general incremental activation paradigm (Proteus) that compresses history via an early bottleneck and gradually unlocks fresh memory capacity as context grows; compatible with existing memory architectures (e.g., SWLA, Comba, Titans, Hope-Attention) at no additional cost.

Result: Across standard language modeling, reasoning tasks, and long-context retrieval/understanding, Proteus improves performance, with gains increasing at longer context lengths, indicating reduced interference and better retention of late context.

Conclusion: Static memory is suboptimal; dynamically scheduling effective memory capacity is a simple, broadly applicable technique for sequence modeling.

Abstract: The quadratic cost of attention-based sequence models for long contexts has motivated a growing line of research on memory-based models that can compress context into a compact state. However, most existing memory models expose a static memory throughout the entire sequence. Because early tokens face no compression pressure, they occupy too many degrees of freedom and "pollute" the memory state, leaving little capacity for later context and increasing interference between what is stored and what arrives next. We study a new paradigm of incremental memory activation, where the effective capacity of memory is progressively expanded as the context grows. Imposing an early bottleneck forces the model to compress history more effectively, while unlocking fresh capacity over time reduces interference and improves retention of later context. We instantiate this paradigm in Proteus, a straightforward mechanism that can be incorporated into a broad class of neural memory architectures at no additional cost. We apply Proteus to state-of-the-art models, including SWLA, Comba, Titans, and Hope-Attention, and observe consistent improvements on standard language modeling and reasoning, as well as on long-context retrieval and understanding, with gains that grow at longer context lengths. Overall, our results show that static memory is suboptimal and that scheduling effective capacity is a simple and broadly applicable tool for sequence modeling.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [445] [FLOPs vs Real Work: The Importance of Replication in AI Efficiency Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14550)
*Enrique Barba Roque,Luís Cruz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Replication confirms FLOPs alone poorly predict execution time; α-FLOPs underestimates time on newer hardware, with instability (jumps/oscillations); replication materials were incomplete; complete replication package provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether α-FLOPs remains a valid estimator of hardware-dependent efficiency on modern hardware and ensure reproducibility of such analyses.

Method: Replicate the original experiments, scrutinize replication materials for transparency (dependencies, regression data), perform fine-grained timing measurements across layers with varying spatial/kernel aspects, compare against α-FLOPs predictions on new hardware.

Result: Raw FLOPs do not map straightforwardly to execution time due to differences in parallelizability; newer hardware shows instabilities and discontinuities in timing; α-FLOPs generally underestimates execution time; replication validates the general thesis but yields negative results for α-FLOPs.

Conclusion: FLOPs alone are insufficient as a cost metric; α-FLOPs is not reliable on modern hardware; emphasizes need for complete, transparent replication packages and provides one for further study.

Abstract: AI efficiency has recently taken the spotlight in both academy and industry due to massive model scales, high energy demands, and environmental costs. While reporting Floating Point Operations (FLOPs) is a traditional approach for assessing computational costs, the relationship between FLOPs and execution time is not straightforward, as layers with the same number of FLOPs may not have the same execution time because some operations are more easily parallelized than others. This paper sets out to replicate the original experiments from a study that proposed the $α-FLOPs$ estimation formula to verify whether the results remain applicable on newer, more powerful hardware.
  During the replication process, we identify limitations in the replication materials provided by the original study, including a lack of specific dependency details and transparency regarding regression data. Our results validate the thesis that raw FLOPs alone are not an appropriate metric for execution time, as spatial dimensions remain more easily parallelized than kernel dimensions. However, fine-grained measurements reveal that the relationship is much less straightforward than previously shown, with newer hardware exhibiting instabilities and discontinuities in execution time, including jumps and oscillations, that the $α-FLOPs$ formula generally underestimates. Ultimately, this work validates the empirical findings from the original study but shows negative results when applying the $α-FLOPs$ estimation. We also highlight the critical need for complete and accurate replication packages for research on hardware-dependent efficiency assessment and provide a complete replication package for our implementation to facilitate further study.

</details>


### [446] [Large Language Models Show Metacognitive Sensitivity in Medical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14552)
*Ahmad Nazzal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A controlled, psychophysics-inspired benchmark evaluates medical LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and confidence in AT-NCD vs DRCI, revealing high accuracy but imperfect calibration and localized confidence errors; provides a framework for evaluating evidence sensitivity and metacognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether LLMs' diagnostic decisions and confidence reflect evidence quality and uncertainty in medical settings, addressing potential miscalibration and overconfidence.

Method: Synthetic 45 vignettes varying evidence strength, conflicts, missing info; three prompt variants; 135 trials; pilot with gpt-4.1-nano; measure diagnostic accuracy, confidence, AUROC2; analyze how confidence tracks evidence distance, missingness, correctness; assess metacognitive sensitivity and calibration; compare models.

Result: Diagnostic accuracy 93.5%; mean confidence 78.4%; AUROC2 0.876; confidence increases with distance from boundary, decreases with missing info; higher on correct vs incorrect after adjusting; evidence of partial metacognitive sensitivity; errors cluster in moderate conflicting AT-NCD cases with shift toward DRCI and overconfidence; confidence quality should be measured directly rather than inferred from accuracy; framework established for evaluating evidence sensitivity and localized calibration failure.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals that medical LLMs show partial metacognitive alignment to evidence but exhibit localized calibration failures; a direct confidence-quality assessment is needed; the framework enables reproducible evaluation of evidence sensitivity and metacognitive calibration in clinical LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated and used in medicine, but clinical usefulness depends on answer accuracy and whether confidence tracks evidence quality and uncertainty. We developed a controlled, psychophysics-inspired clinical benchmark to test diagnostic choice and confidence behavior in a medical LLM. The benchmark focused on probable Alzheimer-type neurocognitive disorder (AT-NCD) versus depression-related cognitive impairment (DRCI). We generated 45 synthetic vignettes varying evidence strength, conflicting evidence, and missing information. Each vignette was presented under three prompt variants, yielding 135 trials. In a pilot run with gpt-4.1-nano, all trials produced valid structured outputs. Across forced-choice trials, diagnostic accuracy was 93.5%, mean confidence was 78.4%, and AUROC2 was 0.876. Confidence increased with evidence distance from the diagnostic boundary, decreased when information was missing, and remained higher on correct than incorrect trials after adjustment for evidence strength and prompt format. These findings indicate partial metacognitive sensitivity rather than globally uninformative confidence. However, errors clustered in moderate, conflicting AT-NCD cases, where the model shifted toward DRCI and retained more confidence than empirical accuracy justified. Model comparison suggested that confidence quality should be measured directly rather than inferred from benchmark accuracy or model capability alone. This study establishes a reproducible framework for evaluating evidence sensitivity, metacognitive sensitivity, and localized calibration failure in medical LLMs.

</details>


### [447] [The Unwritten Benchmark: A New Challenge for Multimodal Machine Learning in Abstract Perceptual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14558)
*Garima Arya Yadav,Nilay Yilmaz,Yezhou Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new benchmark (The Unwritten Benchmark) assesses abstract perceptual reasoning by inferring words from acousto-kinematic signals (pen scratch audio and hand-movement video) with no ink visible. Humans achieve high ordered-letter accuracy while state-of-the-art multimodal models perform poorly, and multimodal input can degrade performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To probe the limits of current multimodal models in abstract perceptual/cognitive reasoning that relies on dynamic generative processes and micro-kinematics, extending beyond static content understanding to causal cross-modal inference.

Method: Define acousto-kinematic word inference across three writing styles. Data consists of audio of pen scratches and video of hand movements with no visible ink. Evaluate humans and models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5-Pro) on ordered-letter accuracy, and analyze single vs. dual-modality inputs to assess fusion effects.

Result: Humans exceed 80% ordered-letter accuracy. Leading models barely reach 10% and often fail to surpass it. A paradoxical fusion effect is observed: providing both modalities can degrade performance rather than improve it, revealing a breakdown in synthesizing complementary cues.

Conclusion: Exposes significant gaps in cross-modal causal reasoning and micro-kinematics comprehension in current models, highlighting a need for methods that capture dynamic, generative perceptual processes for abstract cognitive tasks.

Abstract: Current multimodal models have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in recognizing static visual and auditory content. However, their capacity for abstract perceptual reasoning, inferring unseen information from dynamic, generative processes, remains a critical and underexplored frontier. In this paper, we introduce The Unwritten Benchmark, a new challenge designed to probe this abstract perceptual and cognitive ability. We define the core task as acousto-kinematic word inference: models must decipher words, across 3 different writing styles, being written solely from the audio of pen scratches and the video of hand movements, without any visible ink trace. Our evaluation results reveal a profound gap between human and machine performance: while human participants achieve high ordered letter accuracy (over 80%), leading Multimodal Machine Learning Models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5-Pro, struggle significantly, failing to surpass 10%. Furthermore, we identify a paradoxical fusion effect in the models, where providing both modalities often degrades performance rather than improving it. This finding indicates a fundamental breakdown in their ability to synthesize complementary perceptual cues for this cognitive task. These findings highlight significant limitations in both cross-modal causal reasoning and the understanding of the micro-kinematics essential for such cognitive and intuitive perceptual reasoning.

</details>


### [448] [When to Communicate: Belief Distributions and KL Divergence for Principled Gating in Multi-Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14559)
*Teoman Kaman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KL-based belief divergence gating for inter-agent communication in MARL; gates communication to when agents' latent-world-state beliefs disagree sufficiently, yielding principled, thresholded communication and improved latent representations with mixed task-dependent gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Avoid high-variance, unstable gating from policy-gradient approaches and avoid always-communicate strategies; provide a principled mechanism to trigger communication based on belief disagreement.

Method: Each agent maintains a belief distribution over a latent world state (softmax over LSTM hidden state). Communication is triggered only when the KL divergence between agents' belief distributions exceeds a fixed threshold epsilon. Evaluated on Predator-Prey (IC3Net benchmark) across two sizes with multiple seeds and on MPE simple_spread, comparing to IC3Net, CommNet, and an independent controller.

Result: On PP 10x10, IC3Net outperforms the KL-belief gating. On PP 20x20, threshold ablation (epsilon in {0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0}) shows inverted-U, with epsilon=0.5 achieving 73.84 average steps and 42% success vs IC3Net’s 75.31 steps and 31% (gap of 1.47 steps and 11 percentage points with tighter seed variance). On MPE, the belief head increases mean reward by 12 points and reduces variance by 26× even when gating is inactive. This suggests two orthogonal contributions: principled gating when beliefs can converge, and improved latent representations that benefit coordination regardless.

Conclusion: KL-based gating is a principled alternative to REINFORCE-based or always-on communication. It can improve coordination via better latent representations and trigger communication only when belief disagreement warrants it; performance gains are task- and regime-dependent, indicating complementary benefits of belief-based gating and representation quality.

Abstract: Effective communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning requires agents to decide not only \textit{what} to communicate, but when? Existing approaches either communicate at every timestep or learn a binary gate through REINFORCE policy gradients \cite{singh2019}, a high-variance signal that produces unstable and uninterpretable gating behavior. I propose a principled alternative: agents communicate only when the KL divergence between their learned belief distributions exceeds a fixed threshold. Each agent maintains a belief distribution over a latent world state computed as a softmax over its LSTM hidden state, and communicates only when belief disagreement is large enough to justify information exchange. I evaluate this approach on the Predator-Prey benchmark from IC3Net \cite{singh2019} across two environment sizes with 5 seeds each, and on MPE simple\_spread \cite{lowe2017}, comparing against IC3Net, CommNet, and an independent controller. On PP 10$\times$10, IC3Net outperforms KL-belief at all thresholds. On the harder PP 20$\times$20, a threshold ablation over $\varepsilon \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0\}$ reveals an inverted U-shape: $\varepsilon=0.5$ achieves 73.84 average steps and 42\% success rate versus IC3Net's 75.31 steps and 31\%, a gap of 1.47 steps and 11 percentage points with tighter seed variance. On MPE, the belief head improves mean reward by 12 points and reduces variance by 26$\times$ even when gating is inactive, suggesting two orthogonal contributions: principled gating when beliefs can converge, and improved latent representations that benefit coordination regardless.

</details>


### [449] [Global AI Regulations for FAIR and Ethics in High-Risk Use Cases: A Comparative Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14562)
*Aasish Kumar Sharma,Dimitar Koysev,Christopher Anich,Roshni Kumari Ojha,Julian Kunkel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Cross-jurisdiction AI governance comparison (EU/US/China) identifies interoperability and cross-regime operability gaps; proposes machine-checkable Knowledge Blocks (RDF/OWL, SHACL, PROV-O) for audit-ready compliance-by-design across domains like EEG rehab robotics, CBDC debt-collection, and GPU resource allocation; aims for harmonized, enforceable, risk-based regulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address compliance uncertainty from divergent regimes and enable auditable, interoperable governance of high-stakes AI through a practical, shareable framework.

Method: Construct a comparative matrix across risk triggers, binding obligations, enforcement, and FAIR principles; stress-test with three high-impact domains; base analysis on primary legal texts and implementation evidence; identify recurring gaps; propose Knowledge Blocks as a machine-checkable artefact pattern.

Result: Three recurring gaps identified: (1) weak interoperability mandates; (2) difficulty operationalising cross-regime obligations (AI + sector regulation + data protection); (3) under-specified governance for critical digital infrastructure use cases.

Conclusion: To bridge the implementation gap, propose Knowledge Blocks—machine-checkable compliance artefacts using RDF/OWL, SHACL, and PROV-O—to enable audit-ready, cross-regime compliance-by-design across multiple regimes.

Abstract: AI governance is shifting from voluntary ethics to enforceable, risk-based regulation, yet cross-jurisdictional divergence creates compliance uncertainty for operators of high-stakes AI. We present a comparative matrix for the EU, US, and China that maps (i) risk classification triggers, (ii) binding obligations, (iii) enforcement and accountability mechanisms, and (iv) the degree to which FAIR principles are operationalised in practice. We stress-test the matrix on three high-impact domains: Electroencephalography (EEG)-guided rehabilitation robotics, AI-enabled debt collection in prospective Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) ecosystems, and AI-driven allocation of scarce Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) resources in emerging AI Factory infrastructures. Using primary legal texts and implementation evidence, we identify three recurring gaps: weak interoperability mandates, difficult operationalisation of cross-regime obligations (AI + sector regulation + data protection), and under-specified governance for critical digital infrastructure use cases. To bridge the implementation gap, we outline Knowledge Blocks, a machine-checkable compliance artefact pattern based on Resource Description Framework/Web Ontology Language (RDF/OWL), Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), and Provenance Ontology (PROV-O), enabling audit-ready compliance-by-design across multiple regimes.

</details>


### [450] [Position: AI Lock-In Is in Progress, and We Must Be Prepared](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14565)
*Jaeho Kim,Seokhyun Lee,Jieun Lee,Changhee Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI safety must address AI Lock-In, the systemic vulnerability from over-reliance on AI that can erode human skills and create fragilities when AI is unavailable or disrupted. It uses scenario-based, multi-level analysis to trace how lock-in emerges from individuals to national infrastructure and offers mitigation guidance at each level, advocating proactive, pre-emptive action to preserve autonomy and security.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI safety research concentrates on technical alignment and societal impacts; AI Lock-In represents an underexplored, systemic risk that can undermine human autonomy and national security, especially under service outages or geopolitical stress.

Method: Scenario-driven analysis tracing emergence and escalation of AI Lock-In across multiple levels (individual, societal, national); synthesis of mitigation and preparedness guidance tailored to each level.

Result: Identifies mechanisms by which AI Lock-In arises and escalates; demonstrates potential amplification of risk through AI disruptions and conflicts; provides actionable guidance on mitigating and preparing for these dependencies at different levels.

Conclusion: Proactive attention to AI Lock-In is essential to prevent entrenched dependencies and protect individual autonomy and national security.

Abstract: AI safety research has mainly focused on two areas: technical alignment (ensuring AI systems produce human-aligned outputs) and the regulation of generative AI's societal impacts (including unemployment risk and labor market disruption). However, an equally important dimension remains underexplored: the risk inherent in dependence on AI systems themselves. In this position paper, we argue that AI safety research should address AI Lock-In, the phenomenon whereby excessive reliance on AI systems leads to human deskilling, diminishes human capacity for independent functioning, and creates systemic vulnerabilities when AI systems become unavailable or compromised. We highlight that AI Lock-In is a systemic threat that is already emerging at individual, societal, and national levels, one that could be dramatically amplified by AI service disruptions or geopolitical conflicts. Drawing on detailed scenarios, we investigate how AI Lock-In emerges and escalates across multiple levels, ranging from individual skill atrophy to national-scale infrastructure failures. To address this, we provide guidance on how such risks can be mitigated and prepared for at each level. We contend that proactively addressing AI Lock-In before such dependencies become entrenched, or even irreversible, is essential for preserving individual autonomy and national security.

</details>


### [451] [Position: Evaluations of AI Moral Reasoning Still Miss Half of the Picture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14566)
*Aidan Kierans,Ritam Dutt,Kaley Rittichier,Shiri Dori-Hacohen,Avijit Ghosh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that current LLM ethics work overemphasizes moral values while neglecting normative ethics—the ability to identify and apply context-sensitive moral norms. It reviews benchmarks, identifies gaps, and proposes a research agenda to develop formal normative representations, expert-annotated norm data, and evaluation protocols distinguishing values-level from norms-level competence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the imbalance in LLM ethics research, moving beyond value alignment to normative reasoning and norm application, enabling context-sensitive moral judgments.

Method: Conceptual review of existing benchmarks and methods; gap analysis; proposal of a research agenda including formalized normative representations, expert-annotated norm datasets, and distinct evaluation protocols for values vs norms.

Result: Identification of three gaps (no high-quality norm data, insufficient evaluation of intermediate reasoning, limited identification of morally relevant contextual features) and a concrete agenda for future work.

Conclusion: Advocate for systematic study of normative reasoning in LLMs and the development of resources and protocols to evaluate and train norm-appropriate behavior, complementing value-alignment research.

Abstract: Recent work on evaluating the moral competence of large language models (LLMs) has focused primarily on what we call the moral value problem, i.e., whether model outputs align with human moral values. In contrast, the moral norm problem, i.e., whether models can identify and correctly apply context-sensitive moral norms, remains underexplored. We posit that this imbalance stems from the field's reliance on descriptive ethics frameworks, such as Moral Foundations Theory and Kohlberg's stages of moral development, which emphasize value representation over normative application. We review existing benchmarks and evaluation methods, and show that they cluster heavily around the value problem, while discussion regarding normative ethics remains underrepresented. We identify three crucial gaps: (i) the absence of high-quality ground-truth data for moral norms and their applications, (ii) insufficient evaluation of intermediate reasoning processes, and (iii) limited attention to the identification of morally relevant features in context. Subsequently, we propose a research agenda that includes the development of standardized formal representations for normative theories, the construction of expert-annotated datasets capturing norm application, and evaluation protocols that explicitly distinguish between values-level and norms-level competence. Our goal is to encourage a more systematic study of normative reasoning in LLMs.

</details>


### [452] [From Doyle to AGM: A Survey and an Implementation Roadmap for Belief Change](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14567)
*Yuri Almeida,Arthur Casals*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A targeted narrative review tracing the historical and theoretical foundations of computational belief change from Doyle & London's 1980 taxonomy through AGM and into post-AGM developments, linking pragmatism to formal theory and outlining implications for implementable, guaranteed-belief-change systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain how historical/prior computational approaches relate to AGM theory and identify foundational precedents to guide robust, engineering-focused belief change implementations.

Method: Targeted narrative literature review seeded by Doyle & London 1980 taxonomy; trace evolution of belief revision from computational origins to AGM, analyze post-AGM taxonomy changes, synthesize historical foundations for implementation challenges.

Result: Shows continuity and transformation between pre-AGM pragmatism and AGM constructs; maps evolution of taxonomical categories post-AGM; provides a foundation for computational blueprints with formal guarantees and baselines for implementation analysis.

Conclusion: By integrating historical insights with formal AGM guarantees, the work lays groundwork for systematic, engineering-focused belief change research and robust computational implementations.

Abstract: This paper presents a targeted narrative review establishing the historical and theoretical foundations for computational belief change implementation. Seeded by Doyle and London's foundational 1980 taxonomy, we trace the evolution of belief revision from computational origins through the theoretical transformation of the AGM framework to contemporary approaches. Our analysis demonstrates how pre-AGM computational pragmatism relates to AGM theoretical constructs, revealing both continuities and transformations across this evolution. We analyze how each taxonomical category evolved in the post-AGM era, identifying the theoretical foundations and historical precedents that inform contemporary implementation challenges. This foundation enables subsequent research into robust computational blueprints that synthesize historical insights with formal guarantees, providing the baseline for systematic implementation analysis and engineering-focused belief change research.

</details>


### [453] [Position: AI Governance Needs ISO-like Interoperability Protocols, Not Just Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14568)
*Azmine Toushik Wasi,Mst Rafia Islam,Mahfuz Ahmed Anik,Taki Hasan Rafi,Md Manjurul Ahsan,Dong-Kyu Chae*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Argues for ISO-like interoperability protocols and standardized AI nutrition labels to enable cross-border, machine-readable risk communication, replacing fragmented, law-centric governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current governance is fragmented across jurisdictions, creating compliance complexity for AI systems and SMEs. An interoperable, standards-based framework could harmonize risk communication and foster trust.

Method: Conceptual position paper proposing a modular, versioned set of interoperability protocols akin to ISO standards, plus unified AI nutrition labels (metrics like bias, energy usage, data provenance) and guidance on their deployment across borders.

Result: A framework for interoperable AI governance through standardized, machine-readable manifests that lower SME barriers, reduce regulatory duplication, and build public trust, while preserving innovation via modularity.

Conclusion: Shifts governance from purely legal compliance to technical conformance with a global, shared language for responsible AI deployment.

Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems become deeply integrated into critical global infrastructure, the urgency for robust governance frameworks has intensified. However, current approaches, led by jurisdiction-specific laws, policies, and voluntary frameworks such as the EU AI Act, China's algorithm governance, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework in the U.S., create a fragmented regulatory landscape. In this position paper, we argue that \textbf{\textit{AI governance must be built not on laws alone, but on ISO-like interoperability protocols that enable standardized, machine-readable risk communication across borders}}. Drawing on the success of the GDPR, which was operationalized through standards like ISO 27001 and Privacy by Design, we propose the development of standardized AI \textit{nutrition labels} containing unified metrics for bias, energy usage, and data provenance to facilitate cross-jurisdictional compliance. These manifests would lower barriers for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), reduce redundant regulatory efforts, and build public trust. The paper addresses concerns that standards may stifle innovation by advocating for modular, versioned protocols designed to evolve in tandem with technological change. Overall, we call for a shift from siloed legal compliance toward interoperable technical conformance, enabling a shared global language for responsible AI deployment.

</details>


### [454] [Position: Certified Correctness in Neural Constraint Reasoning Requires Symbolic Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14569)
*Shufeng Kong,Xiaochuan Zhang,Caihua Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Neural CSP solvers show high in-distribution accuracy but fail under distribution shift due to constraint violations; the paper argues for symbolic or neuro-symbolic integration when hard constraints and low verification cost exist, using Sudoku as an NP-complete testbed; proposes bidirectional neural-symbolic collaboration and a multi-agent certified reasoning framework to achieve efficiency and provable correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hard constraints with cheap verification create a gap where purely neural solvers struggle under distribution shifts. Sudoku exemplifies a problem where verification is polynomial while solving is exponential, motivating a shift from pure learning to symbolic or neuro-symbolic approaches to obtain provable correctness.

Method: Conduct a comprehensive survey across deterministic algorithms, metaheuristics, learning-based approaches, and language-conditioned reasoning; advocate bidirectional integration where neural methods learn heuristics and percepts-to-symbols while symbolic methods verify neural outputs; operationalize with a multi-agent certified reasoning framework to balance efficiency and correctness.

Result: The abstract argues that neural-only methods cannot achieve provable correctness on hard CSPs; symbolic and neuro-symbolic methods can provide it. It presents a theoretical position and a proposed framework, rather than reporting empirical results.

Conclusion: Adopt a bidirectional integration: use neural components to aid symbolic solvers and subject neural outputs to symbolic verification; realize this via a multi-agent certified reasoning framework that aims to deliver both computational efficiency and provable correctness.

Abstract: Neural solvers for constraint satisfaction problems have achieved remarkable in-distribution accuracy, yet they suffer from a fundamental limitation persistent constraint violations occur under distribution shifts even when the model reports high confidence. This position paper argues that when hard constraints exist and the cost of verification is relatively low, neural constraint reasoning must prioritize symbolic integration over pure learning. We justify our focus on Sudoku as a representative NP-complete testbed because it exhibits a sharp asymmetry between easy verification and hard solving: checking a candidate solution requires only polynomial time $O(n^{2})$, while finding a solution may require exponential search. Through a comprehensive survey of solving methods spanning deterministic algorithms, metaheuristic optimization, learning-based approaches, and language-conditioned reasoning, we demonstrate that neural-only methods without instance-level certification fail to achieve the provable correctness that symbolic and neuro-symbolic approaches provide. We advocate for a bidirectional integration in which neural methods enhance symbolic solvers by learning heuristics and converting percepts into symbols, while symbolic methods verify neural outputs to ensure their reliability. To operationalize this position, we propose a multi-agent certified reasoning framework that demonstrates how this integration can achieve both computational efficiency and provable correctness.

</details>


### [455] [Position: Want Better ML Reviews? Stop Asking Nicely and Start Incentivizing with a Credit System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14571)
*Shaochen Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A position paper arguing for enforceable procedural safeguards and a currency-like review credit system to curb submissions and improve reviewing in ML, proposing OpenReview Points and two design alternatives alongside four takes on existing mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML faces huge submission volumes, mixed review experiences, and limited public discourse on effective review systems. Existing guidelines are insufficient; robust, enforceable mechanisms and incentives are proposed.

Method: Assess strengths/shortcomings of current mechanisms; present four takes on popular conference mechanisms; propose two alternative designs; introduce a currency-like credit system (OpenReview Points) rewarding good reviews and enabling perks at conferences.

Result: A conceptual reform framework including an OpenReview Points credit system and two concrete design proposals, plus assessment of current mechanisms and directions for implementation (e.g., perks like free registration, review resource access).

Conclusion: Meaningful ML peer-review improvement requires enforceable procedural safeguards paired with a credit-based incentive system rather than relying on polite guidelines alone.

Abstract: With soaring submission counts, stricter reciprocal review policies, widespread adoption of platforms like OpenReview, and without the offsetting pressure of publication fees, the machine learning (ML) community has one of the largest scholarly presences among all scientific fields. And yet, \textbf{almost \textit{everyone} has \textit{many} unpleasant things to share about their review experience.} Worse, there is little public space to seriously discuss, let alone debate, what makes a review system effective or how it might be improved.\quad In this position paper, we expand our discussion from two core problems: \textit{How can we reasonably limit submission volume?} and \textit{How can we incentivize good and discourage bad reviewing?} We first assess the strengths and shortcomings of existing attempts to address such problems. Specifically, we present four takes on some popular conference mechanisms and propose two alternative designs for improvement.\quad Our general position is that meaningful improvement in ML peer review won't come from polite best-practice suggestions tucked into Calls for Papers or Reviewer Guidelines: it requires \textbf{enforceable yet fine-grained procedural safeguards} paired with \textbf{a currency-like credit system (e.g., our proposed \textit{OpenReview Points})}. ML practitioners can ``earn'' such points by contributing good review practices, and ``spend'' them across one or multiple major conferences to redeem different kinds of ``perks,'' such as complimentary registration or the right to request additional review resources.

</details>


### [456] [Longitudinal and Graph-Augmented Prediction of Adolescent Substance Use Onset in the ABCD Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14578)
*Yixuan He,Jinni Su,Yun Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Longitudinal models outperform baseline for predicting adolescent substance-use; a combined approach using temporal XGBoost and Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (T-GCN) with score-level stacking yields the best predictive performance (AUC-ROC > 0.79). Graph signals act as complementary risk information to longitudinal models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To resolve whether baseline characteristics, longitudinal trajectories, and relational context (graphs) differentially contribute to predicting adolescent substance-use, and whether graph-based approaches add value beyond longitudinal modeling.

Method: Using ~11,860 participants from the ABCD study, compare cross-sectional (baseline), longitudinal (temporal models including temporal XGBoost, RNNs), and graph-based approaches (T-GCNs) built on family, school, and feature-similarity graphs to predict sipping, alcohol use, marijuana use, and combined alcohol/marijuana use. Evaluate performance, analyze feature importance, and test score-level stacking combining temporal XGBoost and T-GCN predictions.

Result: Longitudinal models outperform baseline; temporal XGBoost is the strongest standalone model. T-GCNs do not generally outperform temporal XGBoost but provide complementary, graph-derived risk signals. Stacking temporal XGBoost and T-GCN predictions yields the best performance across outcomes (AUC-ROC > 0.79). Feature analyses highlight peer deviance, age, externalizing symptoms, parental monitoring, cultural norms, and neighborhood context as key predictors.

Conclusion: Longitudinal modeling is valuable for predicting substance-use onset in adolescence, and graph-based representations offer useful auxiliary risk signals that can further enhance predictive performance when combined with longitudinal models.

Abstract: Early identification of adolescent substance-use risk is an important prevention challenge, yet the relative value of baseline characteristics, longitudinal trajectories, and relational context remains unclear. Using data from approximately 11,860 participants in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, we compare cross-sectional, longitudinal, and graph-based approaches for predicting alcohol sipping, alcohol use, marijuana use, and alcohol/marijuana use. We evaluate tree-based models, recurrent neural networks, and Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (T-GCNs) constructed from family, school, and feature-similarity graphs. Longitudinal models consistently outperform baseline models, with temporal XGBoost achieving the strongest standalone performance. Although T-GCNs generally do not surpass temporal XGBoost, graph-derived risk scores provide complementary information. Combining temporal XGBoost and T-GCN predictions through score-level stacking yields the best performance across all outcomes, achieving AUC-ROC values above 0.79. Feature analyses identify peer deviance, age, externalizing symptoms, parental monitoring, cultural norms, and neighborhood context as important predictors of substance use onset. These findings demonstrate the value of longitudinal modeling for substance-use prediction and suggest that graph-based representations can provide effective auxiliary risk signals.

</details>


### [457] [SKILL: Self-correcting Knowledge-guided Iterative Large Language Model Agent for Logic Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14579)
*Rui Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-correcting Knowledge-guided Iterative LLM Agent (SKILL) unifies multi-agent LLM reasoning and PPO-based RL for automated logic-synthesis optimization; achieves 12.4% PDA improvement and 86.3% success on up to 500K gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logic synthesis optimization suffers from exponential search spaces, sparse rewards, and diverse logic structures; traditional expert flows lack adaptability; reinforcement learning methods often exhibit low sample efficiency and limited interpretability.

Method: Coordination of three LLMs (GPT-4o for strategic planning; Claude Sonnet 4 for detailed reasoning; Gemini 2.5 Pro for efficient analysis) with a PPO-based RL agent that interacts with synthesis tools; a self-correcting module monitors environment feedback (PDA metrics) to detect suboptimal behaviors and trigger LLM-guided recovery strategies.

Result: Evaluations on IWLS, OpenCores, and EPFL benchmarks show SKILL achieves a 12.4% PDA improvement over expert flows and an 86.3% success rate on logic systems up to 500K gates.

Conclusion: SKILL demonstrates effective unification of LLM-driven planning and reasoning with RL-based environment interaction, augmented by self-correction, yielding improved logic-synthesis optimization performance over traditional expert-driven flows.

Abstract: Logic synthesis optimization poses significant challenges due to exponentially growing search spaces, sparse reward signals, and diverse logic structures. Traditional expert-designed flows lack adaptability, while reinforcement learning (RL) methods often suffer from low sample efficiency and limited interpretability. We introduce SKILL, a Self-correcting Knowledge-guided Iterative Large Language Model Agent that unifies multi-agent LLM reasoning and RL-based environment interaction for automated synthesis optimization. SKILL coordinates three specialized LLMs: GPT-4o for strategic planning, Claude Sonnet 4 for detailed reasoning, and Gemini 2.5 Pro for efficient analysis with a PPO-based RL agent that learns actionable policies through direct interaction with synthesis tools. A novel self-correcting module monitors environment feedback (PDA metrics), detects suboptimal behaviors, and invokes LLM-guided recovery strategies. Evaluations on IWLS, OpenCores, and EPFL benchmarks show SKILL achieves a 12.4 % PDA improvement over expert flows and 86.3% success rate on logic systems up to 500K gates.

</details>


### [458] [OGX: An Open-Source, Vendor-Neutral Generative AI Application Server](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14580)
*Francisco Javier Arceo,Sébastien Han,Matthew Farrellee,Charlie Doern,Yuan Tang,Derek Higgins,Varsha Prasad Narsing,Gordon Sim,Sumanth Kamenani,Ben Browning,Raghotham Murthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-source AI app server/library providing a unified, model-agnostic API surface for OpenAI/Anthropic/Google with pluggable backends; emphasizes server-side agent orchestration via the Responses API.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce coupling between applications and model backends; enable flexible deployment across inference engines, vector stores, and safety backends; support agentic workflows (retrieval-augmented generation, multi-turn agents, tool-calling).

Method: Implements a server and Python library that expose major frontier APIs through pluggable providers; supports the Open Responses API, Anthropic Messages API, and Google GenAI Interactions API; integrates 20+ inference providers, 13 vector stores; provides a Kubernetes Operator for production deployment; targets developer tools.

Result: Demonstrates broad ecosystem adoption and readiness: 8,400+ GitHub stars, 242 contributors, 4,000+ commits over ~2 years; enables self-hosted, model-agnostic backend for agentic AI apps such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and OpenHands.

Conclusion: OGX offers a flexible, vendor-agnostic backend solution for AI-powered developer tooling, decoupling SDKs from deployment choices and supporting scalable, production-grade agentic AI workflows.

Abstract: OGX (Open GenAI Stack) is an open-source AI application server and Python library that implements the APIs of major frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) with pluggable backend providers. Developers building agentic AI applications--such as retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, multi-turn agents, and tool-calling workflows--can develop against a single API surface and deploy with any combination of inference engine, vector database, and safety backend, without changing application code. OGX's primary focus is the Responses API for server-side agentic orchestration, conforming to the Open Responses specification. The server also supports the Anthropic Messages API and Google GenAI Interactions API, decoupling SDK choice from model and deployment decisions. With over 20 inference providers, 13 vector store backends, and a companion Kubernetes Operator for production deployment, OGX serves as the self-hosted, model-agnostic backend for AI-powered developer tools including Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and OpenHands. The project has over 8,400 GitHub stars, 242 contributors, and 4,000 commits across nearly two years of public development.

</details>


### [459] [Euclid-Omni : A Unified Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plane Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14585)
*Zhaoyu Li,Hangrui Bi,Youyuan Zhang,Wenjie Ma,Zenan Li,Zhaolei Zhang,Xujie Si,Kaiyu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unified neuro-symbolic Euclidean geometry system, Euclid-Omni, combining a formal geometry engine with LLMs and VLMs, using Euclidea for symbolic reasoning and a synthetic data pipeline; achieves competitive performance on Olympiad-level tasks with relatively low compute/data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Euclidean geometry requires diagram understanding, axiomatic deduction, and algebra; existing methods typically handle only parts of this, limiting performance on high-difficulty problems.

Method: Develop Euclidea, a symbolic geometry solver for deductive inference and algebra; build a data-generation pipeline that synthesizes symbolic problems/solutions, renders diagrams, and translates them into natural language; train and evaluate LLMs and VLMs on these synthetic datasets across calculation and proving tasks.

Result: VLMs trained on synthetic data excel on calculation tasks; LLMs + Euclidea are competitive with state-of-the-art on Olympiad-level proving problems, with an order of magnitude less compute and data.

Conclusion: Public code available; demonstrates a scalable, unified neuro-symbolic approach to geometric reasoning that spans calculation and proving, with potential for broader reasoning tasks and future enhancements.

Abstract: Euclidean geometry is a compelling testbed for AI reasoning, as it demands the combination of intuitive diagram understanding, axiomatic deduction, and algebraic computation. Yet, existing approaches typically address only a subset of these abilities or struggle with competition-level problems. We introduce \textit{Euclid-Omni}, a unified neuro-symbolic framework that couples a formal geometry system with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to tackle both calculation- and proving-style problems, in formal and natural languages, up to Olympiad-level difficulty. At its core, we develop \textit{Euclidea}, a versatile symbolic geometry solver that automatically generates reasoning steps through deductive inference and algebraic computation. Building on this, we develop a data-generation pipeline that synthesizes symbolic problems and solutions, renders diagrams, and translates them into natural language, producing large-scale, diverse datasets for training LLMs and VLMs across a wide range of reasoning settings. Experiments show that VLMs trained on our synthetic data achieve superior performance on calculation tasks, and that LLMs combined with \textit{Euclidea} are competitive with state-of-the-art systems on Olympiad-level proving problems, despite using orders of magnitude less compute and training data. Code and scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/20171130/Euclid-Omni

</details>


### [460] [An Agentic Framework Using Rules and LLMs for Embedding and Annotating Descriptive Document Layouts: A Plant Science Use Case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14587)
*Nicolas Turenne,Youcef Sklab,Eric Chenin,Jean-Daniel Zucker*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a modular, agent-based pipeline for botanical trait extraction that combines OCR, segmentation/indexing by genus/species, rule-based parsing, and ensemble LLMs to expand trait vocabularies and resolve ambiguities, achieving scalable, explainable extraction across large botanical corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for accurate, scalable, and explainable extraction of plant traits from large document collections, leveraging advances in OCR, IR, and LLMs within an agentic framework.

Method: Pipeline steps: OCR of PDFs; segmentation/indexing by genus/species; rule-based parsers for structured trait extraction; ensembles of LLMs to expand trait vocabularies and resolve ambiguities; an agent-based architecture enabling planning, iterative reasoning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration; evaluation on three regional botanical datasets; emphasis on evaluation, ethics, and trustworthiness.

Result: Extracted 55,737 trait annotations across 4,961 species (avg 9.1 traits/species); LLM enrichment increased coverage for 75% of traits and total annotations by 59%; OCR engine choice had minor impact; counts remained stable, indicating robustness and scalability.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline offers robust, scalable, and explainable large-scale botanical trait extraction, with LLM enrichment enhancing coverage; the agent-based design supports rigorous evaluation and responsible deployment in botany data pipelines.

Abstract: Background: Recent advances in information retrieval (IR) leverage both dense and sparse representations, large language models (LLMs), and specialized retrieval models to improve ranking accuracy, relevance, and cross-lingual performance. Complementary techniques such as passage indexing, document layout analysis, and semantic knowledge representation further enhance retrieval effectiveness by capturing fine-grained contextual and structural information. Emerging agentic LLM frameworks extend these capabilities by enabling planning, iterative reasoning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration, thereby broadening applications across diverse domains. These frameworks also emphasize rigorous evaluation, ethical considerations, and trustworthiness, ensuring responsible deployment in real-world settings. We propose a modular, agent-based pipeline for botanical trait extraction. Optical character recognition (OCR) converts PDFs into machine-readable text, while segmentation and indexing organize content by genus and species. Rule-based parsers extract structured botanical traits, and ensembles of large language models (LLMs) expand trait vocabularies and resolve ambiguities. This approach ensures accurate species recognition, scalable annotation, and explainable integration of textual botanical descriptions, enabling robust and interpretable data extraction across large botanical corpora. Results: Using three regional botanical datasets, our system extracted 55,737 trait annotations across 4,961 species, averaging 9.1 traits per species. Integration of LLM-based enrichment improved coverage for 75% of traits, increasing total annotations by 59%. While the choice of OCR engine had a minor effect on species recognition, overall annotation counts remained stable, demonstrating the robustness, scalability, and reliability of the pipeline for large-scale botanical trait extraction.

</details>


### [461] [The Hallucination Snowball: Modeling Error Propagation as State Transitions in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14588)
*Prabhjot Singh,Bhushan Pawar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hallucination snowball in four-state sequential LLM pipelines; early-stage verification dramatically reduces survival, while detectability decays across stages. Boundary gates outperform end-to-end checks; allocate verification resources primarily to the first handoff (S1→S2).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify structural flaw in chained multi-agent LLM pipelines introduced by handoffs without verification, quantify how injected hallucinations evolve across stages, and provide guidance for efficient verification resource allocation.

Method: Empirical study with 346 automatically injected hallucinations in a 4-agent FinanceBench financial analysis pipeline. Measured per-boundary escape probabilities between stages, compared RAG-based boundary gating versus end-of-pipeline verification, computed detection rates across stages for multiple models (e.g., gpt-4o, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B), calculated Cohen's h for effect sizes, and projected survival in n-agent pipelines.

Result: Stage-wise detectability declines: Stage 1 detection 72.0% (gpt-4o); Stage 4 detection 50.9%; 23.7% of hallucinations survive undetected in final output. Strongest model at Stage 1 detects 87.0% but Stage 4 reaches only ~60–65% detection. Boundary gates (identical RAG verification) reduce survival from 58.4% to 16.2% versus end-of-pipeline checking; end-checks yield only 2.3 percentage points improvement over no verification. About 75.4% of hallucinations remain catchable at S1→S2, while 89.3% have already escaped by S3→S4. A simple model yields predictions for n-agent pipelines and prescribes allocating verification resources to earlier handoffs. 

Conclusion: Verification is more impactful when applied earlier in the pipeline than later checks alone. Prioritize S1→S2 verification to curtail hallucination survival; end-to-end verification has limited incremental benefit. The study provides a first-principles framework (Markov-like four-state model) and practical guidance for resource allocation in multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: Sequential multi-agent LLM pipelines chain specialized agents without verification at handoffs, creating a structural flaw with measurable and severe consequences. We show that hallucinations injected at Stage 1 do not merely persist; they transform: raw numerical facts become derived computations, then narrative prose, then editorially approved conclusions. At each transformation, detectability degrades near-irreversibly. We formalize this as the hallucination snowball effect, a first-order Markov process over four states (Raw Fact $\to$ Derived $\to$ Narrative $\to$ Invisible) with empirically measured per-boundary escape probabilities of 24.6%, 48.3%, and 89.3%. Across 346 automatically injected hallucinations in a 4-agent financial analysis pipeline on FinanceBench, gpt-4o detection drops from 72.0% at Stage 1 to 50.9% at Stage 4, and 23.7% of hallucinations survive completely undetected in the final output. Even the strongest model tested (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, 87.0% at Stage 1) faces a structural ceiling; projected Stage 4 detection is only ${\sim}$60--65%. Critically, boundary gates using identical RAG verification tools reduce hallucination survival from 58.4% to 16.2% versus end-of-pipeline checking (Cohen's $h = -0.911$, $p < 0.000001$), while end-checking alone achieves merely 2.3 pp improvement over no verification. When you verify matters more than whether you verify. Our model predicts survival for $n$-agent linear pipelines and prescribes optimal verification resource allocation: invest at $S_1{\to}S_2$ first, where 75.4% of hallucinations are still catchable, not at $S_3{\to}S_4$ where 89.3% have already escaped.

</details>


### [462] [Toward Safe LLM Agents: A Survey of Specification, Verification, and Enforcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14590)
*Pierre Dantas,Lucas Cordeiro,Ehsan Nowroozi,Tihanyi Norbert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Systematic review of 38 studies (2022–2026) on task-level safety for LLM agents; finds persistent specification bottleneck with only 24–35% semantic correctness, runtime monitoring as the most mature enforcement (40–65% reduction) but not guaranteeing safety, a verifier tax where blocking 94% unsafe actions still yields <5% safe task completion due to unsafe-path alternatives, and no approach achieves soundness, scalability, semantic correctness, and task-level safety simultaneously; provides a three-level taxonomy, comparative analysis, verifier-tax synthesis, and a ten-problem research agenda.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish formally grounded, task-level safety guarantees for LLM agents that perform irreversible real-world actions, addressing fragmentation across specification, verification, and enforcement.

Method: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of 38 studies published 2022–2026, sourced from six academic databases; includes taxonomy development, cross-study comparison, analysis of the verifier tax, and roadmap development.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Specification bottleneck persists; natural-language-to-formal translation yields 24–35% semantic correctness. (2) Runtime monitoring is the most mature enforcement, reducing unsafe actions by 40–65% in controlled settings, but not providing full safety guarantees. (3) Verifier tax shows that blocking 94% of unsafe actions can still leave <5% safe task completion due to alternate unsafe paths. (4) No approach simultaneously achieves soundness, scalability, semantic correctness, and task-level safety. Contributions include a three-level taxonomy, comparative analysis of existing techniques, synthesis of evidence on the verifier tax, and a ten-problem research agenda for trustworthy agentic AI.

Conclusion: No current solution meets all desirable properties; the study provides a structured taxonomy, evidence synthesis, and a concrete research agenda to advance trustworthy, task-level safety for LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly perform irreversible real-world actions, including database updates, API calls, file operations, and autonomous use of tools. However, no existing system provides formally grounded, task-level safety guarantees for the plans these agents generate. Research remains fragmented across specification, verification, and enforcement, limiting understanding of the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. To address this gap, we conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of 38 studies published between 2022 and 2026 and retrieved from six academic databases. Our analysis reveals four key findings. First, the specification bottleneck remains the primary challenge: natural-language-to-formal translation achieves only 24% to 35% semantic correctness, undermining downstream verification. Second, runtime monitoring is the most mature enforcement strategy, reducing unsafe actions by 40% to 65% in controlled settings, but it does not provide complete safety guarantees. Third, the verifier tax shows that blocking 94% of unsafe actions can still result in less than 5% safe task completion because agents exploit alternative unsafe paths. Finally, no existing approach simultaneously achieves soundness, scalability, semantic correctness, and task-level safety preservation. We contribute a three-level taxonomy, a comparative analysis of existing techniques, a synthesis of evidence on the verifier tax, and a ten-problem research agenda for trustworthy agentic AI.

</details>


### [463] [Position: Medical AI Neglects Real Treatment Outcomes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14598)
*Shiva Kaul,Anjum Khurshid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Advocates incorporating real treatment outcomes from observational studies and randomized trials into the training and evaluation of medical AI, rather than relying on expert opinions and literature syntheses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice relies on opinions and texts to capture treatment understanding, which inadequately reflects actual outcomes, limiting AI models and benchmarks and misaligning with clinical goals.
