Method: Conceptual analysis and literature synthesis in a position paper; proposes a framework and concrete steps to integrate outcome data into AI development, including data sources and evaluation strategies.

Result: No empirical results are reported; the paper argues that outcome-informed training/evaluation will improve clinical relevance and benchmark validity and provides recommendations for implementing outcome data into AI pipelines.

Conclusion: Real treatment outcomes should be the downstream objective of medical AI, guiding both training and evaluation and driving improvements in models and benchmarks.

Abstract: Medical AI has rapidly improved its ability to perform diagnostic and prognostic tasks that lead to treatment decisions. But understanding of treatment itself is still inadequately trained and evaluated, using human opinions and syntheses (especially texts such as biomedical publications and clinical practice guidelines) rather than actual underlying data on treatment outcomes. This neglect seriously limits the potential of medical AI, and is already causing deficiencies in both frontier models and major benchmarks, as argued in this position paper. Real treatment outcomes, drawn from sources such as observational databases and randomized experiments, should be substantially incorporated into both training and evaluation. Improving these outcomes should be reemphasized as the downstream goal of all medical AI.

</details>


### [464] [When Do LLMs Apply the Wrong Law? Diagnosing LLM Failures in Temporal Legal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14610)
*Yiqian Huang,Shuyuan Zheng,Qianying Liu,Shaowen Peng,Yuntao Kong,Kotaro Funakoshi,Chuan Xiao,Manabu Okumura,Yang Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study introduces a benchmark for temporal applicable-law determination in legal judgment prediction and exposes surprising behaviors of LLMs: a strong bias to apply the most recent law, not due to temporal understanding or historical knowledge; RLHF-driven explicit reasoning reduces reasoning path diversity and worsens temporal accuracy; stronger general reasoning correlates with worse temporal legal performance, informing future improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal applicability of laws is crucial for accurate legal judgment, yet it is unclear whether LLMs can correctly determine which version of the law applies at different times. The paper seeks to diagnose this capability and its failure modes.

Method: Construct and evaluate a benchmark for temporal applicable-law determination; perform systematic behavioral analysis of LLMs, including the impact of reinforced learning with explicit reasoning (RLHF-style) on reasoning diversity and temporal accuracy; examine correlations between general reasoning ability and temporal legal performance.

Result: 1) LLMs favor applying the most recently enacted law regardless of factual timing. 2) This bias is not due to misunderstanding temporal scope or lack of historical statute knowledge. 3) Explicit reasoning shaped by RLHF may reduce diversity of reasoning paths, driving convergence on the current law. 4) Stronger general reasoning ability inversely correlates with temporal legal reasoning performance.

Conclusion: To advance temporally grounded legal reasoning, future work should study and mitigate the current-law bias, understand why explicit reasoning narrows reasoning options, and design evaluation and training strategies that preserve diverse, temporally accurate reasoning paths.

Abstract: Legal reasoning tasks such as legal judgment prediction (LJP) require identifying the temporally correct version of the law governing a case -- a capability we term temporal applicable-law determination. However, whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably perform this task remains unexplored. In this paper, we construct a benchmark to evaluate LLMs on temporal applicable-law determination, and systematically investigate why they fail at temporal legal reasoning. Our experiments reveal four key findings. First, LLMs exhibit a strong bias toward applying the most recently enacted law, regardless of when the legally relevant facts occurred. Second, this bias does not stem from an inability to understand that laws have temporal scope, nor from a lack of knowledge about historical statutes. Third, we provide behavioral evidence that reinforcement-learning-shaped explicit reasoning may be a key mechanism: while improving general reasoning ability, it reduces the diversity of reasoning paths, causing models to converge on applying the current law. Fourth, this produces a counterintuitive inverse relationship: models with stronger general reasoning ability tend to perform worse on temporal legal reasoning. Our findings offer concrete guidance for future work on improving LLM performance in temporally grounded legal reasoning.

</details>


### [465] [Do LLM Agents Negotiate Rationally? A Mechanism-Design Framework for Verifiable Multi-Agent Interaction over A2A/MCP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14613)
*Wael Albayaydh,Rui Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework that encodes classical negotiation into A2A schemas, adds runtime verification, and benchmarks negotiation/auction tasks; shows verification improves reliability and that incentive-compatibility doesn't guarantee compliant LLM behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MCP/A2A provide transport/discovery but not strategic guarantees. To ensure efficient, individually rational, strategy-proof outcomes in LLM-agent systems, a framework linking classical MAS theory to LLM infrastructures and verifiable interactions is needed, with benchmarks and diagnostics.

Method: Encode alternating-offers bargaining and VCG-style auctions as constraints over A2A message schemas; implement a lightweight runtime verification/repair layer enforcing protocol invariants; create a benchmark suite with known optimal solutions for negotiation and allocation; evaluate multiple LLM backbones across unstructured dialogue, structured protocols, and protocols with verification; analyze outcomes under N=30 per condition for negotiations and auctions, including parser artifact corrections; report negative results for a three-party fair-allocation task.

Result: Verification reduces outcome variance; structured protocols yield 100% success for both models; audited unstructured baselines reach ~97% and 93.3% success after corrections; in auctions, allocations are 100% efficient for both models but truthful bidding varies (one model consistently bids true valuations; the other rarely does); a three-party fair-allocation task yields only 4.2% usable outcomes (negative result with diagnosis).

Conclusion: The work bridges classical multi-agent systems theory and modern LLM-agent infrastructure, introducing verifiable interaction at the A2A protocol layer. It shows that mechanism-level incentive compatibility does not automatically transfer to LLM-agent behavior and highlights the value of a verification/repair layer to achieve reliable, efficient outcomes.

Abstract: Modern LLM-agent frameworks increasingly interoperate through standards such as Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) for agent-to-tool access and Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for agent delegation and negotiation. However, these protocols specify transport and discovery rather than strategic correctness and do not guarantee efficient, individually rational, or strategy-proof outcomes.
  We introduce a framework that (i) encodes classical negotiation mechanisms, including alternating-offers bargaining and Vickrey-Clarke-Groves-style auctions, as constraints over A2A message schemas; (ii) provides a lightweight runtime verification and repair layer that checks messages against protocol invariants; and (iii) offers a benchmark of negotiation and allocation tasks with known optimal solutions for measuring deviations from game-theoretic predictions.
  We evaluate multiple LLM backbones using unstructured dialogue, structured protocols, and structured protocols with verification. Across negotiation trials (N=30 per condition), verification reduces outcome variance, while structured protocols achieve 100 percent success for both models. After correcting parser artifacts, audited unstructured baselines achieve approximately 97 percent and 93.3 percent success.
  In auction experiments (N=30 per model), both models achieve 100 percent efficient allocation but differ sharply in truthful bidding: one bids its exact valuation in every trial, whereas the other does so in only 3.3 percent of trials. Thus, mechanism-level incentive compatibility does not automatically transfer to LLM-agent behavior. A three-party fair-allocation task produced only 4.2 percent usable outcomes; we report this negative result with a diagnosis. This work bridges classical multi-agent systems theory and modern LLM-agent infrastructure and defines verifiable interaction at the A2A protocol layer.

</details>


### [466] [Large Language Models and their Awareness of Mechanics and Spatial Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14615)
*Johannes Gerstmayr,Sebastian Weyrer,Tobias Möltner,Peter Manzl,Michael Pieber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MecEng is a fully automated benchmark for evaluating LLMs on creating simulation-ready multibody models from text, spanning rigid and flexible mechanics tasks, with ground-truth verification across graph structure, numerical solutions, and part-level properties. Open-weight models approach proprietary performance on rigid-body tasks but struggles with flexible, geometry-heavy cases; the study analyzes factors like temperature, reasoning, prompts, model size, and release date, indicating rapid, but imperfect, mechanical engineering awareness in current LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify and systematize LLM capability in mechanics and spatial geometry (mechanical engineering awareness) by building an automated pipeline that converts textual descriptions into simulation-ready multibody models and evaluating LLMs against expert ground truth across diverse tasks.

Method: A pipeline uses Netgen to generate simulation-ready geometry from text descriptions and Exudyn to assemble multibody system models. 84 tasks across three difficulty levels (rigid to flexible with 3D geometry, meshing, and model order reduction) are used. Ground truth verification includes system-graph isomorphism with annotated nodes, numerical solutions, and part-specific measures (mass, geometry, eigenfrequencies). Evaluation covers 32 open-weight and 2 proprietary LLMs.

Result: Best open-weight model: 86.0% overall on rigid-body tasks; strongest proprietary model: 91.4% on rigid tasks. Flexible multibody tasks are significantly harder. Additional analyses show effects of sampling temperature, reasoning, prompt design, model size, and LLM release date on performance.

Conclusion: Mechanical engineering awareness in LLMs is rapidly improving but remains error-prone. MecEng reveals substantial progress in generating simulation-ready models from text, with gaps primarily in complex geometry and advanced modeling tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on established code-generation and mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, but their capabilities in mechanics and spatial geometry, here denoted as mechanical engineering awareness, has not been quantified systematically. We present MecEng, a fully automated benchmark that evaluates LLMs on the creation of multibody simulation models from parameterized textual descriptions. The benchmark comprises 84 generic tasks on three difficulty levels, ranging from rigid-body systems with joints and contact to flexible multibody systems that require exact 3D geometry generation, tetrahedral finite-element meshing, and Hurty-Craig-Bampton model order reduction of machine parts. A dedicated pipeline with LLMs generates simulation-ready geometry from text using Netgen, and builds multibody system models for the code Exudyn, which are then verified against expert ground truth on several levels: system-graph isomorphism including graph node annotations, numerical solutions, and part-specific measures such as mass, geometry, and eigenfrequencies. In total, 32 open-weight and two proprietary LLMs are evaluated. On rigid-body tasks, the best open-weight model obtains an overall success rate of 86.0%, compared to 91.4% for the strongest proprietary model, while flexible multibody tasks remain considerably harder. Additional studies quantify the influence of sampling temperature, reasoning, prompt design, model size, and LLM-release date. The results indicate rapidly improving, but still error-prone, mechanical engineering awareness of current LLMs.

</details>


### [467] [A Human-Centred Approach to Benchmarking LLMs for Parenting Advice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14622)
*Yunke Zhao,Isobel Voysey,Alastair van Heerden,Rob Hughes,Jun Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multidimensional, rubric-based evaluation of 15 LLMs across 100 parenting scenarios in English and Chinese shows that aggregate scores conceal item-level weaknesses, language affects responses, and models may push different parenting styles; emphasizes need for auditable evaluation and informs model selection for direct parenting advice applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parenting is a socially sensitive domain. Standard information-quality benchmarks are insufficient; evaluation should capture relational and behavioral aspects and cross-language effects to ensure safe, appropriate advice.

Method: Evaluate 15 LLMs across 100 parenting scenarios in English and Chinese using an expert-created, multi-dimensional rubric. Use an LLM-as-a-judge approach to assess outputs on multiple dimensions beyond aggregate quality.

Result: Aggregate scores hide item-specific weaknesses; models implicitly encourage different parenting styles; language influences responses.

Conclusion: Evaluation output auditability is critical; highlights challenges in assessing LLM-generated parenting advice and informs model selection for direct user engagement and development of user-facing parenting advice applications.

Abstract: People are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to seek advice, including for parenting. Parenting is a critical and socially sensitive domain. Thus, evaluating advice provided by LLMs requires indicators beyond aggregated information quality benchmarks to consider relational and behavioural elements of the responses. With a multi-dimensional rubric created by parenting experts, this paper evaluates 15 LLMs across 100 parenting scenarios in 2 languages (English and Chinese), using an LLM-as-a-judge method. Results show that aggregate scores can hide rubric item-specific weaknesses, models implicitly encourage different parenting styles, and language influences responses. We highlight the importance of evaluation output auditability and challenges involved in evaluating LLM-generated advice in domains like parenting. Our findings provide important insights for selecting LLMs for direct user engagement and the development of user-facing parenting advice applications.

</details>


### [468] [Learning Agent Execution for KV-Cache Management in Agentic Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14624)
*Rui Zhang,Chaeeun Kim,Shaoting Feng,Kuntai Du,Yuhan Liu,Yi Zhong,Cheng-Wei Ching,Junchen Jiang,Liting Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent-aware KV-cache (CacheScout) for multi-agent LLM serving learns agent execution semantics online to guide eviction and prefetching, improving cache efficiency and latency without changing serving path.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-agent LLM workflows, each agent uses fixed context (system prompts, tools, few-shot examples), causing opportunity for KV-cache reuse but existing systems evict reusable contexts due to prefix-caching and recency-based policies.

Method: Online learning of agent execution transitions without predefined workflow graphs or offline training; an agent-aware KV-cache runtime layer that guides eviction and proactive prefetching while leaving the critical serving path intact; implemented on top of vLLM.

Result: KV-cache hit rate improved by 10-18 percentage points; mean TTFT reduced by 18-45%; mean per-turn latency reduced by 29-38%; peak throughput increased up to 57%; benefits extend to larger models (TTFT reduced by up to 54%; throughput +37%).

Conclusion: CacheScout demonstrates a non-invasive runtime solution that leverages agent semantics to substantially improve KV-cache performance and LLM serving throughput, with positive generalization to larger models.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems have emerged as an important deployment paradigm for AI services, where each user request is decomposed into a sequence of specialized agents. Across these workflows, every agent repeatedly executes a fixed context consisting of system prompts, tool definitions, and few-shot examples, creating substantial opportunities for KV-cache reuse. Existing LLM serving systems, however, manage KV-cache reactively using prefix caching and recency-based replacement, causing reusable agent contexts to be evicted before their next invocation and forcing repeated recomputation. We present CacheScout, an agent-aware KV-cache runtime layer for multi-agent LLM serving. The key insight is that future KV-cache reuse is governed by agent execution semantics rather than cache recency alone. CacheScout captures these semantics by learning agent execution transitions online, without requiring predefined workflow graphs or offline training, and uses the learned execution model to guide both cache eviction and proactive prefetching while leaving the serving critical path unchanged. We implement CacheScout on top of vLLM. Across representative real-world multi-agent workloads, CacheScout improves KV-cache hit rate by 10-18 percentage points, reduces mean TTFT by 18-45%, lowers mean per-turn latency by 29-38%, and increases peak throughput by up to 57%. These benefits also generalize to larger models, reducing TTFT by up to 54% while sustaining 37% higher throughput.

</details>


### [469] [Accuracy and Reliability of Large Language Models in Cosmetic Chemistry and Skin Health: A Benchmarking Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14631)
*Amelia Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: 14 LLMs show limited internalized cosmetic chemistry knowledge without web access; overall performance is poor, with major gaps in quantitative reasoning and structural identification. General skincare questions are plausible but lack technical depth; outputs can be overconfident, risking misinformation. More training data and improved reasoning are needed before deployment as consumer resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate the reliability and safety of general-purpose LLMs as sources of cosmetic chemistry and skincare guidance for consumers; identify specific failure modes and risks.

Method: Benchmark 14 LLMs on a structured set of cosmetic-chemistry topics (chemical properties of ingredients and consumer-relevant scenarios). Web search disabled to isolate internal knowledge. Assess overall accuracy, quantitative reasoning, structural identification, and propensity to produce confidently incorrect answers.

Result: Overall performance was poor. Major deficits observed in quantitative reasoning and structural identification tasks. While models can handle general skincare questions reasonably, they fail to provide the technical depth required for informed consumer decisions. Outputs that are confident but technically incorrect were less likely to trigger skepticism than those that acknowledge uncertainty, indicating a riskier blind trust in authoritative-sounding responses. Training on unverified public data likely contributes to these failures.

Conclusion: General-purpose LLMs currently are not reliable sources for cosmetic chemistry information in consumer contexts. Progress requires fine-tuning on verified chemical and dermatological datasets and substantial improvements in algorithmic reasoning before these tools can be considered suitable resources for public use.

Abstract: As consumers increasingly turn to AI chatbots for skincare advice, the technical accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) in cosmetic chemistry remains largely under-evaluated. We benchmarked 14 LLMs on a structured set of topics related to cosmetic chemistry, including the chemical properties of specific cosmetic ingredients and common cosmetic scenarios that may be of interest to consumers. Web search was disabled throughout to assess each model's internalized knowledge rather than its internet retrieval capacity. Overall performance was poor, with the most pronounced deficits in quantitative reasoning and structural identification tasks. While models handled general skincare questions with reasonability, responses consistently lacked the technical depth required for informed consumer decision-making. Notably, conversation with AI can pose a risk: outputs that sound authoritative but contain technical errors are less likely to generate skepticism compared to responses that explicitly acknowledge uncertainty. These findings suggest that general-purpose LLMs, trained predominantly on unverified public data, are currently not reliable sources of cosmetic chemistry information. Progress on two fronts, fine-tuning verified chemical and dermatological datasets, and substantial improvements to algorithmic reasoning, will likely be needed before these tools can be considered as resources for public use.

</details>


### [470] [Task- and Session-Level Model Routing: A Common-Interface Hybrid Evaluation of Four Open-Source Routers Across Four Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14641)
*Kiran N. Kumar,Santhosh K. Saminathan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Common protocol evaluation of open-source routers across four benchmarks shows most routers stabilize to fixed tiers; vLLM Semantic Router is content-sensitive but not superior; Always-Mid aligns with Aurelio; fixed-tier controls and protocol margins are essential; results are configuration-specific.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of direct comparability due to heterogeneous tasks, pools, and protocols impedes robust evaluation of routing models; propose standardized measurement and cross-benchmark evaluation.

Method: Assess four router implementations (RouterBench, BFCL v4, tau2-bench, WebArena) using 290 frozen tasks against 2,610 candidate outcomes; analyze tier assignments, perform task-level superiority tests (notably for vLLM); compare with content-blind allocation; apply protocol-declared margin (five percentage points) on WebArena.

Result: Three routers produce constant or near-constant tier assignments; only vLLM Semantic Router shows material variation with prompt content and fails to achieve superiority on any benchmark; Always-Mid exactly matches Aurelio on three benchmarks and is within 0.003 on the fourth; for vLLM, there is no task-specific advantage over a share-matched content-blind allocation; equivalence only on WebArena within five-point margin; gains correlate with selected-tier composition rather than task-specific targeting.

Conclusion: Fixed-tier baselines and selected-tier distributions are necessary controls; conclusions are bounded to the specified configurations, candidate pools, and frozen benchmarks; not a universal endorsement or refutation of routing paradigms.

Abstract: Agentic systems increasingly delegate model selection to a router, yet open-source routers are usually evaluated with different tasks, candidate pools, and execution protocols, limiting direct comparison. We present a common measurement protocol and hybrid evaluation of four router implementations across RouterBench, BFCL v4, tau2-bench, and WebArena. We evaluate 290 frozen tasks against a locked matrix of 2,610 candidate outcomes. Three routers emit constant or near-constant tier assignments; only vLLM Semantic Router varies materially with prompt content, and it has the highest observed success rate on none of the four benchmarks. Always-Mid matches Aurelio exactly on three benchmarks and within 0.003 on the fourth. For vLLM, task-level superiority tests detect no task-specific advantage over a share-matched content-blind allocation; equivalence is established only on WebArena at the protocol-declared five-percentage-point margin. The results show that, under these configurations and controls, observed gains track selected-tier composition more closely than demonstrated task-specific targeting. Fixed-tier baselines and selected-tier distributions are therefore necessary controls in router evaluation; the findings are scoped to these configurations, candidate pool, and frozen benchmark samples, not to routing paradigms in general.

</details>


### [471] [Evaluating Multimodal LLMs across Text and Audio Modalities for Accessible Disaster Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14651)
*Anuridhi Gupta,Samara Mansoor,Hemant Purohit*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-weight MM-LLMs are evaluated for cross-modal consistency (text vs audio) in real emergency alert scenarios across four vulnerable personas; none achieve reliable consistency; modality-related inequities emerge; design recommendations proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure reliable, equitable disaster risk communication by AI; current systems fail to meet the needs of people with access/functional needs; cross-modal consistency of multi-modal LLMs is under-examined.

Method: Assess open-weight MM-LLMs on real emergency alert scenarios; four personas; measure consistency of responses across text and audio given the same task scenario.

Result: No model shows reliable cross-modal consistency; larger gaps for personas with access needs; modality-dependent inequity observed; raises concerns for humanitarian value.

Conclusion: Provide concrete design recommendations to build equitable, trustworthy, and inclusive AI tools for disaster risk communication.

Abstract: Effective disaster risk communication is a foundational humanitarian challenge, yet current emergency infrastructure fails to meet the needs of individuals with access and functional needs, including hard-of-hearing individuals, pregnant women, mothers with toddlers, and elderly individuals with dementia. Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MM-LLMs), demonstrate powerful capabilities to serve diverse users across text, audio, image, and video modalities within a single unified system, such as a chatbot. However, their suitability for deployment rests on a property that receives limited scrutiny, i.e., whether these systems produce consistent, actionable outputs regardless of the modality through which a user communicates. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive analysis to understand the status of open-weight MM-LLMs using real emergency alert scenarios across four different vulnerable personas. These state-of-the-art (SOTA) models are evaluated on consistency of responses across text and audio modalities when the same task scenario is given. Findings indicate that no model achieves reliable consistency across modalities, and that performance gaps are heightened for personas with access needs, introducing modality-dependent inequity that undermines the humanitarian value of these systems. These results inform concrete design recommendations for building equitable, trustworthy, and inclusive AI tools for disaster risk communication.

</details>


### [472] [When Uncertainty Isn't Enough: An Empirical Study of Self-Correction in Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14659)
*Pranav Rakasi,Maanas Lalwani,Arnav Srivastava,Arya Palanivel,Tinuade Adeleke,Ruizhe Li,Sean Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Uncertainty estimation methods for code generation were evaluated; multi-sample P(True) best correlates with correctness, while most other methods (including semantic entropy probes) show weak correlation. Three self-correction policies were tested; only verification-based self-correction reliably improves Pass@1 (substantial gains), while uncertainty-based and adaptive decoding often decrease accuracy. Cheap uncertainty estimators are not sufficient to improve correctness and are best used as gates for more expensive verification/execution loops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether uncertainty signals developed for NLP can translate to code generation to improve correctness via selective self-correction, addressing reliability gaps in LLM-based code

Method: Evaluate five uncertainty methods (mean token entropy, verbalized confidence, P(True) with multi-sample, entropy ensembles, semantic entropy probes) on three small code LLMs across HumanEval and BigCodeBench; implement three self-correction policies (adaptive decoding, uncertainty-based regeneration, verification-based regeneration); measure changes in Pass@1

Result: multi-sample P(True) shows strongest correlation with correctness; other uncertainty methods show weak correlation. Uncertainty-based self-correction degrades Pass@1 in 5 of 6 configs; adaptive decoding degrades in 4 of 6. Only verification-based self-correction improves Pass@1, with gains of +6 to +26pp on HumanEval and +8 to +20pp on BigCodeBench, inverse scaling with baseline strength. Results replicate across benchmarks; cheap uncertainty estimators insufficient to independently improve code correctness; best used to gate more expensive execution-based correction loops

Conclusion: Cheap uncertainty estimators alone cannot reliably improve code correctness; their practical value lies in gating costly verification/execution loops rather than replacing verification; findings robust across benchmarks and models

Abstract: Large language models for code generation often produce incorrect solutions without reliable indicators of failure. We study whether uncertainty estimation methods developed for natural language transfer to code generation, and whether such signals can improve code generation via selective self-correction. We evaluate five uncertainty methods: mean token entropy, verbalized confidence, $P(\text{True})$, entropy ensembles, and semantic entropy probes, across three small code LLMs on HumanEval and BigCodeBench. We find that multi-sample $P(\text{True})$ achieves the strongest correlation with correctness, while all the other methods, including semantic entropy probes, yield only weak correlation. We then use these uncertainty signals to drive three self-correction policies: adaptive decoding, uncertainty-based regeneration, and verification-based regeneration. Our results reveal a stronger negative finding than anticipated: uncertainty-based self-correction fails to reliably improve Pass@1, degrading accuracy in 5 of 6 configurations across both benchmarks ($-3$pp to $-10$pp), and adaptive decoding degrades accuracy in 4 of 6 configurations. Only verification-based self-correction reliably improves Pass@1, with gains of $+6$ to $+26$ percentage points on HumanEval and $+8$ to $+20$ percentage points on BigCodeBench, scaling inversely with baseline strength. These findings replicate consistently across both benchmarks and suggest that cheap uncertainty estimators are insufficient on their own to improve code correctness, and that their practical value lies in serving as gating signals for costlier execution-based correction loops rather than as standalone substitutes for verification.

</details>


### [473] [Cross-Domain Industrial Fault Detection by Causal Mechanism Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14666)
*Dhiraj Neupane,Mohamed Reda Bouadjenek,Richard Dazeley,Sunil Aryal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CMR-Mamba is a causal, cross-modal, per-domain state-space encoder approach for unsupervised coupling-fault detection, using kNN on a learned normal manifold and mechanism residuals; it outperforms marginal reconstruction baselines, especially on hard/stealthy faults, across mechanical, hydraulic, and cyber-physical domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Marginal-distribution reconstruction methods miss coupling faults that break inter-sensor relationships while individual sensor statistics remain normal, leading to latent failures that threaten reliability and safety.

Method: Train per-domain Mamba state-space encoders on healthy data. Apply a causal cross-modal predictor to regularise encoders so the effect-channel manifold encodes normal cause-to-effect coupling. Detect anomalies via (i) kNN distance on the effect manifold and (ii) the mechanism residual between observed and predicted effect embedding. Evaluate across electromechanical (Paderborn bearings), hydraulic (ZeMA), and cyber-physical (SWaT) domains. Ablations compare kNN manifold scoring versus reconstruction-error scoring and assess impact of causal regularisation.

Result: kNN manifold scoring yields up to 0.42 AUROC improvement over reconstruction-based baselines; causal regularisation contributes less than kNN scoring; easy faults saturate aggregate AUROC, but the method excels on hard/stealthy faults; CMR-Mamba achieves state-of-the-art performance on Paderborn artificial defects and SWaT stealthy attacks; code and data are publicly available.

Conclusion: CMR-Mamba provides an interpretable, consistently competitive approach for detecting coupling faults across mechanical, hydraulic, and cyber-physical systems, with kNN-based manifold scoring driving most gains and causal regularisation offering secondary benefit.

Abstract: Unsupervised fault detection in industrial systems is dominated by reconstruction based methods that monitor individual sensor marginal distributions. This misses coupling faults, where the physical relationship between sensor groups breaks while marginal statistics remain normal. Such faults evade marginal monitoring and persist as latent failures, with direct consequences for system reliability and safety. We propose CMR-Mamba (Causal Mechanism Representation Mamba), which trains per domain Mamba state-space encoders on healthy data. A causal cross-modal predictor regularises these encoders so that the effect-channel manifold reflects the normal cause-to-effect coupling. Anomalies are scored by k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) distance on this manifold or by the mechanism residual between the observed and the causally predicted effect embedding. We evaluate CMR-Mamba on electromechanical (Paderborn bearings), hydraulic (ZeMA) and cyber-physical (SWaT) coupling-fault domains. Ablations establish two findings. First, k-NN manifold scoring, rather than the encoder family, is the dominant source of gain over reconstruction-error scoring, improving baselines by up to 0.42 AUROC and exceeding the gain from causal regularisation. Second, aggregate AUROC is saturated by easy faults that any strong method solves, so the methods separate only on the low-separability subset. There CMR-Mamba leads the evaluated baselines on Paderborn artificial defects and on SWaT stealthy attacks, which keep every sensor inside its normal range and which marginal methods detect only at chance. CMR-Mamba therefore offers an interpretable and consistently competitive approach to coupling-fault detection across mechanical, hydraulic and cyber-physical systems. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/CMR_Mamba_MFD_1177.

</details>


### [474] [Position: AI Agents in Scientific Teams Should Be Studied as Human-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14667)
*Patrick Emami,Sameera Horawalavithana,Truc Nguyen,Gihan Panapitiya,Bruno Jacob,Siddhisanket Raskar,Saumya Sinha,Jared D. Willard,Andrew Glaws,Nithin Somasekharan,Ling Yue,Brian Lu,Shaowu Pan,Jason Eisner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Advocates studying AI scientists as human–agent systems (HAS) rather than autonomous AI agents, using literature and case studies to show risks of ignoring human–agent dynamics and to propose mathematical frameworks for AI–human synergy in science.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dominant focus on autonomous AI scientists neglects social dynamics of scientific teams; understanding HAS can prevent biases and diversify inquiry.

Method: Literature review and empirical analysis; analysis of real-world case studies to illustrate HAS effects and potential synergy.

Result: Demonstrates that scientists and agents can augment each other's capabilities; neglecting HAS can lead to risks such as reduced diversity of inquiry; provides evidence from literature and cases.

Conclusion: Urges adoption of the HAS lens and development of mathematical frameworks to model and foster human–AI collaboration in scientific discovery.

Abstract: Large language model-based agents are increasingly deployed as collaborators in scientific discovery yet most current work focuses on the autonomous capabilities of "AI Scientists". We argue that this overlooks the social aspects of scientific teamwork, and that studying AI Scientists as human-agent systems (HAS)--where the unit of analysis is the human-agent pair--is both underexplored and undervalued. We establish these points through literature and empirical analysis, and highlight recent incidences and studies which show that deploying agents in science without accounting for human-agent dynamics introduces near-term risks, including reduced diversity of scientific inquiry. Through analysis of real-world case studies, we show that scientists and agents can augment each other's capabilities. We call for new research that adopts the HAS lens to develop mathematical frameworks for understanding and fostering human-AI synergy in scientific discovery.

</details>


### [475] [Beyond Correctness: Toward Automated Novelty Verification with Lean 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14669)
*Ayrton Porto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AViD Journal pipeline formalizes LaTeX articles in Lean 4 to assess novelty via a three-axis decision tree: prior existence in formal (Mathlib) and informal (TheoremSearch/Matlas with LLM judge) corpora, non-triviality via automatic tactics, and structural distance (Jaccard) of premises. Evaluation on withdrawn arXiv papers reveals three practical obstacles: semantic fidelity may not follow from successful compilation, recall is bounded by theorem-index coverage, and source code removal hinders reproducibility of benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To automate novelty assessment in mathematical proofs by bridging formal verification with novelty signaling, addressing the gap where correct proofs may still be known results.

Method: Formalize LaTeX statements in Lean 4, apply a three-dimensional novelty verdict: check prior existence in formal corpus (Mathlib) and informal sources (TheoremSearch, Matlas with temporal filter and an LLM judge); assess non-triviality via automatic tactics; compute structural distance using Jaccard distance over premise sets. Evaluate on papers withdrawn from arXiv to identify limiting obstacles rather than performance metrics.

Result: Three obstacles identified: (1) valid Lean compilation does not guarantee semantic fidelity; (2) recall ceiling governed by theorem-index coverage rather than the similarity metric; (3) arXiv removes source code upon withdrawal, compromising reproducibility of benchmarks.

Conclusion: The AViD pipeline yields insight beyond performance metrics, highlighting substantive barriers to automated novelty detection in formalized mathematics and underscoring the need for improved fidelity checks, broader theorem coverage, and robust reproducibility practices.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems applied to mathematics verify correctness but not novelty: an automatically generated theorem can compile in Lean without errors and yet be an already known result. This article presents AViD Journal, a pipeline that receives a LaTeX article, formalizes its statements in Lean 4, and issues a novelty verdict through a decision tree over three dimensions: prior existence in a formal corpus (Mathlib) and an informal one (TheoremSearch and Matlas, with temporal filter and LLM judge), non-triviality via automatic tactics, and structural distance between proofs measured as Jaccard distance over premise sets.
  Evaluation on papers withdrawn from arXiv due to declared duplication produced a result more informative than any performance measure: the identification of three obstacles that limit the approach regardless of this implementation. First, successful compilation of a Lean file does not guarantee semantic fidelity. Second, the recall ceiling is imposed by the coverage of theorem indices, not by the similarity metric. Third, arXiv removes the source code of articles upon withdrawal, compromising the reproducibility of any benchmark built upon them.

</details>


### [476] [Auditing an AI-Generated Mathematical Proof: A Correction to a Greedy Conditioning Lemma in Quantum Parallel Repetition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14673)
*Mikołaj Sienicki,Krzysztof Sienicki*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Notes a polarity error in a quantitative greedy conditioning lemma used in a chapter claiming an exponential parallel repetition theorem for entangled games; provides a counterexample, identifies the correct continuation condition, and offers a complete corrected proof; meanwhile the repair is local and the main theorem is not independently verified by this note. Illustrates how plausible AI-generated arguments can contain small but decisive reversals between complementary events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clarify and repair a specific lemma that undermined a part of a larger argument; demonstrate that a mathematically plausible AI-generated argument can hide a reversal between complementary events; caution for relying on AI-generated proofs.

Method: Construct a counterexample to the printed continuation test, identify the intended condition on the continuation, and present a corrected, self-contained proof for the lemma; keep the lemma's statement and parameterization intact and decouple the repair from verification of the main theorem.

Result: A concrete counterexample is provided; the intended continuation condition is clarified; a complete corrected proof is supplied; the repair is localized and does not constitute a full independent verification of the main theorem.

Conclusion: The note emphasizes precision in probabilistic conditioning arguments and warns about hidden reversals in AI-generated mathematical reasoning; it reinforces the need for meticulous cross-checking in complex probabilistic proofs.

Abstract: Chapter 6 of OpenAI's *Ten Advances in Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science* claims an exponential parallel-repetition theorem for all finite two-player, one-round entangled games. Early in the proof, the chapter uses a quantitative greedy conditioning lemma. The lemma is meant to select a small set of coordinates (D) such that, after conditioning on winning every coordinate in (D), a randomly chosen remaining coordinate is won with average probability at least (1-δ). The statement is correct, but the proof as printed contains a polarity error. Its continuation test is written in terms of average success, while the next step requires a coordinate with a large conditional failure probability. That implication is false, and even simple examples can leave the printed procedure without a valid next move.
  This note gives an explicit counterexample, identifies the intended continuation condition, and supplies a complete corrected proof. The repair is local: it leaves the statement of the lemma and the parameters used later in the chapter unchanged. It should not, however, be read as an independent verification of the main parallel-repetition theorem. More broadly, the example shows how a mathematically plausible AI-generated argument can hide a small but decisive reversal between complementary events.

</details>


### [477] [When Agentic Executions Fail: Detecting and Localizing Runtime Faults from Telemetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14680)
*Chenkai Zhang,Yiran Li,Yifang Tian,Michalis Bachras,Hans-Arno Jacobsen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A dataset and benchmark (AGENTCHAOSBENCH) for diagnosing runtime faults in agentic systems using execution telemetry; evaluates fault localization across tool/model/guardrail/inter-agent failures; baseline results show poor fault detection ability, highlighting need for robust diagnostics and reproducible evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliability in LLM-based agentic systems depends on the full execution trace (tool calls, model calls, guardrails, inter-agent messages). Outcome-only evaluation misses failure modes and hinders diagnosis; a benchmark with fault injection and execution telemetry enables systematic evaluation and comparison of diagnosis methods.

Method: Five heterogeneous applications coordinate agents via the Agent-to-Agent protocol and Model Context Protocol. Ten fault types are injected at tool, model, guardrail, and inter-agent boundaries plus a no-fault control. 275 sanitized traces (250 faulty, 25 no-fault). Fault-type and location labels held out for diagnosis. Zero-shot LLM baselines (up to 14B params) and a larger model (DeepSeek-v4-pro) evaluated on single-trace inputs to identify fault type and location.

Result: LLMs achieve low fault-type accuracy (13.6–19.2% for detectors; 24.8% for DeepSeek-v4-pro). Joint fault type and location accuracy tops at 22%. Reference-dependent faults, especially bypassed guardrails, remain difficult to diagnose from a single trace. Aligned references improve some relative faults but do not resolve guardrail bypass. The dataset supports reproducible comparison of LLM-based and non-LLM methods.

Conclusion: The AGENTCHAOSBENCH dataset enables standardized evaluation and benchmarking of runtime fault diagnosis in agentic systems. Current LLM-based baselines struggle to localize faults from single traces, particularly guardrail bypasses; aligned references help only partially. The work highlights the need for more robust, multi-trace diagnostics and improved fault-localization techniques.

Abstract: Reliability in LLM-based agentic systems is a property of the whole execution (its tool calls, model calls, guardrails, and inter-agent messages), not of the final answer alone, yet evaluating only task outcomes reveals little about how or why a run fails. We present AGENTCHAOSBENCH, a benchmark for detecting and localizing runtime faults in agentic systems from their execution telemetry. We run five heterogeneous applications that coordinate agents over the Agent-to-Agent protocol and call tools through the Model Context Protocol, and inject ten types of operational fault (unavailable or slow tools, corrupted or oversized responses, and delayed, looped, or misrouted delegations and bypassed guardrails) at their tool, model, guardrail, and inter-agent boundaries, alongside a no-fault control. The resulting dataset contains 275 sanitized traces: 250 faulty executions spanning ten fault types and 25 no-fault controls. Each faulty trace is aligned with the no-fault execution of the same input; fault-type labels and, where applicable, location labels are held out from diagnosis. On structured single-trace inputs, a first set of zero-shot LLM baselines shows the task is far from solved: local detectors up to 14B parameters reach only 13.6-19.2% top-1 fault-type accuracy and the frontier DeepSeek-v4-pro only 24.8%, while jointly identifying the fault type and its location tops out at 22%; reference-dependent faults (above all a bypassed guardrail) stay near-unsolved from a single trace. An aligned reference improves selected relative faults but does not resolve guardrail bypass. The held-out labels and compact prediction format support reproducible comparison of LLM-based and non-LLM diagnosis methods.

</details>


### [478] [A Comprehensive Survey of Wireless Foundation Models for AI-Native 6G Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14694)
*Naveed Khan,Besan Al Sbeihi,Maryam Alshehhi,Nasir Saeed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified survey of wireless foundation models (WFMs) that defines concepts, taxonomy, architectures, training paradigms, and applications; synthesizes datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation approaches; discusses challenges and future directions for AI-native 6G.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models enable scalable, transferable intelligence across wireless tasks; current research is fragmented across architectures and domains; a comprehensive survey is needed to guide design, learning, deployment, and standardization for AI-native 6G networks.

Method: Conceptual grounding of WFMs; taxonomy by model architectures, pre-training paradigms, and applications; literature review of representative architectures, self-supervised pre-training strategies, parameter-efficient adaptation methods, datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation methodologies; analysis of applications across physical-layer signal processing, network intelligence, and cross-layer optimization; discussion of data availability, generalization, interpretability, edge deployment, and standardization as key challenges; outlining future research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and general-purpose WFMs.

Result: Provides a comprehensive, unified reference that clarifies the WFM landscape, connects architectures and training methods to wireless tasks, and highlights datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation methodologies; identifies gaps and standardization needs; outlines research directions for scalable, trustworthy WFMs in AI-native 6G.

Conclusion: Advances in WFMs will enable scalable wireless intelligence; success depends on data availability, generalization, interpretability, efficient edge deployment, and standardization; future work should pursue scalable, trustworthy, and general-purpose WFMs for AI-native 6G networks.

Abstract: Foundation models are emerging as a transformative paradigm for AI-native sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks by enabling scalable, transferable, and data-efficient intelligence across diverse communication tasks. Unlike conventional deep learning models that are trained for individual applications, wireless foundation models (WFMs) learn generalized representations from large-scale heterogeneous wireless data and can be efficiently adapted to communication, sensing, localization, and network optimization tasks with minimal task-specific supervision. Despite rapid progress, current research remains fragmented across architectures, training paradigms, and application domains, with no unified survey dedicated to the design, learning, and deployment of WFMs. This survey presents a comprehensive and unified review of wireless foundation models. We first establish the fundamental concepts of WFMs and introduce a taxonomy that organizes the field according to model architectures, pre-training paradigms, and applications. We then review representative architectures, self-supervised pre-training strategies, parameter-efficient adaptation methods, datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation methodologies, highlighting their roles in enabling transferable wireless intelligence. Furthermore, we examine emerging applications spanning physical-layer signal processing, network intelligence, and cross-layer optimization, and discuss the key challenges of data availability, generalization, interpretability, efficient edge deployment, and standardization. Finally, we outline future research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and general-purpose wireless intelligence for AI-native 6G networks. This survey provides a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners developing next-generation intelligent wireless systems.

</details>


### [479] [Synchronized Logit Steering: Real-world Steganography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14697)
*Andrew Rufail,Aadi Dash,Onir Narahari,Ethan Mui,Mahi Gajare,Prakhar Tiwari,Shrija Makapothula,Nick Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SLS enables prompt-agnostic covert encoding of data into LLM outputs by deriving a proxy prompt from the output and encoding payloads in token rank within high-entropy regions, with periodic bursts to boost capacity; achieves low divergence from greedy distributions and higher payload density, enabling stealthy communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome dependency on identical prompt contexts in steganography for LLMs, especially in production pipelines using retrieval augmentation or system instructions.

Method: Deterministic scheme deriving a proxy prompt from generated output; encode payload values as token ranks within high-entropy regions of the proxy prompt distribution; incorporate periodic recurrence and bursts to scale information density; evaluate on ShareGPT, GSM8K, SWE-bench Verified; measure KL divergence and KS tests.

Result: KL divergence between true and proxy prompt distributions falls below 0.5 nats after 40-token window; encoding does not disrupt convergence vs greedy generation; periodic-burst variant achieves 0.20 bits per token (~10x single-payload); KS tests show outputs are statistically indistinguishable from greedy, indicating covert communication is practical and stealthy.

Conclusion: SLS provides a prompt-agnostic, covert communication channel within LLM outputs with scalable capacity and minimal detectable difference from standard generation; relevance for practical steganography and potential defenses.

Abstract: Steganography in large language models offers a way to embed hidden messages within natural-sounding text. Existing token and logit-level methods typically require the sender and receiver to share an identical prompt context, which is rarely guaranteed in production pipelines that use retrieval-augmented generation or proprietary system instructions. We introduce Synchronized Logit Steering (SLS), a deterministic steganographic scheme that eliminates this dependency by deriving a proxy prompt from the generated output itself, allowing both parties to reconstruct the same logit distribution without access to the original prompt. SLS encodes payload values as token ranks within high-entropy regions of the proxy prompt distribution, and we extend the scheme with periodic recurrence and payload bursts to scale information density. Across ShareGPT, GSM8K, and SWE-bench Verified, we show that the KL divergence between the true and proxy prompt distributions falls below 0.5 nats once the synchronization window reaches 40 tokens, and SLS encoding does not meaningfully disrupt this convergence relative to greedy generation. We also find that the periodic-burst variant achieves 0.20 bits per token, or roughly 10x the capacity of single-payload encoding. Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests further confirm that SLS outputs are statistically difficult to distinguish from greedy generations, demonstrating that covert, prompt-agnostic communication through LLMs is both practical and stealthy.

</details>


### [480] [Semantic Uncertainty-Guided Orchestration in Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14707)
*John Knowlton,Aritra Guha,Risto Miikkulainen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces HASSUM, a semantic-uncertainty-guided orchestration framework for uncertainty-aware coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems; uses semantic entropy and semantic density to gauge trust at the level of answer semantics, enabling adaptive decisions to reduce hallucinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the propagation of errors/hallucinations in multi-agent coordination by moving beyond output-probability uncertainty to semantic-level uncertainty signals that reflect trust in intermediate reasoning. Seeks a general, architecture-agnostic orchestration mechanism.

Method: Proposes semantic entropy and semantic density as uncertainty metrics integrated into a general orchestration framework (HASSUM). Enables adaptive actions (output verification, selective reprompting, deliberation, confidence-aware selection). Implemented within a hierarchical agent framework and evaluated on StrategyQA, JailbreakBench, and TruthfulQA to test complex reasoning under ambiguity.

Result: Uncertainty-guided orchestration yields more reliable outcomes than uncertainty-unaware coordination across tasks requiring complex reasoning and prone to hallucinations. Using semantic entropy and density in tandem outperforms either metric alone. Ablations show thresholds and model sizes influence effectiveness.

Conclusion: Semantic uncertainty is a practical, general-purpose signal for improving robustness and trustworthiness in agentic AI systems; the framework is architecture-agnostic and broadly applicable to hierarchical multi-agent settings.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems become increasingly capable, coordinating agents under uncertainty becomes a fundamental challenge. Existing orchestration strategies typically rely on fixed interaction patterns and often lack mechanisms for assessing the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, allowing errors and hallucinations to propagate through the system. This paper introduces a semantic-uncertainty-guided orchestration approach, HASSUM as a general framework for uncertainty-aware coordination in multi-agent systems. The method estimates uncertainty using semantic entropy and semantic density, which measure trust at the level of answer semantics rather than output probabilities. These signals enable adaptive orchestration decisions, including output verification, selective reprompting, additional deliberation, and confidence-aware response selection. Because the approach operates independently of any particular agent architecture, it can be integrated into a broad range of hierarchical and collaborative multi-agent systems. The evaluations demonstrate an implementation within a hierarchical agent framework and evaluate it on StrategyQA, JailbreakBench, and TruthfulQA benchmarks. Across tasks that require complex reasoning and are prone to ambiguity or hallucinations, uncertainty-guided orchestration yields more reliable outcomes than uncertainty-unaware coordination. Semantic entropy and semantic density in tandem outperformed either metric alone. Ablations testing different thresholds and model sizes demonstrated that both influence the effectiveness of semantic metrics. The results suggest that semantic uncertainty is a practical and general-purpose signal for improving robustness and trustworthiness in agentic AI systems.

</details>


### [481] [Beyond Pass@k: Measuring Reliability and Security of Agentic Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14711)
*Jiajun Jiang,Sharon Zheng,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The abstract targets a misapplication of Chen et al. (2021) pass@k in AI coding benchmarks, introducing reliability@k with independent rollouts, plus a security-adjusted variant. It provides synthetic and real-world evidence of inflated scores under misapplication and suggests careful, powered benchmarking with complementary metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarking AI coding agents requires unbiased, independent evaluation of ability to produce correct solutions. Misusing pass@k by tying n to a single submission’s test suite inflates performance and misleads comparisons.

Method: Diagnose the misapplication, prove the error with counterexamples, and propose reliability@k (n = independent rollouts, c = fully-passing rollouts). Extend with security-adjusted reliability@k (counts only functionally correct and secure rollouts). Validate via (i) synthetic multi-rollout benchmark, (ii) live-API test with three agents, and (iii) a preliminary 5-task SWE-bench pilot. Compare against single-rollout proxies using rank correlations (Spearman).

Result: Demonstrates substantial inflation from misapplied pass@k (reported 0.96–0.98 vs corrected 0.00–0.12). A single-rollout proxy poorly tracks true performance (ρ = 0.417). Live-API rankings remained unchanged under the proposed adjustment, suggesting limited sensitivity in small samples. SWE-bench pilot shows macro-averaged hidden-test pass rate 0.80 vs strict task resolution 0.20, indicating a gap between broad success and task-level determinism.

Conclusion: Properly defining independence in evaluation (reliability@k) and extending with security considerations yields more reliable benchmarking and highlights the need for larger, well-powered experiments to decisively compare agents. The proposed measures complement, rather than replace, existing benchmarks and emphasize alignment between functional correctness and security.

Abstract: AI coding agent benchmarks rank agents with the Chen et al. (2021) pass@k estimator, but current implementations misapply it: they set n to the number of unit tests in a single submission rather than the number of independent rollout attempts, conflating test-suite size with attempt independence. We diagnose this operationalization error, prove it by counterexample, and propose reliability@k, the same estimator applied correctly, with n = independent rollouts and c = fully-passing rollouts per (task, agent) pair. In a synthetic multi-rollout benchmark, the misapplied metric inflates reported scores by 0.85-0.97 in absolute terms (0.96-0.98 reported vs. 0.00-0.12 corrected), and a cheap single-rollout proxy fails to substitute for repeated runs (Spearman $ρ= 0.417$). Motivated by evidence that functional correctness does not imply security safety, we additionally propose security-adjusted reliability@k, which counts only rollouts that are both functionally correct and free of high-severity insecure patterns. In an initial live-API test with three agents, the adjustment did not change any ranking under our current scanner and threshold, so we present it as a proposed complementary lens whose decisive evaluation requires better-powered future runs. Finally, a preliminary 5-task SWE-bench Verified pilot observes the same core concern in a real repository setting: macro-averaged hidden-test pass rate was 0.80 while strict task resolution was 0.20.

</details>


### [482] [Advanced modelling and data analytics in aviation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14746)
*Aziida Nanyonga*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ML/NLP on aviation safety datasets (Socrata, ATSB, NTSB, ASN) to extract patterns, topics, and causal insights; demonstrates improved incident analysis and decision support with interpretable AI and deployment considerations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlock predictive and explanatory insights from heterogeneous aviation safety data to enhance safety management and reduce accidents/near-misses.

Method: Data fusion from multiple sources; apply deep learning and transformer models; NLP for incident narratives; topic modeling; causal inference; interpretable AI frameworks; evaluation in a structured aviation safety context; deployment considerations.

Result: Evidence of detectable patterns and themes in safety records; actionable insights for regulators, airlines, and policymakers; improved interpretability and transparency in ML-driven safety analyses; practical deployment guidance.

Conclusion: Advanced ML/NLP methods are viable for aviation safety analysis, offering data-driven decision support and greater transparency, with potential integration into safety management systems.

Abstract: The aviation industry characterized by its stringent safety standards has seen a growing need for innovative approaches to enhance safety measures. Despite the vast accumulation of aviation safety data over time, its full potential in predicting and preventing incidents has not been fully realized. This research addresses this gap by applying machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to analyze aviation safety data from Socrata, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB), the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), and the Aviation Safety Network (ASN). By leveraging existing ML models, including deep learning and transformer-based architectures alongside NLP methods for mining aviation incident narratives, this study uncovers patterns contributing to safety related incidents such as accidents and near-misses. Additionally, it employs various topic modelling techniques to extract meaningful themes from unstructured safety reports, enhancing the interpretability of incident analysis. Causal inference techniques and interpretable AI frameworks are further explored to improve model transparency and trustworthiness. A key contribution of this work is the deployment of advanced ML methodologies in a structured aviation safety context, assessing their effectiveness and providing insights into their practical implementation. The findings offer valuable insights for aviation stakeholders, including regulators, airlines, and policymakers, by providing data-driven solutions that enhance incident analysis and decision making. Ultimately, this research supports the industry s ongoing efforts to minimize risks, improve passenger and crew security, and integrate AI driven methodologies into aviation safety management.

</details>


### [483] [Agentic Data Cleaning Without a Clean Reference: An Experimental Study of Capabilities and Trade-offs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14765)
*Hadi Fadlallah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an evidence-grounded framework for reference-free data cleaning; evaluates seven configurations across financial, clinical, and environmental-monitoring datasets; finds trade-offs among detection, repair, grounding, conservatism, reproducibility, and cost; no configuration uniformly outperforms others; full conservative policy minimizes unsafe/ unnecessary changes; deterministic profiling achieves best synthetic detection F1; source ranking reduces unsupported rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data cleaning without a trusted clean reference is challenging due to ambiguity between errors and valid observations; need to understand how different agent capabilities interact and what trade-offs emerge when augmenting with reasoning, evidence, and controls.

Method: Proposes an evidence-grounded framework with components: structured context, profiling, LLM reasoning, executable checks, controlled evidence retrieval, source ranking, citation alignment, conservative repair, reversible scripts, provenance logging. Evaluates seven configurations across seven datasets (financial, clinical, environmental-monitoring) using controlled synthetic corruption and original-data descriptive analysis; compares against two baselines and a progressive LLM sequence; analyzes 126 completed runs.

Result: Deterministic profiling baseline achieves highest detection F1-score (0.561) in synthetic evaluation. Among LLM-based configurations, full conservative configuration attains the highest F1 (0.421) but no configuration dominates across all criteria. Source-ranked configurations have the lowest unsupported-rule rates; decision-level citation alignment remains weak. Full conservative configuration yields no unsafe or unnecessary modifications (rates already zero pre-policy) and does not perform direct repairs. Overall, added capabilities entail trade-offs across detection, repair, grounding, conservatism, reproducibility, and cost; framework provides a structured methodology to evaluate these trade-offs.

Conclusion: The study presents a structured framework and empirical methodology for evaluating trade-offs in reference-free agentic data cleaning, highlighting that increased capabilities do not guarantee uniform improvements and that careful design of controls is essential for balancing accuracy, safety, and practicality.

Abstract: Data cleaning without a trusted clean reference is challenging because unusual values may represent either genuine errors or valid observations. This paper studies how different agent capabilities affect reference-free data cleaning and proposes an evidence-grounded framework that combines structured context, profiling, LLM reasoning, executable checks, controlled evidence retrieval, source ranking, citation alignment, conservative repair, reversible scripts, and provenance logging. Seven configurations are evaluated across financial, clinical, and environmental-monitoring datasets using controlled synthetic corruption and original-data descriptive analysis, resulting in 126 completed runs. The evaluation includes two comparison baselines and a progressive LLM-based sequence that adds executable tools, evidence retrieval, evidence controls, and conservative repair. In the synthetic evaluation, the deterministic profiling baseline achieved the highest detection F1-score of 0.561. Among the LLM-based configurations, the full conservative configuration achieved the highest F1-score of 0.421, but no configuration performed best across all evaluation criteria. The source-ranked configurations achieved the lowest unsupported-rule rates, while decision-level citation alignment remained weak. The full conservative configuration produced no unsafe or unnecessary modifications, although these rates were already zero before the conservative policy was added, and it performed no direct repairs. Overall, the results show that additional capabilities introduce trade-offs among detection, repair, evidence grounding, conservative behaviour, reproducibility, and operational cost rather than producing consistent improvements. The study provides a structured framework and empirical methodology for evaluating these trade-offs in reference-free agentic data cleaning.

</details>


### [484] [From Errors to Proofs: Minimal-Core-Guided Repair for Neuro-Symbolic Constraint Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14771)
*Dipankar Sarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A method replacing opaque solver errors with minimal unsatisfiable cores as feedback when translating constraint problems to a solver, achieving faithful translations and dramatically reducing fabrication, with a benchmark showing strong results except in one diagnosable domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Faithful translation from natural language to formal specifications is crucial for reliable constraint solving. Current pipelines only repair crashes and reveal solver errors, which can still yield wrong solutions. Providing a minimal unsat core offers a leakage-free diagnostic signal to localize faults and prevent fabrication.

Method: Translate problems to a formal solver (Answer Set Programming). If the translated program is unsatisfiable, instead of returning an error, extract a minimal unsatisfiable core from the model's own constraints and return that core as the diagnostic signal. Build and test on a benchmark of 77 problems with an exact oracle across seven domains; compare against a strong chain-of-thought baseline.

Result: The approach yields faithful translations on 6 of 7 domains; only the aggregate coverage scheduling domain shows failure in translation. Using a minimal core reduces fabrication (instances where the model fabricates a solution to an infeasible problem) from 79% to 7%. The chain-of-thought baseline matches the symbolic route on accuracy, but its value lies in having certificates and avoiding fabrication rather than improved accuracy.

Conclusion: Minimal unsat cores provide a leakage-free, certifiable feedback signal that guides the model toward faithful problem specification and prevents fabrication, improving reliability beyond plain accuracy. The approach shows strong promise but reveals a diagnosable failure pattern in a specific domain requiring further generalization.

Abstract: Making language models solve constraint problems reliably often means having them translate the problem into a formal specification and delegating the search to a sound solver. But the translation is itself a language-model task, and an unfaithful translation makes the solver faithfully solve the wrong problem. Existing pipelines repair only translations that crash, returning the solver's error message and falling silent when the program runs but is wrong. We replace the error message with a proof: when the generated program is unsatisfiable, we extract a minimal unsatisfiable core over the model's own constraints and hand it back the exact set that cannot hold together, a leakage-free signal that localizes the fault. On a new benchmark of 77 problems with an exact oracle, translation to Answer Set Programming is faithful on six of seven domains and fails only on aggregate coverage scheduling, which concentrates the translation tax in one diagnosable pattern. A minimal core, rather than a bare error, is what stops a weaker model from fabricating solutions to infeasible problems, cutting fabrication from 79% to 7%. A strong chain-of-thought baseline meanwhile matches the symbolic route on accuracy, so the route's value is not accuracy but certificates and its refusal to fabricate.

</details>


### [485] [Task-Driven Three-Layer Distributed Scheduling for Emergency Earth Observation in Large Low-Earth-Orbit Constellations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14789)
*Qian Yin,Xinwei Wang,Guohua Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A distributed task-driven three-layer scheduling framework (T3L-DS) for emergency observation requests in large LEO EO constellations, achieving higher emergency coverage than baseline distributed methods and approaching centralized SA performance, while substantially reducing routine-coverage loss under load.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emergency requests arriving during routine-plan execution necessitate rapid insertion with minimal disruption in large LEO EO constellations. Centralized or standard distributed approaches may struggle under intermittent ground contact and dynamic demand.

Method: T3L-DS represents task demand and sensor footprints on a common geographic grid, forms temporary clusters from observation capabilities and current inter-satellite links, uses onboard dual-plan bidding and joint marginal evaluation for intra-cluster coordination, and employs an inter-cluster coordination mechanism for unresolved demand.

Result: Compared with centralized simulated annealing (SA) and distributed baselines A-SeTVBRP and CNP, T3L-DS achieves the highest emergency coverage among distributed methods, with average relative improvements of ~2.8% over A-SeTVBRP and ~17.1% over CNP; its average relative gap to SA is ~7.1%. Under conflict-enhanced loads, it reduces routine-coverage loss by ~57.9% and ~87.7% relative to A-SeTVBRP and CNP. An ablation study confirms the contribution of the proposed coordination enhancements.

Conclusion: T3L-DS provides an effective distributed approach to the dynamic emergency observation scheduling problem (DEOSP) in large LEO EO constellations.

Abstract: Large low-Earth-orbit (LEO) Earth-observation (EO) constellations offer frequent access to geographically dispersed ground targets, but emergency requests may arrive after committed routine-plan execution has begun. The resulting dynamic emergency observation scheduling problem (DEOSP) requires urgent tasks to be inserted under intermittent ground contact without excessive routine-plan disruption. To address DEOSP, we propose a task-driven three-layer distributed scheduling (T3L-DS) method, which represents task demand and sensor footprints on a common geographic grid and forms temporary clusters from observation capabilities and current inter-satellite links. For intra-cluster coordination, T3L-DS introduces onboard dual-plan bidding and joint marginal evaluation. It also designs an inter-cluster coordination mechanism for unresolved demand. Extensive computational experiments compare T3L-DS with centralised simulated annealing (SA), an adapted selective time-variant better reply process (A-SeTVBRP), and a conventional contract-net protocol (CNP). T3L-DS achieves the highest emergency coverage among the distributed methods, with average relative improvements of approximately 2.8% and 17.1% over A-SeTVBRP and CNP, respectively. Its average relative gap from SA is approximately 7.1%. Under conflict-enhanced loads, it reduces routine-coverage loss by approximately 57.9% and 87.7% relative to A-SeTVBRP and CNP, respectively. The ablation study confirms the contribution of the proposed coordination enhancements. Overall, the results show that T3L-DS provides an effective distributed approach to DEOSP.

</details>


### [486] [CEDAR-GRPO: Process-Aware Reinforcement Learning for General Abductive Reasoning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14791)
*Moein Salimi,Danial Parnian,Shaygan Adim,Amirmohammad Ebrahiminasab,Nima Alighardashi,Parsa Gholami,Sahand Akramipour,Mahdi Jafari Siavoshani,Mohammad Hossein Rohban*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CEDAR-GRPO is a process-aware RL post-training framework that augments abductive reasoning in LLMs by combining final-answer correctness with abductive rewards for evidence coverage and evidence-to-explanation directionality. Across 11 unseen tasks and four open-weight LLMs, it yields transfer gains over base models and correctness-only GRPO, with average improvements of 7.4 and 2.7 points and a maximum of 30.8 points. Ablations show contributions from RL, reward design, and task diversity; process-level metrics reveal stronger abductive behavior (exploration, rival elimination, backtracking, uncertainty marking).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Abduction under uncertainty is central to explanation and discovery, but gains from LLM improvements often fail to transfer beyond benchmark tasks. This work probes whether RL post-training can cultivate transferable abductive reasoning across diverse tasks.

Method: Introduce CEDAR-GRPO, a process-aware RL objective that merges final-answer correctness with abductive rewards (evidence coverage and evidence-to-explanation directionality). Post-train four open-weight LLMs on a controlled, domain-neutral mixture of abductive hypothesis-generation and hypothesis-selection tasks. Evaluate on 11 unseen tasks spanning hypothesis selection, missing-fact generation, defeasible inference, long-context investigation, clinical reasoning, code debugging, and non-abductive controls. Conduct ablations to quantify contributions of RL, reward design, and task diversity; analyze process-level abductive behaviors.

Result: All models improve on every held-out task relative to both their base versions and correctness-only GRPO. Average gains are 7.4 points (abductive rewards) and 2.7 points (correctness-only); maximum gain observed is 30.8 points. Ablations confirm the roles of RL, abductive reward design, and task diversity. Process metrics indicate enhanced abductive behavior, including exploration of alternatives, elimination of rivals, backtracking, and uncertainty marking.

Conclusion: RL-based post-training with abductive rewards and diverse abductive tasks yields transferable enhancements in abductive reasoning across varied domains; the gains stem from the combination of reward shaping, process-awareness, and task heterogeneity.
