Abstract: Abductive reasoning, often characterized as inference to the best explanation, is central to explanation under uncertainty, from everyday sense-making and investigation to scientific discovery. Yet LLM research has mostly studied abduction through narrow, task-specific benchmarks, making it unclear whether observed gains transfer beyond the benchmark family used for training or evaluation. We ask whether RL post-training can improve abduction as a transferable reasoning capability. We introduce CEDAR-GRPO, a process-aware framework that combines final-answer correctness with abductive rewards for evidence coverage and evidence-to-explanation directionality. Four open-weight LLMs are post-trained on a controlled, domain-neutral mixture of abductive hypothesis-generation and hypothesis-selection tasks. We evaluate them on 11 unseen tasks spanning hypothesis selection, missing-fact generation, defeasible inference, long-context investigation, clinical reasoning, code debugging, and non-abductive controls. CEDAR- GRPO improves every model on every held-out task over both base models and correctness-only GRPO, with average gains of 7.4 and 2.7 points, respectively, and a maximum gain of 30.8 points. Ablations confirm that RL, abductive reward design, and task diversity each contribute to transfer. Process-level metrics further show stronger abductive behavior, including exploration of alternatives, elimination of rivals, backtracking, and uncertainty marking.

</details>


### [487] [Individual Disempowerment through an Advice Channel: Control Loss when Influence is Endogenous](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14795)
*Adam M. Oberman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Formal analysis of AI safety via human-in-the-loop where advisor influence models a fraction of human action; shows horizon- and memory-dependent shifts in optimal strategy, with bounds and caps failing to guarantee safety; a small-change horizon example (15 vs 16 rounds) demonstrates sudden cultivation behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge the boxing safety premise by formalizing how a human, embedded in the system, can be influenced by the advisor’s messages, potentially weakening safety guarantees.

Method: Model the advisor’s influence as epsilon_t of behavior following advice in a Markov decision process. Assume a rich channel that can echo any human action. Compare episodic versus long-memory deployments under per-round approval rewards. Derive influence bounds: fixed at deployment (horizon-insensitive) vs exogenous caps and memory resets. Provide a closed-form example.

Result: Increasing epsilon_t weakens the effectiveness of a message-independent fallback. Per-round reward fosters reliance beyond a patience threshold; same reward weights yield different optimal strategies in episodic vs long-memory settings. A bound fixed at deployment is horizon-insensitive and cannot guarantee better performance than a trivial ceiling; exogenous caps or memory resets alter incentives but do not recover prior steering. In a clear example, the optimal oracle avoids cultivation in fifteen rounds but cultivates in sixteen.

Conclusion: The safety of human-in-the-loop advice is fragile to horizon and memory effects. Designing robust safeguards requires accounting for dynamic influence, horizon length, memory resets, and external caps; small changes in deployment horizon can flip optimal objectives, indicating a need for horizon-aware, memory-conscious, and cap-augmented safety guarantees.

Abstract: An AI that can only give advice seems safe: the human is always free to ignore it. That is the premise of the boxing tradition in AI safety, and its long-suspected weak point is that the human who reads the answers is part of the system. We make the fraction $\varepsilon_t$ of behavior that follows the advice a state of a Markov decision process, moved by the advisor's own messages, so that use deepens reliance. Granted a channel rich enough to echo any action the human could take, higher $\varepsilon_t$ weakly lowers every monotone measure of the power of a human with a message-independent fallback. An oracle rewarded by per-round approval cultivates reliance beyond a closed-form patience threshold, so the same reward weights leave the optimal oracle answering in episodic deployments and cultivating in long-memory ones. An influence bound certified once at deployment is blind to that horizon and bounds the loss no lower than its trivial ceiling. An exogenous cap on influence bounds the guarantee the human loses, and a short enough memory reset removes the incentive to cultivate, while neither recovers the value already steered away. In a closed-form example the optimal oracle never cultivates in fifteen-round sessions and does in sixteen.

</details>


### [488] [Generated Context versus Governed State: Functional Conditions for Accountable Longitudinal Clinical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14804)
*Augusto Bernardo Pissarra,Victor Lorena de Farias Souza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A governance- and state-estimation-centric view of clinical AI for LLMs. The paper argues that persistent patient state, not single-task text dialogue, governs clinical AI performance; it defines five interrelated objects (true state, observations, evidence, belief, simulated state), proposes a tiered governance standard and a four-part information requirement to enable accountability, and introduces a six-level maturity framework to separate governable state from computable capability. No empirical results are claimed; the work is analytic and preparatory toward Clinical World Models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of persistent, governed representations of patient state in LLM-based clinical AI, under partial observability, and to provide a rigorous audit-friendly framework for accountability beyond style and fluency.

Method: Conceptual framework: distinguish five objects, define governance tiers, derive an operational accountability decomposition (immutable evidence ledger with time-versioning, distinct belief state, observation-process model, claim-level causal typing), and present a six-level maturity model to separate governable state from computable capability. Explicitly analytic with stated research questions and future work; no empirical evaluation.

Result: An analytic framework that converts accountable clinical AI from slogan to audit instrument. Provides a structured taxonomy and governance architecture (state vs. generated context), a concrete information requirements set for accountability, and a maturity model that maps current LLM-centric practice to higher governance maturity.

Conclusion: The work is analytic and preparatory; it outlines constructs and an audit-oriented architecture for future implementation of Clinical World Models and a buildable core of the framework, laying groundwork for future empirical and architectural development.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the dominant interface of clinical artificial intelligence, yet the interface they expose (text in, text out, one context window at a time) maintains no explicit, persistent, governed representation of what is currently true about a patient. This paper argues that longitudinal clinical reasoning is a state-estimation problem under partial observability, and that the axis on which clinical AI succeeds or fails is not the fluency of the model reading the record but the governance of the patient state it reasons over. We distinguish generated context from governed state; separate five objects that clinical AI habitually conflates (true state, observations, evidence, belief, and simulated state); define a tiered governance standard against which any clinical AI system can be audited; and show that an operational definition of accountability decomposes into four information requirements: an immutable evidence ledger with awareness-time versioning, a belief state distinct from accumulated evidence, an observation-process model, and claim-level causal typing. We are explicit that this decomposition is analytic rather than a necessity theorem, and that its value is conceptual hygiene: it converts "accountable clinical AI" from a slogan into an audit instrument. A six-level maturity framework separates what a system makes governable from what it can compute, locating current LLM-centric practice at high capability but low maturity. The paper is fully self-contained: the four research questions the framework poses are stated in the introduction, and the conclusion records what the paper establishes toward each; future work develops the buildable core of the architecture and the research program toward full Clinical World Models. No empirical result is claimed here.

</details>


### [489] [Do LLMs Know What to Ask and When? Evaluating Multi-Turn Information Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14808)
*Yepeng Huang,Jiawen Zhang,Michelle Dai,Xiaorui Su,Shanghua Gao,Zi Wang,Marinka Zitnik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Formalizes multi-turn information seeking as a k-underspecified constraint satisfaction problem; introduces MT-InfoSeek evaluation suite; reveals models struggle to ask minimally sufficient questions, underestimate required information, and misorder queries; final accuracy hides information-seeking ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate and characterize information-seeking behavior in multi-turn question-answering by formalizing it as constrained information gathering and by separating information-seeking ability from answer generation; highlight limitations of current LLM evaluations in measuring this capability.

Method: Define k-underspecified constraint satisfaction; instantiate MT-InfoSeek with 5,251 problems and 9,006 task instances across mathematics, logic, biology, medicine, and general knowledge; evaluate models on three axes (what they ask, when they ask, and how information affects final answer); analyze minimal sufficient query sets, impact of true k, and ordered dependencies; measure final sufficiency as a separation metric from final answer generation.

Result: Model performance degrades as underspecification increases; models recognize need for more information but underestimate how much; in logic with k=2 they under-predict missing information about four times more often than over-predict; fail to identify minimal sufficient query sets; marginal gains when given true k; incorrect query order reduces final accuracy even if all necessary information is eventually acquired; final sufficiency metric reveals information-seeking ability distinct from final answer accuracy.

Conclusion: The ability to seek information across multiple turns is distinct from answer generation and is not captured by current LLM evaluations; evaluation frameworks should separately measure information sufficiency to accurately assess multi-turn information-seeking capabilities.

Abstract: When a user question is underspecified, a capable model should recognize that its context is insufficient, identify the missing information, ask for it, and respond only once that information determines a unique answer. We formalize multi-turn information seeking as solving a k-underspecified constraint satisfaction problem, where k is the number of variables jointly required to determine the target and therefore measures the degree of missing information. We instantiate the formulation in MT-InfoSeek, a controlled evaluation suite of 5,251 problems and 9,006 task instances spanning mathematics, logic, biology, medicine, and general knowledge. We evaluate models along three axes: what they ask, when they ask it, and how the acquired information affects the final answer. Performance degrades across models and domains as underspecification increases. Models recognize that additional information is needed but underestimate how much, and in logical problems at k = 2 they under-predict the degree of missing information about four times as often as they over-predict it. They also fail to identify a minimal sufficient set of queries, improve only marginally when given the true k, and often stop before acquiring sufficient information. In tasks with ordered dependencies, an incorrect query order reduces final accuracy even when the model eventually acquires all necessary information. We measure information seeking directly through final sufficiency, which records whether the acquired information determines the target independent of answer generation. This separation shows differences between models that final accuracy alone does not capture, and indicates that the ability to seek information over multiple turns is distinct from the ability to generate answers and is not measured by current LLM evaluations.

</details>


### [490] [MINT: Min-Selection Preference Distillation for Balanced Multi-Objective Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14828)
*Tony Tu,Sayan Chakraborty,Ruomeng Xu,Tony Qin,Austin Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIN-selection preference distillation replaces additive ranking with a worst-case criterion, using the p -> -infty limit of generalized means. This yields better-balanced multi-objective optimization for language agents, improving weaker objectives and reducing imbalance across tasks, with strong empirical results in emotional support and negotiation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Additive reward shaping often causes optimization to bias toward the easiest-to-improve objective, neglecting others. There is a need for a ranking criterion that emphasizes balance among multiple objectives while preserving the original objective structure (DPO).

Method: Introduce MIN-selection: rank sampled candidates by their weakest objective rather than a weighted sum. This corresponds to the p -> -infty limit of a generalized-mean (spanning additive to worst-case). Keep the DPO objective unchanged. Apply to cooperative emotional support and adversarial negotiation tasks, and perform turn-by-turn analysis to assess balance dynamics.

Result: MIN-selection consistently improves balance across objectives, lifting the weaker axis (e.g., emotional support) from 0.37 to 0.64 (p < 1e-40) and surpassing human experts; gains persist through full multi-turn rollouts. The central finding is that the improvement scales with the degree of imbalance in the reference policy and endures as long as the interaction remains imbalanced.

Conclusion: A single-line change to preference distillation—focusing on the weakest objective—can effectively mitigate imbalance in multi-objective alignment for language agents, with robust empirical benefits and a principled connection to generalized-mean limits.

Abstract: Aligning a language agent to several objectives at once is a persistent failure mode of preference-based training: when objectives are combined additively, optimization collapses onto whichever is cheapest to improve and sacrifices the rest, so a support agent learns to sound warm while giving no real help. The root issue is that an additive reward has no notion of balance. We introduce Mint (MIN-selection preference disTillation), a one-line change to preference distillation: rather than ranking sampled candidates by a weighted sum of rewards, we rank them by their weakest objective, distilling the best-balanced candidate over the most lopsided one with an unchanged DPO objective. This is the p -> negative infinity limit of a generalized-mean family spanning additive to worst-case selection. Across cooperative emotional support and adversarial negotiation, min-selection lifts both objectives while sharply cutting their imbalance; on emotional support it raises the weaker axis from 0.37 to 0.64 (p < 10^-40), surpassing human experts and persisting across full multi-turn rollouts. A turn-by-turn analysis yields our central finding: min-selection corrects imbalance in proportion to how imbalanced the reference policy is, and its benefit endures over an interaction precisely as long as that imbalance does.

</details>


### [491] [What the Reranker Sees: Multi-Aspect Page Annotation for Long-Document Multimodal Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14841)
*Guanchen Wu,Jiayuan Ding,Subhabrata Mukherjee,Carl Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trident: a two-component LLM-based reranking and generation framework for long-document VQA that substantially improves evidence retrieval and open-ended synthesis; annotation-driven reranking yields consistent gains over baselines, with best config outperforming PageIndex and achieving high cross-judge agreement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long documents pose retrieval challenges: high recall but poor precision; visual data and structure (tables, charts, layout) are often missed by text-only rerankers; need structured evidence records and generation-aware prompting.

Method: Trident-R converts each candidate into an LLM-readable semantic record (visual caption, section path, entity tags, multi-axis hits, snippet) and uses a single adaptive-K rerank; Trident-S prompts the VLM with topical/entity/structure lenses to improve synthesis; evaluation on two long-document VQA benchmarks with annotation+rerank protocol; compare to adaptive-K baselines; assess retrieval F1 and generation accuracy; cross-LLM judge agreement.

Result: Retrieval F1 improved across five pools; all reranked pools beat strongest adaptive-K baseline PageIndex; LLM rerank without annotation barely shifts first-hit ranking, indicating annotation is key; Trident-S yields up to 6.6-point gain in generation accuracy for open-ended synthesis; best Trident config provides strongest downstream QA pipeline with kappa 0.913 between two LLM judges.

Conclusion: Structured annotation-driven reranking plus generation-side prompting yields robust gains in long-document VQA across datasets and judges, establishing Trident as a strong framework for integrative retrieval-and-generation tasks.

Abstract: Long-document visual question answering (VQA) over documents of tens to hundreds of pages mixing text, tables, charts, and figures typically follows retrieve-then-read pipelines. In our setting, the bottleneck shifts from retrieval recall to reranker-side evidence selection: on MMLongBench-Doc, BGE-M3 reaches Recall@20 = 0.86 but only F1@5 = 0.254, and even the visual retriever ColPali reaches only F1@5 = 0.332; a text-only rerank LLM seeing only raw snippets misses table, chart, and layout evidence even when the upstream retriever encoded images. We propose Trident, with two complementary components: Trident-R, a retriever-agnostic LLM reranker that converts each candidate into an LLM-readable semantic record, including a visual caption, section path, entity tags, multi-axis concept hits, and a text snippet, then performs a single adaptive-K rerank call; and Trident-S, a generation-side module that prompts the VLM under topical, entity, and structural lenses before synthesis. On two long-document datasets, the annotation+rerank protocol substantially improves retrieval F1 across five heterogeneous pools, with every reranked pool exceeding the strongest adaptive-K baseline PageIndex. An LLM rerank without the annotation barely changes first-hit ranking, indicating the lift comes from the structured annotation. Trident-S targets open-ended synthesis questions by design, adding up to 6.6 points in generation accuracy on these questions. The best Trident configuration is the strongest downstream QA pipeline in our evaluation, with rankings consistent across two LLM judges (kappa = 0.913).

</details>


### [492] [Discovering High-Quality Chess Puzzles with Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14851)
*Allen Nie,Anirudhan Badrinath,Nicholas Tomlin,Timothy Dai,Carissa Yip,Rose E Wang,Emma Brunskill,Chris Piech*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Offline reinforcement learning on 1.5B puzzle-solving histories to quantify and optimize the pedagogical value of chess puzzles, enabling automatic curation of practice sets for learners; shows gains for beginners and aligns model-discovered puzzles with expert annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pedagogical item creation is costly and requires balancing diverse thinking patterns; many platforms rely on low-value, automatically generated puzzles. The work aims to infer a puzzle value function from large-scale interaction data and to automatically assemble targeted practice sets to improve learner progress.

Method: Train an offline RL policy using a year-long dataset of 1.5 billion puzzle-solving histories to estimate the value of puzzles and learn a policy that selects a set of puzzles for learners. Evaluation relies on offline policy evaluation (OPE) and assessment of impact on beginner players (Elo 100–1000); qualitative analysis via expert annotations of discovered puzzles.

Result: The learned policy significantly benefits beginners, especially those with stagnant growth, within the 100–1000 Elo range. OPE indicates improved pedagogical value of recommended puzzles, and expert ratings corroborate the quality of discovered puzzles.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility of deriving pedagogical value and effective practice-item selection from large-scale user interaction data, paving the way for data-driven, adaptive puzzle curation in educational platforms.

Abstract: Learning and skill mastery require extensive and deliberate practice. In many learning settings, producing high-quality pedagogical materials can require a high level of domain expertise and be very time-consuming. Pedagogical materials often need to train students to engage in different thinking patterns. In some domains, such as chess, puzzles are used to help students practice their skills in calculating the next moves and recognizing known patterns on a board. Giving students a practice set of puzzles to help them learn different modes of thinking is challenging because the teacher needs to carefully balance between different motifs and how many look-ahead steps a student needs to perform. Popular online platforms like Chess.com and Lichess offer players millions of puzzles. Unlike chess tactics puzzles procured by human experts, where chess beginners can learn valuable insights, these puzzles are automatically generated and often regarded as having low pedagogical value. These platforms also rely on a heuristic to recommend puzzles to users for practice. Using the user history data over an entire year, a total of 1.5 billion puzzle-solving histories, we learn the pedagogical value of a puzzle and how to automatically choose a set of puzzles to better support chess learners using insights from offline reinforcement learning. We show that using offline policy evaluation, our trained policy has significant impact on beginners with puzzle-solving Elo range of 100--1000, particularly for the group of beginners whose learning growth was stagnant. We also performed a qualitative analysis of the puzzles discovered by our model by collecting annotation ratings from expert chess players. The success of our pipeline shows promise for a future where we can understand the pedagogical values of practice items given general user interaction data.

</details>


### [493] [JarvisBench: Always-on Intelligence Between Humans and Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14870)
*Chen Chen,Zhehuai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Jarvis, an always-on attention-coordination layer that mediates human attention for long-horizon agents, and JarvisBench, a benchmark to evaluate bidirectional coordination (answering user queries about ongoing work and prompting user judgment at the right time).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the bidirectional coordination problem between intermittent human attention and continuous agent execution, ensuring timely user access to ongoing work and appropriate human judgments when needed.

Method: Proposes Jarvis as a runtime-agnostic attention layer with a full-duplex speech interface, and JarvisBench as a 45-task benchmark (20 single-agent tasks, 25 workstreams in 10 multi-agent projects) spanning 19 domains, designed to integrate with arbitrary agent runtimes without modifying their execution loops; provides a reference implementation for natural user interaction.

Result: Conceptual framework and benchmark design are laid out; no empirical results reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: Separating execution from attention coordination yields a stable evaluation target as agent capabilities improve, and JarvisBench enables evaluation of both directions of coordination (user-initiated questions and timely user judgments).

Abstract: Long-horizon agents can execute continuously, but human attention remains intermittent and scarce. This creates a bidirectional coordination problem: users may need immediate access to an agent while work continues in the background, whereas agents may encounter consequential decisions that require user judgment after the user has stopped monitoring execution. We posit an always-on attention-coordination layer---\textit{Jarvis}\footnote{Named after the fictional AI assistant in \textit{Iron Man}.}---that mediates this interface and allocates human attention across one or more working agents. We introduce \textit{JarvisBench} to evaluate both directions of this coordination: whether an intermediary can accurately and promptly answer user-initiated questions about ongoing work, and whether it can recognize when an agent requires user judgment, solicit that judgment at the right moment, and route it back to improve task outcomes. JarvisBench contains 45 agentic task instances: 20 single-agent tasks and 25 workstreams organized into 10 multi-agent projects. The tasks span 19 domains and were selected and adapted from more than 2,000 public candidates. Crucially, the need for user attention arises naturally during execution rather than from an obvious omission in the initial prompt. JarvisBench is designed to integrate with arbitrary agent runtimes without modifying their underlying execution loops. Our reference implementation further provides a full-duplex speech interface, allowing users to reach Jarvis naturally while timely attention coordination supports agents working in the background. By separating agent execution from attention coordination, JarvisBench provides a stable evaluation target as agent capabilities continue to improve.

</details>


### [494] [Personalized Auto-Research: Towards a True AI Co-Scientist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14881)
*Bo Ni,Franck Dernoncourt,Hongjie Chen,Yu Wang,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Zhengzhong Tu,Tyler Derr,Ryan A. Rossi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for personalized auto-research using graph-grounded representations to tailor every stage of the AI-assisted research pipeline to an individual researcher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research progress hinges on accounting for researchers' tacit knowledge, prior work, and community; current AI co-researchers are researcher-agnostic and may misalign with users' needs.

Method: Proposes three components: (i) graph-grounded researcher representations, (ii) personalization across the full research pipeline (retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, review), (iii) evaluation anchored in the individual; uses a pipeline that threads researcher context through all steps.

Result: A general, flexible framework is proposed; discusses open problems and challenges; no empirical results reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: Personalization is not a convenience but essential for AI to function as a genuine co-scientist; one-size-fits-all fails; future work on open challenges.

Abstract: AI co-scientists that generate hypotheses, retrieve related work, design experiments, execute code, and draft full papers are beginning to change how research is carried out. Despite this rapid progress, state-of-the-art systems remain researcher-agnostic: given a research goal, they optimize novelty, validity, or reviewer score while ignoring the individual scientist who will use the output. This overlooks a fundamental fact about research, namely, that what counts as novel, valuable, or feasible depends on the researcher, including their prior work, methodological repertoire, and the collaborators and communities in which they are embedded. In this work, we introduce the problem of personalized auto-research, which conditions every stage of the research process on a representation of the individual researcher. We argue that personalization is not a convenience layer, but rather the fundamental property that allows an AI system to serve as a genuine co-scientist rather than a generic instrument. To address this problem, we propose a general and flexible framework that threads a graph-grounded researcher context through retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, and review. The framework consists of three fundamental components: (i) graph-grounded researcher representations, (ii) personalization across the full research pipeline, and (iii) evaluation grounded in the individual. Notably, we highlight a one-size-fits-all failure mode where distinct researchers issuing the same goal receive essentially the same research, erasing the tacit knowledge through which novel ideas arise. Finally, we discuss fundamental open problems and challenges.

</details>


### [495] [Frontier AI Forecasting Has a Measurement Problem: An Audit of Progress Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14903)
*Fabricio F Costa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Audits whether public measurement records support links from targets to trends in benchmarks, compute, release, or belief for frontier AI; finds that forecasting rests on versioned, linked measurement systems rather than simple curves.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To validate if dated forecasts genuinely reflect underlying measurement structures or merely fit trends, by constructing an event-centric audit record and testing measurement bridges.

Method: Build a frozen, event-centric audit record through 2026-08-12 with 62 systems, 12 benchmarks, 7 criteria, 144 events, 27 sources, 408 relations; assess training compute availability, METR horizons, benchmark progress, and cross-links using statistical fits (log-scale slope, logit/probit vs linear/log) and power analysis; examine provenance and cross-check with 56 sources.

Result: Found selective bridges with limited power; training compute is missing for most closed systems and absent for open-weight systems; benchmark links show some correlations but inconsistent across link forms; most quantitative events come from a single program and many from lab releases; no single direction provides a universal replacement scalar.

Conclusion: Frontier AI forecasting can be credible only if grounded in a versioned, explicit measurement system with traceable joins and dependencies; a simple fitted curve or calendar date is insufficient for defensible dated forecasts.

Abstract: Quantitative forecasts of frontier artificial intelligence often connect dated targets to trends in benchmark scores, training compute, release time, or expert belief. This paper audits whether the public measurement record supports those connections before another trend is fitted. I construct a frozen, event-centric record through 12 August 2026 with 62 selected systems, 12 versioned benchmarks, seven capability or impact criteria, 144 graded events, 27 source records, and 408 typed relations. The record is an audit sample, not a census. Only seven systems jointly observe estimated training compute and a METR 50 percent task horizon. Training compute is absent for 19 of 27 closed systems, including every selected closed release from 2026, while none of the 35 open-weight systems has a METR horizon observation. Benchmark succession creates a second break: a seven-system link from METR Time Horizon 1.0 to 1.1 has a log-scale slope of 1.206 (95 percent CI 1.021 to 1.390), whereas a six-system MMLU to MMLU-Pro comparison appears shift-like under logit and probit links but not under linear or logarithmic links. The observed bridges have about 80 percent power only for slope departures near 25 percent. Provenance is concentrated: 52 of 71 substantive quantitative events, or 73.2 percent, come from one measurement programme, and 76.1 percent are laboratory releases. A review of 56 methodological and empirical sources identifies 16 complementary measurement directions spanning resources, inference budgets, reliability, agentic work, safety, human preference, field outcomes, and forecast backtesting. No direction supplies a replacement scalar. The result is not that frontier AI forecasting is impossible, but that a defensible dated forecast is a claim about a versioned measurement system with explicit joins, protocols, links, and source dependence, not merely a fitted curve or calendar date.

</details>


### [496] [LLMs Can Predict Failure Risk, But Struggle to Predict Which Collaboration Protocol Pays Off: Cost-Aware Protocol Routing Across Reasoning Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14927)
*Chih-Hsuan Yang,Jingyan Jiang,Cheng-Hau Yang,Vikram Vasudevan,Huihuo Zheng,Venkatram Vishwanath,Rajeev Thakur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates when multi-agent LLM collaboration is worth its cost by comparing four protocols (Baseline, Single, PER, Broadcast) on a large math benchmark and robustness checks; findings show confidence can guide escalation but protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved, with an oracle improving retrospective coverage but limited transfer across protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify the cost-benefit tradeoffs of additional LLM collaboration and develop decision mechanisms for escalating collaboration based on performance signals.

Method: Compare four collaboration protocols across a large problem set (4,181 math problems) and robustness checks across biology and science benchmarks, using fixed/frozen routers and trained routers. Evaluate with post-answer pre-collaboration probes (gpt-oss-120b), pre-answer self-confidence gates, and an oracle to measure retrospective coverage. Report AUROC and AUPRC for failure prediction and any-collaboration benefit, and examine held-out router settings.

Result: Under fixed policies, conservative routing under-escalates while higher-solve frozen routers over-escalate. The post-answer pre-collaboration probe ranks Baseline failures with AUROC 0.8847 (4,151 parseable cases). This probe predicts any collaboration’s benefit (AUROC 0.7683, AUPRC), but poorly predicts PER- or Broadcast-specific gains (AUPRC 0.1674 and 0.1041). The pre-answer self-confidence gate achieves 78.0% solves at 45K tokens, vs. 73.8% at 71.3K for a frozen router, and 92.4% for a retrospective fixed-order oracle. Across 10 settings, the oracle adds 23.2–58.3 points of retrospective coverage over Baseline; held-out router evaluations show 18.5–28.9-point gaps. Confidence can aid initial escalation, but protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved.

Conclusion: Confidence signals enable some escalation decisions, but there is no universal, protocol-agnostic rule for cost-aware collaboration. Decisions appear task-dependent, with limited transfer of gains across protocols; further work is needed to develop reliable, protocol-aware routing policies.

Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can improve reasoning by spending more computation, but deployment requires deciding when extra collaboration is worth its cost. We isolate this decision by running every problem under four protocols while holding the solver fixed within each setting: direct solving (Baseline), iterative self-correction (Single), planner-executor-reviewer collaboration (PER), and multi-agent deliberation (Broadcast). The primary benchmark comprises 4,181 competition-level math problems; paired robustness checks cover four benchmarks spanning competition math, biology, and broader science with two solver families. Across fixed policies, trained routers, and frozen LLM routers, conservative policies under-escalate, whereas higher-solve frozen routers often over-escalate. A post-answer, pre-collaboration gpt-oss-120b probe ranks Baseline failures with 0.8847 AUROC (4,151 parseable cases; 95% CI [0.8732, 0.8955]). The same score remains informative for predicting whether any collaboration helps (0.7683 AUPRC), but is much weaker for identifying PER- or Broadcast-specific value (0.1674 and 0.1041 AUPRC). Separately, the pre-answer self-confidence gate reaches 78.0% solve at 45K tokens, compared with 73.8% at 71.3K for a frozen gpt-oss-120b router and 92.4% for a retrospective fixed-order oracle. Across 10 paired model-condition settings, the oracle adds 23.2-58.3 points of retrospective coverage over Baseline, but protocol profiles vary by task. In the six settings with held-out router evaluations, oracle gaps remain 18.5-28.9 points. Confidence can therefore support initial escalation, while protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved.

</details>


### [497] [Small Models Scout Bottleneck Order for Large-Model Data Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14936)
*Seungmin Choi,Jiwon Sung,Muhammad Umer,Abhiram Rao Gorle,Guijin Son,Youngjae Yu,John M. Cioffi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LogFloor enables phase-ordered bottleneck resolution through first-passage skill training, achieving substantial token savings and transferability across model scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether training trajectories of small proxies reveal a transferable curriculum structure for larger models’ skill bottlenecks, beyond token-cost minimization.

Method: Define first-passage skill training with per-skill floors. Use LogFloor closed-loop controller to steer rounds toward current bottlenecks. Evaluate on five bAbI slices (Qwen2.5-1.5B), 70M-to-12B transfer with path replay, and MMLU-control with a frozen scout path; perform ablations on path collapse and phase reversal.

Result: Average token-cost reduction of 56.2% across five bAbI slices. In transfer, 30.9% (pair mean), 39.4% (pooled), 37.6% (source-cost accounting) saved. MMLU-control: frozen scout path succeeds across eight 12B runs. Ablations removing phase order erase most benefits; bottleneck labels alone are only partially useful.

Conclusion: Phase-ordered bottleneck resolution is a transferable curriculum structure for monitored skill-targeted training, enabling efficient, scalable skill acquisition across model scales.

Abstract: Small proxy models are commonly used to identify data mixtures for larger-scale training. We ask whether their training trajectories reveal another transferable structure: the order in which larger models should resolve skill bottlenecks. We formulate first-passage skill training, where each monitored skill has a target floor and the objective is to minimize the tokens required to reach all floors. We introduce LogFloor, a closed-loop controller that directs each round toward current bottlenecks, producing phase-ordered resolution trajectories. Across five bAbI skill slices on Qwen2.5-1.5B, LogFloor reduces token cost by 56.2% on average. In 70M-to-12B transfer, three-round replay of a 70M scout path reaches every floor in all eight target runs, saving 30.9% by pair mean, 39.4% in pooled training tokens, and 37.6% under source-cost accounting. On MMLU-control, a frozen scout path succeeds across all eight 12B runs. Collapsing a path to its static marginal mixture or reversing its phase order removes most benefits, while bottleneck labels alone remain partially useful. These results identify phase-ordered bottleneck resolution as a transferable curriculum structure for monitored skill-targeted training.

</details>


### [498] [When Is an Agent Evaluation Over? Outcome Finality and Cross-Unit Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14940)
*Avyay M. Casheekar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a completion-based framework for judging final labels in agent evaluations, arguing that end-of-run endpoints are insufficient for final outcomes due to independent factors like outcome finality and cross-run separation. Uses controlled replay and protocol reviews to show endpoint-label divergence and inconsistent documentation, then proposes an open-effects record to track post-endpoint relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation practice treats the end-of-run state as the trial outcome, but this conflates two independent issues: whether the outcome is ultimately final and whether runs can be separated without state carryover. A robust evaluation requires clearly justified final labels that account for any remaining evidence that could change the outcome.

Method: Three-part approach: (1) controlled replay experiments to observe how fixed-action runs yield different endpoint vs terminal labels under delayed operations; (2) review of ten public evaluation protocols to assess how they document run stopping criteria, scoring, unfinished operations, and run separation; (3) proposal of an open-effects record to document post-endpoint dependencies and their potential to affect outcomes or other runs.

Result: Findings indicate: (a) endpoint and terminal labels diverge for every delayed operation in controlled replay; delayed writes can affect the next run’s score when inter-run state persists but not under isolation or verified reset; (b) protocols vary in documenting run stop criteria and scoring, with less consistency on unfinished operations and cross-run separation evidence; (c) introduction of an open-effects record to track ongoing effects and their relation to scored outcomes.

Conclusion: A final label is warranted only when any evidence that could change the claimed outcome is resolved, bounded, or left as uncertainty. The proposed open-effects record provides a concrete tool to manage post-endpoint dependencies and improve cross-run interpretability of evaluations.

Abstract: Current agent evaluations score models on the state visible at the end of a stopped run which they count as one trial. However, interpreting the score as a final result would require two conditions that the endpoint does not itself necessarily establish: outcome finality and cross-unit separation. These conditions are independent, since reconciling a delayed outcome can settle the label while runs still share state and isolating runs can prevent carryover while the scored outcome remains unfinished. We develop a completion argument that specifies the evidence needed for each decision and argue that a final label is justified only when anything that could still change the claimed outcome is resolved, bounded, or retained as uncertainty. First, in a controlled replay to demonstrate the mechanism where an agent's actions were held fixed, we find that the endpoint and terminal labels differ for every delayed operation, while a delayed write changes the next run's score when service state persists between runs but not after isolation or verified reset. Second, in a review of ten public protocols, we find that all protocols identify when a run stops and what is scored, while unfinished operations and the evidence for treating runs as separate trials are documented less consistently. Finally, we propose an open-effects record that lists operations or resources that may remain relevant after the endpoint, their current status, and whether they could change the scored outcome or affect another run.

</details>


### [499] [Skill Blocks: How Should an Agent Load Its Skill? A Caching-Correct Comparison of Pre-load, On-Demand Tool-Loading, Progressive Disclosure, and Hybrid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14943)
*Hironobu Nakasuji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid and other conditional loading methods reduce token usage without universally outperforming, with savings dependent on per-turn usage patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce token costs for agent skills by avoiding loading full skill content on every turn while preserving performance.

Method: Compare four loading strategies (Full, Skill Block, Reference, Hybrid) across five benchmarks (SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, SynthProc). Measure token usage for single-turn input and cache-aware input for multi-turn; assess quality with paired outcome tests.

Result: Hybrid reduces input by 27.4% (SearchQA) and 39.8% (SpreadsheetBench). For large multi-turn skills, Skill Block and Hybrid achieve 62.5%/52.8% on ScienceWorld and 73.0%/66.6% on SynthProc. ALFWorld gains are smaller due to short, frequently reused procedures. Paired tests show no quality differences, though they don't establish equivalence.

Conclusion: Conditional loading yields the largest gains when much of a skill is not needed every turn; there is no universal winner among the four strategies; choose loading method based on usage pattern.

Abstract: Agent skills are often injected in full on every request, increasing token cost. We compare four content-preserving loading methods: Full, Skill Block, Reference, and Hybrid. Across SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SynthProc, we measure token usage using raw input for single-turn tasks and cache-correct effective input for multi-turn tasks. Results show no universal winner. Hybrid reduces input by 27.4% on SearchQA and 39.8% on SpreadsheetBench. On large multi-turn skills, Skill Block and Hybrid achieve substantial reductions, reaching 62.5% and 52.8% on ScienceWorld and 73.0% and 66.6% on SynthProc. ALFWorld shows smaller gains because procedures are short and repeatedly needed. Paired outcome tests detect no quality differences, though they do not establish equivalence. Overall, conditional loading is most beneficial when large portions of a skill are not needed on every turn.

</details>


### [500] [Trust Is Not Enough: Influence Calibration for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14945)
*Qizhen Lan,Xi Xiao,Xiangchen Guan,Mengchen Fan,Moule Lin,Jung Im Choi,Lijing Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICSD introduces influence-based calibration for on-policy self-distillation to address trust–utility mismatch by measuring token-wise first-order impact of teacher perturbations on the RL surrogate, applying batch-adaptive calibration to produce bounded distillation weights without extra model passes, yielding consistent improvements over trust-only allocation across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA (GRPO/GiGPO) with 1.5B–7B models; notable reductions in mass on objective-opposed tokens and higher alignment with RL gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trust-based token allocation in on-policy self-distillation may not align supervision with the policy objective, leading to suboptimal emphasis on tokens that truly support learning. ICSD aims to quantify and exploit the actual utility of supervised tokens by measuring their sensitivity to teacher-directed perturbations and calibrating their influence to remain within action-turn mass constraints.

Method: Compute for each supervised token the first-order response of its importance-weighted RL surrogate contribution to a perturbation in the teacher-directed output. Use batch-adaptive calibration to convert this non-stationary signal into bounded allocation weights, preserving the total auxiliary-loss mass within each action turn. These weights are detached (do not require extra model passes) and affect only the distillation loss. Evaluated under GRPO and GiGPO across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA on model families from 1.5B to 7B.

Result: ICSD consistently improves all matched aggregate metrics versus trust-only allocation across the three domains and two policy-optimization frameworks, and across model sizes up to 7B. At 7B, reported scores reach 96.1% ALFWorld success and 93.1 WebShop score. Frozen-batch analyses show reduced teacher-supported mass on objective-opposed tokens (60.1%→37.8%) and a 0.192 increase in cosine similarity with the RL gradient, indicating stronger alignment of distillation with the objective.

Conclusion: Influence Calibration for Self-Distillation provides a principled, efficient mechanism to align on-policy distillation signals with the policy objective, yielding broad performance gains across domains and model scales, with interpretable reductions in supervision on undesired tokens and improved RL alignment. Code is available in the referenced repository.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) gives language agents dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher on the policy's own trajectories. Existing methods allocate this supervision mainly by teacher trust, but trust does not reveal whether emphasizing a token supports the current policy objective. We call this the trust-utility mismatch and introduce Influence Calibration for Self-Distillation (ICSD). For each supervised token, ICSD measures the first-order response of its importance-weighted RL surrogate contribution to a teacher-directed output perturbation. Batch-adaptive calibration converts this non-stationary signal into a bounded allocation weight while preserving the original auxiliary-loss mass within each action turn. These detached weights affect only the distillation loss and require no additional model pass. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, ICSD improves all matched aggregate metrics over trust-only allocation under Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO), across two model families spanning 1.5B to 7B. At 7B, it reaches 96.1% ALFWorld success and a WebShop score of 93.1. Frozen-batch analyses show that ICSD reduces teacher-supported mass assigned to objective-opposed tokens from 60.1% to 37.8% and raises cosine compatibility with the RL gradient by 0.192. A companion repository is avail- able at https://github.com/lanqz7766/Influence-Calibration-for-On-Policy-Self-Distillation-in-Agentic-RL.

</details>


### [501] [RETRACE: Resilience-Guided Trait-Conditioned Craving Estimation from Wearable Physiology in Opioid Use Disorder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14947)
*Yi Xiao,Harshit Sharma,Dessa Bergen-Cico,Asif Salekin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RETRACE is a resilience-guided, trait-conditioned framework for subject-independent craving estimation from wearable physiology. It uses a dual-encoder with a frozen stress-pretrained encoder and a resilience-conditioned craving encoder, employing feature-level gating and fusion to achieve light personalization without target-user craving labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Craving detection from wearable signals is hard in subject-independent settings due to stress confounds and inter-individual variability. Resilience-related context, which shapes stress regulation and craving vulnerability, is not observable in short-term windows but can be inferred from proxy signals.

Method: A dual-encoder architecture: a frozen stress-pretrained encoder captures generalizable stress physiology; a resilience-conditioned craving encoder interprets craving-specific patterns. Feature-level gating and representation-level fusion integrate the two, enabling lightweight personalization without craving labels or per-user retraining. Evaluated on a novel multimodal OUD dataset with wearable physiology, stress/craving annotations, and autobiographical narratives; LOSO evaluation.

Result: RET RACE achieved up to 7% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline under LOSO on the novel multimodal OUD dataset.

Conclusion: Separating general stress physiology from subject-specific craving interpretation via a resilience-conditioned, trait-aware framework yields improved subject-independent craving estimation and enables lightweight personalization without craving-label data.

Abstract: Detecting opioid craving from wearable physiological signals is critical yet difficult, with the potential to support proactive interventions for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). This challenge is especially pronounced under subject-independent evaluation because craving is subjective, heterogeneous, and often physiologically entangled with stress. Our empirical analysis shows that stress elicits strong and reproducible autonomic responses, while craving-related signals are weaker, sparse, and largely embedded within stress-related physiology. We further show that psychological resilience, which shapes stress regulation and craving vulnerability, is not reliably observable from short-term wearable windows, but can be captured through reusable subject-level proxies, including post-stress heart-rate recovery and autobiographical memory recall.Motivated by these findings, we introduce RETRACE, a resilience-guided trait-conditioned framework for subject-independent craving estimation from wearable physiology. RETRACE reframes craving detection as trait-conditioned physiological interpretation: rather than assuming the same physiological pattern has the same meaning across individuals, it uses resilience-related subject context to guide inference. Technically, RETRACE introduces a novel dual-encoder design that separates generalizable stress physiology from subject-specific craving interpretation. It combines a frozen stress-pretrained encoder with a resilience-conditioned craving encoder, using feature-level gating and representation-level fusion to enable lightweight personalization without target-user craving labels or per-user retraining. We evaluate RETRACE on a novel multimodal OUD dataset containing wearable physiology, stress and craving annotations, and autobiographical narratives. Under LOSO setup, RETRACE achieves up to 7% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline

</details>


### [502] [T-LLM Compiler: Trusted LLM-based Code Optimization and Verification Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14953)
*Zahra Fazel,Sunanda Gamage,Shayan Shirahmad Gale Bagi,Amir H. Ashouri,Tomasz S. Czajkowski,Bryan Chan,Reza Azimi,Yaoqing Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A collaborative T-LLM Compiler integrates LLM-based high-level code transformations with traditional compilers and verification tools to enable reliable, iterative code optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can perform code transformations but struggle with correctness and verification; combining LLMs with compilers and formal verification aims to improve both correctness and performance of optimized code.

Method: An iterative workflow where high-level LLM transformations are guided by traditional compiler passes and verification tools; verification results steer corrective actions; the approach emphasizes collaboration between LLMs, compilers, and verification components and is released as open-source.

Result: On PolyBench/C benchmarks, code optimization accuracy reaches up to 83.3%; speedup up to 16.1%; transformed code averages 26.7% speedup relative to standard baselines; demonstrates enhanced correctness and performance.

Conclusion: A verification-driven, collaborative LLM-assisted compiler workflow can yield substantial improvements in both correctness and performance of code optimizations, with open-source release enabling broader adoption.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened opportunities to apply high-level code transformations to the field of code optimization, and it has since emerged as one of the most fundamental tasks for LLMs to perform; however, at present, LLMs struggle to apply wide-ranging code optimization tasks due to both the complexity of the code and the inability to independently verify the correctness of the transformations. In this paper, we present the Trusted LLM (T-LLM) Compiler, which proposes an advancement in compiler technology through a collaborative effort involving high-level LLM code transformations, traditional compilers, and verification tools. Experimental results reveal that it can significantly improve code correctness when tested on a set of PolyBench/C benchmarks. Our approach facilitates iterative code optimization efforts with verification strategies that enable corrective actions. Through this approach, T-LLM Compiler achieves code optimization accuracy of up to 83.3% and a speedup of up to 16.1\% on the PolyBench/C benchmarks, with the transformed code reaching an average of 26.7% speedup wrt standard baselines. Additionally, we release the project's source code to the open-source community.

</details>


### [503] [Demand-Driven Vertiport Siting and Discrete-Event Fleet Simulation for On-Demand Urban Air Mobility Network Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14974)
*Hossein Z. Saghazadeh,Yonas Ayalew,Reza Ahmari,Parham Kebria,Abdollah Homaifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A demand-driven, integrated framework for on-demand UAM network design linking vertiport siting, fleet simulation, and door-to-door travel-time feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the design challenge of UAM networks by coupling demand estimation, vertiport siting, fleet operations, and energy/time considerations to evaluate feasible systems under varying demand.

Method: Estimate demand from commuter/activity data, convert to spatial trip-end points, cluster with K-means to generate candidate vertiport locations; screen candidates by range constraints and minimum spacing; evaluate candidate networks with a discrete-event simulation including multi-vehicle dispatch, deadhead relocation, battery swaps, and service regularity; compute flight time and energy with a point-mass eVTOL model.

Result: In a Greater Los Angeles case study, the preferred design grows from 4 stations and 4 eVTOLs at low demand to 16 stations and 12 eVTOLs at highest tested demand. Larger fleets improve completion time and vehicle-arrival regularity but do not eliminate deadhead flights, indicating persistent operational burden from spatial demand imbalance. Travel-time savings suggest UAM is most defensible for longer or congested trips where sufficient non-flight time remains after accounting for flight time.

Conclusion: A demand-driven design framework can adapt vertiport networks and fleets to demand, yielding performance gains with larger, denser networks; however, deadhead flights and demand distribution remain key limitations, and UAM value is greatest for longer or heavily congested trips.

Abstract: This paper presents a demand-driven framework for on-demand Urban Air Mobility (UAM) network design that links vertiport siting, fleet simulation, and door-to-door travel-time feasibility. Demand is estimated from commuter and passenger activity data, converted into spatial trip-end points, and clustered using K-means to generate candidate vertiport locations. Candidate networks are screened using range and minimum station-spacing constraints, then evaluated with a discrete-event simulation that models multi-vehicle dispatch, deadhead relocation, battery swaps, and service regularity. Flight time and energy consumption are computed using a point-mass eVTOL performance model. In a Greater Los Angeles case study, the preferred design expands from four stations and four eVTOLs at low demand to sixteen stations and twelve eVTOLs at the highest tested demand level. Results show that larger fleets improve completion time and vehicle-arrival regularity but do not eliminate deadhead flights, indicating that spatial demand imbalance remains an operational burden. The travel-time savings analysis further suggests that UAM is most defensible for longer or congestion-heavy trips where sufficient non-flight time remains after accounting for flight time.

</details>


### [504] [Does a Tool Result Carry More Authority Than Plain Text? Three Prospective Studies of False-Claim Adoption in a Synthetic Assignment Task with Claude Opus 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14992)
*Justin Bronder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tool results are not uniquely more influential than announced inline text for guiding model outputs in a single-model, synthetic task; inline text can yield similar false-code adoption; findings are limited in scope.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether packaging claims as tool results vs. inline text differentially biases LLMs, clarifying if external tool-result metadata carries extra weight.

Method: Four-arm experiment (no target, prior assistant assertion, tool-result record, ten-field metadata wrapper) on a synthetic lookup task using Claude Opus 5; preregistered replication; live-text control with binding swaps; outcomes measured as false-code adoption. Single model/API, one synthetic template.

Result: Adoption rates: 0/24 (no target), 0/22 (prior assertion), 14/24 (tool-result), 15/24 (metadata wrapper). Tool-result trial: 11/12 supported, 14/24 unsupported; replication: 7/24 vs 0/24 (p=0.0047). Tool-result rate declined from 14/24 to 7/24 across runs four days apart. Live control: inline text 60/60 adoption; tool-result 57/60 (p=1 for superiority). Overall, no robust superiority of tool results; inbound data show placement not necessary; generalizability limited (single model, API, synthetic task).

Conclusion: No evidence that tool-result packaging has greater behavioral weight than announced inline text; effects appear contingent on presentation and task; broader validation across models and tasks is needed.

Abstract: Language-model systems increasingly read from stores they also write to, so a claim that was merely written earlier can return looking retrieved. We tested whether the message package carrying an unsupported assignment changes which answer a model gives in a synthetic lookup task. Claude Opus 5 selected a color code for a named item or abstained. In an exploratory four-arm study, false-code adoption was 0/24 with no target claim, 0/22 scorable trials when a prior assistant assertion named the target, 14/24 when a tool-result record named it, and 15/24 when that result used a ten-field metadata wrapper that marked it unchecked. The tool-result arm selected the record's code in 11/12 supported trials and 14/24 unsupported trials, ruling out a fixed output-token bias while leaving substantial planted-token heterogeneity. A document-preregistered replication reproduced the tool-result versus assistant-assertion gap, 7/24 against 0/24, one-sided Fisher exact p = 0.0047. The tool-result rate nevertheless fell from 14/24 to 7/24 across runs made four days apart. A second preregistered study gave the earlier comparison a live text control: both records were announced in advance and placed in the same final user turn, then target binding was swapped between the linked tool result and later inline JSON. Inline text was sufficient for false-code adoption in 60/60 trials; the tool-result condition produced 57/60, so the registered result-first superiority criterion failed, p = 1. The result does not show that tool results have no effect. It shows that native tool-result placement was not necessary and that this experiment did not find greater behavioral weight for the result package than for announced inline text. The findings concern a single model on one synthetic task template, accessed through one API.

</details>


### [505] [S2-MoE: Enabling Efficient Self-Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts on Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15018)
*Haochen Huang,Shengxuan Qiu,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Efficient self-speculative decoding for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) on edge devices; S2-MoE reduces verification overhead and improves expert reuse via routing-aware speculative expansion, reuse-aware gating, and shared-context alignment; implemented in llama.cpp; yields up to 5.3x speedup (avg ≈2x) over standard autoregressive decoding across MoE models on edge hardware; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge devices suffer from severe memory and bandwidth constraints that hinder MoE inference. Naive combinations of speculative decoding and MoE incur large verification overhead and poor expert reuse, particularly in memory-bound settings.

Method: Introduce S2-MoE: routing-aware adaptive speculative expansion to reduce redundant verification; reuse-aware expert gating to improve gating efficiency; and shared-context alignment to synchronize draft and target execution. Implemented within llama.cpp to enable practical deployment on edge devices.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows up to 5.3x speedup, around 2.0x average speedup, for MoE inference across diverse models and datasets on edge devices.

Conclusion: S2-MoE provides a practical, effective framework for edge MoE inference by addressing verification overhead and expert reuse inefficiencies, with an open-source implementation and code release.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) for inference on edge devices is challenging due to severe memory and bandwidth constraints. While speculative decoding and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have been proposed to improve inference efficiency, naively combining them often incurs excessive verification overhead and poor expert reuse, limiting their effectiveness in memory-bound edge settings. In this work, we propose S2-MoE, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for MoE inference on edge devices. S2-MoE reduces redundant verification through routing-aware adaptive speculative expansion, improves verification efficiency with reuse-aware expert gating, and aligns draft and target execution via shared context. Implemented in llama.cpp, S2-MoE achieves up to 5.3x speedup (about 2.0x on average) over standard autoregressive de?coding across diverse MoE models and datasets on edge devices.Code is available at https://github.com/angerybob/S2-MoE.

</details>


### [506] [Gathered, Not Admitted: How Attention Brings a Latent Variable into Verbalizable Form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15022)
*Parsa Mazaheri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: No evidence of a gating entry mechanism; a mid-depth, attention-mediated window yields readable latent variable readout across model arms; a single linear decoder suffices across arms, while readout is not a calibrated measure of use and depends on demand.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether latent quantities in language models are gated (admitted) into a 'workspace' and how readable such latent quantities are across contexts and architectures.

Method: Jacobian-based analysis (Jacobian lenses) on open-weight models; five arms share identical context; assess whether any gate predicts entry; measure percentile rank improvements; train/shared linear decoder decoding the variable from all arms (including controls); analyze attention-mediated depth window separating patch depth from readout depth; compare transport depth across model families (64-layer hybrid vs 62-layer dense); evaluate saturating vs non-saturating readouts; assess dependency of window on demand and across arms.

Result: No gate predicted by the analysis. Demand raises a concept’s lens visibility beyond applying a operator to a provided value: +0.050 [+0.045, +0.057] percentile rank on the primary checkpoint, positive across all four measured arms; yet that arm often reads at ceiling and accuracy-contrast is stronger with that readout. A single shared linear map decodes the variable from every arm (including control) at 6.4–9.0x its selection-corrected floor. The later readable form arises via attention-mediated gathering inside a mid-depth window; separating patch depth from readout depth yields transport at least 17x higher than shallower regions under non-saturating readouts, with no tested MLP output contributing positively inside it. Under saturating percentile rank the same grid fails to localize the window (a property of the measure). An arm that needs the variable for nothing concentrates sevenfold less, indicating demand-specificity. The window has two edges (survival below, destruction above) and occurs at the same fractional depth across a 64-layer hybrid model and a 62-layer dense model from another family. We localize where the variable is installed and read, not the route from the passage. However, readout is not a calibrated measure of use: three components move it to within 12% of one another, yet they differ 7.4x in how they affect the answer.

Conclusion: The data do not support a discrete gate controlling entry to a representational workspace. Instead, readable latent quantities emerge from an attention-driven window located at mid-depth, with a stable linear decodability across arms. The readout signal is not a direct proxy for variable use and is modulated by multiple factors; interpretability claims should account for these complexities and cross-architecture consistency.

Abstract: Language models hold latent quantities in a form they can report on, and more of a quantity is present in that form when the task requires reusing it flexibly. What causes a representation to enter that form is open, and the word workspace invites an admission story: a gate that decides what gets in. Testing it on open-weight models with Jacobian lenses, over a benchmark whose five arms share an identical context, we find no gate where it predicts one. Demand raises a concept's lens visibility beyond what applying an operator to a supplied value produces: +0.050 [+0.045, +0.057] in percentile rank on our primary checkpoint, positive on all four we measure, though that arm answers at ceiling and the accuracymatched contrast is stronger under that readout. At the same time one shared linear map decodes the variable from every arm, the control included, at 6.4-9.0x its selection-corrected floor. What produces the later readable form at the queried position is attention-mediated gathering inside a mid-depth window: separating patch depth from readout depth puts transport there at least 17x above anywhere shallower under non-saturating readouts, with no tested MLP output contributing positively inside it. Under the saturating percentile rank the same grid does not localise the window, which is a fact about that measure. An arm that needs the variable for nothing concentrates sevenfold less, so the window is demand-specific. That window has two measured edges, a survival failure below and destruction above, and it falls at the same fractional depth in a 64-layer hybrid and a 62-layer dense model from another family. We localise where the variable is installed and read, not the route from the passage, which transports nothing. But the readout is not a calibrated measure of use: three components move it to within 12% of one another and differ 7.4x in what they do to the answer.

</details>


### [507] [LLM-Based Hierarchical Coordinated Control with Continuation-Aware Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15041)
*Changhong He,Jinda Gao,Xinkuan Liu,Le Zhang,Xizi Luo,Yu Mei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An LLM-based hierarchical coordination framework with continuation-aware policy learning improves coordination of multiple interacting units under heterogeneous context and constraints, validated on traffic control and energy management; shows consistent gains over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordination of multiple interacting units is hard due to unknown system dynamics, heterogeneous operational information, and strict low-level constraints. A scalable, constraint-aware, long-horizon coordination method is needed.

Method: Use an LLM to guide high-level coordination across heterogeneous contexts; have task-specific controllers/optimizers generate executable, constraint-aware actions; introduce Continuation-Aware GRPO to evaluate future system evolution under the current policy; train on simplified models and evaluate on realistic simulators.

Result: The proposed framework outperforms direct task-specific control/optimization, end-to-end RL, rule-based and RL-based hierarchical coordination, and prompting-only LLM coordinators across multi-ramp traffic control and virtual power plant energy management tasks.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous-context reasoning, hierarchical execution, and continuation-aware policy learning effectively improve coordination of complex, constrained, multi-unit systems and are broadly applicable.

Abstract: Coordinating multiple interacting units in complex engineering systems is challenging when system interactions are difficult to model, operational information is heterogeneous, and low-level actions must satisfy strict constraints. We propose an LLM-based hierarchical framework in which the LLM coordinates interacting units based on heterogeneous operational context, while task-specific controllers or optimizers generate executable and constraint-aware actions. We further introduce Continuation-Aware GRPO to capture the consequences of coordination decisions over subsequent control intervals. Rather than judging a decision only by its immediate outcome, the method also evaluates how the system evolves afterward under the current policy. We validate the framework on multi-ramp traffic control and virtual power plant (VPP) energy management, using simplified system models for training and more realistic simulators for evaluation. Across both tasks, the proposed method consistently outperforms direct task-specific control and optimization, end-to-end reinforcement learning, rule-based and RL-based hierarchical coordination, and prompting-only LLM coordinators, demonstrating the value of heterogeneous-context reasoning, hierarchical execution, and continuation-aware policy learning.

</details>


### [508] [SCOPE: Score-Isolated Agentic Optimization for Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15043)
*Yuhua Jiang,Jiaming Wang,Qingbin Liu,Feifei Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is an auditable inference-time adaptation framework for frozen video world models that treats external controls as a typed state, constrains updates with development evidence, and freezes the policy before held-out evaluation, showing notable gains on Physics-IQ and revealing transferability limits and deployment criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time adaptation of frozen video world models risks leakage from held-out data into policy and makes attribution of gains difficult when prompts, samplers, verifiers, and selectors co-evolve; a principled, auditable approach is needed.

Method: Propose SCOPE: represent external controls as a typed state; update state through bounded changes supported by development evidence; freeze the resulting policy before evaluation; evaluate on Physics-IQ; perform controlled ablations to parse contributions; conduct cross-backbone and prospective analyses.

Result: Physics-IQ: +14.24 improvement over exact frozen base (95% CI [+8.10, +21.23]). Ablations attribute gains to scene specification, sampling, and learned selection; margin over strongest agentic baseline unresolved; cross-backbone and prospective results show updates help but do not transfer uniformly.

Conclusion: Inference-time adaptation gains exist but require a principled mechanism for deciding which updates become deployed; SCOPE provides an auditable framework and highlights transferability challenges; code is available.

Abstract: Video world models are increasingly used as simulators for planning and embodied decision making, yet improving them at inference time introduces a subtle evaluation problem: prompts, samplers, verifiers, and selectors may evolve together, making it difficult to attribute gains or prevent held-out feedback from shaping the final policy. We introduce \scope (\emph{\scopefullname}), a framework for auditable inference-time adaptation of frozen video world models. \scope represents external controls as a typed state, updates this state only through bounded changes supported by development evidence, and freezes the resulting policy before held-out evaluation. On Physics-IQ benchmark, \scope improves over the exact frozen base by $+14.24$ (95\% CI $[+8.10,+21.23]$). Controlled ablations further identify gains from scene specification, sampling, and learned selection, while the margin over the strongest matched agentic baseline remains unresolved. Cross-backbone and prospective evaluations reveal a complementary result: useful inference-time updates exist, but their benefits do not transfer uniformly across models and settings. Together, these findings suggest that reliable inference-time adaptation requires not only better proposals, but also a principled mechanism for deciding which updates should become part of the deployed system. Code is available at https://github.com/YuhuaJiang2002/SCOPE.

</details>


### [509] [Andy: A Mathematical Agent for Rigorous Proof and Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15052)
*Zi'an Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Autonomous agent Andy demonstrates end-to-end automated mathematical research: learning from a published self-triggered impulsive consensus result, formulating a global exponential leader-follower synchronization problem for delayed, heterogeneous networks with switching topologies, and proving a hybrid control scheme (self-triggered impulses with delay and a recovery-phase continuous feedback) achieves synchronization, excluding Zeno behavior, with validation via a numerical example.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Showcase an end-to-end automated workflow for mathematical research, including knowledge acquisition, problem formulation, multistage verification, and rigorous proof construction, and illustrate the agent’s ability to learn from existing results and extend them to new, nontrivial problems.

Method: Hybrid control design combining self-triggered impulses with execution delay and a recovery-phase continuous feedback; after each delayed impulse, the recovery window cancels the delayed error channel; derivation of sufficient conditions for global exponential synchronization; proof that Zeno behavior is excluded for both sampling and impulse sequences; numerical example validating the theoretical results.

Result: Sufficient conditions are established for global exponential synchronization in delayed heterogeneous networks with switching topologies under the proposed hybrid control; Zeno behavior is ruled out for both sampling and impulses; numerical example corroborates the theoretical findings.

Conclusion: The case demonstrates Andy’s ability to learn from existing results, formulate meaningful research problems, and develop and verify rigorous proofs, illustrating a practical workflow for automated mathematical research.

Abstract: Andy is an autonomous mathematical research agent that solves and verifies submitted problems, formulates new research problems, and constructs rigorous proofs. It separates proof generation from correctness evaluation and supports knowledge acquisition, targeted revision, and multistage verification. This paper illustrates the workflow using a published result on self-triggered impulsive consensus as a starting point. Andy formulates a global exponential leader-follower synchronization problem for delayed heterogeneous networks with switching communication topologies. The proposed hybrid control combines self-triggered impulses with execution delay and recovery-phase continuous feedback.
