After each delayed impulse, this feedback cancels the delayed error channel during a recovery window. Sufficient conditions for global exponential synchronization are established, and Zeno behavior is excluded for both the sampling and impulse sequences. A numerical example confirms the result. This case demonstrates Andy's ability to learn from existing results, formulate meaningful research problems, and develop and verify rigorous proofs.

</details>


### [510] [TAHB: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Text-Attributed Hypergraph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15055)
*David Yoon Suk Kang,JungHyun Kim,Juhyun Jeon,Sang-Wook Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TAHB introduces the first public text-attributed hypergraph benchmark with 10 real-world datasets to enable evaluation of text-aware hypergraph learning, and shows that LLM-enhanced semantics plus structural information yield the best performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of public benchmarks for text-attributed hypergraphs, despite the relevance of hypergraphs for higher-order relations and the value of language models for semantic attributes.

Method: Construct 10 real-world text-attributed hypergraph datasets across e-commerce, academia, movies, and politics; systematically evaluate hypergraph representation learning under text-aware settings; test LLM-as-Enhancer and LLM-as-Predictor paradigms.

Result: TAHB preserves key structural properties of real-world hypergraphs; experimental results reproduce trends seen on existing benchmarks; LLM-enhanced textual semantics improve hypergraph learning; joint use of structural and textual information yields the best results for LLM-based prediction.

Conclusion: TAHB provides a foundational benchmark for future research at the intersection of hypergraph learning and language models and enables systematic, text-aware evaluation.

Abstract: Hypergraphs effectively model higher-order groupwise relationships beyond pairwise interactions, while pretrained language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs) provide rich semantic understanding from textual attributes. However, research on combining language models with hypergraph learning remains limited due to the lack of public text-attributed hypergraph benchmarks. To address this limitation, we present TAHB (Text-Attributed Hypergraph Benchmark), the first public benchmark integrating hypergraph structures and raw textual attributes. TAHB contains 10 real-world datasets from four domains - e-commerce, academia, movies, and politics networks - enabling systematic evaluation of text-aware hypergraph representation learning. Experimental results show that TAHB preserves key structural properties of real-world hypergraphs and consistently reproduces performance tendencies observed in existing benchmarks. Furthermore, experiments under both LLM-as-Enhancer and LLM-as-Predictor settings demonstrate that LLM-enhanced textual semantics improve hypergraph learning performance, while structural and textual information jointly provide the best setting for LLM-based prediction. Our benchmark provides a foundation for future research at the intersection of hypergraph learning and language models.

</details>


### [511] [GraphLoom: Reliability-Calibrated Graph Evidence Routing for Multimodal KG-RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15056)
*Zafar Ali,Asad Khan,Aalia Malik,Pavlos Kefalas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reliability-calibrated multimodal RAG framework, GraphLoom, constructs an instance-level multimodal knowledge graph, retrieves bounded, high-utility subgraphs, and routes evidence through hierarchical memory with graph-sequence attention, improving faithfulness and robustness under noisy retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate noise and hallucinations from long, unstructured contexts and indiscriminate evidence expansion in multimodal RAG, and strengthen multi-hop reasoning with faithful evidence routing.

Method: Build an instance-level multimodal knowledge graph from grounded scene descriptions, extracted relational triples, and external commonsense; perform reliability-aware subgraph retrieval with bounded expansion; route high-utility evidence through hierarchical graph memory slots and joint graph-sequence attention in a frozen language model; employ interleaved retrieval with budgeted corrective retrieval for adaptive multi-hop refinement under noisy retrieval.

Result: GraphLoom attains consistent gains in answer quality and evidence faithfulness on ScienceQA, MultiModalQA, and OK-VQA with large distractor pools; improves retrieval quality on MultiModalQA; shows stability under noisy evidence pools; supplementary analyses (MiniCheck-based verification, human evaluation, latency profiling) corroborate reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing as effective compared to strong baselines.

Conclusion: Reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing provides a robust alternative to long-context evidence injection in multimodal RAG, enabling compact, faithful evidence routing and robust performance under noisy retrieval conditions.

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often rely on long unstructured contexts or aggressively expanded evidence graphs, which can introduce noisy evidence, weaken multi-hop reasoning, and increase unsupported generation. We present GraphLoom, a reliability-calibrated multimodal knowledge-graph RAG framework for compact and faithful evidence routing. Given a question and its associated multimodal input, GraphLoom constructs an instance-level multimodal knowledge graph from grounded scene descriptions, extracted relational triples, and external commonsense knowledge. Instead of injecting all retrieved evidence into the generator, GraphLoom performs reliability-aware subgraph retrieval with bounded expansion and selectively routes high-utility evidence through hierarchical graph memory slots and joint graph-sequence attention in a frozen language model. To improve robustness in complex reasoning settings, GraphLoom further combines interleaved retrieval with budgeted corrective retrieval, enabling adaptive multi-hop evidence refinement under noisy retrieval conditions. We evaluate GraphLoom on ScienceQA, MultiModalQA, and OK-VQA, including large distractor evidence pools that approximate noisy external knowledge retrieval. Experimental results show consistent gains in answer quality and evidence faithfulness over strong multimodal RAG, graph-retrieval, and open-source vision-language baselines, with improved retrieval quality on MultiModalQA and stable performance under noisy evidence pools. Additional analyses using MiniCheck-based verification, human evaluation, and latency profiling show that reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing provides an effective alternative to long-context multimodal evidence injection.

</details>


### [512] [LongDocBench: Benchmarking TOC Hierarchy and Contextual Relationship Recovery in Long Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15064)
*Yuefeng Zou,Yichen Lu,Jingxiao Yang,Bingtao Fu,Gaoyang Zhang,Xiongfei Bai,Tian Chen,Xiang Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces LongDocBench for long-document structure recovery, focusing on Table-of-Contents hierarchy and contextual relationships across long documents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks underrepresent long-document structure tasks; need benchmarks that assess cross-page TOC hierarchies and link context between tables/figures and captions/notes across many pages.

Method: Curates 85 real-world long documents (2,582 pages total; up to 105 pages per doc) with human-verified annotations for 3,937 heading nodes and 3,258 contextual relationships across 2,680 table/figure objects; defines evaluation protocols and公開 release; also conducts downstream QA experiments to assess utility and recoverability.

Result: Provides a reproducible testbed and evaluation protocol; human-verified TOC hierarchies and contextual relationships improve long-document QA reasoning; parsers still struggle with these tasks despite strong page-level performance.

Conclusion: LongDocBench fills a critical gap by enabling systematic evaluation of document-level structure recovery in long documents and is publicly released to drive progress.

Abstract: Parsing visual documents into machine-readable representations is fundamental to document intelligence. Existing benchmarks focus on page-level element recognition, reading order, formula recognition, and table structure. Long documents, however, also require document-level structure recovery. This includes reconstructing cross-page table-of-contents (TOC) hierarchies and identifying typed links from tables and figures to their captions, notes, and sources, often in one-to-many form. Because these structures are covered only partially or subsumed within broader parsing protocols, existing benchmarks cannot directly evaluate two key document-level tasks: \emph{Table-of-Contents Hierarchy Recovery} and \emph{Contextual Relationship Recovery}. To benchmark these two tasks, we introduce \textsc{LongDocBench}, comprising 85 real-world financial reports, textbooks, and academic papers spanning 2,582 pages, with up to 105 pages per document. It provides human-verified annotations for 3,937 heading nodes (mean node depth 3.55; maximum depth 9) and 3,258 contextual relationships annotated across 2,680 table and figure objects. We further evaluate both the downstream utility and recoverability of these structures. Long-document question-answering experiments show that human-verified TOC hierarchies and contextual relationships improve reasoning, with their combination providing complementary benefits. Meanwhile, representative document parsers remain limited on both recovery tasks despite strong page-level performance. To support further progress, we publicly release \textsc{LongDocBench} and its evaluation protocol and reproducible testbed for advancing document-level structure recovery in long documents.

</details>


### [513] [Funnel of Thoughts: Efficient Test-Time Scaling via Early Voting and Rollout Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15065)
*Chanhee Park,Sungbin Han,Jeongho Yoon,Seongtae Hong,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FoT (Funnel of Thoughts) reduces per-sample inference cost in multi-sample LRM reasoning by pruning unproductive trajectories using lexical cues, preserving full voted accuracy while cutting attention FLOPs by ~56%, with broad transfer to unseen architectures and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LRMs exhibit diverse, often inconsistent outputs across multiple samples; majority voting across k rollouts is accurate but expensive. A training-free, inference-time strategy is needed to cut cost without sacrificing accuracy.

Method: FoT identifies harmful, hesitation-inducing lexical patterns (e.g., 'Wait', 'Actually', 'perhaps') that correlate with unproductive reasoning trajectories. It prunes affected trajectories before completion using a language-signal-based filter, without additional model fine-tuning or inference, and is shown to generalize across architectures and domains.

Result: Using 115k trajectories from six LRMs, FoT halved attention FLOPs while preserving the 32-trajectory majority-voted accuracy; achieved a 28.8% reduction in full-model inference cost. Online generation FLOPs reduced by 56.1% and wall time by 37.6%. The lexical signal transfers to held-out architectures and out-of-domain tasks without retuning.

Conclusion: A training-free, generalizable signal-based pruning method can drastically reduce inference costs for multi-sample LRM reasoning by identifying and pruning unproductive trajectories, with minimal or no loss in accuracy and broad applicability.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models produce diverse, sometimes inconsistent answers across repeated queries on the same problem, so multi-sample inference is a prerequisite for reliable deployment. Majority voting at k rollouts is the standard solution and the de facto accuracy target for this regime, but it is prohibitively expensive at the scale LRMs require. We introduce Funnel of Thoughts (FoT), an inference-time method that preserves the full 32-trajectory voted accuracy while halving its attention FLOPs, a 28.8% reduction in full-model inference cost. Across 115K reasoning trajectories from six LRMs, we find that unproductive trajectories often reveal themselves through repeated hesitation markers such as "Wait", "Actually", and "perhaps." These trajectories are less likely to reach the correct answer and consume disproportionate attention FLOPs, degenerating into no-answer loops in the worst case. Built on this training-free lexical signal, FoT identifies the vocabulary that captures these pathological patterns and prunes affected trajectories before completion, reducing online generation attention FLOPs by 56.1% and wall time by 37.6% without any additional model inference; the same signal transfers without retuning across held-out architectures and out-of-domain tasks.

</details>


### [514] [Evo-Harness: Context-to-Harness Skill Compilation for Self-Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15071)
*Tianxin Wei,Zhan Shi,Minhua Lin,Bing He,Zewen Liu,Yisi Sang,Yuanchen Bei,Xuying Ning,Jiaru Zou,Ting-Wei Li,Xiao Lin,Yanjun Zhao,Chi Wang,Benoit Dumoulin,Dakuo Wang,Jingrui He,Hanqing Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: One-shot skill harnessing via Evo-Harness enables online harness learning for LLM agents to improve across sequential tasks by distilling noisy, single-shot executions into reusable skills; validated on five realistic benchmarks; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents in realistic environments face novel tasks with highly noisy, one-shot contexts. Prior self-improvement methods struggle to isolate broadly useful lessons from task artifacts. A systematic framework is needed to study self-improvement factors on real tasks.

Method: Introduce online harness learning: a frozen agent updates a structured 'harness' across sequential tasks. Context-to-harness skill compilation distills noisy, single-shot executions into reusable cross-domain skills. Evo-Harness framework enables controlled study of self-improvement factors and cross-domain adaptation; evaluated on five benchmarks.

Result: Empirical demonstration of Evo-Harness effectiveness across five realistic benchmarks (TerminalBench2, SWE-bench, CL-Bench, -bench, WebArena-Infinity). Extensive analysis clarifies how LLM agents learn on the fly; code available at the linked repository.

Conclusion: Evo-Harness provides a principled approach to one-shot skill compilation and online harness learning, enabling systematic investigation of self-improvement drivers in real-world LLM agents.

Abstract: Learning from experience is critical for developing capable, self-improving large language model (LLM) agents. Existing methods typically extract knowledge from accumulated trajectories via reflection, memory, rules, or skills. However, agents in realistic environments continuously encounter novel tasks, often offering only a one-shot opportunity to improve. These executions yield rich but highly noisy contexts, entangling broadly useful lessons with task-specific artifacts. Critically, prior works rarely validate their effectiveness on complex real-world tasks or isolate the underlying drivers of improvement. To address these gaps, we formulate online harness learning, where a frozen agent improves by continually updating a structured harness across sequential tasks. This formulation enables a systematic study of key self-improvement factors through our proposed Evo-Harness. At its core, context-to-harness skill compilation distills noisy, single-shot executions into reusable skill harnesses for cross-domain and topic-level adaptation. To demonstrate the efficacy of one-shot skill compilation, we evaluate across five realistic benchmarks (TerminalBench2, SWE-bench, CL-Bench, -bench, WebArena-Infinity). Our extensive analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of Evo-Harness and provides a principled understanding of how LLM agents can effectively learn on the fly. Our code is available at https://github.com/A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve/tree/release/evo-harness.

</details>


### [515] [Beyond Thresholds: A Quality-Aware Decision Intelligence Framework for Cold Chain IoT Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15082)
*Aashna Sofat,Balwinder Sodhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Quality-Aware Decision Intelligence (QADI) framework for cold chain logistics that translates degradation signals into actionable decisions by combining a structured quality state (L, Q, U, R), a hybrid physics-data microbial model, and a retrieval-augmented reasoning layer; outperforms baselines and enables near-optimal decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cold chain monitoring is reactive and threshold-based; there is a need to relate cumulative product degradation to shelf-life decisions and integrate reasoning for decision support.

Method: Proposes S_q = [L, Q, U, R] representing remaining shelf life, degradation rate, estimation uncertainty, and operational risk; uses a hybrid model combining physics-based microbial kinetics with a data-driven correction; reasoning layer built on Microsoft Phi-4 with retrieval-augmented generation over a structured domain knowledge base; evaluation against five baselines across eight scenarios (milk and broccoli) with ground-truth shelf-life from dairy studies; statistical tests (Wilcoxon, Holm); code link.

Result: Mean absolute shelf-life error 7.2 hours vs 30.9 hours (physics-only); p<0.001; spoilage rate 14.5% vs 16.6% (physics-only and rule-based; p=0.08); oracle-optimal decisions in 99.5% of scenarios; removing LLM reasoning drops optimality to 45.5% (p<0.001); expert-rated explanation quality 83% (κ=0.71). Ablations show hybrid modeling and LLM reasoning contribute distinct gains; RAG retrieval mainly drives explanation quality.

Conclusion: Hybrid QADI with LLM-based reasoning yields substantial improvements in decision quality and explainability; the LLM component is essential for near-optimal decisions; retrieval-augmented generation enhances explanation quality; code is available.

Abstract: Cold chain logistics has advanced technologically, yet most deployed systems remain reactive monitors, not decision-making agents: thresholds trigger alerts, but nothing relates violations to cumulative product degradation or converts degradation signals into logistics decisions. We address this gap with a Quality-Aware Decision Intelligence (QADI) framework combining three capabilities: a structured quality state representation, $S_q = [L, Q, U, R]$ -- remaining shelf life, degradation rate, estimation uncertainty, and operational risk, all derived and computable from the framework equations; a hybrid quality modeling layer combining physics-based microbial kinetics with a data-driven correction term; and a reasoning layer built on Microsoft Phi-4~\cite{Phi4} with retrieval-augmented generation over a structured domain knowledge base.
  We benchmark against five baselines -- threshold monitoring, physics-only, physics-plus-noise, optimisation-based decisions, and a rule-based expert system -- across eight cold chain scenarios, using pasteurised milk as the primary case, with ground truth shelf-life drawn from published dairy studies~\cite{Singh1994, Smigic2015} independent of our model. Comparisons use Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Across milk and broccoli scenarios, the framework attains mean absolute shelf-life error of 7.2 hours (versus 30.9 hours, physics-only; $p<0.001$), spoilage rate of 14.5% (versus 16.6%, physics-only and rule-based; p=0.08), and oracle-optimal decisions in 99.5% of scenarios. Removing the LLM reasoning component drops optimality to 45.5% ($p<0.001$). Expert-rated explanation quality reaches 83% ($κ= 0.71$). Ablations show hybrid modeling and LLM reasoning contribute distinct gains, while RAG retrieval mainly drives explanation quality. Code: https://bit.ly/4d6t44C.

</details>


### [516] [StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a \$15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15089)
*Ziheng Qin,Yaxin Lu,Zhangyang Atlas Wang,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StateM is an agent-native runtime that decouples planning from execution, using durable states, phase-local context, recoverable runbooks, and versioned practices to improve long-horizon task performance with minimal model adaptation. It achieves substantial gains across benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSeek, BusinessBench) and offers cost reductions by enabling reusable runbooks and preconditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address failure modes of long-horizon agents (state drift, forgetting, premature termination) by scaling the execution system rather than re-tuning model weights, and to enable inspectable, reusable procedural knowledge.

Method: Introduce StateM runtime with stateful execution units, phase-local contexts, check transitions, recoverable runbooks, and versioned practices. Evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSeek variants, and BusinessBench using GPT-5.5/5.6/Sol Luna, measuring accuracy, task success, and API/cost metrics; examine transferability and generalization of runbooks.

Result: StateM yields higher accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSeek variants with relatively low adaptation cost. Example: GPT-5.5 xhigh on StateM achieves 92.1% vs 83.1% baseline; with GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh, 95.3% across 445 trials and success on all 89 tasks. Frozen profile improves Luna from 76.7% to 85.4%. Cost-efficient: DeepSeek adaptation <$38; total DeepSeek expenditure ~$52.22 vs hundreds for references. On BusinessBench, runbooks improve macro/micro metrics; cross-family rules generalize.

Conclusion: StateM demonstrates that scalable, inspectable runtime improvements can significantly boost long-horizon agent performance and reduce adaptation costs, with evidence of generalization across domains. The approach decouples execution from model weights and makes learned controls explicit through stateful, verifiable preconditions.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents can fail even when their underlying models can solve the constituent steps. They may lose track of mutable state, fail to reactivate lessons from earlier executions, skip known procedures, or stop prematurely. We bet on harness scaling to improve the execution system around an agent without changing its model weights. We introduce StateM, an agent-native runtime that organizes execution around durable states, phase-local context, checked transitions, recoverable runbooks, and versioned procedural practices that agents and users can inspect together.
  On Terminal-Bench 2.1, StateM raises GPT-5.5 xhigh to 92.1\%, versus 83.1\% reference and GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra at 91.9\%. The runbook transfers unchanged to GPT-5.6. With GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh, StateM reaches 95.3\% raw accuracy across 445 trials and succeeds on all 89 tasks at least once. The frozen profile raises GPT-5.6 Luna from 76.7 to 85.4\%, above the 84.9\% Sol xhigh reference.
  Using the same runtime, runbook structure, and golden rules, less than \$38 of adaptation raises DeepSeek-V4 Flash from 82.7 to 88.1\% under standard timeouts and to 89.1\% on an 88-task common core. Extending only the remaining latency-sensitive task matches the reported 88.8\% GPT-5.6 Sol max result. Final-score API usage is about \$15 versus \$574.68 for the GPT reference; total DeepSeek expenditure is \$52.22.
  On BusinessBench, family-specific runbooks built on development sets yield held-out gains of 0.55 macro and 1.34 micro points; two mechanism-matched families improve by 10.04 points. Concrete rules generalize when tasks share execution structure, while the control methodology applies broadly. StateM turns selected postmortem findings into persistent, executable preconditions and practices, making learned controls explicit and enforceable through stateful controls. Code at github.com/henryqin1997/statem.

</details>


### [517] [Validation-Frontier Representation Selection under Constrained Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15095)
*Wesley Shu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adaptive representation selection under constrained observation improves robustness-efficiency frontier on a focused tabular benchmark but does not universally beat trace baselines; gains are modest and context-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world deployments, observations are incomplete, unstable, or costly. The work seeks to optimize the robustness-efficiency frontier by selecting state representations under observation constraints.

Method: Introduce a validation-frontier selector that combines balanced accuracy with penalties for feature cost, overfit gap, and validation-test instability. Evaluate on a public-tabular benchmark with multiple observation regimes, 45 task cells, 720 candidate actions, and 405 representation rows; compare frontier scores and feature counts to full-trace baselines; also conduct a broader offline stress test.

Result: On the benchmark, frontier score improves by 0.025801 over full trace features; mean feature count decreases by 22.733. Balanced-accuracy difference is small and not statistically significant. Stress tests yield mixed results.

Conclusion: Adaptive representation selection can improve the constrained-observation robustness-efficiency frontier in matched benchmark settings but does not universally dominate trace baselines.

Abstract: AI systems deployed outside clean benchmark settings often rely on observations that are incomplete, unstable, costly, or degraded by monitoring failures. This paper studies representation selection under constrained observation: choosing a state representation when raw accuracy is not the only operational criterion. We propose a validation-frontier selector that combines balanced accuracy with penalties for feature cost, overfit gap, and validation-test instability. In a focused public-tabular benchmark using three scikit-learn datasets, five observation regimes, 45 matched task cells, 720 candidate actions, and 405 representation rows, the adaptive selector improves frontier score over full trace features by 0.025801 while reducing mean feature count by 22.733. Balanced-accuracy difference is small and not statistically significant. A broader offline stress test gives mixed results. The supported claim is therefore bounded: adaptive representation selection can improve a constrained-observation robustness-efficiency frontier in matched benchmark settings, but does not universally dominate trace baselines.

</details>


### [518] [Second-Order Policy Effects as State Transitions: A Source-Linked Benchmark for Policy Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15101)
*Wesley Shu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a second-order policy-effect benchmark and side-effect simulator; shows improved mean policy-effect quality over baselines and highlights transition-state variables in capturing downstream institutional effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy evaluation typically fixes the institutional environment, but real policies trigger adaptation and new equilibria. A benchmark and evaluation protocol for second-order effects is needed to test simulators under downstream institutional changes.

Method: Formalize second-order policy-effect prediction and build a source-linked benchmark with 96 named public-policy cases across eight domains and four actions (implement, modify, pilot, block). Include state variables (benefit, capture, gaming, burden shift, instability, uncertainty, irreversibility, distributional risk, implementation capacity). A runner regenerates outputs from the case table; a simulator avoids reading expert actions. Conduct a protocol-based transition-channel audit (recall, precision, F1-style efficiency, selective top-channel stress diagnostics).

Result: Side-effect simulator achieves mean policy-effect quality 0.945, higher than 0.838 (risk-register baseline) and 0.879 (causal-loop baseline). Gains are strongest in side-effect recall and aggregate transition scoring, but it does not dominate for exact policy-action prediction. Evidence is benchmark-based and supports a bounded claim that transition-state variables increase sensitivity to downstream institutional effects.

Conclusion: Transition-state variables enhance policy simulators' sensitivity to downstream institutional effects; the benchmark provides a structured, source-linked framework for evaluating second-order policy dynamics, though gains are bounded to overall policy-effects rather than exact action prediction.

Abstract: Policy evaluation often estimates direct benefits and costs while treating the institutional environment as fixed. In practice, a policy changes the system it enters: actors adapt, enforcement capacity shifts, burdens move, and new equilibria form around capture, gaming, compliance theater, irreversibility, and repair costs. We formalize this as second-order policy-effect prediction and present a source-linked benchmark for policy simulation. The benchmark contains 96 named public-policy cases across eight domains and four balanced action classes: implement, modify, pilot, and block. Each case includes source locators and state variables for benefit, capture, gaming, burden shift, instability, uncertainty, irreversibility, distributional risk, and implementation capacity. The runner regenerates method outputs and aggregate results from the case table, and the simulator never reads the expert action target. We report a protocol-based transition-channel audit with recall, precision, F1-style efficiency, and selective top-channel stress diagnostics, so universal channel coverage is not mistaken for field validation. The side-effect simulator achieves mean policy-effect quality of 0.945, compared with 0.838 for the risk-register baseline and 0.879 for the causal-loop baseline. Its advantage is concentrated in side-effect recall and aggregate transition scoring; it does not dominate the best structured baselines on exact policy-action choice. The evidence remains benchmark-based, but supports a bounded claim: transition-state variables make policy simulators more sensitive to downstream institutional effects.

</details>


### [519] [Constraint-Aware Synthetic Tabular Data Generation via Inter-Column Constraint Discovery with LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15109)
*Jianxing Zhao,Mao Guan,Dongyu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unified workflow to discover and enforce inter-column constraints for synthetic tabular data, using executable hypotheses and a generator-agnostic postprocessor, to improve constraint violation detection and achieve zero violations for retained constraints while preserving marginals and improving downstream utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic tabular data currently risks violating domain constraints despite high statistical fidelity; there is a need for systematic discovery and enforcement of semantic inter-column constraints (equations, linear inequalities, logical dependencies).

Method: Represent constraints as machine-executable hypotheses; provide a unified interface for full-table validation, deterministic diagnosis, and counterexample-guided revision; deploy a generator-agnostic postprocessor that coordinates repair strategies per constraint family on outputs from unchanged tabular generators; validate via curated audits and end-to-end evaluations.

Result: Improved held-out violation detection over one-shot prompting; postprocessing yields zero measured violations for every retained, applicable constraint; improves downstream utility on most datasets; largely preserves univariate marginals.

Conclusion: An integrated, generator-agnostic constraint enforcement workflow effectively enforces semantic inter-column constraints in synthetic tabular data while maintaining marginal distributions and enhancing downstream utility.

Abstract: Generating structurally valid synthetic tabular data remains difficult: outputs with high statistical fidelity and downstream utility can still violate semantically meaningful domain constraints. We study the discovery and enforcement of three complementary inter-column constraint families---equations, linear inequalities, and logical dependencies. Our unified tool-grounded workflow represents all three as machine-executable hypotheses and applies a common interface for full-table validation, deterministic diagnosis, and counterexample-guided revision. A generator-agnostic postprocessor coordinates family-specific repairs on outputs from unchanged tabular generators. Across curated behavioral audits and end-to-end evaluations, the complete workflow improves held-out violation detection over one-shot direct prompting, while postprocessing yields zero measured violations for every retained, applicable constraint, improves downstream utility on most datasets, and largely preserves univariate marginals.

</details>


### [520] [Anatomy of a Quantized Agent: VRAM Stability and Forecasting in Code-Synthesis Agentic Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15117)
*Anubhab Banerjee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Closed-form VRAM models using two empirical constants (loaded-weight VRAM and fixed activation overhead) can predict peak VRAM during quantized LLM inference with competitive accuracy to learned models across most backbones; peak-memory variance is small; code-synthesis performance is more restricted by LLM capability than memory; no need for complex VRAM predictors in weight-dominated regimes; data released for replication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether simple, analytical VRAM models suffice for forecasting peak VRAM in LLM inference under quantization and realistic usage, and to quantify the relative influence of memory components, quantization, and LLM capacity on compilation/synthesis outcomes.

Method: Strict, measurement-driven study: LangGraph-based CUDA-kernel-synthesis agent (AgentK), 4-bit quantization family (Q4 K M), single NVIDIA H100 GPU, four LLM backbones, 1,920 trajectories. Memory decomposed into weight-storage, KV-cache, and activation terms parameterized by step count, tool invocations, and context growth. Compare a closed-form analytical model (two constants) against learned prompt-feature regression and baselines, using live GPU readings and ground-truth trajectory parameters. Reports peak-memory forecast accuracy (MAPE) and compile success rates across backbones.

Result: Two-constant closed-form model achieves competitive accuracy vs. learned baselines on 3/4 backbones (MAPE 2.2-4.4% vs. 3.4-6.5%, p = 0.76). The smallest backbone (Phi-4-mini) shows an exception due to extremely low VRAM variance (CV 0.3%), where dynamic modeling underperforms. Compile success varies with backbone capacity (5.7% for Phi-4-mini to 62.0% for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B). Overall peak-memory variance is low across backbones (CV 0.3-9.4%), making learned prompt-feature regression statistically insignificant over a constant-mean baseline. Conclusion: no justification for complex VRAM predictors in highly quantized, weight-dominated regimes. Corpus and anonymized framework released for replication.

Conclusion: In highly quantized, weight-dominated LLM inference, simple closed-form VRAM forecasting with two empirical constants suffices for peak memory prediction across a range of backbones; memory variance is small and advanced learned predictors offer little gain. The work highlights that intrinsic LLM capabilities—not memory capacity—limit compile/synthesis success in this regime; data release supports reproducibility.

Abstract: Analytical models of peak VRAM consumption for LLM inference decompose memory into weight-storage, KV-cache, and activation terms parameterized by step count, tool invocations, and context expansion. We evaluate this decomposition empirically within a strictly scoped measurement study: a LangGraph-based CUDA-kernel-synthesis agent (AgentK), a 4-bit quantization family (Q4 K M), a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, and four LLM backbones across 1,920 trajectories. Focusing on peak-memory forecasting behavior, we report two primary observations. First, closed-form analytical models achieve competitive accuracy when provided with two empirical constants: loaded-weight VRAM and a fixed activation-memory overhead. Supplied with live GPU readings and ground-truth trajectory parameters, the closed-form model matches or outperforms the best learned baseline on three of the four backbones (test MAPE 2.2-4.4% vs. 3.4-6.5%, p = 0.76). The exception is the smallest backbone (Phi-4-mini), where minimal VRAM variance (CV 0.3%) causes dynamic modeling to underperform simple regression. Second, compile success strictly bifurcates by backbone capacity (from 5.7% for Phi-4-mini to 62.0% for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B), demonstrating that functional code synthesis remains constrained by intrinsic LLM capabilities rather than available memory. Furthermore, because overall peak-memory variance is remarkably low across all backbones (CV 0.3-9.4%), learned prompt-feature regression offers statistically insignificant improvements over a constant-mean baseline. Consequently, we find no justification for deploying complex predictive VRAM models in highly quantized, weight-dominated regimes. We release the evaluated corpus and anonymized framework to support replication.

</details>


### [521] [Platform Adaptation Under Governance Interventions: Actor Best-Response Modeling and an External Public-Case Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15131)
*Wesley Shu,Peng Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A platform-adaptation model evaluates governance interventions as adaptive transitions in multi-actor information systems, outperforming static baselines across 72 cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy rules on digital platforms are not passively absorbed; actors adapt, creating dynamic, strategic responses. A theory and measurement framework is needed to evaluate governance as adaptive interactions.

Method: Developed a platform-adaptation simulator/model capturing actor best responses, strategic gaming opportunities, moderation burden, user-incentive movement, enforcement response, externality formation, and downstream platform stability; evaluated on 72 external public platform-governance cases across 9 methods and 648 method-case evaluations.

Result: Mean adaptation quality of 0.836338 for the platform-adaptation simulator, vs baselines: 0.669731 (risk-register), 0.589457 (causal-loop analysis), 0.492750 (generic governance critique), 0.369492 (engagement-only optimization), 0.331965 (baseline policy review); paired comparisons show 1.00 win rate against all baselines.

Conclusion: Contributes an information-systems theory and measurement framework that explains why governance evaluation fails when treating policy rules as static controls, and promotes adaptive evaluation of platform governance.

Abstract: Digital platforms govern by changing rules: rankings, monetization thresholds, moderation standards, verification systems, disclosure requirements, appeal processes, and access policies. These interventions are rarely absorbed passively. Creators, sellers, advertisers, moderators, users, developers, and strategic operators adapt to the new reward surface. This paper develops a platform-adaptation model for evaluating governance interventions as transitions in adaptive multi-actor information systems. The model represents actor best response, strategic gaming opportunity, moderation burden, user-incentive movement, enforcement response, externality formation, and downstream platform stability. We evaluate the model on 72 external public platform-governance cases covering media monetization, ranking systems, verification, delivery platforms, marketplaces, app stores, community platforms, and creator ecosystems. Across 9 methods and 648 method-case evaluations, the full platform-adaptation simulator achieves mean adaptation quality of 0.836338, compared with 0.669731 for a risk-register baseline, 0.589457 for causal-loop analysis, 0.492750 for generic governance critique, 0.369492 for engagement-only optimization, and 0.331965 for baseline policy review. Paired comparisons show a win rate of 1.00 against all tested baselines and channel ablations. The contribution is an information-systems theory and measurement framework showing why platform governance evaluation fails when it treats policy rules as static controls rather than interventions into adaptive actor-response fields.

</details>


### [522] [ReForge: Keeping ABR Algorithms Never Finished with Verified Large Language Model Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15138)
*Zhiqiang He,Zhi Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReForge is a continual learning framework that uses an LLM in the loop to iteratively edit a compact, fuzzy-rule page routing decisions among a frozen pool of policies, enabling ABR algorithms to adapt to evolving network scenarios with replay-based validation; achieves near-oracle QoE across sequential 3G/4G/5G arrivals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ABR algorithm design is brittle to new or evolving network environments; traditional one-shot designs fail to generalize as scenarios arrive or change. A continual, safe adaptation mechanism is needed to keep pace with the changing world without breaking previously served networks.

Method: An LLM-in-the-loop iteratively proposes a single small edit to one page of routing rules that dispatch decisions to a frozen policy pool. The LLM generates the initial rule page from measurements, then refines it. Each edit is validated by replaying every network that has been served to date to decide if the change improves overall performance; evaluation is performed on real-world network families arriving 3G→4G→5G, with performance measured via QoE.

Result: With a few edits per arrival, mean QoE improves from 1.23 to 1.74, surpassing the best single policy at 1.66 and reaching 94% of the oracle’s performance. The approach also repairs networks from unseen families (0.30 to 0.80).

Conclusion: ReForge demonstrates effective continual adaptation of ABR algorithms to evolving networks via LLM-guided small edits and replay validation, achieving strong generalization across unseen scenarios while preserving prior functionality; the authors plan to open-source code, data, and experiments.

Abstract: Designing an ABR algorithm for one network scenario takes an engineer months, and large language models now do this work in hours, matching or beating hand-built designs. But either way, the design fits only the world visible at its birth, and fails on the world that arrives after. We ask whether an ABR algorithm can keep pace with the world, redesigned in minutes as each scenario arrives, with every change proven harmless to every scenario already served. In this work, we propose ReForge, a continual heuristic learning framework that adapts to continuously changing scenarios. ReForge runs that routine with a large language model (LLM) in the loop. Each round the LLM reads where the current design falls short and proposes one small edit, and a replay over every network served so far decides. Specifically, what it edits is a single page of fuzzy rules that routes every decision to one of a frozen pool of pre-trained policies. The LLM writes the first page from measurements alone, then keeps improving it on its own. Each round it reads where the current rules fall short and proposes one small edit, and a replay over every network served so far decides whether the edit lands. We evaluate ReForge on nine real-world network families arriving one at a time as 3G, 4G, then 5G. A few edits per arrival lift mean QoE from 1.23 to 1.74, past the best single policy at 1.66 and to 94\% of an oracle, and even repair families the loop never saw, one rising from 0.30 to 0.80. All code, data, and experiment records will be open-sourced upon cleanup.

</details>


### [523] [Translating finite-domain integer constraint models to CP/SMT/ILP/PB/SAT solvers with CPMpy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15143)
*Tias Guns,Ignace Bleukx,Hendrik Bierlee,Jo Devriendt,Emilio Gamba,Orestis Lomis,Wout Piessens,Thomas Sergeys,Dimos Tsouros,Wout Vanroose,Hélène Verhaeghe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Modular cross-paradigm constraint model translation via CPMpy, enabling CP/SMT/ILP/PB/MaxSAT solving from a single high-level language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a unified approach to compare and apply different solving technologies to a given problem without remodelling for each paradigm; address CP global constraints, negation handling, and auxiliary-variable reduction; enable practical benchmarking and solver choice.

Method: Define a high-level language of logical/arithmetic operations and global constraints; implement a modular waterfall of transformations to CP/SMT/ILP/PB/MaxSAT; reuse higher-level transformations in lower-level paradigms; implement and evaluate in the open-source CPMpy library; address negation of arbitrary subexpressions and avoid introducing auxiliary variables; linearize non-linear operators for ILP/PB/SAT.

Result: A CPMpy-based transformation waterfall is implemented and evaluated; constraint models change significantly through the transformations; linearization optimizations are essential for ILP and PB solvers.

Conclusion: A modular, cross-paradigm translation framework enables solving and benchmarking CP/SMT/ILP/PB/MaxSAT problems from a single high-level model; linearization and negation handling are key challenges, effectively addressed within CPMpy.

Abstract: Constraint solving is a declarative approach for solving combinatorial satisfaction and optimization problems. The user specifies their problem through constraints and decision variables, and a generic solver is used to find a solution. Several constraint-solving technologies exist, and certain solvers perform well on certain problems. Therefore, it is useful to try different solvers given a particular application. However, each solving paradigm supports different types of constraints and decision variables.
  Our goal is to translate high-level constraint satisfaction and optimization problems into any lower-level formalism, including CP, SMT QF-LIA, ILP, PB and (Max)SAT. This allows for comparing different solving technologies for a particular problem, without requiring a user to manually remodel it for each solving paradigm.
  We define a high-level language of logical and arithmetic operations, and useful additional functions and constraints, which are known as global constraints in the CP community. We then present a modular framework for transforming our high-level modeling language to CP/SMT/ILP/PB and (Max)SAT solvers. While many transformations are partly described in the literature, we observe that they can be implemented through a modular waterfall of smaller components, where lower-level paradigms reuse the transformations of higher-level paradigms. Two recurring challenges are handling the negation of arbitrary subexpressions and avoiding the introduction of auxiliary variables. Additionally, we take special care linearizing non-linear operators for ILP, PB and SAT-solvers.
  The transformation waterfall is implemented and evaluated in the open-source CPMpy library. Our results show that constraint models significantly change throughout the transformations, and that optimizations to the linearization of constraints are essential for ILP and PB solvers.

</details>


### [524] [ACTS-SQL: Agentic and Critic-Oriented Tree-Structured SQL Correctness with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15145)
*Xinmei Huang,Jie Song,Peng Li,Fuxin Jiang,Jing Zhang,Tieying Zhang,Jianjun Chen,Chenming Liu,Tao Yang,Maoyin Liu,Wenda Li,Hong Chen,Cuiping Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A training-free, plan-guided, tree-structured debugging framework for SQL correction in Text-to-SQL that uses multi-strategy backtracking, execution-based verification, and clause-level diagnostics, achieving strong gains and real-world deployment gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SQL errors in T2S hinder practical deployment; existing methods require data or brittle single-path workflows; need robust, training-free correction suitable for industrial pipelines.

Method: Plan-guided, tree-structured debugging framework maintaining multiple correction strategies with backtracking; execution-based verification; clause-level diagnostics; strategy pruning and error localization.

Result: On BIRD-Critic, achieves 9.42% absolute improvement over SOTA; outperforms strong LLM backbones and agent baselines; deployed in Volcano Engine's TLS as online T2S API; increases real-world execution accuracy from 36.77% to 53.61% with GPT-5.

Conclusion: Training-free, stable SQL correction approach that mitigates error accumulation and performs well in production; demonstrates practicality for industrial Text-to-SQL systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly adopted in Text-to-SQL systems, yet SQL errors remain a major obstacle in real-world Text-to-SQL inference pipelines. Existing SQL correction approaches either rely on large-scale, high-quality training data with substantial overhead, or adopt single-path agentic workflows that are brittle to early mistakes and prone to error propagation.
  To develop a practical SQL correctness system for industrial scenarios, we present a training-free framework that formulates SQL correction as a plan-guided, tree-structured debugging process. By maintaining multiple correction strategies and enabling backtracking, the framework mitigates error accumulation during iterative refinement. We further integrate execution-based verification and clause-level diagnostic tools to support strategy pruning and precise error localization.
  We evaluate the system on the BIRD-Critic benchmark and observe consistent accuracy gains over strong LLM backbones and representative agent-based baselines, achieving a 9.42% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art method. The framework is also deployed in the Torch Log Service (TLS) of Volcano Engine to support an online Text-to-TLS API. In production, it improves execution accuracy from 36.77% to 53.61% on real user queries with a representative strong LLM backbone (GPT-5). These results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our approach in real-world deployments.

</details>


### [525] [Constitutive Priors for Machine Intelligence: A Legitimacy Theory of the Artificial Physical World](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15147)
*Jiang Jiang,Yifu Sun,Qi Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Four-world ontology for constitutive priors in the artificial physical world, with a legitimacy criterion, a four-layer architecture (syntax, concept, knowledge, instance), deployment across five industrial domains using a 32-class failure-mode vocabulary, and five falsifiable predictions. LLMs are readers of the archive, not the archive. First of three companion works.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the physical AI deadlock by leveraging intentionally constituted artifacts that ship with readable archives, enabling data generation and validation from the built world; establish a principled legitimacy check for constitutive prior frameworks.

Method: Develop a four-world ontology; derive a legitimacy criterion based on direction of fit between constitutive norms and instantiated artifacts; prove a four-layer lower bound (syntax, concept, knowledge, instance); document deployment claims across five industrial domains with a 32-class failure-mode taxonomy; propose five falsifiable predictions backed by semi-formal arguments (Gold-type boundary, decidability results, boundary theorem); position large language models as archive readers rather than archive creators.

Result: A testable framework for constitutive priors: a legitimacy criterion; a proven four-layer architecture; deployment mapping across domains with a standardized failure-mode vocabulary; five falsifiable predictions; semi-formal arguments supporting core claims.

Conclusion: The framework reframes LLMs' role to interpret and read archives embedded in engineered artifacts rather than generating or acting as the primary archive; this is the first of three companion works that will address remaining questions.

Abstract: Machine intelligence has conquered the symbolic world but stalled at the physical one. The stall is structural: physical AI faces a cold-start deadlock -- no intelligence without data, no data without deployed intelligence. Our thesis: the deadlock is real but unevenly distributed, and the exception has a name: the artificial physical world. Buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure are intentionally constituted and documented: designed artifacts ship with readable archives that precede and constitute their instances; here, norms are promulgated before instances, not averaged from them. Four contributions. (i) From a four-world ontology we derive a legitimacy criterion for constitutive prior frameworks: prior extraction is legitimate if and only if the object domain is intentionally constituted and has left a readable archive; the criterion is testable through direction of fit -- deviation from a constitutive norm is a violation in the world, not a revision of the model. (ii) We establish a layering lower bound: any such framework has at least four layers -- syntax, concept, knowledge, instance -- because four construction goals pair into mutually incompatible carriers. (iii) We register deployment claims across five industrial domains and a 32-class failure-mode vocabulary. (iv) We stake the framework on five falsifiable predictions, the central one checkable on the public engineering record: if it fails, the framework fails. Semi-formal arguments back these claims (Appendix A): a Gold-type boundary on rule coverage in archiveless worlds, a decidability result for failure reduction over closed concept layers, and a boundary theorem for certificate-anchored calculi. Large language models find an honored place here -- as readers of the archive, not as the archive. First of three companion works; the companions take up the questions deliberately left open.

</details>


### [526] [SkillCommit: Evolving Agent Skills through Behaviorally Validated Scope Expansion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15165)
*Yu He,Weikai Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillCommit is an online skill evolution framework that builds a hierarchical library of reusable skills from LLM agent experiences. It preserves each new skill as an instance-specific patch, then abstracts related skills into higher-level skills only if they share a common mechanism and preserve validated behavior, enabling cross-domain and cross-model transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for consolidating LLM experience rely on semantic similarity or judgments, which can conflate superficially related but behaviorally incompatible strategies, reducing performance. There is a need for online, mechanism-aware skill evolution that preserves validated behavior across cases.

Method: For each incoming skill, store it as an instance-specific patch. Use embedding-based retrieval to identify candidate related skills. Apply cross-instance replay and an LLM-based mechanism to verify whether skills transfer across cases and share a common underlying mechanism. If candidates pass both checks, abstract them into a higher-level skill and commit the new skill only if it preserves the validated behavior of all constituent skills.

Result: Empirical evaluations on RuleArena, OpenExempt, and KOR-Bench show that SkillCommit consistently improves agent performance across diverse domains. The learned skills also transfer across model scales and families, enabling cross-model experience transfer.

Conclusion: SkillCommit successfully creates a hierarchical, evolving skill library from online experience that enhances performance and enables cross-domain and cross-model transfer, by preserving validated behavior while abstracting common mechanisms.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can continually improve without parameter updates by converting historical experience into reusable procedural knowledge. However, existing methods often consolidate experience based on semantic similarity or LLM judgments, which may merge superficially related but behaviorally incompatible strategies and thereby degrade performance. To address the issue, we propose SkillCommit, an online skill evolution framework that continuously transforms experience into a hierarchical library of reusable skills. Each new experience is initially preserved as an instance-specific patch, retaining the behavior validated in its local context. As related skills accumulate, SkillCommit abstracts those sharing a common behavioral mechanism into higher-level skills. Specifically, for each incoming skill, embedding-based retrieval first identifies candidate related skills. Cross-instance replay and an LLM-based mechanism check determine whether these skills transfer across cases and share a common underlying mechanism. Candidates that pass both checks are abstracted into a higher-level skill and committed only if it preserves the validated behavior of all constituent skills. Experiments on RuleArena, OpenExempt and KOR-Bench demonstrate that SkillCommit consistently improves agent performance across diverse domains. Moreover, the learned skills transfer across model scales and families, enabling cross-model experience transfer.

</details>


### [527] [LongRCA Bench: Diagnosing Responsible Roles and Root Causes in Long-Horizon Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15242)
*Yunfei Zhang,Boyu Feng,Changhua Pei,Zexin Wang,Zhihuang Peng,Xinlong Liu,Hengyue Jiang,Difeng Ma,Jiayi Zhang,Yongzhou Yao,Yanan Zhao,Fei Sun,Yintong Huo,Zhaoyang Liu,Jingjing Li,Gaogang Xie,Dan Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces LongRCA Bench for long-horizon failure diagnosis and Root-Cause Trajectory Attribution (RCTA). Provides independently labeled data for responsible role and earliest decisive root-cause step; baseline performance is low, while RCTA (a training-free method) substantially improves attribution metrics. Highlights separation of responsible-role attribution and exact root-step localization as distinct evaluation targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing failure benchmarks focus on short traces and outcome-level evaluation; there is a need to localize the earliest decisive error in long-horizon trajectories to aid developers.

Method: Construct LongRCA Bench with 1,140 failed trajectories across five domains and independently scored human labels for responsible role and earliest decisive root-cause step. Introduce RCTA, a training-free method that retrieves candidate error steps from segment summaries and traces them to prior handoff instructions, evaluated with the same backbone and scoring protocol as the benchmark.

Result: Median trajectory length is 145 steps. The strongest baseline achieves 13.2% exact root-step accuracy; RCTA achieves 51.1% responsible-role accuracy and 24.1% exact root-step accuracy.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the need to treat responsible-role attribution and exact root-step localization as separate targets in long-trajectory failure diagnosis. Presents a viable, training-free method (RCTA) that meaningfully improves attribution while revealing substantial room for improvement.

Abstract: When a long-horizon agent execution fails, outcome-level evaluation reveals the unsuccessful result but not where the decisive error entered the trajectory. Developers must then inspect the full execution to identify the responsible role and localize the earliest decisive root-cause step. Existing failure-attribution benchmarks largely focus on shorter traces, leaving diagnosis across hundreds of recorded steps underexplored. We introduce LongRCA Bench, comprising 1,140 failed trajectories across five domains without injected errors. It provides independently scored human labels for the responsible role and earliest decisive root-cause step. The median trajectory contains 145 steps, and the strongest baseline reaches only 13.2% exact root-step accuracy. We further present Root-Cause Trajectory Attribution (RCTA), a training-free method that retrieves candidate error steps from segment summaries and traces them to available earlier handoff instructions. Using the same backbone, benchmark instances, and scoring protocol, RCTA reaches 51.1% responsible-role accuracy and 24.1% exact root-step accuracy. These results highlight the need to evaluate responsible-role attribution and exact root-step localization as separate targets in long-trajectory failure diagnosis.

</details>


### [528] [Demographic Injection in Medical Language Models under Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15254)
*Diego Mardian,Frank Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A single DEI prompt causes demographic injection in clinical-language-model outputs, misrepresenting patients and often changing the recommended answer; the effect is robust across 47 models and four benchmarks, reproducible with various phrasings, suggesting a general risk of prompting to nudge reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess safety and bias risks of DEI-guided prompting in clinical AI by quantifying unintended demographic disclosure and its impact on answers.

Method: Empirical evaluation across 47 language models, four medical benchmarks, and ~376,000 responses using a validated model-judge pipeline; compare with length-matched controls; analyze effect of phrasing; categorize injected content by general population statements vs patient-specific attributes; measure impact on answer and statistical significance.

Result: The DEI prompt increases demographic injection from 0.7% to 33.1% (47x; across all models), with 18x effect when controlling for length (p=1.4e-14); most injections are general population statements, but a small subset attaches demographics to the patient or shifts the selected option (0.25–2.4% of responses, 99.8% toward the incorrect option); phrasing scales the effect from 14% to 56%. The effect appears to reflect a general mechanism where nudging reasoning can introduce unrequested patient details, not limited to DEI prompts.

Conclusion: DEI prompts illustrate a broader risk: any instruction that nudges model reasoning can introduce unrequested demographic details, potentially affecting clinical recommendations. Flagged outputs are treated as model errors, not clinical guidance; results call for careful prompt design and robust evaluation to ensure safety and reliability.

Abstract: Clinical-AI guidance increasingly recommends prompting language models to reason with attention to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). We measure a side effect that misrepresents patients: a one-sentence DEI prompt appended to a medical question leads models to add patient demographic attributes (race, socioeconomic status, sex) the question never stated, in effect rewriting who the patient is. We call this demographic injection. Across 47 models, four medical benchmarks, and 376,000 responses scored by a validated model-judge pipeline, a single DEI prompt raises the injection rate from 0.7% to 33.1% (47x) in all 47 of 47 models, attributable to the equity content rather than to added length (18x above a length-matched control; p=1.4x10^-14). Most added content is a general population statement that leaves the answer unchanged, but a smaller subset attaches an attribute to the specific patient or changes the selected option (0.25-2.4% of responses, 99.8% toward the incorrect option), where the invented demographic changes the answer the model recommends. Phrasing scales the effect from 14% to 56%. DEI prompts are just one example of a more general mechanism. Any instruction that nudges how a model reasons can make it add unrequested details, including details about the patient. Flagged outputs are treated as model errors under study, not clinical guidance.

</details>


### [529] [Towards Standardized Evaluation in Automated Domain Modeling: Introducing a Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15255)
*Vasiliy Seibert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark for automated domain modeling combining two datasets (Golden UML Modelset and Chen et al. archive) to evaluate NL-to-domain-model generation, with ground-truth models, a comparison metric, and evaluation of heuristic and LLM-based methods; provided as a FAIR4RS-compliant research artifact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standardized benchmarks are lacking for automated domain modeling, hindering fair comparison of approaches across complexity and scale.

Method: Integrate 45-record Golden UML Modelset (via Zenodo/Text2UML) and 8-record Chen et al. archive into a benchmark; for each NL description provide a ground-truth domain model; apply a metric to compare generated graphs to ground truth; assess multiple approaches (heuristic-rule-based, LLM-driven); release as a FAIR4RS-compliant artifact.

Result: Demonstrates utility by evaluating several approaches on the benchmark; no explicit quantitative results in abstract; indicates the benchmark supports cross-domain assessment across complexity/scale.

Conclusion: FAIR4RS-compliant artifact to enable reuse and future research in automated domain modeling; benchmark provides a standardized evaluation framework.

Abstract: Domain modeling plays an essential role in domain-driven design, capturing essential entities and their relationships within a specific domain. Despite advancements in automated domain modeling, the absence of standardized benchmarks has hindered the comparative assessment of existing approaches. This paper introduces a benchmark designed to address this gap. The benchmark combines the 45-record Golden UML Modelset (Verbruggen et al., 2025) on Zenodo, as distributed by the Text2UML project of Calamo, Mecella, and Snoeck (Calamo et al., 2025), with the 8-record reference archive of Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2023a,b), enabling the evaluation of automated domain modeling approaches across different levels of complexity and scale. Given a natural language description, the task is to generate a corresponding domain model. For each description, a reference domain model is provided as ground truth. A metric is used to compare the generated domain model with the corresponding ground-truth model. To demonstrate the utility of the benchmark, we evaluate multiple automated domain modeling approaches, including heuristic rule-based methods and LLM-driven strategies. In accordance with the FAIR4RS recommendations (Chue Hong et al., 2022), the benchmark is provided as a research artifact to encourage reuse and support future research on automated domain modeling.

</details>


### [530] [Decentralized Federated Learning for Heterogeneous Multi-Task Semantic Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15256)
*Lin Yin,Tiejun Lv,Weicai Li,Xi Yu,Xiaoyu He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A personalized DSC framework with task-aware routing and a communication-while-aggregation protocol that uses task affinities to tune aggregation depth, backed by Lyapunov analysis, achieving near-optimal aggregation depth and improved performance over baselines on NYU-v2 and Taskonomy under varying link conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Topology-agnostic aggregation in heterogeneous, multi-task distributed semantic communication leads to negative transfer and overconsensus bias. There is a need to preserve local fidelity while enabling beneficial cross-task knowledge sharing.

Method: 1) Node-level: policy-driven multi-path routing to separate task-specific features from shared representations. 2) Network-level: 'communicationwhile-aggregation' protocol calibrating a column-stochastic consensus matrix using task affinities to absorb complementary knowledge while blocking mismatched updates. 3) Theoretical: unified Lyapunov drift analysis to bound convergence and derive a closed-form optimal aggregation depth. 4) Empirical: tests on NYU-v2, Taskonomy, and imperfect wireless links to study aggregation depth, network size, and link reliability.

Result: On NYU-v2, achieving a 4.77% global relative improvement over the no-aggregation baseline and outperforming FedAvg, FedAMP, and heuristic max aggregation. Additional experiments on Taskonomy and under imperfect wireless conditions show robustness to network size and link reliability.

Conclusion: The framework successfully balances aggregation depth to mitigate negative transfer and OCB, delivering theoretical guarantees and empirical gains over standard and heuristic DS T/Fed learning baselines. It demonstrates the value of task-aware routing and affinity-based aggregation in heterogeneous DSC networks.

Abstract: Collaborative training in distributed semantic communication (DSC) networks typically relies on decentralized federated learning (DFL). However, pushing topology-agnostic aggregation into heterogeneous, multi-task environments creates a fundamental bottleneck: it drives negative transfer and overconsensus bias (OCB). This paper introduces a personalized DSC framework that cuts off this cross-task interference. At the node level, a policy-driven multi-path routing mechanism separates task-specific features from shared representations to preserve local fidelity. Across the network, we deploy a "communicationwhile- aggregation" protocol. It calibrates a column-stochastic consensus matrix using task affinities. This limits the system to absorbing complementary knowledge while actively blocking mismatched parameter updates. To bound the convergence, we derive a unified Lyapunov drift analysis. We reveal a strict Ushaped trade-off: deeper topological mixing reduces variance but amplifies structural OCB. Resolving this tension yields a closed-form expression for the optimal aggregation depth. We evaluate the proposed framework on NYU-v2, where the results reveal a clear trade-off between insufficient aggregation and excessive topological mixing. At the analytically derived optimal aggregation depth, our method achieves a 4.77% global relative improvement over the no-aggregation baseline and outperforms decentralized FedAvg, FedAMP, and heuristic max aggregation. We further evaluate the framework on Taskonomy and imperfect wireless links to examine the effects of network-size variation and wireless-link reliability.

</details>


### [531] [VibeWorlding: Can Multimodal Agents Construct 3D Open Worlds End-to-End?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15265)
*Yansong Ning,Jingwen Ye,Zhongkai Wu,Yang Sun,Yiqin Zhu,Xingyi Li,Weidong Zhang,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces VibeWorlding, a unified framework for benchmarking and training vibe worlding agents in 3D open worlds, including VWE-BENCH and VibeWorlding-Gym; experiments show RL improves performance and open-source models can rival/beat frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to systematically analyze how multimodal agents infer user intent, plan scene layout, invoke 3D tools, and reason over textual/visual 3D world information, beyond idealized queries.

Method: Create VWE-BENCH with 2,616 high-quality 3D assets, 323 human-annotated seed 3D worlds, and 6,828 reverse-synthesized multimodal user queries (verified and unverified with rubrics); develop VibeWorlding-Gym, a joint multimodal RL post-training framework that unifies asset retrieval/editing/rendering as MCP tools and a rubric-based verifier for feasibility and intent fulfillment, enabling evaluation and RL reward services.

Result: Frontier MLLMs perform poorly (below 60% success) on vibe worlding; RL training reduces this gap, enabling open-source MLLMs to reach or exceed frontier performance; VibeWorlder-8B is comparable to frontier models, while VibeWorlder-30B-A3B achieves the best Pass@1.

Conclusion: RL-based training and a standardized benchmark enable fair evaluation and scalable multimodal RL for 3D world editing tasks, bringing high-performance capabilities to open-source models.

Abstract: Constructing an interactive 3D open world from a user query is important. However, existing methods are primarily evaluated on idealized, simple queries, making it difficult to systematically analyze and compare how multimodal agents understand user intent, use 3D tools, and reason over textual and visual 3D world information. To this end, we propose VibeWorlding, a unified framework for benchmarking and training vibe worlding agents: a multimodal agent that can autonomously infer user intent, plan scene layout, invoke 3D tools, and reflect on the multimodal feedback in a multi-turn agent-environment interaction process. To achieve this, we first build VWE-BENCH, a benchmark of 2,616 high-quality 3D assets, 323 human-annotated seed 3D worlds, and 6,828 reverse-synthesized multimodal user queries, split into verified queries with ground-truth and unverified queries with carefully designed rubrics. Moreover, we develop VibeWorlding-Gym, a joint multimodal RL post-training framework that integrates (1) a sandbox environment unifying asset retrieval, editing, and image rendering as MCP tools, and (2) a rubric-based verifier that combines physical feasibility and intent fulfillment verification, supporting both fair model evaluation and scalable multimodal RL reward service. Our experiments show that current frontier MLLMs are far from solving the vibe worlding agent task, with even GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-Max reaching below 60% success rate, and trace the bottleneck to precise 3D world editing. We further find that RL training can ease this weakness and enable open-source MLLMs to even surpass closed-source frontiers: our VibeWorlder-8B is comparable to frontier MLLMs, while our flagship VibeWorlder-30B-A3B attains the best overall Pass@1 among all evaluated models.

</details>


### [532] [$D^{2}R^{2}$: Discrete Diffusion with Regulation Reinforcement for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15288)
*Ninghan Fan,Qi Liu,Xunuo Zhu,Yukai Sun,Luyuan Chen,Xuheng Zhou,Yuetian Du,Ming Kong,Xiaojun Zhu,Jie Liu,Zhan Zhou,Qiang Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces D^2R^2, a discrete diffusion model with reinforcement for gene-wise progression in single-cell perturbation prediction; achieves state-of-the-art on Norman19 and competitive on H1; shows interpretable, biology-guided gene generation order.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods predict full expression profiles without modeling the sequential emergence of gene responses. Modeling gene-wise order with biological priors (gene regulatory networks) can improve accuracy, interpretability, and controllability of perturbation predictions.

Method: Proposes Masked Discrete Diffusion Model that treats expression as ordinal tokens and reconstructs a fully masked profile step-by-step, enabling conditioning on remaining genes. A Regulatory Policy Module initializes and adapts a generation policy from a gene regulatory network inferred from control cells, then group-relative policy optimization refines the ordering using final perturbation-effect agreement as the reward.

Result: D^2R^2 achieves the best performance on all five metrics on Norman19 and remains competitive on H1 across Norman19 and VCC-H1 datasets. Ablations show biology-informed ordering outperforms random and uncertainty-based heuristics; reversing the biologically-prior ordering degrades all metrics. Biological analyses indicate the policy prioritizes regulatory genes early and promotes perturbation-specific transcription factors and responsive genes.

Conclusion: Gene generation order is a valuable, controllable, and biologically interpretable dimension for single-cell perturbation prediction; the proposed framework demonstrates that order-aware generation with regulatory priors yields improved predictive accuracy and interpretability.

Abstract: Predicting single-cell transcriptomic responses to genetic perturbations is central to functional genomics and virtual-cell modeling. Existing approaches, however, typically predict an entire expression profile as a whole, leaving the order in which individual gene responses are generated unmodeled. To address this problem, we introduce \textbf{$D^{2}R^{2}$} (\textbf{D}iscrete \textbf{D}iffusion with \textbf{R}egulation \textbf{R}einforcement), which reformulates perturbation prediction as regulation-guided gene-wise progressive generation. A Masked Discrete Diffusion Model represents expression as ordinal tokens and reconstructs a fully masked profile step by step, allowing generated gene responses to condition those that remain masked. A Regulatory Policy Module initializes the generation policy from a gene regulatory network inferred from control cells and adapts it to the perturbation and current partially generated state. Then, group-relative policy optimization refines only the ordering policy using final perturbation-effect agreement as reward. Across Norman19 and VCC-H1, $D^{2}R^{2}$ achieves the best performance on all five metrics on Norman19 and remains competitive on H1. Controlled ablations holding the generator and generation budget fixed show that biological-prior ordering improves over random ordering and is more reliable than uncertainty-based heuristics, whereas reversing the biological-prior ordering degrades every metric. Biological analyses further show that the refined policy prioritizes regulatory genes early while promoting perturbation-specific transcription factors and responsive genes. These results establish gene generation order as an effective, controllable, and biologically interpretable dimension of single-cell perturbation prediction.

</details>


### [533] [ReasonCast: Agentic Demand Forecasting with Selective Semantic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15291)
*Ziyue Yang,Chaolin Xu,Yijing Wang,Tiankai Gu,Hui Yang,Yanhong Lin,Kaiyuan Liu,Fei Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReasonCast is a structured semantic intervention framework for forecast enhancement using event knowledge, achieving targeted WMAPE improvements with controlled interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitation of prior text-enhanced forecasting that uses generic representations; need forecast-relevant semantics and operations to modify dynamics.

Method: Agent selects whether to apply reasoning; represents event knowledge with structured fields: event relevance, demand direction, temporal shape, amplitude, peak intensity; interacts with time-series via additive (trends/shape) and multiplicative (level shifts) paths; post-training curriculum: schema SFT, semantic-field RL, forecast-utility RL; evaluation using a frozen forecaster.

Result: WMAPE reductions of 3.29/1.25/0.47 percentage points on holiday-sensitive, mega-sale-sensitive, M5 windows; risk of degradation during stable-sales periods if intervention is indiscriminate; suppressing unnecessary intervention preserves baseline performance.
