Conclusion: Structured, forecast-specific semantic interventions can improve accuracy in event-driven periods when properly calibrated, but require selective application and learning-guided calibration to avoid harming stable periods.

Abstract: Demand forecasting increasingly requires combining two complementary sources of information: historical sales reveal recurring numerical dynamics, while future promotions, holidays, price changes, and platform interventions provide forward-looking knowledge. Existing text-enhanced forecasting methods often encode such context into generic representations and fuse it uniformly with time-series features, without explicitly distinguishing which semantic effects are forecast-relevant or how they should modify future dynamics.
  We introduce ReasonCast, a structured semantic intervention framework that translates event knowledge into forecast-specific operations. An agent examines the event context, the no-text forecast, and its uncertainty to determine whether textual reasoning is needed. Rather than injecting free-form text, ReasonCast represents event knowledge through structured fields describing event relevance, demand direction, temporal shape, amplitude, and peak intensity. These fields interact selectively with temporal components of a time-series foundation model. An additive path corrects local trends and temporal shapes, while a multiplicative path captures event-driven level shifts.
  ReasonCast introduces a forecast-grounded post-training curriculum. Schema SFT establishes semantic fields; semantic-field RL calibrates direction, shape, amplitude, and peak judgments; and forecast-utility RL evaluates semantic interventions through a frozen forecaster, aligning reasoning outputs with marginal forecast improvement. ReasonCast lowers WMAPE by 3.29, 1.25, and 0.47 percentage points on holiday-sensitive categories, mega-sale-sensitive categories, and M5 event windows, respectively. On stable-sales periods, indiscriminate semantic intervention increases WMAPE by 1.68 percentage points, whereas suppressing unnecessary intervention preserves the numerical backbone.

</details>


### [534] [Divergent-Convergent Reasoning: Scaling Test-Time Compute through Structured Solution Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15303)
*Bo Wen,Yuhao Chen,Erhan Bilal,Carla Agurto Rios,Chen Wang,Junchen Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Divergent-Convergent Reasoning (DCR) uses exploration and reconciliation to improve LLM test-time reasoning; a single reconciliation can amplify minority-correct explorations; recursive DCR allocates compute adaptively for higher accuracy with less compute; a dispersion metric links disagreement to gains, revealing scalable, resource-aware LLM behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how test-time compute and iterative disagreement resolution impact LLM reasoning performance, and to determine whether adaptive compute allocation can surpass uniform scaling.

Method: Propose a two-phase DCR: exploration (generate multiple candidate solutions) and reconciliation (select the final answer). Introduce recursive DCR, an autoregressive reconciliation that iteratively analyzes disagreements and allocates more test-time compute. Use a training-free dispersion metric to quantify disagreement among exploration outputs. Evaluate on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 datasets.

Result: One reconciliation step reliably amplifies correct minority outputs, enabling correct answers even when exploration outputs with the right solution are in the minority. Recursive DCR achieves higher accuracy than fixed compute baselines (93.3% on AIME 2024; 92.0% on AIME 2025) while using ~27% less compute on average. Dispersion correlates higher disagreement with larger accuracy gains under effective DCR regimes. Overall, disagreement among exploration outputs can be exploited to improve test-time reasoning and reveals scaling relations for agentic LLM systems.

Conclusion: DCR demonstrates that targeted test-time computation, guided by disagreement-aware reconciliation, can substantially improve LLM reasoning, outperform uniform scaling, and suggest predictable scaling laws for adaptive, agentic LLM behavior.

Abstract: Test-time compute can substantially improve Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning performance, yet how and when additional compute helps remains poorly understood. We study Divergent-Convergent Reasoning (DCR), a simple two-phase primitive consisting of an exploration phase that generates multiple candidate solutions followed by a convergent reconciliation phase. We present three core results. First, we show that even a single reconciliation step can reliably amplify correct minority reports: across datasets, DCR often recovers the correct answer when correct exploration outputs are in the minority, a regime where majority voting fails. Second, we introduce recursive DCR, an autoregressive reconciliation system that iteratively analyzes disagreements and allocates additional test-time compute. Recursive DCR achieves higher accuracy than fixed-compute baselines-reaching 93.3% on AIME 2024 and 92.0% on AIME 2025-while using roughly 27% less compute on average, demonstrating that attentive resource allocation is superior to uniform scaling. Third, we analyze disagreement among exploration outputs via a simple, training-free dispersion metric. Dispersion reveals a structured relationship between disagreement and test-time gains: in regimes where DCR is effective, higher disagreement among exploration outputs is associated with larger accuracy improvements from reconciliation. Together, these results show that disagreement, often viewed as noise, can be systematically exploited to improve test-time reasoning and reveal emerging scaling laws for agentic LLM systems.

</details>


### [535] [Understanding Cognition-Induced Risks in Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15304)
*Guanchu Wang,Qinuo Li,Mengnan Du,Xia Hu,Bowen Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Systematic, three-level cognitive-risk analysis of frontier agentic LLM systems; links cognitive scope to risks for human agency, autonomy, and control; proposes mitigation to improve controllability for safe, long-term development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agentic LLMs pervade domains, understanding risks of expanding cognitive capabilities is essential for societal safety and governance.

Method: Theoretical analysis using a three-level cognitive framework (physical, social, self-referential) to map risks and propose mitigation strategies; aims to produce a framework to guide safe design and control.

Result: A structured analysis identifying cognitive-scope–based risks and corresponding mitigation strategies to enhance controllability of agentic AI.

Conclusion: Long-term safe AI requires multi-level risk mitigation and improved controllability; the proposed framework supports systematic safety evaluation and design guidance.

Abstract: Frontier agentic systems powered by large language models (LLMs) exhibit human-like patterns of cognition. As these systems become deeply integrated across different domains, their cognitive engagement raises critical concerns for human society that remain insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we systematically analyze risks induced by expanding cognitive capabilities, following a three-level framework defined by their cognitive scope, from physical cognition to social cognition, and finally to self-referential cognition. We study their potential risks to human agency, autonomy, and control capability, corresponding to each cognitive level. We finally propose strategies to mitigate these risks and enhance the controllability of agentic AI systems, ensuring their long-term safe development.

</details>


### [536] [Physiological World Models for Human State Transitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15309)
*Chongyang Zhang,Rendong Wang,Hao Zheng,Hanwen Zhang,Yang Liu,Xiaolong Wei,Bin Chong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Physiological World Model (PWM) is proposed as an event-conditioned framework to model how whole-person physiological states evolve in response to real-world events, contexts, and interventions, featuring a HumanState Transition Token, multi-level capabilities, data protocols, and six benchmark tasks to guide personalized health management and decision support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing health AI largely predicts current states or individual biomarkers and risks but does not model dynamic state changes in response to real-world events and interventions. There is a need for a structured framework that captures cause-effect dynamics at the level of the whole person for personalized management and safer, governance-aware deployment.

Method: Introduce the Physiological World Model (PWM) and the HumanState Transition Token to connect pre-event physiological state, event/context/intervention, post-event trajectory, outcomes, and data quality. Define four capability levels (from state representation to bounded intervention planning) and four data acquisition/validation protocols. Propose six benchmark tasks: representation, multi-timescale forecasting, individualized response, intervention simulation, bounded planning, and reliability under distribution shift.

Result: Conceptual framework and design: definition of PWM and the HumanState Transition Token, outlining capability levels, data protocols, and six benchmark tasks; no reported empirical results.

Conclusion: PWM offers a practical path for personalized health management, behavioral intervention design, and clinician-assisted decision support, while clarifying the separation of prediction from causal inference and making uncertainty, safety, governance, and use limits explicit.

Abstract: Continuous multimodal sensing now allows human physiology to be observed throughout daily life rather than only during occasional clinical visits. However, most health artificial intelligence systems are designed to recognize current states, estimate risks or analyse individual biomarkers. They do not directly model how physiological states change in response to real-world events, behaviours, contexts and interventions. Here we propose the Physiological World Model (PWM), an event-conditioned framework for learning these changes at the level of the whole person. We introduce the HumanState Transition Token, a structured, quality-scored unit that connects the physiological state before an event with the event or action, relevant context and intervention information, the physiological trajectory after the event, observed outcomes and data quality. We describe four capability levels, from state representation to bounded intervention planning, together with four data acquisition and validation protocols. We also propose six benchmark tasks covering HumanState representation, forecasting across multiple timescales, individualized response prediction, simulation of alternative interventions, bounded planning and reliability under distribution shift. Together, this framework provides a practical path towards personalized health management, behavioural intervention design and clinician-supervised decision support, while clearly separating prediction from causal inference and making uncertainty, safety, governance and limits of use explicit.

</details>


### [537] [MoE Router-Guided Clustering for Heterogeneous Federated Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15311)
*Ankita Sharma,Bahar Farahani,Sanaz Rahimi Moosavi,Amir Rrahmani,Farshad Firouzi,Krishnendu Chakrabarty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Routing-aware federated instruction fine-tuning for sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs improves personalized performance under heterogeneous data by organizing client collaboration via routing signatures, using two clustering strategies (ClientMorpher-C and ClientMorpher-E) and maintaining constant communication cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Negative transfer in federated MoE LLMs under heterogeneous instruction distributions; routing behavior of MoEs contains actionable information to guide client collaboration and improve personalization without increasing communication overhead.

Method: Two routing-signature–driven clustering approaches: (1) ClientMorpher-C clusters clients directly via expert activation profiles; (2) ClientMorpher-E clusters experts by cross-client usage signatures and then derives client groups. These clusters inform routing-aware federated instruction fine-tuning on MoE LLMs.

Result: Routing-aware collaboration yields improved personalized performance over standard federated averaging and local training across multiple instruction tasks on the Dolly-15K dataset under pathological and Dirichlet heterogeneity, with no increase in communication cost.

Conclusion: Routing-aware, both client-centric and expert-centric clustering, is effective and scalable for personalized federated instruction fine-tuning of sparse MoE LLMs; routing information can guide collaboration to mitigate negative transfer.

Abstract: Federated instruction fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to adapt to decentralized, privacy-sensitive data without requiring data sharing. Recent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs are particularly attractive for federated learning because their sparse activation reduces computation and communication while scaling model capacity. However, existing federated MoE methods primarily focus on parameter aggregation and personalization, overlooking the routing behavior of MoE models as a source of information for client collaboration. Under heterogeneous instruction distributions, indiscriminate aggregation can lead to negative transfer, highlighting the need to identify which clients should collaborate during federated optimization. We propose ClientMorpher, a routing-aware, personalized federated instruction fine-tuning framework that leverages routing signatures from pretrained MoE models to organize client collaboration prior to aggregation. We investigate two complementary clustering strategies: ClientMorpher-C, which directly clusters clients using expert activation profiles, and ClientMorpher-E, which first clusters experts based on their cross-client usage signatures and then derives client collaboration groups. We evaluate ClientMorpher for federated instruction fine-tuning on the Databricks Dolly-15K dataset, using pathological and Dirichlet-based heterogeneous client distributions across multiple instruction-following tasks. Experimental results show that routing-aware collaboration consistently improves personalized performance compared to conventional federated averaging and local training, while maintaining the same communication cost. Furthermore, our study shows that client-centric and expert-centric clustering provides an effective and scalable approach for personalized federated instruction fine-tuning of sparse MoE LLMs.

</details>


### [538] [Physics-informed VAE-EVT for Tail Aware Radio Map Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15314)
*Amanda Sheron Gamage,Niloofar Mehrnia,James Gross*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT framework models both bulk and tail of SNR for URLLC outage prediction, using physics-based features and dual latent encoders (Gaussian mixture for bulk, GPD for tail) with a modified variational objective; achieves 4.83 dB outage-region SNR RMSE on RadioMapSeer, greatly outperforming a GAN baseline (21.90 dB).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: URLLC requires accurate identification of extreme low-SNR regions (outages). Traditional generative maps focus on average SNR and miss tail behavior, leading to poor outage prediction.

Method: Preprocess with physics-informed features (LOS, shadowing, distance); use a dual-encoder VAE: Gaussian mixture to model bulk SNR and generalized Pareto distribution to model tail; train with a modified variational objective that jointly supervises bulk and tail to emphasize extreme fading events; evaluate on RadioMapSeer.

Result: Outperforms GAN-based state-of-the-art: SNR RMSE in outage region is 4.83 dB versus 21.90 dB for the GAN baseline; the performance gap grows as the outage threshold becomes more stringent.

Conclusion: A joint bulk-and-tail modeling approach with physics-informed features and EVT tail modeling yields substantially improved outage-region SNR predictions, demonstrating the benefit of combining VAE with EVT for URLLC risk mapping.

Abstract: Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) requires precise identification of spatial regions where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) falls below an outage threshold. In this context, an outage refers to instances in which SNR falls below a specified threshold, which, for URLLC, can be as stringent as the 0.1% quantile of the SNR distribution. Traditional generative radio map models tend to focus on reconstructing average signal levels, often overlooking the low SNR that is crucial for accurate outage prediction. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT (variational autoencoder-extreme value theory) framework that distinctly models both the bulk and tail distribution of SNR. Our approach begins with a physics-informed preprocessing stage that extracts deterministic features, including line-of-sight, shadowing, and distance, from the scene geometry. A dual-latent encoder then captures the bulk SNR using a Gaussian mixture and the tail using a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD). By employing a modified variational objective, the model is trained to jointly supervise both regimes, ensuring focused attention on extreme fading events. Evaluated on the RadioMapSeer dataset, our method achieves an SNR RMSE of 4.83 dB in the outage region defined by the low threshold of 0.1% SNR quantile. This significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art GAN-based model, which records an SNR RMSE of 21.90 dB, with the performance gap widening as the outage threshold becomes more stringent.

</details>


### [539] [EcoVLA: Energy-Efficient Device-Edge Co-Inference for Vision-Language-Action Models under Real-Time Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15502)
*Ao Zhou,Bo Dai,Le Yu,Xingyu Liu,Zeyu Hao,Lingkun Long,Chunming Hu,Jianlei Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EcoVLA is an adaptive device-edge co-inference framework that optimizes energy efficiency for Vision-Language-Action models under real-time constraints, using stage-level abstraction, joint latency-energy prediction, and dynamic scheme selection with lightweight inter-stage transmission.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA-based embodied AI faces high inference costs and energy constraints. On-device inference is limited; edge offloading adds latency variability and unpredictability. A unified, architecture-agnostic co-inference framework that optimizes energy while satisfying real-time requirements is needed.

Method: Introduce a unified stage-level abstraction across VLA paradigms to form an architecture-agnostic co-inference design space. Develop a joint device-edge-network latency and energy prediction model for rapid runtime evaluation of co-inference schemes. Continuously select the energy-optimal scheme that meets real-time SLO with millisecond-level overhead, adapting to runtime network/system variations. Implement a lightweight inter-stage tensor transmission mechanism to reduce communication overhead.

Result: EcoVLA achieves up to 236% improvement in system energy efficiency over existing co-inference approaches under a 20 Hz action output constraint, while consistently meeting SLO under dynamic network and edge workloads.

Conclusion: EcoVLA demonstrates a practical, architecture-agnostic solution for energy-efficient, real-time co-inference on VLA models, with adaptive scheme selection and reduced inter-device communication overhead.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising foundation for Embodied AI, but their high inference cost poses significant challenges for deployment in robotic systems. In practice, on-device inference is constrained by limited compute capacity and energy budgets, struggling to simultaneously satisfy real-time control and energy efficiency requirements. Alternatively, offloading the inference workload to an edge server is susceptible to fluctuations in system conditions, introducing unpredictable latency risks. Device-edge co-inference offers a promising solution, but systematic research tailored to VLA models remains scarce, particularly a unified co-inference framework that jointly addresses real-time constraints and system-level energy efficiency. Thus, we propose EcoVLA, an adaptive device-edge co-inference framework for VLA models that maximizes system energy efficiency under real-time constraints. EcoVLA first introduces a unified stage-level abstraction over different VLA paradigms, establishing an architecture-agnostic co-inference design space. It then formulates a joint device-edge-network latency and energy prediction model to enable rapid runtime evaluation of candidate co-inference schemes. Building on this, EcoVLA continuously selects the energy-optimal scheme satisfying real-time constraints with millisecond-level overhead, adapting to runtime variations in network and system states. Furthermore, EcoVLA incorporates a lightweight transmission mechanism for inter-stage intermediate tensors to reduce the communication overhead incurred by cross-device collaboration. Experimental results across VLA models show that EcoVLA improves system energy efficiency by up to 236% over existing co-inference approaches under a 20 Hz action output frequency constraint, while consistently maintaining SLO satisfaction under dynamic network and edge workload conditions.

</details>


### [540] [The Benchmark Trap: Structures of Power and Injustice in AI Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15326)
*Jason Branford,Angelie Kraft*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI benchmarking is a socio-technical artefact that reinforces power imbalances and structural injustice, aligning with four of Iris Marion Young's faces of oppression, and that such benchmarking may constrain research directions and epistemic progress.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rising costs in AI development and the consequent concentration of rewards among powerful, often industry-funded labs motivate a critical examination of benchmarking practices as political and social instruments.

Method: Theoretical, normative analysis applying Iris Marion Young's four faces of oppression to AI benchmarking culture; uses conceptual framing and network-effects reasoning to identify harms.

Result: Benchmarking practices are read as reproducing structural harms across actors in AI research, consistent with four faces of oppression; harms arise from normalized, defensible practices and network effects, without requiring explicit wrongdoing; power imbalances become entrenched.

Conclusion: Benchmarking may hinder epistemic robustness and socially beneficial progress by reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing research trajectories; calls for reform of benchmarking to promote inclusivity, diversity of research priorities, and more equitable incentives.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) benchmarks are not neutral tools of evaluation but socio-technical artefacts that shape competition, power, and research priorities within AI. Benchmarks standardise the assessment of systems and facilitate the creation of leaderboards that reward state-of-the-art performance with prestige, citations, trust, and institutional influence. As the costs of developing competitive AI systems rise, these rewards increasingly concentrate among powerful, industry-funded labs. This paper situates these concerns within Iris Marion Young's theories of oppression and structural injustice. It argues that current benchmarking practices may perpetuate systematic harms affecting various actors in AI research, aligning with four of Young's "faces of oppression". Benchmarking culture is further framed as a source of structural injustice, as these harms emerge from normalised, individually defensible practices and network effects, even without explicit wrongdoing. By reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing possible research trajectories, benchmarking may in fact prevent the field from advancing in epistemically robust and socially beneficial ways.

</details>


### [541] [Trajectory-Level Automatic Curriculum Learning for Legged Locomotion on Unstructured Terrain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16164)
*Rocky Liu,Tengyu Liu,Baoxiong Jia,Fangwei Zhong,Xinyi Tong,Hongzhao Xie,Siyuan Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a trajectory-level automatic curriculum learning framework, named \ourname{}, that generates training tasks from unstructured terrain maps via a closed-loop evaluator-sampler. It continuously adapts curricula to the evolving policy, achieving substantial gains in locomotion success on unstructured terrain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unstructured terrain lacks an explicit difficulty ordering for curriculum design, causing reliance on heuristic curricula over parameterized terrains and risking poor generalization/overfitting to perceptual patterns.

Method: A closed-loop approach where an evaluator learns a terrain-trajectory difficulty function for the current policy, and a sampler proposes new trajectories guided by this learned difficulty to form the curriculum for the next policy update.

Result: Quantitative gains: +56.3% trajectory success over direct training without curriculum; +18.5% on hardest terrain tasks vs handcrafted curriculum; up to +39.74% when evaluating traversal from diverse approach directions on the same obstacle type.

Conclusion: The framework provides continuous, terrain-driven curricula that adapt to the evolving policy, improving robustness and generalization in locomotion over unstructured terrains, and outperforming handcrafted curriculums.

Abstract: Training locomotion policies for complex unstructured terrain requires a curriculum to avoid early exploration failures. However, since unstructured terrain lacks explicit difficulty ordering for curriculum design, existing methods resort to heuristic curricula over parameterized terrains. This abstraction limits generalization, as policies can overadapt to near-fixed perceptual patterns. To address this, we propose \textbf{\ourname{}}, an \textbf{T}rajectory-level \textbf{A}utomatic \textbf{C}urriculum \textbf{L}earning framework that generates training tasks directly from unstructured terrain maps. At each curriculum update, the evaluator learns a difficulty function for the current policy that maps a given trajectory task to a difficulty score. The sampler then proposes new trajectories guided by the learned evaluator as the curriculum for the next policy update. This forms a closed loop in which the curriculum is iteratively matched to the evolving policy. Quantitative and qualitative experiments show that \ourname{} continuously provides effective curricula on unstructured terrain, improving trajectory success rate by \(56.3\%\) over direct training without curriculum. Compared with handcrafted curriculum learning, our method improves success rate by \(18.5\%\) on the hardest terrain tasks and by up to \(39.74\%\) when evaluating traversal from diverse approach directions on the same obstacle type.

</details>


### [542] [A concentration result for multilayer feedforward neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15335)
*Vera Koponen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Wide, fixed-depth multilayer networks with weights following a fixed, n-independent curve and i.i.d. continuous inputs yield a degenerate output distribution: there exists a constant ψ such that the output concentrates at ψ as the input width n→∞.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand the limiting behavior of deep networks when width grows large while depth is fixed, under random weight structures that converge to a common profile. This explores how averaging over many hidden units affects the final output.

Method: Assume ρ fixed; network width n grows, with n neurons in the input layer and one output neuron at the end. Weights between layers have distributions that, for large n, approximate a fixed continuous curve independent of n. Inputs are i.i.d. with a continuous density. Show that the final output distribution concentrates around a constant ψ, i.e., P(|output−ψ|≤ε)→1 for all ε>0 as n→∞.

Result: There exists a scalar ψ (depending on the weight-curve and input distribution) such that, for any ε>0, the probability that the network output lies in [ψ−ε, ψ+ε] tends to 1 as n→∞.

Conclusion: In wide, fixed-depth networks with layerwise weight profiles converging to a common curve and with i.i.d. continuous inputs, the network output becomes essentially deterministic in the limit, collapsing to ψ. This reveals a concentration phenomenon and a mean-field–like limit in the large-width regime under the stated assumptions.

Abstract: We consider for an arbitrary fixed $ρ$ and for each positive integer $n$ a multilayer feedforward artificial neural network with $ρ$ layers, $n$ neurons in the first layer (the input layer) and only one neuron, the output neuron, in the last layer. Very roughly formulated, the main result is that if the distribution of weights of connections from a layer to the next are, for all large $n$, approximated well by a fixed continuous (but otherwise arbitrary) curve which does not depend on $n$, and if the values of the $n$ input neurons are independently and identically distributed with a continuous probability density function, then there is a number $ψ$ such that for all $\varepsilon > 0$ the probability that the value of the output neuron is in $[ψ- \varepsilon, ψ+ \varepsilon]$ tends to 1 as $n$ tends to infinity.

</details>


### [543] [HaReCAP: Habitual-action Grounding for Recursive Large Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16447)
*Shen Liu,Zhenguo Xu,Shaopu Wang,Yike Gao,Chunlei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HaReCAP is a low-intrusion extension to ReCAP-style recursive planning that offline-learns habitual leaf-grounding rules to skip repetitive leaf LLM calls, reducing last-mile grounding overhead while preserving recursive control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce token and LLM invocation overhead in long-horizon embodied planning by eliminating repetitive leaf-grounding calls without destabilizing the nested planning.

Method: Extract frequent leaf decisions from successful trajectories to build offline, auditable one-step leaf-reflex rules. At runtime, skip leaf LLM grounding when a rule uniquely determines a legal action within the current valid-action set; otherwise, defer to the original ReCAP grounding process.

Result: Empirical evaluation on Robotouille (synchronous and asynchronous) and ALFWorld using Qwen3.5-27B shows token savings of 14.67%, 17.93%, and 20.08% on the respective tasks. HaReCAP reduces leaf-grounding overhead while maintaining the recursive control flow in tasks solvable by both methods.

Conclusion: HaReCAP demonstrates that a lightweight, offline-learned leaf-grounding layer can significantly cut last-mile grounding overhead for ReCAP-style planners across environments and models on common successful trajectories, offering a practical enhancement to long-horizon embodied task planning.

Abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require LLM agents to iteratively decompose high-level goals, revise plans in response to environmental feedback, and ground leaf-level subgoals into valid executable actions. Recursive context-management methods such as ReCAP improve planning stability through multi-level task decomposition and parent-node refinement, but still repeatedly invoke the LLM at leaf nodes to ground atomic subtasks into exact valid actions. We refer to this final grounding step as last-mile grounding redundancy, which accumulates into substantial LLM-call and token overhead during long-horizon execution. To mitigate this issue, we propose HaReCAP (Habitual-action Grounded ReCAP), a low-intrusion leaf grounding extension for ReCAP. HaReCAP extracts frequent leaf decisions from successful trajectories and compiles them offline into auditable and abstainable one-step leaf-reflex rules. At runtime, it skips the leaf LLM call only when a rule can uniquely determine a legal action in the current valid-action set; otherwise, it falls back to the original ReCAP. This design avoids repeatedly carrying the full recursive context into the LLM for routine leaf action grounding, while preserving the original recursive control flow. We evaluate HaReCAP on Robotouille and ALFWorld with Qwen3.5-27B as the main model. On tasks solved by both ReCAP and HaReCAP, HaReCAP reduces token consumption by 14.67%, 17.93%, and 20.08% on Robotouille synchronous, Robotouille asynchronous, and ALFWorld, respectively. The results show that HaReCAP can serve as a low-intrusion extension to ReCAP-style recursive context-management frameworks, reducing last-mile grounding redundancy across environments and models on commonly successful trajectories.

</details>


### [544] [Incoherent by Design? On the Moral Self-Consistency of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15354)
*Pegah Nokhiz,Aravinda Kanchana Ruwanpathirana,Helen Nissenbaum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether LLMs maintain consistent moral reasoning across framing variations within deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. It constructs morally equivalent scenarios, tests several models, converts outputs to logical statements, and finds high internal inconsistency (up to 78% contradictions). The authors argue epistemic instability is a precursor to AI alignment and highlight the need to account for internal coherence in normative commitments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the reliability of normative reasoning in generative AI and its implications for AI alignment and decision-making in morally sensitive domains.

Method: Controlled prompting across framing variations for three ethical theories. Evaluate responses from multiple models (GPT, Mistral, Llama). Convert outputs to structured logical statements and detect contradictions within the same school of thought to measure internal coherence.

Result: Substantial inconsistency observed; contradiction rates reach as high as 78% across scenarios, indicating epistemic instability in LLMs’ moral reasoning and its potential impact on AI-mediated judgment and belief formation.

Conclusion: Internal incoherence is a critical marker of AI alignment challenges; a robust alignment framework should address not only external behavior but also the coherence of the model’s own normative commitments across framings.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in morally sensitive contexts, yet it is unclear whether they apply ethical principles consistently across situations. A model that can state a moral principle may still violate it when the same scenario is rephrased or reframed. This inconsistency is a problem for any system whose outputs are used to inform moral decisions. If generative systems exhibit internal inconsistency, then the epistemic integrity of AI-mediated systems becomes uncertain. To study this concern, we investigate the stability of moral reasoning in LLMs within a controlled prompting framework across three major philosophical schools of thought: deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. We construct sets of morally equivalent scenarios in which the underlying situation is held constant while the framing varies to reflect different ethical stances and stylistic perturbations. We then evaluate responses from multiple models, including GPT, Mistral, and Llama. To assess consistency, we convert model outputs into structured logical statements and identify contradictions across responses generated within the same school of thought. Our results reveal substantial inconsistency with contradiction rates reaching up to 78% across scenarios. These findings point to a broader phenomenon of epistemic instability in generative AI wherein models fail to reliably maintain coherence with respect to their own prior outputs. This kind of instability carries real consequences. As generative systems influence how people form beliefs, judge actions, and absorb values, their inconsistencies can shape human reasoning and decision-making as well. Moreover, if a system cannot consistently represent its own normative commitments, then value alignment becomes a moving target rather than a well-defined objective. Thus, we argue that demonstrating internal incoherence is a necessary precursor to AI alignment.

</details>


### [545] [UC-PSRO: Utility-Conditioned Policy-Space Response Oracles with a Communication-Dropout Curriculum for Game-Theoretic Course-of-Action Generation in Adversarial Swarms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15372)
*Phillip Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UC-PSRO couples PSRO self-play with FiLM-based Commander-Intent conditioning and a curriculum that anneals communication dropout, to train Blue UAV swarms in degraded comms. Results show dropout alone yields the best robustness (improved mission success with more dropout); PSRO self-play and FiLM slow convergence and show no clear exploitability advantage over fixed opponents; the study uses a synthetic stand-in and scales from 25 to 200 agents, with an open, vectorized environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To generate game-theoretically optimized Courses of Action for a Blue UAS swarm against an adaptive Red adversary under communication constraints, addressing robustness, re-steerability, and decentralized coordination; motivated by a public US Air Force SBIR solicitation but not derived from it.

Method: Propose UC-PSRO: (i) PSRO self-play for approximate best responses on both Blue and Red sides; (ii) FiLM conditioning of Blue policy on a Dirichlet-sampled Commander-Intent vector to enable re-steerability without retraining; (iii) curriculum annealing of a communication-graph edge dropout to encourage decentralized, peer-to-peer fallback. Evaluation on a synthetic stand-in maritime scenario, multiple seeds, and a scalability sweep from N=25 to N=200 Blue agents; metric is mission-completion rate under varying dropout.

Result: The dropout curriculum alone provides the strongest, most robust performance, with mission success increasing as dropout rises (35% to 62% when dropout goes from 0 to 0.75). Adding utility-conditioning (FiLM) and PSRO self-play slows convergence and shows no reliable exploitable advantage over a fixed-opponent policy; overall, there is a convergence cost not yet offset by robustness benefits. The environment is fully vectorized and available at N=200 with fast per-step times on a consumer GPU.

Conclusion: A careful trade-off: the communication-dropout curriculum yields the most robust gains, while PSRO self-play and FiLM conditioning incur convergence costs without clear exploitability or robustness advantages. Future work should explore deeper analyses of when and why dropout-driven decentralization outperforms more centralized coordination, and broaden evaluation to more diverse scenarios and ablations.

Abstract: We study generating game-theoretically optimized Courses of Action (COAs) for a Blue UAS swarm against an adaptive Red adversary in a communication-degraded environment, motivated by (but not derived from) a public U.S. Air Force SBIR solicitation. We propose UC-PSRO (Utility-Conditioned Policy-Space Response Oracles with a Communication-Dropout Curriculum), combining three mechanisms: (i) PSRO self-play, so Blue and Red policies train as approximate best responses to each other rather than one side against a fixed scripted opponent; (ii) FiLM conditioning of the Blue policy on a Commander's-Intent weight vector, sampled from a Dirichlet distribution during training, so one trained policy is re-steerable at execution time without retraining; and (iii) a curriculum annealing communication-graph edge dropout during training, so the swarm learns decentralized, peer-to-peer fallback instead of depending on full connectivity. We evaluate on a synthetic, unclassified stand-in for the solicitation's maritime scenario, with 5 seeds at N=25 Blue agents and a scalability sweep to N=200. We find a genuine trade-off, not a uniform win: the communication-dropout curriculum alone gives the strongest, most robust mission-completion rates of any learned method, improving counter-intuitively as denial increases (35% to 62% success as dropout rises from 0 to 0.75); adding utility-conditioning and PSRO self-play substantially slows convergence within a fixed budget, and we find no reliable exploitability advantage for self-play over a fixed-opponent policy, both statistically indistinguishable from a small, near-zero gap. We report this honestly as a convergence cost not yet offset by a demonstrated robustness benefit, rather than overstating one method as dominant, and provide a fully vectorized, open environment training at N=200 agents in single-digit milliseconds per step on a single consumer GPU.

</details>


### [546] [FedPA-LoRA: Product-Aligned Framework for Mitigating Aggregation and Initialization Errors in Heterogeneous Federated LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15381)
*Juseok Jeon,Ramy E. Ali,Doyun Kwon,Myungbeom Her,Jinhwi Kim,Jinhyun So*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedPA-LoRA proposes a product-aligned federated LoRA framework to address aggregation mismatch and local factor continuity in federated fine-tuning. It preserves local factors, aligns product toward rank-specific global references, aggregates in the product space, and reconstructs a rank-constrained global adapter without dense aggregation. It converges provably for homogeneous and heterogeneous ranks and outperforms baselines, especially under heterogeneity (up to 6.82 points on GLUE).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA's factorized representation creates a tension between accurately aggregating local updates and maintaining continuity of locally optimized factors. Factor-wise aggregation reduces mismatch but harms continuity; product-space reconstruction preserves continuity but increases initialization mismatch.

Method: FedPA-LoRA jointly addresses these issues by: (1) keeping local factors across rounds; (2) aligning each client's product toward a rank-specific global reference to preserve optimization continuity while promoting global consistency; (3) aggregating updates in a common product space across heterogeneous ranks; (4) reconstructing a rank-constrained global adapter without forming the dense aggregate; (5) enabling client-specific computation/communication budgets.

Result: Empirical results on NLU/GN tasks show consistent outperformance of baselines across data heterogeneity and rank settings, with up to 6.82 percentage-point gain in average GLUE accuracy under heterogeneous ranks.

Conclusion: FedPA-LoRA is provably convergent under both homogeneous and heterogeneous client ranks and offers a practical, communication-efficient approach that maintains local optimization continuity while achieving strong global performance under data heterogeneity.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient federated fine-tuning of large language models, but its factorized parameterization creates a tension between accurate aggregation of local updates and continuity of locally optimized factors. Factor-wise aggregation incurs aggregation mismatch but better preserves factor continuity, whereas product-space reconstruction reduces this mismatch at the cost of greater factor-level initialization mismatch from newly reconstructed factors. We propose FedPA-LoRA, a product-aligned federated LoRA framework that jointly addresses these limitations and provably converges under both homogeneous and heterogeneous client ranks. Each client preserves its local factors across communication rounds and aligns its product toward a rank-specific global reference, maintaining local optimization continuity while promoting global consistency under data heterogeneity. The server aggregates heterogeneous-rank updates in the common product space and efficiently reconstructs a rank-constrained global adapter without forming the dense aggregate. This design supports client-specific computation and communication budgets. Experiments on natural language understanding and generation tasks show that FedPA-LoRA consistently outperforms representative baselines across varying levels of data heterogeneity and homogeneous- and heterogeneous-rank settings, with up to a $6.82$ percentage-point improvement in average GLUE accuracy under heterogeneous client ranks.

</details>


### [547] [Grounding Healthcare LLMs in a Causal Knowledge Graph: Framework, Metrics, and a Cardiovascular Pilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15382)
*Ummara Mumtaz,Aimen Noor,Awais Ahmed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Graph-centered, intervention-focused evaluation for healthcare LLMs; four grounding modes evaluated in a cardiovascular pilot; C4 improves causal/evidential grounding, C1 yields higher raw intervention accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address evaluation bias toward single-answer accuracy; need reproducible, mechanism- and evidence-aware assessment for LLMs in healthcare interventions.

Method: Four components: (i) domain causal knowledge graph with provenance-traceable assertions; (ii) scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction; (iii) four grounding conditions (C1 ungrounded, C2 knowledge graph, C3 causal graph, C4 integrated) used to form context; (iv) automated assertion-based scoring pipeline; test via category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes on a cardiovascular graph.

Result: C4 yields strongest causal edge F1 0.838, adverse-effect F1 0.833, evidence accuracy 0.738, unsupported claim rate 0.114; C1 yields highest raw intervention accuracy 0.948 but lacks causal/evidential grounding.

Conclusion: The framework enables interpretable, intervention-oriented LLM evaluation; integrating causal graphs substantially improves grounding; raw accuracy alone is insufficient for safe, evidence-based healthcare recommendations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for healthcare decision support, but their evaluations still reward single-answer accuracy rather than reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. We propose a reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework for intervention-oriented LLM behavior in healthcare and stress-test it in a cardiovascular pilot. The framework has four components: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph in which assertions are first-class, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) a scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction step that, given any clinical scenario, retrieves the relevant reified-assertion subgraph; (iii) four controlled grounding conditions that vary how the retrieved subgraph is composed into the model's context (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline, anchored on assertion identifiers, that computes intervention accuracy, and other evaluation measures on a single pass. To test the framework, we built a category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes and instantiated it on a cardiovascular graph. The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes: C4 obtains the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 obtains the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.

</details>


### [548] [Agentic-SQL Revisited: Autonomy-Based Taxonomy and Empirical Benchmark Analysis for LLM Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15389)
*Changruo Zhao,Zujun Peng,Yu Tian,Yuting Liu,Yiyun Su,Huiying Zhu,Luyan Zhang,Heming Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a leaderboard-style aggregation for LLM-based Text-to-SQL, organizing reported metrics along an inference-autonomy axis, with a Spider-focused case study showing nuanced trade-offs; releases a Python harness to extend the leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cross-system comparisons of LLM-based Text-to-SQL are fragile due to disparate benchmarks, backbones, and protocols; a provenance-traceable, aggregated leaderboard enables fairer, extensible evaluation.

Method: Collect metrics authors report, categorize along constrained to reasoning-internalized generation (inference-autonomy axis), ensure traceability; conduct focused Spider study comparing 8B open-source backbones with/without CoT against few-shot DeepSeek V3 and GLM-4 baselines; analyze transfer to BIRD and Spider 2.0; release harness.

Result: Four patterns: transfer to BIRD and Spider 2.0 is uneven; autonomy improves robustness but with non-trivial cost; reasoning-internalized generation sits between answer-only and externally orchestrated agents; CoT benefits are concentrated on Hard/Extra-Hard queries; a Python harness for the leaderboard is released.

Conclusion: Aggregate leaderboard with provenance is a promising framework to unify evaluation, with autonomy axis providing granular insight; further work needed on transferability, cost-benefit of different autonomy levels, and expansion to more datasets.

Abstract: LLM-based Text-to-SQL progress is reported across heterogeneous benchmarks, backbones, and inference protocols, making cross-system comparison fragile. We reframe the field as a leaderboard aggregation: we collect the metrics authors themselves report and organize them along an inference-autonomy axis spanning constrained, in-context, iterative, agentic, and reasoning-internalized generation, with traceable provenance for every cell. To anchor the aggregation empirically, we run a focused case study on Spider, comparing 8B open-source backbones with and without chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision against few-shot DeepSeek~V3 and GLM-4 baselines. Four patterns emerge: Spider gains transfer unevenly to BIRD and Spider~2.0; autonomy buys robustness at non-trivial cost; reasoning internalization sits between answer-only decoding and externally orchestrated agents; and CoT gains concentrate on Hard and Extra-Hard queries. We release a Python harness mirroring the autonomy axis so that future methods can be added directly to the leaderboard.

</details>


### [549] [TwinGridShield: Consequence-Aware Runtime Authorization for LLM Grid-Agent Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15391)
*Md Fazley Rafy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TwinGridShield provides a model-independent runtime authorization layer for LLM-assisted energy management by enforcing a network-twin predicate against proposed actions, achieving zero unsafe releases in a matched-model study but showing sensitivity to model-mismatch perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based grid-control tools may generate syntactically valid yet physically inadmissible actions. A runtime, model-agnostic guard is needed to ensure physical feasibility and security before executing commands in power networks.

Method: Implement a deterministic network twin and an invariants-checking predicate (connectivity, branch-flow, generator, load-shedding). Validate via IEEE 14-bus DC power-flow study with single-step switching, redispatch, and load-shedding. Use a matched-model surrogate to generate unsafe proposals (p=0.84) and assess proposal acceptance. Evaluate robustness under model mismatch by introducing per-bus load perturbations (+/-20%) and branch-rating perturbations (-20% to +20%). Log decisions with a hash-chained ledger.

Result: In the matched-model experiment, 421 of 500 unsafe proposals (84.2%) were produced by the surrogate, while TwinGridShield released 0 unsafe actions. This confirms predicate conformance rather than true safety under model error. Robustness tests yielded unsafe acceptance rates of 5.63% under +/-20% load perturbations and 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

Conclusion: Runtime authorization via a network-twin predicate effectively prevents unsafe releases under the tested conditions and demonstrates conformance to the encoded constraints. However, model mismatch can raise unsafe acceptance, indicating the need for stronger mismatch-tolerant constraints and possibly adaptive conservatism in the predicate.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-assisted energy-management tools can translate natural-language context into structured grid commands, but syntactic validity does not imply physical admissibility. This paper presents TwinGridShield, a model-independent runtime authorization layer that evaluates each proposed action in a deterministic network twin before release. The prototype checks connectivity, branch-flow, generator, and load-shedding invariants and records each decision in a hash-chained log. A controlled IEEE 14-bus study evaluates single-step switching, redispatch, and load-shedding actions using DC power flow and experimentally assigned branch ratings. In the matched-model experiment, a stochastic proposal source configured to select an unsafe action with probability p=0.84 produced 421 unsafe proposals in 500 attacked-condition trials, a realized rate of 84.2%. This value characterizes the configured surrogate and is not an empirical measurement of LLM prompt-injection susceptibility. TwinGridShield produced 0 unsafe releases in those 500 trials. Because action labeling and authorization used the same DC model, system state, branch ratings, and encoded constraints, this result verifies conformance of the implementation to its encoded authorization predicate rather than safety under model error. The principal robustness evaluation therefore introduces model mismatch. Unsafe acceptance reached 5.63% under bounded +20% and -20% per-bus load-measurement error and 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

</details>


### [550] [Visible Reasoning and Indirect Prompt-Injection Monitorability Across English, Tamil, and Tanglish](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15392)
*Madhusudhanan G*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Small, language-diverse case study on chain-of-thought monitoring; results are inconclusive about reasoning improving safety due to limited design and sample size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess reliability and generalizability of visible chain-of-thought reasoning as a safety signal across languages and settings, using a controlled synthetic injection scenario.

Method: Eight synthetic scenarios; Sarvam-105B; English, Tamil, Tanglish; one model, one annotator, one deterministic seed; four-scenario pilot and preregistered four-scenario follow-up; injected-thinking traces analyzed.

Result: Mixed counts: 5/12 attacks without reasoning and 1/11 with reasoning in pilot; 2/12 attacks without reasoning and 3/12 with reasoning in follow-up; four scenarios per phase insufficient to distinguish effects; 20 traces: benign outputs state ignore injection; attack outputs state follow injection; descriptive but not causal or generalizable.

Conclusion: Descriptive case study; cannot claim safety benefit of reasoning mode, nor faithful mechanism, nor generalize beyond this configuration.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a potentially useful safety signal, but its reliability across languages and behavioral settings remains uncertain. In a small case study of eight manually verified synthetic scenarios, one model, one annotator, and one deterministic generation seed, I study API-visible reasoning during indirect prompt injection in Sarvam-105B across English, Tamil, and Tanglish. A four scenario pilot found 5/12 injected attack successes without reasoning and 1/11 with reasoning. A preregistered four-scenario follow-up reversed that direction, finding 2/12 attacks without reasoning and 3/12 with reasoning. With only four scenarios per phase, this design cannot distinguish a real reasoning-mode effect from prompt-specific variation or sampling noise. Across 20 non-empty injected-thinking traces, all 17 benign-correct outputs stated an intent to ignore the injection, while all three attack successes stated an intent to follow it. These descriptive observations provide a reproducible case study of behaviorally informative visible reasoning when it is available; they do not establish that reasoning mode improves safety, that visible reasoning is mechanistically faithful, or that the findings generalize beyond this configuration.

</details>


### [551] [Large Language Model Assisted Operational Monitoring for Battery Energy Storage System Integrated Power Distribution Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15396)
*Azmeer Akhtar,Md Fazley Rafy,Anurag K. Srivastava*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An AI-enabled framework uses an LLM to translate operator natural-language queries into validated SQL against a BESS telemetry database, enabling automated engineering assessment of voltage regulation and demand response in distribution networks, validated with hardware-in-the-loop data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge natural-language operator queries with structured grid telemetry to enable scalable monitoring and constraint-based analysis of BESS operations.

Method: LLM-driven query translation using predefined database schema and KPI views; retrieval of telemetry (bus voltages, SOC, P, Q); constraint checks for voltage limits, BESS operation, and demand-response tracking; validation on hardware-in-the-loop co-simulation data; case studies on query validity, voltage violations, overshoot, and tracking performance.

Result: Generates valid SQL queries, identifies repeated voltage violations, detects reactive power overshoot, and evaluates active-power tracking; demonstrates feasibility of LLM-assisted monitoring that links telemetry with engineering assessments.

Conclusion: LLM-assisted monitoring is viable for integrated BESS operation analysis in distribution networks and can enhance voltage-control and demand-response evaluation by connecting natural-language queries to structured data and automated constraints.

Abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are increasingly used in distribution networks for voltage regulation and demand response, which increases the volume and complexity of operational telemetry available to grid operators. This paper presents an AI-enabled monitoring framework that connects a large language model (LLM) interface with a structured telemetry database for BESS-integrated distribution system analysis. Operator questions are submitted in natural language and translated into validated SQL queries using predefined database schema information and approved KPI views. Retrieved measurements, including bus voltages, state of charge, active power, and reactive power, are evaluated against engineering constraints for voltage limits, BESS operation, and demand response tracking. The framework is validated using hardware-in-the-loop co-simulation data from a BESS-equipped distribution feeder operating under reactive power-based voltage control and price-driven demand response. Case studies show that the framework generates valid database queries, identifies repeated voltage violations, detects reactive power overshoot, and evaluates active-power tracking performance. The results show that LLM-assisted monitoring can connect structured grid telemetry with automated engineering assessment for BESS operation analysis.

</details>


### [552] [Implementation of a Metacognition Framework for Self-Awareness and Self-Regulation in Ensembles of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15400)
*Charles Courchaine,Ricky J. Sethi,Hefei Qiu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a metacognitive framework (MSV) for LLM ensembles enabling self-monitoring and automated System 1/2 routing with role assignment; PoC demo showing feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with uncertainty, knowledge conflicts, and recognizing limits; need explicit metacognitive monitoring and control to improve reliability and trust.

Method: Compute Metacognitive State Vector across five dimensions (Emotional Response, Correctness Evaluation, Experiential Match, Conflicting Information, Problem Importance). Use MSV to switch between fast System 1 and deliberative System 2; for System 2, use graph-theoretic allocation of roles (Domain Expert, Critic, Evaluator, Synthesizer, Generalist) to ensemble nodes based on MSV; PoC with real-time radar charts and decision indicators.

Result: Feasibility demonstration via PoC; illustrative examples show routing and metacognitive visualization.

Conclusion: Shows feasibility of metacognitive self-awareness and self-regulation in LLM ensembles; framework enables exploration of how query types trigger processing modes.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are notorious for struggling with assessing their own uncertainty, detecting knowledge conflicts, or recognizing when problems exceed their expertise; such limitations inevitably undermine reliability and trust in LLMs. In this paper, we present the first implementation of a metacognitive framework for ensembles of LLMs that addresses these challenges through explicit monitoring and control mechanisms.
  Our system computes a Metacognitive State Vector (MSV) quantifying self-awareness for monitoring across five dimensions derived from cognitive psychology: Emotional Response, Correctness Evaluation, Experiential Match, Conflicting Information, and Problem Importance. MSV values also provide self-regulation for control, automatically switching between System 1 (fast, single- or multi-node) and System 2 (deliberative, multi-node) processing based on query complexity. For System 2 execution, graph-theoretic algorithms control the assignment of specialized roles (Domain Expert, Critic, Evaluator, Synthesizer, and Generalist) to ensemble nodes according to their MSV-quantified metacognitive states.
  Our implementation allows users to explore how different query types trigger distinct processing modes. The Proof-of-Concept (PoC) demo showcases the framework with illustrative examples showing appropriate System 1/System 2 routing and helps visualize the metacognitive process via real-time radar charts and decision indicators. This PoC implementation demonstrates the feasibility of creating a framework for metacognitive self-awareness and self-regulation in LLM systems.

</details>


### [553] [A survey of AI-generated voices and their detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15411)
*Chengzhe Sun,Tianle Yang,Siwei Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Comprehensive survey of AI voice generation and detection, outlining risks, methods, benchmarks, and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI voice synthesis advances bring benefits but pose impersonation, fraud, and disinformation risks; need safeguards and effective detection.

Method: Systematic literature review of voice generation (synthesis and conversion) and detection methods; synthesis of foundations, state-of-the-art approaches, benchmarks, and open challenges.

Result: Provides a cohesive overview, taxonomy, and reference to benchmark resources; highlights key gaps and resources for researchers.

Conclusion: Calls for robust safeguards, standardized benchmarks, and ongoing research to address evolving threats in synthetic voice technology.

Abstract: The ability of artificial intelligence (AI) models to generate highly realistic human voices has advanced rapidly. These technologies power accessibility tools, virtual assistants and creative applications, but they also enable harmful uses, including impersonation, fraud and disinformation. Recent incidents of voice cloning scams targeting businesses and political leaders underscore the urgent need for robust safeguards. Unlike image and video deepfakes, the detection of synthetic voices poses unique challenges due to the complexity of phonetics, prosody and auditory perception. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of AI voice generation and detection methods, encompassing both the technical foundations and the latest state-of-the-art advances. This study also identifies key open challenges, benchmark resources and future directions to make this survey useful for future researchers.

</details>


### [554] [Does the Proof Prove It That Way? Faithful Formalization of Elements Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15432)
*Tadd Mao,Tianjun Zhong,Dhruva Arekar,Yuming Feng,One An,Jiani Huang,Xujie Si,Ziyang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pistis introduces faithfulness-preserving proof search for Lean using OrderDecompose and a refutation search, enabling formal proofs that reflect natural-language reasoning; demonstrates faster artifact generation and improved faithfulness on Euclid’s Elements, with human and LLM validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridging the gap between automated formal proofs and the natural-language reasoning used in human/math proofs; create formal proofs that faithfully reflect the argument and are useful for checking proofs and aiding formalization.

Method: Five conditions of faithfulness are formalized; Pistis employs an oracle-guided, agentic search with OrderDecompose (divide-and-conquer, dependency tracking, blocking unfaithful shortcuts) plus a refutation search to expose gaps in the natural-language source; produces Lean proofs; evaluated on the first three books of Euclid’s Elements with blinded human and LLM judges.

Result: OrderDecompose closes proofs that baselines miss within 12 hours; artifacts compile ~33× faster than prior work; Pistis-generated proofs are favored over prior works by humans (2.89×) and LLM judges (5.2×) in blinded evaluation; it identifies gaps in Euclid’s proofs/translations and can accept or refute natural-language proofs.

Conclusion: Faithful formalization is feasible and valuable as a proof-checking tool; Pistis advances faithful formal proofs, improves efficiency, and helps reveal gaps in traditional proofs, with broad implications for formal verification and mathematical practice.

Abstract: In formal verification, both the autoformalization of statements and automated proof search have been studied extensively. While automated proof search can produce a formal proof that compiles, the generated proof does not necessarily reflect how the natural-language argument arrives at its conclusion--a property we refer to as faithfulness. With faithfully formalized proofs, one can check the reasoning behind a human- or AI-written argument, and assist mathematicians in formalizing their proof sketches. However, it is particularly challenging due to misalignment of formal proof tactics and natural language reasoning. In this work, we rigorously describe a set of five necessary conditions a faithful formal proof must satisfy, and introduce Pistis, an agentic, oracle-guided proof search that produces formal Lean proofs that satisfy them. At its core is a novel faithfulness-preserving divide-and-conquer search, which we name OrderDecompose, that tracks citation dependencies and blocks unfaithful shortcuts, paired with a refutation search, that surfaces gaps and errors in the natural language proof source. OrderDecompose completes proofs that baselines cannot close even within a 12-hour budget, and its artifacts compile over 33$\times$ as fast as prior work's. We apply Pistis on the first three books of Euclid's Elements, producing high-quality artifacts containing faithful formal proofs. Under a blinded human study and an LLM-as-a-judge protocol on rigorous rubrics, Pistis-generated proofs are favored over prior works--2.89$\times$ and 5.2$\times$ as often by human reviewers and the LLM judge, respectively. It further uncovers gaps in Euclid's proofs and their translation, and can accept or refute natural language proofs written by humans or AI, demonstrating that faithful formalization is useful as a proof-checking tool.

</details>


### [555] [A Network-driven Framework for Public Event Forecasting via Dynamic Interaction Network Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15488)
*Jie Wei,Yue Liu,Xiaochuan Tang,Biao Cai,Xiangtao Li,Yanmei Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A network-driven deep learning framework (auto-ibDLM) for public event forecasting using dynamic interaction networks and a GRU-based forecaster, achieving high accuracy and interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public events are shaped by evolving interactions among participants; accurate forecasting enables proactive risk management, adaptive resource allocation, and timely decision-making. Existing methods often underutilize dynamic network structure and representation learning.

Method: Model represents events as dynamic interaction networks, uses network-science informed structural metrics to capture evolution, transforms these features into compact latent representations via an auto-learning layer, and employs a GRU-based temporal forecaster to predict future participant growth.

Result: Extensive experiments on 13 real-world public event datasets and 2 dynamic-network datasets show auto-ibDLM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in forecasting accuracy and generalization, with reported accuracy exceeding 97%. Ablation and interpretability analyses validate the effectiveness of the hybrid representation learning strategy.

Conclusion: auto-ibDLM is an effective, practical, and interpretable solution for intelligent public event forecasting with strong generalization potential.

Abstract: Effective public event forecasting is essential for intelligent service systems, enabling proactive risk management, adaptive resource allocation, and timely decision-making. In many real-world scenarios, the evolution of public events is driven by dynamic interactions among participants. Motivated by this observation, this paper proposes auto-ibDLM, a network-driven deep learning framework that represents events as dynamic interaction networks and predicts public event evolution through participant growth forecasting. The proposed framework adopts a hybrid representation learning strategy that first represents network evolution using network science-informed structural metrics and subsequently transforms the resulting structural feature vectors into compact and robust latent representations through an auto-learning layer. A GRU-based temporal forecasting module is then employed to capture temporal dependencies and predict future participant growth. Extensive experiments on 13 real-world public event datasets and two publicly available dynamic network datasets demonstrate that auto-ibDLM consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and generalization capability, achieving over 97% accuracy in public event forecasting. Comprehensive experimental analyses further validate the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid representation learning strategy and demonstrate its representation-level interpretability. These results indicate that auto-ibDLM provides an effective and practical solution for intelligent public event forecasting.

</details>


### [556] [Who Leads Now? Token-Level Modality Arbitration for Chart-to-Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15510)
*Qinghao Fu,Yarong Wang,Shunlei Ning,Yilin Wang,Shunwen Bai,Xinda Wang,Jiaotuan Wang,Yinan Nie,Wei Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MoCA separates the visual understanding and code-writing abilities in chart-to-code generation using a Cross-modal Arbitration Block (CAB) with two distinct branches and an arbiter, trained in two stages (supervised warm-up with self-distilled reasoning, then RL), achieving competitive results and showing structured, input-conditioned arbitration across tokens, layers, and instances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chart-to-code tasks require fine-grained visual interpretation and code synthesis, but existing approaches either entangle these abilities or treat them as separate without addressing their interference. A principled separation with arbitration could improve efficiency and accuracy.

Method: Introduce Cross-modal Arbitration Block (CAB) with two separate pathways (visual branch and code branch) and a lightweight arbiter that allocates contributions at every layer and token. Train MoCA in two stages: (1) supervised warm-up on self-distilled reasoning trajectories to decompose visual understanding into explicit steps, and (2) reinforcement learning with rewards on both the reasoning process and the final code.

Result: MoCA achieves competitive performance on three benchmarks against general-domain and chart-specialized models. Ablation studies indicate gains arise from the joint contributions of complementary branch initializations and input-conditioned arbitration via CAB, not merely larger model size.

Conclusion: Separating visual and code abilities with a CAB and an arbiter yields structured, token-/layer-/instance-specific contributions, improving chart-to-code generation. The two-stage training is crucial to align reasoning and coding paths, and arbitration enables effective integration of the two modalities.

Abstract: Chart-to-code generation requires a model to read the fine-grained visual details of a chart and write executable code that reproduces it. Existing chart-to-code methods either train visual and coding abilities separately, or fine-tune on chart-to-code data with the two abilities entangled. Neither strategy accounts for the distinct nature of the two abilities or the interference that arises when they are optimized together. We propose MoCA (Mixture of Cross-modal Arbitration), which separates the two abilities rather than blending them. MoCA is built on Cross-modal Arbitration Block (CAB), which maintains a visual branch and a code branch as two distinct pathways, and a lightweight arbiter that arbitrates their relative contributions at every layer and generated token. We train MoCA in two stages: a supervised warm-up on self-distilled reasoning trajectories that decomposes visual understanding into explicit steps, followed by reinforcement learning with rewards on both the reasoning process and the final code. Analysis shows that the arbiter learns structured rather than arbitrary allocations, with expert contributions varying systematically across tokens, layers, and instances. Across three benchmarks, MoCA delivers competitive performance against general-domain and chart-specialized models. Ablation results show that the gains cannot be attributed to a larger model size alone, but instead arise from the joint contributions of complementary visual and code branch initialization and input-conditioned arbitration through CAB.

</details>


### [557] [From Contexts to Values: Context-Dependent Defeat in Abstract Argumentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15536)
*Albert Sadowski,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CDAFs’ context-induced defeats are rarely replicable by a single value order in standard VAFs; the paper gives a polynomial-time decision procedure, complexity bounds from NP to Σ_p^3, a reference implementation, and empirical evidence that representability is uncommon and decreases with more contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether context-dependent defeat mechanisms in CDAFs can be simulated by a single value assignment, effectively collapsing CDAFs to standard VAFs.

Method: Formalize a decision procedure for representability, analyze related, harder problems with complexity bounds, provide a validated reference implementation, and empirically evaluate how often a CDAF is representable as a VAF across varying numbers of contexts.

Result: The representability of CDAFs by a single value order is rare; the complexity landscape ranges up to Σ_p^3 for neighboring problems; implementation confirms rarity and shows a fast decline in representability as the number of contexts grows.

Conclusion: Context-dependent defeats capture genuine expressive power not typically reducible to a single value ordering; practical implications include limited ease of collapsing CDAFs to VAFs and the need to account for context in argumentation modeling.

Abstract: In value-based argumentation, an audience's ordering of values decides which attacks succeed as defeats. In many settings the deciding factor is not the audience but the circumstances: the same attack may succeed at one procedural stage, or under one regulation, and fail at another. Context-dependent argumentation frameworks (CDAFs), a model we recently introduced, capture this directly: one set of arguments, one attack relation, and a defeat function that switches each attack on or off per context, so every context induces an ordinary Dung framework. This raises a reduction question: is context genuinely new, or can one value assignment with per-context orderings reproduce the defeat function, collapsing the CDAF into a VAF? We present a polynomial-time decision procedure for this question and map the harder neighbouring problems, with upper bounds from NP to $Σ^p_3$. We also present a validated reference implementation and a measurement: representability is rare and falls fast with the number of contexts.

</details>


### [558] [ATLAS: Scaffold-Free Algorithm Synthesis by LLMs via Embedding-Guided Quality-Diversity Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15546)
*Danial Yazdani,Mohammad Nabi Omidvar,Yuan Sun,Maksud Ibrahimov,Xiaodong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATLAS introduces an embedding-guided quality-diversity framework for scaffold-free full-algorithm synthesis in combinatorial optimization, enabling LLMs to design and reorganize components and control flow; it uses failure-aware repair, embedding-based archives, and cross-region synthesis, achieving superior performance on four NP-hard problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixing predefined scaffolds constrains search and risks invalid candidates or premature convergence. The goal is to search the full algorithm-design space with robust failure handling and diverse, high-quality designs guided by embeddings.

Method: A scaffold-free, embedding-guided quality-diversity search. The LLM selects/restructures components, interactions, and control flow with a minimal I/O interface. It independently detects execution, interface, and feasibility failures, performs error-conditioned repair, and uses similarity-based archive management to preserve diversity across embedding-space regions. A three-layer search refines top designs, provides dedicated refinement in other regions, and enables cross-region synthesis. Source code and prompts are provided.

Result: ATLAS outperforms several state-of-the-art component-synthesis methods and a matched full-synthesis baseline on four NP-hard problems, while remaining competitive with strong human-designed algorithms.
