Each run can preserve multiple diverse algorithms from distinct embedding-space regions, and design differences often lie in primary construction or global-search backbone.

Conclusion: Embedding-guided quality-diversity search makes the enlarged full-algorithm design space practically searchable; the approach is validated by public code and exact prompts at the reported GitHub repository.

Abstract: Most LLM-based automated algorithm design methods optimize a designated component within a human-specified scaffold, fixing overall organization and component interactions. We present ATLAS, an embedding-guided quality-diversity framework for scaffold-free full-algorithm synthesis in combinatorial optimization. The problem specification supplies objectives and constraints; a minimal I/O interface fixes only instance and solution formats; the LLM chooses and restructures components, interactions, and control flow. This freedom enlarges the search space, risking invalid candidates and premature convergence to one design region. ATLAS independently detects execution, interface, and feasibility failures, recomputes objectives, and applies error-conditioned repair; similarity-based archive management preserves algorithms across embedding-space regions to counter premature convergence. Its three-layer search refines the best design, gives other regions dedicated refinement opportunities, and performs cross-region synthesis to recombine components and their interactions. Across four NP-hard problems, ATLAS outperforms several state-of-the-art component-synthesis methods and a matched full-synthesis baseline while remaining competitive with strong human-designed algorithms. One ATLAS run retains several algorithms with comparable performance from distinct embedding-space regions rather than a single design. Code inspection finds that these multi-component designs differ in their primary construction or global-search backbone. Our results suggest that embedding-guided quality-diversity search can make the enlarged full-algorithm design space practically searchable. Source code and exact executable prompts are available at <https://github.com/Danial-Yazdani/ATLAS>.

</details>


### [559] [Admission Without Answers: Label-Free Certification and Experience Learning for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15565)
*Junbo Jacob Lian,Huiling Chen,Hanzhang Qin,Chung-Piaw Teo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AdmitOR introduces a label-free admission gate for optimization-learning agents, using calibrated external behavioral evidence to decide admissions. It uses cross-family agreement over resampled instances, with a calibrated threshold to admit, abstain, or escalate. It shows higher precision and macro accuracy than baselines on multiple benchmarks, but reveals calibration-on-calibration data does not generalize to wild streams; dataset quality issues also affect benchmarking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable reliable, label-free admission control in experience-learning optimization without requiring labeled answers, addressing unreliable natural labels and the risk of poisoned admissions.

Method: Run multiple model families (prompting strategies, solver stacks) on resampled instances from an extracted parameter domain; summarize agreement via a cross-family clique of value-function traces; apply a calibrated false-discovery-target threshold to decide admit/abstain/escalate; compare four admission judges across logs within a state-of-the-art skill learner; assess calibration vs wild streams and dataset quality.

Result: AdmitOR achieves higher admission precision (0.927) and macro accuracy (58.4) than baselines (0.871 precision for majority vote; 53.9 macro accuracy for a ground-truth-labeled library); reduces poisoned admissions by 3.1x (relative) and 8.0x; shows the smallest library while maintaining strong performance; bootstrap validation supports the gain; however, preregistered FDR holds on calibration data but not on wild streams; transfer failure reveals a necessary condition for extension to wild streams; benchmark texts encoding labels are a source of failure.

Conclusion: AdmitOR is the first label-free admission mechanism with an explicitly calibrated false-discovery target, achieving improved admission quality and macro accuracy, while highlighting limits in generalizing calibration to wild streams and underscoring data-quality issues in benchmarks.

Abstract: Experience-learning agents for optimization modeling improve by storing verified skills, but existing learners admit knowledge by checking against known answers, which real ticket streams do not provide. The natural label-free alternatives are unreliable: on a 300-problem label-blind stream, admitting every executable model poisons roughly one admission in four, while single-instance agreement accepts models that match at one value but differ elsewhere. We propose AdmitOR, an admission gate built on calibrated external behavioral evidence. Candidates from three model families, prompting strategies, and solver stacks are run on instances resampled from an extracted parameter domain; agreement across the resulting value-function traces is summarized by a cross-family clique, and a calibrated threshold returns accept, abstain, or escalate. The preregistered false-discovery criterion holds on calibration data but not on the wild stream. We report this negative result in full and trace most failures to benchmark texts that do not faithfully encode their labeled instances. Comparing four admission judges on one collection of logs inside a state-of-the-art skill learner, AdmitOR raises admission precision to 0.927, against 0.871 for majority vote and 0.726 for execution success, yielding 3.1x and 8.0x fewer poisoned admissions. Its library is the smallest and attains the highest macro accuracy across five public benchmarks, 58.4 against 54.8 for majority vote and 53.9 for the ground-truth-labeled library. The 3.5-point gain over majority vote is supported by a paired bootstrap and survives correction for a host-side anomaly. To our knowledge, AdmitOR is the first label-free admission mechanism designed around an explicitly calibrated false-discovery target. The transfer failure identifies a necessary condition for extending it to wild streams.

</details>


### [560] [From Generalist to Specialist: A Context-Fusion Framework for Endoscopic Polyp Reporting with a Frozen VLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15580)
*Ruijie Yang,Yan Zhu,Peiyao Fu,Siyuan Li,Te Luo,Zhihua Wang,Quanlin Li,Pinghong Zhou,Xian Yang,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A context-fusion framework enhances a frozen general-purpose VLM for endoscopic polyp reporting by combining explicit retrieval-based evidence and implicit specialist tokens, achieving strong performance with minimal trainable parameters and outperforming weight-adaptation baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable integrated, quantitative, and standardized polyp reporting within a single record while preserving a frozen pretrained VLM, addressing the limitations of task-specific models and weight-adaptation methods that either require retraining or break the unified interface.

Method: Introduce a context-fusion framework that (1) uses explicit transduction context via a self-supervised polyp encoder to retrieve related image–report pairs as evidence conditioned on the query, and (2) injects implicit instruction context through learned continuous specialist tokens without modifying the VLM weights. Only a tiny fraction of parameters (0.006% of the VLM) are trainable. Evaluation compares against general-purpose VLMs, task-specific predictors, and weight-adaptation baselines on 2,056 expert-annotated endoscopic images.

Result: The framework substantially improves direct frozen-VLM inference across numerical, categorical, and report-generation metrics, achieving the strongest overall performance among evaluated methods. It requires trainable parameters equal to 0.006% of the frozen VLM. When the top-1 retrieved case matches the target category, it reduces errors of the weight-adaptation baseline by 70.5%.

Conclusion: Context-fusion provides a lightweight, effective strategy for specialist adaptation of a frozen VLM, preserving pretrained capabilities while delivering improved polyp-reporting performance. The approach is data-efficient and may generalize to other medical imaging domains requiring unified reporting.

Abstract: Reliable endoscopic polyp reporting requires integrating quantitative lesion sizing, standardized Paris classification, and clinically meaningful morphological description within a single record. General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) offer a unified interface for image understanding and report generation. Existing specialization strategies, however, typically rely on task-specific models or model-weight adaptation, leaving unresolved how to introduce reliable specialist knowledge while preserving both this unified interface and the VLM's pretrained capabilities. We introduce a context-fusion framework that specializes a frozen general-purpose VLM through both implicit instruction context and explicit transduction context without modifying its pretrained weights. Specifically, a self-supervised polyp encoder retrieves related image-report pairs as explicit, query-specific evidence, while learned continuous specialist tokens provide implicit instruction context shared across cases. Experiments were conducted on 2,056 expert-annotated public endoscopic images. We compared the framework with general-purpose VLMs, task-specific predictors, and weight-adaptation methods to assess specialist performance, unified reporting, and adaptation efficiency. Across numerical, categorical, and report-generation metrics, the proposed framework substantially improved direct frozen-VLM inference and achieved the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods. It added trainable parameters equal to only 0.006% of the frozen VLM's parameter count. When the top-1 retrieved case carried the correct target category, our framework corrected 70.5% of the errors made by a weight-adaptation baseline. These findings support the context-fusion framework as a lightweight and effective strategy for specialist adaptation of a frozen VLM.

</details>


### [561] [Agent Gym: A Framework for Continuous Evaluation and Evolution of LLM Agents Through Human-in-the-Loop Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15591)
*Pouya Ghiasnezhad Omran,Michael Zimmermann,Duncan Cambridge,Ashmita Kapoor,Tanya Dixit*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent Gym enables continuous post-deployment evolution of LLM agents through a six-capability loop (Act, Evaluate, Investigate, Correct, Learn, Observe) within a three-zone architecture (constitution, runtime pipeline, learning loop), including a hybrid correction engine, layered investigation, safety checks, and a Spec-to-Note Gap for transparency; demonstrated with an open-source invoice-processing implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLM agents are fixed at deployment while business rules and edge cases evolve; current methods rely on heavy log collection and redesign, reducing agility and value.

Method: Modular framework wrapping existing LLM agents; six capabilities; three architectural zones; hybrid deterministic-LLM correction engine with 21 operators and three-tier actions; three-layer investigation for compliance validation; programmatic safety loop ensuring rule correctness before human approval; Spec-to-Note Gap for transparency; open-source invoice-processing reference implementation.

Result: Fully operational reference implementation; demonstrates end-to-end capability; ready for adoption in real-world workflows (invoice processing).

Conclusion: Enables continuous, safe, and auditable post-deployment evolution of agent behavior without source-code changes, improving adaptability, transparency, and governance; supports domain-agnostic deployment.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents deployed in production environments face a fundamental tension: the agent's behavior is frozen at deployment time, while the business rules and edge cases it must handle continue to evolve. Existing approaches address agent construction and one-time evaluation but provide no structured mechanism for continuous post-deployment behavioral correction without modifying the agent's source code. Most of the approaches offered in the market, require intense collection of logs and traces, and re-examining the agent design by the engineering team, a process which is heavy, long and negates the economical value of agentic transformation. We introduce Agent Gym, a modular, domain-agnostic framework that wraps any existing LLM-based agent in a continuous evaluation-and-evolution loop. The framework provides six composable capabilities --- Act, Evaluate, Investigate, Correct, Learn, and Observe --- organized across three architectural zones: a constitution layer that codifies domain knowledge in configuration artifacts, a runtime inference pipeline that chains acting, investigation, and adaptive correction, and a learning loop that enables subject matter experts to discover and validate new correction rules through natural language interaction. The key technical contributions include a hybrid deterministic-LLM correction engine with 21 condition operators and three-tier actions, a three-layer investigation architecture for ground-truth-free compliance validation, and a programmatic safety loop that guarantees rule correctness before human approval. We further introduce the Spec-to-Note Gap, an autoencoder-inspired view of agentic system transparency. An open-source reference implementation for invoice processing demonstrates that the framework is fully operational and ready for adoption.

</details>


### [562] [Bias-Corrected Ceilings of Emotion Predictability from Human Label Variation Based on Instance-Level Fano Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15619)
*Keito Inoshita*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BACE estimates a bias-corrected ceiling for emotion-recognition from text, separating irreducible vs reducible error and using an anchored Dirichlet-mixture EB estimator; finds saturation claims are not robust and irreducible error is at least ~33% on GoEmotions (and similarly for offensiveness/irony).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether an accuracy ceiling in text emotion recognition is reachable, not via a single metric, but by quantifying dependence on annotation, estimators, noise, and protocol.

Method: Introduce BACE framework; use anchored Dirichlet-mixture empirical Bayes estimator, bracketed between plug-in and NSB; employ annotator splits, noise deconvolution, and a fixed claim gate to attribute error without circularity.

Result: Unconstrained estimates place reachability 0.38–1.03, so saturation cannot be decided by any single estimator; at least ~33% of a representative classifier's error on GoEmotions is irreducible; same pattern for offensiveness and irony.

Conclusion: Only the irreducible-error claim passes the gate; overall study cautions against declaring saturation and provides a bias-corrected framework to decompose error.

Abstract: Emotion recognition from text keeps improving on benchmarks, yet whether an accuracy ceiling has been reached is seldom asked with discipline. Our aim is not to pin this ceiling to a single number, but to quantify how far it depends on finite annotation, estimator choice, annotation noise, and the evaluation protocol, and thereby to discipline how confidently saturation can be claimed. We propose Bias-corrected Affective Ceiling Estimation (BACE), an analysis framework that estimates a bias-corrected ceiling, separates irreducible from reducible error, and disciplines the resulting claims. An anchored Dirichlet-mixture empirical Bayes estimator, bracketed between plug-in and NSB, recovers the human-consensus distribution; an annotator split, a noise deconvolution, and a fixed claim gate then attribute error without circularity. Methodologically, unconstrained point estimates place reachability anywhere from 0.38 to 1.03, so saturation cannot be decided by any single estimator. Substantively, the only assertion passing the claim gate is that at least about 33% of a representative classifier's error on GoEmotions is irreducible, with the same pattern recurring on offensiveness and irony.

</details>


### [563] [Rotation-Invariant Multi-IMU Activity Recognition under Independent Per-Location Orientation Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15621)
*Seungyeol Baek,Yoonbyung Chai,Yonghyeon Lee,Sungjoon Choi,Sungho Suh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A rotation-invariant framework for multi-IMU HAR (TRI-HAR) that handles independent per-location orientation offsets without rotational augmentation; uses an SO(3)-equivariant backbone with per-IMU invariant projection and feature fusion to improve robustness and macro-F1 under deployment shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployment shifts in multi-IMU HAR arise from independent per-location orientation offsets after reattachment, which break standard HAR models. Rotation augmentation is insufficient and calibration pipelines are costly. A structurally invariant model can provide robust recognition without explicit orientation normalization.

Method: Transform each IMU's accel/gyro data into triaxial vectors, apply a shared SO(3)-equivariant backbone, project invariants per IMU location, and fuse the resulting invariant features for activity classification.

Result: In four multi-IMU benchmarks, TRI-HAR preserves macro-F1 under fixed independent per-location SO(3) rotations and outperforms rotation-augmented baselines under this target shift without needing rotational augmentation.

Conclusion: TRI-HAR demonstrates that embedding rotation invariance at the architectural level yields robustness to per-location orientation offsets in multi-IMU HAR, eliminating the need for rotational data augmentation or calibration pipelines.

Abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) with self-administered wearables, such as at-home rehabilitation and exercise monitoring, often requires reattaching inertial measurement units (IMUs) across sessions. In multi-IMU settings, this can induce independent orientation offsets across body locations, a deployment shift that conventional scalar HAR models do not structurally handle. Existing remedies rely on rotation augmentation, whose robustness depends on sampled transformations, or calibration and orientationnormalization pipelines requiring additional reference-frame assumptions or explicit procedures. We present Truly Rotation-Invariant HAR (TRI-HAR), a rotation-invariant framework that makes robustness to independent per-location IMU orientation offsets a structural model property. TRI-HAR reshapes accelerometer and gyroscope streams into triaxial vectors, applies a shared SO(3)-equivariant backbone and invariant projection to each IMU location, and fuses the resulting invariant features for activity classification. Across four multi-IMU benchmarks, TRI-HAR preserves macro-F1 under fixed independent per-location SO(3) rotations and outperforms rotation-augmented baselines under this target shift without requiring rotational augmentation.

</details>


### [564] [Argumentation for Common Ground: Finding Zones of Possible Agreement between Individuals in Conflict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15634)
*Elisa Cavatorta,Antonio Rago*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A bipolar quantitative argumentation framework is proposed to identify Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) in peace talks by merging sides' reasoning; evaluated in Palestinian-Israeli context with survey and LLM data; preliminary results indicate feasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Citizens' acceptability of peace depends on contested narratives; need computational tools to map mutually acceptable clauses under polarized reasoning to identify common ground for conflict resolution.

Method: Develop a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework for each side's reasoning about treaty clauses; merge frameworks to identify ZOPAs; evaluate via theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments using survey data and LLM-generated data.

Result: The framework identifies ZOPAs and demonstrates feasibility of mapping feasible agreements grounded in citizens' reasoning; preliminary results support practical utility for negotiators.

Conclusion: Argumentation-based approach can empower negotiators to map feasible ZOPAs grounded in citizens' reasoning; promising direction requiring further empirical validation.

Abstract: How can common ground between societies in conflict be identified when citizens' acceptability of peace agreements is shaped by contested narratives? Such acceptability is mediated not only by the clauses that agreements include or exclude, but crucially by citizens' subjective reasoning concerning agreements' clauses. In this paper, we leverage computational argumentation to introduce a novel approach to identifying mutually acceptable agreements among individuals in conflict, i.e. a Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA). First, we introduce a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework tailored to represent each side's reasoning about peace agreements. We then show how merging these frameworks can enable negotiators to identify peace agreements that are mutually acceptable. To evaluate our approach under conditions of real-world relevance, we focus on the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, where long-standing policy, practitioner and public interest underscores the demand for methods capable of analysing polarised public reasoning. We show how our framework identifies a ZOPA through theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments using survey data from both existing work and retrieved by a large language model. The results illustrate how argumentation can empower negotiators and conflict-resolution teams in mapping feasible ZOPAs grounded in citizens' reasoning.

</details>


### [565] [A Responsible Artificial Intelligence Framework for Groundwater Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15657)
*Chong Chen,Yulu Zhang,Qingxi Guo,Yihan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Six Responsible AI principles are proposed for groundwater prediction; Transformer-based models outperform LSTM, highlighting practical value of Responsible AI in sustainable groundwater management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure AI deployment in groundwater aligns with human values and ethical standards, addressing the scarcity of Responsible AI research in groundwater and supporting sustainable water management under climate change and human activities.

Method: Develop LSTM and Transformer time-series models using multi-source hydrometeorological data from the Heihe River Basin; evaluate with post-hoc interpretability, Monte Carlo simulation, and scenario analysis to compare performance and interpretability.

Result: Transformer outperforms LSTM in accuracy, robustness, and interpretability; demonstrates operability and practical value of the proposed Responsible AI principles for groundwater prediction.

Conclusion: Responsible AI principles are actionable in groundwater prediction and can inform sustainable water management under climate change and human activity pressures.

Abstract: The rapid development and widespread application of artificial intelligence (AI) have sparked intense discussions on how to deploy responsible AI systems in a manner aligned with human values and ethical standards. Compared to fields like healthcare, energy, or finance, the application of AI in groundwater is relatively limited, and research on responsible AI is even more scarce. Taking the middle reaches of the Heihe River Basin as the study area, this paper proposes six Responsible AI principles: transparency, technical robustness, privacy governance, fairness, accountability, and sustainability. LSTM and Transformer time-series models are developed using multi-source hydrometeorological data, and validated via post-hoc interpretability, Monte Carlo simulation, and scenario analysis. The results show that Transformer outperforms LSTM in accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, demonstrating the operability and practical value of Responsible AI principles in groundwater prediction to support sustainable water management under climate change and human activities.

</details>


### [566] [Large Models for Small Devices: Recent Advances and Empirical Analysis of Edge AI Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15693)
*Subhransu Das,Jiaming Cheng,Arnav Kumar,Sadia Afrose,Mingzhe Han,Michael Silagy,Shreya Palande,Brijesh Soni,Rajiv Ramnath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Edge deployment of large AI models requires task- and hardware-aware compression; no universal winner—quantization often preserves latency and task performance for QA, while pruning can dramatically reduce size for segmentation but may hurt accuracy and inflate latency due to alignment issues; results depend on hardware (GPU/CPU/RPi) and model; an open-source deployment workflow and guidelines are provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between compression research and practical deployment on resource-constrained devices by deriving deployment guidelines from real hardware results across tasks.

Method: Survey dozens of recent works with real hardware results; deploy compact language and image models on GPU, CPU, and Raspberry Pi for question answering and image segmentation; analyze effects with neural-flow graph and prefill-decode latency decomposition; distill task-specific deployment directions; publish code/artifacts.

Result: For QA, Qwen3.5 0.8B achieves 93.85 SQuAD F1 and 92 EM under Q5_K_M GGUF quantization; structured pruning at same precision costs 16 F1 at 1% pruning. For segmentation, quantization leaves parameters/MACs unchanged while pruning reduces model size by ~80% with near-constant mIoU. Pruning can inflate deployed artifact by 21–49% due to misalignment of k-quant super-blocks; longer non-compliant outputs raise Raspberry Pi latency by up to 3.4x. A LoRA-recovered variant remains parseable, delivering 71% BoolQ accuracy but drives 97/100 predictions to a single class with 52.6% balanced accuracy. The effects are explained via neural-flow graph analysis and prefill-decode latency decomposition; guidelines are task-, model-, hardware-specific. Code and artifacts are open source at the provided URL.

Conclusion: Deployment choices must be task-, model-, and hardware-aware. The work consolidates deployment guidelines from a broad survey and provides deployment directions and open-source tooling to enable practical edge deployment.

Abstract: Running large AI models on resource-constrained edge devices requires model compression to reduce model size and computation. What compresses well, however, need not deploy well. We survey dozens of recent works that report compression results on real hardware and extract practical deployment guidelines from them. Following these guidelines, we deploy compact language and image models on GPU, CPU, and Raspberry Pi platforms across question answering and image segmentation. No single technique wins across tasks. For question answering, Qwen3.5 0.8B reaches 93.85 SQuAD F1 and 92 EM under Q5_K_M GGUF quantization, while structured pruning at the same precision costs 16 F1 at a 1% ratio. For segmentation, the ranking reverses: default quantization leaves parameters and MACs unchanged, whereas pruning cuts model size by nearly 80% at near-constant mIoU. Pruning can even inflate the deployed artifact by 21-49% by breaking k-quant super-block alignment; combined with longer, less format-compliant outputs, this raises Raspberry Pi latency up to 3.4x. Compression can also manufacture the appearance of competence rather than destroy it visibly: one LoRA-recovered variant stays fully parseable and holds 71% strict BoolQ accuracy while sending 97 of 100 predictions to a single class, at 52.6% balanced accuracy. We explain these effects through neural-flow graph analysis and prefill-decode-level latency decomposition, and condense them into task-specific deployment research directions. The right technique depends on the task, the model, and the hardware. Our experiment code and artifacts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Arnavvvkumar/deployment

</details>


### [567] [Adaptive Mixing of Policies from Searching and Policies from Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15700)
*Gavin B. Rens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adaptive mixing of NN policy and MCTS (Flexer) reduces search depth based on policy priors, achieving improvements on toy symbolic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distillation from search can be expensive; reduce search depth when network priors are informative to save computation while maintaining performance.

Method: Proposes Flexer: at each step, combine NN policy with MCTS policy; the mixing factor increases when policy imitation error and environment-model variance are high.

Result: Flexer outperforms a version of AlphaZero, DQN, and ADP on three toy symbolic problems.

Conclusion: Adaptive policy mixing can yield empirical gains in resource-constrained or variable-depth search; results are limited to toy tasks, requiring validation on larger benchmarks.

Abstract: Background: Distillation of training targets generated thru search/planning has proven useful in reinforcement learning, but search can take exceedingly long. Objectives: Rather than perform search to the same depth every time (typically at a fixed period of steps), reduce the search depth proportionally to the quality of the policy network priors. Methods: We describe Flexer, an architecture that, for each step, mixes the policy from a neural network and the policy from Monte Carlo tree search. The mixing factor favors the MCTS policy as the policy imitation error of the network and the environment models' variance increases. Results: Flexer outperforms a version of AlphaZero (and DQN and ADP) for some experiments on three toy symbolic problems.

</details>


### [568] [HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15703)
*XinQi Wang,Jinwei Xiao,Sijia Cui,Hongming Zhang,Yanna Wang,Qingyang Zhang,Bo Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyMem is a hierarchical, functionally separated context framework for LLM agents that reduces context growth and enables coherent long-horizon reasoning by using isolated reasoning and memory-management modules, achieving improved Pass@1 on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus with DeepSeek-V4.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the problem of context bloat in long-horizon, multi-step tasks where dense traces crowd the persistent planning context. Flat, compressed contexts often degrade reasoning; a hierarchical separation of context types can preserve high-level planning and execution information.

Method: Introduce HyMem, a hierarchical architecture with distinct functional layers: a planning layer, an isolated reasoning module for subtasks (which does not pollute the persistent planning context), and a memory management module that maintains progress via structured summaries. Integrates with DeepSeek-V4 and evaluates on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus using Pass@1 as the metric.

Result: HyMem achieves average Pass@1 scores of 66.7% (GAIA) and 61.3% (Browsecomp-plus), exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively.

Conclusion: Separating context by function effectively controls reasoning-context growth, enabling stable, coherent long-horizon reasoning within limited context windows and improving task performance across complex domains.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often perform poorly on complex, long-horizon tasks because their context becomes increasingly cluttered over time. As interactions accumulate, detailed execution traces and intermediate outputs dominate the context, making it difficult for the model to retain and use high-level planning information. Most existing methods address this issue through compression or retrieval applied to a single, flat context, which does not clearly separate different types of context information and often leads to degraded reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose HyMem, a hierarchical framework that explicitly separates the agent's context into distinct functional layers. HyMem organizes context by function to separate high-level planning from execution and complex analysis. Its isolated reasoning module handles complex subtasks without adding intermediate reasoning traces to the persistent planning context, while its memory management module preserves task progress across context refreshes through structured summaries. These components reduce redundant context accumulation, retain task-critical information, and support coherent long-horizon reasoning within a limited context window. Experiments on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus show that, with DeepSeek-V4, HyMem achieves average Pass@1 scores of 66.7% and 61.3%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis indicates that HyMem effectively controls the growth of the reasoning context, allowing the model to maintain focus and accuracy across complex, long-horizon tasks.

</details>


### [569] [PLeDO: Pain Level Detection for Osteoarthritis from EMR Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15719)
*Yuhao Chen,Jiahao Cai,Nafiz Sadman,Farhana Zulkernine,John Queenan,David Barber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: We propose SPaDe and PLeDO, two NLP/ML tools to detect OA pain severity from primary care EMRs by extracting pain expressions from unstructured notes and integrating structured data; validated against gold-standard labels, showing feasibility for improving care.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OA pain assessment is subjective and variably expressed; EMR data are split between structured fields (e.g., medications, scales) and unstructured notes; automated, accurate pain level detection can inform diagnosis and treatment in primary care.

Method: SPaDe: synonym-based pain level detection from chart notes; PLeDO: integrated tool combining structured medication data and pain-scale cues from notes; both rely on human-labeled gold standard for evaluation; information extraction, NLP, and ML techniques.

Result: Both SPaDe and PLeDO can detect mild and moderate-to-severe pain from EMR data in the OA context, demonstrating feasibility and potential to improve care quality in primary care settings.

Conclusion: Integrated EMR-based pain level detection is feasible for OA and may enhance diagnosis and treatment decisions; future work to improve accuracy, generalizability, and deployment in clinics.

Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive chronic joint disease resulting in a breakdown of articular cartilage and bone when damaged joint tissues are not able to normally repair themselves. The aim of this pilot research study is to understand the pain severity for OA from patients' primary care Electronic Medical Records (EMR), both from the structured medical data and the unstructured chart note data using information extraction, natural language processing and machine learning techniques. We propose SPaDe, a Synonym-based Pain level Detection tool to categorize patients into having mild or moderate-to-severe pain to understand diagnosis and treatment methods based on only the pain related expressions in the unstructured chart note. Expressions are subjective, objective, and influenced by cultural background and demography which poses a difficult challenge. Therefore, we improve the model by incorporating the medication information from the structured EMR data and pain scale related information from the chart note to propose an integrated pain level detection tool for OA called PLeDO. With the help of human labeled gold standard data, we demonstrate that both SPaDe and PLeDO can detect mild and moderate-to-severe pain from the EMR data to analyze and potentially improve the quality of care in primary care setting.

</details>


### [570] [Toward AI-Friendly Cartography: Understanding How Color Design Influences Foundation Model Spatial Reasoning on Sequential Choropleth Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15736)
*Yonghe Sun,Zhenjia Liu,Hua Liao,Wenjia Xu,Nai Yang,Weihua Dong,Zhiwei Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sequential color ordering and sufficient lightness contrast are essential for machine map understanding; hue alone has limited impact. Disrupting sequential order or reducing lightness contrast degrades multimodal FM performance, especially on compare/rank tasks; LoRA helps but does not remove the sensitivities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether classic cartographic design principles for human perception transfer to foundation models (FMs) for multimodal map understanding, focusing on sequential choropleth maps.

Method: Create a controlled benchmark with 5,760 maps and 28,800 questions across Attribute Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, and Pattern Delineate; evaluate 21 open-source and proprietary multimodal FMs; manipulate hue palette, color ordering, and lightness; apply LoRA fine-tuning; perform factorial experiments to pinpoint error sources.

Result: Hue choice yields limited/inconsistent effects; breaking sequential color ordering substantially reduces performance, especially for comparison and ranking; reducing lightness contrast consistently impairs reasoning; increasing contrast beyond separability offers marginal gains; LoRA improves overall accuracy but preserves sensitivities; errors cluster around color-and-legend decoding, spatial reasoning, and integrating thematic attributes with spatial structure.

Conclusion: Maintaining conventional sequential ordering and adequate lightness contrast remains important for machine map understanding; findings offer empirical guidance for AI-friendly cartographic design and highlight areas (legend decoding, spatial reasoning, attribute-structure integration) where FMs struggle.

Abstract: Foundation models (FMs) increasingly support multimodal and geospatial reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether cartographic principles designed for human perception are equally effective for machines. Focusing on sequential choropleth maps, we examine how hue palette, color ordering, and lightness contrast influence FM spatial reasoning. We construct a controlled benchmark of 5,760 maps and 28,800 questions spanning Attribute Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, and Pattern Delineate, and evaluate 21 open-source and proprietary multimodal FMs. Results show that hue choice has limited and inconsistent effects, whereas disrupting sequential color ordering substantially reduces performance, especially for comparison and ranking. Reduced lightness contrast also consistently impairs reasoning, while increasing contrast beyond sufficient separability provides only marginal gains. LoRA fine-tuning improves overall accuracy but preserves these relative sensitivities. Additional factorial experiments further indicate that errors arise from color-and-legend decoding, spatial reasoning, and the integration of thematic attributes with spatial structure. These findings show that conventional sequential ordering and sufficient contrast remain important for machine map understanding and provide empirical guidance for AI-friendly cartographic design.

</details>


### [571] [Propaganda Forensics: Recovering the Generation Pipeline of an AI-Driven Influence Campaign](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15746)
*Benjamin Icard,Elouan Vuichard,Louis Lefebvre,Lila Sainero,Thomas Girault,Alice Breton,Tanguy Launay,Gauvain Bourgne,Morgane Casanova,Guillaume Gadek,Victor Klötzer,Michel Le Nouy,Guillaume Gravier,Jean-Gabriel Ganascia,Paul Égré*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Forensic analysis of AI-driven propaganda generation; PROPAGIA corpus (2,646 propagandist French articles) analyzed against SIPA to identify propaganda techniques; evidence of prompt leaks and cross-article redundancy; attribution signals point to Llama 3 and possibly Mistral models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how AI-generated propaganda is produced, detected, and attributed, to improve forensic methods and inform policy on AI-driven influence campaigns.

Method: Assemble PROPAGIA (Storm-1516/CopyCop) corpus of 2,646 propagandist French articles and compare with SIPA (mainstream French press). Apply topic modeling, vagueness and sentiment analysis to isolate propaganda techniques; search for prompt instruction leaks across 84 PROPAGIA sites; analyze cross-article redundancy; use rewriting-based detection to attribute generation to Llama 3 and assess Mistral involvement.

Result: PROPAGIA shows higher vagueness, subjectivity, and negativity than SIPA, and cites fewer sources. Found prompt leaks on 50 of 84 PROPAGIA sites, including a verbatim ten-point editorial specification. High cross-article redundancy observed. Rewriting-based detection supports attribution to Llama 3, with possible involvement of Mistral-family models.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a practical forensic pipeline for detecting and attributing AI-driven propaganda, reveals model- and prompt-based leakage signals, and underscores challenges in attribution and detection.

Abstract: We present a forensic analysis of the generation pipeline behind a recent AI-driven influence campaign. We introduce PROPAGIA, a corpus of 2,646 propagandist French articles from the Storm-1516/CopyCop campaign disclosed by VIGINUM and INSIKT GROUP in 2025. For comparison, we rely on SIPA, a corpus of human-written French mainstream press from the same period. Using topic modeling, vagueness and sentiment analysis, we first isolate persuasion techniques characteristic of propaganda, with PROPAGIA far exceeding SIPA in vagueness, subjectivity and negativity, and citing fewer sources. We then find prompt instruction leaks on 50 of the 84 PROPAGIA websites, including a verbatim ten-point editorial specification accounting for several of these differences, together with high cross-article redundancy. Finally, we show that rewriting-based detection supports INSIKT GROUP's attribution to the Llama 3 family, but also suggests the involvement of Mistral-family models.

</details>


### [572] [Intent-Driven Situation Tracking for User-Centric Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15755)
*Meiling Tao,Yiling Tao,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Intent-Driven Situation States (IDSS) is a training-free framework that maintains an explicit, provenance-aware situation state alongside dialogue, separating grounded facts from task-state judgments to improve action feasibility, planning, and efficiency in user-centric multi-turn agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing context-management methods rely on history and implicit inference, often failing to separate facts from task-state judgments. A persistent, explicit situation state could reduce inference burden and improve constraint handling, planning, and reuse of past information.

Method: IDSS maintains an explicit situation state in parallel with dialogue, parses tool outputs into provenance-aware entities and attributes, tracks user intents, required variables, constraints, and execution status, and propagates new facts to task constraints to update action executability. It is training-free.


Result: Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across eight LLMs show that IDSS improves task completion, preference elicitation, and interaction efficiency, with notable gains in multi-entity coordination, evolving user constraints, and constraint-aware replanning. Ablations indicate the benefits arise from the interaction of fact persistence, intent-centered state tracking, and constraint modeling.

Conclusion: Explicit situation tracking offers an effective alternative to history-centric context management for reliable, user-centric multi-turn agents.

Abstract: User-centric multi-turn agents must act on an evolving task situation shaped by changing user intents, accumulated tool-grounded facts, missing information, and execution constraints. Existing context-management methods improve the use of past interaction history, but rarely maintain an explicit situation state that separates grounded facts from task-state judgments. As a result, agents often need to infer fine-grained attributes, task dependencies, and constraint satisfaction implicitly from dialogue traces. We propose Intent-Driven Situation States (IDSS), a training-free framework that maintains an explicit situation state alongside the dialogue. IDSS parses tool returns into provenance-aware entities and attributes, tracks user intents, required variables, constraints, and execution status, and propagates new facts to task constraints to update action executability. This allows agents to avoid infeasible actions, advance dependent goals, and reuse relevant information without repeatedly searching raw history. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across eight LLMs show that IDSS improves task completion, preference elicitation, and interaction efficiency, with clear gains on tasks involving multi-entity coordination, evolving user constraints, and constraint-aware replanning. Ablations and error analyses show that these improvements come from the interaction between fact persistence, intent-centered state tracking, and constraint modeling. These results suggest that explicit situation tracking offers an effective alternative to history-centric context management for reliable user-centric multi-turn agents.

</details>


### [573] [Broken Symmetry in LLM Refusal: Answer Release Is More Local Than Refusal Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15772)
*Yiqi Liu,Yang Wang,Songxin Wang,Chenghao Xiao,Chenghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Refusal is not a simple symmetric switch: hidden states retain recoverable answers, and small local interventions can release them, while enforcing refusal is harder and broader.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand if model refusals erase or merely suppress information, and to quantify the locality and reversibility of interventions between answering and refusing for safety auditing and control.

Method: Use a controlled withhold setting and bidirectional activation patching to compare answering vs. refusing trajectories, analyze local intervention locality, recoverability of hidden-state information, and the geometry of answer/refusal displacement vectors.

Result: Matched answer/refusal trajectories under bidirectional patching reveal a causal asymmetry (broken symmetry). Correct answers remain linearly recoverable from hidden states even when a refusal is generated. Releasing the withheld answer is a highly local operation (single-position patch), whereas enforcing/refusal requires broader interventions; assembling a coherent refusal is more difficult. The displacement vector between answer and refusal is not a reliable, reversible linear control toggle.

Conclusion: Refusal cannot be treated as a symmetric switch. Probe recoverability can overestimate true control; locating refusal-relevant directions does not reliably yield the ability to steer a model from answering to coherent refusal.

Abstract: When a language model refuses to answer a prompt, it is unclear whether the correct answer is erased from its internal representations, or merely suppressed at the output layer. We investigate this mechanism using a controlled withhold setting, which yields perfectly matched answering and refusal trajectories for bidirectional activation patching. We uncover a causal asymmetry in intervention locality under matched causal interventions, which we term broken symmetry. Even when a model generates a clean refusal, the correct answer remains linearly recoverable from its hidden states. Furthermore, releasing this withheld answer is a highly local operation, requiring only a single-position patch. Conversely, the reverse operation is not equally local: reimposing suppression requires broader interventions across multiple positions, and assembling a coherent refusal sequence is more difficult still. We further demonstrate that while an average answer-to-refusal displacement vector marks the geometric difference between these states, it fails to act as a reliable, reversible linear control toggle between behaviours. Taken together, our findings show that refusal does not function as a simple symmetric switch. For safety and auditing, this implies that probe recoverability can overestimate true behavioural control, and locating refusal-relevant directions does not reliably grant the ability to steer a model from answering to coherent refusal.

</details>


### [574] [KV-Rescue: Recovering Reasoning Language Model KV Eviction Loss via Stepwise Interleaving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15797)
*Minsoo Cheong,Woosang Lim,Vincent-Daniel Yun,Sungjoo Yoo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KV eviction is lossy; a low-cost, training-free hybrid approach (KV-Rescue) recovers most of the lost accuracy by interleaving reasoning from an evicted 7B and a full-context 1.5B model using a lightweight helper and a detector to stop incoherent generation. Empirically improves across math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV-cache eviction saves memory but is inherently lossy due to decoding from partial history, causing accuracy drops and potential runaway degeneration. The loss is best described as an information gap from missing context rather than a pure capacity limitation. An oracle between complementary-error models (evicted 7B vs full-context 1.5B) recovers a large portion of the gap.

Method: KV-Rescue is a training-free inference framework that interleaves reasoning steps from two models into a shared trajectory, aided by a lightweight full-context helper. An online detector using entropy and compressibility terminates incoherent or repetitive candidates early, reducing wasted computation.

Result: Across five math benchmarks with Qwen2.5-Math 7B and 72B, KV-Rescue recovers an average of 87% of the accuracy lost to eviction at eviction budget B=64. A decode-cost analysis shows that preventing runaway degeneration reduces base-model token generation by 43% on average. An oracle between the evicted 7B and full-context 1.5B recovers 79% of the accuracy gap to the full-KV 7B model.

Conclusion: KV-Rescue demonstrates that bridging the information gap caused by KV eviction is achievable without retraining, delivering substantial accuracy recovery and efficiency gains through a lightweight, hybrid inference approach.

Abstract: KV-cache eviction caps the memory cost of long reasoning traces but is inherently lossy because the model decodes from a partial view of its history. Under aggressive budgets, this not only lowers accuracy but can also cause runaway degeneration, where the model produces incoherent or repetitive tokens until reaching the length limit. We characterize much of this loss as an information gapf caused by missing context, rather than a capability gap caused by limited model capacity. An evicted 7B model and a full-context 1.5B model make complementary errors, and an oracle choice between their answers recovers 79% of the accuracy gap to the full-KV 7B model. Based on this observation, we propose KV-Rescue, a training-free inference framework that bridges the information gap introduced by KV eviction using a lightweight full-context helper. KV-Rescue interleaves reasoning steps from the two models into a shared trajectory. An online detector uses entropy and compressibility to terminate the generation of incoherent or repetitive base-model candidates early. Across five math benchmarks with Qwen2.5-Math 7B and 72B, KV-Rescue recovers an average of 87% of the accuracy lost to eviction at eviction budget B=64. A decode-cost analysis further shows that preventing runaway degeneration cuts base-model token generation by 43% on average.

</details>


### [575] [Pricing the Risk of Runtime Compression: Anytime-Valid Admission and a Served-Output Law for Compressed Serving State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15810)
*Fanzhe Wei,Li Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An end-to-end framework for runtime precision control and risk accounting in serving systems, combining an anytime-valid ledger, machine-checked design laws, and exchangeable extrapolation to replace conformal certificates; empirical results show meaningful reductions in exact-fallback and practical risk pricing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To balance quality and capacity in large-scale serving stacks while providing statistically meaningful guarantees that remain valid across unseen requests and live traffic.

Method: Proposes an anytime-valid, physically accounted ledger with bounds that hold at every admission call; evaluates via a pre-registered held-out confirmatory round; introduces a machine-checked design law linking target service metrics to a threshold knob; conducts a three-layer audit (operator-norm envelope, ellipsoid replacement, gate operating point); uses exchangeable extrapolation across multiple histories to replace binary conformal certificates; formalization in Lean 4 with extensive theorems; empirical validation on live traffic.

Result: The union-budget bound exhausts on every long request in production; the anytime-valid ledger achieves a bound that holds across 352,333 admissions and halves the exact-fallback rate on a held-out confirmatory round (0.30 → 0.14); a calibrated, priced bound localizes the remaining gap to the operating point (~700x); exchangeable extrapolation yields discriminative calibration risk improvements (0.41 vs 0.51); Lean 4 formalization reports 228 exported theorems; a companion paper evaluates and rejects certifying routing; the shipped product provides risk-with-spend, law-stated bounds that apply to unseen requests.

Conclusion: The work offers a practical framework for pricing and bounding risk in serving systems, with a legible law and provable guarantees that survive unseen requests; it formalizes the guarantees and demonstrates empirical benefits, while surfacing that certifying routing may be inferior to the proposed approach.

Abstract: Runtime compression of serving state trades quality for capacity with no priced guarantee: systems adapt precision on load signals with no soundness statement, and certified approaches budget request-level risk by a union bound over a pre-declared event count. We show the union budget exhausts on every long request in a production serving stack (100% of requests), and replace it with an anytime-valid, physically accounted ledger whose bound holds at every one of 352,333 admission calls on live traffic and which, in a pre-registered held-out confirmatory round, halves the exact-fallback rate at matched risk (0.30 -> 0.14) -- coverage is bought at a price the account states. We then price the remaining distance from the certified witness to what a user experiences: a machine-checked design law (TV <= tanh(a_q w_thr)) turns the served-TV target into a threshold knob, and a three-layer audit of its instantiation -- an operator-norm query envelope measured 1.5x from tight, a measured-ellipsoid replacement for the Cauchy-Schwarz ball that buys nothing (0.89x, held-out sound), and the gate's operating point (~700x) -- localizes the entire 1064x gap to the operating point, a price the law now states rather than an unknown. A priced bound is worth nothing on a request one has not seen, so the third link is the quantifier: exchangeable extrapolation across 80 serving histories replaces binary conformal prediction's vacuous certificates with order-statistic bounds that discriminate (0.41 against 0.51 calibration risk). All probabilistic kernels are Lean 4-checked (228 exported theorems, no sorry); which object deserves this machinery at all is settled empirically in a companion paper that adjudicates -- and rejects -- the natural alternative of certifying routing. What ships is an account: risk you can spend, a gap you can read off a law, and a bound that survives the request you have not seen.

</details>


### [576] [RLCascadeRouter: Quality-Estimator-Free Cascade Routing via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15817)
*Shihong Huang,Shengjie Wang,Hong Ma,Zhou Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLCascadeRouter reframes cascade routing as a quality-estimator-free reinforcement learning problem, using a cascade policy network to directly optimize the performance-cost objective via an MDP, enabling adaptive stopping and model selection without retraining for unseen models; it outperforms baselines across many benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Routing queries among heterogeneous LLMs efficiently is challenging due to varied capabilities and costs. One-shot routers and fixed-order cascades are inflexible and predictive-error-based; a method that directly optimizes the routing decision for cost-performance without relying on separate quality estimators is needed.

Method: Formulate cascade routing as a Markov decision process with actions {stop, select model_i}. Use trajectory returns and advantages to optimize a Cascade Policy Network that encodes model complementarity and remaining-action value. No independent post-hoc response-quality estimators are used, and the approach supports unseen models without retraining.

Result: Empirically superior on ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs, achieving better performance-cost trade-offs than strong baselines. Ablations confirm the utility of both policy components, and the model handles unseen models without retraining.

Conclusion: A quality-estimator-free RL cascade routing framework can directly optimize the cost-performance objective, providing adaptive stopping and model selection with strong generalization to new models and robust empirical gains over existing methods.

Abstract: The growing ecosystem of large language models (LLMs) offers huge potential to optimize performance-cost trade-offs. However, their heterogeneous capabilities and inference costs make efficiently routing queries a significant challenge. Existing paradigms are inflexible: one-shot routers commit before observing responses, whereas conventional cascades stop adaptively but follow a fixed model order. Cascade routing removes both restrictions by reconsidering whether to stop or invoke another model after each response. Current methods use a predict-then-optimize pipeline estimating response quality and future model utility. However, prediction loss for quality or utility is not equivalent to routing-decision loss. A lower prediction error does not necessarily yield a better action; a small boundary-crossing error can reverse a ``stop'' or model-selection decision. Therefore, we propose RLCascadeRouter, a quality-estimator-free framework that formulates cascade routing as a Markov decision process with actions comprising ``stop'' and model selection. It uses trajectory returns and advantages to directly optimize the performance-cost objective. Its Cascade Policy Network models candidate complementarity for model selection and remaining-action value for stopping, eliminating independent post-hoc response-quality estimators. Evaluated across ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs, RLCascadeRouter outperforms strong baselines and achieves superior performance-cost trade-offs. It incorporates unseen models without retraining, and ablation studies validate both policy components.

</details>


### [577] [Schema-Agnostic Graph Reasoning Agent for Hybrid Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15834)
*Marius Dragic,Ruben Ifrah,Alexandre Rio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRA (Graph Reasoning Agent) uses seven generic tools to explore hybrid knowledge graphs and outperforms a full-context agent on the UFK-M benchmark (88.4% vs 83.3%), while reading far fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve reasoning over hybrid knowledge graphs by leveraging uniform primitive operations and selective tool use to reduce context size and improve accuracy in industrial QA tasks.

Method: Employ seven generic tools (listing, reading, searching) to navigate graphs whose nodes are textual concepts or relational tables; compare against a full-context agent and a graph-free control on UFK-M benchmark of 258 analytical SQL-driven questions; measure accuracy and token usage.

Result: GRA achieves 88.4% accuracy, surpassing the full-context agent by 5.1 percentage points, while reading under a third of the input tokens; selective access rather than graph topology drives gains; the graph-free control highlights the importance of reliable tool driving.

Conclusion: Selective navigation over structured substrates with tool-driven reasoning can outperform exhaustive context and is effective for industrial QA tasks requiring SQL execution; the results support building agents that operate via a standard set of primitives over graphs and relational data.

Abstract: Tool-calling LLM agents navigate unfamiliar codebases with a handful of generic primitives for listing, reading and searching files (ls, cat, grep). A knowledge graph admits the same interface: listing neighbours, reading node content and searching descriptions are the same operations on a different substrate. Building on this correspondence, we present GRA, a Graph Reasoning Agent that explores hybrid knowledge graphs, whose nodes are either textual concepts or relational tables, with seven generic tools, discovering everything domain-specific at run time. On UFK-M (Unified Factory Knowledge Model), an industrial benchmark of 258 analytical questions whose gold answers are produced by executing validated SQL programs, GRA beats a full-context agent by 5.1 pp (88.4% vs. 83.3%), while reading under a third of its input tokens. A graph-free control shows the gain comes chiefly from selective agentic access rather than graph topology, and that the effect depends on a model able to drive tools reliably. Seeing less, the agent answers better: selective navigation over a structured substrate beats exhaustive context.

</details>


### [578] [CoupVisor: Strategy Optimization by Round and Challenge Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15868)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoupVisor unifies event representation to support play, replay, simulation, belief tracking, advice, and learning in the hidden-information game Coup; it estimates claim truthfulness from role probabilities and remaining cards; experiments show win-oriented rewards yield the best policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve decision support in hidden-information games by integrating multiple components (manual play, replay, simulation, belief tracking, advisory guidance, and learning) around a single event description, and address detection of dubious claims.

Method: Use a single event description shared across manual play, replay of recorded games, simulation, belief tracking, advisor recommendations, and learning-based policies. Estimate truthfulness of a claim by combining prior role probabilities with the number of cards the claimant holds. Compare a rule-based advisor with several learned and heuristic players across many simulated games and opponent styles.

Result: The choice of reward shaping (short-term vs win-oriented) determines which learning approach performs best; a win-oriented reward yields a policy that outperforms all baselines.

Conclusion: Reward shaping is critical for learning in this domain; a win-focused objective leads to superior policies, and a unified event description enables cross-component integration (play, replay, simulation, belief tracking, advice, and learning).

Abstract: This paper presents CoupVisor, a decision-support system for the hidden-information card game Coup. It addresses two questions: what a player should do on each turn, and when a player should challenge an opponent's claim. The system is built around a single description of game events, which is shared across manual play, replay of recorded games, simulation, belief tracking, advisor recommendations, and learning-based policies. CoupVisor estimates the chance that a claim is truthful by combining how likely each role is with how many cards the claimant still holds, which corrects a case where the very first claim of a game was flagged as suspicious despite no evidence. We compare a rule-following advisor and several learned and heuristic players across many simulated games and different opponent styles. Our main finding is that the choice of reward, whether it rewards short-term gains or ultimately winning the game, decides which learning approach performs best, and that a win-oriented reward produces a policy that outperforms all baselines.

</details>


### [579] [Dear Algo: A Precision-First Agentic Intent Layer for Unified Search and Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15877)
*Rui Wang,Jiazhou Wang,Zheng Wei,Chenglin Lu,Fangcheng Sun,Ivy Sun,Jin Sun,Hui Geng,Lillian Zhang,Chao Yang,Lei Chen,Shahin Sefati,Reem Helou,Joe Zhou,Babak Shakibi,Yiyi Pan,Bi Xue,Hong Yan,Shujian Bu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A production Dear Algo on Threads uses an explicit agentic intent layer to convert open-ended NL requests into an executable retrieval and reranking plan, bridging search and recommendation and delivering high precision and improved candidate quality under a precision-first objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify search and recommendation by treating user intent as a grounded, executable plan; enable open-ended requests to steer the feed rather than produce a one-shot result, and evaluate the approach in a production-like, precision-centric setting.

Method: An intent layer compiles explicit, inferred, negative, and compound NL intents into an executable plan of retrieval and optional semantic/multimodal reranking. It maintains an intent-to-retrieval contract that spans both search-like and recommendation-like modes without a single model/serving path. Evaluation uses a blinded audit of 300 public request–item pairs (296 evaluable), 72 request clusters, LLM-as-judge gate for exact-Relevant precision, and a candidate-randomized serving-path study focusing on the reranker path.

Result: Exact-Relevant precision reached 94.4% in the blinded audit. Across 72 clusters, the full configuration yielded 7.73 judge-qualified candidates per 20 slots vs 6.61 for a baseline, a gain of 1.11 (with 0.12–2.12 confidence). In the candidate-randomized study, Irrelevant admissions dropped from 4.78% to 2.80% (−1.97 points, CI −3.02 to −0.94) and Exact-Relevant share was 2.24 percentage points higher (CI 0.08–4.41).

Conclusion: Explicit natural-language intent can be carried into feed recommendations under a precision-first evaluation. An intent-to-retrieval contract helps bridge search and recommendation modes without requiring a single model or path, enabling more precise and relevant recommendations driven by user-specified intent.

Abstract: Search and recommendation serve a shared discovery objective but encode intent differently. We study this boundary through Dear Algo on Threads, a deployed product where open-ended requests such as \emph{more NBA news} or \emph{less politics} steer subsequent feed recommendations rather than return a one-shot result list. Its agentic intent layer compiles explicit, inferred, negative, and compound intent into a grounded executable plan, then invokes conventional retrieval and optional semantic or multimodal reranking. The layer shares an intent-to-retrieval contract without requiring one model or serving path across search-like and recommendation-like modes.
  We evaluate Dear Algo under a precision-first objective. In a blinded audit of 300 public request-item pairs (296 evaluable), a strict categorical LLM-as-a-judge gate achieved 94.4\% exact-Relevant precision [88.8\%, 98.9\%]. Across 72 normalized request clusters, the full configuration produced 7.73 judge-qualified candidates per 20 slots versus 6.61 for an LLM-derived-query baseline, a gain of 1.11 [0.12, 2.12]. In a candidate-randomized serving-path study restricted to the reranker path's first 72 eligible hours, the user-weighted judge-Irrelevant share among judged admissions was 2.80\% versus 4.78\% off (-1.97 points [-3.02, -0.94]), while Exact-Relevant share was 2.24 points higher [0.08, 4.41].
  Together, these studies show how explicit natural-language intent can be carried into feed recommendation under a precision-first evaluation framework

</details>


### [580] [UI-Mate: Advancing Open-Weight Foundation GUI Agents with In-Context Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15930)
*Zihan Ding,Longxu Dou,Qi Gao,Xiangwu Guo,Shengchao Hu,Zilong Huang,Zihang Jiang,Lei Ke,Mengcheng Lan,Weixian Lei,Hanxuan Li,Honglin Li,Xiyun Li,Zaitang Li,Leowei Liang,Xin Luo,Haozhe Ma,Jiayi Mao,Zhoujie Pan,Can Qin,Tianyuan Qu,Weiqi Wang,Wenkai Wang,Yonglin Wang,Yuxin Wang,Chenxu Wu,Yingchen Yu,Chenyu Zhang,Yuhao Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UI-Mate proposes a scalable environment-grounded training stack with in-context demonstration learning for foundation GUI agents, plus OSWorkerBench/OSWorld benchmarks, achieving strong long-horizon performance across many apps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address data scarcity, bias, and variability in GUI agent training; enable robust, long-horizon task automation across diverse user environments via environment-grounded data and demonstrations.

Method: 1) Scalable environment-grounded training stack: closed-loop data engine automates task generation, environment construction, rollout, filtering, capability balancing, SFT, and online RL across massively parallel environments via unified task-verifier bundles. 2) In-Context Demonstration Learning: transforms multimodal demonstrations into flexible subtask-level workflows, follows demonstrated steps, and re-plans from the live interface. 3) OSWorkerBench Benchmark and Insights: 100 long-horizon office tasks across 41 applications; evaluation with instruction-only and demonstration-guided settings; resources include 33-task self-demo (from strong-agent rollouts) and 45-task variant-demo (from human recordings of related tasks).

Result: UI-Mate-27B achieves state-of-the-art open-weight performance on general computer-use benchmarks (77.0% OSWorld-Verified; 66.2% WindowsAgentArena); on OSWorkerBench it attains 41.0% strict success and 76.9% progress, outperforming Qwen3.6-27B by 17.7 and 24.5 points; in the 33-task self-demo subset, a single demonstration raises strict success from 17.2% to 35.4% and progress from 67.9% to 81.1%.

Conclusion: A scalable, environment-grounded training stack combined with in-context demonstration learning yields improved long-horizon GUI automation across many applications; the OSWorkerBench/OSWorld benchmarks provide robust evaluation and demonstrate significant reliability gains for open-weight GUI agents.

Abstract: Foundation GUI agents can automate complex digital tasks, but deployment is hindered by scarce and biased training data, ambiguous prompts, and unreliable execution. Routine workflows rely on user-specific tools and tacit conventions, so unstated instructions can produce arbitrary variations across runs. We present UI-Mate, a foundation GUI agent that integrates an environment-grounded training stack with in-context demonstration learning. UI-Mate makes three contributions: A Scalable Environment-Grounded Training Stack: A closed-loop data engine automates task generation, environment construction, rollout, filtering, capability balancing, SFT, and online RL across massively parallel environments via unified task-verifier bundles. In-Context Demonstration Learning: A mechanism that transforms multimodal demonstrations into flexible subtask-level workflows, follows relevant demonstrated steps, and re-plans from the live interface. OSWorkerBench Benchmark and Insights: A benchmark of 100 long-horizon office tasks across 41 applications that supports instruction-only and demonstration-guided evaluation. Its demonstration resources separate a 33-task self-demo setting, built from successful strong-agent rollouts of the same targets, from a 45-task variant-demo setting, built from human recordings of related but non-identical tasks. Experiments show that UI-Mate-27B sets a new open-weight state of the art on general computer-use benchmarks, scoring 77.0% on OSWorld-Verified and 66.2% on WindowsAgentArena. On OSWorkerBench, it reaches 41.0% strict success and 76.9% progress, outperforming its Qwen3.6-27B base by 17.7 and 24.5 points. On the 33-task self-demo subset, one demonstration raises strict success from 17.2% to 35.4% and progress from 67.9% to 81.1%, substantially improving long-horizon reliability. Project page: https://ui-mate.github.io.

</details>


### [581] [Augmenting Text to Increase Translation Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15932)
*William Kalikman,Šimon Sukup,Michal Tešnar,Vilém Zouhar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Adversarial Translation Optimization (ATO) to create harder MT benchmarks by gradient-guided token substitutions, yielding lower xCOMET scores and more challenging translations; releases two datasets and code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MT benchmarks saturate; need more challenging evaluations to discriminate model quality.

Method: Adversarial optimization using a differentiable translation difficulty estimator; gradient steps to replace tokens; each step branches over substitutions; tree search via Beam Search; avoids LLM prompting; uses gradient-based objective combining translation difficulty and fluency.

Result: Benchmark translation quality decreases from xCOMET 0.93 to 0.82; paraphrasing baseline yields 0.88; zero-shot baseline 0.86; human evaluation: texts less natural but grammatical; two datasets of 350 English texts; code released.

Conclusion: ATO provides a gradient-based alternative to LLM-driven dataset creation; produces harder, still plausible translations; facilitates robust MT evaluation; datasets and code released.

Abstract: As state-of-the-art machine translation models saturate standard benchmarks, the field needs more challenging evaluations to distinguish between models of varying quality. We propose augmenting existing benchmarks to increase translation difficulty by combining adversarial optimization with a differentiable translation difficulty estimator. Our Adversarial Translation Optimization (ATO) uses gradients from a combined difficulty and fluency objective to iteratively replace tokens. Because each step branches over candidate substitutions at every position, optimization becomes a tree search problem, which we address with Beam Search. ATO offers a gradient-based alternative to LLM-based dataset creation without LLM prompting, expensive human curation, or task-specific model training. Our ATO-modified benchmark lowers average translation quality (xCOMET) from 0.93 to 0.82, compared to 0.88 for paraphrasing and 0.86 for a zero-shot baseline. Human evaluation shows the modified texts are somewhat less natural than the baselines but remain reasonably grammatical and plausible while being substantially harder to translate. We release two datasets of 350 English texts each, generated by our methods, as well as the code.

</details>


### [582] [Navigation-Informed Embeddings: Dense-Retriever Adaptation from Agent Search Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15956)
*Shrey Shah,Levent Ozgur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trace-derived NIE adapters enable zero-label adaptation of dense retrievers to changing distributions, yielding consistent gains on target benchmarks and BEIR HotpotQA without extra labeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapt deployed dense retrievers to evolving workflow distributions using existing retrieval traces, avoiding new relevance labels, synthetic queries, or LLM judgments.

Method: Introduce Navigation-Informed Embeddings (NIE) with two objectives. NIE-Stop treats the stopping document as a soft positive; NIE-Path uses preceding path documents as hard comparisons and enforces ordinal constraints with geometric decay. A BGE encoder adapted from retained source trajectories is used. Evaluations include an independent target benchmark and BEIR HotpotQA, with a shuffled-order control to test the importance of path order.

Result: Target benchmark Recall@20 improves from 72.2 to 78.0 overall. NIE-Stop: 76.9 overall; 52.3 on long paths. NIE-Path: long-path 55.4 (vs 46.7 for unadapted). Shuffled-order control loses 3.2 points. Without public-benchmark training, nDCG@10 on BEIR HotpotQA improves by 1.9.

Conclusion: NIE offers a lightweight, zero-label adaptation channel when trajectories are retained, delivering measurable retrieval gains with no incremental labeling cost.

Abstract: Agentic retrieval workflows produce query, retrieval, and stopping traces as a byproduct of answering questions. We study how these traces can adapt a deployed dense retriever to changing workflow distributions without new relevance labels, synthetic queries, or LLM judgments. We introduce Navigation-Informed Embeddings (NIE), a family of trace-derived objectives. NIE-Stop turns the stopping document into a soft positive; NIE-Path additionally uses preceding path documents as hard comparisons and imposes ordinal constraints with geometric decay. A BGE encoder adapted from retained source trajectories improves support Recall@20 on an independent target benchmark from 72.2 to 78.0 overall. NIE-Stop reaches 76.9 overall and 52.3 on long paths; NIE-Path raises long-path performance to 55.4, compared with 46.7 for the unadapted encoder. A shuffled-order control under the full path objective loses 3.2 points. Without public-benchmark training, the same adapter also improves nDCG@10 by 1.9 points on standard BEIR HotpotQA. NIE therefore provides a lightweight adaptation channel for settings where trajectories are already retained, with zero incremental labeling cost.

</details>


### [583] [Solvable Sokoban Without a Solver via Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15958)
*Sina Baghal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A diffusion-based model trained on tile completion, without solvers or solvability labels, achieves high solvability on Sokoban puzzles and reveals non-local solvable structure via non-fixed-order generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sokoban solvability is PSPACE-complete and fragile to changes, making it hard to certify or generate solvable puzzles; a data-driven approach that yields solvable puzzles without explicit solvability supervision could simplify puzzle generation and analysis.

Method: Transformer-based discrete diffusion model trained on masked tile completion (no solver or solvability labels), using a random subset of cells for training so p(c_k|any subset) is learned. Generation proceeds in any order, conditioned on already placed cells. Adapted MD4 pipeline; trained on DeepMind Boxoban dataset.
